label: Algebraic iff Continuous and For Every Way Below Exists Compact Between
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Then $L$ is algebraic : $L$ is continuous and: $\forall x, y \in S: x \ll y \implies \exists k \in \map K L: x \preceq k \preceq y$ where $\ll$ denotes the way below relation, $\map K L$ denotes the compact subset of $L$.

label: Algorithm to determine whether Polynomial Diophantine Equation has Integer Solution
snippet: There is no algorithm to determine whether a given polynomial Diophantine equation with integer coefficients has an integer solution.

label: All Elements Self-Inverse then Abelian
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Suppose that every element of $G$ is self-inverse. Then $G$ is abelian.

label: All Factors Divide Integer then Whole Divides Integer
snippet: Let $S = \set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_r} \subseteq \Z$ be a finite subset of the integers. Let $S$ be pairwise coprime. Let: $\forall j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, r}: a_r \divides b$ where $\divides$ denotes divisibility. Then: $\ds \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^r a_j \divides b$

label: All Horses are the Same Colour
snippet: == Paradox == All horses are the same colour.

label: All Infima Preserving Mapping is Upper Adjoint of Galois Connection
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a complete lattice. Let $\struct {T, \precsim}$ be an ordered set. Let $g: S \to T$ be an all infima preserving mapping. Then there exists a mapping $d: T \to S$ such that $\struct {g, d}$ is Galois connection and: $\forall t \in T: \map d t = \map \min {g^{-1} \sqbrk {t^\succsim} }$ where: $\min$ denotes the minimum $g^{-1} \sqbrk {t^\succsim}$ denotes the image of $t^\succsim$ under relation $g^{-1}$ $t^\succsim$ denotes the upper closure of $t$

label: All Nontrivial Zeroes of Riemann Zeta Function are on Critical Strip
snippet: All of the nontrivial zeroes of the Riemann $\zeta$ function lie on the critical strip.

label: All Normal Vectors of Simple Closed Contour Cannot Point into Interior
snippet: Let $C$ be a simple closed contour in the complex plane $\C$ with parameterization $\gamma: \closedint a b \to \C$. Let $t \in \openint a b$ such that $\gamma$ is complex-differentiable at $t$. Let $S \in \set {-1,1}$. Let $\Int C$ denote the interior of $C$. Then there exists $r_0 \in \R_{>0}$ such that: for all $\epsilon \in \openint 0 {r_0}$, we have $\map \gamma {t} + \epsilon i S \map {\gamma '}{ t } \in \Int C$ there exists $r_1 \in \R_{>0}$ such that: for all $\epsilon \in \openint 0 {r_1}$, we have $\map \gamma {t} - \epsilon i S \map {\gamma '}{ t } \notin \Int C$.

label: All Suprema Preserving Mapping is Lower Adjoint of Galois Connection
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\struct {T, \precsim}$ be a complete lattice. Let $d: T \to S$ be all suprema preserving mapping. Then there exists a mapping $g: S \to T$ such that $\tuple {g, d}$ is Galois connection and: $\forall s \in S: \map g s = \map \max {d^{-1} \sqbrk {s^\preceq} }$ where $\min$ denotes the maximum $d^{-1} \sqbrk {s^\preceq}$ denotes the image of $s^\preceq$ under relation $d^{-1}$ $s^\preceq$ denotes the lower closure of $t$

label: Almost-Everywhere Equality Relation for Lebesgue Space is Equivalence Relation
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space, and let $p \in \closedint 1 \infty$. Let $\map {\mathcal L^p} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be the Lebesgue $p$-space of $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$. We define the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality relation $\sim_\mu$ on $\map {\mathcal L^p} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ by: $\forall f, g \in \mathcal L^p: f \sim_\mu g$ $\norm {f - g}_p = 0$ where $\norm {\, \cdot \,}_p$ is the $p$-seminorm. Then $\sim_\mu$ is an equivalence relation.

label: Almost-Everywhere Equality Relation for Measurable Sets is Equivalence Relation
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. We define the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality relation $\sim_\mu$ on $\Sigma$ by: $A \sim_\mu B$ $\map \mu {A \symdif B} = 0$ where $\symdif$ denotes set symmetric difference. Then: $\sim_\mu$ is an equivalence relation.

label: Almost-Everywhere Equality Relation for Real-Valued Functions is Equivalence Relation
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\map {\mathcal M} {X, \Sigma, \R}$ be the real-valued $\Sigma$-measurable functions on $X$. Let $\sim_\mu$ be the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality relation on $\map {\mathcal M} {X, \Sigma, \R}$ by: $f \sim_\mu g$ $\map f x = \map g x$ for $\mu$-almost all $x \in X$. That is: $\map \mu {\set {x \in X : \map f x \ne \map g x} } = 0$ Then $\sim_\mu$ is an equivalence relation.

label: Almost All Real Numbers are Absolutely Normal
snippet: Almost all real numbers are absolutely normal.

label: Almost All Real Numbers are Normal
snippet: Almost all real numbers are normal.

label: Almost All Real Numbers are Not Computable
snippet: Almost all real numbers are not computable.

label: Almost All Real Numbers are Transcendental
snippet: Almost all real numbers are transcendental.

label: Almost Convergent Sequence/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Almost Convergent Sequence ==

label: Almost Sure Convergence implies Convergence in Probability
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be almost surely convergent to $X$. Then $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is also convergent in probability to $X$.

label: Alternating Bilinear Form is Reflexive
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $b$ be a bilinear form on $V$. Let $b$ be alternating. Then $b$ is reflexive.

label: Alternating Even-Odd Digit Palindromic Prime
snippet: Let the notation $\paren {abc}_n$ be interpreted to mean $n$ consecutive repetitions of a string of digits $abc$ concatenated in the decimal representation of an integer. The integer: $\paren {10987654321234567890}_{42} 1$ has the following properties: it is a palindromic prime with $841$ digits its digits are alternately odd and even.

label: Alternating Group is Generated by 3-Cycles
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ such that $n \ge 3$. Let $A_n$ denote the alternating group on $n$ letters. Then $A_n$ can be generated by the set of $3$-cycles: $\set {\tuple {1, i, n}: i \in \set {2, 3, \ldots, n - 1} }$

label: Alternating Group is Normal Subgroup of Symmetric Group
snippet: Let $n \ge 2$ be a natural number. Let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters. Let $A_n$ be the alternating group on $n$ letters. Then $A_n$ is a normal subgroup of $S_n$ whose index is $2$.

label: Alternating Group is Set of Even Permutations
snippet: Let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters. Let $A_n$ be the alternating group on $n$ letters. Then $A_n$ consists of the set of even permutations of $S_n$.

label: Alternating Group is Simple except on 4 Letters
snippet: Let $n$ be an integer such that $n \ne 4$. Then the $n$th alternating group $A_n$ is simple.

label: Alternating Group on 3 Letters
snippet: == Group Example == Let $S_3$ denote the symmetric group on $3$ letters. The alternating group on $3$ letters $A_3$ is the kernel of the mapping $\sgn: S_3 \to C_2$. $A_3$ consists of the $3$ elements: $A_3 = \set {e, \tuple {123}, \tuple {132} }$ where the tuples denote cycle notation. Thus $A_3$ is an instance of the cyclic group of order $3$.

label: Alternating Group on 4 Letters
snippet: == Group Example == Let $S_4$ denote the symmetric group on $4$ letters. The alternating group on $4$ letters $A_4$ is the kernel of the mapping $\sgn: S_4 \to C_2$.

label: Alternating Group on More than 3 Letters is not Abelian
snippet: Let $n$ be an integer such that $n > 3$. Then the $n$th alternating group $A_n$ is not abelian.

label: Alternating Series Test
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}_{N \mathop \ge 0}$ be a decreasing sequence of positive terms in $\R$ which converges with a limit of zero. That is, let $\forall n \in \N: a_n \ge 0, a_{n + 1} \le a_n, a_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ Then the series: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {-1}^{n - 1} a_n = a_1 - a_2 + a_3 - a_4 + \dotsb$ converges.

label: Alternating Sum and Difference of Binomial Coefficients for Given n
snippet: $\ds \forall n \in \Z_{\geq 0}: \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n \paren {-1}^i \binom n i = \delta_{n 0}$ where: $\dbinom n i$ is a binomial coefficient $\delta_{n 0}$ denotes the Kronecker delta.

label: Alternating Summation of Binomial Coefficient of Summation of Binomial Coefficient of Sequence
snippet: Let $\sequence a, \sequence b$ be real sequences which satisfy the condition: $a_n = \ds \sum_{r \mathop = 0}^n \binom n r b_r$ Then: $\ds \paren {-1}^n b_n = \sum_{s \mathop = 0}^n \binom n s \paren {-1}^s a_s$

label: Alternative Definition of Ordinal

snippet: Let $\ds \map \lambda s = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac {a_n} {n^s}$ be a Dirichlet series Let $c \in \R$ be greater than the abscissa of absolute convergence of $\lambda$ and greater than $0$. label: Analytic Continuation of Riemann Zeta Function using Dirichlet Eta Function
snippet: Let $\zeta$ be the Riemann zeta function. Let $\eta$ be the Dirichlet Eta Function. Then: $\dfrac 1 {1 - 2^{1 - s} } \map \eta s$ defines an analytic continuation of $\zeta$ to the half-plane $\map \Re s > 0$ minus $s = 1$.

label: Analytic Continuation of Riemann Zeta Function using Mellin Transform of Fractional Part
snippet: Let $\zeta$ denote the Riemann zeta function. The analytic continuation of $\zeta$ to the half-plane $\map \Re s > 0$ is given by: $\ds \frac s {s - 1} - s \int_1^\infty \fractpart x x^{-s - 1} \rd x$ where: $x^{-s - 1}$ takes the principal value $e^{-\map \ln x \paren {s + 1} }$ $\fractpart x$ is the fractional part of $x$.

label: Angle of Intersection of Circles is Equal at Both Points

label: Annihilator is Submodule of Algebraic Dual
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $G$ be a module over $R$. Let $M$ be a submodule of $G$. Let $G^*$ be the algebraic dual of $G$. Then the annihilator $M^\circ$ of $M$ is a submodule of $G^*$.

label: Annihilator of Annihilator on Algebraic Dual of Subspace is Image under Evaluation Isomorphism
snippet: Let $G$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space over a field. Let $G^*$ be the algebraic dual of $G$. Let $G^{**}$ be the algebraic dual of $G^*$. Let $J: G \to G^{**}$ be the evaluation isomorphism. Let $M$ be an $m$-dimensional subspace of $G$. Let $M^\circ$ be the annihilator of $M$. Then: $M^{\circ \circ} = J \sqbrk M$ where $J \sqbrk M$ denotes the image of $M$ under $J$.

label: Annihilator of Subspace of Banach Space as Intersection of Kernels
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $M$ be a vector subspace of $X$. Let $X^\ast$ be the normed dual space of $X$. Let $M^\bot$ be the annihilator of $M$. Then: $\ds M^\bot = \bigcap_{x \mathop \in M} \map \ker {x^\wedge}$ where $x^\wedge$ denotes the evaluation linear transformation evaluated at $x$.

label: Annihilator of Subspace of Banach Space is Subspace of Normed Dual
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $M$ be a vector subspace of $X$. Let $X^\ast$ be the normed dual space of $X$. Let $w^\ast$ be the weak-$\ast$ topology on $X^\ast$. Let $M^\bot$ be the annihilator of $M$. Then $M^\bot$ is a linear subspace of $X^\ast$.

label: Annihilator of Subspace of Banach Space is Weak-* Closed
snippet: Let $X$ be a Banach space. Let $M$ be a vector subspace of $X$. Let $X^\ast$ be the normed dual space of $X$. Let $w^\ast$ be the weak-$\ast$ topology on $X^\ast$. Let $M^\bot$ be the annihilator of $M$. Then $M^\bot$ is closed in $\struct {X^\ast, w^\ast}$.

label: Annihilator of Subspace of Banach Space is Zero iff Subspace is Everywhere Dense
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $M$ be a vector subspace of $X$. Let $X^\ast$ be the normed dual space of $X$. Let $M^\bot$ be the annihilator of $M$. Then: $M^\bot = \set { {\mathbf 0}_{X^\ast} }$ $M$ is everywhere dense in $X$.

label: Antisymmetric Quotient of Preordered Set is Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \precsim}$ be a preordered set. Let $\sim$ be the equivalence relation $S$ induced by $\precsim$. Let $\struct {S / {\sim}, \preceq}$ be the antisymmetric quotient of $\struct {S, \precsim}$. Then: $\struct {S / {\sim}, \preceq}$ is an ordered set. $\forall P, Q \in S / {\sim}: \paren {P \preceq Q} \land \paren {p \in P} \land \paren {q \in Q} \implies p \precsim q$ This second statement means that we could just as well have defined $\preceq$ by letting $P \preceq Q$ : $\forall p \in P: \forall q \in Q: p \precsim q$

label: Approximation of Lower Darboux Integral by Continuous Function
snippet: Let $f : \closedint a b \to \R$ be a bounded real function. Then, for each $\epsilon > 0$, there is a continuous real function $g : \closedint a b \to \R$ such that: $\paren 1 \quad$ For all $x \in \closedint a b$, $\map g x \le \map f x$. $\paren 2 \quad$ The infimums of $f$ and $g$ on $\closedint a b$ are the same. $\paren 3 \quad \ds \underline {\int_a^b} \map f x \rd x < \int_a^b \map g x \rd x + \epsilon$. where $\ds \underline {\int_a^b}$ denotes the lower Darboux integral, and $\ds \int_a^b$ the ordinary Darboux integral.

label: Arc Length for Parametric Equations
snippet: Let $x = \map f t$ and $y = \map g t$ be real functions of a parameter $t$. Let these equations describe a curve $\CC$ that is continuous for all $t \in \closedint a b$ and continuously differentiable for all $t \in \openint a b$. Suppose that the graph of the curve does not intersect itself for any $t \in \openint a b$. Then the arc length of $\CC$ between $a$ and $b$ is given by: $\ds s = \int_a^b \sqrt {\paren {\frac {\d x} {\d t} }^2 + \paren {\frac {\d y} {\d t} }^2} \rd t$ for $\dfrac {\d x} {\d t} \ne 0$.

label: Arc Length for Polar Curve
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers. Let $\CC$ be a simple curve continuous on $\closedint a b$ and continuously differentiable on $\openint a b$. Let $\CC$ be described by the parametric equations: $\begin {cases} x & = r \cos \theta \\ y & = r \sin \theta \end {cases}$ where: $r$ is a function of $\theta$ $\theta \in \closedint a b$. Then the length $s$ of $\CC$ is given by: $\ds s = \int_a^b \sqrt {r^2 + \paren {\frac {\d r} {\d \theta} }^2} \rd \theta$

label: Arc Length on Circle forms Metric
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R^2$ be the set defined as: $A = \set {\tuple {x_1, x_2}: x_1^2 + y_2^2 = 1}$ Thus from Equation of Unit Circle, $A$ is the unit circle embedded in the Cartesian plane. Let $d: A^2 \to \R$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall \tuple {x, y} \in A^2: \map d {x, y} = \begin {cases} 0 & : x = y \\ \pi & : x = -y \\ l & : \text {otherwise} \end {cases}$ where: $x$ and $y$ are of the form $\tuple {x_1, x_2}$ $l$ denotes the length of the minor arc of $A$ between $x$ and $y$. label: Arcsine Function in terms of Gaussian Hypergeometric Function
snippet: Let $\map F {a, b; c; x}$ denote the Gaussian hypergeometric function of $x$: $\ds \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^\infty \dfrac {a^{\overline k} b^{\overline k} } {c^{\overline k} } \dfrac {x^k} {k!}$ Then: $\arcsin x = x \map F {\dfrac 1 2, \dfrac 1 2; \dfrac 3 2; x^2}$ where: $x$ is a real number such that $\size x \le 1$ $\arcsin$ denotes the arcsine function.

label: Arcsine Logarithmic Formulation
snippet: For any real number $x: -1 \le x \le 1$: $\arcsin x = \dfrac 1 i \map \ln {i x + \sqrt {1 - x^2} }$ where $\arcsin x$ is the arcsine and $i^2 = -1$.

label: Arcsine as Integral
snippet: $\ds \map \arcsin x = \int_0^x \frac {\d x} {\sqrt {1 - x^2} }$

label: Arcsine in terms of Arctangent
snippet: $\arcsin x = \map \arctan {\dfrac x {\sqrt {1 - x^2} } }$ where $x$ is a real number with $-1 < x < 1$.

label: Arcsine in terms of Twice Arctangent
snippet: $\arcsin x = 2 \map \arctan {\dfrac x {1 + \sqrt {1 - x^2} } }$ where $x$ is a real number with $-1 < x < 1$.

label: Arctangent Function in terms of Gaussian Hypergeometric Function
snippet: Let $\map F {a, b; c; x}$ denote the Gaussian hypergeometric function of $x$: $\ds \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^\infty \dfrac {a^{\overline k} b^{\overline k} } {c^{\overline k} } \dfrac {x^k} {k!}$ Then: $\arctan x = x \map F {\dfrac 1 2, 1; \dfrac 3 2; -x^2}$ where: $x$ is a real number such that $\size x < 1$ $\arctan$ denotes the arctangent function.

label: Arctangent Logarithmic Formulation
snippet: For any real number $x$: $\arctan x = -\dfrac i 2 \map \ln {\dfrac {1 + i x} {1 - i x} }$ where $\arctan x$ is the arctangent and $i^2 = -1$.

label: Arctangent in terms of Arcsine
snippet: $\arctan x = \map \arcsin {\dfrac x {\sqrt {1 + x^2} } }$ where $x$ is a real number.

label: Arctangent of Imaginary Number
snippet: Let $x$ belong to the open real interval $\openint {-1} 1$. Then: $\map {\tan^{-1} } {i x} = \dfrac i 2 \map \ln {\dfrac {1 + x} {1 - x} }$ where $\tan$ is the complex tangent function, $\ln$ is the real natural logarithm, and $i$ is the imaginary unit.

label: Are All Perfect Numbers Even?
snippet: == Open Question == By the Theorem of Even Perfect Numbers, it is known that an even number is perfect it is of the form: $2^{n - 1} \paren {2^n - 1}$ where $2^n - 1$ is prime. It is not known whether there exist any odd perfect numbers. None have ever been found.

label: Are Irrational Square Roots Normal?
snippet: == Open Question == It is not known whether irrational square roots are normal.

label: Are there Integers which are Sum of 2 Fifth Powers in 2 Ways?
snippet: == Open Question == It is not known whether there exists an integer which equals the sum of two fifth powers in $2$ different ways. That is, it is not known whether the Diophantine equation: $a^5 + b^5 = c^5 + d^5$ has a solution.

label: Are there any Palindromic Fifth Powers?
snippet: == Open Question == It is not known whether there exist any palindromic fifth powers of an integer.

label: Are there any Palindromic Fourth Powers with Non-Palindromic Roots?
snippet: == Open Question == It is not known whether there exist any palindromic fourth powers of a non-palindromic integer.

label: Area Enclosed by First Turn of Archimedean Spiral
snippet: Let $S$ be the Archimedean spiral defined by the equation: $r = a \theta$ The area $\AA$ enclosed by the first turn of $S$ and the polar axis is given by: $\AA = \dfrac {4 \pi^3 a^2} 3$ 500px

label: Area Sampling/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Area Sampling ==

label: Area between Radii and Curve in Polar Coordinates
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve expressed in polar coordinates $\polar {r, \theta}$ as: $r = \map g \theta$ where $g$ is a real function. Let $\theta = \theta_a$ and $\theta = \theta_b$ be the two rays from the pole at angles $\theta_a$ and $\theta_b$ to the polar axis respectively. Then the area $\AA$ between $\theta_a$, $\theta_b$ and $C$ is given by: $\ds \AA = \int \limits_{\theta \mathop = \theta_a}^{\theta \mathop = \theta_b} \frac {\paren {\map g \theta}^2 \rd \theta} 2$ as long as $\paren {\map g \theta}^2$ is integrable.

label: Area between Radii and Whorls of Archimedean Spiral
snippet: Let $S$ be the Archimedean spiral defined by the equation: $r = a \theta$ Let $\theta = \theta_1$ and $\theta = \theta_2$ be the two rays from the pole at angles $\theta_1$ and $\theta_b$ to the polar axis respectively. Let $R$ be the figure enclosed by: $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ the $n$th turn of $S$ and the $n+1$th turn of $S$ The area $\AA$ of $R$ is given by: $\AA = a^2 \pi \paren {\theta_2 - \theta_1} \paren {\theta_2 + \theta_1 + 2 \pi \paren {2 n + 1} }$

label: Area between Smooth Curve and Line with Fixed Endpoints is Maximized by Arc of Circle
snippet: Let $y$ be a smooth curve, embedded in $2$-dimensional Euclidean space. Let $y$ have a total length of $l$. Let it be contained in the upper halfplane with an exception of endpoints, which are on the x-axis and are given. Suppose, $y$, together with a line segment connecting $y$'s endpoints, maximizes the enclosed area. Then $y$ is an arc of a circle.

label: Area of Circle
snippet: The area $A$ of a circle is given by: $A = \pi r^2$ where $r$ is the radius of the circle.

label: Area of Ellipse
snippet: Let $K$ be an ellipse whose major axis is of length $2 a$ and whose minor axis is of length $2 b$. The area $\AA$ of $K$ is given by: $\AA = \pi a b$

label: Area of Integer Heronian Triangle is Multiple of 6
snippet: Let $\triangle {ABC}$ be an integer Heronian triangle. Then the area of $\triangle {ABC}$ is a multiple of $6$.

label: Area of Isosceles Triangle in terms of Sides
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be an isosceles triangle whose apex is $A$. Let $r$ be the length of a leg of $\triangle ABC$. Let $b$ be the length of the base of $\triangle ABC$. Then the area $\AA$ of $\triangle ABC$ is given by: $\AA = \dfrac b 4 \sqrt {4 r^2 - b^2}$

label: Area of Parallelogram
snippet: The area of a parallelogram equals the product of one of its bases and the associated altitude.

label: Area of Parallelogram from Determinant
snippet: Let $OABC$ be a parallelogram in the Cartesian plane whose vertices are located at: {{eqn | l = O | r = \tuple {0, 0} }} {{eqn | l = A | r = \tuple {a, c} }} {{eqn | l = B | r = \tuple {a + b, c + d} }} {{eqn | l = C | r = \tuple {b, d} }} The area of $OABC$ is given by: $\map \Area {OABC} = \begin {vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end {vmatrix}$ where $\begin {vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end {vmatrix}$ denotes the determinant of order $2$.

label: Area of Quadrilateral in Determinant Form
snippet: Let $A = \tuple {x_1, y_1}$, $B = \tuple {x_2, y_2}$, $C = \tuple {x_3, y_3}$ and $D = \tuple {x_4, y_4}$ be points in the Cartesian plane. Let $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ form the vertices of a quadrilateral. The area $\AA$ of $\Box ABCD$ is given by: $\AA = \dfrac 1 2 \paren {\size {\paren {\begin{vmatrix} x_1 & y_1 & 1 \\ x_2 & y_2 & 1 \\ x_3 & y_3 & 1 \\ \end{vmatrix} } } + \size {\paren {\begin{vmatrix} x_1 & y_1 & 1 \\ x_4 & y_4 & 1 \\ x_3 & y_3 & 1 \\ \end{vmatrix} } } }$

label: Area of Quadrilateral with Given Sides is Greatest when Quadrilateral is Cyclic
snippet: Let $Q$ be a quadrilateral whose sides are $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$. Let $\AA$ be the area of $Q$. Then: $Q$ is a cyclic quadrilateral $\AA$ is the greatest area possible for one with sides $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$.

label: Area of Regular Hexagon
snippet: Let $H$ be a regular hexagon. Let the length of one side of $H$ be $s$. Let $\AA$ be the area of $H$. Then: $\AA = \dfrac {3 \sqrt 3} 2 s^2$

label: Area of Regular Polygon
snippet: Let $P$ be a regular $n$-sided polygon whose side length is $b$. Then the area of $P$ is given by: $\Box P = \dfrac 1 4 n b^2 \cot \dfrac \pi n$ where $\cot$ denotes cotangent.

label: Area of Regular Polygon by Circumradius
snippet: Let $P$ be a regular $n$-gon. Let the circumradius of $P$ be $r$. Then the area $\AA$ of $P$ is given by: $\AA = \dfrac 1 2 n r^2 \sin \dfrac {2 \pi} n$

label: Area of Regular Polygon by Inradius
snippet: Let $P$ be a regular $n$-gon. Let $C$ be an incircle of $P$. Let the radius of $C$ be $r$. Then the area $\AA$ of $P$ is given by: $\AA = n r^2 \tan \dfrac \pi n$

label: Area of Right Parabolic Segment
snippet: Let $ABC$ be a right parabolic segment where: $AB$ is the defining chord $\LL$ of $ABC$ $C$ is the vertex of the defining parabola $\PP$ of $ABC$. 480px The area $\AA$ of $ABC$ is given by: $\AA = \dfrac {2 a b} 3$ where: $a$ is the length of the line segment $CF$, where $F$ is the point at which the axis of $\PP$ intersects $AB$ $b$ is the length of the line segment $AB$.

label: Area of Sector
snippet: Let $\CC = ABC$ be a circle whose center is $A$ and with radii $AB$ and $AC$. Let $BAC$ be the sector of $\CC$ whose angle between $AB$ and $AC$ is $\theta$. 300px Then the area $\AA$ of sector $BAC$ is given by: $\AA = \dfrac {r^2 \theta} 2$ where: $r = AB$ is the length of the radius of the circle $\theta$ is measured in radians.

label: Area of Smallest Square accommodating Re-Entrant Knight's Tour
snippet: The area of the smallest square chessboard on which a re-entrant knight's tour is possible is $6 \times 6 = 36$ squares.

label: Area of Square
snippet: A square has an area of $L^2$ where $L$ is the length of a side of the square. Thus we have that the area is a function of the length of the side: $\forall L \in \R_{\ge 0}: \map \Area L = L^2$ where it is noted that the domain of $L$ is the set of non-negative real numbers.

Area of Triangle
snippet: This page gathers a variety of formulas for the area of a triangle.

label: Area of Triangle Inscribed in Parabola
snippet: Let $T$ be the parabola which is the locus of points $\tuple {x, y}$ satisfying $y = x^2$. Let $A$ and $B$ be two arbitrary points on $T$ with coordinates: $A = \tuple {u, u^2}$ $B = \tuple {v, v^2}$, with $u > v$ Let $C$ be a third point on $T$ whose $x$-coordinate is the average of those of $A$ and $B$. The area of $\triangle ABC$ is: $\map \AA {\triangle ABC} = \dfrac 1 8 \paren {u - v}^3$

label: Area of Triangle in Determinant Form
snippet: Let $A = \tuple {x_1, y_1}, B = \tuple {x_2, y_2}, C = \tuple {x_3, y_3}$ be points in the Cartesian plane. The area $\AA$ of the triangle whose vertices are at $A$, $B$ and $C$ is given by: $\AA = \dfrac 1 2 \size {\paren {\begin {vmatrix} x_1 & y_1 & 1 \\ x_2 & y_2 & 1 \\ x_3 & y_3 & 1 \\ \end {vmatrix} } }$

label: Area of Triangle in Determinant Form with Vertex at Origin
snippet: == Example of Area of Triangle in Determinant Form == Let $A = \tuple {0, 0}, B = \tuple {b, a}, C = \tuple {x, y}$ be points in the Cartesian plane. Let $T$ the triangle whose vertices are at $A$, $B$ and $C$. Then the area $\AA$ of $T$ is: $\map \Area T = \dfrac {\size {b y - a x} } 2$

label: Area of Triangle in Terms of Circumradius
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle whose sides are $a$, $b$ and $c$ opposite vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively. Then the area $\AA$ of $\triangle ABC$ is given by: $\AA = \dfrac {a b c} {4 R}$ where $R$ is the circumradius of $\triangle ABC$.

label: Area of Triangle in Terms of Exradius
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle whose sides are $a$, $b$ and $c$ opposite vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively. Let $\rho_a$ be the exradius of $\triangle ABC$ the excircle which is tangent to $a$. Let $s$ be the semiperimeter of $\triangle ABC$. Then the area $\AA$ of $\triangle ABC$ is given by: $\AA = \rho_a \paren {s - a}$

label: Area of Triangle in Terms of Inradius
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle whose sides are $a$, $b$ and $c$ opposite vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively. Then the area $\AA$ of $\triangle ABC$ is given by: $\AA = r s$ where: $r$ is the inradius of $\triangle ABC$ $s = \dfrac {a + b + c} 2$ is the semiperimeter of $\triangle ABC$.

label: Area of Triangle in Terms of Inradius and Exradii
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle whose sides are $a$, $b$ and $c$ opposite vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively. Then the area $\AA$ of $\triangle ABC$ is given by: $\AA = \sqrt {r \rho_a \rho_b \rho_c}$ where: $r$ is the inradius $\rho_a$, $\rho_b$ and $\rho_c$ are the exradii of $\triangle ABC$ $a$, $b$ and $c$ respectively.

label: Area of Triangle in Terms of Side and Altitude
snippet: The area of a triangle $\triangle ABC$ is given by: $\dfrac {c \cdot h_c} 2 = \dfrac {b \cdot h_b} 2 = \dfrac {a \cdot h_a} 2$ where: $a, b, c$ are the sides $h_a, h_b, h_c$ are the altitudes from $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively.

label: Area of Triangle in Terms of Two Sides and Angle
snippet: == Corollary to Area of Triangle in Terms of Side and Altitude == The area of a triangle $ABC$ is given by: $\dfrac 1 2 a b \sin C$ where: $a, b$ are two of the sides $C$ is the angle of the vertex opposite its other side $c$.

label: Area under Acceleration-Time Graph
snippet: Let $P$ be a particle moving in a straight line. Let the acceleration of $P$ as a function of time be $\map a t$. Let the velocity of $P$ as a function of time be $\map v t$. Let the motion of $P$ be plotted on an acceleration-time-graph $G$. Let $v_1$ and $v_2$ be the velocities of $P$ at times $t_1$ and $t_2$ respectively. Then the area under $G$ between times $t_1$ and $t_2$ is equal to $v_2 - v_1$.

label: Area under Curve
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function which is defined and (Darboux) integrable on the closed interval $\closedint a b$. Consider the graph of $f$ embedded in a Cartesian plane. Let $\AA$ denote the area between the curve $\map f x$, the straight lines $x = a$ and $x = b$, and the $x$-axis. Then: $\AA = \ds \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$ where $\ds \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$ denotes the (Darboux) definite integral of $f$ from $a$ to $b$.

Areas of Triangles and Parallelograms Proportional to Base
snippet: Let $ABC$ and $ACD$ be triangles. Let $EC, CF$ be parallelograms under the same height. Then: $AC : CD = \triangle ABC : \triangle ACD = \Box EC : \Box CF$ where: $AC : CD$ denotes the ratio of the length of $AC$ to that of $CD$ $\triangle ABC : \triangle ACD$ denotes the ratio of the area of $\triangle ABC$ to that of $\triangle ACD$ $\Box EC : \Box CF$ denotes the ratio of the area of parallelogram $EC$ to that of parallelogram $CF$.

label: Arens-Fort Space is Countable
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be the Arens-Fort space. Then $S$ is countably infinite.

label: Arens-Fort Space is Separable
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be the Arens-Fort space. Then $T$ is a separable space.

label: Argument Principle
snippet: Let $\gamma$ be a closed contour. Let $D$ be the region enclosed by $\gamma$. Let $f$ be a function meromorphic on $D$. Let $f$ be holomorphic with no zeroes on $\gamma$. Let $N$ denote the number of zeroes of $f$ in $D$, counted up to multiplicity. Let $P$ denote the number of poles of $f$ in $D$, counted up to order. Then: $\ds N - P = \frac 1 {2\pi i} \oint_\gamma \frac {\map {f'} z} {\map f z} \rd z$

label: Argument of Complex Conjugate equals Argument of Reciprocal
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. Then: $\arg {\overline z} = \arg \dfrac 1 z$ where: $\arg$ denotes the argument of a complex number $\overline z$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z$.

label: Argument of Complex Conjugate equals Negative of Argument
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. Then: $\arg {\overline z} = -\arg z$ where: $\arg$ denotes the argument of a complex number $\overline z$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z$.

label: Argument of Exponential is Imaginary Part plus Multiple of 2 Pi
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. Let $\exp z$ denote the complex exponential of $z$. Let $\arg z$ denote the argument of $z$. Then: $\map \arg {\exp z} = \set {\Im z + 2 k \pi: k \in \Z}$ where $\Im z$ denotes the imaginary part of $z$.

label: Argument of Product equals Sum of Arguments
snippet: Let $z_1, z_2 \in \C$ be complex numbers. Let $\arg$ be the argument operator. Then: $\map \arg {z_1 z_2} = \map \arg {z_1} + \map \arg {z_2} + 2 k \pi$ where $k$ can be $0$, $1$ or $-1$.

label: Argument of Quotient equals Difference of Arguments
snippet: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be complex numbers. Then: $\map \arg {\dfrac {z_1} {z_2} } = \map \arg {z_1} - \map \arg {z_1} + 2 k \pi$ where: $\arg$ denotes the argument of a complex number $k$ can be $0$, $1$ or $-1$.

label: Argument of x to the n Equals n Times The Argument
snippet: Let $z$ be a complex number. Then: $\forall n \in \N_{>0}: \map \arg {z^n} = n \map \arg z$

label: Arithmetic Average of Second Chebyshev Function
snippet: Let $x \ge 1$ be a real number. Then: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop \le x} \map \psi {x/n} = x \ln x - x + \map \OO {\map \ln {x + 1} }$ where: the summation extends over all strictly positive integers $n$ such that $n \le x$ $\OO$ is big-O notation $\psi$ is the second Chebyshev function.

label: Arithmetic Mean is Weighted Mean with Equal Weights
snippet: Let $S = \sequence {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a set of real numbers. Let $W$ be a weight function to be applied to the terms of $S$ such that: $\forall x \in S: \map W x = c$ where $c$ is a real constant. Let $\bar x$ denote the weighted mean of $S$ $W$. Then: $\bar x = A_n$ where $A_n$ denotes the arithmetic mean of $S$.

label: Arithmetic Mean of two Real Numbers is Between them
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{\ne 0}$ be real numbers such that $a < b$. Let $\map A {a, b}$ denote the arithmetic mean of $a$ and $b$. Then: $a < \map A {a, b} < b$

label: Arithmetic Sequence of 16 Primes
snippet: The $16$ integers in arithmetic sequence defined as: $2\,236\,133\,941 + 223\,092\,870 n$ are prime for $n = 0, 1, \ldots, 15$.

label: Art Gallery Problem
snippet: == Classic Problem == Consider an whose shape is a (simple) polygon. The Art Gallery Problem asks: What is the minimum number of security guards needed, positioned on the perimeter of the , so that every point within the can be seen by at least one of the guards? That is, for a given (simple) polygon $P$: What is the smallest set $S$ of points on the perimeter of $P$ such that for every point $p \in P$ there exists some $q \in S$ such that there exists a straight line segment $p q$ lying wholly inside $P$? Category:Classic Problems Category:Plane Geometry

label: Arzelà-Ascoli Theorem
snippet: Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space. Let $Y$ be a metric space. Let $\CC$ be the set of all continuous functions $X \to Y$. Consider $\CC$ as a metric space with the supremum metric: $\ds \map {d_\infty} {f, g} := \sup_{x \mathop \in X} \map d {\map f x, \map g x}$ Then a set $F \subseteq \CC$ is relatively compact it is pointwise equicontinuous and pointwise relatively compact.

label: Associated Legendre Function
snippet: An associated Legendre function $P_l^m$ is related to a Legendre polynomial $P_l$ by the equation: $ \map {P^m_l} x = \paren {1 - x^2}^{m / 2} \dfrac {\d^m \map {P_l} x} {\d x^m}, \qquad 0 \le m \le l$ Although extensions are possible, in this article $l$ and $m$ are restricted to integer numbers. For even $m$ the associated Legendre function is a polynomial, for odd $m$ the function contains the factor $\paren {1 - x^2}^\frac 1 2$ and hence is not a polynomial. The associated Legendre functions are important in quantum mechanics and potential theory.

label: Associated Legendre Function of the First Kind/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Associated Legendre Functions of the First Kind ==

label: Associatehood is Equivalence Relation
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \circ}$ be an integral domain whose zero is $0_D$ and whose unity is $1_D$. Let $\sim$ be the relation defined on $D$ as: $\forall x, y \in D: x \sim y$ $x$ is an associate of $y$ Then $\sim$ is an equivalence relation.

label: Associative Idempotent Anticommutative
snippet: Let $\circ$ be a binary operation on a non-empty set $S$. Let $\circ$ be associative. Then $\circ$ is anticommutative : $(1): \quad \circ$ is idempotent and: $(2): \quad \forall a, b \in S: a \circ b \circ a = a$

label: Associative Law of Addition
snippet: Let $\mathbb F$ be one of the standard number sets: $\N, \Z, \Q, \R$ and $\C$. Then: $\forall x, y, z \in \mathbb F: x + \paren {y + z} = \paren {x + y} + z$ That is, the operation of addition on the standard number sets is associative.

label: Associative Law of Multiplication
snippet: Let $\mathbb F$ be one of the standard number sets: $\N, \Z, \Q, \R$ and $\C$. Then: $\forall x, y, z \in \mathbb F: x \times \paren {y \times z} = \paren {x \times y} \times z$ That is, the operation of multiplication on the standard number sets is associative.

label: Associativity of Group Direct Product
snippet: The group direct product $G \times \paren {H \times K}$ is (group) isomorphic to $\paren {G \times H} \times K$.

label: Associativity on Indexing Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a commutative semigroup. Let $\family {x_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in A}$ be a family of terms of $S$ indexed by a finite non-empty set $A$. Let $\family {B_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be a family of distinct subsets of $A$ forming a partition of $A$. Then: $\ds \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n \paren {\prod_{a \mathop \in B_k} x_\alpha} = \prod_{\alpha \mathop \in A} x_\alpha$

label: Astroid is Envelope of Line Segment whose End Points lie on Coordinate Axes
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a line segment of length $a$. Let the endpoints of $\LL$ be constrained to lie on the coordinate axes of a Cartesian plane: one on the $x$-axis and one on the $y$-axis The envelope of $\LL$ forms an astroid whose cusps lie on the points at which the coordinate axes intersect a circle of radius $a$ whose center is at the origin.

label: Asymmetric Relation is Antireflexive
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation on $S$. Let $\RR$ be asymmetric. Then $\RR$ is also antireflexive.

label: Asymptotes to Hyperbola in Reduced Form
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a hyperbola embedded in a cartesian plane in reduced form with the equation: $\dfrac {x^2} {a^2} - \dfrac {y^2} {b^2} = 1$ $\KK$ has two asymptotes which can be described by the equation: $\dfrac {x^2} {a^2} - \dfrac {y^2} {b^2} = 0$ that is: $y = \pm \dfrac b a x$

label: Asymptotic Formula for Bernoulli Numbers
snippet: The Bernoulli numbers with even index can be approximated by the asymptotic formula: $B_{2 n} \sim \paren {-1}^{n + 1} 4 \sqrt {\pi n} \paren {\dfrac n {\pi e} }^{2 n}$ where: $B_n$ denotes the $n$th Bernoulli number $\sim$ denotes asymptotically equal.

label: Asymptotic Growth of Euler Phi Function
snippet: Let $\phi$ be the Euler $\phi$ function. For any $\epsilon > 0$ and sufficiently large $n$: $n^{1 - \epsilon} < \map \phi n < n$

label: At Least One Third of Zeros of Riemann Zeta Function on Critical Line
snippet: At least $\dfrac 1 3$ of the nontrivial zeroes of the Riemann $\zeta$ function lie on the critical line.

label: Atlas Belongs to Unique Differentiable Structure

snippet: Let $M$ be the Mandelbrot set. Let $T_c: \C \to \C$ be the complex function defined as: $\forall z \in \C: \map {T_c} z = z^2 + c$ Let $c \in M$. Then $T_c$ has an attractor which is either a fixed point or a set of $n$ periodic points of period $n$.

label: Autocorrelation Matrix is Positive Definite
snippet: Let $S$ be a strictly stationary stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. Let $\sequence {s_n}$ be a sequence of $n$ successive values of $T$: $\sequence {s_n} = \tuple {z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_n}$ Let $\mathbf P_n$ denote the autocorrelation matrix associated with $S$ for $\sequence {s_n}$. Then $\mathbf P_n$ is a positive definite matrix.

label: Autocovariance Matrix for Stationary Process is Variance by Autocorrelation Matrix
snippet: Let $S$ be a strictly stationary stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. Let $\sequence {s_n}$ be a sequence of $n$ successive values of $T$: $\sequence {s_n} = \tuple {z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_n}$ Let $\boldsymbol \Gamma_n$ denote the autocovariance matrix associated with $S$ for $\sequence {s_n}$. Let $\mathbf P_n$ denote the autocorrelation matrix associated with $S$ for $\sequence {s_n}$. Then: $\boldsymbol \Gamma_n = \sigma_z^2 \mathbf P_n$ where $\sigma_z^2$ denotes the variance of $S$.

label: Automorphic Numbers in Base 10
snippet: If leading zeroes are allowed, there are exactly $4$ $n$-digit automorphic numbers in base $10$: $00 \dots 00$ $00 \dots 01$ $5^{2^{n - 1} } \pmod {10^n}$ $6^{5^{n - 1} } \pmod {10^n}$

snippet: Let $\struct {S, *}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\Aut S$ be the automorphism group of $\struct {S, *}$. Then $\Aut S$ is a subgroup of the symmetric group $\struct {\Gamma \paren S, \circ}$ on $S$.

label: Auxiliary Approximating Relation has Interpolation Property
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a complete lattice. Let $x, z \in S$ such that: $x \ll z \land x \ne z$ Let $\RR$ be an auxiliary approximating relation on $S$. Then $\exists y \in S: \tuple {x, y} \in \RR \land \tuple {y, z} \in \RR \land x \ne y$

label: Auxiliary Approximating Relation has Quasi Interpolation Property
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a complete lattice. Let $x, z \in S$. Let $\RR$ be an auxiliary approximating relation on $S$ such that $\tuple {x, z} \in \RR \land x \ne z$ Then: $\exists y \in S: x \preceq y \land \tuple {y, z} \in \RR \land x \ne y$

label: Axes of Symmetry for Ellipse
snippet: Let $K$ be an ellipse. Then $K$ has exactly $2$ axis of bilateral symmetry: the major axis of $K$ the minor axis of $K$.

label: Axes of Symmetry of Hyperbola
snippet: The hyperbola has $2$ axis of bilateral symmetry: the transverse axis the conjugate axis. When expressed in reduced form in a cartesian plane, these correspond respectively with the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis.

snippet: The aleph hypothesis is the proposition: $\aleph_{\alpha} = \beth_{\alpha}$ for all ordinals $\alpha$ where $\aleph_\alpha$ is the Aleph ($\aleph$) mapping and $\beth_\alpha$ is the Beth ($\beth$) mapping.

snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\RR \subseteq \powerset S$ be a set of subsets of $S$. $\RR$ is an algebra of sets the following axioms hold: {{axiom | n = \text {AS} 1 | lc= Unit: | m = S \in \RR }} {{axiom | n = \text {AS} 2 | lc= Closure under Union: | q = \forall A, B \in \RR | m = A \cup B \in \RR }} {{axiom | n = \text {AS} 3 | lc= Closure under Complement Relative to $S$: | q = \forall A \in \RR | m = \relcomp S A \in \RR }} These criteria are called the algebra of sets axioms.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Abstraction
snippet: The states: Given any property $P$, there exists a unique set which consists of all and only those objects which have property $P$: $\set {x: \map P x}$ From the definition of a set: A set is any aggregation of objects, called elements, which can be precisely defined in some way or other.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Choice/Formulation 1
snippet: For every set of non-empty sets, it is possible to provide a mechanism for choosing one element of each element of the set. $\ds \forall s: \paren {\O \notin s \implies \exists \paren {f: s \to \bigcup s}: \forall t \in s: \map f t \in t}$ That is, one can always create a choice function for selecting one element from each element of the set.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Choice/Formulation 2
snippet: Let $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of sets all of which are non-empty, indexed by $I$ which is also non-empty. Then there exists an indexed family $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ such that: $\forall i \in I: x_i \in X_i$ That is, the Cartesian product of a non-empty family of sets which are non-empty is itself non-empty.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Choice/Formulation 3
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a set of non-empty pairwise disjoint sets. Then there exists a set $C$ such that for all $S \in \SS$, $C \cap S$ has exactly one element. Symbolically: $\forall s: \paren {\paren {\O \notin s \land \forall t, u \in s: t = u \lor t \cap u = \O} \implies \exists c: \forall t \in s: \exists x: t \cap c = \set x}$ That is, there exists a choice set $C$ for $\SS$.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Choice/Formulation 4
snippet: Let $A$ be a non-empty set. Then there exists a mapping $f: \powerset A \to A$ such that: for every non-empty proper subset $x$ of $A$: $\map f x \in x$ where $\powerset A$ denotes the power set of $A$.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Choice/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on == exposited the in order to prove what is now known as Zermelo's Well-Ordering Theorem. He himself did not invent the idea of the choice function; he explains that he is merely formalizing a concept ubiquitous in mathematics. Formulation 1 and formulation 2 are written in a letter from to , postmarked $24$ September $1904$: Der vorliegende Beweis beruht auf der Voraussetzung [...] daß es auch für eine unendliche Gesamtheit von Mengen immer Zuordnungen gibt, bei denen jeder Menge eines ihrer Elemente entspricht, oder formal ausgedrückt, daß das Produkt einer unendlichen…

label: Axiom:Axiom of Choice for Finite Sets
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a non-empty set of finite, non-empty sets. Then there exists a choice function for $\SS$.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Choice for Finite Sets/Proof from Hall's Marriage Theorem
snippet: Suppose that Hall's Marriage Theorem holds for all sets of finite sets. Let $\SS$ be a non-empty set of finite, non-empty sets. Then there exists a choice function for $\SS$.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Countable Choice/Form 1
snippet: Let $\sequence {S_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of non-empty sets. The axiom of countable choice states that there exists a sequence: $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that $x_n \in S_n$ for all $n \in \N$.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Countable Choice/Form 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a countable set of non-empty sets. Then $S$ has a choice function.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Countable Choice for Finite Sets
snippet: Let $S$ be a countable set of non-empty finite sets. Then $S$ has a choice function.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Dependent Choice/Left-Total
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a binary relation on a non-empty set $S$. Suppose that: $\forall a \in S: \exists b \in S: a \mathrel \RR b$ that is, that $\RR$ is a left-total relation (specifically a serial relation). The axiom of dependent choice states that there exists a sequence $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $S$ such that: $\forall n \in \N: x_n \mathrel \RR x_{n + 1}$ Dependent Choice

label: Axiom:Axiom of Dependent Choice/Right-Total
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a binary relation on a non-empty set $S$. Suppose that: $\forall a \in S: \exists b \in S: b \mathrel \RR a$ that is, that $\RR$ is a right-total relation. The axiom of dependent choice states that there exists a sequence $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $S$ such that: $\forall n \in \N: x_{n + 1} \mathrel \RR x_n$ Dependent Choice

label: Axiom:Axiom of Extension/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on == The nature of the , or as it is frequently called, suggests that the ought in fact to be the preferred name, as it gives a precise definition of the extent of a collection. However, the word extensionality is a term in logic which determines equality of objects by its external features, as opposed to intensionality, which is more concerned with internal structure. label: Axiom:Axiom of Extension/Set Theory
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. The states that: $A$ and $B$ are equal they contain the same elements. That is, : every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$ and: every element of $B$ is also an element of $A$. This can be formulated as follows:

label: Axiom:Axiom of Extension/Set Theory/Formulation 1
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. The axiom of extension can be formulated as: $\forall x: \paren {x \in A \iff x \in B} \iff A = B$

label: Axiom:Axiom of Extension/Set Theory/Formulation 2
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. The can be formulated as: $\forall x: \paren {\paren {A = B \land A \in x} \implies B \in x}$ This formulation is used in set theories that define $=$ instead of admitting it as a primitive.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Foundation
snippet: For all non-empty sets, there is an element of the set that shares no element with the set. That is: $\forall S: \paren {\paren {\exists x: x \in S} \implies \exists y \in S: \forall z \in S: \neg \paren {z \in y} }$ The antecedent states that $S$ is not empty.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Foundation (Classes)
snippet: For any non-empty class, there is an element of the class that shares no element with the class. $\forall X: X \ne \O \implies \exists y: y \in X \land y \cap X = \O$

label: Axiom:Axiom of Infinity/Class Theory/Formulation 1
snippet: Let $\omega$ be the class of natural numbers as constructed by the Von Neumann construction: Then $\omega$ is a set.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Infinity/Class Theory/Formulation 3
snippet: Not every set is a natural number.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Infinity/Set Theory
snippet: There exists a set containing: $(1): \quad$ a set with no elements $(2): \quad$ the successor of each of its elements. That is: $\exists x: \paren {\paren {\exists y: y \in x \land \forall z: \neg \paren {z \in y} } \land \forall u: u \in x \implies u^+ \in x}$ In this context, the successor of the set $u$, written $u^+$, is defined as $u^+ := u \cup \set u$. The symbol $\cup$ represents set union and $\set u$ represents the singleton containing $u$.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Limitation of Size
snippet: For any class $\CC$, a set $x$ such that $x = \CC$ exists there is no bijection between $\CC$ and the universal class. Limitation of Size

label: Axiom:Axiom of Pairing/Class Theory
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be sets. Then the class $\set {a, b}$ is likewise a set.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Pairing/Set Theory/Strong Form
snippet: For any two sets, there exists a set to which only those two sets are elements: $\forall a: \forall b: \exists c: \forall z: \paren {z = a \lor z = b \iff z \in c}$ That is, let $a$ and $b$ be sets. Then there exists a set $c$ such that $c = \set {a, b}$. Thus it is possible to create a set whose elements are two sets that have already been created.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Pairing/Set Theory/Weak Form
snippet: For any two sets, there exists a set to which those two sets are elements: $\forall a: \forall b: \exists c: \forall z: \paren {z = a \lor z = b \implies z \in c}$ That is, let $a$ and $b$ be sets. Then there exists a set $c$ such that $a \in c$ and $b \in c$. Thus it is possible to create a set that contains as elements two sets that have already been created.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Powers/Class Theory
snippet: Let $x$ be a set. Then its power set $\powerset x$ is also a set.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Powers/Set Theoretical and Class Theoretical
snippet: == Axiom of Unions: Difference between Formulations == Recall the two formulations of the axiom of powers:

label: Axiom:Axiom of Powers/Set Theory
snippet: For every set, there exists a set of sets whose elements are all the subsets of the given set. $\forall x: \exists y: \paren {\forall z: \paren {z \in y \iff \forall w: \paren {w \in z \implies w \in x} } }$

label: Axiom:Axiom of Replacement/Also known as

label: Axiom:Axiom of Replacement/Class Theory/Formulation 1
snippet: For every mapping $f$ and set $x$ in the domain of $f$, the image $f \sqbrk x$ is a set. Symbolically: $\forall Y: \map {\text{Fnc}} Y \implies \forall x: \exists y: \forall u: u \in y \iff \exists v: \tuple {v, u} \in Y \land v \in x$ where: $\map {\text{Fnc}} X := \forall x, y, z: \tuple {x, y} \in X \land \tuple {x, z} \in X \implies y = z$ and the notation $\tuple {\cdot, \cdot}$ is understood to represent Kuratowski's formalization of ordered pairs.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Replacement/Class Theory/Formulation 2
snippet: For every mapping $f$ and set $x$, the restriction $f \restriction x$ is a set.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Replacement/Class Theory/Formulation 3
snippet: Every mapping whose domain is a set is also a set.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Replacement/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Axiom of Replacement == The axiom of replacement was added to the axioms of Zermelo set theory by , and also independently by . The resulting system of axiomatic set theory is now referred to as Zermelo-Fraenkel Set Theory.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Replacement/Set Theory
snippet: For every mapping $f$ and subset $S$ of the domain of $f$, there exists a set containing the image $f \sqbrk S$. More formally, let us express this as follows: Let $\map P {x, z}$ be a propositional function, which determines a mapping. That is, we have: $\forall x: \exists ! y : \map P {x, y}$. Then we state as an axiom: $\forall A: \exists B: \forall y: \paren {y \in B \iff \exists x \in A : \map P {x, y} }$

label: Axiom:Axiom of Segment Construction
snippet: Let $\equiv$ be the relation of equidistance. Let $\mathsf{B}$ be the relation of betweenness. The axiom of segment construction is given by the following statement: $\forall a, b, c, q: \exists x: \mathsf{B} qax \land ax \equiv bc$ where $a, b, c, q, x$ are points.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Specification
snippet: For every set and every condition, there corresponds a set whose elements are exactly the same as those elements of the original set for which the condition is true. Because we cannot quantify over functions, we need an axiom for every condition we can express. Therefore, this axiom is sometimes called an axiom schema, as we introduce a lot of similar axioms. This axiom schema can be formally stated as follows:

label: Axiom:Axiom of Specification/Also known as
snippet: The is also known as: The Axiom of Subsets (although this unnecessarily reduces the scope of this axiom to pure set theory) The Axiom of Comprehension The Axiom of Selection (this axiom allows one to select the elements of a subset) The Axiom of Separation or Separation Principle (although this can be confused with the Tychonoff separation axioms, which arise in topology, so this name is deprecated on ) The Axiom of Segregation, under its German name Aussonderungsaxiom The limited abstraction principle, in apposition to the unlimited abstraction principle, also known as the axiom of…

label: Axiom:Axiom of Specification/Class Theory
snippet: The is an axiom schema which can be formally stated as follows: Let $\map \phi {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n, x}$ be a propositional function such that: $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ are a finite number of free variables whose domain ranges over all classes $x$ is a free variable whose domain ranges over all sets Then the gives that: $\forall A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n: \exists B: \forall x: \paren {x \in B \iff \map \phi {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n, x} }$ where each of $B$ ranges over arbitrary classes.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Specification/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on == The was created by as a replacement for the of Frege set theory. The latter had been demonstrated, via Russell's Paradox, to lead to the conclusion that Frege Set Theory is Logically Inconsistent. Thus, rather than allowing a set to be constructed of any elements at all which satisfy a given property $P$, the elements in question are restricted to being elements of some pre-existing set. This in turn leads to the further question of how to create such a pre-existing set in the first place.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Specification/Set Theory
snippet: The axiom of specification is an axiom schema which can be formally stated as follows: For any well-formed formula $\map P y$, we introduce the axiom: $\forall z: \exists x: \forall y: \paren {y \in x \iff \paren {y \in z \land \map P y} }$ where each of $x$, $y$ and $z$ range over arbitrary sets. This means that if you have a set, you can create a set that contains some of the elements of that set, where those elements are specified by stipulating that they satisfy some (arbitrary) condition.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Specification/Set Theory/Also presented as
snippet: == : Also presented as == The can also be specified as follows: If $\phi$ is a property (with parameter $p$), then for any $X$ and $p$ there exists a set: $Y = \paren {u \in X: \map \phi {u, p} }$ that contains all those $u \in X$ that have the property $\phi$. $\forall X: \forall p: \exists Y: \forall u: \paren {u \in Y \iff \paren {u \in X \land \map \phi {u, p} } }$

label: Axiom:Axiom of Swelledness
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. $V$ is a swelled class. That is, every subclass of a set which is an element of $V$ is a set in $V$. Briefly: Every subclass of a set is a set.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Transitivity
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. $V$ is a transitive class. That is, every set $S$ which is an element of $V$ is a subclass of $V$. Briefly: Every set is a class.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Triangle Existence
snippet: Let $\equiv$ be the relation of equidistance. Let $\mathsf{B}$ be the relation of betweenness. Then the following axiom holds: $\forall a,a',b,b',c',p: ab \equiv a'b' \implies$ $\exists c,x: \left({ac \equiv a'c' \land bc \equiv b'c' \land \mathsf{B}cxp}\right) \land \left({\mathsf{B}abx \lor \mathsf{B}bxa \lor \mathsf{B}xab}\right)$ where $a, b, c, a', b', c', x, p$ are points.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Union
snippet: Let $x$ and $y$ be sets. Then their union $x \cup y$ is a set.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Unions/Class Theory
snippet: Let $x$ be a set (of sets). Then its union $\bigcup x$ is also a set.

label: Axiom:Axiom of Unions/Set Theoretical and Class Theoretical
snippet: == Axiom of Unions: Difference between Formulations == Recall the two formulations of the axiom of unions:

label: Axiom:Axiom of Unions/Set Theory
snippet: For every set of sets $A$, there exists a set $x$ (the union set) that contains all and only those elements that belong to at least one of the sets in the $A$: $\forall A: \exists x: \forall y: \paren {y \in x \iff \exists z: \paren {z \in A \land y \in z} }$

label: Axiom:Axiom of the Empty Set
snippet: The posits the existence of a set which has no elements. Depending on whether this axiom is declared in the context of set theory or class theory, it exists in different forms.

label: Axiom:Axiom of the Empty Set/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. The empty class $\O$ is a set, that is: $\O \in V$

label: Axiom:Axiom of the Empty Set/Set Theory
snippet: There exists a set that has no elements:

label: Axiom:Axiom of the Empty Set/Set Theory/Formulation 1
snippet: There exists a set that has no elements: $\exists x: \forall y \in x: y \ne y$

label: Axiom:Axiom of the Empty Set/Set Theory/Formulation 2
snippet: There exists a set that has no elements: $\exists x: \forall y: \paren {\neg \paren {y \in x} }$

label: Axiom:Five-Segment Axiom
snippet: Let $\equiv$ be the relation of equidistance. Let $\mathsf B$ be the relation of betweenness. Let $=$ be the relation of equality. This axiom asserts that: $\forall a, b, c, d, a', b', c', d':$ $\paren {\neg \paren {a = b} \land \paren {\mathsf B a b c \land \mathsf B a' b' c'} \land \paren {a b \equiv a' b' \land b c \equiv b' c' \land a d \equiv a' d' \land b d \equiv b' d'} }$ $\implies c d \equiv c' d'$ where $a, b, c, d, a', b', c', d'$ are points.

label: Axiom:Group Axioms/Also known as
snippet: == Group Axioms: Also known as == The group axioms are also known as the group postulates, but the latter term is less indicative of the nature of these statements. The numbering of the group axioms themselves is to a certain extent arbitrary. For example, some sources do not include $\text G 0$ on the grounds that it is taken for granted that $\circ$ is closed in $G$. However, in the treatment of more abstract aspects of group theory it is recommended that this axiom be taken into account.

label: Axiom:Gödel-Bernays Axioms
snippet: The Gödel-Bernays axioms are a conservative extension of the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms with the (ZFC) that allow comprehension of classes. Although not the standard axioms of set theory, particularly in category theory, they spare us any paradoxes of the Russell's Paradox type.

label: Axiom:Hilbert's Axioms
snippet: Hilbert's Axioms are a series of axioms whose purpose is to provide a rigorous basis for the definition of Euclidean geometry. In the following the primitive objects are: points (denoted by $A, B, C \ldots$) lines (denoted by $a, b, c \ldots$) planes (denoted by $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \ldots$) the composite objects are segment ray angle the primitive relations are: distinct (binary)(defined for all objects) betweenness (ternary)(point between two other points) lies on (binary)(point lies on line, point lies on ray, segment lies on line) congruence (binary)(defined for segments and angles).

snippet: Let $\equiv$ be the relation of equidistance. Let $\mathsf{B}$ be the relation of betweenness. label: Axiom:Parallel Postulate
snippet: If two straight lines are drawn which intersect a third in such a way that the sum of the measures of the two interior angles on one side is less than the sum of the measures of two right angles, then the two lines must intersect each other on that side if extended far enough.

label: Axiom:Pasch's Axiom (Euclidean Geometry)
snippet: Let a triangle and a straight line lie in the same plane such that the line does not go through any of the vertices of the triangle. Then if the line intersects one side of the triangle, it intersects another. 600px That is, such a straight line intersects two of the triangle's sides or none.

label: Axiom:Playfair's Axiom
snippet: Exactly one straight line can be drawn through an arbitrary point not on a given line parallel to the given straight line in a plane. Or: Given any straight line and a point not on it, there exists one and only one line which passes through this point and does not intersect the first line no matter how far they are extended. This unique line is defined as being parallel to the original line in question. Or: Two straight lines which intersect one another cannot both be parallel to one and the same straight line.

label: Axiom:Playfair's Axiom/Also known as
snippet: == Playfair's Axiom: Also known as == Playfair's Axiom is often referred to as Euclid's fifth postulate. However, it bears noting that while they are equivalent, these two formulations differ in structure.

label: Axiom:Playfair's Axiom/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Playfair's Axiom == Playfair's axiom was not actually originated by . He merely published it. However, when he did so, he credited others, specifically , for having used it earlier. It is a frequently seen alternative presentation of Euclid's Fifth Postulate. It can easily seen to be equivalent to that given by , and it can be argued that it is easier to understand. Texts on analytic geometry often gloss over its intrinsic significance, merely deducing it from the general equation of a straight line and the point of intersection of two such.

label: Axiom:Propositions of Incidence
snippet: == Axioms == The propositions of incidence are basic properties of projective geometry which are accepted as true. It is possible to derive these propositions from the basics of linear algebra.

label: Axiom:Propositions of Incidence/Line
snippet: A (straight) line contains an infinite number of is points, and is completely determined by any two distinct points of that line. Thus, if a line determined by points $A$ and $B$ also contains the points $X$ and $Y$, then the line determined by points $X$ and $Y$ is the same line, and also contains the points $A$ and $B$.

label: Axiom:Propositions of Incidence/Line in Plane
snippet: A line defined by any two distinct points in a plane lies entirely within that plane.

label: Axiom:Propositions of Incidence/Plane
snippet: A plane consists of an infinite number of points, and is completely determined by any three distinct points of that plane which are not collinear.

label: Axiom:Propositions of Incidence/Plane and Line
snippet: A plane and a (straight) line which does not lie in that plane have exactly one point in common. That is, a point is completely determined by any two of the infinite number of distinct (straight) lines which intersect at that point.

label: Axiom:Propositions of Incidence/Point
snippet: Any two distinct (straight) lines lying in a plane have exactly one point in common. That is, a point is completely determined by any two of the infinite number of distinct (straight) lines which intersect at that point.

label: Axiom:Propositions of Incidence/Space
snippet: A (three-dimensional) space is completely determined by any four distinct points of that space which are not coplanar.

snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\Sigma$ be a system of subsets over $X$.

label: Axiom:Sigma-Algebra Axioms/Formulation 1
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\Sigma$ be a system of subsets over $X$. $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-algebra over $X$ the following axioms are satisfied: {{axiom | n = \text {SA 1} | lc= Unit: | m = X \in \Sigma }} {{axiom | n = \text {SA 2} | lc= Closure under Complement: | q = \forall A \in \Sigma | m = \relcomp X A \in \Sigma }} {{axiom | n = \text {SA 3} | lc= Closure under Countable Unions: | q = \forall A_n \in \Sigma: n = 1, 2, \ldots | m = \bigcup_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty A_n \in \Sigma }} These criteria are called the $\sigma$-algebra axioms.

label: Axiom:Sigma-Ring Axioms/Formulation 1

label: Axiom:Sigma-Ring Axioms/Formulation 2
snippet: Let $\Sigma$ be a system of sets. $\Sigma$ is a $\sigma$-ring the following axioms are satisfied: {{axiom | n = \text {SR} 1' | lc= Empty Set: | m = \O \in \Sigma }} {{axiom | n = \text {SR} 2' | lc= Closure under Set Difference: | q = \forall A, B \in \Sigma | m = A \setminus B \in \Sigma }} {{axiom | n = \text {SR} 3' | lc= Closure under Countable Disjoint Unions: | q = \forall A_n \in \Sigma: n = 1, 2, \ldots | m = \bigsqcup_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty A_n \in \Sigma }} These criteria are called the $\sigma$-ring axioms.

label: Axiom:Strict Ordering Axioms/Formulation 2
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. $\RR$ is a strict ordering on $S$ $\RR$ satisfies the axioms: {{axiom | n = 1 | lc= Antireflexivity | q = \forall a \in S | m = \neg \paren {a \mathrel \RR a} }} {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= Transitivity | q = \forall a, b, c \in S | m = \paren {a \mathrel \RR b} \land \paren {b \mathrel \RR c} \implies a \mathrel \RR c }} These criteria are called the strict ordering axioms.

snippet: == Axioms == The Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel axioms are a basis for axiomatic set theory. By convention, a variable denoting a class is written as an uppercase letter, and a variable denoting a set is written as a lowercase letter. label: Axiom:Zermelo-Fraenkel Axioms
snippet: == Axioms == The Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms are the most well-known basis for axiomatic set theory. There is no standard numbering for them, and their exact formulation varies. Certain of these axioms can in fact be derived from other axioms, so their status as "axioms" can be questioned. The axioms are as follows:

label: Axiom of Archimedes
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number. Then there exists a natural number greater than $x$. $\forall x \in \R: \exists n \in \N: n > x$ That is, the set of natural numbers is unbounded above.

snippet: The axiom of choice implies the axiom of dependent choice.

snippet: The axiom of dependent choice implies the axiom of countable choice.

label: Axiom of Subsets Equivalents
snippet: The Axiom of Specification states that: $\forall z: \forall \map P y: \exists x: \forall y: \paren {y \in x \iff \paren {y \in z \land \map P y} }$ We will prove that this statement is equivalent to the following statements: $\forall z: \forall A: \paren {\paren {z \cap A} \in U}$ $\forall z: \forall A: \paren {A \subseteq z \implies A \in U}$ In the above statements, the universe is $U$.

label: Axiomatize all of Physics
snippet: == Hilbert $23$: Problem $6$ == Mathematical treatment of the axioms of physics: $(1): \quad$ An axiomatic treatment of probability with limit theorems for foundation of statistical physics $(2): \quad$ The rigorous theory of limiting processes "which lead from the atomistic view to the laws of motion of continua".

label: B-Algebra Power Law with Zero
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \circ}$ be a $B$-algebra. Let $n, m \in \N_{>0}$ such that $n > m$. Then: $\forall x \in X: n, m \in \N_{>0} \implies x^m \circ x^n = 0 \circ x^{n - m}$ where $x^k$ for $k \in \N_{>0}$ denotes the $k$th power of the element $x$.

label: Babbage's Congruence
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $a, b \in \Z$ be integers. Then: $\dbinom {a p} {b p} \equiv \dbinom a b \pmod {p^2}$ where $\dbinom a b$ denotes a binomial coefficient.

label: Babczyński Theorem
snippet: Let $n$ be a $6$-digit integer of the form $\sqbrk {xyxyxy}$ for digits $x$ and $y$. Then $n$ is divisible by $3$, $7$, $13$ and $37$.

label: Backward Path of Well-Ordering is Finite
snippet: Let $A$ be a class under a well-ordering $\preccurlyeq$. Let $S$ be a backward path of $\preccurlyeq$ in $A$. Then $S$ is finite.

label: Baer's Criterion
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $M$ be a left $R$-module. Then $M$ is injective the following condition holds: For all left ideals $I$ of $R$ with inclusion map $\iota : I \to R$, and for all $R$-module homomorphisms $f : I \to M$, there exists an $R$-module homomorphism $\tilde f : R \to M$ such that: $\tilde f \circ \iota = f$

label: Baire-Osgood Theorem
snippet: Let $X$ be a Baire space. Let $Y$ be a metrizable topological space Let $f: X \to Y$ be a mapping which is the pointwise limit of a sequence $\sequence {f_n}$ in $\map C {X, Y}$. {{explain|$\map C {X, Y}$}} Let $\map D f$ be the set of points where $f$ is discontinuous. Then $\map D f$ is a meager subset of $X$.

label: Baire Category Theorem
snippet: The Baire Category Theorem consists of two statements, each of which is independent of the other:

label: Baire Characterisation Theorem
snippet: A real-valued function $f$ defined on a Banach space $X$ is a Baire-$1$ function : for every non-empty closed subset $K$ of $X$, the restriction of $f$ to $K$ has a point of continuity relative to the topology of $K$.

label: Baire Space iff Open Sets are Non-Meager
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Then $T$ is a Baire space every non-empty open set of $T$ is non-meager in $T$.

label: Baire Space is Non-Meager
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a Baire space (in the context of topology). Then $T$ is non-meager in $T$.

label: Balanced Hull is Intersection of Balanced Sets containing Set
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $A \subseteq X$ be a non-empty set. Let $\map {\operatorname {bal} } A$ be the balanced hull of $A$. Then: $\ds \map {\operatorname {bal} } A = \bigcap \set {B \supseteq A: B \text { is balanced} }$

label: Balanced Set in Vector Space is Symmetric
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $C \subseteq X$ be a balanced set. Then $C$ is symmetric.

label: Balanced Subset of Complex Plane is Bounded or Entire Space
snippet: Consider $\C$ as a vector space over $\C$. Let $E$ be a balanced subset of $\C$. Then $E$ is bounded, or $E = \C$.

label: Balanced Subset of Real Numbers is Bounded or Entire Space
snippet: Consider $\R$ as a vector space over $\R$. Let $E$ be a balanced subset of $\R$. Then $E$ is bounded, or $E = \R$.

label: Banach-Alaoglu Theorem
snippet: Let $X$ be a separable normed vector space. Then the closed unit ball in its normed dual $X^*$ is sequentially compact with respect to the weak-$\ast$ topology.

label: Banach-Dieudonné Theorem
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Let $B_{X^\ast}^-$ be the closed unit ball in $X^\ast$. Let $w^\ast$ be the weak-$\ast$ topology in $X^\ast$. Let $A$ be a convex set in $X^\ast$ such that: $A \cap n B_{X^\ast}^-$ is $w^\ast$-closed for each $n \in \N$. Then $A$ is $w^\ast$-closed.

label: Banach-Schauder Theorem
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \norm \cdot_Y}$ be Banach spaces. Let $T : X \to Y$ be a surjective bounded linear transformation. Then $T$ is an open mapping.

label: Banach-Tarski Paradox
snippet: Let $\mathbb D^3 \subset \R^3$ be a unit ball in real Euclidean space of $3$ dimensions. Then $\mathbb D^3$ is equidecomposable to the union of two such unit balls.

label: Banach Algebra of Continuous Functions on Compact Hausdorff Space is Banach Algebra
snippet: Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space. Let $\map \CC X = \map \CC {X, \C}$ be the vector space of continuous functions on $X$. Let $\ast$ be pointwise multiplication on $\C^X$. Let $\norm {\, \cdot \,}_\infty$ be the supremum norm on $\map \CC X$. Then $\struct {\map \CC X, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ is a Banach algebra.

snippet:
Let $\mathbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot}$ be a non-trivial Banach algebra over $\mathbb F$. Suppose that $X$ has an identity element $\mathbf 1_X$. Then there exists a norm $
orm \cdot '$ on $X$ equivalent to $
orm \cdot$ such that $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot '}$ is a unital Banach algebra. That is: $(1): \quad
orm \cdot$ and $
orm \cdot '$ are equivalent $(2): \quad\struct {X, 
orm \cdot '}$ is a Banach algebra $(3): \quad
orm {\mathbf 1_X}' = 1$

label: Banach Fixed-Point Theorem
snippet: Let $\struct {M, d}$ be a complete metric space. Let $f: M \to M$ be a contraction. That is, there exists $q \in \hointr 0 1$ such that for all $x, y \in M$: $\map d {\map f x, \map f y} \le q \, \map d {x, y}$ Then there exists a unique fixed point of $f$.

label: Banach Isomorphism Theorem
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \norm \cdot_Y}$ be Banach spaces. Let $T : X \to Y$ be a bijective bounded linear transformation. Then the inverse of $T$ is a bounded linear transformation. That is, $T$ is a normed vector space isomorphism.

label: Banach Space-Valued Function Constant on each Set in Countable Partition of Domain is Bochner Measurable
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $\sequence {\Omega_n'}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of Lebesgue measurable subsets of $I$ such that: $\ds \bigcup_{n \mathop \in \N} \Omega_n' = I$ Let $f : I \to X$ be a function that is constant on each $\Omega_n'$. Then $f$ is Bochner measurable.

label: Banach Space-Valued Simple Function has Standard Representation
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a simple function. Then $f$ is a simple function there exists: disjoint Lebesgue measurable sets $\Omega_1, \ldots, \Omega_n \subseteq I$ of finite Lebesgue measure $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in X$ such that: $\ds \map f t = \sum_{r \mathop = 1}^n x_r \map {\chi_{\Omega_r} } t$ for each $t \in I$.

label: Banach Space-Valued Simple Function is Bochner Measurable
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $f : I \to X$ be a simple function. Then $f$ is Bochner measurable.

label: Banach Space-Valued Simple Function takes Finitely Many Values
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a simple function. Then $\Img f$ is a finite set.

label: Banach Space Valued Function is Analytic iff Weakly Analytic
snippet: Let $U$ be an open set of $\C$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a Banach space over $\C$. Let $f : U \to X$ be a function. Then $f$ is analytic it is weakly analytic.

label: Banach Space is Reflexive iff Normed Dual is Reflexive
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\Bbb F$. Let $X^\ast$ be the normed dual space of $X$. Then: $X$ is reflexive $X^\ast$ is reflexive.

label: Banach Space with Schur Property is Weakly Sequentially Complete
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space with the Schur property. Then $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ is weakly sequentially complete.

label: Banach Space with Weak Topology has Countable Tightness
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $w$ be the weak topology on $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Then $\struct {X, w}$ has countable tightness.

label: Barlow's Prediction
snippet: == Prediction == ascertained that $2^{31} - 1 = 2147483647$ is a prime number; and this is the greatest at present known to be such, and, consequently, the last of the above perfect numbers [that is, $2^{30}\left({2^{31} - 1}\right)$], which depends upon this, is the greatest perfect number known at present, and probably the greatest that ever will be discovered; for, as they are merely curious without being useful, it is not likely that any person will attempt to find one beyond it. label: Barycentric Coordinates are Unique iff Vertices are Affinely Independent
snippet: Let $V = \tuple {v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_k}$ be a set of $k + 1$ vertices in $\mathbb R^k$. Let $x$ be any point in $\mathbb R^k$. Let $\tuple {\lambda_0, \lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_k}$ be the barycentric coordinates of $x$ the vertices. Then the barycentric coordinates are unique $V$ is affinely independent.

label: Barycentric Coordinates of Centroid of Triangle
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ be the position vectors of the $3$ vertices of a triangle $T$ in the plane. Let $p$ be the centroid of $T$. Let $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ be the barycentric coordinates of $p$ $T$ Then: $\alpha = \beta = \gamma = \dfrac 1 3$

label: Barycentric Coordinates of Point inside Triangle
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ be the position vectors of the $3$ vertices of a triangle $T$ in the plane. Let $p$ be an arbitrary point inside $T$. Then the barycentric coordinates of $p$ $T$ are all positive.

label: Basel Problem
snippet: $\ds \map \zeta 2 = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty {\frac 1 {n^2} } = \frac {\pi^2} 6$ where $\zeta$ denotes the Riemann zeta function.

label: Bases of Finitely Generated Vector Space have Equal Cardinality
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $G$ be a finitely generated $K$-vector space. Then any two bases of $G$ are finite and equivalent.

label: Bases of Free Module have Equal Cardinality
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be a free $R$-module. Let $B$ and $C$ be bases of $M$. Then $B$ and $C$ are equivalent. That is, they have the same cardinality.

label: Bases of Vector Space have Equal Cardinality
snippet: Let $R$ be a division ring. Let $V$ be a vector space over $R$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be bases of $V$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are equivalent. That is, $X$ and $Y$ have the same cardinality.

label: Basic Separating Hyperplane Theorem
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $A, B \subseteq X$ be disjoint convex sets such that $A$ has an internal point. Let $X^\#$ be the algebraic dual of $X$. Then there exists a linear functional $\hat f \in X^\#$ such that the affine hyperplane $\sqbrk {\hat f = \alpha}$ properly separates $A$ and $B$.

label: Basic Sequence Congruent to Complemented Basic Sequence is Complemented
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be Banach spaces over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a complemented basic sequence. Let $\sequence {y_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a basic sequence in $Y$ that is congruent to $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. Then $\sequence {y_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is complemented in $Y$.

label: Basic Universe has Infinite Number of Elements
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Then $V$ has an infinite number of elements.

snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Then $V$ is not a set.
