label: Definition:Abstract Algebra
snippet: Abstract algebra is a branch of mathematics which studies algebraic structures and algebraic systems. It can be roughly described as the study of sets equipped with operations.

label: Definition:Abstract Algebra/Also known as
snippet: == Abstract Algebra: Also known as == Abstract algebra is also sometimes referred to as modern algebra, particularly in older texts.

label: Definition:Abstract Machine
snippet: An abstract machine is a hypothetical computing machine defined in terms of the operations it performs rather than its internal physical structure.

label: Definition:Abstract Space
snippet: An abstract space is: a set of objects together with: a set of axioms which define operations on and relations between those objects.

label: Definition:Abundance
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. Let $\map {\sigma_1} n$ be the divisor sum function of $n$. That is, let $\map {\sigma_1} n$ be the sum of all positive divisors of $n$. Then the abundance of $n$ is defined as $\map A n = \map {\sigma_1} n - 2 n$.

label: Definition:Abundancy Index
snippet: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Let $\map {\sigma_1} n$ be the divisor sum function of $n$. That is, let $\map {\sigma_1} n$ be the sum of all positive divisors of $n$. Then the abundancy index of $n$ is defined as $\dfrac {\map {\sigma_1} n} n$.

label: Definition:Abundant Number
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer.

label: Definition:Abuse of Notation
snippet: Mathematical notation can be considered in two ways: As an aid to mathematical understanding, no more and no less than a useful convention to encapsulate more or less complicated ideas in a completely unambiguous format; As the reason for mathematical effort, so as to encapsulate a truth as a documented piece of aesthetic beauty in its own right. Abuse of notation is a technique of using a system of symbology in a way different from that for which it was originally defined.

label: Definition:Acceleration
snippet: The acceleration $\mathbf a$ of a body $M$ is defined as the first derivative of the velocity $\mathbf v$ of $M$ relative to a given point of reference time $t$: $\mathbf a = \dfrac {\d \mathbf v} {\d t}$ Colloquially, it is described as the rate of change of velocity. It is important to note that as velocity is a vector quantity, then it follows by definition of derivative of a vector that so is acceleration.

label: Definition:Acceleration (Continuum Mechanics)
snippet: In the context of continuum mechanics, the acceleration of a point $P$ in a body $B$ is the material derivative of the velocity of $P$ evaluated at $P$.

label: Definition:Acceptance Region
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some population $P$. Let $\Omega$ be the parameter space of $\theta$. Let $\mathbf X$ be a random sample from $P$. Let $T = \map f {\mathbf X}$ be a sample statistic. Let $\delta$ be a hypothesis test of the form: accept $H_0$ if $T \in A$ for some null hypothesis $H_0$ and some $A \subset \Omega$. We refer to $A$ as the acceptance region of $\delta$.

label: Definition:Accounting
snippet: Accounting is the branch of mathematics concerned with processing of information about economic entities, such as businesses and corporations.

label: Definition:Accumulation Point
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Accumulation Point/Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence in $A$. Let $x \in S$. Then $x \in S$ is an accumulation point of $\sequence {x_n}$ : $\forall U \in \tau: x \in U \implies \set {n \in \N: x_n \in U}$ is infinite

label: Definition:Accumulation Point/Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. Let $x \in S$. Then $x$ is an accumulation point of $A$ : $x \in \map \cl {A \setminus \set x}$ where $\cl$ denotes the (topological) closure of a set.

label: Definition:Accuracy
snippet: Accuracy is a measure of how closely a reported number matches the true value of that number.

label: Definition:Accuracy/Decimal Places
snippet: A representation $y$ in decimal notation of a number $x$ is: accurate to $n$ decimal places the number $n$ of digits after the decimal point of $x$ match the first $n$ digits after the decimal point of $y$, without rounding.

label: Definition:Accuracy/Significant Figures
snippet: A representation $y$ in decimal notation of a number $x$ is accurate to $n$ significant figures the first $n$ digits of $x$ match, after rounding, the first $n$ digits of $y$. In this context it is usual for $y$ to be expressed only by $n$ digits.

label: Definition:Ackermann-Péter Function
snippet: The Ackermann-Péter function $A: \Z_{\ge 0} \times \Z_{\ge 0} \to \Z_{> 0}$ is an integer-valued function defined on the set of ordered pairs of positive integers as: $\map A {m, n} = \begin{cases} n + 1 & : m = 0 \\ \map A {m - 1, 1} & : m > 0, n = 0 \\ \map A {m - 1, \map A {m, n - 1} } & : \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$

label: Definition:Acnode/Also known as
snippet: == Acnode: Also known as == An acnode is also known as an isolated point, but the latter term has a wider application in the field of topology, of which the acnode is an example.

label: Definition:Acoustics
snippet: Acoustics is the branch of physics which studies the properties of sound.

label: Definition:Action (Dynamics)
snippet: The action for a given segment from point $A$ to point $B$ on the trajectory of a dynamical system is defined by the line integral: $\ds \sum_i \int_A^B p_i \rd q_i$ where: $q_i$ are the generalized coordinates $p_i$ are the generalized momenta.

label: Definition:Acute Angle
snippet: An acute angle is an angle which has a measure between that of a right angle and that of a zero angle.

label: Definition:Acyclic
snippet: Category Theory: Acyclic Object Acyclic Resolution Graph Theory: Acyclic Graph Topology: Acyclic Sheaf

label: Definition:Acyclic Graph
snippet: An acyclic graph is a graph or digraph with no cycles.

label: Definition:Acyclic Object
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an abelian category with enough injectives. Let $\mathbf B$ be an abelian category. Let $F : \mathbf A \to \mathbf B$ be a left exact functor. Let $X$ be an object of $\mathbf A$. Then $X$ is $F$-acyclic $\mathrm R^i \map F X = 0$ for all positive integers $i \in \Z_{i \mathop \ge 1}$. In the above $\mathrm R^i F$ denotes the $i$-th right derived functor of $F$. Category:Definitions/Homological Algebra

label: Definition:Acyclic Resolution
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an abelian category with enough injectives. Let $\mathbf B$ be an arbitrary abelian category. Let $F : \mathbf A \to \mathbf B$ be a left-exact functor. Let $X$ be an object in $\mathbf A$. An $F$-acyclic resolution of $X$ is a cochain complex $P := \family {d^i : I^i \to I^{i + 1} }_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ in $\mathbf A$, such that: $(1): \quad \forall i $\begin{xy} \xymatrix{ \dots \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & X \ar[r]^{\varepsilon} & I^0 \ar[r]^{d^0} & I^1 \ar[r]^{d^1} & I^2 \ar[r]^{d^2} & \dots } \end{xy}$ is exact.

label: Definition:Acyclic Sheaf
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be an abelian sheaf on $X$. Let $\map \Gamma {X, -} : \map {\mathbf {Ab} } X \to \mathbf {Ab}$ be the global sections functor on $X$. Then $\FF$ is acyclic $\FF$ is $\map \Gamma {X, -}$-acyclic in the category of abelian sheaves $\map {\mathbf {Ab} } X$ on $X$.

label: Definition:Adapted Stochastic Process/Discrete Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is an (discrete-time) adapted stochastic process : $X_n$ is $\FF_n$-measurable random variable for each $n \in \N$.

label: Definition:Adapted Stochastic Process at Stopping Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}, \Pr}$ be a filtered probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \ge 0}$ be an $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}$-adapted stochastic process. Let $T$ be a stopping time with respect to $\sequence {\FF_n}_{n \ge 0}$. We define the random variable $X_T$ by: $\map {X_T} \omega = \map {X_{\map T \omega} } \omega \map {\chi_{\set {\omega \in \Omega : \map T \omega < \infty} } } \omega$ That is: $\map {X_T} \omega = \begin{cases} \map {X_{\map T \omega} } \omega & : \map T \omega < \infty \\ 0 &: \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$

label: Definition:Adaptive Quadrature
snippet: Adaptive quadrature is a numerical integration algorithm for evaluating definite integrals of an integrand $f$ where the points at which $f$ are evaluated are chosen adaptively. Hence if $f$ changes rapidly around a point $x$ in the interval of integration, the algorithm chooses small subintervals near $x$. However, if $f$ changes slowly, the algorithm chooses larger subintervals near $x$.

label: Definition:Addition
snippet: Addition is the basic operation $+$ everyone is familiar with. For example: $2 + 3 = 5$ $47 \cdotp 3 + 191\cdotp 4 = 238 \cdotp 7$

label: Definition:Addition/Complex Numbers
snippet: The addition operation in the domain of complex numbers $\C$ is written $+$. Let $z = a + i b, w = c + i d$ where $a, b, c, d \in \R, i^2 = -1$. Then $z + w$ is defined as: $\paren {a + i b} + \paren {c + i d} = \paren {a + c} + i \paren {b + d}$

label: Definition:Addition/Integers
snippet: The addition operation in the domain of integers $\Z$ is written $+$. We have that the set of integers is the Inverse Completion of Natural Numbers. Thus it follows that elements of $\Z$ are the isomorphic images of the elements of equivalence classes of $\N \times \N$ where two tuples are equivalent if the difference between the two elements of each tuple is the same. Thus addition can be formally defined on $\Z$ as the operation induced on those equivalence classes as specified in the definition of integers.

label: Definition:Addition/Rational Numbers
snippet: The addition operation in the domain of rational numbers $\Q$ is written $+$. Let: $a = \dfrac p q, b = \dfrac r s$ where: $p, q \in \Z$ $r, s \in \Z_{\ne 0}$ Then $a + b$ is defined as: $\dfrac p q + \dfrac r s = \dfrac {p s + r q} {q s}$ This definition follows from the definition of and proof of existence of the field of quotients of any integral domain, of which the set of integers is an example.

label: Definition:Addition/Real Modulo Addition
snippet: Let $z \in \R$. Let $\R_z$ be the set of residue classes modulo $z$ of $\R$. The addition operation is defined on $\R_z$ as follows: $\eqclass a z +_z \eqclass b z = \eqclass {a + b} z$ This operation is called addition modulo $z$.

label: Definition:Addition/Real Numbers
snippet: The addition operation in the domain of real numbers $\R$ is written $+$. From the definition, the real numbers are the set of all equivalence classes $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers. Let $x = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}, y = \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$, where $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ and $\eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$ are such equivalence classes. Then $x + y$ is defined as: $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} + \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n + y_n} } {}$

label: Definition:Addition/Sum
snippet: Let $a + b$ denote the operation of addition on two objects $a$ and $b$. Then the result $a + b$ is referred to as the sum of $a$ and $b$. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

label: Definition:Addition/Summand
snippet: Let $a + b$ denote the operation of addition on two objects. The objects $a$ and $b$ are known as the summands of $a + b$. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

label: Definition:Addition of Cuts
snippet: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be cuts. Let the operation of addition be defined on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ as: $\gamma := \alpha + \beta$ where $\gamma$ is the set of all rational numbers $r$ such that: $\exists p \in \alpha, q \in \beta: r = p + q$ In this context, $\gamma$ is known as the sum of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

label: Definition:Additive Category
snippet: Let $A$ be a preadditive category.

label: Definition:Additive Function
snippet: Analysis: Additive Function (Algebra): $\map f {x + y} = \map f x + \map f y$ Definition:Number Theory: Definition:Additive Arithmetic Function Definition:Additive Function on UFD Definition:Completely Additive Function Definition:Additive Function on Class of Modules In measure theory, the concept has a completely different meaning: Additive Function (Measure Theory): $A \cap B = \O \implies \map f {A \cup B} = \map f A + \map f B$ In this context, also see Sigma-Additive Function.

label: Definition:Additive Function (Measure Theory)
snippet: Let $\SS$ be an algebra of sets. Let $f: \SS \to \overline \R$ be a function, where $\overline \R$ denotes the set of extended real numbers. Then $f$ is defined to be an additive function : $\forall S, T \in \SS: S \cap T = \O \implies \map f {S \cup T} = \map f S + \map f T$ That is, for any two disjoint elements of $\SS$, $f$ of their union equals the sum of $f$ of the individual elements.

label: Definition:Additive Function on Class of Modules
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\CC$ be a class of $R$-modules. Let $G$ be an abelian group. Let $\lambda : \CC \to G$ be a mapping. Then $\lambda$ is called an additive function : for all $M' ', M, M' \in \CC$: $0 \to M' ' \to M \to M' \to 0$ is a short exact sequence $\implies \map \lambda {M' '} - \map \lambda M + \map \lambda {M'} = 0$

label: Definition:Additive Group/Also defined as
snippet: == Additive Group: Also defined as == Some sources make special issue of the nature of a group when its underlying set is a subset of, or derived directly from, numbers themselves. In such treatments, a group whose operation is addition is then referred to as an additive group. On we consider all groups, whatever their nature, to be instances of the same abstract concept, and therefore make no such distinction.

label: Definition:Additive Group of Complex Numbers
snippet: The additive group of complex numbers $\struct {\C, +}$ is the set of complex numbers under the operation of addition.

label: Definition:Additive Group of Integers
snippet: The additive group of integers $\struct {\Z, +}$ is the set of integers under the operation of addition. Thus integer addition is: Well-defined on $\Z$ Closed on $\Z$ Associative on $\Z$ Commutative on $\Z$ The identity of $\struct {\Z, +}$ is $0$ Each element of $\struct {\Z, +}$ has an inverse.

label: Definition:Additive Group of Integers Modulo 4
snippet: The additive group of integers modulo $4$ $\struct {\Z_4, +_4}$ is the set of integers modulo $4$ under the operation of addition modulo $4$.

label: Definition:Additive Group of Integers Modulo m
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ such that $m > 1$. The additive group of integers modulo $m$, denoted $\struct {\Z_m, +_m}$, is the set of integers modulo $m$ under the operation of addition modulo $m$.

label: Definition:Additive Group of Integers Modulo m/Also denoted as
snippet: == Additive Group of Integers Modulo $m$: Also denoted as == The additive group of integers modulo $m$ is denoted by some sources as $\struct {\N_m, +_m}$. Hence this defines the underlying set as a subset of the natural numbers rather than the integers: $\N_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ As can be seen, $\Z_m$ and $\N_m$ are the same thing. Category:Definitions/Additive Groups of Integers Modulo m

label: Definition:Additive Group of Rational Numbers
snippet: The additive group of rational numbers $\struct {\Q, +}$ is the set of rational numbers under the operation of addition.

label: Definition:Additive Group of Real Numbers
snippet: The additive group of real numbers $\struct {\R, +}$ is the set of real numbers under the operation of addition.

label: Definition:Additive Inverse/Also defined as
snippet: == Additive Inverse: Also defined as == Some sources make special issue of the nature of a group when its underlying set is a subset of, or derived directly from, numbers themselves. In such treatments, the inverses of a group whose operation is addition are then referred to as additive inverses. On we consider all groups, whatever their nature, to be instances of the same abstract concept, and therefore make no such distinction.

label: Definition:Additive Inverse/Field
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a field whose addition operation is $+$. Let $a \in R$ be any arbitrary element of $F$. The additive inverse of $a$ is its inverse under addition, denoted $-a$: $a + \paren {-a} = 0_F$ where $0_F$ is the zero of $R$.

label: Definition:Additive Inverse/Number
snippet: Let $\Bbb F$ be one of the standard number systems: $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$, $\C$. Let $a \in \Bbb F$ be any arbitrary number. The additive inverse of $a$ is its inverse under addition, denoted $-a$: $a + \paren {-a} = 0$

label: Definition:Additive Inverse/Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring whose ring addition operation is $+$. Let $a \in R$ be any arbitrary element of $R$. The additive inverse of $a$ is its inverse under ring addition, denoted $-a$: $a + \paren {-a} = 0_R$ where $0_R$ is the zero of $R$.

label: Definition:Additive Monoid of Natural Numbers
snippet: The additive monoid of natural numbers $\left({\N, +}\right)$ is the set of natural numbers under the operation of addition.

label: Definition:Additive Notation
snippet: Additive notation is a convention often used for representing a commutative binary operation of an algebraic structure. The symbol used for the operation is $+$. Let $\struct {S, +}$ be such an algebraic structure, and let $x, y \in S$. $x + y$ is used to indicate the result of the operation $+$ on $x$ and $y$. $e$ or $0$ is used for the identity element. Note that in this context, $0$ is not a zero element. $-x$ is used for the inverse element. $n x$ is used to indicate the $n$th power of $x$. This notation is usual in group theory when discussing a general abelian group.

label: Definition:Adherent Point/Filter
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a filter on $\struct {X, \tau}$. Let $\cl$ be closure taken in $\struct {X, \tau}$. We say that $x$ is an adherent point of $\FF$ : $\ds x \in \bigcap \set {\map \cl F : F \in \FF}$

label: Definition:Adherent Point of Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Adherent Point of Set/Definition by Closure
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. A point $x \in S$ is an adherent point of $H$ $x$ is an element of the closure of $H$.

label: Definition:Adherent Point of Set/Definition by Neighborhood
snippet: Let $T = \struct{S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. A point $x \in S$ is an adherent point of $H$ every neighborhood $N$ of $x$ satisfies: $H \cap N \ne \O$

label: Definition:Adherent Point of Set/Definition by Open Neighborhood
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. A point $x \in S$ is an adherent point of $H$ every open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ satisfies: $H \cap U \ne \O$

label: Definition:Adjacency Matrix
snippet: An adjacency matrix is a matrix which describes a graph by representing which vertices are adjacent to which other vertices. The adjacency matrix of a graph $G$ of order $n$ is a square matrix of order $n$, where each row and column corresponds to a vertex of $G$. The element $a_{i j}$ of such a matrix specifies the number of edges from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$. An adjacency matrix for a simple graph and a loop-digraph is a logical matrix, that is, one whose elements are all either $0$ or $1$. An adjacency matrix for an undirected graph is symmetrical about the main diagonal.

label: Definition:Adjacent
snippet: Adjacent (Graph Theory): Two vertices are said to be adjacent there exists an edge to which they are both incident. Two edges are said to be adjacent there exists an vertex to which they are both incident. Two faces of a planar graph are said to be adjacent or neighboring there exists an edge to which they are both incident. Adjacent (Geometry): Two angles are adjacent they share a line. Similarly: Adjacent in Polygons: The two sides of a polygon that form a particular vertex are adjacent to that vertex. The two vertices of a polygon that terminate a particular side are adjacent to that side.

label: Definition:Adjacent (Graph Theory)/Faces
snippet: 220px Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a planar graph. Two faces of $G$ are adjacent they are both incident to the same edge (or edges). In the above diagram, $BCEF$ and $ABF$ are adjacent, but $BCEF$ and $AFG$ are not adjacent. Note that faces which are both incident to the same vertex are not considered adjacent unless they are also both incident to the same edge.

label: Definition:Adjacent Faces
snippet: Graph Theory: Adjacent Faces of Graph: Two faces of a planar graph are said to be adjacent or neighboring there exists an edge to which they are both incident. Solid Geometry: Adjacent Faces of Polyhedron: Two faces of a polyhedron that meet at the same vertex are adjacent to each other.

label: Definition:Adjacent Sides/Also known as
snippet: == Adjacent Sides: Also known as == Adjacent sides (in a polygon) are also known as consecutive sides. Some sources use the term coterminal.

label: Definition:Adjacent Vertices of Polygon/Also known as
snippet: == Adjacent Vertices of Polygon: Also known as == Adjacent vertices (in a polygon) are also known as consecutive vertices or consecutive angles. The term adjacent angles can also be seen, but as this is used for a different concept, it is preferred that it is not used in this context.

label: Definition:Adjoint Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ be locally small categories. Let $F : \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ and $G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be functors. Then $F$ and $G$ are adjoint functors there exists an adjunction $\struct {F, G, \alpha}$. In this case: $F$ is the left adjoint functor of $G$ and: $G$ is the right adjoint functor of $F$.

label: Definition:Adjoint Linear Transformation
snippet: Let $\HH$ and $\KK$ be Hilbert spaces. Let $\map \BB {\HH, \KK}$ be the set of bounded linear transformations from $\HH$ to $\KK$. Let $A \in \map \BB {\HH, \KK}$ be a bounded linear transformation. By Existence and Uniqueness of Adjoint, there exists a unique bounded linear transformation $A^* \in \map \BB {\KK, \HH}$ such that: $\forall h \in \HH, k \in \KK: {\innerprod {\map A h} k}_\KK = {\innerprod h {\map {A^*} k} }_\HH$ where $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_\HH$ and $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_\KK$ are inner products on $\HH$ and $\KK$ respectively. $A^*$ is called the adjoint of $A$.

label: Definition:Adjoint of Densely-Defined Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\Bbb F$. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a densely defined linear operator on $\HH$. For each $y \in \HH$, define the linear functional $f_x : \map D T \to \Bbb F$ by: $\map {f_y} x = \innerprod {T x} y$ for each $x \in \map D T$.

label: Definition:Adjugate Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_n$ be a square matrix of order $n$. Let $\mathbf C$ be its cofactor matrix. The adjugate matrix of $\mathbf A$ is the transpose of $\mathbf C$: $\adj {\mathbf A} = \mathbf C^\intercal$

label: Definition:Adjunction/Adjunct
snippet: Let $\mathbf {Set}$ be the category of sets. Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ be locally small categories. Let $\tuple {F, G, \alpha}$ be an adjunction between $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$. Let $D \in \mathbf D$ and $C \in \mathbf C$ be objects. Let $f : FD \to C \in \mathbf C$ and $g : D \to GC \in \mathbf D$ be morphisms: $g = \map {\alpha_{\tuple{D^\text{op}, C} } } f$ The morphisms $f$ and $g$ are called adjuncts: $g$ is called the right adjunct of $f$. $f$ is called the left adjunct of $g$.

label: Definition:Adjunction/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf {Set}$ be the category of sets. Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ be locally small categories. An adjunction between $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ is a triple $\tuple {F, G, \alpha}$, where $F : \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ is a covariant functor. $G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ is a covariant functor.

label: Definition:Admissible Family of Curves
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I = \closedint a b$ is a closed real interval. Let $J$ is an open real interval. Let $\Gamma : I \times J \to M$ be a one-dimensional family of curves, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product. Let $\tuple {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{n - 1}, a_n}$ be a finite subdivision of $I$ such that for all $i \in \N_{> 0} : i \le n$ the mapping $\Gamma$ is smooth on $J \times \closedint {a_{i - 1}} {a_i}$. Suppose that for all $s \in J$ the mapping $\map {\Gamma_s} t = \map \Gamma {s, t}$ is an admissible curve.

label: Definition:Admissible Subdivision of Family of Curves
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I = \closedint a b$ is a closed real interval. Let $J$ is an open real interval. Let $\Gamma : I \times J \to M$ be a one-dimensional family of curves, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product. Let $\tuple {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{n - 1}, a_n}$ be a finite subdivision of $I$ such that for all $i \in \N_{> 0} : i \le n$ the mapping $\Gamma$ is smooth on $J \times \closedint {a_{i - 1}} {a_i}$. Suppose that for all $s \in J$ the mapping $\map {\Gamma_s} t = \map \Gamma {s, t}$ is an admissible curve.

label: Definition:Aerodynamics
snippet: Aerodynamics is the branch of fluid mechanics concerned with the behaviour of bodies in motion through a gaseous medium, usually air.

label: Definition:Aether (Physics)
snippet: An aether was a hypothetical weightless fluid which was supposed to pervade the whole of the physical universe, including all matter. Its purpose was to attempt to explain the phenomenon of action at a distance.

label: Definition:Aether (Physics)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Aether == The existence of an aether, as a hitherto undetected entity in physics, was still being posited as late as the $20$th century as a medium through which electromagnetic radiation was able to travel. Its existence was disproved by the Michelson-Morley Experiment. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Affine Algebraic Set
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $A = K \sqbrk {X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ be the ring of polynomial functions in $n$ variables over $K$. Then a subset $X \subseteq K^n$ is an affine algebraic set it is the zero locus of some set $T \subseteq A$.

label: Definition:Affine Algebraic Variety
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Let $n \ge 1$ be an Integer.

label: Definition:Affine Algebraic Variety/Definition 1
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Let $n \ge 1$ be an Integer. An affine algebraic set $X \subseteq k^n$ is an affine algebraic variety $X$ is irreducible the Zariski topology.

label: Definition:Affine Algebraic Variety/Definition 2
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Let $n \ge 1$ be an Integer. An affine algebraic set $X \subseteq k^n$ is an affine algebraic variety the associated ideal $\map I X$ is prime.

label: Definition:Affine Functional
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $f : X \to K$ be a linear functional. Let $c \in K$. Define $g : X \to K$ by: $\forall x \in X: \map g x = \map f x + c$ We say that $g$ is an affine functional on $X$.

label: Definition:Affine Geometry
snippet: Affine geometry is the study of the geometry of affine spaces. Hence it is the study of properties and types of geometric figures which are invariant under an affine transformation. It provides a modern axiomatic approach to the study of configurations of lines, planes and hypersurfaces. In particular an affine space can be thought of as a finite dimensional vector space with no distinguished origin, and its affine transformations are those that preserve collinearity. It can be considered as projective geometry which preserves the line at infinity.

label: Definition:Affine Group of One Dimension
snippet: Let $S$ be the set of mappings $f_{a b}: \R \to \R$ defined as: $S := \set {f_{a b}: x \mapsto a x + b: a \in \R_{\ne 0}, b \in \R}$ The algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$, where $\circ$ denotes composition of mappings, is called the $1$-dimensional affine group on $\R$ and can be denoted $\map {\operatorname {Af}_1 } \R$.

label: Definition:Affine Hull
snippet: == Definition == Let $S$ be a set.

label: Definition:Affine Hull/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The affine hull of $S$ is the smallest affine set containing $S$.

label: Definition:Affine Hull/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The affine hull of $S$ is the intersection of all affine sets of which $S$ is a subset.

label: Definition:Affine Hyperplane
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a linear functional. Let $\alpha \in \R$. Define: $\sqbrk {f = \alpha} = \set {x \in X : \map f x = \alpha}$ We say that $\sqbrk {f = \alpha}$ is the affine hyperplane associated with $f$ and $\alpha$.

label: Definition:Affine Hyperplane Separating Two Sets
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a linear functional. Let $\alpha \in \R$. Let $\sqbrk {f = \alpha}$ be the affine hyperplane generated by $f$ and $\alpha$. Let $\sqbrk {f \le \alpha}$ and $\sqbrk {f \ge \alpha}$ be the corresponding weak half-spaces. Let $A, B \subseteq X$. We say that $\sqbrk {f = \alpha}$ separates $A$ and $B$ : $A \subseteq \sqbrk {f \le \alpha}$ and $B \subseteq \sqbrk {f \ge \alpha}$ or: $A \subseteq \sqbrk {f \ge \alpha}$ and $B \subseteq \sqbrk {f \le \alpha}$.

label: Definition:Affine Hyperplane Separating Two Sets/Proper Separation
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a linear functional. Let $\alpha \in \R$. Let $A, B \subseteq X$. Let: $H = \sqbrk {f = \alpha}$ be the affine hyperplane generated by $f$ and $\alpha$. We say that $\sqbrk {f = \alpha}$ properly separates $A$ and $B$ $A \cup B \not \subseteq H$.

label: Definition:Affine Hyperplane Separating Two Sets/Strict Separation
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a linear functional. Let $\alpha \in \R$. Let $\sqbrk {f = \alpha}$ be the affine hyperplane generated by $f$ and $\alpha$. Let $\sqbrk {f \alpha}$ be the corresponding strict half-spaces. Let $A, B \subseteq X$. We say that $\sqbrk {f = \alpha}$ strictly separates $A$ and $B$ : $A \subseteq \sqbrk {f \alpha}$ or: $A \subseteq \sqbrk {f > \alpha}$ and $B \subseteq \sqbrk {f < \alpha}$.

label: Definition:Affine Hyperplane Separating Two Sets/Strong Separation
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a linear functional. Let $\alpha \in \R$. Let $\epsilon > 0$. Let $\sqbrk {f = \alpha}$ be the affine hyperplane generated by $f$ and $\alpha$. Let $\sqbrk {f \le \alpha}$ and $\sqbrk {f \ge \alpha + \epsilon}$ be weak half-spaces generated by $f$. Let $A, B \subseteq X$. We say that $\sqbrk {f = \alpha}$ strong separates $A$ and $B$ : $A \subseteq \sqbrk {f \le \alpha}$ and $B \subseteq \sqbrk {f \ge \alpha + \epsilon}$ or: $A \subseteq \sqbrk {f \ge \alpha + \epsilon}$ and $B \subseteq \sqbrk {f \le \alpha}$.

label: Definition:Affine Monoid
snippet: An affine monoid is a monoid that is: finitely generated and: isomorphic to a submonoid of a free abelian group $\Z^d$, for some $d \in \Z_{\ge 0}$.

label: Definition:Affine Open Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a scheme. Let $U \subset X$ be an open subset. We say, that $U$ is an affine open subset, if the restriction $\struct {U, \OO_X {\restriction U}}$ of $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $U$ is an affine scheme.

label: Definition:Affine Scheme
snippet: An affine scheme is a ringed space which is isomorphic to the spectrum of a commutative ring with unity.

label: Definition:Affine Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The affine set induced by $S$ is the set which contains all the points on the entire straight line through a given pair of elements of $S$.

label: Definition:Affine Space/Associativity Axioms
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\struct {V, +_V, \circ}$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $\EE$ be a set on which two mappings are defined: $+ : \EE \times V \to \EE$ $- : \EE \times \EE \to V$ satisfying the following associativity conditions: {{axiom | n = \text A 1 | q = \forall p, q \in \EE | m = p + \paren {q - p} = q }} {{axiom | n = \text A 2 | q = \forall p \in \EE: \forall u, v \in V | m = \paren {p + u} + v = p + \paren {u +_V v} }} {{axiom | n = \text A 3 | q = \forall p, q \in \EE: \forall u \in V | m = \paren {p - q} +_V u = \paren {p + u} - q }} Then the ordered triple $\struct {\EE, +,…

label: Definition:Affine Space/Group Action
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\struct {V, +_V, \circ}$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $\EE$ be a set. Let $\phi: \EE \times V \to \EE$ be a free and transitive group action of $\struct {V, +_V}$ on $\EE$. Then the ordered pair $\struct {\EE, \phi}$ is an affine space.

label: Definition:Affine Space/Notation
snippet: == Affine Space: Notation == Almost invariably the same symbol (usually $+$) is used for the addition $+_V: V \times V \to V$ in the vector space and the addition $+: \EE \times V \to \EE$ in the affine space. This does not allow any ambiguity as the two mappings have different domains. For elements $p, q \in \EE$, it is common to write $\vec {p q} = q - p$. Category:Definitions/Affine Spaces

label: Definition:Affine Space/Weyl's Axioms
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\struct {V, +_V, \circ}$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $\EE$ be a set on which a mapping is defined: $- : \EE \times \EE \to V$ satisfying the following associativity conditions: {{axiom | n = \text W 2 | q = \forall p, q, r \in \EE | m = \paren {r - q} +_V \paren {q - p} = r - p }} Then the ordered pair $\tuple {\EE, -}$ is an affine space.

label: Definition:Affine Span
snippet: Let $\VV$ be a vector space. Let $\WW$ be a subset of $\VV$. The affine span $\SS$ of $\WW$ is the smallest affine subspace of $\VV$ such that $\WW$ is a subset of $\SS$.

label: Definition:Affine Subspace
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an affine space with tangent space $E$. Let $\FF \subseteq \EE$ be a subset of $\EE$.

label: Definition:Affine Subspace/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an affine space with tangent space $E$. Let $\FF \subseteq \EE$ be a subset of $\EE$. $\FF$ is an affine subspace of $\EE$ there exists a point $p \in \EE$ such that: $F_p := \set {q - p: q \in \FF}$ is a vector subspace of the vector space $E$.

label: Definition:Affine Subspace/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an affine space with tangent space $E$. Let $\FF \subseteq \EE$ be a subset of $\EE$. $\FF$ is an affine subspace of $\EE$ $\FF$ contains all straight lines between every point of $\FF$.

label: Definition:Affine Subspace of Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $U \subseteq X$ be a vector subspace of $X$. Let $x \in X$. We say that $x + U = \set {x + u : u \in U}$ is an affine subspace of $X$.

label: Definition:Affine Transformation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\EE$ and $\FF$ be affine spaces with difference spaces $E$ and $F$ respectively. Let $\LL: \EE \to \FF$ be a mapping. $\LL$ is an affine transformation there exists a linear transformation $L: E \to F$ such that for every pair of points $p, q \in \EE$: $\map \LL q = \map \LL p + \map L {\vec {p q} }$

label: Definition:Affinely Dependent
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be the $n$-dimensional real Euclidean space. Let $S = \set {x_1, \dots, x_r}$ be a finite subset of $\R^n$. An element $x \in \R^n$ is affinely dependent on $S$ there exist real numbers $\set {\lambda_i: 1 \le i \le r}$ such that: $(1): \quad x = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^r \lambda_i x_i$ $(2): \quad \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^r \lambda_i = 1$

label: Definition:Affinely Dependent/Independent
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be the $n$-dimensional real Euclidean space. Let $X = \set {x_1, \dots, x_r}$ be a finite subset of $\R^n$. The subset $X$ is affinely independent no element $x \in X$ is affinely dependent on $X \setminus \set x$.

label: Definition:Age
snippet: Applied mathematics and various sciences: Age: the period of time over which a physical object has been in existence. Model Theory Age: a class of $\LL$-structures with certain properties

label: Definition:Aggregate/Also known as
snippet: == Aggregate: Also known as == An aggregate is also known as a aggregation. Category:Definitions/Sets

label: Definition:Aggregate/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Aggregate == The word aggregate was used by when translating 's use of the word Menge from the German. It has since been superseded by the more compact and streamlined set. Category:Linguistic Notes

label: Definition:Aggregation
snippet: Algebra: Aggregation: a collection of a number of terms into a parenthetical expression. Set Theory: Aggregation, or aggregate, is the word for set that was used since 's translation of up until the mid $20$th century, since which time set is all but universal. Physics: Aggregation: a discrete set of (usually) particles which are to be considered as under the same or well-definedly similar conditions at the introduction of an exposition. Category:Definitions/Language Definitions

label: Definition:Aggregation (Physics)
snippet: An aggregation, in the context of physics, is a set of bodies (but usually particles) all of which are under the same or similar conditions, and which are assumed to behave (in certain aspects) as one body. The concept is deliberately left vague.

label: Definition:Agreement between Observers
snippet: Let two observers $A$ and $B$ independently classify each of a set of observations into $2$ or more categories. Let $A$ and $B$ both assign an observation $x$ into the same category. Then $A$ and $B$ are in agreement over $x$.

label: Definition:Aleph-Null
snippet: Aleph-null is the cardinal number of a set which is in one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers $\N$.

label: Definition:Aleph/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Aleph == Aleph, $\aleph$, is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It is pronounced al-eph, with the stress on the first syllable. Category:Linguistic Notes

label: Definition:Aleph Mapping
snippet: Let $\NN'$ denote the class of infinite cardinals. Then $\aleph$ (that is: aleph) is defined as the unique order isomorphism between the two ordered structures $\struct {\On, \in}$ and $\struct {\NN', \in}$ where $\On$ denotes the class of all ordinals.

label: Definition:Aleph Number
snippet: An aleph number is an infinite cardinal.

label: Definition:Aleph Number/Also known as
snippet: == Aleph Number: Also known as == An aleph number is also known as an aleph.

label: Definition:Aleph Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Aleph Number == The concept and notation of aleph numbers are due to . He defined the notion of cardinality. He was the first to realize that infinite sets can have different cardinalities.

label: Definition:Aleph Number/Symbol
snippet: == Aleph Number: Symbol == The symbol used to denote an aleph number is the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet aleph: $\aleph$.

label: Definition:Alexander-Conway Polynomial
snippet: An Alexander-Conway polynomial is a polynomial associated with a knot.

label: Definition:Alexandroff Extension
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a non-empty topological space. Let $p$ be a new element not in $S$. Let $S^* := S \cup \set p$. Let $\tau^*$ be the topology on $S^*$ defined such that $U \subseteq S^*$ is open : $U$ is an open set of $T$ or $U$ is the complement in $T^*$ of a closed and compact subset of $T$. This topology is called the Alexandroff extension on $T$.

label: Definition:Alexandroff Extension/Also known as
snippet: == Alexandroff Extension: Also known as == The Alexandroff extension on a topological space $T$ is also known as: the one point compactification topology (or one-point compactification topology) on $T$ the Alexandroff compactification topology (or just Alexandroff compactification) on $T$ although that latter appellation is also used for a subtly different concept.

label: Definition:Alexandroff Extension of Real Number Line
snippet: The Alexandroff extension of the real number line $\R^*$ is defined as: $\R^* := \R \cup \set \infty$ that is, the set of real numbers together with an element $\infty$ which is not in $\R$.

label: Definition:Algebra
snippet: Algebra: The field of mathematics concerned with manipulation of equations. Abstract Algebra: The subfield of algebra concerned with abstract algebraic structures. Linear Algebra: The subfield of abstract algebra concerned with modules. Vector Algebra: The subfield of linear algebra concerned with vectors. Algebra may also refer to structures in various branches of mathematics, for example: Algebraic Structure Algebra Loop Algebra of Sets The Algebra of Sets Sigma-Algebra Borel Sigma-Algebra B-Algebra

label: Definition:Algebra/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Algebra == The word algebra originates from the Arabic word al-ğabr, meaning balancing, reduction or restoration. It originates from the name of a book, circa , by : (The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing)

label: Definition:Algebra (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: In the context of abstract algebra, in particular ring theory and linear algebra, the following varieties of algebra exist: Definition:Boolean Algebra Definition:Algebra over Ring: an $R$-module $G_R$ over a commutative ring $R$ with a bilinear mapping $\oplus: G^2 \to G$. Definition:Algebra over Field: a vector space $G_F$ over a field $F$ with a bilinear mapping $\oplus: G^2 \to G$. Definition:Real Algebra: an algebra over a field where the field in question is the field of real numbers $\R$.

label: Definition:Algebra (Mathematical Branch)
snippet: Algebra is the branch of mathematics which studies the techniques of manipulation of objects and expressions.

label: Definition:Algebra (Mathematical Branch)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Algebra == The study of algebra dates back to , who published his (The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing) in around . made significant advances in the use of algebraic notation in the $16$th century.

label: Definition:Algebra Defined by Ring Homomorphism
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Let $\struct {S, +, *}$ be a ring. Let $f : R \to S$ be a ring homomorphism. Let the image of $f$ be a subset of the center of $S$. Let $S_R$ be the module defined by the ring homomorphism $f$. The algebra defined by $f$ is the algebra over $R$ defined as: $\struct {S_R, *}$

label: Definition:Algebra of Limits
snippet: The algebra of limits is a collection of theorems relating to algebraic rules of convergence of sequences, either real or complex, to limits. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ and $\sequence {y_n}$ be sequences, either real or complex, such that: {{eqn | l = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n | r = l }} {{eqn | l = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} y_n | r = m }} Then the following rules apply:

label: Definition:Algebra of Sets/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\RR \subseteq \powerset S$ be a set of subsets of $S$. $\RR$ is an algebra of sets over $S$ $\RR$ satisfies the algebra of sets axioms:

label: Definition:Algebra of all Mappings
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {A, +_A, \circ_A, \ast_A}$ be an $R$-algebra. Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {A^S, +, \circ}$ be the $R$-module of all mappings from $S$ to $A$. For each $f, g \in A^S$, define: $\map {\paren {f \ast g} } x = \map f x \ast_A \map g x$ for each $x \in S$. We call $\struct {A^S, +, \circ, \ast}$ the $R$-algebra of all mappings from $S$ to $A$.

label: Definition:Algebra over Field
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. An algebra over $F$ is an ordered pair $\struct {A, *}$ where: $A$ is a vector space over $F$ $*: A^2 \to A$ is a bilinear mapping That is, it is an algebra $\struct {A, *}$ over the ring $F$ where: $F$ is a field the $F$-module $A$ is a vector space. The symbol $A$ is often used for such an algebra, more so as the level of abstraction increases.

label: Definition:Algebra over Field/Also defined as
snippet: == Algebra over Field: Also defined as == Some sources insist that an algebra over a field requires that the bilinear mapping $*$ must have an identity element $1_A$ such that: $\forall a \in A: a * 1_A = 1_A * a = a$ that is, that $\struct {A, *}$ has to be a unitary algebra. It is worth being certain of what is meant in any works read. Especially in commutative algebra, an algebra over a field is often defined as a unital associative commutative algebra.

label: Definition:Algebra over Field/Multiplication
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. Let $\struct {A, *}$ be an algebra over $F$ such that: $A$ is a vector space over $F$ $* : A^2 \to A$ is a bilinear mapping. The bilinear mapping $*$ is often referred to as multiplication.

label: Definition:Algebra over Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. An algebra over $R$ is an ordered pair $\struct {A, *}$ where: $A$ is an $R$-module $*: A^2 \to A$ is an $R$-bilinear mapping

label: Definition:Algebraic (Model Theory)
snippet: Let $\MM$ be an $\LL$-structure with universe $M$. Let $A$ be a subset of $M$. and let $\bar b$ be an ordered $n$-tuple of elements from $M$. Let $\LL_A$ be the language formed by adding constant symbols to $\LL$ for each element of $A$. $\bar b$ is algebraic over $A$ there is an $\LL_A$-formula $\map \phi {\bar x}$ with $n$ free variables such that: $\MM \models \map \phi {\bar b}$ and: the set $\set {\bar m \in M^n : \MM \models \map \phi {\bar m} }$ has only finitely many elements.

label: Definition:Algebraic (Model Theory)/Saturated Model
snippet: Let $\MM$ be an $\LL$-structure with universe $M$. Let $A$ be a subset of $M$. and let $\bar b$ be an ordered $n$-tuple of elements from $M$. Let $\LL_A$ be the language formed by adding constant symbols to $\LL$ for each element of $A$. Let $\MM$ be a saturated model. Then $\bar b$ is algebraic over $A$ it has only finitely many images under $A$-automorphisms.

label: Definition:Algebraic Closure
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. An algebraic closure of $K$ is an algebraically closed algebraic field extension of $K$. An algebraic closure of $K$ can be denoted $\overline K$.

label: Definition:Algebraic Complement of Vector Subspace
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $U_1$ be a vector subspace of $X$. We say that $U_2$ is an algebraic complement of $U_1$ : $X = U_1 \oplus U_2$ where $\oplus$ denotes the internal direct sum. That is: for each $x \in X$, there exists $u_1 \in U_1$ and $u_2 \in U_2$ such that $x = u_1 + u_2$ and: $U_1 \cap U_2 = \set { {\mathbf 0}_X}$

label: Definition:Algebraic Curve
snippet: An algebraic curve is a curve which is the locus of a set of polynomial equations.

label: Definition:Algebraic Dual/Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $\phi: V \to K$ be a linear mapping. The set of all such $\phi$ is called the (vector) algebraic dual (of $V$) and is denoted by $V^*$.

label: Definition:Algebraic Geometry
snippet: Algebraic geometry is the branch of geometry which studies objects in multi-dimensional space using the techniques of abstract algebra. In particular, techniques from commutative algebra are mainly used. It also encompasses the study of algebraic varieties.

label: Definition:Algebraic Geometry/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Algebraic Geometry == The foundations for the theory of algebraic geometry were laid in 's paper . It was further developed in the $19$th century by .

label: Definition:Algebraic Integer
snippet: Let $K / \Q$ be an algebraic number field. {{explain|The notation at this point needs to be expanded and explained. The concept is pitched at a level more abstract than can easily be comprehended by someone who is merely exploring for example $\Z \sqbrk {\sqrt 2}$. It is also worth adding further definitions which may serve to bring it down to earth.}} Then $\alpha \in K$ is an algebraic integer it satisfies a monic polynomial $f \in \Z \sqbrk X$. The set of all algebraic integers in $K$ is denoted $\OO_K$.

label: Definition:Algebraic Integer/Quadratic
snippet: Let $K / \Q$ be an algebraic number field. Let $K / \Q$ have degree two. Then an algebraic integer in $K$ is a quadratic integer.

label: Definition:Algebraic Logic
snippet: Algebraic logic is a branch of mathematical logic which is the reasoning obtained by manipulating equations with free variables.

label: Definition:Algebraic Matroid
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. Let $S \subseteq L$ be a finite subset of $L$. Let $\struct{S, \mathscr I}$ be the matroid induced by Algebraic Independence over $K$ on $S$. From Matroid Induced by Algebraic Independence is Matroid, $\struct{S, \mathscr I}$ is a matroid. Then any matroid isomorphic to $\struct{S, \mathscr I}$ is called an algebraic matroid.

label: Definition:Algebraic Number
snippet: An algebraic number is an algebraic element of the field extension $\C / \Q$. That is, it is a complex number that is a root of a polynomial with rational coefficients. The set of algebraic numbers can often be seen denoted as $\mathbb A$.

label: Definition:Algebraic Number/Degree
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be an algebraic number. By definition, $\alpha$ is the root of at least one polynomial $P_n$ with rational coefficients. The degree of $\alpha$ is the degree of the minimal polynomial $P_n$ whose coefficients are all in $\Q$.

label: Definition:Algebraic Number Field
snippet: An algebraic number field is a finite extension of the field of rational numbers $\Q$.

label: Definition:Algebraic Number Theory
snippet: Algebraic number theory is the branch of abstract algebra which studies structures in which the usual number fields are embedded. As such it can also be considered to be a branch of number theory.

label: Definition:Algebraic Number Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Algebraic Number Theory == The field of algebraic number theory was initiated by , with his papers of $1828$ and $1832$ on biquadratic residues.

label: Definition:Algebraic Number over Field
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. Let $z$ be a complex number. $z$ is algebraic over $F$ $z$ is a root of a polynomial with coefficients in $F$.

label: Definition:Algebraic Structure
snippet: An algebraic structure with $n$ operations is an ordered tuple: $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n}$ where: $S$ is a set $\circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots, \circ_n$ are $n$ binary operations which are defined on all the elements of $S \times S$.

label: Definition:Algebraic Structure/Also defined as
snippet: == Algebraic Structure: Also defined as == Some sources define an algebraic structure such that the underlying set is specifically non-empty. Others allow the concept of an empty algebraic structure, while acknowledging that it is usual for it to be non-empty. Some sources categorize modules and vector spaces as algebraic structures, but in the strict definition as given on , technically they are not.

label: Definition:Algebraic Structure/Also known as
snippet: == Algebraic Structure: Also known as == Some sources refer to an algebraic structure as an abstract algebra, but this term is more generally used for the branch of mathematics that studies these structures. Some sources use the term algebraic system, which reserves for a slightly more general concept. Some sources use the variant term algebraic structure with $n$ compositions. Some sources use the notation $\gen {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots}$ for $\struct {S, \circ_1, \circ_2, \ldots}$ and so on.

label: Definition:Algebraic Structure/One Operation
snippet: An algebraic structure with $1$ operation is an ordered pair: $\struct {S, \circ}$ where: $S$ is a set $\circ$ is a binary operation defined on all the elements of $S \times S$.

label: Definition:Algebraic Structure/Two Operations
snippet: An algebraic structure with $2$ operations is an ordered triple: $\struct {S, \circ, *}$ where: $S$ is a set $\circ$ and $*$ are binary operations defined on all the elements of $S \times S$.

label: Definition:Algebraic System
snippet: An algebraic system is a mathematical system $\SS = \struct {E, O}$ where: $E$ is a non-empty set of elements $O$ is a set of finitary operations on $E$.

label: Definition:Algebraic Topology
snippet: Algebraic topology is a branch of topology which uses tools from abstract algebra to study topological spaces.

label: Definition:Algebraic Variety
snippet: An algebraic variety is the solution set of a system of simultaneous polynomial equations: {{eqn | l = \map {P_1} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} | r = 0 }} {{eqn | l = \map {P_2} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} | r = 0 }} {{eqn | l = \map {P_k} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} | r = 0 }}

label: Definition:Algebraic Variety/Also defined as
snippet: == Algebraic Variety: Also defined as == Some sources define an algebraic variety as the zero set of a polynomial to which a commutative ring can be associated.

label: Definition:Algebraic Variety/Also known as
snippet: == Algebraic Variety: Also known as == An algebraic variety is also known just as a variety.

snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Then $K$ is algebraically closed :

label: Definition:Algebraically Independent
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. Let $A \subseteq L$ be a subset of $L$. Let $\map K {\set {X_\alpha: \alpha \in A} }$ be the field of rational functions in the indeterminates $\family {X_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in A}$. Then $A$ is algebraically independent over $K$ there exists a homomorphism: $\phi: \map K {\set {X_\alpha: \alpha \in A} } \to L$ such that, for all $\alpha \in A$: $\map \phi {X_\alpha} = \alpha$

label: Definition:Algorism
snippet: Algorism is an archaic term which means the process of doing arithmetic using Arabic numerals.

label: Definition:Algorism/Algorist
snippet: During the middle ages, an algorist was an arithmetician who used algorism, as opposed to an abacist who calculated using an abacus. By the time of , the term had evolved to mean a mathematician who devised algorithms for more complicated operations than those of the classical algorithms.

label: Definition:Algorithm
snippet: An algorithm is a finite set of instructions (or rules) that defines a sequence of operations for solving a particular computational problem for all problem instances for some problem set. An algorithm must have the following properties:

label: Definition:Algorithm/Action
snippet: In an algorithm, an action is part of a step of that algorithm. It is an operation which changes the state of the algorithm in some manner.

label: Definition:Algorithm/Analysis
snippet: There are two primary methods for analyzing algorithms formally:

label: Definition:Algorithm/Analysis/Complexity
snippet: The complexity of an algorithm is defined as the number of discrete steps needed to terminate as a function of the number of inputs. An algorithm may be analysed in the context of its complexity. This is typically via measures of run-times using big-$\OO$, or big-$\Omega$, or $\Theta$ notation. Complexity can be through 3 main types of analysis: Average-Case Analysis, using a distribution of cases to find an average case of the algorithm run-time for analysis Best-Case Analysis, using the best possible problem instance of the algorithm for analysis Worst-Case Analysis,using the worst possible…

label: Definition:Algorithm/Analysis/Correctness
snippet: The primary method of validity for algorithms is using a Proof of Correctness. This is correctness through verification of the algorithm accomplishing its purpose formally, and terminating in $k$ finite steps. Category:Definitions/Algorithms

label: Definition:Algorithm/Comment
snippet: In an algorithm, a comment is a piece of explanatory information that helps the reader of that algorithm understand it better.

label: Definition:Algorithm/Condition
snippet: In an algorithm, a condition is part of a step of that algorithm. It is an operation which determines the outcome of a decision as to which step to execute next,

label: Definition:Algorithm/Definiteness
snippet: Each step of an algorithm must be precisely defined.

label: Definition:Algorithm/Effectiveness
snippet: An algorithm is supposed to be effective. That is, its operations must be basic enough to be able to be done exactly and in a finite length of time by, for example, somebody using pencil and paper.

label: Definition:Algorithm/Finiteness
snippet: An algorithm must terminate after a finite number of steps.

label: Definition:Algorithm/Formal Specification
snippet: An algorithm can be implemented formally as a computational method $\left({Q, I, \Omega, f}\right)$ as follows: Let $A$ be a finite set of symbols. Let $A^*$ be the set of all collations on $A$: $\left\{ {x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n: n \ge 0, \forall j: 1 \le j \le n: x_j \in A}\right\}$ The states of the computation are encoded so as to be represented by elements of $A^*$. Let $N \in \Z_{\ge 0}$. Let $Q$ be the set of all ordered pairs $\left({\sigma, j}\right)$ where $\sigma \in A^*, j \in \Z: 0 \le j \le N$. Let $I \subseteq Q$ such that $j = 0$. Let $\Omega \subseteq Q$ such that $j = N$.

label: Definition:Algorithm/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Algorithm == The word algorithm is a recent addition to the English language. It was still absent from major dictionaries as late as $1957$.

label: Definition:Algorithm/Input
snippet: An algorithm has zero or more inputs. These are values supplied either: before the algorithm starts as the algorithm runs. These inputs are taken from specified sets of objects.

label: Definition:Algorithm/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Algorithm == The word algorithm ultimately derives from the name . It is strongly believed that it is the result of linguistic evolution of the archaic term algorism, with which algorithm ought not be confused (although some sources do not make the distinction). The term was seen in German literature in its Latin form algorithmus at around the time of , where the classical algorithms were referenced.

label: Definition:Algorithm/Operation
snippet: In an algorithm, an operation is part of a step of that algorithm. It consists of one of two things: an action or: a condition. Category:Definitions/Algorithms

label: Definition:Algorithm/Output
snippet: An algorithm has one or more outputs. These are values which are specifically determined by the inputs.

label: Definition:Algorithm/Step
snippet: An algorithm consists of a finite set of steps, uniquely identified by means of a label, conventionally numeric. A step of an algorithm consists of: an operation an instruction as to what the algorithm is to do next, which will be one of the following: $(1): \quad$ By default: to move onto the next step in the sequence $(2): \quad$ Based on the result of a condition, the specific step to perform next $(3): \quad$ To terminate. It is usual to include a statement in natural language which briefly describes the purpose of this step. A step may also contain a comment.

label: Definition:Algorithm/Termination
snippet: The termination of an algorithm is the point at which it has finished.

label: Definition:Algorithmic Analysis
snippet: The field of algorithmic analysis is a subfield of computer science which studies the performance characteristics of algorithms.

label: Definition:Algorithmic Complexity/Motivation
snippet: == Algorithmic Complexity: Motivation== The increase in use of computers for all sorts of automation projects requires that the algorithms used are as efficient as possible, using as few computer resources as possible. The study of algorithmic complexity as a way of comparing algorithms has come into prominence as a result.

label: Definition:Algorithmic Computability
snippet: The concept of algorithmic computability is an intuitive one. An algorithmically computable function is a function which can be carried by means of an algorithm, theoretically by a person using pencil and paper. The concept arose in the decades before the invention of digital computers. Much of the theoretical groundwork was done in the 1930s by such as , and . The term used by when he discussed the issue in how his famous Church's Thesis was effectively calculable.

label: Definition:Almost-Everywhere Equality Relation/Lebesgue Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space, and let $p \in \closedint 1 \infty$. Let $\map {\LL^p} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be the Lebesgue $p$-space of $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$. We define the $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality relation $\sim_\mu$ on $\map {\LL^p} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ by: $f \sim_\mu g$ $\norm {f - g}_p = 0$ where $\norm {\, \cdot \,}_p$ is the $p$-seminorm. From Almost-Everywhere Equality Relation for Lebesgue Space is Equivalence Relation, $\sim_\mu$ is shown to be an equivalence relation. Category:Definitions/Almost-Everywhere Equality Relation

label: Definition:Almost All/Set Theory/Uncountable
snippet: Let $S$ be an uncountably infinite set. Let $P: S \to \set {\text {true}, \text {false} }$ be a property of $S$ such that: $\set {s \in S: \neg \map P s}$ is countable (either finite or countably infinite). Then $P$ holds for almost all of the elements of $S$. Category:Definitions/Set Theory

label: Definition:Almost Discrete Space
snippet: Let $S \ne \O$ be a set. Let $\tau = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be discrete except for a set of measure zero. Then $\struct {S, \tau}$ is an almost discrete space.

label: Definition:Almost Everywhere
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. A property $\map P x$ of elements of $X$ is said to hold ($\mu$-)almost everywhere if the set: $\set {x \in X: \neg \map P x}$ of elements of $X$ such that $P$ does not hold is contained in a $\mu$-null set.

label: Definition:Almost Perfect Number
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer.

label: Definition:Almost Perfect Number/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Almost Perfect Numbers == The sequence of almost perfect numbers begins: $1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, \ldots$ Category:Definitions/Almost Perfect Numbers

label: Definition:Almost Separately Valued Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $f : I \to X$ be a function. Let $\lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure on $I$. We say that $f$ is almost separately valued : there exists a $\lambda$-null set $\Omega_0 \subseteq I$ such that $f \sqbrk {I \setminus \Omega_0}$ is separable.

label: Definition:Almost Sure Convergence
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ almost surely converges to $X$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \ds \map \Pr {\lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \size {X_n - X} < \epsilon} = 1$ This is written: $X_n \xrightarrow {\text {a.s.}} X$

label: Definition:Almost Uniform Convergence
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $D \in \Sigma$. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}, f_n: D \to \R$ be a sequence of $\Sigma$-measurable functions. Then $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is said to converge almost uniformly on $D$ : For all $\epsilon > 0$, there is a measurable subset $E_\epsilon \subseteq D$ of $D$ such that: $(1): \quad \map \mu {E_\epsilon} < \epsilon$ $(2): \quad \sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges uniformly to $f$ on $D \setminus E_\epsilon$.

label: Definition:Alphabet
snippet: Formal Languages: Alphabet: a set of symbols from which collations in a given formal languages may be constructed. Natural Languages: Alphabet: the set of letters used to represent the sounds of a given natural language. Category:Definitions/Formal Systems Category:Definitions/Language Definitions

label: Definition:Alphabet of Natural Language
snippet: The alphabet of a natural language $\LL$ is the set of symbols, called letters, which are used to represent the sounds of $\LL$.

label: Definition:Altered Long Line
snippet: Let $\struct {L, \preccurlyeq, \tau}$ denote the long line. Let $p$ be a point which is not an element of $L$. Consider the set $S := L \cup \set p$. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_p}$ be the topological space whose topology $\tau_p$ is defined as follows: The open sets of $T$ are the open sets of $L$ together with those generated by the following neighborhoods of $P$: $\ds \map {U_s} p := \set p \cup \set {\bigcup_{\alpha \mathop = \beta}^\Omega \openint \alpha {\alpha + 1}: 1 \le \beta < \Omega}$ where $\Omega$ denotes the first uncountable ordinal.

label: Definition:Alternant
snippet: Propositional Logic: Alternant (Logic): a synonym for a disjunct: one of the substatements of a compound statement whose main connective is a disjunction. Linear Algebra: Alternant (Linear Algebra): a determinant constructed from $n$ functions and $n$ points such that its $\tuple {i, j}$th entry is the value of the $i$th function at the $j$th point, or vice versa.

label: Definition:Alternating Bilinear Form
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $b$ be a bilinear form on $V$. Then $b$ is alternating : $\forall v \in V: b \left({v, v}\right) = 0$

label: Definition:Alternating Group
snippet: Let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters. For any $\pi \in S_n$, let $\map \sgn \pi$ be the sign of $\pi$. The kernel of the mapping $\sgn: S_n \to C_2$ is called the alternating group on $n$ letters and denoted $A_n$.

label: Definition:Alternating Series
snippet: Let $\ds s = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ be a series in the real numbers $\R$. The series $s$ is an alternating series the terms of $\sequence {a_n}$ alternate between positive and negative.

label: Definition:Alternative
snippet: Logic: Alternative (Logic): A synonym for disjunct. Abstract Algebra: Alternative Operation: an operation which is associative on $2$ elements.

label: Definition:Alternative Hypothesis
snippet: In the context of a hypothesis test, the alternative hypothesis, usually denoted $H_1$ or $\mathrm H_1$, is the hypothesis which is to be accepted if the null hypothesis is demonstrated not to hold.

label: Definition:Altitude of Cylinder
snippet: 400px An altitude of a cylinder is a line segment drawn perpendicular to the base and its opposite plane. In the above diagram, $HJ$ is an altitude of the cylinder $ACBDFE$.

label: Definition:Altitude of Geometric Figure
snippet: The altitude of a geometric figure $\FF$ is the length of a line segment giving the height of $\FF$.

label: Definition:Altitude of Geometric Figure/Also defined as
snippet: == Altitude of Geometric Figure: Also defined as == The word altitude is often used in the context of a geometric figure to mean the height. However, on it is preferred if the terms altitude and height are used specifically to mean respectively the perpendicular and its length, to avoid confusion.

label: Definition:Altitude of Polygon
snippet: An altitude of a polygon is the longest perpendicular from the base to a vertex most distant from the base.

label: Definition:Altitude of Pyramid
snippet: 400px An altitude of a pyramid is a straight line perpendicular to the plane of the base to its apex. In the above diagram, an altitude is a straight line length is $h$.

label: Definition:Altitude of Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. Let a perpendicular be dropped from $\angle A$ to its opposite side $a$ or its production: 760px The line $h_a$ so constructed is called the altitude of $\angle A$.

label: Definition:Altitude of Triangle/Foot
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. Let $h_a$ be the altitude of $A$: 760px The point at which $h_a$ meets $BC$ (or its production) is the foot of the altitude $h_a$.

label: Definition:Ambivalent Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Then $G$ is ambivalent every element of $G$ is conjugate to its inverse: $\forall g \in G : \exists h \in G : h g h^{-1} = g^{-1}$ That is, every element of $G$ is real.

label: Definition:Amount of Substance
snippet: The amount of a particular substance in a body composed of that substance is ultimately measured by a count of the number of elementary units it comprises.

label: Definition:Amount of Substance/Dimension
snippet: == Dimension of Amount of Substance == Amount of substance is one of the fundamental dimensions of physics. In dimensional analysis it is assigned the symbol $\mathsf N$. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Amount of Substance

label: Definition:Amphiboly
snippet: An amphiboly is an ambiguity resulting from poor syntax.

label: Definition:Amplitude
snippet: Complex Analysis: Another word for Argument of Complex Number Analysis Amplitude of Periodic Real Function Amplitude of Incomplete Elliptic Integral of the First Kind Physics: Amplitude of Simple Harmonic Motion Polar Coordinates: Another word for angular coordinate

label: Definition:Anagram
snippet: Let $b \in \Z_{>1}$ be an integer greater than $1$. Let $m$ be an integer expressed in base $b$. An anagram base $b$ of $m$ is an integer formed by the digits of $m$ written in a different order. When the number base of $m$ is not specified, base $10$ is assumed.

label: Definition:Analysis
snippet: Analysis is a branch of mathematics that studies continuous change, and the use of limits. It subsumes the fields of calculus, differential equations, the calculus of variations, power series, Fourier series, real analysis and complex analysis. It is one of the main branches of mathematics, alongside geometry, number theory and algebra.

label: Definition:Analysis/Complex
snippet: Complex analysis is a branch of mathematics that studies complex functions.

label: Definition:Analysis/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Analysis == The field of analysis was put into its modern shape by the work of , , and .

label: Definition:Analysis/Real
snippet: Real analysis is a branch of mathematics that studies real functions.

label: Definition:Analysis of Variance
snippet: Analysis of variance is the statistical technique of partitioning the variance of a set of data into a number of components. Each such component is associated with a particular source of variance, such as: treatments design groupings error and so on.

label: Definition:Analytic Basis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. An analytic basis for $\tau$ is a subset $\BB \subseteq \tau$ such that: $\forall U \in \tau: \exists \AA \subseteq \BB: U = \bigcup \AA$ That is, such that for all $U \in \tau$, $U$ is a union of sets from $\BB$.

label: Definition:Analytic Basis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\BB \subseteq \tau$. Then $\BB$ is an analytic basis for $\tau$ : $\forall U \in \tau: \forall x \in U: \exists V \in \BB: x \in V \subseteq U$

label: Definition:Analytic Continuation
snippet: Let $U \subset \C$ be an open set. Let $f: U \to \C$ be an analytic function. Let $V$ be an open subset of $\C$ such that $U \subset V$. An analytic continuation of $f$ to $V$ is an analytic function $F: V \to \C$ such that $\map F z = \map f z$ for $z \in U$.

label: Definition:Analytic Function/Banach Space Valued Function
snippet: Let $U$ be an open subset of $\C$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a Banach space over $\C$. Let $f : U \to X$ be a mapping. We say that $f$ is analytic the limit: $\ds \lim_{w \mathop \to z} \frac {\map f w - \map f z} {w - z}$ exists for each $z \in U$.

label: Definition:Analytic Function/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $U \subset \C$ be an open set. Let $f : U \to \C$ be a complex function. Then $f$ is analytic in $U$ for every $z_0 \in U$ there exists a sequence $\sequence {a_n}: \N \to \C$ such that the series: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a_n \paren {z - z_0}^n$ converges to $\map f z$ in a neighborhood of $z_0$ in $U$.

label: Definition:Analytic Function/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is smooth on the open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi \in \openint a b$. Let $\openint c d \subseteq \openint a b$ be an open interval such that: $(1): \quad \xi \in \openint c d$ $(2): \quad \ds \forall x \in \openint c d: \map f x = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {\paren {x - \xi}^n} {n!} \map {f^{\paren n} } x$ Then $f$ is an analytic (real) function at the point $\xi$. That is, a real function is an analytic real function at a point $\xi$ it equals its Taylor series expansion in some open interval containing $\xi$.

label: Definition:Analytic Geometry
snippet: Analytic geometry is the study of geometry by algebraic manipulation of systems of ordered tuples of variables representing points in Cartesian space. Traditionally, the subject is divided into two main branches:

label: Definition:Analytic Number Theory
snippet: Analytic number theory is a branch of number theory which uses tools from analysis to solve problems about the integers.

label: Definition:Analytic Number Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Analytic Number Theory == Some consider that the field of analytic number theory was effectively created by in $1737$, on the occasion of his discovery of two results: Sum of Reciprocals of Powers as Euler Product and: Sum of Reciprocals of Primes is Divergent. Others place its origins with , with Dirichlet's Theorem on Arithmetic Sequences. Other important results in the field include: the Prime Number Theorem the Bertrand-Chebyshev Theorem the Hardy-Littlewood Circle Method.

label: Definition:Analytic Proof
snippet: An analytic proof is a proof using algebra or analysis only, without dependence upon axioms, particularly geometric ones.

label: Definition:Analytic Real Function/Space
snippet: The set of all analytic real functions is called the space of analytic (real) functions and is denoted $\mathrm C^\omega$.

label: Definition:Analytical Mechanics
snippet: Analytical mechanics is a subfield of mathematical physics which uses techniques of analysis, in particular the calculus of variations, to solve problems in mechanics. Hence, instead of solving equations in vector quantities, it involves solutions of differential equations of scalar quantities.

label: Definition:Analytics
snippet: Analytics is the branch of data science which applies mathematical techniques to large sets of data with the aim of devising strategies for competitive advantage and value creation, particular in relation to commerce.

label: Definition:Ancient Egyptian Papyrus
snippet: Most of our knowledge of the mathematics of has come to us through a number of documents written on .

label: Definition:Angelic Topological Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\cl$ be closure in $\struct {X, \tau}$. We say that $\struct {X, \tau}$ is angelic for each $A \subseteq X$: for each $x \in \map \cl A$ there exists a sequence $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $A$ such that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges to $x$.

label: Definition:Angle
snippet: Let $\LL_1$ and $\LL_2$ be two lines which intersect at a point $\PP$. The angle between $\LL_1$ and $\LL_2$ is defined as the inclination between $\LL_1$ and $\LL_2$ at $\PP$. '

label: Definition:Angle/Adjacent
snippet: Two angles are adjacent if they have an intersecting line in common: 250px

label: Definition:Angle/Arm
snippet: Each of the two intersecting lines or line segments that form an angle are called its arms.

label: Definition:Angle/Directed versus Undirected
snippet: The most basic definition of angle is an undirected angle on the interval $\closedint {0 \degrees} {180 \degrees}$ or $\closedint 0 \pi$. This definition is often insufficient, in cases such as the external angles of a polygon. Therefore, angles are most commonly defined in one of two ways: $(1): \quad$ Undirected angles on the interval $\closedint {0 \degrees} {360 \degrees}$ or $\closedint 0 {2 \pi}$. $(2): \quad$ Directed angles, with the positive direction being anticlockwise from a given line (or, if no line is specified, from the $x$-axis).

label: Definition:Angle/Subtend
snippet: Let $AB$ be a line segment and $C$ be a point: 250px The line segment $AB$ is said to subtend the angle $\angle ACB$.

label: Definition:Angle/Types
snippet: Angles can be divided into categories:

label: Definition:Angle/Vertex
snippet: The point at which the arms of an angle meet is known as the vertex of that angle.

label: Definition:Angle Between Vectors in Inner Product Space
snippet: Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be an inner product space. Let $v,w \in V$ be such that $\size v, \size w \ne 0$, where $\size {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the inner product norm. Then the real number $\theta \in \closedint 0 \pi$ is called the angle (between $v$ and $w$) : $\map \cos \theta = \dfrac {\innerprod v w} {\size v \size w}$

label: Definition:Angle Bisector
snippet: 300px Let $\angle ABC$ be an angle. The angle bisector of $\angle ABC$ is the straight line which bisects $\angle ABC$. In the above diagram, $BD$ is the angle bisector of $\angle ABC$. Thus $\angle ABD \cong \angle DBC$ and $\angle ABD + \angle DBC = \angle ABC$.

label: Definition:Angle Inscribed in Circle
snippet: 300px Let $AB$ and $BC$ be two chords of a circle which meet at $B$. The angle $\angle ABC$ is the angle inscribed at $B$ (with respect to $A$ and $C$). Category:Definitions/Circles
