label: Definition:Angle of Contingence
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be two points on a plane curve. 400px The angle of contingence $A$ and $B$ is defined as the angle between the positive directions of the tangents to the curve at $A$ and $B$.

label: Definition:Angle of Depression
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be points in space such that $A$ is lower than $B$. The angle of depression of $A$ from $B$ is the angle between the line $AB$ and the horizontal.

label: Definition:Angle of Elevation
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be points in space such that $A$ is higher than $B$. The angle of elevation of $A$ from $B$ is the angle between the line $AB$ and the horizontal.

label: Definition:Angle of Elevation/Also known as
snippet: == Angle of Elevation: Also known as == The angle of elevation of a point can also be seen referred to as its elevation. However, the term elevation is ambiguous, so it not endorsed in this context on .

label: Definition:Angle of Friction
snippet: Let $B$ be a body at rest on a plane surface $S$ on which friction acts. Let $\mu_s$ denote the coefficient of static friction between $B$ and $S$. The angle of friction is the angle $\lambda$ defined as: $\tan \lambda = \mu_s$

label: Definition:Angle of Intersection of Circles
snippet: Let $\CC$ and $\CC'$ be circles whose centers are at $C$ and $C'$ respectively. Let $\CC$ and $\CC'$ intersect at $A$ and $B$. The angle of intersection of $\CC$ and $\CC'$ is the angle between the tangents at the point of intersection. 540px Of the two angles formed by the tangents, the angle taken is between: the half-line of one tangent that passes completely outside both circles and: the half-line of the other tangent that passes through the interior of one circle.

label: Definition:Angular Acceleration
snippet: Angular acceleration is the rate of increase of angular velocity with time.

label: Definition:Angular Distance
snippet: The angular distance between two points $A$ and $B$ a reference point $P$ is the angle between the straight lines $AP$ and $BP$, that is: $\angle APB$

label: Definition:Angular Frequency
snippet: Let $f$ be a physical process that can be modelled by a periodic function whose nature is that of a sinusoid. The angular frequency of $f$ is a measure of the rate of oscillation of $f$ equal to $2 \pi \nu$, where $\nu$ is the frequency of $f$.

label: Definition:Angular Measure
snippet: The usual units of measurement for angle are as follows:

label: Definition:Angular Measure/Radian
snippet: The radian is the SI unit of plane angle. It can be symbolized either by the word $\radians$ or without any unit. Radians are pure numbers, as they are ratios of lengths. The addition of $\radians$ is merely for clarification. $1 \radians$ is the angle subtended at the center of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the radius: 360px

label: Definition:Angular Momentum/Aggregation of Particles
snippet: Let $\PP = \set {P_i: i \in I}$ be an aggregation of particles, indexed by $I$, all in motion relative to a point $O$. For all $i \in I$, let: the mass of particle $P_i$ be $m_i$ the velocity of particle $P_i$ relative to $O$ be $\mathbf v_i$. The angular momentum of $\PP$ relative to (or about) $O$ is defined as the sum of the angular momenta of each of the particles in $\PP$: $\ds \mathbf L = \sum_{i \mathop \in I} \mathbf r_i \times \mathbf p_i = m \paren {\mathbf r_i \times \mathbf v_i}$ where: $\mathbf p_i$ denotes the (linear) momentum of particle $P_i$ for $i \in I$ $\mathbf r_i$…

label: Definition:Angular Momentum/Particle
snippet: Let $P$ be a particle of mass $m$ moving with velocity $\mathbf v$ relative to a point $O$. The angular momentum of $P$ relative to (or about) $O$ is defined as: $\mathbf L = \mathbf r \times \mathbf p = m \paren {\mathbf r \times \mathbf v}$ where: $\mathbf p$ denotes the (linear) momentum of $P$ $\mathbf r$ denotes the position vector of $P$ $O$ $\times$ denotes the vector cross product.

label: Definition:Angular Momentum/Rigid Body
snippet: The angular momentum of a rigid body about a point $O$ is the vector cross product of its moment of inertia $\mathbf I$ about $O$ by its angular velocity $\omega$ about $O$: $\mathbf L = \mathbf I \times \omega$

label: Definition:Angular Momentum of Particle/Also presented as
snippet: Some sources present the definition of the angular momentum of a particle $P$ relative to a point $A$ as: $\mathbf L = \paren {\mathbf r - \mathbf r_A} \times m \mathbf v$ where: $m$ denotes the mass of $P$ $\mathbf v$ velocity of $P$ relative to the frame of reference in which the motion of $P$ is defined $\mathbf r$ denotes the position vector of $P$ $\mathbf r_A$ denotes the position vector of $A$ $\times$ denotes the vector cross product.

label: Definition:Angular Speed
snippet: Angular speed is defined as the magnitude of angular velocity.

label: Definition:Angular Velocity
snippet: Let $P$ be a particle moving in the plane. Let $O$ be a distinguished point in the plane. Let $\map {\mathbf r} t$ be the position vector of $P$ $O$ as a function of time. Let $\map {\mathbf v} t$ be the velocity of $P$ $O$ as a function of time. 600px The vector $\bsomega = \dfrac {\mathbf r \times \mathbf v} {\size {\mathbf r}^2}$ is known as the angular velocity of $P$ $O$.

label: Definition:Angular Velocity/Dimension
snippet: Angular velocity has dimension $\mathsf T^{-1}$. Category:Definitions/Angular Velocity Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement

label: Definition:Angular Velocity/Symbol
snippet: == Angular Velocity: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote angular velocity is $\bsomega$.

label: Definition:Angular Velocity/Unit
snippet: The unit of measurement of angular velocity is the radian per second. Category:Definitions/Angular Velocity Category:Definitions/Units of Measurement

label: Definition:Annihilator
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Let $M$ and $N$ be modules over $R$. Let $B : M \times N \to R$ be a bilinear mapping. The annihilator of $D \subseteq M$ is the set defined and denoted as: $\map {\operatorname {Ann}_N} D := \set {n \in N : \forall d \in D: \map B {d, n} = 0}$

label: Definition:Annihilator of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \times}$ be a ring or, more usually, a field. Let $B: R \times \Z$ be a bilinear mapping defined as: $B: R \times \Z: \tuple {r, n} \mapsto n \cdot r$ where $n \cdot r$ defined as an integral multiple of $r$: $n \cdot r = r + r + \cdots \paren n \cdots r$ Note the change of order of $r$ and $n$: $\map B {r, n} = n \cdot r$ Let $D \subseteq R$ be a subring of $R$.

label: Definition:Annihilator of Subspace of Banach Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a Banach space. Let $M$ be a vector subspace of $X$. Let $X^\ast$ be the normed dual space of $X$. The annihilator is defined and denoted: $M^\bot = \set {g \in X^\ast : \map g x = 0 \text { for all } x \in M}$

label: Definition:Annihilator of Subspace of Normed Dual Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a Banach space. Let $X^\ast$ be the normed dual space of $X$. Let $N$ be a vector subspace of $X^\ast$. The annihilator of $N$ is defined and denoted: ${}^\bot N = \set {x \in X : \map g x = 0 \text { for all } g \in N}$

label: Definition:Annulus
snippet: Geometry: Annulus: the region between two concentric circles Topology: Annulus: a topological space which is homeomorphic with an annulus in the context of geometry Abstract Algebra: Annulus: another word for a ring

label: Definition:Annulus (Geometry)/Also known as
snippet: == Annulus: Also known as == The more contemporary word ring can sometimes be seen for annulus. However, as the term ring is ubiquitous in the field of abstract algebra to refer to an algebraic structure of a particular type, it is the policy of to use the term annulus instead, so as to reduce the possibility of confusion.

label: Definition:Annulus (Geometry)/Center
snippet: 400px The center of an annulus is the common center of the $2$ concentric circles that form its boundary. In the above diagram, the center is the point $O$. Category:Definitions/Annuli

label: Definition:Annulus (Topology)
snippet: An annulus in the context of topology is a topological space which is homeomorphic with an annulus in the context of geometry. 400px

label: Definition:Anomalous Cancellation
snippet: Let $r = \dfrac a b$ be a fraction where $a$ and $b$ are integers expressed in conventional decimal notation. Anomalous cancellation is a phenomenon whereby deleting (that is, cancelling) common digits from the numerator $a$ and the denominator $b$ of $r$, the value of $r$ the fraction does not change.

label: Definition:Ansatz
snippet: An Ansatz is a guessed solution, or general form of a solution, to a mathematical problem. A mathematician making the Ansatz will then attempt to prove that the Ansatz is indeed a solution to the original problem. If he or she succeeds, the Ansatz is justified retroactively.

label: Definition:Antecedent/Also known as
snippet: == Antecedent: Also known as == The terms: premise assumption hypothesis can often be found in the literature as a word for antecedent, but on we reserve the use of premise, assumption and hypothesis for elements of the structure of logical arguments. The term antecedent clause can sometimes be seen, particularly when the conditional it is part of consists of a statement in natural language. The archaic terms implicans and protasis can sometimes be found.

label: Definition:Anti-Self-Dual 2-Form
snippet: Let $M$ be a $4$-dimensional oriented Riemannian manifold. Let $\omega$ be a $2$-form on $M$. Let $*$ be the Hodge star operator. Suppose: $* \omega = -\omega$ Then $\omega$ is known as the anti-self-dual $2$-form.

label: Definition:Antiassociative Operation
snippet: Let $\circ$ be a binary operation on the set $S$. $\circ$ is an antiassociative operation on $S$ : $\forall x, y, z \in S: \paren {x \circ y} \circ z \ne x \circ \paren {y \circ z}$

label: Definition:Antichain
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. An antichain in $S$ is a subset $A \subseteq S$ such that no two distinct elements in $A$ are comparable. That is: $\forall x, y \in A: x \ne y \implies \lnot \paren {x \preccurlyeq y} \land \lnot \paren {y \preccurlyeq x}$

label: Definition:Anticlastic Surface
snippet: Let $S$ be a surface in space. Let $P$ be a point at which the Gaussian curvature of $S$ at $P$ is negative. Then $S$ is described as being anticlastic at $P$.

label: Definition:Anticlockwise
snippet: Anticlockwise is this direction: 400px

label: Definition:Anticompact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is anticompact every compact subset of $T$ is finite.

label: Definition:Antilexicographic Order/Also known as
snippet: == Antilexicographic Order: Also known as == Antilexicographic order can also be referred to as colexicographic order. Some sources classify the antilexicographic order as a variety of order product. Hence the term antilexicographic product can occasionally be seen. Some sources which focus more directly on real analysis refer to this merely as the ordered product, or order product. This is because the other types of order product as documented on are not of such importance in that context.

label: Definition:Antilogarithm
snippet: Let $x \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $b \in \R_{>1}$ be a real number which is greater than $1$. Let $y = \log_b x$ be the logarithm of $x$ base $b$. Then $x$ is the antilogarithm of $y$ base $b$.

label: Definition:Antinomy
snippet: An antinomy is a self-contradictory statement which arises as the result of a valid argument from a set of premises which contains an inherent ambiguity or contradiction. Such apparent paradoxes can also often be classified as fallacies.

label: Definition:Antipodal Points
snippet: Two points at opposite ends of a diameter of an ellipsoid are referred to as antipodal.

label: Definition:Antiprism
snippet: An antiprism is a prismatoid which has $2$ congruent polygonal bases: One such base is rotated to the other one so the lateral faces are triangles.

label: Definition:Antiprism/Also defined as
snippet: == Antiprism: Also defined as == Some sources define an antiprism as having: regular polygons for bases. isosceles triangles for lateral faces. That is, as defines a right-regular antiprism.

label: Definition:Antisymmetric Relation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is antisymmetric : $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR \land \tuple {y, x} \in \RR \implies x = y$ that is: $\set {\tuple {x, y}, \tuple {y, x} } \subseteq \RR \implies x = y$

label: Definition:Ap-
snippet: Let $A$ be a body in elliptical orbit $O$ around another body $B$. Ap- and apo- are prefixes which indicates the more distant of the two apsides of $O$ from the center of mass of $B$.

label: Definition:Aperiodic Tiling
snippet: An aperiodic tiling is a set of tiles which can tile the plane, but can never form a periodic tiling.

label: Definition:Apex
snippet: The apex of a geometric figure is the point which is distinguished from the others by dint of it being furthest away from its base. Not all figures have a discernible apex. For example, parallelograms, prisms and parallelepipeds do not.

label: Definition:Apothem/Also known as
snippet: == Apothem: Also known as == The apothem of a regular polygon is also known as its short radius.

label: Definition:Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a > b$. Then $a - b$ is an apotome : $(1): \quad \dfrac a b \notin \Q$ $(2): \quad \paren {\dfrac a b}^2 \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers.

label: Definition:Apotome/Fifth Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a - b$ is an apotome. Then $a - b$ is a fifth apotome : $(1): \quad b \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \notin \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

label: Definition:Apotome/First Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a - b$ is an apotome. Then $a - b$ is a first apotome : $(1): \quad a \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

label: Definition:Apotome/Fourth Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a - b$ is an apotome. Then $a - b$ is a fourth apotome : $(1): \quad a \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \notin \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

label: Definition:Apotome/Second Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a - b$ is an apotome. Then $a - b$ is a second apotome : $(1): \quad b \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

snippet:

label: Definition:Apotome/Third Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a - b$ is an apotome. Then $a - b$ is a third apotome : $(1): \quad a \notin \Q$ $(2): \quad b \notin \Q$ $(3): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

label: Definition:Apotome/Warning
snippet: It is a mistake to suggest that $a$ and $b$ may be any real numbers such that $\dfrac a b \notin \Q$ and $\paren {\dfrac a b}^2 \in \Q$. For example, let $a = \pi \sqrt 2$ and $b = \pi$. Then we see that: $(1): \quad \dfrac a b = \sqrt 2 \notin \Q$ $(2): \quad \paren {\dfrac a b}^2 = 2 \in \Q$ But $a - b = \pi \paren {\sqrt 2 - 1}$ is not an apotome.

label: Definition:Apotome of Medial/First Apotome
snippet: Let $a, b \in \set {x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}$ be two rationally expressible numbers such that $a > b$ be in the forms: $a = k^{1/4} \rho$ $b = k^{3/4} \rho$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a - b$ is a first apotome of a medial.

label: Definition:Apotome of Medial/Second Apotome

label: Definition:Approximation

label: Definition:Apsis

label: Definition:Apéry's Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Apéry's Constant == Apéry's constant was first investigated by , who tried but failed to calculate its value. Its precise value is still unknown. label: Definition:Arbitrarily Large
snippet: Let $P$ be a property of real numbers. We say that: $\map P x$ holds for arbitrarily large $x$ or: there exist arbitrarily large $x$ such that $\map P x$ holds $\forall a \in \R: \exists x \in \R: x \ge a: \map P x$ That is: For any real number $a$, there exists a (real) number not less than $a$ such that the property $P$ holds. or, more informally and intuitively: However large a number you can think of, there will be an even larger one for which $P$ still holds. or: $\set {x: \map P x}$ is not bounded above.

label: Definition:Arbitrarily Small
snippet: Let $P$ be a property of real numbers. We say that: $\map P x$ holds for arbitrarily small $\epsilon$ or: there exist arbitrarily small $x$ such that $\map P x$ holds $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{> 0}: \exists x \in \R: \size x \le \epsilon: \map P x$ That is: For any real number $a$, there exists a (real) number not more than $a$ such that the property $P$ holds. or, more informally and intuitively: However small a number you can think of, there will be an even smaller one for which $P$ still holds.

label: Definition:Arbitrary Constant
snippet: An arbitrary constant is a symbol used to represent an object which is neither a specific number nor a variable. It is used to represent a general object (usually a number, but not necessarily) whose value can be assigned when the expression is instantiated.

snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \preceq_2}$ be complete lattices. Let $\phi: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping between the underlying sets of $L_1$ and $L_2$. label: Definition:Arc
snippet: Graph theory: An arc of a directed graph is a line, with a directional arrow, that joins one vertex to another. Geometry: An arc is a specific part of a general curve. Particular usages: Arc of Circle: any part of its circumference; Arc of Cycloid: one of the parts of a cycloid between two cusps. Topology: An arc from $a$ to $b$ in a topological space is a continuous injection $f: I \to T$ such that $\map f 0 = a$ and $\map f 1 = b$.

label: Definition:Arc-Connected
snippet: Arc-connectedness is a property of a topological space $T$ which relates to the existence of certain homeomorphic embeddings from a closed real interval (in practice, usually just the closed unit interval) into $T$.

label: Definition:Arc-Connected/Points
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $a, b \in S$ be such that there exists an arc from $a$ to $b$. That is, there exists a homeomorphic embedding $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that $\map f 0 = a$ and $\map f 1 = b$. Then $a$ and $b$ are arc-connected. It is also declared that any point $a$ is arc-connected to itself.

label: Definition:Arc-Connected/Subset
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $U \subseteq S$ be a subset of $T$. Let $T' = \struct {U, \tau_U}$ be the subspace of $T$ induced by $U$. Then $U$ is arc-connected in $T$ every two points in $U$ are arc-connected in $T'$. That is, $U$ is arc-connected : for every $x, y \in U$, there exists a homeomorphic embedding $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that $\map f 0 = x$ and $\map f 1 = y$.

label: Definition:Arc-Connected/Topological Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is arc-connected every two points in $T$ are arc-connected in $T$. That is, $T$ is arc-connected : $\forall x, y \in S: \exists$ a homeomorphic embedding $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that $\map f 0 = x$ and $\map f 1 = y$.

label: Definition:Arc (Topology)

label: Definition:Arc Component
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let us define the relation $\sim$ on $T$ as follows: $x \sim y \iff x$ and $y$ are arc-connected. We have that $\sim $ is an equivalence relation, so from the Fundamental Theorem on Equivalence Relations, the points in $T$ can be partitioned into equivalence classes. These equivalence classes are called the arc components of $T$. If $x \in T$, then the arc component of $T$ containing $x$ (that is, the set of points $y \in T$ with $x \sim y$) can be denoted by $\map {\operatorname {AC}_x} T$.

label: Definition:Arc Distance

label: Definition:Argument of Complex Number
snippet: Let $z = x + i y$ be a complex number. An argument of $z$, or $\arg z$, is formally defined as a solution to the pair of equations: $(1): \quad \dfrac x {\cmod z} = \map \cos {\arg z}$ $(2): \quad \dfrac y {\cmod z} = \map \sin {\arg z}$ where $\cmod z$ is the modulus of $z$. From Sine and Cosine are Periodic on Reals, it follows that if $\theta$ is an argument of $z$, then so is $\theta + 2 k \pi$ where $k \in \Z$ is any integer. Thus, the argument of a complex number $z$ is a continuous multifunction.

label: Definition:Argument of Complex Number/Also known as
snippet: == Argument of Complex Number: Also known as == The argument of a complex number is also seen as: its amplitude, denoted $\am z$ its phase, denoted $\ph z$

label: Definition:Argument of Complex Number/Principal Argument
snippet: Let $R$ be the principal range of the complex numbers $\C$. The unique value of $\theta$ in $R$ is known as the principal argument, of $z$. This is denoted $\Arg z$. Note the capital $A$. The standard practice is for $R$ to be $\hointl {-\pi} \pi$. This ensures that the principal argument is continuous on the real axis for positive numbers. Thus, if $z$ is represented in the complex plane, the principal argument $\Arg z$ is intuitively defined as the angle which $z$ yields with the real ($y = 0$) axis.

label: Definition:Argument of Complex Number/Principal Range
snippet: It is understood that the argument of a complex number $z$ is unique only up to multiples of $2 k \pi$. With this understanding, we can limit the choice of what $\theta$ can be for any given $z$ by requiring that $\theta$ lie in some half open interval of length $2 \pi$. The most usual of these are: $\hointr 0 {2 \pi}$ $\hointl {-\pi} \pi$ but in theory any such interval may be used. This interval is known as the principal range.

snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Let $\struct {A_R, *}$ be an algebra over $R$. Then $\struct {A_R, *}$ is an associative algebra $*$ is an associative operation. That is: $\forall a, b, c \in A_R: \paren {a * b} * c = a * \paren {b * c}$

label: Definition:Associative Operation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\circ : S \times S \to S$ be a binary operation. Then $\circ$ is associative : $\forall x, y, z \in S: \paren {x \circ y} \circ z = x \circ \paren {y \circ z}$

label: Definition:Assumption
snippet: An assumption is a statement which is introduced into an argument, whose truth value is (temporarily) accepted as true. In mathematical expositions, the keyword let is often the indicator here that an assumption is going to be introduced.

label: Definition:Astronomical Distance Units/Astronomical Unit
snippet: The astronomical unit is a derived unit of length. It is defined as being $149 \, 597 \, 870 \, 700$ metres. The astronomical unit is the standard unit of measurement used by astronomers when discussing distances within the solar system. It is derived as the approximate mean distance from the center of Earth to the center of the Sun.

label: Definition:Astronomical Triangle
snippet: Let $P$ be a point on the celestial sphere $\CC$. Consider the following $3$ great circles on $\CC$: the great circle between $P$ and the zenith the great circle between $P$ and the north celestial pole the great circle between the zenith and the north celestial pole. The spherical triangle formed by these $3$ great circles is called the astronomical triangle $P$.

label: Definition:Astronomy
snippet: Astronomy is the branch of physics which studies the features which can be seen in the sky that are outside the atmosphere of Earth. Certain of its mathematical aspects can be considered a subfield of solid geometry.

label: Definition:Astrophysics
snippet: Astrophysics is the branch of physics which studies the internal nature of celestial bodies as opposed to their positions and movements.

label: Definition:Asymptote
snippet: $y$-axis, and the line $x = y$ (red)]] Let $C$ be a curve in the plane. Let $L$ be a line (usually straight) such that the distance between $C$ and $L$ approaches zero as they tend to infinity. Then $L$ is an asymptote to (or of) $C$.

label: Definition:Asymptote/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Asymptote == The word asymptote is derived from the Greek ἀσύμπτωτος (asumptōtos) which means not falling together. It was coined by during his analysis of conic sections. The adjectival form of asymptote is asymptotic.

label: Definition:Asymptotic Distribution
snippet: For all $n \in \N$, Let $Z_n$ be a random variable. The asymptotic distribution of $Z_n$ is the limiting probability distribution as $n \to \infty$.

label: Definition:Asymptotic Equality/General Definition/Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $V$ be a normed vector space over $\R$ or $\C$ with norm $\norm {\, \cdot \,}$. Let $f, g: S \to V$ be mappings. Let $x_0 \in X$. Then: $f$ is asymptotically equal to $g$ as $x \to x_0$ $f - g = \map \oo g$ as $x \to x_0$ where $\oo$ denotes little-$\oo$ notation.

label: Definition:Asymptotic Equality/Sequences/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ be sequences in $\R$. Let $b_n \ne 0$ for all $n$. $\sequence {a_n}$ is asymptotically equal to $\sequence {b_n}$ : $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \dfrac {a_n} {b_n} = 1$

label: Definition:Asymptotic Equality/Sequences/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ be sequences in $\R$. $\sequence {a_n}$ is asymptotically equal to $\sequence {b_n}$ : $a_n - b_n = \map \oo {b_n}$ where $\oo$ denotes little-$\oo$ notation.

label: Definition:Asymptotics
snippet: Suppose the task to evaluate a certain number is sufficiently unwieldy that it becomes impractical to calculate it directly. In such cases it is frequently useful to have a completely different method to calculate an approximation to that number. Let the accuracy of this approximation improve as the number of operations involved in its calculation increases. The field of mathematics concerned with studying such techniques is called asymptotics.

label: Definition:Atlas
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. An atlas of class $C^k$ and dimension $d$ on $M$ is a set of $d$-dimensional charts $\mathscr F = \family {\struct {U_\alpha, \phi_\alpha}: \alpha \in A}$ indexed by some set $A$ such that: $(1): \quad \ds \bigcup_{\alpha \mathop \in A} U_\alpha = M$ $(2): \quad$ Every two charts $\struct {U, \phi}$ and $\struct {V, \psi}$ are $C^k$-compatible.

label: Definition:Atlas/Maximal Atlas
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a $d$-dimensional atlas of class $C^k$ of $M$.

label: Definition:Atlas/Maximal Atlas/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a $d$-dimensional atlas of class $C^k$ of $M$. $A$ is a maximal $C^k$-atlas of dimension $d$ $A$ is not strictly contained in another $C^k$-atlas.

label: Definition:Atlas/Maximal Atlas/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a $d$-dimensional atlas of class $C^k$ of $M$. $A$ is a maximal $C^k$-atlas $A$ contains all charts of $M$ that are $C^k$-compatible with $A$.

label: Definition:Atlas/Maximal Atlas/Definition 3
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a $d$-dimensional atlas of class $C^k$ of $M$. $A$ is a maximal $C^k$-atlas $A$ is a maximal element of some differentiable structure, partially ordered by inclusion. That is, a maximal element of some equivalence class of the set of atlases of class $\CC^k$ on $M$ under the equivalence relation of compatibility.

label: Definition:Atlas/Smooth Atlas
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. A smooth atlas on $M$ is a $C^\infty$-atlas on $M$.

label: Definition:Atmospheric Pressure
snippet: Atmospheric pressure is the physical property defined as the pressure at a point in the atmosphere (of Earth, usually) caused by the gravitational force on the air.

label: Definition:Atom
snippet: Logic: Atom: a concept at an irreducible level of simplicity, for example: a simple statement in propositional logic Measure theory: Atom of a measure Abstract algebra: Atom of a $\sigma$-algebra Irreducible element of an integral domain Lattice Theory: Atom of a lattice Physics: Atom: the smallest piece of matter that can exist of a particular type of substance Whatever this is: Definition:Atomic Formula

label: Definition:Atom (Logic)
snippet: In a particular branch of logic, certain concepts are at such a basic level of simplicity they can not be broken down into anything simpler. Those concepts are called atoms or described as atomic. Different branches of logic admit different atoms.

label: Definition:Atom (Logic)/Propositional Logic
snippet: In propositional logic, the atoms are simple statements.

label: Definition:Atom (Physics)
snippet: An atom (in the context of physics and chemistry) is the smallest piece of matter that can exist of a particular type of substance. Atoms can be subdivided into smaller particles, but then it ceases to be that substance.

label: Definition:Atom of Countably Generated Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\Sigma$ be a countably generated $\sigma$-algebra of $X$. Let $x \in X$. Then: $ \ds \sqbrk x_\Sigma = \bigcap \set {A \mathop \in \Sigma : x \in A }$ is called the atom of $\Sigma$ containing $x$.

label: Definition:Atom of Propositional Logic/Also defined as
snippet: == Atom of Propositional Logic: Also defined as == Some sources define an atom of propositional logic to mean what is defined in as a literal: a statement variable or the negation of a statement variable. Category:Definitions/Atoms of Propositional Logic

label: Definition:Atom of Propositional Logic/Also known as
snippet: == Atom of Propositional Logic: Also known as == An atom of propositional logic is also known by some sources in the longer form atomic sentence. Some sources use the term indecomposable sentence.

label: Definition:Atomic Electric Field
snippet: Let $B$ be a body of matter. Let $P$ be a point inside $B$. The atomic electric field $\mathbf E_{\text {atomic} }$ at $B$ is the electric field at $P$ caused by the atomic charge density due to the electric charges within the atoms that make up $B$.

label: Definition:Atomic Physics
snippet: Atomic physics is the branch of physics concerned with the structure and behaviour of the atom.

label: Definition:Atomic WFF of Predicate Logic
snippet: An atomic WFF of predicate logic is a WFF not containing any connectives or quantifiers. In the formal grammar of predicate logic, the atomic WFFs are precisely those WFFs which can be formed by only applying the rule $\mathbf W ~ \PP_n$.

label: Definition:Attainable Set
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, A}$ be a digraph. Let $u \in V$. The attainable set of $u$ is the set of all vertices of $G$ which are reachable from $u$.

label: Definition:Attractor
snippet: Let $S$ be a dynamical system in a space $X$. Let $T$ be an iterated mapping in $S$: $x_{n + 1} = \map T {x_n}$ An attractor is an invariant set $A$ in $X$ towards which nearby points $x$ converge, that is: $T \sqbrk A = A$ $x_n = \map {T^n} x$ approaches $A$ as $n$ increases for points close to $A$.

label: Definition:Augmented Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $n \times m$. Let $\mathbf B$ be a matrix of order $n \times k$. The augmented matrix of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ is the block matrix $\begin {pmatrix} \mathbf A & \mathbf B \end {pmatrix}$ of order $n \times \paren {m + k}$.

label: Definition:Aurifeuillian Factorization
snippet: An Aurifeuillian factorization is an operation to find the prime factors of integers of various forms based upon the identity: $a^2 + b^2 = \paren {a - \sqrt {2 a b} + b} \paren {a + \sqrt {2 a b} + b}$ $a^3 + b^3 = \paren {a + b} \paren {a - \sqrt {3 a b} + b} \paren {a + \sqrt {3 a b} + b}$

label: Definition:Autocorrelation Matrix
snippet: Let $S$ be a strictly stationary stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. Let $\sequence {s_n}$ be a sequence of $n$ successive values of $T$: $\sequence {s_n} = \tuple {z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_n}$ The autocorrelation matrix associated with $S$ for $\sequence {s_n}$ is: $\mathbf P_n = \begin {pmatrix} 1 & \rho_1 & \rho_2 & \cdots & \rho_{n - 1} \\ \rho_1 & 1 & \rho_1 & \cdots & \rho_{n - 2} \\ \rho_2 & \rho_1 & 1 & \cdots & \rho_{n - 3} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \rho_{n - 1} & \rho_{n - 2} & \rho_{n - 3} & \cdots & 1 \end {pmatrix}$ where $\rho_k$ is the…

label: Definition:Autocovariance Matrix
snippet: Let $S$ be a strictly stationary stochastic process giving rise to a time series $T$. Let $\sequence {s_n}$ be a sequence of $n$ successive values of $T$: $\sequence {s_n} = \tuple {z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_n}$ The autocovariance matrix associated with $S$ for $\sequence {s_n}$ is: $\boldsymbol \Gamma_n = \begin {pmatrix} \gamma_0 & \gamma_1 & \gamma_2 & \cdots & \gamma_{n - 1} \\ \gamma_1 & \gamma_0 & \gamma_1 & \cdots & \gamma_{n - 2} \\ \gamma_2 & \gamma_1 & \gamma_0 & \cdots & \gamma_{n - 3} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \gamma_{n - 1} & \gamma_{n - 2} & \gamma_{n - 3} &…

label: Definition:Automorphic Function (Group Theory)
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\phi: G \times X \to X$ be a group action: $\forall \tuple {g, x} \in G \times X: g * x := \map \phi {g, x} \in X$ Let $f: X \to X$ be a mapping. Then $F$ is an automorphic function : $\forall \tuple {g, x} \in G \times X: \map f {g * x} = \map f x$

label: Definition:Automorphic Number
snippet: An automorphic number is a positive integer all of whose powers end in that number.

label: Definition:Automorphic Number/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Automorphic Numbers == The sequence of automorphic numbers begins as:

label: Definition:Automorphism (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: An automorphism is an isomorphism from an algebraic structure to itself. This applies to the term isomorphism as used both in the sense of bijective homomorphism as well as that of an order isomorphism. Hence an automorphism is a permutation which is either a homomorphism or an order isomorphism, depending on context.

label: Definition:Automorphism (Abstract Algebra)/Also defined as
snippet: == Automorphism: Also defined as == An automorphism is defined by some sources as: a bijection mapping the elements of a set onto itself, so the domain and codomain are the same that is, as defines a permutation. However, this makes no mention of the structure imposed on that set, which is essential for this definition to be of any use.

label: Definition:Automorphism Group/Group
snippet: Let $\struct {S, *}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\mathbb S$ be the set of automorphisms of $S$. Then the algebraic structure $\struct {\mathbb S, \circ}$, where $\circ$ denotes composition of mappings, is called the automorphism group of $S$. The structure $\struct {S, *}$ is usually a group. However, this is not necessary for this definition to be valid.

label: Definition:Autoregressive Model

label: Definition:Autoregressive Model/Autoregressive Operator

Let the values of $S$ at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ be $z_t, z_{t - 1}, z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ Let $\tilde z_t, \tilde z_{t - 1}, \tilde z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be deviations from a constant mean level $\mu$: $\tilde z_t = z_t - \mu$ Let $a_t, a_{t - 1}, a_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be a sequence of independent shocks at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ Let $M$ be an autoregessive model on $S$ of order $p$: $\tilde z_t = \phi_1 \tilde z_{t - 1} + \phi_2 \tilde z_{t - 2} + \dotsb + \phi_p \tilde z_{t - p} + a_t$ The parameters of…

label: Definition:Auxiliary
snippet: Differential equations: Auxiliary equation Order theory: Auxiliary relation Geometry: Auxiliary circle Trigonometry: Auxiliary angle

label: Definition:Auxiliary Circle
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a central conic, that is, an ellipse or a hyperbola. The auxiliary circle of $\KK$ is the eccentric circle whose diameter coincides with the major axis of $\KK$.

label: Definition:Auxiliary Circle/Ellipse
snippet: Let $E$ be an ellipse. The auxiliary circle of $E$ is the eccentric circle whose diameter coincides with the major axis of $E$: 400px In the above diagram, the auxiliary circle of $E$ is the circle $C$.

label: Definition:Auxiliary Circle/Hyperbola
snippet: Let $H$ be a hyperbola. The auxiliary circle of $H$ is the eccentric circle whose diameter coincides with the major axis of $H$: 400px In the above diagram, the auxiliary circle of $H$ is the circle $C$.

label: Definition:Auxiliary Equation
snippet: Let: $(1): \quad y' ' + p y' + q y = 0$ be a constant coefficient homogeneous linear second order ODE. The auxiliary equation of $(1)$ is the quadratic equation: $m^2 + p m + q = 0$

label: Definition:Average Acceleration
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion. Let $\Bbb I = \closedint {t_1} {t_2}$ be a time interval. Let $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ be the velocity of $B$ at $t_1$ and $t_2$ respectively. The average acceleration of $B$ during $\Bbb I$ is defined as the change of velocity during $\Bbb I$ divided by the length of $\Bbb I$: $\overline {\mathbf a} := \dfrac {\mathbf v_2 - \mathbf v_1} {t_2 - t_2}$

label: Definition:Average Velocity
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion. Let $\Bbb I = \closedint {t_1} {t_2}$ be a time interval. Let $\mathbf s_1$ and $\mathbf s_2$ be the displacement of $B$ at $t_1$ and $t_2$ respectively. The average velocity of $B$ during $\Bbb I$ is defined as the change of displacement during $\Bbb I$ divided by the length of $\Bbb I$: $\overline {\mathbf v} := \dfrac {\mathbf s_2 - \mathbf s_1} {t_2 - t_2}$

label: Definition:Axiom
snippet: In all contexts, the definition of the term axiom is by and large the same. That is, an axiom is a statement which is accepted as being true. A statement that is considered an axiom can be described as being axiomatic.

label: Definition:Axiom/Nonlogical
snippet: An axiom which deals with some specific subject matter is known as a nonlogical axiom. Hence it is a statement which is accepted as true for a particular branch of mathematics. Different fields of mathematics usually have different sets of statements which are considered as being axiomatic. So statements which are taken as axioms in one branch of mathematics may be theorems, or irrelevant, in others.

label: Definition:Axiomatic Set Theory
snippet: Axiomatic set theory is a system of set theory which differs from so-called naive set theory in that the sets which are allowed to be generated are strictly constrained by the axioms. The best known systems of axiomatic set theory are: ZF (Zermelo-Fraenkel) ZFC (Zermelo-Fraenkel with the Axiom of Choice). Lesser known examples include: Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel Set Theory

label: Definition:Axiomatization
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be an $\LL$-theory. An axiomatization of $\FF$ is a subset $\AA \subseteq \FF$ such that: $\FF = \set {\phi \in \LL: \AA \models_{\mathscr M} \phi}$ That is, all of $\FF$ is a semantic consequence of $\AA$.

label: Definition:Axis/Positive Direction
snippet: Consider a coordinate system whose axes are each aligned with an instance of the real number line $\R$. The direction along an axis in which the corresponding elements of $\R$ are increasing is called the positive direction. Category:Definitions/Coordinate Axes

label: Definition:Axis/X-Axis
snippet: In a cartesian coordinate system, the $x$-axis is the one usually depicted and visualised as going from left to right. It consists of all the points in the real vector space in question (usually either $\R^2$ or $\R^3$) at which all the elements of its coordinates but $x$ are zero.

label: Definition:Axis/Y-Axis
snippet: In a cartesian coordinate system, the $y$-axis is the one usually depicted and visualised as going from "bottom" to "top" of the paper (or screen). It consists of all the points in the real vector space in question (usually either $\R^2$ or $\R^3$) at which all the elements of its coordinates but $y$ are zero.

label: Definition:Axis/Z-Axis
snippet: In a cartesian coordinate system, the $z$-axis is the axis passing through $x = 0, y = 0$ which is perpendicular to both the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis. It consists of all the points in the real vector space in question (usually $\R^3$) at which all the elements of its coordinates but $z$ are zero. As the visual field is effectively two-dimensional, it is not possible to depict a three-dimensional space on a visual presentation (paper, screen and so on) directly. Therefore the representation of the third axis of such a cartesian coordinate system is necessarily a compromise.

label: Definition:Axis of Pencil of Planes
snippet: The line of intersection of a pencil of planes $P$ is called the axis of $P$.

label: Definition:Azimuth (Astronomy)
snippet: Let $X$ be a point on the celestial sphere. The spherical angle between the principal vertical circle and the vertical circle on which $X$ lies is the azimuth of $X$. The azimuth is usually measured in degrees, $0 \degrees$ to $180 \degrees$ either west or east, depending on whether $X$ lies on the eastern or western hemisphere of the celestial sphere.

label: Definition:BIDMAS
snippet: BIDMAS is a mnemonic for determining the binding priority of the operations of arithmetic: $(1): \quad$ Brackets $(2): \quad$ Indices $(3)$ and $(4): \quad$ Division and Multiplication $(5)$ and $(6): \quad$ Addition and Subtraction

label: Definition:Babylonian Clay Tablets/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Babylonian Clay Tablets == There are about a million Babylonian clay tablets that have been dug up from the ground in . Of these, a few hundred are concerned with mathematics and astronomy. They indicate that the had a sophisticated knowledge of astronomy, and a number system which could express numbers to high precision. They also indicate that they had the knowledge of how to solve quadratic equations.

label: Definition:Babylonian Mathematics
snippet: Babylonian mathematics is the name given to the mathematics of the . Its content was arithmetical and algebraical, and considerably in advance of the mathematics of the approximately contemporaneous .

label: Definition:Babylonian Number System/Also denoted as
snippet: == Babylonian Number System: Also denoted as == When representing numbers using the Babylonian number system, it is laborious to represent the actual symbols themselves. Hence it is commonplace to use their decimal counterparts, separated by commas, so that the number represented, for example, in as: 30px 30px 30px would be represented as: $7, 7, 7$ In such a system, the radix point is represented by a semicolon.

label: Definition:Back-Substitution
snippet: Let $S$ be a system of simultaneous linear equations: $\ds \forall i \in \closedint 1 m: \sum _{j \mathop = 1}^n {\alpha_{i j} x_j} = \beta_i$ where all of $\alpha_1, \ldots, a_n, x_1, \ldots x_n, \beta_i, \ldots, \beta_m$ are elements of a field $K$. Let $S$ be expressed in matrix representation: $\sqbrk \alpha_{m n} \sqbrk x_{n 1} = \sqbrk \beta_{m 1}$ where $\sqbrk a_{m n}$ is an $m \times n$ matrix in echelon form.

label: Definition:Backward Path (Class Theory)
snippet: Let $A$ be a class under a total ordering $\preccurlyeq$. Let $S = \sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $A$ (either finite or infinite) such that: $\forall i \in \N: x_i \in S \implies x_{i + 1} \prec x_i$ Then $S$ is referred to as a backward path of $\preccurlyeq$ (in $A$).

label: Definition:Backward Reparametrization of Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $I, I' \subseteq \R$ be real intervals. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Let $\phi : I' \to I$ be a diffeomorphism. Let $\tilde \gamma$ be a curve defined by: $\tilde \gamma := \gamma \circ \phi : I' \to M$ where $\circ$ denotes the composition of mappings $\gamma$ and $\phi$. Suppose $\phi$ is decreasing. Then $\tilde \gamma$ is called the backward reparametrization of $\gamma$.

label: Definition:Baire Category
snippet: The Baire category of a topological space $T$ is a way of specifying how dense $T$ is:

label: Definition:Baire Category/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Baire Category == The concept of categorizing topological spaces into meager and non-meager was introduced by , during his work to define what is now known as a Baire space. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Baire Function
snippet: Let $X \subseteq \R$. For each $n$, let $f_n : X \to \R$ be a continuous function. Suppose that the sequence $\sequence {f_n}$ converges pointwise to a function $f : X \to \R$. We call $f$ a Baire function.

label: Definition:Baire Product Metric
snippet: Let $X := \R^\omega$ be the set defined as: $\ds \R^\omega = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty \R_i$ where each $\R_i$ is a copy of the real number line under the Euclidean metric. We define the Baire product metric on $X$ as: $\map d {\family {x_i}, \family {y_i} } = \dfrac 1 j$ where $j \in \N$ is the smallest such that $x_j \ne y_j$.

label: Definition:Baire Property
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then $H$ has the Baire property there exists an open set $U \in \tau$ such that the symmetric difference $U \symdif H$ is meager.

label: Definition:Baire Space
snippet: A Baire Space (Topology): A topological space such that the intersection of each countable collection of open subsets which are everywhere dense is also everywhere dense. The Baire Space (Set Theory): The set of all infinite sequences of natural numbers.

label: Definition:Baire Space (Set Theory)
snippet: The Baire space $\mathbf B$ is defined as the set of all infinite sequences of natural numbers. It can also be defined as the Cartesian product of a countably infinite number of copies of the set of natural numbers.

label: Definition:Baire Space (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a Baire space the union of any countable set of closed sets of $T$ whose interiors are empty also has an empty interior.

label: Definition:Baire Space (Topology)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a Baire space the intersection of any countable set of open sets of $T$ which are everywhere dense is everywhere dense.

label: Definition:Baire Space (Topology)/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a Baire space the interior of the union of any countable set of closed sets of $T$ which are nowhere dense is empty.

label: Definition:Baire Space (Topology)/Definition 4
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a Baire space , whenever the union of any countable set of closed sets of $T$ has an interior point, then one of those closed sets must have an interior point.

label: Definition:Baker's Dozen
snippet: A baker's dozen is another name for a set whose cardinality is $13$.

label: Definition:Balance
snippet: A balance is a tool for measuring the mass of a body by comparing its weight against that of a set of weights whose mass is known. 600px

label: Definition:Balanced Hull
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $A \subseteq X$ be a non-empty set. We define the balanced hull of $A$ as the $\subseteq$-smallest balanced set containing $A$. We denote this by: $\map {\operatorname {bal} } A$

label: Definition:Balanced Prime/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\left({p_{n - 1}, p_n, p_{n + 1} }\right)$ be a triplet of consecutive prime numbers. $p_n$ is a balanced prime : $p_n = \dfrac {p_{n - 1} + p_{n + 1} } 2$ $p$ is a balanced prime it is the arithmetic mean of the prime numbers on either side of it.

label: Definition:Balanced Prime/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\paren {p_{n - 1}, p_n, p_{n + 1} }$ be a triplet of consecutive prime numbers. $p_n$ is a balanced prime : {{eqn | l = p_{n - 1} + d | r = p_n | c = }} {{eqn | l = p_{n - 1} + 2 d | r = p_{n + 1} | c = }} for some $d \in \Z$. That is, $p_n$ is the middle term of a $3$-term arithmetic sequence in which the $1$st and last terms are the previous and following primes.

label: Definition:Balanced Prime/Definition 3
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. $p$ is a balanced prime the prime gaps either side of it are equal.

label: Definition:Balanced Set
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $A \subseteq X$. We say that $A$ is balanced : $s A \subseteq A$ for all $s \in \GF$ with $\cmod s \le 1$ where $s A$ is the dilation of $A$ by $s$.

label: Definition:Balanced Set/Also defined as
snippet: == Balanced Set: Also defined as == A subset $A$ of a vector space $V$ over a field $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$ is also by some sources defined as a balanced set : $\forall x \in A: \forall s \in \GF: \cmod s < 1 \implies s x \in A$

label: Definition:Balanced Signed Graph
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a signed graph. Then $G$ is balanced it is possible to partition $V$ into two subsets $A, B$ such that: the positive edges have both ends in $A$ or both ends in $B$; the negative edges have one end in $A$ and the other end $B$. It is a frequent practice to apply a different colour to the vertices in each set to enhance clarity.

label: Definition:Balanced Ternary Representation
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Balanced ternary representation is the unique representation of $n$ in the form: $\sqbrk {r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0}$ such that: $\ds n = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^m r_j 3^j$ where: $m \in \Z_{>0}$ is a strictly positive integer such that $3^m \le \size n < 3^{m + 1}$ all the $r_j$ are such that $r_j \in \set {\underline 1, 0, 1}$, where $\underline 1 := -1$.

label: Definition:Ball/Also known as
snippet: == Ball: Also known as == Instead of ball, some sources use the term disk (or disc in British English), and prefer to use $\Bbb D$ for $B$. Some sources use disk (or disc) specifically to mean closed ball, and use open disk (or open disc) for open ball. prefers to reserve the term disk, if at all, for a disk in the complex plane, as there is an intuitive $2$-dimensional nuance to the word disk, while ball guides intuition down the path of $3$ dimensions.

label: Definition:Ballistics
snippet: Ballistics is the branch of applied mathematics involved in the study of the motion of projectiles.

label: Definition:Banach *-Algebra
snippet:
Let $\struct {A, \ast}$ be a $\ast$-algebra over $\C$. Let $
orm {\, \cdot \,}$ be an algebra norm on $A$ such that $\struct {A, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ is a Banach algebra and: $
orm {a^\ast} = 
orm a$ for each $a \in A$. We say that $\struct {A, \ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ a Banach $\ast$-algebra.

label: Definition:Banach Algebra
snippet:
Let $R$ be either the real numbers $\R$ or the complex numbers $\C$.. Let $\struct {A, \circ}$ be an algebra over $R$ which is also a Banach space. Then $\struct {A, \circ}$ is a Banach algebra : $ orall a, b \in R: 
orm {a \circ b} \le 
orm a 
orm b$ where $
orm {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the norm on $A$.

label: Definition:Banach Algebra/Also known as
snippet: == Banach Algebra: Also known as == Some sources refer to a Banach algebra as a normed ring, but on this term is used to mean a ring with a norm on it.

label: Definition:Banach Algebra of Continuous Functions on Compact Hausdorff Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a compact $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space. Let $\map \CC X = \map \CC {X, \C}$ be the vector space of continuous functions on $X$. Let $\ast$ be pointwise multiplication on $\C^X$. Let $\norm {\, \cdot \,}$ be the supremum norm on $\map \CC X$. We call $\struct {\map \CC X, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ the Banach algebra of continuous functions on $X$.

label: Definition:Banach Limit
snippet:
Let $\struct {\map {\ell^\infty} \R, 
orm \cdot_\infty}$ be the normed vector space of bounded sequences on $\R$. Let $\struct {\paren {\map {\ell^\infty} \R}^\ast, 
orm \cdot_{\paren {\ell^\infty}^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {\map {\ell^\infty} \R, 
orm \cdot_\infty}$. Let $S: \map {\ell^\infty} \R 	o \map {\ell^\infty} \R$ be the left shift operator on $\map {\ell^\infty} \R$. Let $\mathbf 1$ be the sequence with ${\mathbf 1}_n = 1$ for each $n \in \N$.

label: Definition:Banach Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu: \Sigma \to \overline \R$ be a mapping, where $\overline \R$ denotes the set of extended real numbers. {{axiom | n = 2 | q = \forall n \in \N: \forall \tuple {S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n} \subseteq \Sigma: \forall i, j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}: S_i \cap S_j = \O | ml= \map \mu {\bigcup_{k \mathop = 1}^n S_k} | mo= = | mr= \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \map \mu {S_k} | rc= that is, $\mu$ is a finitely additive function }}

label: Definition:Banach Space
snippet: A Banach space is a complete normed vector space. That is, a Banach space is a normed vector space where every Cauchy sequence is convergent.

label: Definition:Banach Space/Also defined as
snippet: == Banach Space: Also defined as == Some sources additionally specify that the normed vector space over which a Banach space is defined also has to be over the real or complex numbers. This distinction is of limited importance, as it is vanishingly rare for a Banach space to be used in a different context.

label: Definition:Band Matrix
snippet: A band matrix is a matrix whose elements outside a band of diagonals around the leading diagonal are all zero.

label: Definition:Bar
snippet: Statistics Bar of a bar chart: one of the vertical or horizontal lines or rectangles to indicate a statistic. Physics: Bar: a unit of measurement of atmospheric pressure. Mechanics: Bar: a straight rigid body whose length in one dimension is substantially greater than its width in the other two dimensions.

label: Definition:Barrel (Vector Space)
snippet: Let $V$ be a normed vector space or a topological vector space. Let $W \subseteq V$ be a subset of $V$. Then $W$ is a barrel : $W$ is closed $W$ is convex $W$ is absorbing $W$ is balanced.

label: Definition:Barycenter (Locally Convex Space)
snippet: Let $X$ be a locally convex vector space over $\R$. Let $K \subseteq X$ be a convex subset. Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $K$. Then $x \in K$ is the barycenter of $\mu$ : $\ds \forall \ell \in X^\ast : \map \ell x = \int_K \map \ell u \rd \map \mu u$ where: $X^\ast$ is the dual space of $X$ It is also said that $\mu$ represents $x$ in the weak sense.

label: Definition:Barycentric Coordinate Interpolation
snippet: Let $\tuple {x_0, x_1, ..., x_k}$ be a set of $k+1$ affinely independent points in $\mathbb R^k$. Let $f : \mathbb R^k \to \mathbb R$ be a real-valued function. Let $\tuple {y_0, y_1, ..., y_k}$ be a set of $k+1$ known values of $f$ at $x_0, x_1, ..., x_k$, respectively. Let $x'$ be a point in $\mathbb R^k$. Let the barycentric coordinates of $x'$ $\tuple {x_0, x_1, ..., x_k}$ be $\tuple {\lambda_0, \lambda_1, ..., \lambda_k}$. Then, the barycentric coordinate interpolation of $f$ at $x'$ is given by $\ds y' = \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^k \lambda_i y_i$

label: Definition:Barycentric Coordinates
snippet: Barycentric coordinates are a set of numbers representing the position of a point in a Euclidean space a set of fixed points. In $n$ dimensional space a total of $n + 1$ points must be used.

label: Definition:Barycentric Coordinates/2 Dimensions
snippet: In the plane, barycentric coordinates are a set of $3$ numbers representing the position of a point as follows: Let $\mathbf a$, $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ be the position vectors of the $3$ vertices of a triangle in the plane. Then the position vector of an arbitrary point $p$ can be expressed uniquely in the form: $\mathbf p = \alpha \mathbf a + \beta \mathbf b + \gamma \mathbf c$ such that: $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1$ The set $\set {\alpha, \beta, \gamma}$ consists of the barycentric coordinates of $p$.

label: Definition:Barycentric Coordinates/3 Dimensions
snippet: In $3$ dimensional space, barycentric coordinates are a set of $4$ numbers representing the position of a point as follows: Let $p_0, p_1, p_2, p_3$ be fixed non-coplanar points, such that $p_i = \tuple {x_i, y_1, z_i}$. Then an arbitrary point $p$ can be expressed in the form: $p = \lambda_0 p_0 + \lambda_1 p_1 + \lambda_2 p_2 + \lambda_3 p_3$ such that: $\lambda_0 + \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 = 1$ The set $\set {\lambda_0, \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3}$ consists of the barycentric coordinates of $p$.

label: Definition:Barycentric Refinement
snippet: Let $\CC \subseteq \powerset S$ be a cover for a set $S$.

label: Definition:Barycentric Refinement/Also known as
snippet: == Barycentric Refinement: Also known as == A barycentric refinement of $\CC$ over a set $S$ is also known as a star refinement by some authors. However, a star refinement is generally defined a general subset of $S$, rather than a single element.

label: Definition:Barycentric Refinement/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\CC \subseteq \powerset S$ be a cover for a set $S$. $\VV$ is a barycentric refinement of $\CC$ $\VV$ is a cover for $S$ such that: $\forall x \in S: \exists U \in \CC: \Star x \VV \subseteq U$ where $\Star x \VV$ is the star of $x$ with respect to $\VV$.

label: Definition:Barycentric Refinement/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\CC \subseteq \powerset S$ be a cover for a set $S$. $\VV$ is a barycentric refinement of $\CC$ $\VV$ is a refinement of $\CC$ such that: $\VV = \set {\Star x \VV: x \in S}$ where $\Star x \VV$ is the star of $x$ with respect to $\VV$.

label: Definition:Base
snippet: Geometry: The base of a geometric figure, for example: Base of a triangle (Plane geometry) Base of an isosceles triangle (Plane geometry) Base of a parallelogram (Plane geometry) Base of a segment of a circle (Plane geometry) Base of a cone (Solid geometry) Base of a right circular cone (Solid geometry) Base of a pyramid (Solid geometry) Base of a hemisphere (Solid geometry) Base angles of an isosceles triangle (Plane geometry) Number theory: Number Base (Number theory and arithmetic) Analysis: Base of Logarithm Matroid Theory: Base of Matroid

label: Definition:Base Field (Linear Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a vector space, where: $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ is a field $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group $\struct {G, +_G}$ $\ast: K \times G \to G$ is a binary operation. Then the field $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ is called the base field of $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$. If the base field is understood, then $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ can be rendered $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}$.

label: Definition:Basic Null Sequence
snippet: The sequences defined as: $\sequence {\dfrac 1 {n^r} }_{n \mathop \in \N}$ for $r \in \R: r > 0$ $\sequence {\alpha^n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ for $\alpha \in \C: \cmod {\alpha} < 1$ are known as the basic null sequences.

label: Definition:Basic Open Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\BB \subseteq \tau$ be a basis for $T$. Let $U \in \BB$. Then $U$ is a basic open set of $T$. That is, a basic open set of a topology is an open set of that topology which is an element of a basis for that topology. The basis itself needs to be specified for this definition to make sense. Category:Definitions/Topology Category:Definitions/Topological Bases

label: Definition:Basic Proposition
snippet: Let $f: \mathbb B^k \to \mathbb B$ be a boolean function, where: $\mathbb B = \set {0, 1}$ is a boolean domain $k$ is a natural number. A basic proposition is one of the projection functions $\pr_j: \mathbb B^k \to \mathbb B$, defined as follows: Let $X = \tuple {p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k} \in \mathbb B^k$. Then: $\map {\pr_j} X = p_j$ That is, a basic proposition is one of the elements of the $k$-tuple $\tuple {p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k}$.

label: Definition:Basic Sequence
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be an normed vector space over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $\sqbrk {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be the closed linear span of $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We say that $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a basic sequence if it is a Schauder basis for $\sqbrk {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$.

label: Definition:Basic WFF of Predicate Logic
snippet: Let $\LL$ be the language of predicate logic. A WFF $\mathbf A$ of $\LL$ is called basic it does not start with a logical connective. Basic WFFs are useful to consider as atoms when analysing propositional logic within the larger context of predicate logic. Expressed more formally, we can take the basic WFFs as the vocabulary of the language of propositional logic. Do note that e.g. $\forall x: x = x \land x = x$ is considered basic even though it contains the logical connective $\land$. This is because $\land$ is not the main connective.

label: Definition:Basis
snippet: Topology Basis (Topology) Linear Algebra: Basis (Linear Algebra): Definition:Basis of Vector Space Definition:Basis of Module Definition:Basis of Square Matrix Hilbert Spaces: Basis (Hilbert Space) Definition:Transcendence Basis

label: Definition:Basis/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Basis == The plural of basis is bases. This is properly pronounced bay-seez, not bay-siz.

label: Definition:Basis (Hilbert Space)
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. A basis for $H$ is a maximal orthonormal subset of $H$. Thus, $B$ is a basis for $H$ for all orthonormal subsets $B'$ of $H$: $B \subseteq B' \implies B = B'$

label: Definition:Basis (Linear Algebra)/Also known as
snippet: == Basis in context of Linear Algebra: Also known as == The phrase basis for $G$ can also be seen instead of basis of $G$.

label: Definition:Basis (Topology)/Specification of Topology
snippet: As a way of specifying a particular topology on a set, we can say: Let $\tau$ be the topology which has the sets ... as a basis. In such a case, those sets should all satisfy the axioms for a synthetic basis $\paren {\text B 1}$ and $\paren {\text B 2}$.

label: Definition:Basis (Topology)/Synthetic Basis
snippet: == Definition == Let $S$ be a set.

label: Definition:Basis Constant
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a Schauder basis for $X$. Let $\sequence {S_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be the projections associated with $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. Let $\map \BB X$ be the space of bounded linear transformations on $X$. Let $
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{\map \BB X}$ be the norm on $\map \BB X$. We define the basis constant for $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$, $K_b$, by: $\ds K_b = \sup_{n \mathop \in \N} 
orm {S_n}_{\map \BB X}$

label: Definition:Basis Expansion/Negative Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x \in \R: x < 0$. We take the absolute value $y$ of $x$, that is: $y = \size x$ Then we take the expansion of $y$ in base $b$: $\size {s . d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ where $s = \floor y$. Finally, the expansion of $x$ in base $b$ is defined as: $-\sqbrk {s . d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$

label: Definition:Basis Expansion/Positive Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \ge 0$. Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let us define the recursive sequence: $\forall n \in \N: n \ge 1: \sequence {f_n} = \begin {cases} b \paren {x - \floor x} & : n = 1 \\ b \paren {f_{n - 1} - \floor {f_{n - 1} } } & : n > 1 \end{cases}$ Then we define: $\forall n \in \N: n \ge 1: \sequence {d_n} = \floor {f_n}$ It follows from the method of construction and the definition of the floor function that: $\forall n: 0 \le f_n < b$ and hence $\forall n: 0 \le d_n \le b - 1$ $\forall n: f_n = 0 \implies f_{n + 1} = 0$ and hence $d_{n + 1} = 0$.

label: Definition:Basis Expansion/Recurrence
snippet: Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let $x$ be a real number. Let the basis expansion of $x$ in base $b$ be: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ Let there be a finite sequence of $p$ digits of $x$: $\tuple {d_{r + 1} d_{r + 1} \ldots d_{r + p} }$ such that for all $k \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ and for all $j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, p}$: $d_{r + j + k p} = d_{r + j}$ where $p$ is the smallest $p$ to have this property.

label: Definition:Basis Expansion/Recurrence/Non-Recurring Part
snippet: Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let $x$ be a real number. Let the basis expansion of $x$ in base $b$ be recurring: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots d_r d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p} d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p } d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p} d_{r + 1} \ldots}_b$ The non-recurring part of $x$ is: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots d_r}$

label: Definition:Basis Expansion/Recurrence/Notation
snippet: Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let $x$ be a real number. Let the basis expansion of $x$ in base $b$ be: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ such that $x$ is recurring. Let the non-recurring part of $x$ be: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots d_r}_b$ Let the recurring part of $x$ be: $\sqbrk {\ldots d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p} \ldots}_b$ Then $x$ is denoted: $x = s.d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots d_r \dot d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots \dot d_{r + p}$ That is, a dot is placed over the first and last digit of the first instance of the recurring part. This notation is referred to as recurrence notation

label: Definition:Basis Expansion/Recurrence/Period
snippet: Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let $x$ be a rational number. Let the basis expansion of $x$ in base $b$ be: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ From Basis Expansion of Rational Number, $x$ either terminates or recurs. The period of recurrence is the number of digits in the recurring part after which it repeats itself. Category:Definitions/Basis Expansions

label: Definition:Basis Expansion/Recurrence/Recurring Part
snippet: Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. Let $x$ be a real number. Let the basis expansion of $x$ in base $b$ be recurring: $\sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots d_r d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p} d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p } d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p} d_{r + 1} \ldots}_b$ The recurring part of $x$ is: $\sqbrk {d_{r + 1} d_{r + 2} \ldots d_{r + p}}$

label: Definition:Basis Representation
snippet: Let $b \in \Z$ be an integer such that $b > 1$. Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer such that $n \ne 0$. The (basis) representation of $n$ to the base $b$ is the unique string of digits: $\pm \sqbrk {r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0}_b$ where $\pm$ is: the negative sign $-$ $n 0$ If $n = 0$, then $n$ is represented simply as $0$.

label: Definition:Basis Vector
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_K$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $\BB$ be a basis of $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_K$. Let $\mathbf v$ be an element of $\BB$. Then $\mathbf v$ is known as a basis vector of $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_K$ ( $\BB$).

label: Definition:Basis for Neighborhood System
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $a \in A$ be a point in $M$. Let $\BB_a$ be a set of neighborhoods of $a$ in $M$. Then $\BB_a$ is a basis for the neighborhood system at $a$ : $\forall N_a \subseteq M: \exists B \in \BB_a: B \subseteq N_a$ where $N_a$ denotes a neighborhood of $a$ in $M$. That is, $\BB_a$ is a basis for the neighborhood system at $a$ every neighborhood of $a$ contains an element of $\BB_a$ as a subset.

label: Definition:Basis for Open Sets (Metric Space)
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\BB$ be a set of open sets of $M$. Then $\BB$ is a basis for the open sets of $M$ : for each open set $U$ of $M$, $U$ is the union of sets of $\BB$.

label: Definition:Basis for the Induction
snippet: == Terminology of Mathematical Induction == Consider a proof by mathematical induction: The step that establishes the truth of $Q$ for $w_0$ is called the basis for the induction. Expressed in the various contexts of mathematical induction:

label: Definition:Basis of Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be a unitary $R$-module.

label: Definition:Basis of Module/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be a unitary $R$-module. A basis of $G$ is a linearly independent subset of $G$ which is a generator for $G$.

label: Definition:Basis of Module/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be a unitary $R$-module. Let $\BB = \family {b_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of elements of $M$. Let $\Psi: R^{\paren I} \to M$ be the homomorphism given by Universal Property of Free Module on Set. Then $\BB$ is a basis of $G$ $\Psi$ is an isomorphism.

label: Definition:Basis of Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_K$ be a vector space over $K$.

label: Definition:Basis of Vector Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be an vector space over $R$. A basis of $G$ is a linearly independent subset of $G$ which is a generator for $G$.

label: Definition:Basis of Vector Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be an vector space over $R$. A basis is a maximal linearly independent subset of $G$.

label: Definition:Bayes' Factor
snippet: Let $D$ be a set of data which may be assumed to have arisen from one of only $2$ possible models: $M_1$ or $M_2$. Let the prior probabilities of $M_1$ and $M_2$ be denoted $\map \Pr {M_1}$ and $\map \Pr {M_2}$ such that $\map \Pr {M_2} = 1 - \map \Pr {M_1}$. Let the posterior probabilities be denoted $\condprob {M_1} D$ and $\condprob {M_2} D$ such that $\condprob {M_2} D = 1 - \condprob {M_1} D$.

label: Definition:Bayesian Decision Theory
snippet: Bayesian decision theory is a branch of decision theory which is informed by Bayesian probability. It is a statistical system that tries to quantify the tradeoff between various decisions, making use of probabilities and costs.

label: Definition:Bayesian Probability Model
snippet: The Bayesian probability model is a mathematical model that defines the probability of an event occurring as a degree of belief. That is, that probability is defined as the degree of which it is rational to believe certain statements based on intuition, experience, judgment, or opinion.

label: Definition:Bayesian Statistics
snippet: Bayesian statistics is a type of statistics in which the parameters of the probability distributions themselves are considered as having probability distributions.

label: Definition:Bearing
snippet: Let $A$ be a point on the surface of Earth such that $P$ is neither the North Pole nor the South Pole. Let $B$ be another point on the surface of Earth. The bearing of $B$ $A$ is defined as the angle measured clockwise between $AB$ and $AN$, where $N$ is the North Pole. 300px

label: Definition:Bearing/Warning
snippet: == Bearing: Warning == For the concept of a bearing to make proper sense, it is important to note that $B$ must be sufficiently close to $A$ so as to allow the surface of Earth to be approximated to a plane. Category:Definitions/Bearing

label: Definition:Beatty Sequence/Complementary
snippet: Let $x$ be an irrational number. Let $\BB_x$ be the Beatty sequence on $x$. The complementary Beatty sequence on $x$ is the integer sequence formed by the integers which are missing from $\BB_x$.

label: Definition:Bei Function
snippet: Let $J_n$ denote the Bessel function of the first kind. The Bei function is defined as: $\map {\Bei_n} x = \map \Im {\map {J_n} {x \map \exp {\dfrac {3 \pi i} 4} } }$ where: $\exp$ denotes the exponential function $x$ is real $\map \Im z$ denotes the imaginary part of $z$.

label: Definition:Bell Number
snippet: The Bell Numbers $B_n$ are a sequence of natural numbers defined as the number of ways a set with $n$ elements can be partitioned.

label: Definition:Below
snippet: Numbers: Number $a$ is below number $b$ $a$ is less than $b$. Solid Geometry: Point $a$ is below point $b$ the height of $a$ a given frame of reference $R$ is less than the height of $b$ $R$. Plane Geometry: Point $a$ is below Point $b$ the $y$ coordinate of $a$ is less than the $y$ coordinate of $b$.

label: Definition:Below (Number)
snippet: In the context of numbers, below means less than. Note that this applies to: the natural numbers $\N$ the integers $\Z$ the rational numbers $\Q$ the real numbers $\R$ but specifically not the complex numbers $\C$ because the complex numbers do not have a usual ordering.

label: Definition:Below (Plane Geometry)
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be points in the cartesian plane $\R^2$. Then: $a$ is below $b$ the $y$ coordinate of $a$ is less than the $y$ coordinate of $b$.

label: Definition:Below (Solid Geometry)
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be points in $3$-dimensional Euclidean space $\R^3$. Let $P$ be an arbitrary plane embedded in $S$ be distinguished and defined as horizontal. Then: $a$ is below $b$ the height of $a$ $P$ is less than the height of $b$ $P$.

label: Definition:Ber Function
snippet: Let $J_n$ denote the Bessel function of the first kind. The Ber function is defined as: $\map {\Ber_n} x = \map \Re {\map {J_n} {x \map \exp {\dfrac {3 \pi i} 4} } }$ where: $\exp$ denotes the exponential function $x$ is real $\map \Re z$ denotes the real part of $z$.

label: Definition:Bernoulli's Equation (Fluid Mechanics)
snippet: Bernoulli's equation is a statement of conservation of energy in the context of fluid mechanics: $\ds \int \dfrac {\d p} \rho + \dfrac 1 2 v^2 + V = C$ where: $p$ is the pressure of the fluid $\rho$ is the density of the fluid $V$ is the gravitational potential $C$ is constant for a given stream line.

label: Definition:Bernoulli Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable on a probability space. Then $X$ has the Bernoulli distribution with parameter $p$ : $(1): \quad X$ has exactly two possible values, for example $\Img X = \set {a, b}$ $(2): \quad \map \Pr {X = a} = p$ $(3): \quad \map \Pr {X = b} = 1 - p$ where $0 \le p \le 1$. That is, the probability mass function is given by: $\map {p_X} x = \begin {cases} p & : x = a \\ 1 - p & : x = b \\ 0 & : x \notin \set {a, b} \\ \end {cases}$ If we allow: $\Img X = \set {0, 1}$ then we can write: $\map {p_X} x = p^x \paren {1 - p}^{1 - x}$
