label: Definition:Bernoulli Numbers/Generating Function
snippet: The Bernoulli numbers $B_n$ are a sequence of rational numbers defined by the exponential generating function: $\ds \frac x {e^x - 1} = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {B_n x^n} {n!}$

label: Definition:Bernoulli Numbers/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bernoulli Numbers == The Bernoulli numbers were introduced by in his investigations into the power series expansion of the tangent function.

label: Definition:Bernoulli Numbers/Recurrence Relation
snippet: The Bernoulli numbers $B_n$ are a sequence of rational numbers defined by the recurrence relation: $B_n = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 0 \\ \ds - \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \binom n k \frac {B_k} {n + 1 - k} & : n > 0 \end {cases}$ or equivalently: $B_n = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 0 \\ \ds - \frac 1 {n + 1} \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \binom {n + 1} k B_k & : n > 0 \end {cases}$

label: Definition:Bernoulli Numbers/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Bernoulli numbers begins: {{eqn | l = B_4 | ro= - | r = \dfrac 1 {30} | c = }} {{eqn | l = B_6 | r = \dfrac 1 {42} | c = }} {{eqn | l = B_8 | ro= - | r = \dfrac 1 {30} | c = }} {{eqn | l = B_{10} | r = \dfrac 5 {66} | c = }} {{eqn | l = B_{12} | ro= - | r = \dfrac {691} {2730} | c = }} The odd index Bernoulli numbers, apart from $B_1$, are all equal to $0$.

label: Definition:Bernoulli Polynomial
snippet: The Bernoulli polynomials $\map {B_n} x$ are the terms of the sequence of polynomials defined as: $\ds \map {B_n} x = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n \binom n k B_{n - k} x^k$ where $B_k$ are the Bernoulli numbers.

label: Definition:Bernoulli Trial
snippet: A Bernoulli trial is an experiment whose sample space has two elements, which can be variously described, for example, as: Success and failure True and False $1$ and $0$ the classic heads and tails. Formally, a Bernoulli trial is modelled by a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ such that: $\Omega = \set {a, b}$ $\Sigma = \powerset \Omega$ $\map \Pr a = p, \map \Pr b = 1 - p$ where: $\powerset \Omega$ denotes the power set of $\Omega$ $0 \le p \le 1$ That is, $\Pr$ obeys a Bernoulli distribution.

label: Definition:Bessel's Equation
snippet: == Equation == Bessel's equation is a second order ODE of the form: $x^2 \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + \paren {x^2 - n^2} y = 0$ The parameter $n$ may be any arbitrary real or complex number.

label: Definition:Bessel's Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bessel's Equation == Bessel's equation occurs in a number of applications in the fields of physics and engineering. In particular, it arises in the analysis of the harmonics of the vibration of a circular drum.

label: Definition:Bessel's Modified Equation
snippet: == Equation == Bessel's modified equation is a second order ODE of the form: $x^2 \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} + x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} - \paren {x^2 + n^2} y = 0$ The parameter $n$ may be any arbitrary real or complex number.

label: Definition:Bessel Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Bessel Functions == Bessel functions were introduced by in $1824$. They arise in many problems of physics and engineering. However, despite bearing the name of , they were first studied by . He encountered them during his study of the vibrations of a stretched circular membrane.

label: Definition:Best-Response Function
snippet: Let a strategic game $G$ be modelled by: $G = \stratgame N {A_i} {\succsim_i}$ Let $a^*$ be a Nash equilibrium of $G$: $\forall i \in N: \forall a_i \in A_i: \tuple {a^*_{-i}, a^*_i} \succsim_i \tuple {a^*_{-i}, a_i}$ For any $a_{-1} \in A_{-i}$, let $\map {B_i} {a_{-i} }$ be the set of player $i$'s best moves, defined as: $\map {B_i} {a_{-i} } = \set {a_i \in A_i: \forall a'_i \in A_i: \tuple {a_{-i}, a_i} \precsim_i \tuple {a_{-i}, a'_i} }$ Then $B_{-i}$ is known as the best-response function of player $i$.

label: Definition:Best Approximation
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $B \subsetneq A$ be a proper subset of $A$. Let $x \in A \setminus B$ be an element of $A$ which is outside $B$. The best approximation to $x$ $B$ is the element $y$ of $B$ such that the distance between $x$ and $y$ is smallest. That is, it is the element of $B$ which lies closest to $x$.

label: Definition:Best Rational Approximation
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be an (irrational) real number. The rational number $a = \dfrac p q$ is a best rational approximation to $x$ : $(1): \quad a$ is in canonical form, that is $p$ is coprime to $q$: $p \perp q$ $(2): \quad \left\vert{x - \dfrac p q}\right\vert = \min \left\{ {\left\vert{x - \dfrac {p'} {q'} }\right\vert: q' \le q}\right\}$ That is: $\left\vert{x - \dfrac p q}\right\vert$ is smaller than for any $\dfrac {p'} {q'}$ where $q' \le q$ where $\left\vert{x}\right\vert$ denotes the absolute value of $x$.

label: Definition:Beta Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \closedint 0 1$. $X$ is said to have a beta distribution it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} X = \dfrac {x^{\alpha - 1} \paren {1 - x}^{\beta - 1} } {\map \Beta {\alpha, \beta} }$ for $\alpha, \beta > 0$, where $\Beta$ denotes the beta function. This is written: $X \sim \BetaDist \alpha \beta$

label: Definition:Beta Function
snippet: The beta function $\Beta: \C \times \C \to \C$ is defined for $\map \Re x, \map \Re y > 0$ as:

label: Definition:Beta Function/Also defined as
snippet: == Beta Function: Also known as == The beta function can also be defined as: $\map \Beta {m, n} := \dfrac {\paren {n - 1}! \paren {m - 1}!} {\paren {m + n - 1}!}$ when $m$ and $n$ are (strictly) positive integers.

label: Definition:Beta Function/Also known as
snippet: == Beta Function: Also known as == The beta function can also be referred to as the Eulerian integral of the first kind.

label: Definition:Beta Function/Definition 1
snippet: The beta function $\Beta: \C \times \C \to \C$ is defined for $\map \Re x, \map \Re y > 0$ as: $\ds \map \Beta {x, y} := \int_{\mathop \to 0}^{\mathop \to 1} t^{x - 1} \paren {1 - t}^{y - 1} \rd t$

label: Definition:Beta Function/Definition 2
snippet: The beta function $\Beta: \C \times \C \to \C$ is defined for $\map \Re x, \map \Re y > 0$ as: $\ds \map \Beta {x, y} := 2 \int_0^{\pi / 2} \paren {\sin \theta}^{2 x - 1} \paren {\cos \theta}^{2 y - 1} \rd \theta$

label: Definition:Beta Function/Definition 3
snippet: The beta function $\Beta: \C \times \C \to \C$ is defined for $\map \Re x, \map \Re y > 0$ as: $\map \Beta {x, y} := \dfrac {\map \Gamma x \map \Gamma y} {\map \Gamma {x + y} }$ where $\Gamma$ is the gamma function.

label: Definition:Beta Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Beta Function == The beta function $\map \Beta {x, y}$ was discovered by .

label: Definition:Between (Geometry)
snippet: Betweenness is one of the undefined terms in Tarski's Geometry. Intuitively, a point $b$ is between two others $a$ and $c$ it lies on the line segment $a c$. However as line segment has not yet been defined, we are not allowed to call upon it at this stage. We offer an ostensive definition: File:Betweenness.png In the picture, point $b$ is between the two points $a, c$, and we write: $\mathsf{B}abc$ However, point $d$ is not between the two points $a$ and $c$, and we write: $\map \neg {\mathsf B a d c}$

label: Definition:Between (Geometry)/N-dimensional Euclidean space Intuition
snippet: The intuition behind this definition comes from the fact that when we think that $B$ is between $A$ and $C$, we think of three things. The first thing is that $A$, $B$ and $C$ are collinear. So: $\size {\map \cos {\angle {BAC} } } = 1$ Hence, from Cosine Formula for Dot Product, we should have: $\size {\vec{AB} \cdot \vec{AC} } = \norm {\vec {AB} } * \norm {\vec {AC} }$ Secondly, the vectors $\vec {AB}$ and $\vec {AC}$ have the same direction. Therefore, their dot product should be positive.

label: Definition:Bi-Invariant Riemannian Metric
snippet: Let $G$ be a Lie group. Let $\struct {G, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Suppose $g$ is both left-invariant and right-invariant. Then $g$ is said to be bi-invariant.

label: Definition:Bi-Orthogonal Sequences
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ be sequences in $\HH$. $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ are described as bi-orthogonal : $\forall m, n \in \N: \innerprod {a_m} {b_n} = \begin {cases} 1 & : m = n \\0 & : m \ne n \end {cases}$ where $\innerprod {a_m} {b_n}$ denotes inner product of $a_m$ and $b_n$.

label: Definition:Biadditive Mapping
snippet: Let $M, N, P$ be abelian groups. Let $M \times N$ be the cartesian product. A biadditive mapping $f : M \times N \to P$ is a mapping such that: $\forall m_1, m_2 \in M : \forall n \in N: \map f {m_1 + m_2, n} = \map f {m_1, n} + \map f {m_2, n}$ $\forall m \in M: \forall n_1, n_2 \in N: \map f {m, n_1 + n_2} = \map f {m, n_1} + \map f {m, n_2}$

label: Definition:Bias
snippet: Bias is defined as a prejudice or a lack of objectivity or randomness causing an imbalance which makes it likely that the outcome will tend to be distorted. This can happen in statistics when a process contains some systematic imbalance, resulting in the outcome not being equal to the true value being sought.

label: Definition:Bias/Estimator
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some statistical model. Let $\mathbf X$ be a random sample from this population. Let $\delta$ be an estimator of $\theta$. The bias in $\delta$ is defined as: $\map {\operatorname {bias} } \delta = \expect {\map \delta {\mathbf X} } - \theta$

label: Definition:Bicentral Tree
snippet: A tree $T$ is bicentral it has a bicenter.

label: Definition:Biconnected Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a connected set in $T$. Then $H$ is biconnected it is not the union of two disjoint non-degenerate connected sets.

label: Definition:Bifunctor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$, $\mathbf E$ be categories. Then: a bifunctor is a functor $F:\mathbf C \times \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$, from a product $\mathbf {C \times D}$ to a category $E$. A bifunctor is often viewed as a functor of two variables.

label: Definition:Bifunctor/Substitution of First Variable
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$, $\mathbf E$ be categories. Let $F:\mathbf C \times \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$ be a bifunctor. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Then: $\map F {C, -}$ denotes the functor from $\mathbf D$ to $\mathbf E$ defined as: {{DefineFunctor |ob = for each object $D \in \mathbf D : \map {\map F {C, -} } D := \map F {C, D}$ |mor = for each morphism $g \in \mathbf D : \map {\map F {C, -} } g := \map F {\operatorname{id}_C, g}$ }}

label: Definition:Bifunctor/Substitution of Second Variable
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$, $\mathbf E$ be categories. Let $F:\mathbf C \times \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$ be a bifunctor. Let $D$ be an object of $\mathbf D$. Then: $\map F {-, D}$ denotes the functor from $\mathbf C$ to $\mathbf E$ defined as: {{DefineFunctor |ob = for each object $C \in \mathbf C : \map {\map F {-, D} } C := \map F {C, D}$ |mor = for each morphism $f \in \mathbf C : \map {\map F {-, D} } f := \map F {f, \operatorname{id}_D}$ }}

label: Definition:Bifurcation/Flip
snippet: A flip bifurcation is a bifurcation in which a family of mappings $T_\lambda$, indexed by a real bifurcation parameter $\lambda$, has an repelling fixed point replaced by a pair of periodic points of period $2$, forming an attractor.

label: Definition:Bifurcation/Hopf
snippet: A Hopf bifurcation is a bifurcation in which a family of flows $\map {x_\lambda} t$, indexed by a real bifurcation parameter $\lambda$, has an attractor consisting of: a fixed point replaced by a circle a repelling fixed point for a small change in the index.

label: Definition:Bifurcation Theory
snippet: Bifurcation theory is the mathematical study of changes in the qualitative or topological structure of a given family, such as the integral curves of a family of vector fields, and the solutions of a family of differential equations.

label: Definition:Big-O Notation/Also denoted as
snippet: == Also denoted as == In analytic number theory, sometimes Vinogradov's notations $f \ll g$ or $g \gg f$ are used for big-$\OO$ notation, to mean $f = \map \OO g$. This can often be clearer for estimates leading to typographically complex error terms. Some sources use an ordinary $O$: $f = \map O g$

label: Definition:Big-O Notation/Complex/Infinity
snippet: Let $f$ and $g$ be complex functions defined for all complex numbers whose modulus is sufficiently large. The statement: $\map f z = \map \OO {\map g z}$ as $\cmod z \to \infty$ is equivalent to: $\exists c \in \R_{\ge 0}: \exists r_0 \in \R: \forall z \in \C: \paren {\cmod z \ge r_0 \implies \cmod {\map f z} \le c \cdot \cmod {\map g z} }$ That is: $\cmod {\map f z} \le c \cdot \cmod {\map g z}$ for all $z$ in a neighborhood of infinity in $\C$. label: Definition:Big-O Notation/Sequence/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_n}$ be sequences of real or complex numbers. $a_n$ is big-$\OO$ of $b_n$ : $\exists c \in \R_{\ge 0}: \exists n_0 \in \N: \forall n \in \N: \paren {n \ge n_0 \implies \size {a_n} \le c \cdot \size {b_n} }$ That is: $\size {a_n} \le c \cdot \size {b_n}$ for all sufficiently large $n$. label: Definition:Big Data
snippet: Big data is a generic term for extremely large sets of data in the context of data science.

label: Definition:Big Model
snippet: Let $\MM$ be an $\LL$-structure with universe $M$. Let $\kappa$ be a cardinal. $\MM$ is $\kappa$-big if for every subset $A \subset M$ with cardinality $\card A < \kappa$, the following holds: if $\LL_A$ is the language obtained from $\LL$ by adding new constant symbols for each $a \in A$, then for every language $\LL_A^*$ obtained by adding a new relation symbol $R$ to $\LL_A$, and for every $\LL_A^*$-structure $\NN$ such that $\MM$ and $\NN$ are elementary equivalent as $\LL_A$-structures, there is a relation $R^\MM$ on $M$ such that $\struct {\MM, R^\MM}$ is elementary equivalent to $\NN$…

label: Definition:Bijection/Also known as
snippet: The terms biunique correspondence bijective correspondence bijective mapping are sometimes seen for bijection. Authors who prefer to limit the jargon of mathematics tend to use the term one-one and onto mapping for bijection. If a bijection exists between two sets $S$ and $T$, then $S$ and $T$ are said to be in one-to-one correspondence. Some sources refer to exact correspondence to mean exactly this. Some sources refer to it just as a correspondence.

label: Definition:Bijection/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be classes. Let $f: A \to B$ be a class mapping from $A$ to $B$. Then $f$ is said to be a bijection : $f$ is both a class injection and a class surjection.

label: Definition:Bilateral Shift
snippet: Let $T$ be a linear operator acting on a sequence. Let $T$ be such that if $\sequence v = \map T {\sequence u}$, then $v_k = u_{k - 1}$ for all $k$. Then $T$ is a bilateral shift.

label: Definition:Bilinear Form (Polynomial Theory)/Also known as
snippet: == Bilinear Form in context of Polynomial Theory: Also known as == A bilinear form in the context of polynomial theory is also known as a bilinear function. However, that term is also used as a synonym for a Möbius transformation, so to avoid ambiguitty and misunderstanding it is recommended it not be used.

label: Definition:Bilinear Space
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. A bilinear space over $\mathbb K$ is a pair $\struct {V, f}$ where: $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$ of finite dimension $n > 0$ $f$ is a bilinear form on $V$.

label: Definition:Bimedial/First Bimedial
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be in the forms: $a = k^{1/4} \rho$ $b = k^{3/4} \rho$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a + b$ is a first bimedial.

label: Definition:Bimedial/Second Bimedial
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be in the forms: $a = k^{1/4} \rho$ $b = \dfrac {\lambda^{1/2} \rho} {k^{1/4} }$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. $\lambda$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a + b$ is a second bimedial.

label: Definition:Bimodule
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ and $\struct {S, +_S, \times_S}$ be rings. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $\circ_R : R \times G \to G$ and $\circ_S : G \times S \to G$ be binary operations such that: {{item|(1):|$\struct {G, +_G, \circ_R}$ is a left module}} {{item|(2):|$\struct {G, +_G, \circ_S}$ is a right module}} {{item|(3):|$\forall \lambda \in R: \forall \mu \in S: \forall x \in G: \paren {\lambda \circ_R x} \circ_S \mu \lambda \circ_R \paren {x \circ_S \mu}$}} Then $\struct {G, +_G, \circ_R, \circ_S}$ is a bimodule over $\tuple {R, S}$.

label: Definition:Bin/Width
snippet: The length of the subintervals of a set of grouped data that form the bins of that grouped data is known as the bin width.

label: Definition:Bin Packing Problem
snippet: The bin packing problem is a type of scheduling problem of how to pack a number of boxes into a number of bins. The boxes with the same cross-section as the bins, but of various heights. The aim is to use as few bins as possible.

label: Definition:Binary Biproduct
snippet: Let $A$ be a category. Let $a_1, a_2$ be objects of $A$.

label: Definition:Binary Code
snippet: A binary code is a character encoding consisting of a set of codewords each of which is a sequence of instances of $0$ and $1$. It is usual in a given binary code for each of the codewords to be the same length.

label: Definition:Binary Coproduct UMP

An object $P$ and morphisms $i_1: A \to P$, $i_2: B \to P$: $\begin{xy} +{A} = "A", +{P} = "P", +{B} = "B", "A";"P" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/^.8em/{i_1}, "B";"P" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/_.8em/{i_2}, \end{xy}$ satisfy the (binary coproduct) universal mapping property (or UMP) :

label: Definition:Binary Mess
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $I$ be the set of all finite subsets of $S$. Let $\Bbb B$ be a Boolean domain. Let $M$ be a set defined as: $\ds M \subseteq \bigcup_{P \mathop \in I} \Bbb B^P$ where $\Bbb B^P$ denotes the set of all mappings from $P$ to $\Bbb B$. That is, such that $M$ is a set of mappings from finite subsets of $S$ to $\Bbb B$. Suppose that $M$ satisfies the binary mess axioms: Then $M$ is a binary mess on $S$.

label: Definition:Binary Mess/Consistent Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $M$ be a binary mess on $S$. Let $f : S \to \Bbb B$ be a mapping from $S$ to a Boolean domain. Then, $f$ is consistent with $M$ , for every finite subset $P \subseteq S$: $f {\restriction_P} \in M$ where $f {\restriction_P}$ denotes the restriction of $f$ to $P$.

label: Definition:Binary Notation
snippet: Binary notation is the positional number system whose base is $2$. That is, every number $x \in \R$ is expressed in the form: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z} r_j 2^j$ where $\forall j \in \Z: r_j \in \set {0, 1}$.

label: Definition:Binary Notation/Also known as
snippet: == Binary Notation: Also known as == Binary notation is also known as binary representation.

label: Definition:Binary Notation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Binary Notation == The earliest known reference to binary notation appears to be in a Chinese book dating from approximately $3000$ B.C.E. In Europe, binary notation was invented by . He associated God with $1$ and nothingness with $0$, and believed that it was mystically significant that all numbers could be built from $1$-ness and $0$-ness.

label: Definition:Binary Notation/Motivation
snippet: Binary notation, like hexadecimal notation, has particular relevance in the field of computer science. This is because the two binary digits, $0$ and $1$, can be represented by two well-defined states of a component.

label: Definition:Binary Number
snippet: A binary number is a number expressed in binary notation.

label: Definition:Binary Product UMP (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $A$ and $B$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. An object $P$ and morphisms $p_1: P \to A$, $p_2: P \to B$: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+1em@L+3px{ A & P \ar[l]_*+{p_1} \ar[r]^*+{p_2} & B }\end{xy}$ satisfy the (binary product) universal mapping property (or UMP) :

label: Definition:Binary Product UMP (Category Theory)/Property
snippet: == Property for Binary Product UMP == For any object $X$ and morphisms $x_1:X \to A, x_2: X \to B$ like so: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+1em@L+3px{ A & X \ar[l]_*+{x_1} \ar[r]^*+{x_2} & B }\end{xy}$ there is a unique morphism $u: X \to P$ such that: $x_1 = p_1 \circ u$ and $x_2 = p_2 \circ u$ That is: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+1em@L+3px{ & X \ar[ld]_*+{x_1} \ar@{-->}[d]^*+{u} \ar[rd]^*+{x_2} \\ A & P \ar[l]^*+{p_1} \ar[r]_*+{p_2} & B }\end{xy}$ is a commutative diagram

label: Definition:Binary Search Algorithm
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a finite sequence of length $n$ from an ordered set $\struct {\EE, \preccurlyeq}$. Let $\SS$ be sorted into order by $\preccurlyeq$. Let $x$ be an element of $\EE$ which may or may not be present in $\SS$. The binary search algorithm $\AA$ is an algorithm whose purpose is to see whether $\SS$ contains $x$: $(1): \quad x$ is compared $\preccurlyeq$ with the element $m$ of $\SS$ closest to the middle. $(2): \quad$ If $x = m$ then we have found $x$ in $\SS$. $(3): \quad$ If $x \ne m$ then either $x \prec m$ or $m \prec x$.

label: Definition:Binary System
snippet: A binary system is a number system in which the base is $2$.

label: Definition:Binary Tuple
snippet: A binary tuple is an ordered tuple whose domain is the set $\set {0, 1}$. That is, it is an ordered $n$-tuple $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ such that each $x_i$ is either $0$ or $1$. The set of all binary $n$-tuples can often be seen denoted $V_n$: $V_n := \set {\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}: \forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots n}: x_i \in \set {0, 1} }$

label: Definition:Binary Variable
snippet: A binary variable is a random variable which can take one of only $2$ values. It is conventional for the purposes of data analysis to encode such binary variables by use of a random variable which takes the values $0$ and $1$.

label: Definition:Binding Constraint
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a weak inequality on some set $S$. Let $a \mathrel \RR b$ be a constraint given by a weak inequality $\RR$. Let $P \in S$ such that $P \mathrel \RR b$ is an equality. Then $a \mathrel \RR b$ is binding at $P$.

label: Definition:Binding Priority/Arithmetic
snippet: The binding priority convention used for arithmetic and algebra is: $(1): \quad$ the exponential and power operators take highest binding priority $(2): \quad \times$ and $\div$ bind more tightly than $+$ and $-$ $(3): \quad$ In all other cases, expressions are evaluated from left to right.

label: Definition:Binding Priority/Propositional Logic
snippet: The binding priority convention which is almost universally used for the connectives of propositional logic is: Note that there is no overall convention defining which of $\land$ and $\lor$ bears a higher binding priority, and therefore we consider them to have equal priority. Because of this fact, unless specifically defined, expressions such as $p \land q \lor r$ can not be interpreted unambiguously, and parenthesis must be used to determine the exact priorities which are to be used to interpret particular statements which may otherwise be ambiguous.

label: Definition:Binding Priority (Propositional Logic)/Also defined as
snippet: == Binding Priority for Propositional Logic: Also defined as == When defining binding priority for propositional logic, some sources do impose a priority of $\land$ over $\lor$. Similarly, some sources also impose a priority of $\implies$ over $\iff$. However, these are not a universal convention, and such a binding priority is artificial. Some sources express the binding priority rules by saying that $\iff$ and $\implies$ dominate $\land$ and $\lor$.

label: Definition:Binomial
snippet: Euclidean number theory: A binomial is a term in the form $a + b$ where $\dfrac a b$ and $a + b$ are irrational, but $\paren {\dfrac a b}^2$ is rational. The concept is considered archaic. Algebra: A binomial is an expression with two terms, that is, of the form $a + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are such that $a + b$ cannot be simplified. Definition:Binomial Coefficient Probability theory: Definition:Binomial Distribution

label: Definition:Binomial (Euclidean)
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that: $(1): \quad \dfrac a b \notin \Q$ $(2): \quad \left({\dfrac a b}\right)^2 \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. Then $a + b$ is a binomial.

snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be two (strictly) positive real numbers such that $a + b$ is a binomial. Then $a + b$ is a second binomial : $(1): \quad b \in \Q$ $(2): \quad \dfrac {\sqrt {a^2 - b^2}} a \in \Q$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. '

label: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Complex Numbers
snippet: Let $z, w \in \C$. Then $\dbinom z w$ is defined as: $\dbinom z w := \ds \lim_{\zeta \mathop \to z} \lim_{\omega \mathop \to w} \dfrac {\map \Gamma {\zeta + 1} } {\map \Gamma {\omega + 1} \map \Gamma {\zeta - \omega + 1} }$ where $\Gamma$ denotes the Gamma function. When $z$ is a negative integer and $w$ is not an integer, $\dbinom z w$ is infinite.

label: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Integers/Definition 1
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ and $k \in \Z$. Then the binomial coefficient $\dbinom n k$ is defined as: $\dbinom n k = \begin {cases} \dfrac {n!} {k! \paren {n - k}!} & : 0 \le k \le n \\ & \\ 0 & : \text { otherwise } \end{cases}$ where $n!$ denotes the factorial of $n$.

label: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Integers/Definition 2
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ and $k \in \Z$. The number of different ways $k$ objects can be chosen (irrespective of order) from a set of $n$ objects is denoted: $\dbinom n k$ This number $\dbinom n k$ is known as a binomial coefficient.

label: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Multiindices
snippet: Let $k = \sequence {k_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ and $\ell = \sequence {\ell_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ be multiindices. Let $\ell \le k$. Then $\dbinom k \ell$ is defined as: $\ds \binom k \ell = \prod_{j \mathop \in J} \binom {k_j} {\ell_j}$ Note that since by definition only finitely many of the $k_j$ are non-zero, the product in the definition of $\dbinom k \ell$ is convergent. Category:Definitions/Binomial Coefficients Category:Definitions/Polynomial Theory

label: Definition:Binomial Coefficient/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $r \in \R, k \in \Z$. Then $\dbinom r k$ is defined as: $\dbinom r k = \begin {cases} \dfrac {r^{\underline k} } {k!} & : k \ge 0 \\ & \\ 0 & : k < 0 \end {cases}$ where $r^{\underline k}$ denotes the falling factorial. That is, when $k \ge 0$: $\ds \dbinom r k = \dfrac {r \paren {r - 1} \cdots \paren {r - k + 1} } {k \paren {k - 1} \cdots 1} = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^k \dfrac {r + 1 - j} j$ It can be seen that this agrees with the definition for integers when $r$ is an integer. For most applications the integer form is sufficient.

label: Definition:Binomial Distribution
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_i}$ be a finite binomial experiment of length $n$ such that each of the $X_i$ in the sequence is a Bernoulli trial with parameter $p$ such that $0 \le p \le 1$. Let $X$ be the discrete probability distribution that models the number of successes in $\sequence {X_i}$ . Then $X$ is a binomial distribution with parameters $n$ and $p$.

label: Definition:Binomial Expansion
snippet: Consider the binomial theorem, which in one of its various forms is given here: $\paren {1 + x}^\alpha = 1 + \dbinom \alpha 1 x + \dbinom \alpha 2 x^2 + \dbinom \alpha 3 x^3 + \cdots$ The above algebraic expansion is known as the binomial expansion.

label: Definition:Binomial Experiment
snippet: A binomial experiment is a sequence (either finite or infinite) of Bernoulli trials, each of which has the same parameter $p$. That is, a binomial experiment (with parameter $p$) is a sequence $\sequence {X_i}$ (either finite or infinite) such that: $(1): \quad$ the value of each $X_i$ is one of two values (for example: $a$ or $b$). $(2): \quad$ the probability that $X_i = a$ is the same for all $i$ (for example: $p$). $(3): \quad$ the outcomes of all the Bernoulli trials are independent. That is, it is a sequence of experiments, all of which can be modelled by the same Bernoulli distribution.

label: Definition:Binomial Series
snippet: Consider the Binomial Theorem, which in one of its various forms is given here: $\paren {1 + x}^\alpha = 1 + \dbinom \alpha 1 x + \dbinom \alpha 2 x^2 + \dbinom \alpha 3 x^3 + \cdots$ for arbitrary real $\alpha$. The above infinite series is known as the binomial series.

label: Definition:Biometry
snippet: Biometry is the branch of statistics concerned with the development and application of statistical methods to biologial problems. This includes the design of experiments and the analysis and interpretation of the results.

label: Definition:Bipartite Graph
snippet: A bipartite graph is a graph $G = \struct {V, E}$ where: $V$ is partitioned into two sets $A$ and $B$ such that: each edge is incident to a vertex in $A$ and a vertex in $B$. That is: no two vertices in $A$ are adjacent and no two vertices in $B$ are adjacent. It is a common practice when illustrating such a graph to draw the vertices of $A$ in one colour, and those of $B$ in another. $G$ can be denoted $G = \struct {A \mid B, E}$ to emphasise that $A$ and $B$ partition $V$.

label: Definition:Bipartite Graph/Partite Set
snippet: Let $G = \struct {A \mid B, E}$ be a bipartite graph. Then $A$ and $B$ are called the partite sets of $G$.

label: Definition:Biquadrate
snippet: A biquadrate number (or just biquadrate) is a number which can be expressed as the fourth power of an integer. The sequence of positive biquadrates begins: $1, 16, 81, 256, 625, 1297, 2401, 4096, 6561, 10000, \ldots$

label: Definition:Biquadratic Residue
snippet: Let $p$ be an odd prime. Let $a \in \Z$ be an integer such that $a \not \equiv 0 \pmod p$. Then $a$ is a biquadratic residue of $p$ $x^4 \equiv a \pmod p$ has a solution. That is, : $\exists x \in \Z: x^4 \equiv a \pmod p$

label: Definition:Birectangular Spherical Triangle
snippet: A spherical triangle is described as birectangular it has $2$ right angles.

label: Definition:Birth-Death Process
snippet: A birth-death process is a Markov process which models changes in population caused by births and deaths.

label: Definition:Bisection
snippet: To bisect a finite geometrical object is to cut it in half, that is, into two equal parts. The act of cutting in half is known as bisection.

label: Definition:Bit
snippet: A bit is a binary digit.

label: Definition:Bit/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Bit == The word bit derives directly from the term Binary digIT.

label: Definition:Bitangent
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve in the plane. A bitangent is a straight line which is tangent to $\CC$ at two distinct points.

label: Definition:Bivariate
snippet: An expression is bivariate it involves two variables. The term is usually encountered when the variables concerned are random.

label: Definition:Bivariate Distribution
snippet: A bivariate distribution is the joint distribution of two random variables $X$ and $Y$.

label: Definition:Black-Scholes Equation
snippet: The Black-Scholes equation is a second-order partial differential equation whose purpose is to model a financial market in order to provide estimates for stock options. It is of the form: $\dfrac {\partial V} {\partial t} + \dfrac 1 2 \sigma^2 S^2 \dfrac {\partial^2 V} {\partial S^2} + r S \dfrac {\partial V} {\partial S} - r V = 0$ where: $V$ is the price of the stock option $S$ is the price of the stock $r$ is the interest rate $\sigma$ represents the volatility of the stock price $t$ represents time.

label: Definition:Block Basic Sequence
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a Schauder basis for $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$. Let $\sequence {p_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a strictly increasing sequence and let $p_0 = 0$. Let $\sequence {\alpha_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $\GF$. Define: $\ds u_n = \sum_{j \mathop = p_{n - 1} + 1}^{p_n} \alpha_j e_j$ for each $n \in \N$. We say that $\sequence {u_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a block basic sequence of $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$.

label: Definition:Block Design
snippet: Let $S$ be a set with $n$ elements. A block design is a collection of subsets $B_r$ of a set $S$ such that: each $B_r$ contains the same number $k$ of elements for every subset $T$ of $S$ with exactly $t$ elements, $T$ is a subset of exactly $\lambda$ of the $B_r$. The numbers $k$, $t$, $\lambda$ and $n$ are characteristic of the particular block design.

label: Definition:Block Matrix
snippet: A block matrix is a representation of a matrix as an array of submatrices. This may be defined as follows: Let $S$ be a set. Let $m, n \ge 1$ be positive integers. Let $A = \sqbrk {A_{i j} }$ be an $m \times n$ matrix of matrices over $S$. Let for every $i \in \set {1, \ldots, m}$, the elements of the $i$th row of $A$ have equal height $m_i$. Let for every $j \in \set {1,\ldots, n}$ the elements of the $j$th column of $A$ have equal width $n_i$. Define $M = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^m m_i$ and $N = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n n_i$ as indexed summations.

label: Definition:Block Multiplication
snippet: Block multiplication is (conventional) matrix multiplication in which the matrices involved are block matrices. That is, the entries are submatrices rather than single elements. The submatrices still multiply together as though they were single elements.

label: Definition:Bochner Integrable Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $\lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure on $I$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a Bochner measurable function. We say that $f$ is Bochner integrable there exists simple functions $s_n : I \to X$ such that: $\map {s_n} t \to \map f t$ for each $t \in I$ and: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \int_I \norm {\map f t - \map {s_n} t}_X \rd \map \lambda t = 0$

label: Definition:Bochner Integral
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $\lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure on $I$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a Bochner integrable function. Let $\sequence {s_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of simple functions such that: $\map {s_n} t \to \map f t$ for each $t \in I \setminus \Omega_0$ and: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \int_I \norm {\map f t - \map {s_n} t}_X \rd \map \lambda t = 0$ where $\Omega_0$ is a Lebesgue measurable set with $\map \lambda {\Omega_0} = 0$.

label: Definition:Bochner Integral of Simple Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $\lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure on $I$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a simple function. Take: Lebesgue measurable subsets $\Omega_1, \ldots, \Omega_n$ of $I$ with finite Lebesgue measure $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in X$ such that: $\ds f = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n x_j \chi_{\Omega_j}$ We define the Bochner integral of $f$ over $I$ by: $\ds \int_I f \rd \lambda = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n x_j \map \lambda {\Omega_j}$

label: Definition:Bochner Measurable Function
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $I$ be a real interval. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $f : I \to X$ be a function. We say that $f$ is Bochner measurable there exists a sequence of simple functions $\sequence {s_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that: $\ds \map f t = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map {s_n} t$ for almost all $t \in I$.

label: Definition:Body
snippet: In the context of physics and applied mathematics, a body is an object (possibly idealized) which is imagined to have a material existence in the physical universe. A body can be considered as an aggregate of particles to which it is possible to apply a force.

label: Definition:Body-Centered Cubic Lattice
snippet: 300px A body-centered cubic lattice is a set of points in Cartesian $3$-space whose coordinates are of the form: $\tuple {\dfrac 1 2 a x, \dfrac 1 2 a y, \dfrac 1 2 a z}$ such that: $a$ is a positive real constant $x$, $y$ and $z$ are all either even integers or odd integers.

label: Definition:Body/Deformable
snippet: A deformable body is a body $B$ which is not rigid. That is, when under the influence of a force, the distance between any two points of $B$ may not remain constant.

label: Definition:Body/Rigid
snippet: A rigid body is a body $B$ with the property that the distance between any two points of $B$ remains constant regardless of any external forces.

label: Definition:Boolean Algebra/Also defined as
snippet: == Boolean Algebra: Also defined as == Some sources define a Boolean algebra to be what on is called a Boolean lattice. It is a common approach to define (the) Boolean algebra to be an algebraic structure consisting of: a boolean domain (that is, a set with two elements, typically $\set {0, 1}$) together with: the two operations addition $+$ and multiplication $\times$ defined as follows: $\begin{array}{c|cc} + & 0 & 1 \\ \hline 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ \end{array} \qquad \begin{array}{c|cc} \times & 0 & 1 \\ \hline 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{array}$ Hence expositions discussing such a…

label: Definition:Boolean Algebra/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Boolean algebra

label: Definition:Boolean Domain
snippet: A Boolean domain is a $2$-element set of (Aristotelian) truth values, usually defined and denoted as: $\Bbb B = \set {\T, \F}$

label: Definition:Boolean Domain/Also known as
snippet: == Boolean Domain: Also known as == Some sources refer to a Boolean domain as the set of truth values of propositional logic. Category:Definitions/Boolean Domains

label: Definition:Boolean Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Then $R$ is called a Boolean ring $R$ is an idempotent ring with unity.

label: Definition:Boolean Satisfiability Problem
snippet: Let $X$ be a set of propositional variables. Let $L$ be a set of one or more propositional formulas constructed using only: elements of $X$ the $4$ unary logical connectives $\operatorname{True}$, $\operatorname{False}$, identity, and $\neg$ the $16$ binary logical connectives. The problem is to find truth values for all $x \in X$ such that all the formulas in $L$ are true. Such a problem is known as a boolean satisfiability problem.

label: Definition:Bordered Matrix
snippet: A bordered matrix is a matrix to which one or more extra rows or columns have been added at the edges.

label: Definition:Bordering/Motivation
snippet: Bordering can improve computational efficiency when determining properties of a matrix.

label: Definition:Borel Algebra
snippet: A Borel algebra is sometimes used as another name for a $\sigma$-algebra or $\delta$-algebra. Can be confused with Borel $\sigma$-Algebra, which is a specific kind of $\sigma$-algebra.

label: Definition:Borel Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\map \BB {X, \tau}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\struct {X, \tau}$. Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\map \BB {X, \tau}$ such that: $\map \mu K < \infty$ for all compact $K \subseteq X$. We say that $\mu$ is a Borel measure.

label: Definition:Borel Probability Space
snippet: A probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ is a Borel probability space : $\Omega$ is a dense subset of a compact metric space $M$ and: $\Sigma$ is the trace $\sigma$-algebra of $\Omega$ in the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $M$.

label: Definition:Borel Sigma-Algebra/Also known as
snippet: The Borel $\sigma$-algebra is also found with the name topological $\sigma$-algebra, or even just $\sigma$-algebra. When the set $S$ or the topology $\tau$ are clear from the context, one may encounter $\map \BB \tau$, $\map \BB S$ or even just $\BB$. Some authors write $\BB^n$ for $\map \BB {\R^n, \tau}$. Category:Definitions/Borel Sigma-Algebras

label: Definition:Borel Sigma-Algebra/Borel Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\map \BB {S, \tau}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\struct {S, \tau}$. The elements of $\map \BB {S, \tau}$ are called the Borel (measurable) sets of $\struct {S, \tau}$.

label: Definition:Borel Sigma-Algebra/Metric Space
snippet: Let $\struct {S, d}$ be a metric space. The Borel sigma-algebra (or $\sigma$-algebra) on $\struct {S, d}$ is the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the open sets in $\powerset S$. By the definition of a topology induced by a metric, this definition is a particular instance of the definition of a Borel $\sigma$-algebra on a topological space.

label: Definition:Borel Sigma-Algebra/Topological Space
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space The Borel sigma-algebra $\map \BB {S, \tau}$ of $\struct {S, \tau}$ is the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\tau$. That is, it is the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the set of open sets in $S$.

label: Definition:Bottom (Logic)
snippet: Bottom is a constant of propositional logic interpreted to mean the canonical, undoubted contradiction whose falsehood nobody could possibly ever question. The symbol used is $\bot$.

label: Definition:Bottom (Logic)/Truth Table
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the bottom constant $\bot$ of propositional logic is as follows: $\begin{array}{|c|} \hline \bot \\ \hline \F \\ \hline \end{array}$

label: Definition:Boubaker Polynomials
snippet: The Boubaker polynomials are the components of the following sequence of polynomials: {{eqn | l = \map {B_0} x | r = 1 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_1} x | r = x }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_2} x | r = x^2 + 2 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_3} x | r = x^3 + x }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_4} x | r = x^4 - 2 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_5} x | r = x^5 - x^3 - 3 x }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_6} x | r = x^6 - 2 x^4 - 3 x^2 + 2 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_7} x | r = x^7 - 3 x^5 - 2 x^3 + 5 x }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_8} x | r = x^8 - 4 x^6 + 8 x^2 - 2 }} {{eqn | l = \map {B_9} x | r = x^9 - 5 x^7 + 3 x^5 + 10 x^3 - 7 x }}

label: Definition:Bound Variable
snippet: A bound variable is a variable which, when it occurs in an expression, can be replaced with another variable without changing the meaning of the statement.

label: Definition:Bound Variable/Predicate Logic
snippet: In predicate logic, a bound variable is a variable which exists in a WFF only as bound occurrences.

label: Definition:Bound of Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $f$ be bounded. Then $B$ is a bound for $f$ : $\forall x \in S: B \ge \size {\map f x}$

label: Definition:Bound of Subset of Real Numbers
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers $\R$. Let $S$ be bounded. Then $K$ is a bound for $S$ : $\forall x \in S: \size x \le K$

label: Definition:Boundary
snippet: Geometry: Boundary: The line that goes around a geometric figure. Topology: Boundary: The elements in the closure of a set which are not in the interior of that set. Graph Theory: Boundary: The set of all the vertices of a simple graph that are adjacent to a given vertex.

label: Definition:Boundary (Geometry)
snippet: For example, the endpoints of a line segment are its boundaries.

label: Definition:Boundary (Graph Theory)/Simple Graph
snippet: Let $G = \tuple {V, E}$ be a simple graph. Let $v \in V$ be a vertex of $G$. Then the boundary of $v$ is the set of all vertices of $G$ which are adjacent to $v$: $\map B v = \set {u \in V: \set {u, v} \in E}$

label: Definition:Boundary (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Also defined as
snippet: == Boundary in the context of Topology: Also defined as == Some sources define the boundary of a subset of a topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ as: the set of elements of $S$ which can be approached from within $S$ and from outside $S$. However, this definition is of little use without rigorous definitions of approach, inside and outside. Consequently, such imprecise definitions are not used on .

label: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Also known as
snippet: == Boundary in the context of Topology: Also known as == The boundary of a subset $H$ of a topological space $T$ is also seen referred to as the frontier of $H$.

label: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The boundary of $H$ consists of all the points in the closure of $H$ which are not in the interior of $H$. Thus, the boundary of $H$ is defined as: $\partial H := H^- \setminus H^\circ$ where $H^-$ denotes the closure and $H^\circ$ the interior of $H$.

label: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The boundary of $H$ is the set of all the boundary points of $H$.

label: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The boundary of $H$ is the intersection of the closure of $H$ with the closure of the complement of $H$ in $T$: $\partial H = H^- \cap \paren {\overline H}^-$

label: Definition:Boundary (Topology)/Definition 4
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The boundary of $H$ consists of all the points in $H$ which are not in either the interior or exterior of $H$. Thus, the boundary of $H$ is defined as: $\partial H := H \setminus \paren {H^\circ \cup H^e}$ where: $H^\circ$ denotes the interior of $H$ $H^e$ denotes the exterior of $H$.

label: Definition:Boundary Condition
snippet: Let $\Phi$ be a differential equation to which a particular solution is to be found. A boundary condition is an equation relating particular values of the dependent and independent variables which the particular solution to $\Phi$ must satisfy. It is usual for such boundary condition to correspond to the physical extremities of bodies, aspects of whose internal nature is being modelled by means of $\Phi$.

label: Definition:Boundary Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Boundary Point/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. $x \in S$ is a boundary point of $H$ every neighborhood $N$ of $x$ satisfies: $H \cap N \ne \O$ and $\overline H \cap N \ne \O$ where $\overline H$ is the complement of $H$ in $S$.

label: Definition:Boundary Point/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. $x \in S$ is a boundary point of $H$ $x$ is an element of the boundary of $H$ in $S$.

label: Definition:Boundary Point (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the complex plane. Let $z_0 \in \C$. $z_0$ is a boundary point of $S$ every $\epsilon$-neighborhood $\map {N_\epsilon} {z_0}$ of $z_0$ contains points of $\C$ in $S$ and also points of $\C$ which are not in $S$.

label: Definition:Boundary Value Problem
snippet: A boundary value problem is a differential equation for which a particular solution is to be found, such that the particular solution must satisfy certain boundary conditions.

label: Definition:Bounded Above Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping whose codomain is an ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq}$. Then $f$ is bounded above on $S$ by the upper bound $H$ : $\forall x \in S: \map f x \preceq H$ That is, $f \sqbrk S = \set {\map f x: x \in S}$ is bounded above by $H$.

label: Definition:Bounded Above Mapping/Real-Valued
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. $f$ is bounded above on $S$ by the upper bound $H$ : $\forall x \in S: \map f x \le H$ That is, the set $\set {\map f x: x \in S}$ is bounded above in $\R$ by $H$.

label: Definition:Bounded Above Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded above : $\exists M \in T: \forall i \in \N: x_i \preceq M$

label: Definition:Bounded Above Sequence/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded above there exists no $M$ in $T$ such that: $\forall i \in \N: x_i \preceq M$ Category:Definitions/Unbounded Above Sequences Category:Definitions/Sequences

label: Definition:Bounded Above Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is bounded above (in $S$) $T$ admits an upper bound (in $S$).

label: Definition:Bounded Above Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. A subset $T \subseteq \R$ is bounded above (in $\R$) $T$ admits an upper bound (in $\R$).

label: Definition:Bounded Above Set/Real Numbers/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T \subseteq \R$ be a subset of $\R$ . $T \subseteq \R$ is unbounded above (in $\R$) it is not bounded above.

label: Definition:Bounded Above Set/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is unbounded above (in $S$) it is not bounded above.

label: Definition:Bounded Below
snippet: Bounded Below Set Bounded Below Subset of Real Numbers Bounded Below Mapping Bounded Below Real-Valued Function Bounded Below Sequence Bounded Below Real Sequence

label: Definition:Bounded Below Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping whose codomain is an ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq}$. Then $f$ is said to be bounded below (in $T$) by the lower bound $L$ : $\forall x \in S: L \preceq \map f x$ That is, iff $f \sqbrk S = \set {\map f x: x \in S}$ is bounded below by $L$.

label: Definition:Bounded Below Mapping/Real-Valued
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Then $f$ is bounded below on $S$ by the lower bound $L$ : $\forall x \in S: L \le \map f x$ That is, the set $\set {\map f x: x \in S}$ is bounded below in $\R$ by $L$.

label: Definition:Bounded Below Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded below : $\exists m \in T: \forall i \in \N: m \preceq x_i$

label: Definition:Bounded Below Sequence/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded below there exists no $m$ in $T$ such that: $\forall i \in \N: m \preceq x_i$ Category:Definitions/Unbounded Below Sequences Category:Definitions/Sequences

label: Definition:Bounded Below Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is bounded below (in $S$) $T$ admits a lower bound (in $S$).

label: Definition:Bounded Below Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. A subset $T \subseteq \R$ is bounded below (in $\R$) $T$ admits a lower bound (in $\R$).

label: Definition:Bounded Below Set/Real Numbers/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T \subseteq \R$ be a subset of $\R$ . $T \subseteq \R$ is unbounded below (in $\R$) it is not bounded below.

label: Definition:Bounded Below Set/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is unbounded below (in $S$) it is not bounded below.

label: Definition:Bounded Class/Bounded Subset of Class
snippet: Let $B$ be a class. Let $B$ be a subclass of a class $A$. Then $B$ is a bounded subset of $A$ : there exists a set $x \in A$ such that $B$ is bounded by $x$ That is, every element of $B$ is a subset of $x$.

label: Definition:Bounded Class/Bounded by Set
snippet: Let $B$ be a class. Let $x$ be a set. $B$ is bounded by $x$ : every element of $B$ is a subset of $x$.

label: Definition:Bounded Euclidean Space/Unbounded
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset of a Euclidean space under the usual metric. $A$ is unbounded (in $\R^n$) $A$ is not bounded (in $\R^n$).

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let the image of $f$ be bounded. Then $f$ is bounded. That is, $f$ is bounded it is both bounded above and bounded below.

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M$ be a metric space. Let $f: X \to M$ be a mapping from any set $X$ into $M$. Then $f$ is a bounded mapping $f \sqbrk X$ is bounded in $M$.

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Metric Space/Warning
snippet: == Warning concerning Bounded Mapping to Metric Space == From Real Number Line is Metric Space, we can in theory consider defining boundedness on a real-valued function in terms of boundedness of a mapping into a metric space. However, as a metric space is itself defined in terms of a real-valued function in the first place, this concept can be criticised as being a circular definition. Category:Definitions/Metric Spaces

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Normed Vector Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space over $R$. Let $S$ be a set. Let $f : S 	o X$ be a mapping. We say that $f$ is bounded there exists a real number $M > 0$ such that: $
orm {\map f x} \le M$ for each $x \in S$.

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function.

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued/Attaining its Bounds
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a bounded real-valued function. Let $T$ be a subset of $S$. Suppose that: $\exists a, b \in T: \forall x \in S: \map f a \le \map f x \le \map f b$ Then $f$ attains its bounds on $T$.

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. $f$ is bounded on $S$ : $\exists K \in \R_{\ge 0}: \forall x \in S: \size {\map f x} \le K$ where $\size {\map f x}$ denotes the absolute value of $\map f x$.

label: Definition:Bounded Mapping/Real-Valued/Unbounded
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function.

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Also defined as
snippet: == Bounded Metric Space: Also defined as == Some sources place no emphasis on the fact that the subset $B$ of the underlying set $A$ of $M$ is in fact itself a subspace of $M'$, and merely refer to a bounded set. This, however, glosses over the facts that: {{item|\text{(a)}:|from Subspace of Metric Space is Metric Space, any such subset is also a metric space by dint of the induced metric $d_B$}} {{item|\text{(b)}:| without reference to such a metric, boundedness is not defined.}} Hence strives to ensure that boundedness is consistently defined in the context of a metric space, and not just a…

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Complex
snippet: Let $D$ be a subset of the complex plane $\C$. Then $D$ is bounded (in $\C$) there exists $M \in \R$ such that: $\forall z \in D: \cmod z \le M$

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Complex/Unbounded
snippet: Let $D$ be a subset of the complex plane $\C$. Then $D$ is unbounded (in $\C$) : $\nexists M \in \R: \forall z \in D: \cmod z \le M$ That is, if $D$ is not bounded in $\C$.

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Definition 1
snippet: A subspace $M' = \struct {B, d_B}$ of a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists a \in A, K \in \R: \forall x \in B: \map {d} {x, a} \le K$ That is, there exists an element of $A$ within a finite distance of all elements of $B$.

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Definition 2
snippet: A subspace $M' = \struct {B, d_B}$ of a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists K \in \R: \forall x, y \in M': \map {d_B} {x, y} \le K$ That is, there exists a finite distance such that all pairs of elements of $B$ are within that distance.

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Definition 3
snippet: A subspace $M' = \struct {B, d_B}$ of a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists x \in A, \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: B \subseteq \map {B_\epsilon} {x; d}$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} {x; d}$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ the metric of $M$. That is, $M'$ can be fitted inside an open ball in $M$.

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Definition 4
snippet: A subspace $M' = \struct {B, d_B}$ of a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists K \in \R: \forall x \in B: \map d {x, a} \le K$ for some $a \in A$.

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Definition 5
snippet: A subspace $M' = \struct {B, d_B}$ of a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is bounded (in $M$) : $\exists x \in B, \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: B = \map {B_\epsilon} {x; d_B}$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} {x; d_B}$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ the metric of $M'$. That is, $M'$ is equal to an open ball of itself.

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Euclidean
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset of a Euclidean space under the usual metric. $A$ is bounded (in $\R^n$) : $\exists N \in \R: \forall x \in A: \size x \le N$ That is, every element of $A$ is within a finite distance of any point we may choose for the origin.

label: Definition:Bounded Metric Space/Unbounded
snippet: Let $M = \struct {X, d}$ be a metric space. Let $M' = \struct {Y, d_Y}$ be a subspace of $M$. Then $M'$ is unbounded (in $M$) $M'$ is not bounded in $M$.

label: Definition:Bounded Region of Plane
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \R^2$ be a subset of the plane. $D$ is bounded there exists a circle in the plane which completely encloses $D$.

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence
snippet: A special case of a bounded mapping is a bounded sequence, where the domain of the mapping is $\N$. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded $\exists m, M \in T$ such that $\forall i \in \N$: $(1): \quad m \preceq x_i$ $(2): \quad x_i \preceq M$ That is, it is bounded above and bounded below.

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M$ be a metric space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $M$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is a bounded sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded in $M$. That is: $\exists K \in \R: \forall n, m \in \N: \map d {x_n, x_m} \le K$

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Metric Space/Unbounded
snippet: Let $M$ be a metric space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $M$. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded it is not bounded.

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Normed Division Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded : $\exists K \in \R$ such that $\forall n \in \N: \norm {x_n} \le K$

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Normed Division Ring/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {R, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded it is not bounded.

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $X$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is bounded : $\exists K \in \R$ such that $\forall n \in \N: \norm {x_n} \le K$

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Normed Vector Space/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $R$. $\sequence {x_n}$ is unbounded it is not bounded.

label: Definition:Bounded Sequence/Unbounded
snippet: A sequence which is not bounded is unbounded. Category:Definitions/Boundedness

label: Definition:Bounded Sesquilinear Form
snippet: Let $\HH, \KK$ be Hilbert spaces over $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $u: \HH \times \KK \to \Bbb F$ be a sesquilinear form. Then $u$ is a bounded sesquilinear form, or to be bounded, : $\exists M \in \R: \forall h \in \HH, k \in \KK: \size {\map u {h, k} } \le M \norm h_\HH \norm k_\KK$ A constant $M$ satisfying the above is called a bound for $u$.

label: Definition:Bounded Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T \subseteq S$ be both bounded below and bounded above in $S$. Then $T$ is bounded in $S$.

label: Definition:Bounded Set/Also known as
snippet: == Bounded Set/Also known as == A bounded set can also be referred to as a bounded ordered set. However, it is unnecessary to refer specifically to the ordered nature of such a set, as boundedness cannot be applied to a set which has no ordering. The term bounded poset can also be found. Some sources use the term order-bounded set. Category:Definitions/Bounded Sets

label: Definition:Bounded Set/Real Numbers/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T \subseteq \R$ be both bounded below and bounded above in $\R$. Then $T$ is bounded in $\R$.

label: Definition:Bounded Set/Real Numbers/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T \subseteq \R$ be a subset of $\R$ such that: $\exists K \in \R: \forall x \in T: \size x \le K$ where $\size x$ denotes the absolute value of $x$. Then $T$ is bounded in $\R$.

label: Definition:Bounded Set/Real Numbers/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T \subseteq \R$ be a subset of $\R$ . $T \subseteq \R$ is unbounded (in $\R$) it is not bounded.

label: Definition:Bounded Set/Unbounded
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $T \subseteq S$ is unbounded (in $S$) it is not bounded.

label: Definition:Bounded Subset of Connected Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a connected Riemannian manifold. Let $A \subseteq M$ be a subset. Let $p,q \in M$ be points. Let $d_g$ be the Riemannian distance. Let $C \in \R$ be a constant. Suppose: $\exists C \in \R : \forall p, q \in A : \map {d_g} {p, q} \le C$ Then $A$ is said to be bounded.

label: Definition:Bounded Subset of Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}}$ be a normed vector space. Let $M' \subseteq X$.

label: Definition:Bounded Subset of Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\mathbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {V, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\mathbb F$. A subset $B \subseteq V$ is bounded : for each $U \in \tau$ such that $\mathbf 0_V \in U$ there is an $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ such that: $\epsilon B \subseteq U$ where: $\bf 0_V$ denotes the zero vector of $V$ $\epsilon B$ denotes the dilation of $B$ by $\epsilon$

label: Definition:Bounded Variation/Closed Bounded Interval
snippet: Let $a, b$ be real numbers with $a < b$. Let $f : \closedint a b \to \R$ be a real function.

label: Definition:Bounded Variation/Closed Bounded Interval/Definition 1
snippet: Let $a, b$ be real numbers with $a < b$. Let $f : \closedint a b \to \R$ be a real function. For each finite subdivision $P$ of $\closedint a b$, write: $P = \set {x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ with: $a = x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_{n - 1} < x_n = b$ Also write: $\ds \map {V_f} {P ; \closedint a b} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \size {\map f {x_i} - \map f {x_{i - 1} } }$ We say $f$ is of bounded variation there exists an $M \ge 0$ such that: $\map {V_f} {P ; \closedint a b} \le M$ for all finite subdivisions $P$.

label: Definition:Bounded Variation/Closed Bounded Interval/Definition 2
snippet: Let $a, b$ be real numbers with $a < b$. Let $f : \closedint a b \to \R$ be a real function. For each finite non-empty subset $\SS$ of $\closedint a b$, write: $\SS = \set {x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ with: $a \le x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_{n - 1} < x_n \le b$ Also write: $\ds \map {V_f^\ast} {\SS; \closedint a b} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \size {\map f {x_i} - \map f {x_{i - 1} } }$ We say $f$ is of bounded variation there exists an $M \ge 0$ such that: $\map {V_f^\ast} {\SS; \closedint a b} \le M$ for all finite non-empty subsets $\mathcal S$ of $\closedint a b$.

label: Definition:Bounded Variation/Closed Unbounded Interval
snippet: Let $I$ be an unbounded closed interval or $\R$. Let $f : I \to \R$ be a real function. For each finite non-empty subset $\SS$ of $I$, write: $\SS = \set {x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ with: $x_0 < x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_{n - 1} < x_n$ Also write: $\ds \map {V_f^\ast} {\SS; I} = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \size {\map f {x_i} - \map f {x_{i - 1} } }$ for $n \ge 1$, and $\map {V_f^\ast} {\SS ; I} = 0$ otherwise. We say $f$ is of bounded variation there exists an $M \ge 0$ such that: $\map {V_f^\ast} {\SS; I} \le M$ for all finite non-empty subsets $\SS$ of $I$.

label: Definition:Bowley Skewness
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with quartiles $Q_1$, $Q_2$ and $Q_3$, denoting the lower quartile, median and upper quartile respectively. Then the Bowley skewness of $X$ is defined as: $\dfrac {Q_3 - 2 Q_2 + Q_1} {Q_3 - Q_1}$

label: Definition:Bowley Skewness/Also presented as
snippet: == Bowley Skewness: Also known as == The Bowley skewness is also presented in the following forms: $\dfrac {\paren {Q_3 - Q_2} - \paren {Q_2 - Q_1} } {Q_3 - Q_1}$ $\dfrac {Q_3 - 2 M + Q_1} {Q_3 - Q_1}$ where $M$ denotes the median.

label: Definition:Box-Jenkins Model
snippet: The Box-Jenkins model is a very general mathematical model for time series analysis in forecasting and prediction.

label: Definition:Box-Jenkins Model/ARIMA
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process based on an equispaced time series. Let the values of $S$ at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ be $z_t, z_{t - 1}, z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ Let $a_t, a_{t - 1}, a_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be a sequence of independent shocks at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ Let: $w_t = \nabla^d z_t$ where $\nabla^d$ denotes the $d$th iteration of the backward difference operator.

label: Definition:Box Topology
snippet: Let $\family {\struct {X_i, \tau_i}}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of topological spaces. Let $X$ be the cartesian product of $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$, that is: $\ds X := \prod_{i \mathop \in I} X_i$ Define: $\ds \BB := \set {\prod_{i \mathop \in I} U_i: \forall i \in I: U_i \in \tau_i}$ Then $\BB$ is a synthetic basis on $X$, as shown on Basis for Box Topology. The box topology on $X$ is defined as the topology $\tau$ generated by the synthetic basis $\BB$.

label: Definition:Brachistochrone
snippet: Let a point $A$ be joined by a wire to a lower point $B$. Let the wire be allowed to be bent into whatever shape is required. Let a bead be released at $A$ to slide down without friction to $B$. The shape of the wire so that the bead takes least time to descend from $A$ to $B$ is called the brachistochrone.

label: Definition:Braid Group
snippet: The braid group on $n$ strands is generated by $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \ldots, \sigma_{n-1}$ and the following relations: $\sigma_i \sigma_j = \sigma_j\sigma_i, \forall i, j: |i-j| \ge 2$ $\sigma_i \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i = \sigma_{i+1} \sigma_i \sigma_{i+1}, \forall i \in \{ 1, 2, \ldots, n-2 \}$

label: Definition:Braid Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Braid Theory == related the study of braids to group theory in the $1930$s. In the $1960$s, pointed out the relevance of braid theory the theory of mappings. Thus, if $n$ points are moved continuously in the plane back to their original positions, the motion can be interpreted as a braid. Hence showed how the roots of a polynomial vary according to how the polynomial coefficients are varied. Also in the $1930$s, established the close relationship between braid theory and knot theory. This was then exploited in the $1980$s by .

label: Definition:Branch
snippet: Graph Theory: Branch of a rooted tree: A path from the root node of a rooted tree to one of its leaf nodes Set Theory: Branch of a set-theoretical tree: A maximal chain in a set-theoretical tree Mapping Theory: Branch of a multifunction Branch point of complex multifunction Complex Analysis: Holomorphic Branch Analytic Geometry: Branch of a curve Branch point of a curve Branch of a hyperbola

label: Definition:Branch Point of Complex Multifunction/Definition 1
snippet: Let $U \subseteq \C$ be an open set. Let $f: U \to \C$ be a complex multifunction. A branch point of $f$ is a point $a$ in $U$ such that: $f$ has more than one value at one or more points in every neighborhood of $a$ $f$ has exactly one value at $a$ itself.

label: Definition:Branch Point of Complex Multifunction/Definition 2
snippet: Let $U \subseteq \C$ be an open set. Let $f: U \to \C$ be a complex multifunction. Let $a$ be a point of $f$ such that there does not exist a holomorphic branch of $f$ on some punctured $\epsilon$-disk $\set {z \in \C: 0 < \cmod {z - a} < \epsilon}$ around $a$. Then $a$ is a branch point of $f$.

label: Definition:Branch and Bound Method
snippet: The branch and bound method is an algorithmic procedure for solving the knapsack problem which works as follows: It constructs a branching method that terminates each branch once the constraint limit has been reached It allows items to be added in a predetermined order. This reduces the number of combinations that need to be tried. The algorithm works as follows. Let $\KK$ be a knapsack with maximum weight capacity of $C$ (arbitrary) units. Let $S = \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a finite set of $n$ items, with a weight $w: S \to \R$ and a value $v: S \to \R$.

label: Definition:Branch of Curve/Branch Point
snippet: A branch point of a curve $\CC$ is a point on $\CC$ at which two or more branches of $\CC$ meet.

label: Definition:Bravais Lattice
snippet: A Bravais lattice is a model of the way the structure of a crystal is replicated throughout space.

label: Definition:Bridge
snippet: Graph Theory: Definition:Bridge (Graph Theory) Recreational Mathematics Definition:Bridge (Game)

label: Definition:Brill-Noether Theory
snippet: Brill-Noether Theory is the branch of algebraic geometry which studies special divisors.

label: Definition:British Units of Length
snippet: The British units of length consists of a system of length based on the yard. As such, they form a subset of the imperial system.

snippet: 700px Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle such that $A \to B \to C \to A$ travels anticlockwise around $\triangle ABC$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the first and second Brocard points of $\triangle ABC$ respectively. Let: From Brocard Angle is Unique: $\omega = \omega'$ This angle $\omega = \omega'$ is the Brocard angle of $\triangle ABC$.

label: Definition:Brocard Points
snippet: 700px Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle such that $A \to B \to C \to A$ travels anticlockwise around $\triangle ABC$.

label: Definition:Brocard Points/First
snippet: 700px Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle such that $A \to B \to C \to A$ travels anticlockwise around $\triangle ABC$. Let the point $P$ be constructed such that: $\angle PAB = \angle PBC = \angle PCA$ Then $P$ is the first Brocard point of $\triangle ABC$.

label: Definition:Brocard Points/Second
snippet: 700px Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle such that $A \to B \to C \to A$ travels anticlockwise around $\triangle ABC$. Let the point $Q$ be constructed such that: $\angle QAC = \angle QCB = \angle QBA$ Then $Q$ is the second Brocard point of $\triangle ABC$.

label: Definition:Broken Line
snippet: A broken line is a line which is formed from a number of discrete straight line segments joined together. Hence a curve may be approximated by a broken line, like how a circle can be approximated by a regular polygon.

label: Definition:Brown Numbers
snippet: Brown numbers are pairs of integers $\left({m, n}\right)$ such that: $n! + 1 = m^2$ There are only $3$ known such pairs: $\left({5, 4}\right)$ $\left({11, 5}\right)$ $\left({71, 7}\right)$

label: Definition:Brownian Motion
snippet: Brownian motion is the physical phenomenon of random jittery motion of microscopic particles suspended in a fluid, such as pollen grains in water. This is caused by the random motion of the molecules of the fluid impacting on the particles. It may be modelled as a stochastic process.

label: Definition:Brun's Constant
snippet: Brun's constant is the sum of the series consisting of the reciprocals of the twin primes: $B_2 := \paren {\dfrac 1 3 + \dfrac 1 5} + \paren {\dfrac 1 5 + \dfrac 1 7} + \paren {\dfrac 1 {11} + \dfrac 1 {13} } + \paren {\dfrac 1 {17} + \dfrac 1 {19} } + \paren {\dfrac 1 {29} + \dfrac 1 {31} } + \cdots$ Its approxmiate decimal expansion is: $B_2 \approx 1 \cdotp 90216 \, 05831 \, 04 \ldots$ Estimates of its value are occasionally refined as further work is done to establish its nature.

snippet: The bubble sort is an algorithm for arranging a finite set $S$ of objects into an ordered set $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$, where $\preccurlyeq$ is an arbitrary (total) ordering. It uses repeated passes through $S$ to exchange adjacent elements if they are not in the required order. label: Definition:Buoyancy
snippet: Let $B$ be immersed (either fully or partly) in a fluid $F$. The buoyancy of $B$ is defined as the upward force on $B$ exerted by $F$.

label: Definition:Buoyancy/Center
snippet: Let $B$ be immersed (either fully or partly) in a fluid $F$. The center of buoyancy of $B$ is defined as the center of gravity of the displaced volume of $F$.

label: Definition:Burnout Height
snippet: Let $R$ be a rocket which is propelled by backwards expulsion of the exhaust products of the burning of its internal fuel supply. Let $R$ be fired straight up from the surface of a planet. The burnout height of $R$ is the height attained by $R$ at the instant when its fuel has become exhausted.

label: Definition:Burnout Velocity
snippet: Let $R$ be a rocket which is propelled by backwards expulsion of the exhaust products of the burning of its internal fuel supply. Let $R$ be fired straight up from the surface of a planet. The burnout velocity of $R$ is the velocity attained by $R$ at the instant when its fuel has become exhausted.

label: Definition:By Hypothesis
snippet: When demonstrating a proof, it is frequently necessary to refer to the specification of the result which is to be proved. This result often contains wording along the lines Suppose that ... or Let ... It is convenient to refer back to these specifications during the course of the proof. To do that, the term by hypothesis is often used.

label: Definition:Bézout Numbers
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$ such that $a \ne 0$ or $b \ne 0$. Let $d$ be the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$. By Bézout's Identity: $\exists x, y \in \Z: a x + b y = d$ The numbers $x$ and $y$ are known as Bézout numbers of $a$ and $b$.
