label: Definition:Compatible Atlases
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $\mathscr F, \mathscr G$ be $d$-dimensional atlases of class $C^k$ on $M$.

label: Definition:Compatible Atlases/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $\mathscr F, \mathscr G$ be $d$-dimensional atlases of class $C^k$ on $M$. $\mathscr F, \mathscr G$ are $C^k$-compatible their union $\mathscr F \cup \mathscr G$ is an atlas of class $C^k$.

label: Definition:Compatible Atlases/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $\mathscr F, \mathscr G$ be $d$-dimensional atlases of class $C^k$ on $M$. $\mathscr F$ and $\mathscr G$ are $C^k$-compatible every pair of charts $\struct {U, \phi} \in \mathscr F$ and $\struct {V, \psi} \in \mathscr G$ are $C^k$-compatible.

label: Definition:Compatible Charts
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological space. Let $d$ be a natural number. Let $\struct {U, \phi}$ and $\struct {V, \psi}$ be $d$-dimensional charts of $M$. Then $\struct {U, \phi}$ and $\struct {V, \psi}$ are $C^k$-compatible their transition mapping: $\psi \circ \phi^{-1}: \map \phi {U \cap V} \to \map \psi {U \cap V}$ is of class $C^k$.

label: Definition:Compatible Family of Sections on Topological Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\map {\mathbf {Ouv} } T$ be the category of open sets of $T$. Let $\map {\mathbf {Ouv} } T ^{\mathrm {op} }$ be the dual category of $\map {\mathbf {Ouv} } T$. Let $\FF : \map {\mathbf {Ouv} } T ^{\mathrm {op} } \to \mathbf {Set}$ be a presheaf of sets on $T$. Let $U \subset S$ be an open subset of $T$. Let $\family {U_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an open cover of $U$. Let $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ with $f_i \in \map \FF {U_i}$ for $i \mathop \in I$ be a family.

label: Definition:Compatible Module Structures
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be rings. Let $\struct {M, +}$ be an abelian group. Let $* : A \times M \to M$ and $\circledast: B \times M \to M$ be left or right linear ring actions so that: $(1): \quad \struct {M, +, *}$ is a left or right module over $A$ $(2): \quad \struct {M, +, \circledast}$ is a left or right module over $B$

label: Definition:Compatible Module Structures/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be rings. Let $\struct {M, +}$ be an abelian group. Let $* : A \times M \to M$ and $\circledast: B \times M \to M$ be left or right linear ring actions so that: $(1): \quad \struct {M, +, *}$ is a left or right module over $A$ $(2): \quad \struct {M, +, \circledast}$ is a left or right module over $B$ The module structures are compatible for all $a \in A$, $b \in B$, the homotheties $h_a$ and $h_b$ commute. That is, for all $m \in M$, $a \in A$, $b \in B$: $a * \paren {b \circledast m} = b \circledast \paren {a * m}$

label: Definition:Compatible Module Structures/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be rings. Let $\struct {M, +}$ be an abelian group. Let $* : A \times M \to M$ and $\circledast: B \times M \to M$ be left or right linear ring actions so that: $(1): \quad \struct {M, +, *}$ is a left or right module over $A$ $(2): \quad \struct {M, +, \circledast}$ is a left or right module over $B$ The module structures are compatible for all $a \in A$, the homothety $h_a : M \to M$ is an endomorphism of the $B$-module $M$.

label: Definition:Compatible Module Structures/Definition 3
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be rings. Let $\struct {M, +}$ be an abelian group. Let $* : A \times M \to M$ and $\circledast: B \times M \to M$ be left or right linear ring actions so that: $(1): \quad \struct {M, +, *}$ is a left or right module over $A$ $(2): \quad \struct {M, +, \circledast}$ is a left or right module over $B$ The module structures are compatible for all $b \in A$, the homothety $h_b : M \to M$ is an endomorphism of the $A$-module $M$. That is, the image of the ring representation $B \to \map \End M$ is contained in the endomorphism ring $\map {\End_A} M$.

label: Definition:Compatible Quasiuniformities
snippet: Let $\UU_1$ and $\UU_2$ be quasiuniformities on a set $S$. Let $\struct {\struct {S, \UU_1}, \tau_1}$ and $\struct {\struct {S, \UU_2}, \tau_2}$ be the quasiuniform spaces generated by $\UU_1$ and $\UU_2$. Then $\UU_1$ and $\UU_2$ are compatible (with each other) their topologies are equal. That is, $\tau_1 = \tau_2$.

label: Definition:Complement
snippet: Geometry: Complementary angles: two angles whose measures add up to the measure of a right angle. Complements of Parallelograms: The extra bits that need to be added to a pair of parallelograms sharing a line for their diagonals that need to be added to make one big parallelogram. Relation Theory: Complement of Relation: for a relation $\RR$, its complement is all those pairs which are not in $\RR$. Set Theory: Set Complement or Relative Complement: two related concepts: all the elements of a set which are not in a given subset.

label: Definition:Complementary Angles
snippet: 360px Let $\angle BAC$ be a right angle. Let $\angle BAD + \angle DAC = \angle BAC$. That is: $\angle DAC = \angle BAC - \angle BAD$ Then $\angle DAC$ is the complement of $\angle BAD$. Hence, for any angle $\alpha$ (whether less than a right angle or not), the complement of $\alpha$ is $\dfrac \pi 2 - \alpha$. Measured in degrees, the complement of $\alpha$ is $90 \degrees - \alpha$. If $\alpha$ is the complement of $\beta$, then it follows that $\beta$ is the complement of $\alpha$. Hence we can say that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are complementary.

label: Definition:Complementary Event
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A \in \Sigma$ be an event in $\EE$. The complementary event to $A$ is defined as $\relcomp \Omega A$. That is, it is the subset of the sample space of $\EE$ consisting of all the elementary events of $\EE$ that are not in $A$.

label: Definition:Complementary Idempotent
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A$ be an idempotent operator on $\HH$. Then the complementary idempotent (operator) of $A$ is the bounded linear operator $I - A$, where $I$ is the identity operator on $H$.

label: Definition:Complementary Projection
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A$ be a projection on $\HH$. Then the complementary projection (operator) of $A$ is the bounded linear operator $I - A$, where $I$ is the identity operator on $\HH$.

label: Definition:Complementary Subspace
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space. Let $N, Y \subseteq X$ be subspaces. Then $Y$ is a complementary subspace of $N$ $X$ is the direct sum: $X = N \oplus Y$ That is, for each $x \in X$, there exist unique $n \in N$ and $y \in Y$ such that: $x = n + y$

label: Definition:Complemented Basic Sequence
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a basic sequence in $X$. Let $\sqbrk {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be the closed linear span of $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is complemented $\sqbrk {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a topologically complemented subspace of $X$.

label: Definition:Complete
snippet: Topology: Complete Metric Space: a metric space in which every Cauchy sequence is convergent. Topologically Complete Space: a topological space induced by a complete metric space Complete Topological Group Differential Geometry: Complete Vector Field Order Theory: Complete Ordered Set: an ordered set whose subsets all admit both a supremum and an infimum (also known as a Complete Lattice) Dedekind Completeness Property: the property of an ordered set whose non-empty subsets which are bounded above all admit a supremum Chain Complete Set: an ordered set in which every chain has an upper bound…

label: Definition:Complete Bipartite Graph
snippet: A complete bipartite graph is a bipartite graph $G = \struct {A \mid B, E}$ in which every vertex in $A$ is adjacent to every vertex in $B$. The complete bipartite graph where $A$ has $m$ vertices and $B$ has $n$ vertices is denoted $K_{m, n}$.

label: Definition:Complete Category
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a category. Then $\CC$ is (small-)complete for all small categories $\II$ and all diagrams $D : \II \to \CC$ there exists a limit of $D$ in $\CC$.

label: Definition:Complete Connected Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a connected Riemannian manifold. Suppose $M$ is geodesically complete or metrically complete. Then $M$ is said to be complete.

label: Definition:Complete Disconnected Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a disconnected Riemannian manifold. Suppose $M$ is geodesically complete or that every disconnected component is a complete metric space. Then $M$ is said to be complete.

label: Definition:Complete Distributive Lattice
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Then $S$ is a complete distributive lattice $(1): \quad S$ is a complete lattice $(2): \quad S$ is a distributive lattice.

label: Definition:Complete Graph
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a simple graph such that every vertex is adjacent to every other vertex. Then $G$ is called complete. The complete graph of order $p$ is denoted $K_p$.

label: Definition:Complete Join Semilattice
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is a complete join semilattice : $\forall S' \subseteq S: \sup S' \in S$ That is, all subsets of $S$ have a supremum.

label: Definition:Complete Lattice/Also known as
snippet: == Complete Lattice: Also known as == A complete lattice is also known as a complete ordered set. Category:Definitions/Complete Lattices

label: Definition:Complete Lattice/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is a complete lattice : $\forall T \subseteq S: T$ admits both a supremum and an infimum.

label: Definition:Complete Lattice/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is a complete lattice : $\forall S' \subseteq S: \inf S', \sup S' \in S$ That is, all subsets of $S$ have both a supremum and an infimum.

label: Definition:Complete Lattice/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Greatest and Smallest Elements == The greatest element and smallest element of a complete lattice are denoted on by $\top$ and $\bot$ respectively. Some sources use $1$ for the greatest element and $0$ for the smallest element.

label: Definition:Complete Lattice Homomorphism
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct {S_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct {S_2, \preceq_2}$ be complete lattices. Let $\phi: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping between the underlying sets of $L_1$ and $L_2$. Then: $\phi$ is a complete lattice homomorphism from $L_1$ to $L_2$, denoted $\phi: L_1 \to L_2$ $\phi$ satisfies the complete lattice homomorphism axioms:

label: Definition:Complete Lattice Isomorphism
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct {A_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct {A_2, \preceq_2}$ be complete lattices. Let $\phi: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping.

label: Definition:Complete Lattice Isomorphism/Definition 1
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct {A_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct {A_2, \preceq_2}$ be complete lattices. Let $\phi: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping. We say $\phi: L_1 \to L_2$ is a complete lattice isomorphism $\phi : L_1 \to L_2$ is a bijective complete lattice homomorphism.

label: Definition:Complete Lattice Isomorphism/Definition 2
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct {A_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct {A_2, \preceq_2}$ be complete lattices. Let $\phi: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping. We say $\phi : L_1 \to L_2$ is a complete lattice isomorphism $\phi : L_1 \to L_2$ is an order isomorphism.

label: Definition:Complete Lattice Isomorphism/Definition 3
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct {A_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct {A_2, \preceq_2}$ be complete lattices. Let $\phi: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping. We say $\phi : L_1 \to L_2$ is a complete lattice isomorphism : $\phi : \struct {A_1, \vee_1, \wedge_1, \preceq_1} \to \struct {A_2, \vee_2, \wedge_2, \preceq_2}$ is a lattice isomorphism where $\wedge_1, \vee_1$ denote the meet and join on $L_1$ $\wedge_2, \vee_2$ denote the meet and join on $L_2$

label: Definition:Complete Logistic System
snippet: A complete logistic system is a logistic system in which every valid WFF is a theorem.

label: Definition:Complete Matching
snippet: Let $B$ be a bipartite graph. Let $M$ be a matching on $B$ such that every vertex of $B$ is used. Then $M$ is known as a complete matching.

label: Definition:Complete Measure Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let the family of $\mu$-null sets $\NN_\mu$ satisfy the condition: $\forall N \in \NN_\mu: \forall M \subseteq N: M \in \NN_\mu$ That is, any subset of a $\mu$-null set is again a $\mu$-null set. Then $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ is said to be a complete measure space.

label: Definition:Complete Meet Semilattice
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is a complete meet semilattice : $\forall S' \subseteq S: \inf S' \in S$ That is, all subsets of $S$ have an infimum.

label: Definition:Complete Metric Space/Also known as
snippet: == Complete Metric Space: Also known as == A complete metric space is also known as a complete space.

label: Definition:Complete Metric Space/Definition 1
snippet: A metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is complete every Cauchy sequence is convergent.

label: Definition:Complete Metric Space/Definition 2
snippet: A metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is complete the intersection of every nested sequence of closed balls whose radii tend to zero is non-empty.

label: Definition:Complete Normed Division Ring
snippet:
A normed division ring $\struct {R, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ is complete the metric space $\struct {R, d}$ is a complete metric space where $d$ is the metric induced by the norm $
orm {\, \cdot \,}$. That is, a normed division ring $\struct {R, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ is complete every Cauchy sequence is convergent.

label: Definition:Complete Order Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a complete ordered set. Let $\tau$ be the order topology on $\struct {S, \preceq}$. Then $\tau$ is a complete order topology. Hence $\struct {S, \preceq, \tau}$ is a complete order space.

label: Definition:Complete Orthonormal Basis
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be an orthonormal sequence in $\HH$ which is also a Schauder basis. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is known as a complete orthonormal basis.

label: Definition:Complete Quadrangle/Diagonal Point
snippet: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ be the points of a complete quadrangle $ABCD$. The diagonal points of $ABCD$ are the points of intersection of the lines: $AB$ and $CD$ $AC$ and $BD$ $AD$ and $BC$.

label: Definition:Complete Quadrilateral
snippet: A complete quadrilateral is a quadrilateral whose $4$ lines are extended so as to form $6$ points of intersection. 380px In the above diagram, $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ and $DA$ are the initial $4$ straight lines forming the quadrilateral, whose further intersections are $E$ and $F$.

label: Definition:Complete Quadrilateral/Diagonal
snippet: 380px The diagonals of a complete quadrilateral $Q$ are the lines joining the points of $Q$ which do not already have lines joining them. In the above diagram, $AC$ and $BD$ form two of the diagonals, while $EF$ forms the $3$rd diagonal.

label: Definition:Complete Ritz Sequence
snippet: Let $\MM$ be a normed linear space. Let $\sequence {\phi_n}$ be a Ritz sequence in $\MM$. Let $\MM_n$ be an $n$-dimensional linear subspace of $\MM$, spanned by the first $n$ mappings of $\sequence {\phi_n}$. Let $\eta_n$ be of the form: $\eta_n = \boldsymbol \alpha \boldsymbol \phi$ where $\boldsymbol \alpha$ is an $n$-dimensional real vector. Let $\sequence {\phi_n}$ be such that: $\forall y \in \MM: \forall \epsilon > 0: \exists \map n \epsilon \in \N: \exists \eta_n \in \MM_n: \size {\eta_n - y} < \epsilon$ Then the sequence $\sequence {\phi_n}$ is called complete in $\MM$.

label: Definition:Complete Set of Events
snippet: Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of events in a probability space indexed by $I$. $\family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is a complete set of events : $\ds \map \Pr {\bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} A_i} = 1$

label: Definition:Completed Riemann Zeta Function
snippet: The completed Riemann zeta function $\xi: \C \to \C$ is defined on the complex plane $\C$ as: $\ds \forall s \in \C: \map \xi s := \begin{cases} \dfrac 1 2 s \paren {s - 1} \pi^{-s/2} \map \Gamma {\dfrac s 2} \map \zeta s & : \map \Re s > 0 \\ \map \xi {1 - s} & : \map \Re s \le 0 \end{cases}$ where $\map \zeta s$ is the Riemann zeta function.

label: Definition:Completely Metrizable Space
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. The space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is said to be a completely metrizable (topological) space there exists a metric $d$ such that: $\struct {S, d}$ is a complete metric space and: $\tau$ is the topological space induced by the metric $d$. Such a $\tau$ itself is referred to as a completely metrizable topology.

snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a completely regular space : $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_{3 \frac 1 2}$ space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_1$ space. That is:

snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a completely regular space : $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_{3 \frac 1 2}$ space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_2$ space. That is:

snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A, d}$ and $M_2 = \struct {\tilde A, \tilde d}$ be metric spaces. Then $M_2$ is a completion of $M_1$, or $M_2$ completes $M_1$, : {{item|(4):|$\forall x, y \in A : \map {\tilde d} {x, y} \map d {x, y}$. label: Definition:Complex
snippet: Complex Analysis: the realm of mathematics which explores the properties of functions of complex numbers. Complex number Complex function Complex conjugate and so on. Abstract Algebra: Complex: another word for a subset product. Group Theory: Complex: another word for a subset of a group. Homological Algebra: Differential complex: another word for a null sequence. Algebra and Arithmetic: Complex fraction: a fraction such that the numerator or denominator or both are themselves fractions (also known as a compound fraction).

label: Definition:Complex-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a function. Let $S_1 \subseteq S$ such that $f \left({S_1}\right) \subseteq \C$. Then $f$ is defined as complex-valued on $S_1$. That is, $f$ is defined as complex-valued on $S_1$ if the image of $S_1$ under $f$ lies entirely within the set of complex numbers $\C$. A complex-valued function is a function $f: S \to \C$ whose codomain is the set of complex numbers $\C$. That is $f$ is complex-valued iff it is complex-valued over its entire domain.

label: Definition:Complex (Group Theory)
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $K \subseteq G$ be a subset of $G$. Then $K$ is referred to by some sources as a complex of elements of $G$.

label: Definition:Complex (Group Theory)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Complex (Group Theory) == The concept of a complex in the context of group theory as a synonym for a subset of a group is old-fashioned and perhaps even idiosyncratic. Beyond documenting the idea, will not be exploring the concept, as a treatment using the concept of a subset is well-developed and mathematically mainstream. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Complex Algebra
snippet: Complex algebra is the branch of algebra which specifically involves complex arithmetic. Thus it is the branch of mathematics which studies the techniques of manipulation of expressions in the domain of complex numbers.

label: Definition:Complex Analysis/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Complex Analysis == The field of complex analysis, and the theory of functions of a complex variable was in effect created by . rebuilt the entire mathematical discipline from the ground up in the process of his studies into Abelian functions.

label: Definition:Complex Arithmetic
snippet: Complex arithmetic is the branch of arithmetic which concerns the manipulation of complex numbers

label: Definition:Complex Conjugate
snippet: Let $z = a + i b$ be a complex number. Then the (complex) conjugate of $z$ is denoted $\overline z$ and is defined as: $\overline z := a - i b$ That is, you get the complex conjugate of a complex number by negating its imaginary part.

label: Definition:Complex Conjugate/Also known as
snippet: == Complex Conjugate: Also known as == The complex conjugate of a complex number is usually just called its conjugate when (as is usual in the context) there is no danger of confusion with other usages of the word conjugate. The notation $z^*$ is a frequently encountered alternative to $\overline z$. The notation $\hat z$ is also occasionally seen.

label: Definition:Complex Conjugate/Complex Conjugation
snippet: The operation of complex conjugation is the mapping: $\overline \cdot: \C \to \C: z \mapsto \overline z$. where $\overline z$ is the complex conjugate of $z$. That is, it maps a complex number to its complex conjugate. Category:Definitions/Complex Conjugates

label: Definition:Complex Conjugate/Conjugate Pair
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. Let $\overline z$ be the complex conjugate of $z$. Then $z$ and $\overline z$ are a conjugate pair.

label: Definition:Complex Conjugate Coordinates
snippet: Let $P$ be a point in the complex plane. $P$ may be located using complex conjugate coordinates $\tuple {z, \overline z}$ based on: {{eqn | l = x | r = \dfrac {z + \overline z} 2 | c = Sum of Complex Number with Conjugate }} {{eqn | l = y | r = \dfrac {z - \overline z} {2 i} | c = Difference of Complex Number with Conjugate }} where $P = \tuple {x, y}$ is expressed in Cartesian coordinates.

label: Definition:Complex Conjugate of Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk \alpha_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over the complex numbers $\C$. Let $\overline {\mathbf A}$ denote the matrix formed from $\mathbf A$ by replacing each entry of $\mathbf A$ with its complex conjugate: $\overline {\mathbf A} = \sqbrk \beta_{m n}: \forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, m}, j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}: \beta_{i j} = \overline {\alpha_{i j} }$ where $\overline {\alpha_{i j} }$ denotes the complex conjugate of $\alpha_{j i}$. Then $\overline {\mathbf A}$ is the complex conjugate of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Complex Conjugate of Matrix/Also denoted as
snippet: == Complex Conjugate of Matrix: Also denoted as == The complex conjugate of a matrix $\mathbf A$ can also be seen denoted by $\mathbf A^*$.

label: Definition:Complex Cross-Ratio/Riemann Sphere
snippet: == Complex Cross-Ratio: Definition on Riemann Sphere == The concept of the complex cross-ratio can be extended to the Riemann sphere by allowing one of the points $z_1$, $z_2$, $z_3$ or $z_4$ to be the point at infinity.

label: Definition:Complex Disk
snippet: A (complex) disk is a ball in the complex plane. Let $a \in \C$ be a complex number. Let $R > 0$ be a real number.

label: Definition:Complex Disk/Closed
snippet: A closed (complex) disk is a closed ball in the complex plane. Let $a \in \C$ be a complex number. Let $R > 0$ be a real number. The closed (complex) disk of center $a$ and radius $R$ is the set: $\map {\overline B} {a, R} = \set {z \in \C: \cmod {z - a} \le R}$ where $\cmod {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes complex modulus.

label: Definition:Complex Disk/Open
snippet: An open (complex) disk is an open ball in the complex plane. Let $a \in \C$ be a complex number. Let $R > 0$ be a real number. The open (complex) disk of center $a$ and radius $R$ is the set: $\map B {a, R} = \set {z \in \C: \cmod {z - a} < R}$ where $\cmod {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes complex modulus.

label: Definition:Complex Embedding
snippet: Let $K$ be a subfield of the set of complex numbers $\C$. A complex embedding of $K$ is a ring monomorphism of $K$ into $\C$. That is, a complex embedding is an injective field homomorphism $\sigma: K \to \C$.

label: Definition:Complex Function
snippet: A complex function is a function whose domain and codomain are subsets of the set of complex numbers $\C$.

label: Definition:Complex Function Theory
snippet: Complex function theory is the branch of complex analysis which studies complex functions.

label: Definition:Complex Half-Plane
snippet: Let $\C$ denote the complex plane. A complex half-plane is a half-plane of $\C$ whose edge is an infinite straight line of $\C$. Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis

label: Definition:Complex Inverse Hyperbolic Function
snippet: Let $h: \C \to \C$ be one of the hyperbolic functions on the set of complex numbers. The inverse hyperbolic function $h^{-1} \subseteq \C \times \C$ is actually a multifunction, as in general for a given $y \in \C$ there is more than one $x \in \C$ such that $y = \map h x$. As with the inverse trigonometric functions, it is usual to restrict the codomain of the multifunction so as to allow $h^{-1}$ to be single-valued. There are six basic hyperbolic functions, so each of these has its inverse functions:

label: Definition:Complex Matrix
snippet: A complex matrix is a matrix whose elements are all complex numbers.

label: Definition:Complex Modulus
snippet: Let $z = a + i b$ be a complex number, where $a, b \in \R$. The (complex) modulus of $z$ is written $\cmod z$, and is defined as the square root of the sum of the squares of the real and imaginary parts: $\cmod z := \sqrt {a^2 + b^2}$ The (complex) modulus is a real-valued function, and, as and when appropriate, can be referred to as the (complex) modulus function. It is to be noted that the modulus of a complex number $z$ is the distance between the origin and the point representing $z$ on an Argand diagram.

label: Definition:Complex Modulus/Also known as
snippet: == Complex Modulus: Also known as == The (complex) modulus is also known as the absolute value. Others use that term only for the absolute value of a real number. The notation $\bmod z$ is sometimes seen for $\cmod z$, but on $\cmod z$ is preferred. It is to be noted that the term complex modulus is technically inaccurate, on the grounds that it is not the modulus itself which is complex. However, it has been chosen for for its relative ambiguity when distinguishing it from other uses of the term modulus.

label: Definition:Complex Natural Logarithm/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Complex Natural Logarithm == In $1702$, encountered solutions of the primitive $\ds \int \dfrac {\d x} {a x^2 + b x + c}$ which seemed to require logarithms of complex numbers, which at that time had not been considered. and both investigated, and by $1712$ they had developed opposing viewpoints on how to handle the logarithm of a negative number. used the argument: $\dfrac {\map \d {-x} } {-x} = \dfrac {\map \d x} x$, so by integration $\map \ln {-x} = \map \ln x$ while insisted that the integration was only valid for positive $x$.

label: Definition:Complex Number/Complex Plane/Imaginary Axis
snippet: Let the set $\C$ of complex number be expressed as an ordered pairs on the complex plane. Complex numbers of the form $\tuple {0, y}$, being wholly imaginary, appear as points on the points on the $y$-axis. Hence the $y$-axis of the complex plane is known as the imaginary axis.

label: Definition:Complex Number/Complex Plane/Real Axis
snippet: Let the set $\C$ of complex number be expressed as an ordered pairs on the complex plane. Complex numbers of the form $\tuple {x, 0}$, being wholly real, appear as points on the $x$-axis. Hence the $x$-axis of the complex plane is known as the real axis.

label: Definition:Complex Number/Construction from Cayley-Dickson Construction
snippet: The complex numbers can be defined by the Cayley-Dickson construction from the set of real numbers $\R$. From Real Numbers form Algebra, $\R$ forms a nicely normed $*$-algebra. Let $a, b \in \R$. Then $\tuple {a, b} \in \C$, where: $\tuple {a, b} \tuple {c, d} = \tuple {a c - d \overline b, \overline a d + c b}$ $\overline {\tuple {a, b} } = \tuple {\overline a, -b}$ where: $\overline a$ is the conjugate of $a$ and $\overline {\tuple {a, b} }$ is the conjugation operation on $\C$.

label: Definition:Complex Number/Definition 1
snippet: A complex number is a number in the form $a + b i$ or $a + i b$ where: $a$ and $b$ are real numbers $i$ is a square root of $-1$, that is, $i = \sqrt {-1}$.

label: Definition:Complex Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Complex Number == The concept of a complex number originated in the $16$th century as during the course of developing the solution to the general cubic equation. In his of $1545$, considered the simultaneous equations: $\begin {cases} x + y & = 10 \\ x y & = 40 \end {cases}$ and obtained the solution: $\begin {cases} x & = 5 + \sqrt {-15} \\y & = 5 - \sqrt {-15} \end {cases}$ He made no attempt to interpret the meaning of the square root of a negative number, dismissing it with the comment: So progresses arithmetic subtlely, the end result of which ...

label: Definition:Complex Number/Imaginary Part
snippet: Let $z = a + i b$ be a complex number. The imaginary part of $z$ is the coefficient $b$ (note: not $i b$). The imaginary part of a complex number $z$ is usually denoted on by $\map \Im z$ or $\Im z$.

label: Definition:Complex Number/Imaginary Unit
snippet: Let $\C = \set {a + b i: a, b \in \R}$ be the set of complex numbers. The entity $i := 0 + 1 i$ is known as the imaginary unit.

label: Definition:Complex Number/Irrational
snippet: A complex number is classified as irrational its imaginary part is non-zero.

label: Definition:Complex Number/Notation
snippet: == Complex Number: Also denoted as == The set of complex numbers is usually denoted $\C$. Variants on $\C$ are often seen, for example $\mathbf C$, $\CC$ and $\mathfrak C$, or even just $C$. When $a$ and $b$ are symbols representing variables or constants, the form $a + i b$ is usually (but not universally) seen. Similarly, when $a$ and $b$ are actual numbers, for example $3$ and $4$, it is usually (but not universally) written $3 + 4 i$. In the field of electronics, the letter $j$ is usually used instead of $i$, as $i$ is generally used as the symbol denoting electric current.

snippet: A complex number $z = a + i b$ is wholly imaginary $a = 0$.

label: Definition:Complex Number/Wholly Real
snippet: A complex number $z = a + i b$ is wholly real $b = 0$.

label: Definition:Complex Number as Vector
snippet: Let $z = x + i y$ be a complex number. Then $z$ can be considered as a vector $OP$ in the complex plane such that: its initial point is the origin its terminal point $P$ is the point $\tuple {x, y}$. Two vectors which have the same magnitude and direction, but different initial points, are considered equal.

snippet: == Complex Plane: Also known as == Some sources refer to the complex plane as an Argand plane, for . It is also sometimes known as a Gauss plane, or Gaussian plane, for . label: Definition:Complex Point at Infinity
snippet: The zero in the set of complex numbers $\C$ has no inverse for multiplication. That is, the expression: $\dfrac 1 0$ has no meaning. The (complex) point at infinity is the element added to $\C$ in order to allow $\C$ to be closed under division: $\forall x, y \in \C: \dfrac x y \in \C$ The set $\C$ with that point added is known as the extended complex plane. Conceptually, it can be imagined as a point which is at infinity in all directions. It can also be considered as the $N$ point on the Riemann sphere which does not map to the complex plane. This point can be denoted $\infty$.

label: Definition:Complex Root
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number such that $z \ne 0$. Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $w \in \C$ such that: $w^n = z$ Then $w$ is a (complex) $n$th root of $z$, and we can write: $w = z^{1 / n}$

label: Definition:Complex Sequence
snippet: A complex sequence is a sequence (usually infinite) whose codomain is the set of complex numbers $\C$.

label: Definition:Complex System
snippet: A complex system is a system with many interacting constituent parts. Complex systems are often modeled using a network, using nodes for subsystems and edges as the interactions between them.

label: Definition:Complex Transformation
snippet: A complex transformation is a mapping on the complex plane $f: \C \to \C$ which is specifically not a multifunction. Let $z = x + i y$ be a complex variable. Let $w = u + i v = \map f z$. Then $w$ can be expressed as: $u + i v = \map f {x + i y}$ such that: $u = \map u {x, y}$ and: $v = \map v {x, y}$ are real functions of two variables. Thus a point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ in the complex plane is transformed to a point $P' = \tuple {\map u {x, y}, \map v {x, y} }$ by $f$. Thus $P'$ is the image of $P$ under $f$.

snippet: == Complex Vector Inner Product: Also denoted as == In the field of quantum mechanics, the complex vector inner product is usually written using Dirac notation: $\braket {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b}$.

label: Definition:Component (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let the relation $\sim $ be defined on $T$ as follows: $x \sim y$ $x$ and $y$ are connected in $T$. That is, there exists a connected set of $T$ that contains both $x$ and $y$.

label: Definition:Component (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let the relation $\sim $ be defined on $T$ as follows: $x \sim y$ $x$ and $y$ are connected in $T$. That is, there exists a connected set of $T$ that contains both $x$ and $y$. From Connectedness of Points is Equivalence Relation, $\sim$ is an equivalence relation. From the Fundamental Theorem on Equivalence Relations, the points in $T$ can be partitioned into equivalence classes. These equivalence classes are called the (connected) components of $T$.

label: Definition:Component (Topology)/Definition 2

The component of $T$ containing $x$ is defined as: $\ds \map {\operatorname{Comp}_x} T = \bigcup \leftset {A \subseteq S: x \in A \land A}$ is connected $\rightset{}$

label: Definition:Composable Morphisms
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $f, g \in \mathbf C_1$ be morphisms of $\mathbf C$. Then $f$ is said to be composable with $g$ : $\Cdm f = \Dom g$ that is, the codomain of $f$ is the domain of $g$. When the order of composition is to be made more explicit, one says that $\tuple {g, f}$ is a composable pair. The collection of all such composable pairs in $\mathbf C$ is denoted $\mathbf C_2$.

label: Definition:Composant

label: Definition:Composant/Continuum
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a continuum in $T$. Let $C \subseteq H$ be a subset of $H$. $C$ is a composant of $H$ : there exists some $p \in H$ such that $C$ contains all points $x \in S$ such that $x$ and $p$ are both contained in some proper subcontinua of $H$.

label: Definition:Composant/Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a continuum in $T$. Let $C \subseteq H$ be a subset of $H$. Let $p \in H$. Then $C$ is the composant of $p$ : $C$ is the union of all proper subcontinua of $H$ that contain $p$.

label: Definition:Composite Hypothesis
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some population. Let the parameter space of $\theta$ be $\Omega$. Let $\Omega_0$ and $\Omega_1$ be disjoint subsets of $\Omega$ such that $\Omega_0 \cup \Omega_1 = \Omega$. Consider the hypotheses: $H_0: \theta \in \Omega_0$ $H_1: \theta \in \Omega_1$ We call $H_i$, for $i \in \set {0, 1}$, a composite hypothesis if $\Omega_i$ contains more than a single element.

Then $g$ defines a composition functor $g_* : \map {\mathbf{Sub}_{\mathbf C} } C \to \map {\mathbf{Sub}_{\mathbf C} } D$: That it is in fact a functor is shown on Composition Functor on Categories of Subobjects is Functor.

label: Definition:Composition Series/Composition Length
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $\HH$ be a composition series for $G$. The composition length of $G$ is the length of $\HH$.

label: Definition:Composition Series/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a finite group. A composition series for $G$ is a normal series for $G$ which has no proper refinement.

label: Definition:Composition Series/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a finite group. A composition series for $G$ is a sequence of normal subgroups of $G$: $\set e = G_0 \lhd G_1 \lhd \cdots \lhd G_n = G$ where: $G_{i - 1} \lhd G_i$ denotes that $G_{i - 1}$ is a proper normal subgroup of $G_i$ such that: for all $i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$, $G_{i - 1}$ is a proper maximal normal subgroup of $G_i$.

label: Definition:Composition of Densely-Defined Linear Operators
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\struct {\map D S, S}$ and $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be densely-defined linear operators. Let: $\map D {S T} = \set {x \in \map D T : T x \in \map D S}$ Define $S T : \map D {S T} \to \HH$ by: $\map {\paren {S T} } x = \map {\paren {S \circ T} } x$ for each $x \in \map D {S T}$. We say that $\struct {\map D {S T}, S T}$ is the composition of $\struct {\map D S, S}$ and $\struct {\map D T, T}$.

label: Definition:Composition of Functors
snippet: Let $\mathbf C, \mathbf D$ and $\mathbf E$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ and $G: \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$ be (covariant) functors. The composition of $G$ with $F$ is the functor $GF: \mathbf C \to \mathbf E$ defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = $\map {GF} C := \map G {FC}$ for all objects $C$ of $\mathbf C$ |mor = $\map {GF} f := \map G {Ff}$ for all morphisms $f: C_1 \to C_2$ of $\mathbf C$ }} $GF$ is said to be a composite functor.

label: Definition:Composition of Mappings
snippet: Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_2$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_1$.

label: Definition:Composition of Mappings/Also known as
snippet: == Composition of Mappings: Also known as == Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_2$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_1$. Let $f_2 \circ f_1$ denote the composition of $f_1$ with $f_2$. In the context of analysis, this is often found referred to as a function of a function, which (according to some sources) makes set theorists wince, as it is technically defined as a function on the codomain of a function. Such a composition is also known as a composite mapping or composite function.

label: Definition:Composition of Mappings/Commutative Diagram
snippet: Let $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ be sets. Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_2$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_1$. The concept of composition of mappings can be illustrated by means of a commutative diagram. This diagram illustrates the specific example of $f_2 \circ f_1$: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+1em{ S_1 \ar[r]^*+{f_1} \ar@{-->}[rd]_*[l]+{f_2 \mathop \circ f_1} & S_2 \ar[d]^*+{f_2} \\ & S_3 }\end{xy}$

label: Definition:Composition of Mappings/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ be sets. Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_2$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_1$. The composite mapping $f_2 \circ f_1$ is defined as: $\forall x \in S_1: \map {\paren {f_2 \circ f_1} } x := \map {f_2} {\map {f_1} x}$ 850px

label: Definition:Composition of Mappings/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ be sets. Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_2$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_1$. The composite of $f_1$ and $f_2$ is defined and denoted as: $f_2 \circ f_1 := \set {\tuple {x, z} \in S_1 \times S_3: \tuple {\map {f_1} x, z} \in f_2}$ 850px

label: Definition:Composition of Mappings/Definition 3
snippet: Let $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ be sets. Let $f_1: S_1 \to S_2$ and $f_2: S_2 \to S_3$ be mappings such that the domain of $f_2$ is the same set as the codomain of $f_1$. The composite of $f_1$ and $f_2$ is defined and denoted as: $f_2 \circ f_1 := \set {\tuple {x, z} \in S_1 \times S_3: \exists y \in S_2: \map {f_1} x = y \land \map {f_2} y = z}$ That is: $f_2 \circ f_1 := \set {\tuple {x, z} \in S_1 \times S_3: \exists y \in S_2: \tuple {x, y} \in f_1 \land \tuple {y, z} \in f_2}$ 850px

label: Definition:Composition of Morphisms
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $\tuple {g, f}$ be a pair of composable morphisms. Then the composition of $f$ and $g$ is a morphism $g \circ f$ of $\mathbf C$ subject to: $\map {\operatorname{dom} } {g \circ f} = \operatorname{dom} f$ $\map {\operatorname{cod} } {g \circ f} = \operatorname{cod} g$ This composition of morphisms can be thought of as an abstraction of both composition of mappings and transitive relations.

label: Definition:Compound Distribution
snippet: Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_N$ be pairwise independent random variables such that: the $X_i$ may or may not have the same probability distribution $N$ itself may also be a (discrete) random variable. Let: $S_N : X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_N$ Then the probability distribution of $S_N$ is known as a compound distribution.

label: Definition:Computable
