label: Definition:Computable Complex Number
snippet: Let: $z = a + b i$ be a complex number. Suppose that both $a$ and $b$ are computable real numbers. Then $z$ is a computable complex number.

label: Definition:Computable Rational Sequence
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \in \N}$ be a infinite sequence of rational numbers. Then, $\sequence {x_n}$ is a computable rational sequence there exist total recursive functions $f, g : \N \to \N$ such that, for all $n \in \N$: $x_n = \dfrac {k_n} {\map g n + 1}$ where $\map f n$ codes the integer $k_n$.

label: Definition:Computable Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset of real cartesian $n$-space. Let $f : D \to \R$ be a real-valued function on $D$. Suppose that $f$ is both sequentially computable and computably uniformly continuous. Then, $f$ is computable.

label: Definition:Computable Real Number
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. Suppose there exists a total recursive function $f : \N \to \N$ such that: For every $n \in \N$, $\map f n$ codes an integer $k$ such that: $\dfrac {k - 1} {n + 1} < x < \dfrac {k + 1} {n + 1}$ Then $x$ is a computable real number.

label: Definition:Computably Uniformly Continuous Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset of real cartesian $n$-space. Let $f : D \to \R$ be a real-valued function on $D$. Suppose there exists a total recursive function $d : \N \to \N$ such that: For every $n \in \N$ and $\bsx, \bsy \in D$ such that: $\norm {\bsx - \bsy} < \dfrac 1 {\map d n + 1}$ where $\norm \cdot$ is the Euclidean norm, it holds that: $\size {\map f \bsx - \map f \bsy} < \dfrac 1 {n + 1}$ Then $f$ is computably uniformly continuous.

label: Definition:Computably Uniformly Continuous Real Function
snippet: Let $f : \R \to \R$ be a real function. Suppose there exists a total recursive function $d : \N \to \N$ such that: For every $n \in \N$ and $x, y \in \R$ such that: $\size {x - y} < \dfrac 1 {\map d n + 1}$ it holds that: $\size {\map f x - \map f y} < \dfrac 1 {n + 1}$ Then $f$ is computably uniformly continuous.

label: Definition:Computational Group Theory
snippet: Computational group theory is the study of groups by means of computers. It is concerned with designing and analysing algorithms and data structures to compute information about groups.

label: Definition:Computational Method
snippet: A computational method is an ordered quadruple $\left({Q, I, \Omega, f}\right)$ in which: $Q$ is a set representing the states of the computation $I$ is a set representing the input to the computation $\Omega$ is a set representing the output from the computation $f: Q \to Q$ is a mapping representing the computational rule subject to the following constraints: $I \subseteq Q$ and $\Omega \subseteq Q$ $\forall x \in \Omega: f \left({x}\right) = x$

label: Definition:Computational Method/Computational Sequence
snippet: Consider the computational method $\left({Q, I, \Omega, f}\right)$ in which: $Q$ represents the set of states of the computation $I$ represents the input to the computation $\Omega$ represents the output from the computation $f: Q \to Q$ represents the computational rule Each $x \in I$ defines a computational sequence $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots$ as follows: $x_0 = x$ $\forall k \ge 0: x_{k+1} = f \left({x_k}\right)$

label: Definition:Computational Method/Computational Sequence/Termination
snippet: A computational sequence $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots$ is said to terminate in $k$ steps if $k$ is the smallest integer for which $x_k \in \Omega$. In this case, it produces the output $x_k$ from $x$. Some computational sequences may never terminate.

label: Definition:Computational Number Theory
snippet: Computational Number Theory is a branch of number theory which investigates problems by means of computational techniques.

label: Definition:Computational Problem
snippet: A computational problem is a mathematical object which represents a collection of questions that are to be solved by algorithmic techniques.

label: Definition:Computer
snippet: A computer is a device for executing logical and arithmetical calculations according to a precise sequence of instructions.

label: Definition:Computer Algebra/General Purpose
snippet: A computer algebra program which is designed to be used on any mathematical problem is classified as general purpose.

label: Definition:Computer Algebra/Specialized
snippet: A computer algebra program which is designed to be used for a specific type of mathematical problem, for example group theory, is classified as specialized.

label: Definition:Computer Programming
snippet: Computer programming is a branch of engineering and computer science. It consists of planning and producing a set of instructions to solve a problem by using a computer.

label: Definition:Computer Science
snippet: Computer science is the branch of mathematics concerning computation. As such it can be considered as an offshoot of both mathematical logic and discrete mathematics.

label: Definition:Computer Science/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Computer Science == The origin of computer science can be traced back to the design of algorithms by . Even further back, the Babylonians employed the techniques of asymptotic complexity and reducibility. The discipline became of great importance with the advent of the digital computer in the $20$th century.

label: Definition:Computer Software
snippet: Computer software is a generic term for the sequences of instructions that are used to control a computer.

label: Definition:Concatenation
snippet: Topology: Concatenation: the joining together of two maps on the unit order-$n$ cube Concatenation of Paths: an instance of such topological concatenation Vector Analysis: Concatenation of Contours: the joining together of two contours to form a longer contour. Formal Systems: Concatenation (Formal Systems): the placing of symbols next to each other to form a string. Set Theory, Abstract Algebra and so on: Concatenation of Ordered Tuples: putting together two ordered tuples to form a new one. Mathematical Logic: Concatenation of URM Programs

label: Definition:Concatenation (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $c_1, c_2: \closedint 0 1^n \to S$ be maps. Let $c_1$ and $c_2$ both satisfy the concatenation criterion: $\map c {\partial \closedint 0 1^n} = x_0$. Then the concatenation $c_1 * c_2$ is defined as: $\map {\paren {c_1 * c_2} } {t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n} = \begin {cases} \map {c_1} {2 t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_n} & : t_1 \in \closedint 0 {1/2} \\ \map {c_2} {2 t_1 - 1, t_2, \ldots, t_n} & : t_1 \in \closedint {1/2} 1 \end{cases}$ where $\tuple {t_1, \ldots, t_n}$ are coordinates in the $n$-cube.

label: Definition:Concatenation of Contours/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C$ and $D$ be contours in the complex plane $\C$. Thus: $C$ is a (finite) sequence of directed smooth curves $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ $D$ is a (finite) sequence of directed smooth curves $\sequence {D_1, \ldots, D_m}$. Let $C_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path: $\gamma_i: \closedint {a_i} {b_i} \to \C$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$ Let $D_i$ be parameterized by the smooth path: $\sigma_i: \closedint {c_i} {d_i} \to \C$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, m}$ Let $\map {\gamma_n} {b_n} = \map {\sigma_1} {c_1}$.

label: Definition:Concatenation of Ordered Tuples
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $w, w'$ be ordered tuples in $S$ of lengths $n$ and $n'$, respectively. Then the concatenation of $w$ and $w'$, denoted $w * w'$ or simply $w w'$, is the ordered tuple of $n + n'$ terms defined by: $\quad \map {w * w'} i := \begin{cases} \map w i & : \text {if } 1 \le i \le n \\ \map {w'} {i - n} & : \text {if } n < i \le n + n' \end{cases}$

label: Definition:Concatenation of Paths
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $f, g: \closedint 0 1 \to X$ be paths. Let $\map f 1 = \map g 0$. The concatenation of $f$ and $g$ is the mapping $f * g: \closedint 0 1 \to X$ defined by: $\ds \map {\paren {f * g} } s = \begin {cases} \map f {2 s} & : 0 \le s \le \dfrac 1 2 \\ \map g {2 s - 1} & : \dfrac 1 2 \le s \le 1 \end {cases}$

label: Definition:Concave
snippet: Geometry: Concave Geometric Figure Concave Polygon Concave Polyhedron Real Analysis Concave Real Function

label: Definition:Concave Circumference of Circle/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Concave Circumference == The concept of the concave circumference arises in as a way of rigorously specifying the relationship between a point and the circumference of the circle under investigation. As such it is not specifically defined in , but is tacitly understood. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Concave Polygon
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. $P$ is a concave polygon : at least one internal angle of $P$ is greater than $180 \degrees$.

label: Definition:Concave Polyhedron/Definition 1
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. $P$ is a concave polyhedron : at least one face of $P$ lies in a plane which intersects at least one other face.

label: Definition:Concave Polyhedron/Definition 2
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. $P$ is a concave polyhedron : at least one face of $P$ lies in a plane such that $P$ does not lie completely on one side of that plane.

label: Definition:Concave Real Function/Definition 1/Strictly
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is strictly concave on $I$ : $\forall x, y \in I, x \ne y: \forall \alpha, \beta \in \R_{>0}, \alpha + \beta = 1: \map f {\alpha x + \beta y} > \alpha \map f x + \beta \map f y$ 700px The geometric interpretation is that any point on the chord drawn on the graph of any strictly concave function always lies below the graph.

label: Definition:Concave Real Function/Geometric Interpretation
snippet: == Geometric Interpretation of Concave Real Function == Let $f$ be a concave real function. Then: for every pair of points $A$ and $B$ on the graph of $f$, the chord $AB$ lies entirely below the graph.

label: Definition:Concave Real Function/Point
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. Let $a \in I$ be a point in the domain of $f$. Then: $f$ is concave at $a$ there exists a neighborhood of $a$ on which $f$ is concave.

label: Definition:Concave Real Function/Vector Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $C \subseteq X$ be a convex set. Let $f: C \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. We say that $f$ is concave : $\map f {t x + \paren {1 - t} y} \ge t \map f x + \paren {1 - t} \map f y$ for each $t \in \openint 0 1$ and $x, y \in C$.

label: Definition:Concentric/Circles
snippet: Circles are said to be concentric if they both have the same point as the center. 320px

label: Definition:Concentric Circle Topology
snippet: Open Set of $T$ Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ be concentric circles in the Cartesian plane $\R^2$ such that $C_1$ is inside $C_2$. Let $S = C_1 \cup C_2$. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets consisting of: all singleton sets of $C_2$ all open intervals on $C_1$ each together with its projection from the center of the circles onto $C_2$ except for the midpoint. $\BB$ is then taken to be the sub-basis for a topology $\tau$ on $S$. Thus $\tau$ is referred to as the concentric circle topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the concentric circle space.

label: Definition:Concentric Spheres
snippet: Spheres are said to be concentric if they both have the same point as the center.

label: Definition:Conchoid
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve. Let $P$ be a fixed point which may or may not lie on $\CC$ itself. A conchoid is the locus of points $p$ such that: each $p$ is on a straight line $\LL$ that passes through $P$ and intersects $\CC$ the distance from $p$ to the point of intersection with $\CC$ is a specified constant. As there are in general $2$ such points $p$ which satisfy the criteria, a conchoid has in most cases two branches.

label: Definition:Conchoid/Branch
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a conchoid. The two parts of $\KK$ corresponding to the loci of the points at either endpoint of the generating line segment are referred to as the branches of $\KK$.

label: Definition:Conchoid of Nicomedes
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a straight line. Let $P$ be a fixed point not on $\CC$ but a perpendicular distance $a$ from $\CC$. The conchoid of Nicomedes is the conchoid defined as the locus of points $Q$ such that a straight line segment between $Q$ and $\CC$ passing through $P$ has a constant length $b$. 520px

label: Definition:Conchoid of Nicomedes/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Conchoid of Nicomedes == designed the curve now known as the conchoid of Nicomedes specifically for solving the problem of Doubling the Cube. It can also be used for Trisecting the Angle.

label: Definition:Conclusion
snippet: A conclusion is a statement that is obtained as the result of the process of an argument.

label: Definition:Conclusion/Statistics
snippet: In the context of statistics, a conclusion is a decision as to accept or reject a statistical hypothesis on the basis of the available evidence.

label: Definition:Concrete Category/Definition 1
snippet: A concrete category $\mathbf C$ is a category such that:

label: Definition:Concrete Number
snippet: A concrete number is a number which is used to enumerate a specific set of physical objects.

label: Definition:Concrete Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Concrete Number == The concrete number is the first stage of the appreciation of a number as an abstract concept.

label: Definition:Concurrent
snippet: Concurrent means having a common point.

label: Definition:Concurrent Lines
snippet: A set of $3$ or more (straight) lines through a single point are concurrent. Such lines are said to concur.

label: Definition:Concyclic Points
snippet: A set of $4$ or more points $S = \set {P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n}$ is concyclic if they all lie on the circumference of a circle. 320px In the above diagram, points $A, B, C, D$ are concyclic, as they all lie on the circumference of the circle centered at $O$.

label: Definition:Condensation Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq X$. A condensation point of $A$ is a limit point $x$ of $A$ such that every open set containing $x$ also contains an uncountable number of points of $A$.

label: Definition:Condition Number
snippet: A condition number is a coefficient which measures the degree of ill-conditioning of a mathematical problem.

label: Definition:Conditional/Language of Conditional/Strong
snippet: In a conditional $p \implies q$, the statement $p$ is stronger than $q$.

label: Definition:Conditional Entropy of Finite Partitions
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\xi, \eta$ be finite partitions of $\Omega$. The (conditional) entropy of $\xi$ given $\eta$ is defined as: $\ds \map H {\xi \mid \eta} := \sum_{\substack {B \mathop \in \eta \\ \map \Pr B \mathop > 0}} \map \Pr B \sum_{A \mathop \in \xi} \map \phi {\dfrac {\map \Pr {A \cap B} } {\map \Pr B} }$ where $\phi : \closedint 0 1 \to \R _{\ge 0}$ is defined by: $\map \phi x := \begin {cases} 0 & : x = 0 \\ -x \map \ln x & : x \in \hointl 0 1 \end {cases}$ Here $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm.

label: Definition:Conditional Entropy of Finite Sub-Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\AA, \BB \subseteq \Sigma$ be finite sub-$\sigma$-algebras. The (conditional) entropy of $\AA$ given $\BB$ is defined as: $\ds \map H {\AA \mid \BB} := \map H {\map \xi \AA \mid \map \xi \BB}$ where: $\map H {\cdot \mid \cdot}$ on the denotes the conditional entropy of finite partitions $\map \xi \cdot$ denotes the generated finite partition

label: Definition:Conditional Expectation/Discrete Case
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a discrete random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $B$ be an event in $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ such that $\map \Pr B > 0$. The conditional expectation of $X$ given $B$ is written $\expect {X \mid B}$ and defined as: $\expect {X \mid B} = \ds \sum_{x \mathop \in \image X} x \condprob {X = x} B$ where: $\condprob {X = x} B$ denotes the conditional probability that $X = x$ given $B$ whenever this sum converges absolutely.

label: Definition:Conditional Expectation/General Case
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be an integrable random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$.

label: Definition:Conditional Expectation/General Case/Event
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be an integrable random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A \in \Sigma$. Then we define the conditional expectation of $X$ given $A$: $\expect {X \mid A} = \expect {X \mid \map \sigma A}$ where: $\map \sigma A$ denotes the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $A$ $\expect {X \mid \map \sigma A}$ denotes the conditional expectation of $X$ given $\map \sigma A$ $=$ is understood to mean almost-sure equality. Category:Definitions/Conditional Expectation

label: Definition:Conditional Expectation/General Case/Random Variable
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be an integrable random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\SS$ be a set of real-valued random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Then we define the conditional expectation of $X$ given $\SS$: $\expect {X \mid \SS} = \expect {X \mid \map \sigma \SS}$ where: $\map \sigma \SS$ denotes the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\SS$ $\expect {X \mid \map \sigma \SS}$ denotes the conditional expectation of $X$ given $\map \sigma \SS$ $=$ is understood to mean almost-sure equality.

label: Definition:Conditional Expectation/General Case/Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be an integrable random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\GG \subseteq \Sigma$ be a sub-$\sigma$-algebra of $\Sigma$. We say that $Z$ is a version of the conditional expectation of $X$ given $\GG$, or version of $\expect {X \mid \GG}$ : $(1): \quad \expect {\cmod Z} < \infty$ $(2): \quad$ $Z$ is $\GG$-measurable $(3): \quad \ds \forall G \in \GG: \int_G Z \rd \Pr = \int_G X \rd \Pr$ From Existence and Essential Uniqueness of Conditional Expectation Conditioned on Sigma-Algebra, any two versions of the…

label: Definition:Conditional Inequality
snippet: A conditional inequality is an inequality which is true for only certain values of the variables.

label: Definition:Conditional Preference
snippet: Let $G$ be a lottery. Let $P$ be a player of $G$. Let $X$ denote the set of prizes which $P$ may receive. Let $\Omega$ denote the set of possible states of $G$. Let $\Xi$ be the event space of $G$. Let $L$ be the set of all plays of $G$. Let $f$ and $g$ be two lotteries in $G$. Let $S \subseteq \Xi$ be an event. A conditional preference is a preference relation $\succsim_S$ such that: $f \succsim_S g$ $f$ would be at least as desirable to $P$ as $g$, if $P$ was aware that the true state of the world was $S$.

label: Definition:Conditional Probability
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events of $\EE$. We write the conditional probability of $A$ given $B$ as $\condprob A B$, and define it as: the probability that $A$ has occurred, given that $B$ has occurred.

label: Definition:Conditionally Convergent Series
snippet: A series which is convergent, but not absolutely convergent, is said to be conditionally convergent.

label: Definition:Conduction Electron
snippet: A conduction electron is an electron, typically in a metal, which is able to flow freely through the substance it is part of. This gives rise to an electric current when a potential difference is applied to separate points on that substance.

label: Definition:Cone
snippet: Geometry: Cone (Geometry) Topology and Analysis: Cone (Analysis) Category Theory: Cone (Category Theory)

label: Definition:Cone (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $D: \mathbf J \to \mathbf C$ be a $\mathbf J$-diagram in $\mathbf C$. A cone to $D$ comprises an object $C$ of $\mathbf C$, and a morphism: $c_j: C \to D_j$ for each object of $\mathbf J$, such that for each morphism $\alpha: i \to j$ of $\mathbf J$: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+0.5em@L+2px{ C \ar[d]_*+{c_i} \ar[dr]^*+{c_j} \\ D_i \ar[r]_*+{D_\alpha} & D_j }\end{xy}$ is a commutative diagram.

label: Definition:Cone (Geometry)
snippet: A cone is a three-dimensional geometric figure which consists of the set of all straight lines joining the boundary of a plane figure $PQR$ to a point $A$ not in the same plane of $PQR$: 300px

label: Definition:Cone (Geometry)/Altitude
snippet: 320px Let a perpendicular $AE$ be dropped from the apex of a cone to the plane containing its base. The line segment $AE$ is an altitude of the cone.

label: Definition:Cone (Geometry)/Apex
snippet: Consider a cone consisting of the set of all straight lines joining the boundary of a plane figure $PQR$ to a point $A$ not in the same plane of $PQR$: 300px In the above diagram, the point $A$ is known as the apex of the cone.

label: Definition:Cone (Geometry)/Base
snippet: Consider a cone consisting of the set of all straight lines joining the boundary of a plane figure $PQR$ to a point $A$ not in the same plane of $PQR$: 300px The plane figure $PQR$ is called the base of the cone.

label: Definition:Cone (Geometry)/Double Napped Cone
snippet: A double napped cone is a cone where the lines joining the apex to the circumference of the base extend indefinitely in either dimension: 300px

label: Definition:Cone (Geometry)/Elliptical
snippet: An elliptical cone is a cone which has a base whose shape is an ellipse.

label: Definition:Cone (Geometry)/Generatrix
snippet: Let $K$ be a cone. Let $A$ be the apex of $K$. Let $B$ be the base of $K$. Then a line joining the apex of $K$ to its directrix is a generatrix of $K$.

label: Definition:Cone (Geometry)/Height
snippet: 320px Let a perpendicular $AE$ be dropped from the apex of a cone to the plane containing its base. The length $h$ of the line $AE$ is the height of the cone.

label: Definition:Cone (Topology)
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. The cone on $X$ is defined and denoted as: $C X = T \ast X$ where: $T$ denotes the trivial topological space $T \ast X$ denotes the join of $T$ and $X$

label: Definition:Cone (Vector Space)
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $P \subseteq X$. We say that $P$ is a cone : for all $\alpha \in \R_{\ge 0}$ and $v \in P$, we have $\alpha v \in P$.

label: Definition:Confidence Interval/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable. Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of $X$ whose distribution is unknown. A $100 \paren {1 - \alpha}$ percent confidence interval for $\theta$ is an interval formed by a rule which ensures that, in the long run, $100 \paren {1 - \alpha}$ percent of such intervals will include $\theta$. This confidence interval is derived from the information obtained from a random sample of observations of $X$.

label: Definition:Confidence Interval/Level
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable. Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of $X$ whose distribution is unknown. Consider a $100 \paren {1 - \alpha}$ percent confidence interval for $\theta$. The confidence level associated with this confidence interval is the coefficient $100 \paren {1 - \alpha}$.

label: Definition:Confidence Region
snippet: A confidence region is an extension of the concept of a confidence interval to more than one random variable.

label: Definition:Configuration
snippet: A configuration is a particular arrangement of geometric objects such as points, lines, curves, and so on.

label: Definition:Confirmation
snippet: In the context of statistics, the evidence from a hypothesis test may support belief in a given hypothesis. In such a case, the evidence is said to confirm the hypothesis. However, care needs to be taken not to imply that the hypothesis has been proven beyond doubt.

label: Definition:Conflation
snippet: A conflation is a mistake in which two or more separate but similar ideas become confused with one another.

label: Definition:Confocal Conics
snippet: Let $F$ be a set of conic sections. Then $F$ is a set of confocal conics they all share the same foci.

label: Definition:Confocal Ellipses
snippet: Let $F$ be a set of ellipses. Then $F$ is a set of confocal ellipses they all share the same foci. Category:Definitions/Conic Sections

label: Definition:Confocal Hyperbolas
snippet: Let $F$ be a set of hyperbolas. Then $F$ is a set of confocal hyperbolas they all share the same foci. Category:Definitions/Conic Sections

label: Definition:Conformable Matrices
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be matrices. Let the order of $\mathbf A$ be $a_r \times a_c$. Let the order of $\mathbf B$ be $b_r \times b_c$. Then $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ are conformable if either: $a_r = b_c$ or: $b_r = a_c$ or both. That is, if the number of rows of one is equal to the number of columns of the other.

label: Definition:Conformal Transformation between Riemannian Manifolds
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ and $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $\phi : M \to \tilde M$ be a diffeomorphism. Let $f \in \map {C^\infty} M$ be a positive smooth real function. Suppose $\phi$ pulls $\tilde g$ back to a metric that is conformal to $g$: $\exists f \in \map {C^\infty} M : f > 0 : \phi^* \tilde g = f g$ Then $\phi$ is called a conformal transformation.

label: Definition:Confounding
snippet: Confounding is a technique which can increase the efficiency of a factorial experiment. It allows the use of blocks containing selected subsets of factor-level combinations. Certain components of interaction, usually assumed to be negligible, then become confounded with differences between blocks

label: Definition:Congruence
snippet: Geometry: Congruence: Two geometric figures are congruent they are both "the same size and shape". Metric Spaces: Congruence (Metric Spaces): Two subsets of a space are congruent there exists an isometry between them. Abstract Algebra: Congruence Modulo Ideal: A concept in ideal theory. Congruence Relation: An equivalence on an algebraic structure which is compatible with its operation.

label: Definition:Congruence (Geometry)
snippet: In the field of Euclidean geometry, two geometric figures are congruent : they are, informally speaking, both "the same size and shape" they differ only in position in space one figure can be overlaid on the other figure with a series of rotations, translations, and reflections. Specifically: all corresponding angles of the congruent figures must have the same measurement all corresponding sides of the congruent figures must be be the same length.

label: Definition:Congruence (Metric Spaces)
snippet: Let $\struct {X, d}$ be a metric space. Two subsets $A, B \subseteq X$ of $X$ are said to be congruent there exists an isometry $f: X \to X$ such that $\map {f^\to} A = B$. Such an isometry is called a congruence.

label: Definition:Congruence (Number Theory)/Historical Note
snippet: The concept of congruence modulo an integer was first explored by . He originated the notation $a \equiv b \pmod m$ in his work , published in $1801$.

label: Definition:Congruence (Number Theory)/Integers
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{> 0}$.

label: Definition:Congruence (Number Theory)/Integers/Integer Multiple
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{> 0}$ be an integer. Let $x, y \in \Z$. $x$ is congruent to $y$ modulo $m$ their difference is an integer multiple of $m$: $x \equiv y \pmod m \iff \exists k \in \Z: x - y = k m$

label: Definition:Congruence (Number Theory)/Integers/Modulo Operation
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$. Let $\bmod$ be defined as the modulo operation: $x \bmod m := \begin {cases} x - m \floor {\dfrac x m} & : m \ne 0 \\ x & : m = 0 \end {cases}$ Then congruence modulo $m$ is the relation on $\Z$ defined as: $\forall x, y \in \Z: x \equiv y \pmod m \iff x \bmod m = y \bmod m$ The integer $m$ is called the modulus.

label: Definition:Congruence (Number Theory)/Integers/Remainder after Division
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{> 0}$ be an integer. Congruence modulo $m$ is defined as the relation $\equiv \pmod m$ on the set of all $a, b \in \Z$: $a \equiv b \pmod m := \set {\tuple {a, b} \in \Z \times \Z: \exists k \in \Z: a = b + k m}$ That is, such that $a$ and $b$ have the same remainder when divided by $m$.

label: Definition:Congruence (Number Theory)/Modulo Operation
snippet: Let $z \in \R$. Let $\bmod$ be defined as the modulo operation: $x \bmod y := \begin {cases} x - y \floor {\dfrac x y} & : y \ne 0 \\ x & : y = 0 \end {cases}$ Then congruence modulo $z$ is the relation on $\R$ defined as: $\forall x, y \in \R: x \equiv y \pmod z \iff x \bmod z = y \bmod z$ The real number $z$ is called the modulus.

label: Definition:Congruence (Number Theory)/Remainder after Division
snippet: Let $z \in \R$. We define a relation $\RR_z$ on the set of all $x, y \in \R$: $\RR_z := \set {\tuple {x, y} \in \R \times \R: \exists k \in \Z: x = y + k z}$ This relation is called congruence modulo $z$, and the real number $z$ is called the modulus. When $\tuple {x, y} \in \RR_z$, we write: $x \equiv y \pmod z$ and say: $x$ is congruent to $y$ modulo $z$. Similarly, when $\tuple {x, y} \notin \RR_z$, we write: $x \not \equiv y \pmod z$ and say: $x$ is not congruent (or incongruent) to $y$ modulo $z$.

label: Definition:Congruence (Number Theory)/Residue
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{\ne 0}$ be a non-zero integer. Let $a, b \in \Z$. Let $a \equiv b \pmod m$. Then $b$ is a residue of $a$ modulo $m$. Residue is another word for remainder, and is any integer congruent to $a$ modulo $m$.

label: Definition:Congruence Modulo Ideal
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring, and let $J$ be an ideal of $R$. The notation: $a \equiv b \pmod J$ is used to mean: $a + \paren {-b} \in J$

label: Definition:Congruence Modulo Subgroup/Additive Group of Ring
snippet: == Comment on Congruence Modulo Subgroup == Let $G$ be a group, and let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. Some authors introduce the concept of congruence modulo $H$ in the context of ring theory. In this case, the group $G$ is taken to be the additive group of a ring. This is acceptable, but such a treatment does presuppose that $G$ is abelian. In such a context, all the richness of the analysis of normal subgroups is disappointingly bypassed. Category:Definitions/Group Theory

label: Definition:Congruence Relation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\RR$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. Then $\RR$ is a congruence relation for $\circ$ : $\forall x_1, x_2, y_1, y_2 \in S: \paren {x_1 \mathrel \RR x_2} \land \paren {y_1 \mathrel \RR y_2} \implies \paren {x_1 \circ y_1} \mathrel \RR \paren {x_2 \circ y_2}$

label: Definition:Congruent Sequences
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be normed vector spaces over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$ and $\sequence {y_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $Y$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ and $\sequence {y_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ are congruent : there exists a linear isomorphism $T : X \to Y$ such that: $T x_n = y_n$ for each $n \in \N$.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Also known as
snippet: == Conic Section: Also known as == A conic section is also known just as a conic.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Center
snippet: The center of a conic section is the point midway between the foci.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Directrix
snippet: Let $K$ be a conic section specified in terms of: a given straight line $D$ a given point $F$ a given constant $e$ where $K$ is the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ and the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$ are related by the condition: $q = e p$ The line $D$ is known as the directrix of the conic section.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Eccentricity
snippet: Let $K$ be a conic section specified in terms of: a given straight line $D$ a given point $F$ a given constant $e$ where $K$ is the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ and the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$ are related by the condition: $q = e p$ The constant $e$ is known as the eccentricity of the conic section.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Focus
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a conic section specified in terms of: a given straight line $D$ a given point $F$ a given constant $\epsilon$ where $K$ is the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ and the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$ are related by the condition: $q = \epsilon \, p$ The point $F$ is known as the focus of $\KK$.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Focus-Directrix Property
snippet: A conic section is a plane curve which can be specified in terms of: a given straight line $D$ known as the directrix a given point $F$ known as a focus a given constant $\epsilon$ known as the eccentricity. Let $K$ be the locus of points $b$ such that the distance $p$ from $b$ to $D$ and the distance $q$ from $b$ to $F$ are related by the condition: $(1): \quad q = \epsilon \, p$ Then $K$ is a conic section. Equation $(1)$ is known as the focus-directrix property of $K$.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Focus-Directrix Property/Circle
snippet: 400px It is not possible to define the circle using the focus-directrix property. This is because as the eccentricity $e$ tends to $0$, the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ tends to infinity. Thus a circle can in a sense be considered to be a degenerate ellipse whose foci are at the same point, that is, the center of the circle.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Focus-Directrix Property/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Focus-Directrix Property of Conic Section == The focus-directrix definition of a conic section was first documented by . It appears in his . As he was scrupulous in documenting his sources, and he gives none for this construction, it can be supposed that it originated with him.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Conic Section == The conic sections were first studied, by in around . He was the first to identify them as different types of slices through a right circular cone. Other early investigations were made by at around . made an extensive study of them in around , the results of which he published his book . He demonstrated rigorously that they can all be generated by different sections of the surface of a right circular cone. was also the first to recognise that a double napped cone is used to generate the hyperbola.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Intersection with Cone
snippet: 600px Let $C$ be a double napped right circular cone whose base is $B$. Let $\theta$ be half the opening angle of $C$. That is, let $\theta$ be the angle between the axis of $C$ and a generatrix of $C$. Let a plane $D$ intersect $C$. Let $\phi$ be the inclination of $D$ to the axis of $C$. Let $K$ be the set of points which forms the intersection of $C$ with $D$. Then $K$ is a conic section, whose nature depends on $\phi$.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Intersection with Cone/Circle/Transverse Section
snippet: 400px Let $\phi = \dfrac \pi 2$, thereby making $D$ perpendicular to the axis of $C$. The plane $D$ which is parallel to $B$, whose intersection with the cone is a circle, is known as a transverse section of the cone.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Intersection with Cone/Degenerate Hyperbola
snippet: 400px Let $\phi < \theta$, that is: so as to make $K$ a hyperbola. However, let $D$ pass through the apex of $C$. Then $K$ degenerates into a pair of intersecting straight lines.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Intersection with Cone/Ellipse
snippet: 400px Let $\theta < \phi < \dfrac \pi 2$. That is, the angle between $D$ and the axis of $C$ is between that for which $K$ is a circle and that which $K$ is a parabola. Then $K$ is an ellipse.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Intersection with Cone/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Conic Section: Intersection with Cone == 600px This construction of a conic section was documented by . It appears in his .

label: Definition:Conic Section/Intersection with Cone/Hyperbola
snippet: 400px Let $\phi < \theta$. Then $K$ is a hyperbola. Note that in this case $D$ intersects $C$ in two places: one for each nappe of $C$.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Intersection with Cone/Slicing Plane
snippet: 600px Let $C$ be a double napped right circular cone whose base is $B$. Let $D$ be a plane which intersects $C$. Let $K$ be the conic section formed by the intersection of $C$ with $D$. The plane $D$ is known as the slicing plane of $C$ for $K$.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Intersection with Cone/Tilting Angle
snippet: 600px Let $C$ be a double napped right circular cone whose base is $B$. Let $D$ be a plane which intersects $C$. Let $D$ be inclined at an angle $\phi$ with the axis of $C$. Let $K$ be the conic section formed by the intersection of $C$ with $D$. The inclination $\phi$ of the slicing plane with the axis of $C$ is known as the tilting angle of $D$ for $K$.

label: Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form
snippet: Let $K$ be a conic section. Let $K$ be embedded in a cartesian plane such that: $(1)$ the center is at the origin $(2)$ the foci are at $\left({\pm c, 0}\right)$ for some $c \in \R_{\ge 0}$. This can be interpreted in the contexts of the specific classes of conic section as follows:

label: Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form/Ellipse
snippet: Let $K$ be an ellipse embedded in a cartesian plane. $K$ is in reduced form : $(1): \quad$ its major axis is aligned with the $x$-axis $(2): \quad$ its minor axis is aligned with the $y$-axis. 500px

label: Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form/Hyperbola
snippet: Let $K$ be a hyperbola embedded in a cartesian plane. $K$ is in reduced form : $(1)$ its major axis is aligned with the $x$-axis $(2)$ its minor axis is aligned with the $y$-axis. 500px

label: Definition:Conic Section/Reduced Form/Parabola
snippet: Let $K$ be a parabola embedded in a cartesian plane. As a Parabola has no Center, it is not possible to define the reduced form of a parabola in the same way as for the other classes of conic section. Instead, $K$ is in reduced form : $(1)$ its focus is at the point $\tuple {c, 0}$ $(2)$ its directrix is aligned with the line $x = -c$ for some $c \in \R_{> 0}$. 400px

label: Definition:Conical Surface
snippet: A conical surface is a surface which is generated by all the straight lines passing through a given point $A$, called the apex, and a curve which does not pass through $A$, called the directrix.

label: Definition:Conicoid
snippet: A conicoid is a $3$-dimensional figure whose plane sections are all conic sections.

label: Definition:Conjugacy Action
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. The (left) conjugacy action of $G$ is the left group action $* : G \times G \to G$ defined as: $\forall g, x \in G: g * x = g \circ x \circ g^{-1}$ The right conjugacy action of $G$ is the right group action $* : G \times G \to G$ defined as: $\forall x, g \in G: x * g = g^{-1} \circ x \circ g$

label: Definition:Conjugacy Action/Subgroups
snippet: Let $X$ be the set of all subgroups of $G$. The (left) conjugacy action on subgroups is the group action $* : G \times X \to X$: $g * H = g \circ H \circ g^{-1}$ The right conjugacy action on subgroups is the group action $* : X \times G \to X$: $H * g = g^{-1} \circ H \circ g$

label: Definition:Conjugacy Action/Subsets
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $\powerset G$ be the power set of $G$. The (left) conjugacy action on subsets is the group action $* : G \times \powerset G \to \powerset G$: $g * S = g \circ S \circ g^{-1}$ The right conjugacy action on subsets is the group action $* : \powerset G \times G \to \powerset G$: $S * g = g^{-1} \circ S \circ g$

label: Definition:Conjugacy Class
snippet: The equivalence classes into which the conjugacy relation divides its group into are called conjugacy classes. Thus the conjugacy class of an element $x$ of a group $G$ consists of all $y \in G$ such that $y$ is a conjugate of $x$. The conjugacy class of an element $x \in G$ can be denoted $\conjclass x$.

label: Definition:Conjugacy Class/Also denoted as
snippet: == Conjugacy Class: Also denoted as == Some authors denote a conjugacy class with the notation $\map {\operatorname {cl} } x$, but this can be confused with the notation for closure in the context of topology, so its use is not recommended. Variants on the $\mathrm C$ motif can be seen: $C_x$ or $\map C x$ are fairly common.

label: Definition:Conjugacy Class/Technical Note
snippet: == Technical Note for Conjugacy Class == {{LatexFor|for = \conjclass {x} }} When the subscript is a single character, it is usual to omit the braces: \conjclass x This command is specific to . Category:Technical Notes

label: Definition:Conjugate
snippet: Geometry: The conjugate of an angle $\theta$ is the angle $2 \pi - \theta$, that is, the angle that makes a full angle with it. The conjugate axis of a hyperbola. Conjugate points: Points which line on each other's polar with respect to a circle Conjugate lines: polars with respect to a circle whose poles lie on each other Conjugate diameters in a central conic. Abstract algebra: The conjugate Group theory: The conjugate of an element or subset $X$ of a group $G$ by a given element $a$ is defined as $a X a^{-1}$.

label: Definition:Conjugate (Group Theory)/Element
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group.

label: Definition:Conjugate (Group Theory)/Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $S \subseteq G, a \in G$. Then the $G$-conjugate of $S$ by $a$ is: $S^a := \set {y \in G: \exists x \in S: y = a \circ x \circ a^{-1} } = a \circ S \circ a^{-1}$ That is, $S^a$ is the set of all elements of $G$ that are the conjugates of elements of $S$ by $a$. When $G$ is the only group under consideration, we usually just refer to the conjugate of $S$ by $a$.

label: Definition:Conjugate Angles
snippet: The conjugate of an angle $\theta$ is the angle $\phi$ such that: $\theta + \phi = 2 \pi$ where $\theta$ and $\pi$ are expressed in radians. That is, it is the angle that makes the given angle equal to a full angle when added to it. Equivalently, the conjugate of an angle $\theta$ is the angle $\phi$ such that: $\theta + \phi = 360 \degrees$ where $\theta$ and $\pi$ are expressed in degrees. Thus, conjugate angles are two angles whose measures add up to the measure of $4$ right angles. That is, their measurements add up to $360$ degrees or $2 \pi$ radians.

label: Definition:Conjugate Arcs
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be points on the boundary $\BB$ of a simple closed curve $\CC$ in the plane. Let $a$ and $b$ divide $\BB$ into a major arc and a minor arc. The two arcs together are referred to as conjugate arcs.

label: Definition:Conjugate Axis of Hyperbola/Also defined as
snippet: == Conjugate Axis of Hyperbola: Also defined as == Some sources do not consider the minor axis of a hyperbola separately from the conjugate axis, and instead define the conjugate axis as the infinite straight line that coincides with it. From : There is no minor axis, but the other axis of symmetry, the $y$-axis, is called the conjugate axis. However, on we prefer to keep the concepts separate. Some sources use the term conjugate axis to mean any arbitrary line segment on the minor axis.

label: Definition:Conjugate Diameters
snippet: Let $K$ be a conic section. Let $D_1$ and $D_2$ be diameters of $K$ such that: $D_1$ belongs to the system of parallel chords whose midpoints define $D_2$ and: $D_2$ belongs to the system of parallel chords whose midpoints define $D_1$. Then $D_1$ and $D_2$ are known as conjugate diameters.

label: Definition:Conjugate Gradient Method
snippet: The conjugate gradient method is an iterative technique of solving a system of simultaneous linear equations $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \mathbf b$ in which the matrix of coefficients $\mathbf A$ is symmetric and positive definite. Its use is particularly appropriate when $\mathbf A$ is sparse, because each iteration involves a single product between the matrix and a vector.

label: Definition:Conjugate Linear Mapping
snippet: Let $\Bbb F$ be a subfield of $\C$. Let $V$ and $W$ be a vector spaces over $\Bbb F$. A conjugate linear mapping is a function $f: V \to W$ subject to: $\forall \alpha \in \Bbb F, \mathbf x_1, \mathbf x_2 \in V: \map f {\alpha \mathbf x_1 + \mathbf x_2} = \bar \alpha \map f {\mathbf x_1} + \map f {\mathbf x_2}$ where $\bar \alpha$ is the complex conjugate of $\alpha$

label: Definition:Conjugate Lines of Conic Section
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a conic section. Let $\PP$ and $\QQ$ be the straight lines in the plane of $\KK$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the poles of $\PP$ and $\QQ$ respectively $\KK$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be such that $P$ lies on $\QQ$ and $Q$ lies on $\PP$. Then $\PP$ and $\QQ$ are known as conjugate lines $\KK$.

label: Definition:Conjugate Pair
snippet: Complex Numbers: Conjugate Pair: a pair of complex numbers $z$ and $\overline z$, where $\overline z$ is the complex conjugate of $z$. Analytic Geometry: Conjugate Pair: another name for harmonic conjugates.

label: Definition:Conjugate Point (Calculus of Variations)/Definition 1
snippet: Let: $-\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {P h'} + Q h = 0$ with boundary conditions: $\map h a = 0, \quad \map h c = 0, \quad a < c \le b$ Suppose: $\map h x = 0 \quad \neg \forall x \in \closedint a b$ Suppose: $\map h a = 0, \quad \map h {\tilde a} = 0, \quad a \ne \tilde a$ Then the point $\tilde a$ is called conjugate to the point $a$ solution to the aforementioned differential equation.

label: Definition:Conjugate Point (Calculus of Variations)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $y = \map y x$ and $y^* = \map {y^*} x$ be extremal functions. Let: $M = \tuple {a, \map y a}$ $\tilde M = \tuple {\tilde a, \map y {\tilde a} }$ Let $y$ and $y^*$ both pass through the point $M$. Let: $\map {y^*} {x - \tilde a} - \map y {x - \tilde a} = \epsilon \size {\map {y^*} {x - \tilde a} - \map y {x - \tilde a} }_1$ where: $\size {\map {y^*} {x - \tilde a} - \map y {x - \tilde a} }_1 \to 0 \implies \epsilon \to 0$ Then $\tilde M$ is conjugate to $M$.

label: Definition:Conjugate Point (Calculus of Variations)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $y = \map y x$ and $y = \map {\tilde y} x$ be extremal functions. Let: $M = \paren {a, \map y a}$ $\tilde M = \paren {\tilde a, \map y {\tilde a} }$ Let both $y = \map y x$ and $y = \map {\tilde y} x$ pass through the point $M$. Let $\ds \lim_{\norm {\map y x - \map {\tilde y} x}_{1, \infty} \to 0} \sqbrk {\paren {x, \map y x}: \map y x - \map {\tilde y} x = 0} = \tilde M$ In other words, let $\tilde M$ be the limit points of intersection of $y = \map y x$ and $y = \map {\tilde y} x$ as $\norm {\map y x - \map {\tilde y} x}_{1, \infty} \to 0$.

label: Definition:Conjugate Point (Calculus of Variations)/Dependent on N Functions
snippet: Let $K$ be a functional such that: $\ds K \sqbrk h = \int_a^b \paren {\mathbf h'\mathbf P \mathbf h' + \mathbf h \mathbf Q \mathbf h} \rd x$ Consider Euler's equation related to the functional $K$: $-\map {\dfrac \d {\d x} } {\mathbf P \mathbf h'} + \mathbf Q \mathbf h = 0$ where $\mathbf P$ and $\mathbf Q$ are symmetric matrices.

label: Definition:Conjugate Points (Geometry)
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a conic section. Let $P$ and $Q$ be points in the plane of $\KK$. Let: $P$ lie on the polar of $Q$ $Q$ lie on the polar of $P$. $P$ and $Q$ are known as conjugate points $\KK$.

label: Definition:Conjugate Points (Geometry)/Circle
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle. Let $P$ and $Q$ be points in the plane of $\CC$. Let: $P$ lie on the polar of $Q$ $Q$ lie on the polar of $P$. $P$ and $Q$ are known as conjugate points with respect to $\CC$.

label: Definition:Conjugate Quaternion
snippet: Let $\mathbf x = a \mathbf 1 + b \mathbf i + c \mathbf j + d \mathbf k$ be a quaternion. The conjugate quaternion of $\mathbf x$ is defined as: $\overline {\mathbf x} = a \mathbf 1 - b \mathbf i - c \mathbf j - d \mathbf k$.

label: Definition:Conjugate Quaternion/Matrix Form
snippet: Let $\mathbf x$ be a quaternion defined in matrix form as: $\mathbf x = \begin {bmatrix} a + b i & c + d i \\ -c + d i & a - b i \end {bmatrix}$ The conjugate quaternion of $\mathbf x$ is defined as: $\overline {\mathbf x} = \begin {bmatrix} a - b i & -c - d i \\ c - d i & a + b i \end {bmatrix}$ That is, if: $\mathbf x = \begin {bmatrix} p & q \\ -\overline q & \overline p \end {bmatrix}$ then: $\overline {\mathbf x} = \begin {bmatrix} \overline p & -q \\ \overline q & p \end {bmatrix}$ Category:Definitions/Quaternions

label: Definition:Conjugate Quaternion/Ordered Pair
snippet: Let $\mathbf x$ be a quaternion defined as an ordered pair $\left({a, b}\right)$ of complex numbers. The conjugate quaternion of $\mathbf x$ is defined as: $\overline {\mathbf x} = \overline {\left({a, b}\right)} = \left({\overline a, -b}\right)$

label: Definition:Conjugate Symmetric Mapping
snippet: Let $\C$ be the field of complex numbers. Let $\F$ be a subfield of $\C$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\F$ Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \mathbb F$ be a mapping. Then $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \mathbb F$ is conjugate symmetric : $\forall x, y \in V: \quad \innerprod x y = \overline {\innerprod y x}$ where $\overline {\innerprod y x}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $\innerprod x y$.

label: Definition:Conjugate Triangles
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle. Let $\triangle PQR$ be a triangle. Let: $P'$ be the pole of $QR$ $Q'$ be the pole of $PR$ $R'$ be the pole of $PQ$ with respect to $\CC$. Then $\triangle PQR$ and $\triangle P'Q'R'$ are said to be conjugate triangles with respect to $\CC$.

label: Definition:Conjugate of Quadratic Irrational/Also presented as
snippet: == Conjugate of Quadratic Irrational: Also presented as == A quadratic irrational and its conjugate can also be presented in the form: $a + \sqrt b$, $a - \sqrt b$ where $b$ is a rational number which is not the square of another rational number.

label: Definition:Conjugation on Algebra
snippet: Let $A = \struct {A_F, \oplus}$ be an algebra over a field $F$. Let $C: A_F \to A_F$ be a mapping such that: $\forall a \in A: \map C {\map C a} = a$ $\forall a, b \in A: \map C {a \oplus b} = \map C b \oplus \map C a$ Then $C$ is called a conjugation on $A$.

label: Definition:Conjunction/General Definition
snippet: Let $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ be statements. The conjunction of $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ is defined as: $\ds \bigwedge_{i \mathop = 1}^n \ p_i = \begin {cases} p_1 & \text{if } n = 1 \\ & \\ \ds \paren {\bigwedge_{i \mathop = 1}^{n - 1} p_i} \land p_n & \text{if } n > 1 \end {cases}$ That is: $\ds \bigwedge_{i \mathop = 1}^n \ p_i = p_1 \land p_2 \land \cdots \land p_{n - 1} \land p_n$ In terms of the set $P = \set {p_1, \ldots, p_n}$, this can also be rendered: $\ds \bigwedge P$ and is referred to as the conjunction of $P$.

label: Definition:Conjunctive Transformation
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be square matrices over the complex numbers $\C$. A conjunctive transformation is an operation of changing $\mathbf B$ to $\mathbf A$ by multiplying $\mathbf B$ by a nonsingular matrix $\mathbf Y$ and its Hermitian conjugate $\mathbf Y^*$ such that: $\mathbf A = \mathbf Y^* \mathbf B \mathbf Y$

label: Definition:Connected
snippet: In relation theory: Connected relation In topology: Topological connectedness: Connected topological space Connected set Connected points Connected sum: A topological concept concerning manifolds In complex analysis: Connected set In graph theory: Connected: Connected graph: A graph which has a walk between every pair of vertices. Connected vertices: A pair of vertices between which there is a walk.

label: Definition:Connected Between Two Points
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $a, b \in S$. $T$ is connected between (the) two points $a$ and $b$ each separation of $T$ includes a single open set $U \in \tau$ which contains both $a$ and $b$.

label: Definition:Connected Domain (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers. Then $D$ is a connected domain $D$ is open and connected.

label: Definition:Connected Domain (Complex Analysis)/Simply Connected Domain
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \C$ be a connected domain. Then $D$ is called a simply connected domain $D$ is simply connected.

label: Definition:Connected Manifold/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological manifold. $M$ is called a (path-) connected manifold $M$ is a path-connected topological space.

label: Definition:Connected Points (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $a, b \in S$. Then $a$ and $b$ are connected (in $T$) there exists a connected set in $T$ containing both $a$ and $b$.

label: Definition:Connected Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation on a set $S$. Then $\RR$ is connected : $\forall a, b \in S: a \ne b \implies \tuple {a, b} \in \RR \lor \tuple {b, a} \in \RR$ That is, every pair of distinct elements is comparable.

label: Definition:Connected Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Connected Relation: Also known as == Some sources use the term weakly connected, using the term strictly connected relation for what is defined on as a total relation. A set on which $\RR$ is connected can be referred to as an $\RR$-connected set. Category:Definitions/Connected Relations

label: Definition:Connected Set (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers.

label: Definition:Connected Set (Complex Analysis)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers. $D$ is connected every pair of points in $D$ can be joined by a staircase contour.

label: Definition:Connected Set (Complex Analysis)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers. $D$ is connected every pair of points in $D$ can be joined by a polygonal path all points of which are in $D$.

label: Definition:Connected Set (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$.

label: Definition:Connected Set (Topology)/Also known as
snippet: == Connected Set: Also known as == A connected set of a topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is often found referred to as a connected subset (of $T$). Some sources refer to the concept of a connected subspace, which is no more than a connected set under the subspace topology. On , if the distinction is required, it will be specified explicitly. Category:Definitions/Connected Sets (Topology)

label: Definition:Connected Set (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. $H$ is a connected set of $T$ it is not the union of two non-empty separated sets of $T$.

label: Definition:Connected Set (Topology)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. $H$ is a connected set of $T$ it is not disconnected in $T$.

label: Definition:Connected Set (Topology)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. $H$ is a connected set of $T$ : the topological subspace $\struct {H, \tau_H}$ of $T$ is a connected topological space.

label: Definition:Connected Set (Topology)/Definition 4
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. $H$ is a connected set of $T$ : there do not exist disjoint, non-empty subsets $X$ and $Y$ of $H$ such that $X \cup Y = H$ such that: no limit point of $X$ is an element of $Y$ no limit point of $Y$ is an element of $X$.

label: Definition:Connected Set (Topology)/Definition 5
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. $H$ is a connected set of $T$ : $H$ cannot be partitioned into $2$ non-empty subsets so that each subset has no element in common with the closure of the other.

label: Definition:Connected Sum
snippet: The connected sum of two manifolds $A^n, B^n$ of dimension $n$ is defined as follows: Let $\Bbb D^n$ be a closed $n$-ball. Let $\alpha: \Bbb D^n \to A^n$ be a continuous (or, in the case of smooth manifolds, a smooth) injection. Let $\beta: \Bbb D^n \to B^n$ be a similar function. Define the set: $S = \paren {A^n \setminus \map \alpha {\paren {\Bbb D^n}^\circ} } \cup \paren {B^n \setminus \map \beta {\paren {\Bbb D^n}^\circ} }$ where: $\setminus$ denotes set difference $\paren {\Bbb D^n}^\circ$ denotes the interior of $\Bbb D^n$.

label: Definition:Connected Surface
snippet: A connected surface is a surface $\SS$ where there is a continuous path between any two points on $\SS$ which does not cross the boundary of $\SS$.

label: Definition:Connected Topological Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is connected it admits no separation. That is, $T$ is connected there exist no open sets $A, B \in \tau$ such that: $A, B \ne \O$ $A \cup B = S$ $A \cap B = \O$.

label: Definition:Connected Topological Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is connected it has no two disjoint nonempty closed sets whose union is $S$.

label: Definition:Connected Topological Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is connected its only subsets whose boundary is empty are $S$ and $\O$.

label: Definition:Connected Topological Space/Definition 4
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is connected its only clopen sets are $S$ and $\O$.

label: Definition:Connected Topological Space/Definition 5
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is connected there are no two non-empty separated sets whose union is $S$.

label: Definition:Connected Topological Space/Definition 6
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is connected there exists no continuous surjection from $T$ onto a discrete two-point space.

label: Definition:Connected Topological Space/Definition 7
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is connected : there do not exist disjoint, non-empty open sets $X$ and $Y$ of $T$ such that $X \cup Y = S$.

label: Definition:Connection/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Connection == The idea of a connection was investigated by in his efforts to unify the theory of relativity and that of electromagnetism. Subsequently, connections were used in the study of vector bundles, and as a result have shown themselves to be basic to the development of gauge theory.

label: Definition:Connection Coefficients
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $\dim M$ be the dimension of $M$. Let $U \subseteq M$ be an open subset. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. For all $i \in \N_{>0} : i \le \dim M$ let $\tuple {E_i}$ be a smooth local frame for $TM$. Let $\nabla$ be the connection on $M$. For all $i, j, k \in \N_{> 0} : i, j, k \le \dim M$ let $\Gamma_{ij}^k : U \to \R$ be a smooth real function such that: $\ds \nabla_{E_i} E_j = \Gamma^k_{ij} E_k$ where Einstein summation convention has been imposed.
