orm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_2} }$ be normed vector spaces. Let $f: X_1 	o X_2$ be a mapping from $X_1$ to $X_2$. Let $a \in X_1$ be a point in $X_1$. $f$ is continuous at $a$ (with respect to the norms $
orm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_1}$ and $
orm {\,\cdot\,}_{X_2}$) : $ orall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}:  orall x \in X_1: 
orm {x - a}_{X_1} 0}$ denotes the set of all strictly positive real numbers.

label: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$.

label: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Also known as
snippet: If it is necessary to distinguish between multiple topologies on the same set, then the terminology $\tuple {\tau_1, \tau_2}$-continuous can be used to define a continuous mapping.

label: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Everywhere
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$.

label: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Everywhere/Open Sets
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. The mapping $f$ is continuous on $S_1$ : $U \in \tau_2 \implies f^{-1} \sqbrk U \in \tau_1$ where $f^{-1} \sqbrk U$ denotes the preimage of $U$ under $f$.

label: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Everywhere/Pointwise
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. The mapping $f$ is continuous everywhere (or simply continuous) $f$ is continuous at every point $x \in S_1$.

label: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Point
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. Let $x \in S_1$.

label: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Point/Filters
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. Let $x \in S_1$. The mapping $f$ is continuous at (the point) $x$ : for any filter $\FF$ on $T_1$ that converges to $x$, the corresponding image filter $f \sqbrk \FF$ converges to $\map f x$.

label: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Point/Neighborhood Inverse
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. Let $x \in S_1$. The mapping $f$ is continuous at (the point) $x$ ( the topologies $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$) : For every neighborhood $N$ of $\map f x$ in $T_2$, $f^{-1} \sqbrk N$ is a neighborhood of $x$.

label: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Point/Neighborhoods
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. Let $x \in S_1$. The mapping $f$ is continuous at (the point) $x$ ( the topologies $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$) : For every neighborhood $N$ of $\map f x$ in $T_2$, there exists a neighborhood $M$ of $x$ in $T_1$ such that $f \sqbrk M \subseteq N$.

label: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Point/Open Sets
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. Let $x \in S_1$. The mapping $f$ is continuous at (the point) $x$ ( the topologies $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$) : For every open set $U_2$ of $T_2$ such that $\map f x \in U_2$, there exists an open set $U_1$ of $T_1$ such that $x \in U_1$ and $f \sqbrk {U_1} \subseteq U_2$.

label: Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)/Set
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping from $S_1$ to $S_2$. Let $S$ be a subset of $S_1$. The mapping $f$ is continuous on $S$ $f$ is continuous at every point $x \in S$.

label: Definition:Continuous Mapping Space
snippet: Let $X, Y$ be topological spaces. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a continuous mapping. Then the set of all such mappings $f$ is known as continuous mapping space and is denoted by $C \paren {X,Y}$: $C \paren {X, Y} = \set {f : X \to Y}$

label: Definition:Continuous Real-Valued Function Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a continuous real valued mapping. Then the set of all such mappings $f$ is known as the continuous real-valued function space on $X$ and is denoted by $\map C X$: $\map C X := \map C {X, \R} = \set {f : X \to \R}$

label: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Closed Interval
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on a closed interval $\closedint a b$. $f$ is continuous on $\closedint a b$ it is: $(1): \quad$ continuous at every point of the open interval $\openint a b$ $(2): \quad$ continuous on the right at $a$ $(3): \quad$ continuous on the left at $b$. That is, if $f$ is to be continuous over the whole of a closed interval, it needs to be continuous at the end points. Because we only have "access" to the function on one side of each end point, all we can do is insist on continuity on the side of the end points on which the function is defined.

label: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Informal Definition
snippet: The concept of continuity makes precise the intuitive notion that a function has no "jumps" or "holes" at a given point. Loosely speaking, a real function $f$ is continuous at a point $p$ the graph of $f$ does not have a "break" at $p$.

label: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Left-Continuous
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be an open subset of the real numbers $\R$. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Let $x_0 \in A$. Then $f$ is said to be left-continuous at $x_0$ the limit from the left of $\map f x$ as $x \to x_0$ exists and: $\ds \lim_{\substack {x \mathop \to x_0^- \\ x_0 \mathop \in A} } \map f x = \map f {x_0}$ where $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to x_0^-}$ is a limit from the left. Furthermore, $f$ is said to be left-continuous : $\forall x_0 \in A$, $f$ is left-continuous at $x_0$

label: Definition:Continuous Real Function/One Side
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be an open subset of the real numbers $\R$. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function.

label: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Point
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be any subset of the real numbers. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Let $x \in A$ be a point of $A$.

label: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Right-Continuous
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \R$ be an open subset of the real numbers $\R$. Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real function. Let $x_0 \in S$. Then $f$ is said to be right-continuous at $x_0$ the limit from the right of $\map f x$ as $x \to x_0$ exists and: $\ds \lim_{\substack {x \mathop \to x_0^+ \\ x_0 \mathop \in A}} \map f x = \map f {x_0}$ where $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to x_0^+}$ is a limit from the right. Furthermore, $f$ is said to be right-continuous : $\forall x_0 \in S$, $f$ is right-continuous at $x_0$

label: Definition:Continuous Real Function/Subset
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be any subset of the real numbers. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Then $f$ is continuous on $A$ $f$ is continuous at every point of $A$.

label: Definition:Continuous Real Function at Point/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Let $x \in A$ be a point of $A$. $f$ is continuous at $x$ the limit $\ds \lim_{y \mathop \to x} \map f y$ exists and: $\ds \lim_{y \mathop \to x} \map f y = \map f x$

label: Definition:Continuous Real Function at Point/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \R$ be any subset of the real numbers. Let $f: A \to \R$ be a real function. Let $x \in A$ be a point of $A$. $f$ is continuous at $x$ the limit $\ds \lim_{y \mathop \to x} \map f y$ exists and: $\ds \lim_{y \mathop \to x} \map f y = \map f {\lim_{y \mathop \to x} y}$

label: Definition:Continuous Spectrum of Densely-Defined Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a densely-defined linear operator. We define the continuous spectrum $\map {\sigma_s} T$ as the set of $\lambda \in \C$ such that: $T - \lambda I$ is injective, $\map {\paren {T - \lambda I} } {\map D T}$ is everywhere dense in $\HH$ but $\paren {T - \lambda I}^{-1}$ is not bounded.

label: Definition:Continuous Total Preordering
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\precsim$ be a total preordering on $S$. Let $\precsim$ be such that: $a \precsim b$ whenever there exist sequences $\sequence {a^k}_k$ and $\sequence {b^k}_k$ that converge to $a$ and $b$ respectively for which $a^k \precsim b^k$ for all $k$. Then $\precsim$ is continuous.

label: Definition:Continuously Differentiable
snippet: A differentiable function $f$ is continuously differentiable $f$ is of differentiability class $C^1$. That is, if the first order derivative of $f$ (and possibly higher) is continuous.

label: Definition:Continuum
snippet: A continuum is an object which is continuous.

label: Definition:Continuum/Also defined as
snippet: == Continuum: Also defined as == Some sources define a continuum specifically as either: the set of real numbers an arbitrary real interval, whether open, closed or half-open. However, this usage is considered archaic.

label: Definition:Continuum/Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be both compact and connected in $T$. Then $H$ is a continuum.

label: Definition:Continuum (Topology)/Also defined as
snippet: == Continuum in context of Topology: Also known as == Some sources insist that a topological space need to be a $T_2$ space, as well as both compact and connected, in order to be considered to be a continuum.

label: Definition:Continuum Mechanics
snippet: Continuum mechanics is the branch of applied mathematics concerned with the mechanical behavior of materials considered as a continuous mass rather than as discrete particles.

label: Definition:Contour/Closed/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C$ be a contour in $\C$ defined by the (finite) sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ of directed smooth curves in $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k} {b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. $C$ is a closed contour the start point of $C$ is equal to the end point of $C$: $\map {\gamma_1} {a_1} = \map {\gamma_n} {b_n}$

label: Definition:Contour/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ be directed smooth curves in the complex plane $\C$. For each $k \in \set{ 1, \ldots, n}$, let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k}{b_k} \to \C$. For each $k \in \set{ 1, \ldots, n-1}$, let the endpoint of $\gamma_k$ equal the start point of $\gamma_{k + 1}$: $\map {\gamma_k}{b_k} = \map {\gamma_{k + 1} }{a_{k + 1} }$ Then the finite sequence $\sequence{C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ is a contour.

label: Definition:Contour/Endpoints/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ be directed smooth curves in $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k}{b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set{ 1, \ldots, n}$. Let $C$ be the contour defined by the finite sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$. The start point of $C$ is $\map {\gamma_1}{a_1}$. The end point of $C$ is $\map {\gamma_n}{b_n}$. Collectively, $\map {\gamma_1}{a_1}$ and $\map {\gamma_n}{b_n}$ are referred to as the endpoints of $C$.

label: Definition:Contour/Image/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C$ be a contour in $\C$ defined by the (finite) sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ of directed smooth curves in $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k} {b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. The image of $C$ is defined as: $\ds \Img C := \bigcup_{k \mathop = 1}^n \Img {\gamma_k}$ where $\Img {\gamma_k}$ denotes the image of $\gamma_k$. If $\Img C \subseteq D$, where $D$ is a subset of $\C$, we say that $C$ is a contour in $D$.

label: Definition:Contour/Parameterization/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ be directed smooth curves in the complex plane $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k} {b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. Let $C$ be the contour defined by the finite sequence $C_1, \ldots, C_n$. The parameterization of $C$ is defined as the function $\gamma: \closedint {a_1} {c_n} \to \C$ with: $\map {\gamma \restriction_{\closedint {c_k} {c_{k + 1} } } } t = \map {\gamma_k} t$ where $\ds c_k = a_1 + \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k b_j - \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k a_j$ for $k \in \set {0, \ldots, n}$.

label: Definition:Contour/Simple/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ be directed smooth curves in the complex plane $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k} {b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. Let $C$ be the contour defined by the finite sequence $C_1, \ldots, C_n$. $C$ is a simple contour : $(1): \quad$ For all $j, k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}, t_1 \in \hointr {a_j} {b_j}, t_2 \in \hointr {a_k} {b_k}$ with $t_1 \ne t_2$, we have $\map {\gamma_j} {t_1} \ne \map {\gamma_j} {t_2}$.

label: Definition:Contour Integral
snippet: Let $OA$ be a curve in a vector field $\mathbf F$. Let $P$ be a point on $OA$. Let $\d \mathbf l$ be a small element of length of $OA$ at $P$. Let $\mathbf v$ be the vector induced by $\mathbf F$ on $P$. Let $\mathbf v$ make an angle $\theta$ with the tangent to $OA$ at $P$. 350px Hence: $\mathbf v \cdot \d \mathbf l = v \cos \theta \rd l$ where: $\cdot$ denotes dot product $v$ and $\d l$ denote the magnitude of $\mathbf v$ and $\d \mathbf l$ respectively.

label: Definition:Contour Integral/Complex
snippet: Let $C$ be a contour defined by a finite sequence $C_1, \ldots, C_n$ of directed smooth curves in the complex plane $\C$. Let $C_k$ be parameterized by the smooth path: $\gamma_k: \closedint {a_k} {b_k} \to \C$ for all $k \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$. Let $f: \Img C \to \C$ be a continuous complex function, where $\Img C$ denotes the image of $C$. The contour integral of $f$ along $C$ is defined by: $\ds \int_C \map f z \rd z = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \int_{a_k}^{b_k} \map f {\map {\gamma_k} t} \map {\gamma_k'} t \rd t$

label: Definition:Contour Plot
snippet: Let $f: \R^2 \to \R$ be a real function of $2$ variables. A contour plot is a diagram in the Cartesian plane $\CC$ in which points in $\CC$ with the same values of $f$ are joined by curves for a selection of some specific values

label: Definition:Contour Plot/Contour Line
snippet: Consider a contour plot of a real function $f$ of $2$ variables. Each of the curves joining points with the same values under $f$ are known as contour lines.

label: Definition:Contractible Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space.

label: Definition:Contractible Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. $X$ is called a contractible space the identity map $\operatorname {id}_X$ is homotopic to a constant map $X \to X$.

label: Definition:Contractible Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. $X$ is called a contractible space it is homotopy equivalent to a point.

label: Definition:Contraction
snippet: Let $G$ be a vector space over a field $K$. Let $\beta \in K$. Let $s_\beta: G \to G$ be a similarity mapping on $G$: $\forall \mathbf x \in G: \map {s_\beta} {\mathbf x} = \beta \mathbf x$ Let the scale factor $\beta$ be such that $0 < \beta \le 1$. Then $s_\beta$ is called a contraction.

label: Definition:Contraction Mapping
snippet: Metric Spaces: Contraction Mapping (Metric Space) Linear Algebra: Contraction

label: Definition:Contraction Mapping (Metric Space)
snippet: Let $\struct {X, d_1}$ and $\struct {Y, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a contraction (mapping) there exists $\kappa \in \R: 0 \le \kappa < 1$ such that: $\forall x, y \in X: \map {d_2} {\map f x, \map f y} \le \kappa \map {d_1} {x, y}$ That is, $f$ is Lipschitz continuous for a Lipschitz constant less than $1$.

label: Definition:Contradiction
snippet: A contradiction is a statement which is always false, independently of any relevant circumstances that could theoretically influence its truth value. This has the form: $p \land \neg p$ or, equivalently: $\neg p \land p$ that is: $p$ is true and, at the same time, $p$ is not true. An example of a "relevant circumstance" here is the truth value of $p$. The archetypal contradiction can be symbolised by $\bot$, and referred to as bottom.

label: Definition:Contradictory/Propositional Formulas
snippet: Let $\Delta$ be a set of propositional formulas. Then $\Delta$ is contradictory there exists some propositional formula $P$ such that $P \in \Delta$ and $\neg P \in \Delta$.

label: Definition:Contranormal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. Then $H$ is a contranormal subgroup the normal closure of $H$ is the whole of $G$.

label: Definition:Contrapositive Statement
snippet: The contrapositive of the conditional: $p \implies q$ is the statement: $\neg q \implies \neg p$

label: Definition:Contravariant Functor/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. A contravariant functor $F : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ consists of: An object functor $F_0$ that assigns to each object $X$ of $\mathbf C$ an object $FX$ of $\mathbf D$. An arrow functor $F_1$ that assigns to each arrow $f : X \to Y$ of $\mathbf C$ an arrow $Ff : FY \to FX$ of $\mathbf D$.

label: Definition:Contravariant Hom Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Set}$ be the category of sets. Let $\mathbf C$ be a locally small category. Let $C \in \mathbf C_0$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. The contravariant hom functor based at $C$: $\map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {\cdot, C}: \mathbf C \to \mathbf {Set}$ is the contravariant functor defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = $\map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {B, C} = \map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {B, C}$ |mor = $\map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {f, C}: \map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {B, C} \to \map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {A, C}, g \mapsto g \circ f$…

label: Definition:Contravariant Power Set Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Set}$ be the category of sets. The contravariant power set functor $\overline \PP: \mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Set}$ is the contravariant functor which sends: {{DefineFunctor |ob = An object $x$ to its power set $\powerset x$. |mor = A morphism $f : x \to y$ to the inverse image mapping $\map {\overline \PP} f : \powerset y \to \powerset x$ }}

label: Definition:Control
snippet: A control is an implementation of a technique to rule out the effects of a random variable other than the factors that a particular experiment is designed to investigate. This may be done either by: directly controlling one or more of the possible factors which may influence the outcome or matching pairs of experimental units, and applying a treatment to one but not the other. Randomization can then be employed to ensure that any residual confounding variables do not introduce any systemic bias.

label: Definition:Control Group
snippet: A control group is a set of experimental units in an experimental design which are specifically not given the treatment under investigation. It provides a baseline to assess what would happen to a typical experimental unit to compare those which are subject to that treatment. The control group and the experimental groups should be allocated either randomly, or, if possible, balanced.

label: Definition:Convenience Sampling
snippet: Convenience sampling is the technique of gathering a sample from the most conveniently available set of possible subjects. Data collected in this way cannot be expected to be representative of a more comprehensive population.

label: Definition:Convergence Almost Everywhere
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $D \in \Sigma$. Let $f: D \to \R$ be a $\Sigma$-measurable function. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f_n: D \to \R$. Then $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is said to converge almost everywhere (or converge a.e.) on $D$ to $f$ : $\map \mu {\set {x \in D : \sequence {\map {f_n} x}_{n \mathop \in \N} \text { does not converge to } \map f x} } = 0$ and we write $f_n \stackrel{a.e.} \to f$. In other words, the sequence of functions converges pointwise outside of a $\mu$-null set.

label: Definition:Convergence in Distribution
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. For each $n \in \N$, let $F_n$ be the cumulative distribution function of $X_n$. Let $F$ be the cumulative distribution function of $X$. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges in distribution to $X$ : $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map {F_n} x = \map F x$ for all $x$ for which $F$ is continuous.

label: Definition:Convergence in Mean
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a $\mu$-integrable function. For each $n \in \N$, let $f_n : X \to \R$ be a $\mu$-integrable function. We say that the sequence $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges in mean to $f$ : $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \int \size {f_n - f} \rd \mu = 0$

label: Definition:Convergence in Mean Square
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is convergent in mean square to $X$ : $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \expect {\size {X_n - X}^2} = 0$ where $\expect X$ denotes the expectation of $X$. This is written: $X_n \xrightarrow {\text {L2} } X$

label: Definition:Convergence in Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}, f_n: X \to \R$ be a sequence of $\Sigma$-measurable functions. Then $f_n$ is said to converge in measure to a measurable function $f: X \to \R$ : $\ds \forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map \mu {\set {x \in D : \size {\map {f_n} x - \map f x} \ge \epsilon} } = 0$ for all $D \in \Sigma$ with $\map \mu D < + \infty$.

label: Definition:Convergence in Probability
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges in probability to $X$ : $\ds \forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map \Pr {\size {X_n - X} < \epsilon} = 1$ This is written: $X_n \xrightarrow p X$ or: $X_n \xrightarrow P X$

label: Definition:Convergent Filter
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a filter on $S$. Then $\FF$ converges to a point $x \in S$ : $\forall N_x \subseteq S: N_x \in \FF$ where $N_x$ is a neighborhood of $x$. That is, a filter converges to a point $x$ every neighborhood of $x$ is an element of that filter. If there is a point $x \in S$ such that $\FF$ converges to $x$, then $\FF$ is convergent.

label: Definition:Convergent Filter Basis
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\BB$ be a filter basis of a filter $\FF$ on $S$. Then $\BB$ converges to a point $x \in S$ : $\forall N_x \subseteq S: \exists B \in \BB: B \subseteq N_x$ where $N_x$ is a neighborhood of $x$. That is, a filter basis is convergent to a point $x$ if every neighborhood of $x$ contains some set of that filter basis.

label: Definition:Convergent Mapping/Complex Function
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function defined everywhere on $\C$ except possibly at $c$. Let $\map f z$ tend to the limit $L$ as $z$ tends to $c$. Then $f$ converges to the limit $L$ as $z$ tends to $c$.

label: Definition:Convergent Mapping/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $c$ be a limit point of $M_1$. Let $f: A_1 \to A_2$ be a mapping from $A_1$ to $A_2$ defined everywhere on $A_1$ except possibly at $c$. Let $\map f x$ tend to the limit $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$. Then $f$ converges to the limit $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$.

label: Definition:Convergent Net
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\struct {\Lambda, \preceq}$ be a directed set. Let $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ be a net. We say that $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$ converges to $x \in X$ in $\struct {X, \tau}$, denoted $\ds x_\lambda \to x$ or $\lim x_\lambda = x$, : $\forall U \in \tau: x \in U \implies \exists \lambda_0 \in \Lambda: \forall \lambda \succeq \lambda_0: x_\lambda \in U$ That is, for every open $U$ with $x \in U$, there exists an $\lambda_0 \in \Lambda$ such that forall $\lambda \succeq \lambda_0$, $x_\lambda \in U$.

label: Definition:Convergent Net/Cluster Point
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\struct {\Lambda, \preceq}$ be a directed set. Let $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ be a net. Let $x \in X$. We say that $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ clusters at $x \in X$, denoted $x_\lambda \mathop {\longrightarrow_{\text{cl} } } x$, : $\forall U \in \tau, \lambda_0 \in \Lambda: x \in U \implies \exists \lambda \succeq \lambda_0: x_\lambda \in U$ That is, for every open $U$ with $x \in U$, and for every $\lambda_0 \in \Lambda$, there is an $\lambda \ge \lambda_0$ such that $\lambda \in U$.

label: Definition:Convergent Product/Arbitrary Field/Arbitrary Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a valued field. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of elements of $\mathbb K$. The infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ is convergent : there exists $n_0 \in \N$ such that the sequence of partial products of $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = n_0}^\infty a_n$ converges to some $b \in \mathbb K \setminus \set 0$. The sequence of partial products of $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ is then convergent to some $a \in \mathbb K$. Category:Definitions/Convergent Products

label: Definition:Convergent Product/Arbitrary Field/Nonzero Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a valued field. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of nonzero elements of $\mathbb K$. The infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ is convergent its sequence of partial products converges to a nonzero limit $a \in \mathbb K \setminus \set 0$. Category:Definitions/Convergent Products

label: Definition:Convergent Product/Normed Algebra
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a division ring with norm $\norm {\,\cdot\,}_{\mathbb K}$. Let $\struct {A, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be an associative normed unital algebra over $\mathbb K$. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence in $A$.

label: Definition:Convergent Product/Number Field/Arbitrary Sequence
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q, \R, \C$. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of elements of $\mathbb K$. The infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ is convergent : there exists $n_0 \in \N$ such that the sequence of partial products of $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = n_0}^\infty a_n$ converges to some $b \in \mathbb K \setminus \set 0$. The sequence of partial products of $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ is then convergent to some $a \in \mathbb K$. Category:Definitions/Convergent Products

label: Definition:Convergent Product/Number Field/Nonzero Sequence
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q, \R, \C$. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of nonzero elements of $\mathbb K$. Then: The infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ is convergent its sequence of partial products converges to a nonzero limit $a \in \mathbb K \setminus \set 0$. Category:Definitions/Convergent Products

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Complex Numbers/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\sequence {z_k}$ be a sequence in $\C$. $\sequence {z_k}$ converges to the limit $c \in \C$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R: n > N \implies \cmod {z_n - c} < \epsilon$ where $\cmod z$ denotes the modulus of $z$.

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Complex Numbers/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\sequence {z_k} = \sequence {x_k + i y_k}$ be a sequence in $\C$. $\sequence {z_k}$ converges to the limit $c = a + i b$ both: $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R: n > N \implies \size {x_n - a} < \epsilon \text { and } \size {y_n - b} < \epsilon$ where $\size {x_n - a}$ denotes the absolute value of $x_n - a$.

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or a pseudometric space. Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $A$.

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Metric Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or a pseudometric space. Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $A$. $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in A$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: \forall n \in \N: n > N \implies \map d {x_n, l} < \epsilon$

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Metric Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or a pseudometric space. Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $A$. $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in A$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: \forall n \in \N: n > N \implies x_n \in \map {B_\epsilon} l$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} l$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $l$.

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Metric Space/Definition 3
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or a pseudometric space. Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $A$. $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in A$ : $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map d {x_n, l} = 0$

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Metric Space/Definition 4
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or a pseudometric space. Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $A$. $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in A$ : for every $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$, the open $\epsilon$-ball about $l$ contains all but finitely many of the $x_k$.

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Normed Division Ring/Definition 3
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $R$. The sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $x \in R$ in the norm $
orm {\, \cdot \,}$ : the real sequence $\sequence {
orm {x_n - x} }$ converges to $0$ in the reals $\R$

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\,\cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $L \in X$. The sequence $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges to the limit $L \in X$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: \forall n \in \N: n > N \implies \norm {x_n - L} < \epsilon$

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Note on Domain of N
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence. $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n \to l$ be the limit of $\sequence {x_k}$. That is: $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: n > N \implies \map d {x_n, l} < \epsilon$ Some sources insist that $N \in \N$ but this is not strictly necessary and can make proofs more cumbersome.

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/P-adic Numbers
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $\Q_p$.

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/P-adic Numbers/Definition 1
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $\Q_p$. The sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $x \in \Q_p$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: \forall n \in \N: n > N \implies \norm {x_n - x}_p < \epsilon$

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/P-adic Numbers/Definition 2
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $\Q_p$. The sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $x \in \Q_p$ : $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $x$ in the $p$-adic norm

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/P-adic Numbers/Definition 3
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $\Q_p$. The sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $x \in \Q_p$ : $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $x$ in the $p$-adic metric

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/P-adic Numbers/Definition 4
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $\Q_p$. The sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $x \in \Q_p$ : the real sequence $\sequence {\norm {x_n - x}_p }$ converges to $0$ in the reals $\R$

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Rational Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $\Q$. $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in \R$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: n > N \implies \size {x_n - l} < \epsilon$ where $\size x$ is the absolute value of $x$.

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_k}$ be a sequence in $\R$. The sequence $\sequence {x_k}$ converges to the limit $l \in \R$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R_{>0}: n > N \implies \size {x_n - l} < \epsilon$ where $\size x$ denotes the absolute value of $x$.

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Test Function Space
snippet: Let $\map \DD {\R^d}$ be the test function space with the compact support $K \subseteq \R^d$. Let $\sequence {\phi_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $\map \DD {\R^d}$. Let $\phi \in \map \DD {\R^d}$ be a test function. Let $D^k := \dfrac {\partial^{k_1 + k_2 + \ldots + k_d}} {\partial x_1^{k_1} \partial x_2^{k_2} \ldots \partial x_d^{k_d} }$ be a partial differential operator with the multiindex $k = \tuple {k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_d}$.

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence in $A$.

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Topology/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence in $A$. $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $\alpha \in S$ : $\forall U \in \tau: \alpha \in U \implies \paren {\exists N \in \R_{>0}: \forall n \in \N: n > N \implies x_n \in U}$

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence/Topology/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence in $A$. $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to the limit $\alpha \in S$ : $\forall U \in \tau: \alpha \in U \implies \set {n \in \N: x_n \notin U}$ is finite.

label: Definition:Convergent Sequence in Weak Operator Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $\mathbb K = \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\map {CL} {X, Y}$ be a continuous linear transformation space. Let $\tau$ be the weak operator topology on $\map {CL} {X, Y}$. Suppose $\sequence {T_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a sequence in $\map {CL} {X, Y}$. Suppose $T \in \map {CL} {X, Y}$.

label: Definition:Convergent Series
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ, \tau}$ be a topological semigroup. Let $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ be a series in $S$. This series is said to be convergent its sequence of partial sums $\sequence {s_N}$ converges in the topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$. If $s_N \to s$ as $N \to \infty$, the series converges to the sum $s$, and one writes $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n = s$.

label: Definition:Convergent Series/Normed Vector Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $V$ be a normed vector space. Let $d$ be the induced metric on $V$. Let $\ds S := \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ be a series in $V$. $S$ is convergent its sequence $\sequence {s_N}$ of partial sums converges in the metric space $\struct {V, d}$.

label: Definition:Convergent Series/Number Field
snippet: Let $S$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q, \R, \C$. Let $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$ be a series in $S$. Let $\sequence {s_N}$ be the sequence of partial sums of $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n$. It follows that $\sequence {s_N}$ can be treated as a sequence in the metric space $S$. If $s_N \to s$ as $N \to \infty$, the series converges to the sum $s$, and one writes $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n = s$. A series is said to be convergent it converges to some $s$.

label: Definition:Convergent of Continued Fraction
snippet: Let $F$ be a field, such as the field of real numbers. Let $n \in \N \cup \set \infty$ be an extended natural number. Let $C = \sqbrk {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ be a continued fraction in $F$ of length $n$. Let $k \le n$ be a natural number.

label: Definition:Converse Statement
snippet: The converse of the conditional: $p \implies q$ is the statement: $q \implies p$

label: Definition:Conversion Factor
snippet: A conversion factor is a (usually real) constant which is used to multiply the value of a physical quantity in a given unit of measurement in order to express it in a different unit of measurement.

label: Definition:Convex
snippet: Geometry: Convex Geometric Figure Convex Polygon Convex Polyhedron Order Theory: Order-Convex Set Vector Spaces: Convex Set (Vector Space) Real Analysis Convex Real Function

label: Definition:Convex Balanced Hull
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $A \subseteq X$ be a non-empty set. We define the convex balanced hull of $A$ as the $\subseteq$-smallest convex balanced set including $A$. We denote the convex balanced hull by $\map {\operatorname {cobal} } A$.

label: Definition:Convex Circumference of Circle/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Convex Circumference == The concept of the convex circumference arises in as a way of rigorously specifying the relationship between a point and the circumference of the circle under investigation. As such it is not specifically defined in , but is tacitly understood. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Convex Combination
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $\family {\mathbf v_\alpha}_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \subseteq V$ be a family of elements of $V$ indexed by an indexing set $I$. Let $\ds \sum_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \lambda_\alpha \mathbf v_\alpha$ be a linear combination of $\family {\mathbf v_\alpha}$. Then $\ds \sum_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \lambda_\alpha \mathbf v_\alpha$ is a convex combination of $\family {\mathbf v_\alpha}$ : $(1): \quad \forall \alpha \in I: \lambda_\alpha > 0$ $(2): \quad \ds \sum_{\alpha \mathop \in I} \lambda_\alpha = 1$

label: Definition:Convex Component
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. The maximally order-convex sets into which $H$ is partitioned are the convex components of $H$.

label: Definition:Convex Cone
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $P \subseteq X$ be a cone in $X$. We say that $P$ is a convex cone : for each $v, v' \in P$, we have $v + v' \in P$.

label: Definition:Convex Geometric Figure
snippet: A geometric figure is convex a line segment joining two points on its boundary lies entirely inside it.

label: Definition:Convex Hull
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $U \subseteq V$.

label: Definition:Convex Hull/Definition 1
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $U \subseteq V$. The convex hull of $U$ is defined and denoted: $\ds \map {\operatorname {conv} } U = \set {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_j u_j : n \in \N, \, u_j \in U \text { and } \lambda_j \in \R_{> 0} \text { for each } j, \, \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_j = 1}$ That is, it is the set of all convex combinations of elements of $U$.

label: Definition:Convex Hull/Definition 2
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $U \subseteq V$. The convex hull of $U$ is defined and denoted: $\map {\operatorname {conv} } U = $ the intersection of all convex sets $C \subseteq V$ of $V$ such that $U \subseteq C$. That is, it is the intersection of all convex sets containing $U$.

label: Definition:Convex Hull/Definition 3
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $U \subseteq V$. The convex hull of $U$ is defined and denoted: $\map {\operatorname {conv} } U = $ the smallest convex set $C$ such that $U \subseteq C$.

label: Definition:Convex Polygon/Definition 1
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. $P$ is a convex polygon : For all points $A$ and $B$ located inside $P$, the line $AB$ is also inside $P$.

label: Definition:Convex Polygon/Definition 2
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. $P$ is a convex polygon : every internal angle of $P$ is not greater than $180 \degrees$.

label: Definition:Convex Polygon/Definition 3
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. $P$ is a convex polygon : the region enclosed by $P$ lies entirely on the same side of each side of $P$

label: Definition:Convex Polygon/Definition 4
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. $P$ is a convex polygon : the region enclosed by $P$ is the intersection of a finite number of half-planes. Note that an intersection of a finite number of half-planes is not necessarily a polygon.

label: Definition:Convex Polygon/Definition 5
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. $P$ is a convex polygon : the region enclosed by $P$ is the intersection of all half-planes that contain $P$ and that are created by all the lines that are tangent to $P$. By tangent we mean any line $l$ that contain one or more point of $P$ and has $P$ entirely in one of the half-planes created by $l$. In this sense any line, that is spanned by a side of $P$, is tangent to $P$.

label: Definition:Convex Polyhedron
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron.

label: Definition:Convex Polyhedron/Definition 1
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. $P$ is a convex polyhedron : For all points $A$ and $B$ located inside $P$, the line $AB$ is also inside $P$.

label: Definition:Convex Polyhedron/Definition 2
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. $P$ is a convex polyhedron : For every face of $P$, the plane in which it is embedded does not intersect the interior of $P$.

label: Definition:Convex Polyhedron/Definition 3
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. $P$ is a convex polyhedron : For each face of $P$, the whole of $P$ lies on one side of the plane of that face.

label: Definition:Convex Polyhedron/Definition 4
snippet: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. $P$ is a convex polyhedron : For each face of $P$, the plane containing that face does not intersect any other face of $P$.

label: Definition:Convex Real-Valued Function/Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be an $n$-dimensional real vector space. Let $S \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset. Let $f: S \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. $f$ is convex its epigraph is a convex subset of $\R^{n+1}$.

label: Definition:Convex Real Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is convex on $I$ : $\forall x, y \in I: \forall \alpha, \beta \in \R_{>0}, \alpha + \beta = 1: \map f {\alpha x + \beta y} \le \alpha \map f x + \beta \map f y$ 700px The geometric interpretation is that any point on the chord drawn on the graph of any convex function always lies on or above the graph.

label: Definition:Convex Real Function/Definition 1/Strictly
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. $f$ is strictly convex on $I$ : $\forall x, y \in I, x \ne y: \forall \alpha, \beta \in \R_{>0}, \alpha + \beta = 1: \map f {\alpha x + \beta y} < \alpha \map f x + \beta \map f y$ 700px The geometric interpretation is that any point on the chord drawn on the graph of any convex function always lies above the graph.

label: Definition:Convex Real Function/Geometric Interpretation
snippet: == Geometric Interpretation of Convex Real Function == Let $f$ be a convex real function. Then: for every pair of points $A$ and $B$ on the graph of $f$, the chord $AB$ lies entirely above the graph.

label: Definition:Convex Real Function/Point
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is defined on a real interval $I$. Let $a \in I$ be a point in the domain of $f$. Then: $f$ is convex at $a$ there exists a neighborhood of $a$ on which $f$ is convex.

label: Definition:Convex Real Function/Vector Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $C \subseteq X$ be a convex set. Let $f: C \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. We say that $f$ is convex : $\map f {t x + \paren {1 - t} y} \le t \map f x + \paren {1 - t} \map f y$ for each $t \in \openint 0 1$ and $x, y \in C$ whenever $\set {\map f x, \map f y} \ne \set {-\infty, \infty}$.

label: Definition:Convex Set (Geometry)
snippet: Let $S$ be a subset of an $n$-dimensional real Euclidean space $\R^n$. Let $S$ be such that for every pair of points in $S$, the straight line segment $AB$ lies entirely inside $S$. Then $S$ is a convex set of $S$.

label: Definition:Convex Set (Vector Space)
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $C \subseteq V$.

label: Definition:Convex Set (Vector Space)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $C \subseteq V$. We say that $C$ is convex : $t x + \paren {1 - t} y \in C$ for each $x, y \in C$ and $t \in \closedint 0 1$.

label: Definition:Convex Set (Vector Space)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $C \subseteq V$. We say that $C$ is convex : $t C + \paren {1 - t} C \subseteq C$ for each $t \in \closedint 0 1$, where $t C + \paren {1 - t} C$ denotes a linear combination of $C$.

label: Definition:Convex Set (Vector Space)/Line Segment
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over $\R$ or $\C$. Let $x, y \in V$. The set: $\set {t x + \paren {1 - t} y: t \in \closedint 0 1}$ is called the (straight) line segment joining $x$ and $y$. A convex set can thus be described as a set containing all straight line segments between its elements.

label: Definition:Convolution
snippet: Real Analysis Convolution Integral Convolution of Real Sequences Convolution of Fourier Transforms Convolution of Laplace Transforms Measure Theory Definition:Convolution (Measure Theory) Definition:Convolution of Measurable Functions Definition:Convolution of Measurable Function and Measure Definition:Convolution of Measures Arithmetic Functions Definition:Dirichlet Convolution Abstract Algebra Definition:Convolution of Mappings on Divisor-Finite Monoid Probability Theory Definition:Convolution of Random Variables

label: Definition:Convolution (Measure Theory)
snippet: Let $\BB^n$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R^n$, and let $\lambda^n$ be Lebesgue measure on $\R^n$.

label: Definition:Convolution of Measurable Functions
snippet: Let $\BB^n$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R^n$, and let $\lambda^n$ be Lebesgue measure on $\R^n$. Let $f, g: \R^n \to \R$ be $\BB^n$-measurable functions such that for all $x \in \R^n$: $\ds \int_{\R^n} \map f {x - y} \map g y \rd \map {\lambda^n} y$ is finite. The convolution of $f$ and $g$, denoted $f * g$, is the mapping defined by: $\ds f * g: \R^n \to \R, \map {f * g} x := \int_{\R^n} \map f {x - y} \map g y \rd \map {\lambda^n} y$

label: Definition:Conway Circle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. Let: $AB$ be produced: from $A$ by length $BC$ from $B$ by length $AC$ $BC$ be produced: from $B$ by length $AC$ from $C$ by length $AB$ $AC$ be produced: from $A$ by length $BC$ from $C$ by length $AB$ The Conway circle is the circle on whose circumference lie these $6$ new points so generated: 500px

label: Definition:Conway Life
snippet: A cellular evolution deriving from a stencil shaped as: $(1): \quad X := \Z^2$ $(2): \quad S_X := 2 := \set {0, 1}$ $(3): \quad \map S 0 \in \paren {\Z^2 \to 2}$ $(4): \quad \Delta := \tuple {\tuple {0, 0}, \tuple {0, 1}, \tuple {1, 1}, \tuple {1, 0}, \tuple {1, -1}, \tuple {0, -1}, \tuple {-1, -1}, \tuple {-1, 0}, \tuple {-1, 1} }$ $(5): \quad \map \delta {m, n_1, n_2, n_3, n_4, n_5, n_6, n_7, n_8} := \tuple {m, \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^8 n_i} \in \set {\tuple {0, 3}, \tuple {1, 2}, \tuple {1, 3} } \mathrel ? 1 : 0$ is called a Conway life.

label: Definition:Conway Life/Also known as
snippet: == Conway Life: Also known as == A Conway life is also known as the Game of Life, but there now exist several variants which have been developed since devised the original. Hence, while you will generally be understood when you talk about the Game of Life, it is prudent on to be specific.

label: Definition:Coordinate/Also denoted as
snippet: == Coordinates: Also denoted as == It is usual to use the subscript technique to denote the coordinates where $n$ is large or unspecified: $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ However, note that some texts (often in the fields of physics and mechanics) prefer to use superscripts: $\tuple {x^1, x^2, \ldots, x^n}$ While this notation is documented here, its use is not endorsed by because: there exists the all too likely subsequent confusion with notation for powers one of the philosophical tenets of is to present a system of notation that is as completely consistent as possible.

label: Definition:Coordinate Domain
snippet: Let $M$ be a topological manifold. Let $\struct {U, \phi}$ be a chart of $M$. Then $U$ is known as the coordinate domain of each of its points.

label: Definition:Coordinate System
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\sequence {a_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be an ordered basis of a free unitary $R$-module $G$. Then $\sequence {a_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ can be referred to as a coordinate system.

label: Definition:Coordinate System/3-Space
snippet: In physics and applied mathematics, it is usual for the coordinate system under discussion to be considered as superimposed on ordinary space of $3$ dimensions.

label: Definition:Coordinate System/3-Space/Curvilinear
snippet: Recall that we can define Cartesian $3$-space by means of perpendicular planes. Let us superimpose onto this coordinate system $3$ other one-parameter families of surfaces. In each of these families, the surfaces need not be parallel and they need not be planes. These families are such that every point in (ordinary) $3$-dimensional space can then be uniquely identified as the intersection of $3$ such surfaces: one surface from each family. Hence every point is identified as the ordered triple $\tuple {q_1, q_2, q_3}$, where $q_1$, $q_2$ and $q_3$ are the parameters of each of the families.

label: Definition:Coordinate System/Origin
snippet: The origin of a coordinate system is the zero vector. In the $x y$-plane, it is the point: $O = \tuple {0, 0}$ and in general, in the Euclidean space $\R^n$: $O = \underbrace {\tuple {0, 0, \ldots, 0} }_{\text{$n$ coordinates} }$ Thus it is the point where the axes cross over each other.

label: Definition:Coordinate Transformation
snippet: Let $\CC_\alpha$ and $\CC_\beta$ be coordinate systems over a space $\EE$ of $n$ dimensions. Let $P$ be a point in $\EE$ such that: $P$ is expressed as $\tuple {\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n}$ in $\CC_\alpha$ $P$ is expressed as $\tuple {\beta_1, \beta_2, \ldots, \beta_n}$ in $\CC_\beta$ A coordinate transformation is a mapping $\phi: \EE \to \EE$ such that: $\map \phi {\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n} = \tuple {\beta_1, \beta_2, \ldots, \beta_n}$ for all such points in $\EE$.

label: Definition:Coordinate Vector
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $M$ be a unitary $R$-module of dimension $n$. Let $B = \sequence {b_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be an ordered basis of $M$. Let $x \in M$. Let $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n\in R$ be such that $\ds x = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \lambda_i b_i$. Then $\tuple {\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n} \in R^n$ is the coordinate vector of $x$ $B$. This can be denoted: $\sqbrk x_B$

label: Definition:Copeland-Erdős Constant
snippet: The Copeland-Erdős constant is the real number whose decimal expansion is formed by concatenating the prime numbers in ascending order: $C_{10} = 0 \cdotp 23571 \, 11317 \, 19232 \, 93137 \, 4143 \ldots$

label: Definition:Copenhagen Interpretation
snippet: == Philosophical Position == The Copenhagen interpretation is the philosophical position that the quantum state of a particle is represented by Schrödinger's equation. This provides a probabilistic description of the particle's quantum state, which is undetermined until measured. The act of measurement collapses the wave function.

label: Definition:Coplanar
snippet: Coplanar means in the same plane.

label: Definition:Coplanar/Lines
snippet: Two (or more) lines are coplanar there exists a plane $P$ such that all the lines lie in $P$. In this context, these lines may be understood as encompassing straight lines and plane curves.

label: Definition:Coplanar/Points
snippet: Four or more points which belong to the same plane are coplanar.

label: Definition:Coplanar Vectors
snippet: Three or more vectors are coplanar they can be embedded in the same plane. Formally:

label: Definition:Coplanar Vectors/Non-Coplanar
snippet: Three or more vectors are non-coplanar if they are not coplanar. That is if they cannot be embedded in the same plane.

label: Definition:Coprime/Integers
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be integers. Let $\gcd \set {a, b}$ denote the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$. Then $a$ and $b$ are coprime : $\gcd \set {a, b}$ exists and: $\gcd \set {a, b} = 1$. '

label: Definition:Coprime/Integers/Relatively Composite
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be integers such that $b \ne 0$ and $a \ne 0$ (i.e. they are both non-zero). Let $\gcd \set {a, b}$ be the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$. If $\gcd \set {a, b} > 1$, then $a$ and $b$ are relatively composite. That is, two integers are relatively composite if they are not coprime. ' Category:Definitions/Number Theory Category:Definitions/Coprime Integers

label: Definition:Coproduct/Also Known As
snippet: == Coproduct: Also known as == If $\CC = \family {C_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ is a set, indexed by some indexing set $J$, the notations $\ds \coprod_{j \mathop \in J} C_j$ and $\ds \coprod_j C_j$ are often seen. In this situation, one writes $i_j$ for $i_{C_j}$ and calls it the $j$th injection. Category:Definitions/Coproducts

label: Definition:Coproduct/Binary Coproduct
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $A$ and $B$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. A coproduct diagram for $A$ and $B$ comprises an object $P$ and morphisms $i_1: A \to P$, $i_2: B \to P$: $\begin{xy} +{A} = "A", +{P} = "P", +{B} = "B", "A";"P" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/^.8em/{i_1}, "B";"P" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/_.8em/{i_2}, \end{xy}$ subjected to the following universal mapping property: In this situation, $P$ is called a coproduct of $A$ and $B$ and may be denoted $A + B$. We generally write $\sqbrk {x_1, x_2}$ for the unique morphism $u$ determined by above diagram.

label: Definition:Coproduct/Binary Coproduct Injection
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $A$ and $B$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. Let object $P$ and morphisms $i_1: A \to P$, $i_2: B \to P$ denote a binary coproduct of $A$ and $B$. The morphisms $i_1: A \to P$, $i_2: B \to P$ are called (binary coproduct) injections; if necessary, $i_1$ can be called the first injection and $i_2$ the second injection. The injections $i_1$ and $i_2$ are often taken to be implicit.

label: Definition:Coproduct/General Definition
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $\CC$ be any collection of objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC$ be the discrete category on $\CC$, considered as a subcategory of $\mathbf C$. A coproduct for $\CC$, denoted $\ds \coprod \CC$, is a colimit for the inclusion functor $D: \map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC \to \mathbf C$, considered as a diagram.

label: Definition:Coproduct/Injection
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $\CC$ be any collection of objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC$ be the discrete category on $\CC$, considered as a subcategory of $\mathbf C$. Let the object $\ds \coprod \CC$ and morphisms $i_C: C \to \ds \coprod \CC$ for each object $C \in \CC$ denote the coproduct of $\CC$. For an object $C$ in $\CC$, the associated morphism $i_C: \ds C \to \coprod \CC$ is called the injection on $C$.

label: Definition:Coproduct/Sets
snippet: Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be sets. A coproduct $\struct {C, i_1, i_2}$ of $S_1$ and $S_2$ comprises a set $C$ together with mappings $i_1: S_1 \to C$, $i_2: S_2 \to C$ such that: for all sets $X$ and mappings $f_1: S_1 \to X$ and $f_2: S_2 \to X$: there exists a unique mapping $h: C \to X$ such that: $h \circ i_1 = f_1$ $h \circ i_2 = f_2$ Hence: $\begin{xy} \xymatrix@L+2mu@+1em{ & C \ar@{-->}[dd]_*{h} & \\ S_1 \ar[ru]^*{i_1} \ar[rd]_*{f_1} & & S_2 \ar[lu]_*{i_2} \ar[ld]^*{f_2} \\ & X & }\end{xy}$ is a commutative diagram.

label: Definition:Coproduct UMP
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $\CC$ be any collection of objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC$ be the discrete category on $\CC$, considered as a subcategory of $\mathbf C$. An object $\ds \coprod \CC$ and morphisms $i_C: C \to \ds \coprod \CC$ for each object $C \in \CC$: $\begin{xy} +{\ds \coprod \CC} = "CC", +{\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC} = "BLL", +{C} = "BL", +{\ldots} = "BC", +{C'} = "BR", "BL";"CC" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/_1em/{i_C}, "BR";"CC" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/^1em/{i_{C'} }, \end{xy}$ satisfy the (coproduct) universal mapping property or (UMP) :

label: Definition:Coproduct UMP/Property
snippet: == Property for Coproduct UMP == For any object $A$ together with morphisms $a_C: C \to A$ for each object $C \in \CC$, then there exists a unique morphism $a: \ds \coprod \CC \to A$ such that: for each $C \in \CC: a_C = a \circ i_C$ That is: $\begin{xy} +{A} = "TC", +{\ds \coprod \CC} = "CC", +{\map {\mathbf {Dis} } \CC} = "BLL", +{C} = "BL", +{\ldots} = "BC", +{C'} = "BR", "BL";"CC" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/^1em/{i_C}, "BR";"CC" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/_1em/{i_{C'} }, "CC";"TC" **@{--} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.4)*!/^.5em/{a}, "BL";"TC" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?<>(.5)*!/_1em/{a_C}, "BR";"TC" **@{-} ?>*@{>}…

label: Definition:Coproduct of Morphisms
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $A, A'$ and $B, B'$ be pairs of objects admitting binary coproducts: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@R-1em@C+1em@L+3px{ A \ar[r]^*+{i_1} & A \sqcup A' & A' \ar[l]_*+{i_2} \\ B \ar[r]^*+{j_1} & B \sqcup B' & B' \ar[l]_*+{j_2} }\end{xy}$ Let $f: A \to B$ and $f': A' \to B'$ be morphisms.

label: Definition:Copunctal
snippet: Copunctal means having a common point.

label: Definition:Copunctal/Lines
snippet: Three (or more) lines are copunctal there exists a point $P$ that lies on all the lines. In this context, these lines may be understood as encompassing straight lines and plane curves.

label: Definition:Copunctal/Planes
snippet: Three (or more) planes are copunctal there exists a point $P$ that lies on all the planes.

label: Definition:Coriolis Force
snippet: A Coriolis force is an inertial force that arises when a body $B$ moves in a rotating frame of reference $\FF$. The Coriolis force acts on $B$ at right angles to both the axis of rotation and the direction of motion of $B$ in $\FF$.

label: Definition:Corollary
snippet: A corollary is a proof which is a direct result, or a direct application, of another proof. It can be considered as being a proof for free on the back of a proof which has been paid for with blood, sweat and tears.

label: Definition:Correlation
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. The correlation between $X$ and $Y$ is a measure of how much the value of one is dependent upon the other. That is, it is a measure of the extent to which a change in $X$ tends to correspond to a change in $Y$, and vice versa.

label: Definition:Correlation/High
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables presented as data pairs. Such data pairs are highly correlated, or show a high correlation, if the values show a close relationship.

label: Definition:Correlation/Negative
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. $X$ and $Y$ show a negative correlation a change in $X$ corresponds to a change in $Y$ in the opposite direction, and vice versa.

label: Definition:Correlation/Positive
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. $X$ and $Y$ show a positive correlation a change in $X$ corresponds to a change in $Y$ in the same direction, and vice versa.

label: Definition:Correlation Coefficient
snippet: A correlation coefficient is a statistical coefficient which provides a measure of a particular aspect of correlation amongst a set of data.

label: Definition:Correlation Matrix
snippet: Let $\sequence a_n$ and $\sequence b_n$ be sequences of $n$ observations. A correlation matrix $\mathbf C$ is a square matrix of order $n$ defined as: $\sqbrk c_{i j} = r_{i j}$ where $r_{i j}$ denotes the sample correlation coefficient between $a_i$ and $b_j$.

label: Definition:Correspondence/Also defined as
snippet: == Correspondence: Also defined as == Some sources define a correspondence as a relation with no restrictions upon it. That is, a correspondence from $S$ to $T$ is an arbitrary subset of the Cartesian product $S \times T$. In order to reduce confusion, it is recommended that this usage of correspondence is not used.

label: Definition:Corresponding Conditional
snippet: Let $p_1, p_2, p_3, \ldots, p_n \vdash q$ be a sequent of propositional logic. It can be expressed as a theorem as follows: $\vdash p_1 \implies \paren {p_2 \implies \paren {p_3 \implies \paren {\ldots \implies \paren {p_n \implies q} \ldots } } }$ This is known as the sequent's corresponding conditional.

label: Definition:Corresponding Sides
snippet: Let $\PP$ and $\QQ$ be similar $n$-sided polygons. The corresponding sides of $\PP$ and $\QQ$ are the $n$ pairs of sides for which the ratio of the side of $\PP$ to the side of $\QQ$ is the same in each case. This also covers the case where $\PP$ and $\QQ$ are congruent, where the ratio in this case is $1 : 1$.

label: Definition:Cosecant/Complex Function
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. The complex function $\csc z$ is defined as: $\csc z = \dfrac 1 {\sin z}$ where $\sin z$ is the sine of $z$. The definition is valid for all $z \in \C$ such that $\sin z \ne 0$.

label: Definition:Cosecant/Definition from Circle/First Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the first quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {0, 1}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the cosecant of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $OB$. Hence in the first quadrant, the cosecant is positive.

label: Definition:Cosecant/Definition from Circle/Fourth Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the fourth quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {0, 1}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the cosecant of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $OB$. Hence in the fourth quadrant, the cotangent is negative.

label: Definition:Cosecant/Definition from Circle/Second Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the second quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {0, 1}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the cosecant of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $OB$. Hence in the second quadrant, the cosecant is positive.

label: Definition:Cosecant/Definition from Circle/Third Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the third quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {0, 1}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the cosecant of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $OB$. As $OP$ needs to be produced in the opposite direction to $P$, the cosecant is therefore a negative function in the third quadrant.

label: Definition:Cosecant/Real Function
snippet: Let $x \in \C$ be a real number. The real function $\csc x$ is defined as: $\csc x = \dfrac 1 {\sin x}$ where $\sin x$ is the sine of $x$. The definition is valid for all $x \in \R$ such that $\sin x \ne 0$.

label: Definition:Coset/Left Coset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\struct {H, \circ}$ be a subgroup of $\struct {S, \circ}$. The left coset of $x$ modulo $H$, or left coset of $H$ by $x$, is: $x \circ H = \set {y \in S: \exists h \in H: y = x \circ h}$ That is, it is the subset product with singleton: $x \circ H = \set x \circ H$

label: Definition:Coset Product
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $N$ be a normal subgroup of $G$. Let $a, b \in G$. The coset product of $a \circ N$ and $b \circ N$ is defined as the binary operation on the left coset space $G / N$ defined as: $\paren {a \circ N} \circ \paren {b \circ N} = \paren {a \circ b} \circ N$ where $a \circ N$ and $b \circ N$ are the left cosets of $a$ and $b$ by $N$.

label: Definition:Coset Space/Left Coset Space
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. The left coset space (of $G$ modulo $H$) is the quotient set of $G$ by left congruence modulo $H$, denoted $G / H^l$. It is the set of all the left cosets of $H$ in $G$.

label: Definition:Coset Space/Notation
snippet: == Coset Space: Notation == If we are (as is usual) concerned at a particular time with only the right or the left coset space, then the superscript is usually dropped. Thus the notation $G / H$ is used for both the right and left coset space. If, in addition, $H$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, then $G / H^l = G / H^r$ and the notation $G / H$ is then unambiguous anyway. Some sources use $G \divides H$ for the left coset space, reserving $G / H$ for the right coset space. Some sources even use $H \divides G$ for the left coset space.

label: Definition:Coset Space/Right Coset Space
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. The right coset space (of $G$ modulo $H$) is the quotient set of $G$ by right congruence modulo $H$, denoted $G / H^r$. It is the set of all the right cosets of $H$ in $G$.

label: Definition:Coset Space of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S$ be a subring of $R$. For $a \in R$, let $\paren {a + S}$ denote the coset of $S$ by $a$. The coset space of $R$ $S$ is defined as the set of all cosets of $S$ in $R$: $\set {\paren {a + S}: a \in R}$

label: Definition:Cotangent/Complex Function
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. The complex function $\cot z$ is defined as: $\cot z = \dfrac {\cos z} {\sin z} = \dfrac 1 {\tan z}$ where: $\sin z$ is the sine of $z$ $\cos z$ is the cosine of $z$ $\tan z$ is the tangent of $z$ The definition is valid for all $z \in \C$ such that $\sin z \ne 0$.

label: Definition:Cotangent/Definition from Circle/First Quadrant

Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {0, 1}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the cotangent of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $AB$. Hence in the first quadrant, the cotangent is positive.

label: Definition:Cotangent/Definition from Circle/Fourth Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the fourth quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. As $OP$ needs to be produced in the opposite direction to $P$, the cotangent is therefore a negative function in the fourth quadrant.

label: Definition:Count
snippet: To count a set $S$ is to establish a bijection between $S$ and an initial segment $\N_n$ of the natural numbers $\N$. If $S \sim \N_n$ (where $\sim$ denotes set equivalence) then we have counted $S$ and found it has $n$ elements. If $S \sim \N$ then $S$ is infinite but countable.

label: Definition:Countability Axioms
snippet: == Definitions == Countability axioms is the common name used to refer to a set of properties of a topological space which have to do with the existence of countable sets, or countable families of open sets, satisfying certain conditions. They are not axioms in the strict sense of the word, but they are usually named as such because one may think of them as additional basic properties that one can ask from a topological space.

label: Definition:Countable/Also defined as
snippet: Some sources define countable to be what is defined on as countably infinite. That is, they use countable to describe a collection which has exactly the same cardinality as $\N$. Thus under this criterion $X$ is said to be countable there exists a bijection from $X$ to $\N$, that is, $X$ is equivalent to $\N$. However, as the very concept of the term countable implies that a collection can be counted, which, plainly, a finite can be, it is suggested that this interpretation may be counter-intuitive.

label: Definition:Countable Basis
snippet: A countable (analytic) basis for a topology $\tau$ is an analytic basis for $\tau$ which is a countable set.

label: Definition:Countable Chain Condition
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. $T$ satisfies the countable chain condition every disjoint set of open sets of $T$ is countable.

label: Definition:Countable Complement Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be an infinite set whose cardinality is usually taken to be uncountable. Let $\tau$ be the set of subsets of $S$ defined as: $H \in \tau \iff \relcomp S H$ is countable, or $H = \O$ where $\relcomp S H$ denotes the complement of $H$ relative to $S$. In this definition, countable is used in its meaning that includes finite. Then $\tau$ is the countable complement topology on $S$, and the topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countable complement space.

label: Definition:Countable Complement Topology/Countable
snippet: It is possible to define the countable complement topology on a countable set set $S$, but as every subset of a countable set has a countable complement, it is clear that this is trivially equal to the discrete space. This is why the countable complement topology is usually understood to apply to uncountable sets only. Category:Definitions/Countable Complement Topologies

label: Definition:Countable Finite Intersection Axiom
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $T$ be such that: Every countable set $V_\alpha$ of closed sets of $T$ such that $\ds \bigcap V_\alpha = \O$ contains a finite subset $V_\beta \subseteq V_\alpha$ such that $\ds \bigcap V_\beta = \O$. Then $T$ satisfies the countable finite intersection axiom.

label: Definition:Countable Ordinal
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be an ordinal. Then $\alpha$ is said to be countable it is a countable set.

label: Definition:Countable Set
snippet: == Definition == Let $S$ be a set.

label: Definition:Countable Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. $S$ is countable there exists an injection: $f: S \to \N$

label: Definition:Countable Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. $S$ is countable it is finite or countably infinite.

label: Definition:Countable Set/Definition 3
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. $S$ is countable there exists a bijection between $S$ and a subset of $\N$. That is, if it can be shown that it is possible to exhaustively count its elements.

label: Definition:Countable Tightness
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\cl$ be closure in $\struct {X, \tau}$. We say that $\struct {X, \tau}$ has countable tightness for each $A \subseteq X$ and $x \in \map \cl A$, there exists a countable set $S \subseteq A$ such that $x \in \map \cl S$.

label: Definition:Countable Topological Space
snippet: A countable topological space is a topological space whose underlying set is countable, whether finite or countably infinite.

label: Definition:Countably Additive Function
snippet: Let $\Sigma$ be a $\sigma$-algebra. Let $f: \Sigma \to \overline \R$ be a function, where $\overline \R$ denotes the set of extended real numbers. Then $f$ is defined as countably additive : $\ds \map f {\bigcup_{n \mathop \in \N} E_n} = \sum_{n \mathop \in \N} \map f {E_n}$ where $\sequence {E_n}$ is any sequence of pairwise disjoint elements of $\Sigma$. That is, for any countably infinite set of pairwise disjoint elements of $\Sigma$, $f$ of their union equals the sum of $f$ of the individual elements.

label: Definition:Countably Compact Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countably compact space : every countable open cover of $S$ has a finite subcover.

label: Definition:Countably Compact Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countably compact space : every countable set of closed sets of $T$ whose intersection is empty has a finite subset whose intersection is empty. That is, $T$ satisfies the countable finite intersection axiom.

label: Definition:Countably Compact Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countably compact space : every infinite sequence in $S$ has an accumulation point in $S$.

label: Definition:Countably Compact Space/Definition 4
snippet: A topological space $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ is a countably compact space : every countably infinite subset of $S$ has an $\omega$-accumulation point in $S$.

label: Definition:Countably Compact Space/Definition 5
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countably compact space : every infinite subset of $S$ has an $\omega$-accumulation point in $S$.

label: Definition:Countably Generated Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\Sigma$ be a $\sigma$-algebra of $X$. $\Sigma$ is countably generated : $\Sigma$ is generated by a countable collection $\GG \subseteq \Sigma$.

label: Definition:Countably Infinite/Also known as
snippet: When the terms denumerable and enumerable are encountered, they generally mean the same as countably infinite. Sometimes the term enumerably infinite can be seen. Some modern pedagogues (for example and ) use the term listable, but this has yet to catch on.

label: Definition:Countably Infinite/Set
snippet: == Definition == Let $S$ be a set.

label: Definition:Countably Infinite Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. $S$ is countably infinite there exists a bijection: $f: S \to \N$ where $\N$ is the set of natural numbers. That is, it is an infinite set of the form: $\set {s_0, s_1, \ldots, s_n, \ldots}$ where $n$ runs over all the natural numbers. An infinite set is countably infinite if it is countable, and is uncountable otherwise.

label: Definition:Countably Infinite Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. $S$ is countably infinite there exists a bijection: $f: S \to \Z$ where $\Z$ is the set of integers. An infinite set is countably infinite if it is countable, and is uncountable otherwise.

label: Definition:Countably Infinite Topological Space/Also known as
snippet: == Countably Infinite Topological Space: Also known as == A countably infinite topological space is also known as. Some sources use the term countable topological space, but 's usage of countable specifically includes the finite case.

label: Definition:Countably Metacompact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countably metacompact space : every countable open cover of $T$ has an open refinement which is point finite.

label: Definition:Countably Paracompact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a countably paracompact space : every countable open cover of $T$ has an open refinement which is locally finite.

label: Definition:Countably Subadditive Function
snippet: Let $\Sigma$ be a $\sigma$-algebra over a set $X$. Let $f: \Sigma \to \overline \R$ be a function, where $\overline \R$ denotes the set of extended real numbers. Then $f$ is defined as countably subadditive for any sequence $\sequence {E_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ of elements of $\Sigma$: $\ds \map f {\bigcup_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty E_n} \le \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \map f {E_n}$

label: Definition:Counterexample
snippet: Let $X$ be the universal statement: $\forall x \in S: \map P x$ That is: For all the elements $x$ of a given set $S$, the property $P$ holds. Such a statement may or may not be true. Let $Y$ be the existential statement: $\exists y \in S: \neg \map P y$ That is: There exists at least one element $y$ of the set $S$ such that the property $P$ does not hold. It follows immediately by De Morgan's laws that if $Y$ is true, then $X$ must be false. Such a statement $Y$ is referred to as a counterexample to $X$.

label: Definition:Counts
snippet: Counts are a statistic which simply records the count of instances of various events. These can then be used as the basis of more sophisticated statistical investigation, for example the analysis of contingency tables.

label: Definition:Coupled Equations
snippet: Coupled equations are a pair of simultaneous equations, usually differential equations.

label: Definition:Covariance
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Let $\mu_X = \expect X$ and $\mu_Y = \expect Y$, the expectations of $X$ and $Y$ respectively, exist and be finite. Then the covariance of $X$ and $Y$ is defined by: $\cov {X, Y} = \expect {\paren {X - \mu_X} \paren {Y - \mu_Y} }$ where this expectation exists.

label: Definition:Covariance Matrix
snippet: Let $\sequence a_n$ and $\sequence b_n$ be sequences of $n$ observations. A covariance matrix $\mathbf C$ is a square matrix of order $n$ defined as: $\sqbrk c_{i j} = \cov {x_i, y_i}$ where $\cov {x_i, y_i}$ denotes the covariance of $x_i$ and $y_j$.
