label: Definition:Discrete/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Discrete == Be careful with the word discrete. A common homophone horror is to use the word discreet instead. However, discreet means cautious or tactful, and describes somebody who is able to keep silent for political or delicate social reasons. Category:Linguistic Notes

label: Definition:Discrete (Word)
snippet: Discrete is a word used to define an object which is not continuous. That is, it takes only finite or countably infinite values.

label: Definition:Discrete Extension of Reals
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $D$ be an everywhere dense subset of $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ with an everywhere dense complement in $\R$. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets defined as: $\BB = \tau_d \cup \set {\set x: x \in D}$ Let $\tau*$ be the topology generated from $\BB$. $\tau^*$ is referred to as a discrete extension of $\R$. It is usual to focus attention on the two specific cases where $D$ is either the set of rational numbers or the set of irrational numbers:

label: Definition:Discrete Extension of Reals/Rational
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $\Q$ denote the set of rational numbers. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets defined as: $\BB = \tau_d \cup \set {\set x: x \in \Q}$ Let $\tau*$ be the topology generated from $\BB$. $\tau^*$ is referred to as the discrete rational extension of $\R$.

label: Definition:Discrete Fourier Transform
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be a finite sequence of complex numbers for some $n \in \N_{>0}$. The discrete Fourier transform of $\sequence {x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ is the sequence $\sequence {\hat x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ where: $\hat x_k = \ds \sum_{r \mathop = 1}^n x_r \map \exp {\dfrac {-2 \pi i k r} n}$

label: Definition:Discrete Fourier Transform/Inverse
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be a finite sequence of complex numbers for some $n \in \N_{>0}$. Let $\sequence {\hat x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ be the discrete Fourier transform of $\sequence {x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$. The inverse discrete Fourier transform of $\sequence {\hat x_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ is: $x_k = \ds \dfrac 1 n \sum_{r \mathop = 1}^n \hat x_r \map \exp {\dfrac {2 \pi i k r} n}$

label: Definition:Discrete Geometry
snippet: Discrete geometry is a branch of geometry that studies constructive methods of discrete geometric objects.

label: Definition:Discrete Group
snippet: A discrete group is a topological group whose topology is discrete.

label: Definition:Discrete Logarithm
snippet: Let $g$ be a generator of a cyclic group $G$. Let $y \in G$ such that: $y = g^x$ The integer $x$ is known as the discrete logarithm of $y$ to base $g$. It is usual for $G$ to be the multiplicative group of a finite field. In particular, the multiplicative group $\Z'_p$ for prime $p$ is often used as the canonical example.

label: Definition:Discrete Logarithm Problem
snippet: Let $g$ be a generator of a cyclic group $G$. The discrete logarithm problem is to find the discrete logarithm of a given $y \in G$ to base $g$.

label: Definition:Discrete Logarithm Problem/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Discrete Logarithm Problem == The discrete logarithm problem is known to be a "very difficult" problem to solve for a large cyclic group. Hence its usefulness in the field of cryptography, where, for example, the Diffie-Hellman-Merkle key exchange technique utilises this very difficulty.

label: Definition:Discrete Logarithm Problem/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Discrete Logarithm Problem == The discrete logarithm problem is so called because its solution is equivalent to the problem of solving $y = e^x$ where $x$ and $y$ are real numbers and whose solution is $x = \ln y$.

label: Definition:Discrete Mathematics
snippet: Discrete mathematics is the branch of mathematics which studies mathematical structures that are discrete rather than continuous. Is is usually applied to areas of mathematics such as combinatorics and graph theory. Computer science has applications of discrete mathematics on account of the discrete nature of computer states.

label: Definition:Discrete Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Then $\mu$ is said to be a discrete measure it is a series of Dirac measures. That is, there exist: a sequence $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $X$ and: a sequence $\sequence {\lambda_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $\R$ such that: $(1):\quad \forall E \in \Sigma: \map \mu E = \ds \sum_{n \mathop \in \N} \lambda_n \, \map {\delta_{x_n} } E$ where $\delta_{x_n}$ denotes the Dirac measure at $x_n$. By Series of Measures is Measure, defining $\mu$ by $(1)$ yields a measure.

label: Definition:Discrete Probability Distribution
snippet: A discrete probability distribution is a probability distribution of a discrete random variable.

label: Definition:Discrete Probability Measure
snippet: Let $\Omega$ be a countable set. Let $\powerset \Omega$ be its power set, regarded as a $\sigma$-algebra. Let $\paren {p_\omega}_{\omega \mathop \in \Omega} \subseteq \closedint 0 1$ be a subset of the closed unit interval in $\R$, indexed by $\Omega$. Suppose that $\ds \sum_{\omega \mathop \in \Omega} p_\omega = 1$.

label: Definition:Discrete Random Variable/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ be a measurable space. A discrete random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ is a mapping $X: \Omega \to S$ such that: $(1): \quad$ The image of $X$ is a countable subset of $S$ $(2): \quad$ $\forall x \in S: \set {\omega \in \Omega: \map X \omega = x} \in \Sigma$ Alternatively, the second condition can be written as: $(2): \quad$ $\forall x \in S: X^{-1} \sqbrk {\set x} \in \Sigma$ where $X^{-1} \sqbrk {\set x}$ denotes the preimage of $\set x$.

label: Definition:Discrete Random Variable/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ be a measurable space. Let $X$ be a random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$. Then we say that $X$ is a discrete random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ : the image of $X$ is a countable subset of $\Omega'$.

label: Definition:Discrete Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then $H$ is a discrete set every point of $H$ is an isolated point of $H$.

label: Definition:Discrete Set of Subsets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $\FF$ is discrete each element of $S$ has a neighborhood which intersects at most one of the sets in $\FF$.

label: Definition:Discrete Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a topological group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. Then $H$ is called a discrete subgroup it is a discrete group for the induced topology.

label: Definition:Discrete Topology
snippet: Let $S \ne \O$ be a set. Let $\tau = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. That is, let $\tau$ be the set of all subsets of $S$: $\tau := \set {H: H \subseteq S}$ Then $\tau$ is called the discrete topology on $S$. The topological space $\struct {S, \tau} = \struct {S, \powerset S}$ is called the discrete space on $S$, or just a discrete space.

label: Definition:Discrete Topology/Countable
snippet: Let $S$ be an infinite set. Let $\tau = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. That is, let $\tau$ be the set of all subsets of $S$: $\tau := \set {H: H \subseteq S}$ Let $S$ be a countably infinite set. Then $\tau = \powerset S$ is a countable discrete topology, and $\struct {S, \tau} = \struct {S, \powerset S}$ is a countable discrete space.

label: Definition:Discrete Topology/Finite
snippet: Let $S \ne \O$ be a set. Let $\tau = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. That is, let $\tau$ be the set of all subsets of $S$: $\tau := \set {H: H \subseteq S}$ Let $S$ be a finite set. Then $\tau = \powerset S$ is a finite discrete topology, and $\struct {S, \tau} = \struct {S, \powerset S}$ is a finite discrete space.

label: Definition:Discrete Topology/Infinite
snippet: Let $S \ne \O$ be a set. Let $\tau = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. That is, let $\tau$ be the set of all subsets of $S$: $\tau := \set {H: H \subseteq S}$ Let $S$ be an infinite set. Then $\tau = \powerset S$ is an infinite discrete topology, and $\struct {S, \tau} = \struct {S, \powerset S}$ is an infinite discrete space.

label: Definition:Discrete Topology/Uncountable
snippet: Let $S \ne \O$ be a set. Let $\tau = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. That is, let $\tau$ be the set of all subsets of $S$: $\tau := \set {H: H \subseteq S}$ Let $S$ be an uncountably infinite set. Then $\tau = \powerset S$ is an uncountable discrete topology, and $\struct {S, \tau} = \struct {S, \powerset S}$ is an uncountable discrete space.

label: Definition:Discrete Topology on Two-Point Set
snippet: == Example of Finite Discrete Space == Let $S = \set {0, 1} = 2$ be an instance of an arbitrary doubleton. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be the topological space on $S$ where $\tau = \powerset S$ is the power set of $S$. Then $\tau$ is the discrete topology on a two-point space. The topological space $T$ itself is hence referred to as the discrete two-point space.

label: Definition:Discrete Uniformity
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The discrete uniformity on $S$ is the uniformity $\UU$ defined as: $\UU := \set {u \subseteq S \times S: \Delta_S \subseteq u}$ that is, all subsets of the cartesian product on $S$ which contain the diagonal relation on $S$. Hence from Relation Contains Diagonal Relation iff Reflexive it can be considered as the set of all reflexive relations on $S$.

label: Definition:Discriminant
snippet: Polynomial Theory: Discriminant of Polynomial Abstract Algebra: Discriminant of Number Field Discriminant of Bilinear Form Discriminant of Quadratic Form Linear Algebra: Discriminant of Matrix Analytic Geometry: Discriminant of Conic Section Statistics: Discriminant Function

label: Definition:Discriminant Function
snippet: A discriminant function is a function which assigns a given individual to one of a number of populations according to the data appertaining to that individual. It is based on measurements on individuals for whom the population to which each one belongs is known. It is chosen to minimize the probabilities or costs of misclassification.

label: Definition:Discriminant of Bilinear Form
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$ of finite dimension $n>0$. Let $b : V\times V \to \mathbb K$ be a bilinear form on $V$. Let $A$ be the matrix of $b$ relative to an ordered basis of $V$. If $b$ is nondegenerate, its discriminant is the equivalence class of the determinant $\det A$ in the quotient group $\dfrac {\mathbb K^\times} {\paren {\mathbb K^\times}^2}$. If $b$ is degenerate, its discriminant is $0$.

label: Definition:Discriminant of Conic Section
snippet: Let $K$ be a conic section embedded in a Cartesian plane with the general equation: $a x^2 + 2 h x y + b y^2 + 2 g x + 2 f y + c = 0$ where $a, b, c, f, g, h \in \R$. The discriminant of $K$ is defined as the determinant calculated as: $\Delta = \begin {vmatrix} a & h & g \\ h & b & f \\ g & f & c \end {vmatrix}$

label: Definition:Discriminant of Cubic Equation/Reduced Form
snippet: Let $P$ be a cubic equation expressed in the form: $x^3 + p x^2 + q x + r = 0$ The discriminant of $P$ is given by: $D = 4 q^3 + 4 p^3 r + 27 r^3 - p^2 q^2 - 18 p q r$

label: Definition:Discriminant of Cubic Equation/Reduced Form/Also presented as
snippet: == Discriminant of Cubic Equation: Reduced Form: Also presented as == Let $P$ be a cubic equation expressed in the form: $x^3 + p x^2 + q x + r = 0$ Some sources present the discriminant of $P$ in the form: $D = p^2 q^2 + 18 p q r - 4 q^3 - 4 p^3 r - 27 r^3$ under which regime the sign of $D$ is interpreted inversely.

label: Definition:Discriminant of Polynomial

Let $\map f X \in k \sqbrk X$ be a polynomial of degree $n$: $a_n x^n + a_{n - 1} x^{n - 1} + a_{n - 2} x^{n - 2} + \cdots + a_1 x + a_0$ Let $\overline k$ be an algebraic closure of $k$. Let the roots of $f$ in $\overline k$ be $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_n$. Then the discriminant $\map \Delta f$ of $f$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = \map \Delta f | r = {a_n}^{2 n - 2} \prod_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop < j \mathop \le n} \paren {\alpha_i - \alpha_j}^2 | c = }} {{eqn | r = {a_n}^{2 n - 2} \paren {\alpha_1 - \alpha_2}^2 \paren {\alpha_1 - \alpha_3}^2 \paren {\alpha_1 -…

label: Definition:Discriminant of Polynomial/Cubic Equation
snippet: Let $P$ be the cubic equation: $a x^3 + b x^2 + c x + d = 0$ with $a \ne 0$ Let: {{eqn | l = Q | r = \dfrac {3 a c - b^2} {9 a^2} }} {{eqn | l = R | r = \dfrac {9 a b c - 27 a^2 d - 2 b^3} {54 a^3} }} The discriminant of the cubic equation is given by: $D := Q^3 + R^2$

label: Definition:Discriminant of Polynomial/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == discriminant (of a polynomial equation)

label: Definition:Discriminant of Polynomial/Quadratic Equation
snippet: Consider the quadratic equation: $a x^2 + b x + c = 0$ The expression $b^2 - 4 a c$ is called the discriminant of the equation.

label: Definition:Discriminatory Test
snippet: In the context of statistics, a discriminatory test is a statistical test whose power is greater than some previously specified level.

label: Definition:Disjoint
snippet: A pair of properties is described as disjoint each one can't happen if the other holds.

label: Definition:Disjoint Events
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be events in a probability space. Then $A$ and $B$ are disjoint : $A \cap B = \O$ It follows by definition of probability measure that $A$ and $B$ are disjoint : $\map \Pr {A \cap B} = 0$ That is, two events are disjoint the probability of them both occurring in the same experiment is zero. That is, $A$ and $B$ can't happen together.

label: Definition:Disjoint Sets
snippet: Two sets $S$ and $T$ are disjoint : $S \cap T = \O$ That is, disjoint sets are sets such that their intersection is the empty set -- they have no elements in common.

label: Definition:Disjoint Sets/Family
snippet: Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of sets indexed by $I$. Then $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is disjoint their intersection is empty: $\ds \bigcap_{i \mathop \in I} S_i = \O$

label: Definition:Disjoint Union (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a collection of pairwise disjoint sets. That is, for all sets $A, B \in \CC: A \ne B \implies A \cap B = \O$. Then the union of all sets in $\CC$ is called their disjoint union: $\ds \bigsqcup_{A \mathop \in \CC} A \equiv \bigcup_{A \mathop \in \CC} A$ That is, in this context the term disjoint union means union of sets which are pairwise disjoint.

label: Definition:Disjoint Union (Set Theory)
snippet: Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of sets. The disjoint union of $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is defined as the set: $\ds \bigsqcup_{i \mathop \in I} S_i = \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} \set {\tuple {x, i}: x \in S_i}$ where $\bigcup$ denotes union. Each of the sets $S_i$ is canonically embedded in the disjoint union as the set: ${S_i}^* = \set {\tuple {x, i}: x \in S_i} = S_i \times \set i$ that is, the cartesian product of $S_i$ and $\set i$. For distinct $i, j \in I$, the sets ${S_i}^*$ and ${S_j}^*$ are disjoint even if $S_i$ and $S_j$ are not.

label: Definition:Disjoint Union (Set Theory)/2 Sets
snippet: Let $I$ be a doubleton, say $I := \set {0, 1}$. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of sets. Then the disjoint union of $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is defined as the set: {{eqn | l = \bigsqcup_{i \mathop \in I} S_i | r = \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} \set {\tuple {x, 0}, \tuple {y, 1} : x \in S_0, y \in S_1} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \bigcup \set {S_0 \times \set 0, S_1 \times \set 1} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \paren {S_0 \times \set 0} \cup \paren {S_1 \times \set 1} | c = }}

label: Definition:Disjoint Union (Set Theory)/Also known as
snippet: == Disjoint Union: Also known as == A disjoint union in the context of set theory is also called a discriminated union. In 's original words: We denote the uniting of many aggregates $M, N, P, \ldots$, which have no common elements, into a single aggregate by $\tuple {M, N, P, \ldots}$. The elements in this aggregate are, therefore, the elements of $M$, of $N$, of $P$, $\ldots$, taken together.

label: Definition:Disjoint Union (Set Theory)/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Disjoint Union (Set Theory) == The notations: $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ and $\ds \coprod_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ can also be seen for the disjoint union of a family of sets. When two sets are under consideration, the notation: $A \sqcup B$ or: $A \coprod B$ are usually used. Some sources use: $A \vee B$ The notations: $A + B$ or $A \oplus B$ are also encountered sometimes. This notation reflects the fact that, from the , the cardinality of the disjoint union is the sum of the cardinalities of the terms in the family.

label: Definition:Disjunction/General Definition
snippet: Let $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ be statements. The disjunction of $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ is defined as: $\ds \bigvee_{i \mathop = 1}^n \ p_i = \begin{cases} p_1 & : n = 1 \\ & \\ \ds \paren {\bigvee_{i \mathop = 1}^{n - 1} \ p_i} \lor p_n & : n > 1 \end{cases}$ That is: $\ds \bigvee_{i \mathop = 1}^n \ p_i = p_1 \lor p_2 \lor \cdots \lor p_{n - 1} \lor p_n$ In terms of the set $P = \set {p_1, \ldots, p_n}$ this can also be rendered: $\ds \bigvee P$ and is referred to as the disjunction of $P$.

label: Definition:Disk
snippet: A disk in the pure geometrical context is a circular region of the plane, which may or may not include its boundary.

label: Definition:Disk/Also defined as
snippet: == Disk: Also defined as == Many sources define a disk in the context of a general metric space as the set of points within a given distance of a given point. That is, with the definition that uses for ball. It needs to be appreciated that when the metric space in question is a Euclidean plane, the two definitions coincide. In fact, when the metric space in question is the complex plane, the term complex disk is used to mean the ball with the given radius and center.

label: Definition:Disk/Radius
snippet: The radius of a disk is the radius of the circle that forms its boundary.

label: Definition:Dispersion
snippet: Statistics: Dispersion Topology: Dispersion point

label: Definition:Dispersion (Statistics)
snippet: Let $S$ be a sample of a population in the context of statistics. The dispersion of $S$ is a general term meaning how much the data describing the sample are spread out. The word can also be applied to a random variable. Measures of dispersion include the following:

label: Definition:Dispersion Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a connected set in $T$ and let $p \in H$. Let $p \in H$ such that $H \setminus \set p$ is totally disconnected, where $\setminus$ denotes set difference. Then $p$ is a dispersion point of $H$.

label: Definition:Displacement
snippet: The (physical) displacement of a body is a measure of its position relative to a given point of reference in a particular frame of reference. Displacement is a vector quantity, so it specifies a magnitude and direction from the point of reference. In Cartesian coordinates, the direction is implicit, as it occurs as a result of the combined distances from the various axes of the frame of reference.

label: Definition:Dissection
snippet: A dissection is a partition of a geometric figure into two or more components.

label: Definition:Dissection Proof
snippet: A dissection proof is a proof in geometry that involves dissection of a geometric figure into multiple parts which can then be reassembled into a different geometric figure.

label: Definition:Distance
snippet: Complex Analysis: Distance between Complex Numbers Metric spaces: A distance function in a measure defining a metric space. The distance between sets is the minimum distance between elements in two subsets of a metric space. Metrical Geometry: The distance between two points $A$ and $B$ is the length of a line segment joining $A$ and $B$. The distance between two lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ in ordinary space is the length of the shortest line segment joining $L_1$ and $L_2$.

label: Definition:Distance-Preserving Mapping
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces, pseudometric spaces, or quasimetric spaces. Let $\phi: M_1 \to M_2$ be a mapping such that: $\forall a, b \in M_1: \map {d_1} {a, b} = \map {d_2} {\map \phi a, \map \phi b}$ Then $\phi$ is called a distance-preserving mapping.

label: Definition:Distance/Points/Complex Numbers
snippet: Let $x, y \in \C$ be complex numbers. Let $\cmod {x - y}$ be the complex modulus of $x - y$. Then the function $d: \C^2 \to \R$: $\map d {x, y} = \cmod {x - y}$ is called the distance between $x$ and $y$.

label: Definition:Distance/Points/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Let $\size {x - y}$ be the absolute value of $x - y$. Then the function $d: \R^2 \to \R$: $\map d {x, y} = \size {x - y}$ is called the distance between $x$ and $y$.

label: Definition:Distance/Sets/Metric Spaces
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $x \in A$. Let $S, T$ be subsets of $A$. The distance between $x$ and $S$ is defined and annotated $\ds \map d {x, S} = \inf_{y \mathop \in S} \paren {\map d {x, y} }$. The distance between $S$ and $T$ is defined and annotated $\ds \map d {S, T} = \inf_{\substack {x \mathop \in S \\ y \mathop \in T} } \paren {\map d {x, y} }$.

label: Definition:Distance/Sets/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $S, T$ be a subsets of the set of real numbers $\R$. Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The distance between $x$ and $S$ is defined and annotated $\ds \map d {x, S} = \map {\inf_{y \mathop \in S} } {\map d {x, y} }$, where $\map d {x, y}$ is the distance between $x$ and $y$. The distance between $S$ and $T$ is defined and annotated $\ds \map d {S, T} = \map {\inf_{\substack {x \mathop \in S \\ y \mathop \in T} } } {\map d {x, y} }$.

label: Definition:Distance (Geometry)
snippet: Distance, in the context of geometry, is a measure of the length of a line segment between a pair of objects.

label: Definition:Distance Function/Also defined as
snippet: == Distance Function: Also defined as == The term distance function is usually encountered at elementary level in the context solely of the metric space. However, as such abstract spaces proliferate with respect to the nature of its structure, it is convenient to reserve a term for the overall category into which this sort of mapping occurs. Hence the decision at to implement the term distance function for a mapping which is one of: .

label: Definition:Distance across Surface
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be points on a surface $\SS$. The distance from $A$ to $B$ across $S$ is defined as the length of the geodesic of $\SS$ between $A$ and $B$.

label: Definition:Distance between Point and Curve
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve, which may be either straight or curved. Let $P$ be a point not on $\CC$. The distance between $P$ and $\CC$ is the length of the shortest straight line segment that can be constructed between $\CC$ and $P$.

label: Definition:Distance between Point and Surface
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a surface, which may or may not be a plane. Let $P$ be a point not on $\SS$. The distance between $P$ and $\SS$ is the length of the shortest straight line segment that can be constructed between $\SS$ and $P$.

label: Definition:Distance between Points
snippet: The distance between two points $A$ and $B$ in space is defined as the length of a straight line segment that would be drawn from $A$ to $B$.

label: Definition:Distinct/Plural
snippet: Two objects $x$ and $y$ are distinct $x \ne y$. If $x$ and $y$ are distinct, then that means they can be distinguished, or identified as being different from each other.

label: Definition:Distinct/Plural/Pairwise Distinct
snippet: A set $S$ of objects is pairwise distinct : for each pair $\set {x, y} \subseteq S$ of elements of $S$, $x$ and $y$ are distinct. Category:Definitions/Set Theory Category:Definitions/Distinct

label: Definition:Distinct/Singular
snippet: Let $x \in S$ be an element of a set of objects $S$. Then: $x$ is distinguished from the other elements of $S$ $x$ is endowed with a property that the other elements of $S$ are specifically deemed not to possess. Such an element is identified as being distinct from the others.

label: Definition:Distinguished Element
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A distinguished element of $S$ is an element which is distinguished in some manner, by the imposition of some property or properties on $S$, from the other elements of $S$.

label: Definition:Distribution-Free Method/Limitations
snippet: == Distribution-Free Method: Limitations == Many distribution-free methods have analogues where the assumption is that the samples are from a given family of probability distributions. When that assumption is valid, the distribution-free tests are generally less efficient. However, a distribution-free test is often more efficient than a parametric test when those assumptions break down. A distribution-free method requires considerable computational power, which at one time was a serious problem. However, in the days of modern computer developments, this is not such a problem that it was.

label: Definition:Distribution Space
snippet: Let $\map \DD {\R^d}$ be the test function space. Let $T: \map \DD {\R^d} \to \C$ be a Schwartz distribution. Then the set of all $T$ is called the distribution space and is denoted by $\map {\DD'} {\R^d}$.

label: Definition:Distributional Derivative
snippet: Let $\phi \in \map \DD \R$ be a test function. Let $T \in \map {\DD'} \R$ be a Schwartz distribution. The distributional derivative $\dfrac {\d T} {\d x} \in \map {\DD'} \R$ is defined by: $\map {\dfrac {\d T} {\d x} } \phi := - \map T {\dfrac {\d \phi} {\d x}}$

label: Definition:Distributive Operation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set on which is defined two binary operations, defined on all the elements of $S \times S$, which we will denote as $\circ$ and $*$. The operation $\circ$ is distributive over $*$, or distributes over $*$, : $\circ$ is right distributive over $*$ and: $\circ$ is left distributive over $*$.

label: Definition:Distributive Operation/Distributand
snippet: Let $S$ be a set on which is defined two binary operations, defined on all the elements of $S \times S$, which we will denote as $\circ$ and $*$. Let $\circ$ be distributive over $*$. Then $*$ is a distributand of $\circ$.

label: Definition:Distributive Operation/Distributor
snippet: Let $S$ be a set on which is defined two binary operations, defined on all the elements of $S \times S$, which we will denote as $\circ$ and $*$. Let $\circ$ be distributive over $*$. Then $\circ$ is a distributor of $*$. Category:Definitions/Distributive Operations

label: Definition:Distributive Operation/Left
snippet: Let $S$ be a set on which is defined two binary operations, defined on all the elements of $S \times S$, denoted here as $\circ$ and $*$. The operation $\circ$ is left distributive over the operation $*$ : $\forall a, b, c \in S: a \circ \paren {b * c} = \paren {a \circ b} * \paren {a \circ c}$

label: Definition:Distributive Operation/Right
snippet: Let $S$ be a set on which is defined two binary operations, defined on all the elements of $S \times S$, denoted here as $\circ$ and $*$. The operation $\circ$ is right distributive over the operation $*$ : $\forall a, b, c \in S: \paren {a * b} \circ c = \paren {a \circ c} * \paren {b \circ c}$

label: Definition:Divergence Operator/Also known as
snippet: == Divergence Operator: Also known as == The divergence of a vector field $\mathbf V$ is usually vocalised div $\mathbf V$. Category:Definitions/Divergence Operator

label: Definition:Divergence Operator/Cartesian 3-Space
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of Cartesian $3$-space $\R^3$. Let $\map {\mathbf V} {x, y, z}$ be a vector field acting over $R$. The divergence of $\mathbf V$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = \operatorname {div} \mathbf V | o = := | r = \nabla \cdot \mathbf V }} {{eqn | r = \dfrac {\partial V_x} {\partial x} + \dfrac {\partial V_y} {\partial y} + \dfrac {\partial V_z} {\partial z} | c = }}

label: Definition:Divergence Operator/Geometrical Representation
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of space embedded in a Cartesian coordinate frame. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field acting over $R$. The divergence of $\mathbf V$ at a point $A$ in $R$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = \operatorname {div} \mathbf V | o = := | r = \nabla \cdot \mathbf V | c = }} {{eqn | r = \dfrac {\partial V_x} {\partial x} + \dfrac {\partial V_y} {\partial y} + \dfrac {\partial V_z} {\partial z} | c = }} where: $\nabla$ denotes the Del operator $\cdot$ denotes the dot product $V_x$, $V_y$ and $V_z$ denote the magnitudes of the components of $\mathbf V$ at $A$ in the directions of the…

label: Definition:Divergence Operator/Integral Form
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of space embedded in a Cartesian coordinate frame. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field acting over $R$. The divergence of $\mathbf V$ at a point $A$ in $R$ is defined as: $\ds \operatorname {div} \mathbf V := \lim_{\delta \tau \mathop \to 0} \dfrac {\int_S \mathbf V \cdot \d S} {\delta \tau}$ where: $S$ is the surface of a volume element $\delta \tau$ containing $A$ $\cdot$ denotes the dot product $\ds \int_S$ denotes the surface integral over $S$.

label: Definition:Divergence Operator/Physical Interpretation
snippet: Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field acting over a region of space $R$. The divergence of $\mathbf V$ at a point $P$ is the total flux away from $P$ per unit volume. It is a scalar field.

label: Definition:Divergence Operator/Riemannian Manifold/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold equipped with a metric $g$. Let $\mathbf X : \map {\CC^\infty} M \to \map {\CC^\infty} M$ be a smooth vector field. The divergence of $\mathbf X$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = \operatorname {div} \mathbf X | o = := | r = \nabla \cdot \mathbf X }} {{eqn | r = \star^{−1}_g \d_{\d R} \star_g \map g {\mathbf X} }} where: $\star_g$ is the Hodge star operator of $\struct {M, g}$ $\d_{\d R}$ is de Rham differential.

label: Definition:Divergence Operator/Riemannian Manifold/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an oriented Riemannian manifold. Let $\rd V_g$ be the volume form of $\struct {M, g}$. Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. Then the divergence of $X$, denoted by $\operatorname {div} X$, is defined by: $\paren {\operatorname {div} X} \rd V_g := \map d {X \mathop \lrcorner \rd V_g}$ where: $\lrcorner$ denotes interior multiplication $\map \rd {X \mathop \lrcorner \rd V_g}$ denotes the exterior derivative of $X \mathop \lrcorner \rd V_g$.

label: Definition:Divergent Product/Divergence to Zero
snippet: Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a valued field. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of elements of $\mathbb K$. If either: there exist infinitely many $n \in \N$ with $a_n = 0$ there exists $n_0 \in \N$ with $a_n \ne 0$ for all $n > n_0$ and the sequence of partial products of $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = n_0 + 1}^\infty a_n$ converges to $0$ the product diverges to $0$, and we assign the value: $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n = 0$ Category:Definitions/Divergent Products Category:Definitions/Infinite Products

label: Definition:Divergent Sequence
snippet: A sequence which is not convergent is divergent.

label: Definition:Divergent Series
snippet: A series which is not convergent is divergent.

Let $\map \phi {\bar x, \bar b}$ be an $\LL$-formula with free variables $\bar x$ and parameters $\bar b$ from the universe of $\mathfrak C$. Let $\map {\operatorname{tp} } {\bar b / A}$ denote the type of $\bar b$ over $A$.

label: Definition:Divisibility/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Divisibility == The concept of divisibility has been studied for over $3000$ years. From before the time of , the ancient Greeks were considering questions about: odd and even numbers perfect numbers amicable numbers prime numbers as well as many others. Even today, some of those questions remain unanswered.

label: Definition:Divisible Abelian Group
snippet: Let $\struct{A, +}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct{A, +, \circ}$ be the $\Z$-module associated with $A$. Then $\struct{A, +}$ is a divisible abelian group $\struct{A, +, \circ}$ is a divisible $\Z$-module. Category:Definitions/Group Theory Category:Definitions/Abelian Groups

label: Definition:Divisible Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be a left $R$-module. Let $M$ be such that: for all $m \in M$ for all non zero divisors $r \in R$ there exists some $m' \in M$ such that $r m' = m$. Then $M$ is a divisible module.

label: Definition:Division
snippet: The concept of division can be defined in the following ways, according to context:

label: Definition:Division/Field/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, +, \times}$ be the field of real numbers. The operation of division is defined on $\R$ as: $\forall a, b \in \R \setminus \set 0: a / b := a \times b^{-1}$ where $b^{-1}$ is the multiplicative inverse of $b$ in $\R$.

label: Definition:Division/Standard Number Field
snippet: The concept of division over a field is usually seen in the context of the standard number fields:

label: Definition:Division Product
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\struct {U_R, \circ}$ be the group of units of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$. Then we define the following notation: $\forall x \in U_R, y \in R$, we have: $\dfrac y x := y \circ \paren {x^{-1} } = \paren {x^{-1} } \circ y$ $\dfrac y x$ is a division product, and $\dfrac y x$ is voiced $y$ divided by $x$. We also write (out of space considerations) $y / x$ for $\dfrac y x$. This notation is usually used when $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is a field.

label: Definition:Division Ring/Definition 2
snippet: A division ring is a ring with unity $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ such that: $\forall x \in R^*: \exists! x^{-1} \in R^*: x^{-1} \circ x = x \circ x^{-1} = 1_R$ where $R^*$ denotes the set of elements of $R$ without the ring zero $0_R$, that is: $R^* = R \setminus \set {0_R}$ That is, every non-zero element of $R$ has a (unique) non-zero product inverse.

label: Definition:Division Ring/Definition 3
snippet: A division ring is a ring with unity $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ such that: Every non-zero element of $R$ is a unit.

label: Definition:Division Ring/Definition 4
snippet: A division ring is a ring with unity $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ such that: $R$ has no proper elements.

label: Definition:Division Subring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. A division subring of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is a subset $S$ of $R$ such that $\struct {S, +_S, \circ_S}$ is a division ring.

label: Definition:Division in Ratio
snippet: Let a quantity $X$ be partitioned into parts which are in a given ratio to one another. Then $X$ is divided in (the given) ratio.

label: Definition:Division in Ratio/Straight Line
snippet: Let $A$, $B$ and $P$ be collinear points. Then: $P$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $m : n$ $AP : PB = m : n$ where $AP$ and $PB$ are directed line segments.

label: Definition:Division in Ratio/Straight Line/External
snippet: Let $A$, $B$ and $P$ be collinear points. Let $P$ not lie between $A$ and $B$. Then $P$ divides $AB$ externally in the ratio $\size m : \size n$ $AP : PB = m : n$ and the ratio $m : n$ is negative.

label: Definition:Division in Ratio/Straight Line/Internal
snippet: Let $A$, $B$ and $P$ be collinear points. Let $P$ lie between $A$ and $B$. Then $P$ divides $AB$ internally in the ratio $m : n$ $AP : PB = m : n$ and the ratio $m : n$ is positive.

label: Definition:Division of Line Segment
snippet: Let $AB$ be a line segment. A division is the construction of a point $E$ on the straight line containing $AB$ such that $AE : EB$ is a specified ratio. There are two types of division of a line segment:

label: Definition:Divisor-Finite Monoid
snippet: Let $\struct {M, *}$ be a monoid. Then $M$ is divisor-finite for all $m \in M$ the set: $\set {\tuple {x, y} \in M^2 : x*y = m}$ is finite.

label: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Integer
snippet: Let $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ be the ring of integers. Let $x, y \in \Z$. Then $x$ is a divisor of $y$ is defined as: $x \divides y \iff \exists t \in \Z: y = t \times x$

label: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Integer/Aliquant Part
snippet: An aliquant part of an integer $n$ is a positive integer which is less than $n$ but is not a divisor of $n$.

label: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Integer/Aliquot Part
snippet: An aliquot part of an integer $n$ is a divisor of $n$ which is strictly not equal to $n$.

label: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Real Number
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $x, y \in \R$. Then $x$ divides $y$ is defined as: $x \divides y \iff \exists t \in \Z: y = t \times x$ where $\Z$ is the set of integers. That is, that $y$ is an integer multiple of $x$.

label: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Ring with Unity
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be an ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $x, y \in D$. We define the term $x$ divides $y$ in $R$ as follows: $x \mathrel {\divides_R} y \iff \exists t \in R: y = t \circ x$ When no ambiguity results, the subscript is usually dropped, and $x$ divides $y$ in $R$ is just written $x \divides y$.

label: Definition:Divisor (Algebra)/Terminology
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \times}$ be a ring. Let $x, y \in R$. Let $x \divides y$ denote that $x$ is a divisor of $y$. Then the following terminology can be used: $x$ divides $y$ $y$ is a multiple of $x$ $y$ is divisible by $x$. In the field of Euclidean geometry, in particular: $x$ measures $y$. To indicate that $x$ does not divide $y$, we write $x \nmid y$.

label: Definition:Divisor Count Function
snippet: Let $n$ be an integer such that $n \ge 1$. The divisor count function is defined on $n$ as being the total number of positive integer divisors of $n$. It is denoted on as $\sigma_0$ (the Greek letter sigma). That is: $\ds \map {\sigma_0} n = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} 1$ where $\ds \sum_{d \mathop \divides n}$ is the sum over all divisors of $n$.

label: Definition:Divisor Sum Function
snippet: Let $n$ be an integer such that $n \ge 1$. The divisor sum function $\map {\sigma_1} n$ is defined on $n$ as being the sum of all the positive integer divisors of $n$. That is: $\ds \map {\sigma_1} n = \sum_{d \mathop \divides n} d$ where $\ds \sum_{d \mathop \divides n}$ is the sum over all divisors of $n$.

label: Definition:Divisor Topology
snippet: Let $S = \set {x \in \Z: x \ge 2}$ denote the set of integers greater than $1$. Let $\BB$ be the set of all sets $U_n$ defined for all $n \ge 2$ as: $U_n = \set {x \in \Z_{>0}: x \divides n}$ where $\divides$ denotes the divisor relation. Then $\BB$ is the basis for a topology $\tau$ on $S$. Then $\tau$ is referred to as the divisor topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the divisor space.

label: Definition:Divisor of Polynomial
snippet: Let $D$ be an integral domain. Let $D \sqbrk x$ be the polynomial ring in one variable over $D$. Let $f, g \in D \sqbrk x$ be polynomials. Then: $f$ divides $g$ $f$ is a divisor of $g$ $g$ is divisible by $f$ $\exists h \in D \sqbrk x : g = f h$ This is denoted: $f \divides g$

label: Definition:Dodeca-/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Use of Dodeca- == The prefix dodeca- can be found in the following contexts: dodecagon: a polygon with $12$ sides and hence $12$ vertices dodecahedron: a polyhedron with $12$ faces Category:Definitions/Number Prefixes

label: Definition:Dodecagon/Regular
snippet: A regular dodecagon is a dodecagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with $12$ sides. That is, a dodecagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: 300px

label: Definition:Dodecahedron/Regular
snippet: A regular dodecahedron is a dodecahedron whose $12$ faces are all congruent regular pentagons. It has: $12$ faces $30$ edges $20$ vertices.

label: Definition:Domain
snippet: Set theory: The concept of domain in the contexts of mapping theory, relation theory and abstract algebra. The domain of a variable. Category theory The concept of domain. Abstract algebra: The concept of integral domain in ring theory. Analysis: Domain: another term for an open region.

label: Definition:Domain (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $f: X \to Y$ be a morphism. Then the domain of $f$ is defined to be the object $X$. This is usually denoted $X = \Dom f$ or $X = \map D f$.

label: Definition:Domain (Set Theory)/Binary Operation
snippet: Let $\circ: S \times S \to T$ be a binary operation. The domain of $\circ$ is the set $S$ and can be denoted $\Dom \circ$. This definition can be considered as the same as that for the domain of a mapping, where the domain would be defined as $S \times S$. Category:Definitions/Abstract Algebra

label: Definition:Domain (Set Theory)/Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. The domain of $f$ is $S$, and can be denoted $\Dom f$.

label: Definition:Domain (Set Theory)/Relation/General Definition
snippet: Let $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ be the cartesian product of sets $S_1$ to $S_n$. Let $\ds \RR \subseteq \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ be an $n$-ary relation on $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$. The domain of $\RR$ is the set defined as: $\ds \Dom \RR := \set {\tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n - 1} } \in \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^{n - 1} S_i: \exists s_n \in S_n: \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in \RR}$ The concept is usually encountered when $\RR$ is an endorelation on $S$: $\ds \Dom \RR := \set {\tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n - 1} } \in S^{n - 1}: \exists s_n \in S_n: \tuple {s_1, s_2,…

label: Definition:Domain of Exponential Map
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g, \nabla}$ be a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold without boundary endowed with the Levi-Civita connection. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $v \in T_p M$. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be an open real interval. Let $\gamma_v : I \to M$ be the unique maximal geodesic such that: $\map {\gamma '} 0 = v$ where $\gamma'$ is the velocity of $\gamma$. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$.

label: Definition:Domain of Relation/Also defined as
snippet: It is usual, as here, to define the domain of $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ as the subset of $S$ that bears some element of $S$ to $T$. However, it appears to make sense to define it to be the whole of the set $S$. Using this definition, $s \in \Dom \RR$ whether or not $\exists t \in T: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR$. It would then be possible to refer to $\set {s \in S: \exists t \in T: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR}$ as the preimage of $\RR$. This appears never to be done in the literature that has so far been studied as source work for .

label: Definition:Dominate (Analysis)
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence in $\R$. Let $\sequence {z_n}$ be a sequence in $\C$. Then $\sequence {a_n}$ dominates $\sequence {z_n}$ : $\forall n \in \N: \cmod {z_n} \le a_n$ Category:Definitions/Analysis Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis

label: Definition:Dominate (Set Theory)
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets.

label: Definition:Dominate (Set Theory)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Then $S$ is dominated by $T$ there exists an injection from $S$ to $T$. The notation $S \preccurlyeq T$ is used to indicate that $S$ dominates $T$.

label: Definition:Dominate (Set Theory)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Then $S$ is dominated by $T$ $S$ is equivalent to some subset of $T$. That is, there exists a bijection $f: S \to T'$ for some $T' \subseteq T$. The notation $S \preccurlyeq T$ is used to indicate that $S$ dominates $T$.

label: Definition:Dominate (Set Theory)/Strictly Dominate
snippet: Let $S, T$ be sets. $S$ is strictly dominated by set $T$ $S \preccurlyeq T$ but $\neg T \preccurlyeq S$. This can be written $S \prec T$ or $S < T$. Category:Definitions/Set Theory

label: Definition:Domino
snippet: A domino is a $2$-omino: 200px That is, it is a polyomino consisting of exactly $2$ unit squares.

label: Definition:Dominoes
snippet: Dominoes are a set of (usually) wooden tiles: in the shape of an oblong $2$ units by $1$ unit (of the order of an inch) with two numbers, usually in the form of dots, usually between $0$ and $6$, one at each end, divided by a line between them, on one side only such that each of the numbers appears paired with every number (including itself) exactly once such that the opposite sides of the dominoes are unmarked so as to make them indistinguishable when upside down (although of course they may have a pretty design on them).

label: Definition:Dominoes/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Domino == The singular of dominoes is domino. Note that in the field of recreational mathematics, the term domino may in fact be used just for the $2$-by-$1$ oblong shape, in its context of being two squares joined together by an edge. An older meaning of the word domino is a carnival costume featuring a black robe and a mask, often white, that covers the eyes. It is supposed that the name of the game dominoes may have derived from the carnival costume meaning. Category:Linguistic Notes

label: Definition:Dominoes/Pips
snippet: The dots on the faces of a set of dominoes are usually referred to as pips.

label: Definition:Dot Product
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $n$ dimensions: {{eqn | l = \mathbf a | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n a_k \mathbf e_k }} {{eqn | l = \mathbf b | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n b_k \mathbf e_k }} where $\tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$.

label: Definition:Dot Product/Also known as
snippet: == Dot Product: Also known as == The dot product is also known as: The scalar product (but this can be confused with multiplication by a scalar so is less recommended) The standard inner product. Some sources refer to it as just the inner product, but this is a more general term of which the dot product is merely an example. The symbol used for the dot is variously presented; another version is $\mathbf a \bullet \mathbf b$, which can be preferred if there is ambiguity between the dot product and standard multiplication.

label: Definition:Dot Product/Complex
snippet: Let $z_1 := x_1 + i y_1$ and $z_2 := x_2 + i y_2$ be complex numbers.

label: Definition:Dot Product/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $z_1 := x_1 + i y_1$ and $z_2 := x_2 + i y_2$ be complex numbers. The dot product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \circ z_2 = x_1 x_2 + y_1 y_2$

label: Definition:Dot Product/Complex/Definition 3
snippet: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be complex numbers. The dot product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \circ z_2 := \map \Re {\overline {z_1} z_2}$ where: $\map \Re z$ denotes the real part of a complex number $z$ $\overline {z_1}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z_1$ $\overline {z_1} z_2$ denotes complex multiplication.

label: Definition:Dot Product/Complex/Definition 4
snippet: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be complex numbers. The dot product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \circ z_2 := \dfrac {\overline {z_1} z_2 + z_1 \overline {z_2} } 2$ where: $\overline {z_1}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z_1$ $\overline {z_1} z_2$ denotes complex multiplication.

label: Definition:Dot Product/General Context
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $n$ dimensions: {{eqn | l = \mathbf a | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n a_k \mathbf e_k }} {{eqn | l = \mathbf b | r = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n b_k \mathbf e_k }} where $\tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$.

label: Definition:Double-Headed Coin
snippet: A double-headed coin is an extreme example of a biased coin such that instead of a head and a tail, both sides are heads. Hence: the probability of landing heads is $1$ the probability of landing tails is $0$.

label: Definition:Double Centralizer Generated by Element of C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $c \in A$. Define $L_c : A \to A$ and $R_c : A \to A$ by: $\map {L_c} a = c a$ and: $\map {R_c} a = a c$ for each $a \in A$. We say that $\tuple {L_c, R_c}$ is the double centralizer generated by $c$.

label: Definition:Double Centralizer of C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $L, R : A \to A$ be bounded linear transformations such that: $\map L {a b} = \map L a b$ $\map R {a b} = a \map R b$ $\map R a b = a \map L b$ for each $a, b \in A$. We call $\tuple {L, R}$ a double centralizer for $A$.

label: Definition:Double Factorial
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer.

label: Definition:Double Pointed Countable Complement Topology on Real Numbers
snippet: == Example of Double Pointed Topology == A particular example of a double pointed topology is the topological space $T \times D$ where: {{item||$T \struct {\R, \tau}$ is the countable complement space on the real numbers $\R$}} {{item||$D \struct {\set {0, 1}, \set {\O, \set {0, 1} } }$ is the indiscrete space on $\set {0, 1}$.}}

label: Definition:Double Pointed Topology
snippet: Let $T_S = \struct {S, \tau_S}$ be a topological space. Let $A = \set {a, b}$ be a doubleton. Let $D = \struct {A, \set {\O, A} }$ be the indiscrete space on $A$. Let $\struct {T_S \times D, \tau}$ be the product space of $T_S$ and $D$. Then: $\tau$ is known as the double pointed topology on $T_S$ $\struct {T_S \times D, \tau}$ is known as the double pointed space on $T_S$. It is seen that $T_S \times D$ is conceptually equivalent to taking the space $T_S$ and replacing each point with a pair of topologically indistinguishable points.

label: Definition:Double Precision
snippet: A number is held in a digital computer to double precision it uses $2$ blocks to hold it.

label: Definition:Doubleton
snippet: A doubleton is a set that contains exactly two elements. The doubleton containing the distinct elements $a$ and $b$ can be written $\set {a, b}$. The set $\set {a, b}$ is known as the doubleton of $a$ and $b$.

label: Definition:Doubleton/Class Theory
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be sets. The class $\set {a, b}$ is a doubleton (class). It is defined as the class of all $x$ such that $x = a$ or $x = b$: $\set {a, b} = \set {x: x = a \lor x = b: a \ne b}$

label: Definition:Down Run
snippet: A down run is a run such that the sequence is decreasing.

label: Definition:Dozen
snippet: A dozen is another name for a set whose cardinality is $12$.

label: Definition:Drag
snippet: Drag is defined as the resistance to motion of a body $B$ through a fluid $F$. The amount of drag depends on: the velocity of $B$ the size and shape of $B$ the density and viscosity of $F$. There is no adequate formula for drag which can be applied in every situation.

label: Definition:Drift Velocity of Electrons
snippet: In an electrical conductor, some of the electrons are more or less free to move between atoms. In a state of electric neutrality, such electrons move randomly. Under the influence of a potential difference, the electrons are influenced to move in a direction towards positive charge and away from negative charge. So, while the electrons are still moving in all directions at random, there is a tendency for the motion to drift towards the positive. The drift velocity is defined as the mean velocity of all the electrons within a given volume.

label: Definition:Dual Code
snippet: Let $C$ be a binary linear code of length $n$. The dual code to $C$ is the set of all binary strings $b_1 b_2 \cdots b_n$ such that: $a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + \cdots + a_n b_n = 0 \pmod 2$ for all codewords $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ in $C$.

label: Definition:Dual Elements
snippet: In the context of geometry, dual elements are types of object such that one type of object has a specific connection with the other type of object.

label: Definition:Dual Elements/Plane Geometry
snippet: In the context of plane geometry, dual elements are: straight lines, which can be defined by two points points, which can be defined by the intersection of two straight lines.

label: Definition:Dual Elements/Solid Geometry
snippet: In the context of solid geometry, dual elements are: planes, which can be defined by two straight lines points, which can be defined by the intersection of two straight lines.

label: Definition:Dual Graph
snippet: Let $G$ be a planar graph. The dual graph to $G$ is a planar graph $G^*$ created from $G$ as follows: $(1): \quad$ Inside every face of $G$, place a vertex of $G^*$. $(2): \quad$ For every edge of $G$ separating two faces of $G$, construct an edge of $G^*$ incident with the vertices of $G^*$ corresponding to those two faces. Then $G^*$ is the dual graph to $G$.

label: Definition:Dual Mapping
snippet: Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces. Let $V^*$ and $W^*$ denote the algebraic dual of $V$ and $W$ respectively. Let $T: V \to W$ be a linear transformation from $V$ to $W$. Let $T^*: V^* \to W^*$ be the mapping from $V^*$ to $W^*$ defined as: $\forall \phi \in W^*: \forall v \in V: \map {\paren {T^* \phi} } v = \map \phi {T v}$ Then $T^*$ is known as the dual (mapping) of $T$.

label: Definition:Dual Matroid
snippet: Let $M = \struct {S, \mathscr I}$ be a matroid. Let $\mathscr B$ be the set of bases of the matroid $M$. The dual of $M$, denoted $M^* = \struct{S, \mathscr I^*}$, is the matroid whose bases is the set: $\mathscr B^* = \set{S \setminus B : B \in \mathscr B}$

label: Definition:Dual Operations
snippet: In the context of geometry, dual operations are types of operation such that one type of operation has a specific connection with the other type of operation.

label: Definition:Dual Operations/Plane Geometry
snippet: In the context of plane geometry, dual operations are: the connection of two points to define a straight line the intersection of two straight lines to define a point.

label: Definition:Dual Ordering/Notation
snippet: To denote the dual of an ordering, the conventional technique is to reverse the symbol. Thus: $\succeq$ denotes $\preceq^{-1}$ $\succcurlyeq$ denotes $\preccurlyeq^{-1}$ $\curlyeqsucc$ denotes $\curlyeqprec^{-1}$ and so: $a \preceq b \iff b \succeq a$ $a \preccurlyeq b \iff b \succcurlyeq a$ $a \curlyeqprec b \iff b \curlyeqsucc a$ Similarly for the standard symbols used to denote an ordering on numbers: $\ge$ denotes $\le^{-1}$ $\geqslant$ denotes $\leqslant^{-1}$ $\eqslantgtr$ denotes $\eqslantless^{-1}$ and so on.

label: Definition:Dual Ordering/Strict/Notation
snippet: To denote the dual of an strict ordering, the conventional technique is to reverse the symbol. Thus: $\succ$ denotes $\prec^{-1}$ and so: $a \prec b \iff b \succ a$ Similarly for the standard symbol used to denote a strict ordering on numbers: $>$ denotes $<^{-1}$ and so on.

label: Definition:Dual Statements
snippet: In the context of geometry, dual statements are statements in which: the name of each object is replaced by its dual element each operation is replaced by its dual operation.

label: Definition:Dual System
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $E$ and $F$ be vector spaces over $K$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot : E \times F \to K$ be a bilinear mapping. We say that the tuple $\tuple {E, F, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ is a dual system over $K$ : {{item||$\innerprod {x_0} y {\mathbf 0}_K$ for all $y \in F$ implies that $x_0 {\mathbf 0}_E$}} {{item||$\innerprod x {y_0} {\mathbf 0}_K$ for all $x \in E$ implies that $y_0 {\mathbf 0}_F$}} The dual system $\tuple {E, F, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ is frequently denoted as $\innerprod E F$.

label: Definition:Duality (Geometry)
snippet: Duality in the context of geometry is a property that conceptually connects types of object with other types of object.

label: Definition:Duality (Geometry)/Plane Geometry
snippet: In the context of plane geometry, the straight line and the point are dual elements: a straight line can be defined by two points a point can be defined by the intersection of two straight lines.

label: Definition:Duality (Geometry)/Solid Geometry
snippet: In the context of solid geometry, the plane and the point are dual elements: a plane can be defined by two straight lines a point can be defined by the intersection of two straight lines.

label: Definition:Dudeney Number
snippet: A Dudeney number is a natural number which is equal to the sum of the digits of its cube when expressed in decimal notation.

label: Definition:Duodecimal Notation/Symbols
snippet: In order to be able to represent numbers in a duodecimal system conveniently and readably, it is necessary to render the digits $10$ and $11$ using single characters. The following techniques accomplish this: $\mathrm T$ and $\mathrm E$ that is, the initial letters of ten and eleven. $\mathrm A$ and $\mathrm B$ Hence this is consistent with the common form for hexadecimal notation. $\mathrm X$ and $\mathrm E$ This was the suggestion from the Duodecimal Society in $1944$.

label: Definition:Duodecimal System/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Duodecimal System == A $12$-based system is easier than a $10$-based system to divide into thirds, quarters and sixths. This partly offsets the clear advantage of a $10$-based system that it makes it easy to use the fingers for counting. Hence the duodecimal system has been suggested several times during the course of history to replace the decimal system as the basis of a universal counting system. , in describing his ideal state, determined that the system of coinage and weights and measures should be based on a duodecimal system.

label: Definition:Dyad
snippet: A dyad is an instance of the number $2$.

label: Definition:Dyadic Rational
snippet: A dyadic rational is a rational number whose denominator, when expressed in canonical form, is an integral power of $2$. That is, $a \in \Q$ is dyadic : $\exists p \in \Z, q \in \Z_{>0}: a = \dfrac p {2^q}$

label: Definition:Dynamic Equilibrium
snippet: A body $B$ is in dynamic equilibrium : $B$ is moving with constant (non-zero) velocity the vector sum of all the forces acting upon $B$ is zero.

label: Definition:Dynamical System
snippet: A dynamical system is a nonlinear system in which a function describes the time dependence of a point in a geometrical space $X$. It is an iterative procedure consisting of: a mapping $T$ of a $X$ onto itself and: an iteration $x_{n + 1} = \map T {x_n}$. Hence positions of points in $X$ evolve iteratively under $T$.

label: Definition:Dynamical System/Flow
snippet: In a dynamical system, a set of time-dependent equations is known as flow.

label: Definition:Dynamical System/Orbit
snippet: Let $S$ be a dynamical system consisting of a mapping $T$ and iteration $x_{n + 1} = \map T {x_n}$. The orbit of $x_0$ is the set of points $\set {x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots}$ When $T$ is invertible, the orbit usually includes the points $x_{-1} = \inv T x, x_{-2} = \inv T {x_{-1} }, \ldots$ For a flow, the orbit of a point $x$ is the union of all the points $\map x t$ for all $t$.

label: Definition:Dynamical Systems
snippet: Dynamical systems is a branch of mathematics which studies the long-term behavior of a state space that evolves in time according to a prescribed rule. A dynamical system can be viewed as a tuple $(T, X, f)$ where $T$ is a semigroup that represents time, $X$ is the underlying state space, and $f:T\times X\to X$ is a semigroup action that describes the rule. Typically, $T$ is commutative, $X$ is a topological space, and $f$ is a continuous map.

label: Definition:Dynamical Systems Theory
snippet: Dynamical systems theory is the branch of mathematics which studies dynamical systems.

label: Definition:Dynamics/Also defined as
snippet: == Dynamics: Also defined as == Some sources treat kinematics as a separate branch of classical mechanics, while handling dynamics and kinetics as the same thing.

label: Definition:Dynkin System
snippet: Let $X$ be a set, and let $\DD \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Then $\DD$ is called a Dynkin system (on $X$) it satisfies the following conditions: {{item|(3):|For all pairwise disjoint sequences $\sequence {D_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $\DD$, $\ds \bigcup_{n \mathop \in \N} D_n \in \DD$}}

label: Definition:Dynkin System Generated by Collection of Subsets
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\GG \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Then the Dynkin system generated by $\GG$, denoted $\map \delta \GG$, is the smallest Dynkin system on $X$ that contains $\GG$. That is, $\map \delta \GG$ is subject to: $(1):\quad \GG \subseteq \map \delta \GG$ $(2):\quad \GG \subseteq \DD \implies \map \delta \GG \subseteq \DD$ for any Dynkin system $\DD$ on $X$ In fact, $\map \delta \GG$ always exists, and is unique, as proved on Existence and Uniqueness of Dynkin System Generated by Collection of Subsets.

label: Definition:EMV Algorithm
snippet: The emv algorithm proceeds as follows. Let a decision tree be complete with all payoffs and probabilities of probabilistic outcomes known. Determine the expected monetary value for each of the chance nodes, starting with the payoffs. At each decision node, the player takes the decision which maximizes the expected monetary value.

label: Definition:Ear
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. Let $A, B, C$ be vertices of $P$ such that $\angle BAC$ is an internal angle of the vertex $A$. Let $BC$ be a chord of $P$. Then the triangle $\triangle ABC$ is an ear of $P$.

label: Definition:Earth
snippet: Earth is the planet on which we live. It is the third planet of the solar system from the sun. Its orbit lies between those of Venus and Mars.

label: Definition:Earthworm Sequence
snippet: The earthworm sequence is the integer sequence $\sequence {h_n}$ defined as follows. Let $h: \Z \to \Z$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall a \in \Z: \map h a = 2 a \pmod {100}$ Then: $h_n = \begin {cases} x: x \in \set {10, 11, \dotsc, 99} & : n = 0 \\ \map h {n - 1} & : n > 0 \end {cases}$ That is: $h_0$ is an arbitrary integer between $10$ and $99$ $h_n$ is the result of multiplying the previous term in the sequence by $2$ and keeping only the last two digits.

label: Definition:Earthworm Sequence/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Earthworm Sequence == The earthworm sequence was invented by , and appears in his $1991$ work . His interest is specifically in whether each of the integers selected for $h_1$ ever returns to its starting point. He fails to document the details of what happens for $h_0 = 50$. The only reason this sequence appears here is because prime.mover found a piece of paper with his analysis on it in a big pile of material which is in the process of being recycled.

label: Definition:East Point of Horizon
snippet: Let an observer $O$ be facing the north point of the horizon $N$, facing directly away from the south point of the horizon $S$. Let the celestial equator meet the celestial horizon at the points $E$ and $W$. Let $E$ be the point on the right of $O$. This is called the east point of the horizon. 480px In the above diagram, the east point of the horizon is indicated by $E$.

label: Definition:Eastern Hemisphere
snippet: The eastern hemisphere of Earth is the hemisphere immediately to the east of the prime meridian. Points in the eastern hemisphere have longitude between $0 \degrees \, \mathrm E$ (the prime meridian itself) and $180 \degrees \, \mathrm E$.

label: Definition:Eccentric/Circles
snippet: Circles are said to be eccentric if their centers are at different points. 320px Circles $K_1$ and $K_2$, whose centers are $C_1$ and $C_2$, are eccentric.

label: Definition:Eccentric/Ellipses
snippet: Ellipses are said to be eccentric if their centers are at different points. 320px Ellipses $E_1$ and $E_2$, whose centers are $C_1$ and $C_2$, are eccentric.

label: Definition:Eccentric Angle
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a central conic. Let $P$ be a point on $\KK$. Let $\CC$ be the auxiliary circle of $\KK$. The eccentric angle of $P$ $\KK$ is defined as follows:

label: Definition:Eccentric Angle/Ellipse
snippet: Let $\KK$ be an ellipse with foci at $F_1$ and $F_2$. Let $P$ be a point on $\KK$. Let $\CC$ be the auxiliary circle of $\KK$ with center $O$. Let $PQ$ be dropped perpendicular to the major axis $F_1 F_2$ of $\KK$ such that $Q$ lies on $F_1 F_2$. Let $QP$ be produced so as to meet $\CC$ at $P'$. The angle $QOP'$ is the eccentric angle of $P$ $\KK$. 480px In the above diagram, $\alpha$ is the eccentric angle of $P$ $\KK$.

label: Definition:Eccentric Angle/Hyperbola
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a hyperbola with foci at $F_1$ and $F_2$. Let $P$ be a point on $\KK$. Let $\CC$ be the auxiliary circle of $\KK$ with center $O$. Let $PQ$ be dropped perpendicular to the major axis $F_1 F_2$ of $\KK$ such that $Q$ lies on $F_1 F_2$. Let $QP'$ be drawn tangent to $\CC$ such that $P'$ is the point of tangency with $\CC$. The angle $QOP'$ is the eccentric angle of $P$ $\KK$. 480px In the above diagram, $\alpha$ is the eccentric angle of $P$ $\KK$.

label: Definition:Eccentric Circle of Central Conic/Ellipse
snippet: Let $\KK$ be an ellipse whose center is at $O$. The eccentric circles of $\KK$ are the two circles whose center is at $O$ and whose diameter coincides with either the major axis of $\KK$ or the minor axis of $\KK$. 480px

label: Definition:Eccentric Circle of Central Conic/Hyperbola
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a hyperbola whose center is at $O$. The eccentric circles of $\KK$ are the two circles whose center is at $O$ and whose diameter coincides with either the major axis of $\KK$ or the minor axis of $\KK$. 480px

label: Definition:Eccentricity
snippet: Analytic Geometry: Eccentricity of Conic Section Graph Theory: Eccentricity of Vertex

label: Definition:Eccentricity of Conic Section/Also denoted as
snippet: == Eccentricity: Also denoted as == Some sources use $\epsilon$ for the eccentricity of a conic section. Category:Definitions/Conic Sections

label: Definition:Eccentricity of Ellipse/Shape
snippet: The eccentricity of an ellipse determines its shape: 610px In the above: the semiminor axis $b$ is kept constant and arbitrarily allocated a length of $1$ the linear eccentricity $c$ is varied from $1$ to $4$ the eccentricity is calculated using Eccentricity of Ellipse in terms of Semiminor Axis and Linear Eccentricity as: $e = \dfrac c {\sqrt {b^2 + c^2} }$ As can be seen, the greater $e$ is, the longer the ellipse its width.

label: Definition:Echelon Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Echelon Matrix: Also known as == An echelon matrix and a matrix in echelon form are the same thing. A matrix in echelon form is also sometimes seen as being in row echelon form. The definition of column echelon form is directly analogous.
