label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/19 - Axis of Cone
snippet: The axis of the cone is the straight line which remains fixed and about which the triangle is turned.

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/21 - Cylinder
snippet: When, one side of those about the right angle in a rectangular parallelogram remaining fixed, the parallelogram is carried round and restored again to the same position from which it began to be moved, the figure so comprehended is a cylinder.

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/25 - Cube
snippet: A cube is a solid figure contained by six equal squares.

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/3 - Line at Right Angles to Plane
snippet: A straight line is at right angles to a plane when it makes right angles with all the straight lines which meet it and are in the plane.

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/4 - Plane at Right Angles to Plane
snippet: A plane is at right angles to a plane when the straight lines drawn, in one of the planes, at right angles to the common section of the planes are at right angles to the remaining plane.

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/5 - Inclination of Straight Line
snippet: The inclination of a straight line to a plane is, assuming a perpendicular drawn from the extremity of the straight line which is elevated above the plane to the plane, and a straight line joined from the point thus arising to the extremity of the straight line which is in the plane, the angle contained by the straight line so drawn and the straight line standing up.

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/6 - Inclination of Plane
snippet: The inclination of a plane to a plane is the acute angle contained by the straight lines drawn at right angles to the common section at the same point, one in each of the planes.

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book XI/7 - Similarly Inclined
snippet: A plane is said to be similarly inclined to a plane as another is to another when the said angles of the inclinations are equal to one another.

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (II)/1 - First Binomial
snippet: Given a rational straight line and a binomial, divided into its terms, such that the square on the greater term is greater than the square on the lesser by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the greater, then, if the greater term be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, let the whole be called a first binomial straight line;

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (II)/4 - Fourth Binomial
snippet: Again, if the square on the greater term be greater than the square on the lesser by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with the greater, then, if the greater term be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, let the whole be called a fourth binomial;

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (III)/1 - First Apotome
snippet: Given a rational straight line and an apotome, if the square on the whole be greater than the square on the annex by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the whole, and the whole be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, let the apotome be called a first apotome.

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (III)/2 - Second Apotome
snippet: But if the annex be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, and the square on the whole be greater than that on the annex by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with the whole, let the apotome be called a second apotome.

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (III)/3 - Third Apotome
snippet: But if neither be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, and the square on the whole be greater than the square on the annex by the square on a straight line commensurable with the whole, let the apotome be called a third apotome.

label: Definition:Euclid's Definitions - Book X (III)/4 - Fourth Apotome
snippet: Again, if the square on the whole be greater than the square on the annex by the square on a straight line incommensurable with the whole, then, if the whole be commensurable in length with the rational straight line set out, let the apotome be called a fourth apotome;

label: Definition:Euclid Number
snippet: A Euclid number is a natural number of the form: $E_n := p_n\# + 1$ where $p_n\#$ is the primorial of the $n$th prime number.

label: Definition:Euclid Number/Also defined as
snippet: == Euclid Numbers: Also known as == The term Euclid number is also used by some sources to denote an even perfect number. On , the term Euclidean number is preferred for that concept.

label: Definition:Euclid Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euclid Number == The name Euclid number derives from 's proof of the Infinitude of Prime Numbers. It is often stated (erroneously) that this proof relies on these numbers. However, recall that did not begin by assuming that the set of all primes is finite. His proof, found in as , proceeded as follows: Take any finite set of primes (it could be any set, for example $\set {3, 211, 65537}$). Then it follows that at least one prime exists that is not in that set. However, the numbers themselves are mildly interesting in their own right.

label: Definition:Euclid Number/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Euclid numbers begins as follows: Category:Definitions/Euclid Numbers

label: Definition:Euclid Prime
snippet: A Euclid prime is a natural number which is both a Euclid number and a prime number.

label: Definition:Euclid Prime/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Euclid primes begins: $2, 3, 7, 31, 211, 2311, 200 \, 560 \, 490 \, 131, \ldots$ This sequence can be better comprehended as: $\sequence {p_n \# + 1}$ where: $p_n \#$ denotes the primorial of the $n$th prime number $n$ is the sequence: $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 11, 75, 171, 172, 384, 457, 616, 643, \ldots$

label: Definition:Euclidean
snippet: Geometry: Euclidean Geometry Euclidean Space Topology: Euclidean Topology Euclidean Metric Euclidean Distance Euclidean Norm Abstract Algebra: Euclidean Domain Euclidean Relation All the above are related in some way to, or derived from, the concept of Euclidean geometry. Additional concepts bearing the adjective Euclidean: Number Theory: Euclidean Algorithm

label: Definition:Euclidean Directional Derivative
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be the $n$-dimensional real vector space. Let $p \in \R^n$ be a point. Let $T_p \R^n$ be tha tangent space of $\R^n$ at $p$. Let $v \in T_p \R^n$ be a vector. Let $\map {\mathfrak{X}} {\R^n}$ be the space of smooth vector fields of $\R^n$. Let $Y \in \map {\mathfrak{X}} {\R^n}$ be a vector field.

label: Definition:Euclidean Domain/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euclidean Domain == A Euclidean domain is so named because, as an algebraic structure, it sustains the concept of the Euclidean Algorithm. himself made no mention of the concept, which is an abstract algebraic concept defined in (mathematically speaking) modern times. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Euclidean Geometry
snippet: Euclidean geometry is the branch of geometry in which the parallel postulate applies. An assumption which is currently under question is whether or not ordinary space is itself Euclidean. Euclidean geometry adheres to Euclid's postulates.

label: Definition:Euclidean Geometry/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euclidean Geometry == Euclidean geometry was initially developed in Greece between about $600$ and $300$ BCE. It was codified at the end of this period and published as . As a system, it was regarded as logically sound for some $2000$ years, although there are in fact a number of unstated and concealed assumptions. re-cast Euclidean geometry in $1899$, in his , which used: three undefined entities: point, line and plane $28$ assumptions, known as Hilbert's axioms.

label: Definition:Euclidean Group
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space. Let $\map E n$ be the set of all isometries of $M$. Then $\map E n$ is called the Euclidean group (of order $n$).

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric
snippet: Let $M_{1'} = \struct {A_{1'}, d_{1'} }$ and $M_{2'} = \struct {A_{2'}, d_{2'} }$ be metric spaces. Let $A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$ be the cartesian product of $A_{1'}$ and $A_{2'}$. The Euclidean metric on $A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$ is defined as: $\map {d_2} {x, y} := \paren {\paren {\map {d_{1'} } {x_1, y_1} }^2 + \paren {\map {d_{2'} } {x_2, y_2} }^2}^{1/2}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2} \in A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$.

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $\C$ be the complex plane. The Euclidean metric on $\C$ is defined as: $\forall z_1, z_2 \in \C: \map d {z_1, z_2} := \size {z_1 - z_2}$ where $\size {z_1 - z_2}$ denotes the modulus of $z_1 - z_2$.

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric/General Definition
snippet: Let $M_{1'} = \struct {A_{1'}, d_{1'} }, M_{2'} = \struct {A_{2'}, d_{2'} }, \ldots, M_{n'} = \struct {A_{n'}, d_{n'} }$ be metric spaces. Let $\ds \AA = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_{i'}$ be the cartesian product of $A_{1'}, A_{2'}, \ldots, A_{n'}$. The Euclidean metric on $\ds \AA = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_{i'}$ is defined as: $\ds \map {d_2} {x, y} := \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {\map {d_{i'} } {x_i, y_i} }^2}^{\frac 1 2}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n} \in \AA$.

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note == himself did not in fact conceive of the Euclidean metric and its associated Euclidean space, Euclidean topology and Euclidean norm. They bear that name because the geometric space which it gives rise to is Euclidean in the sense that it is consistent with Euclid's fifth postulate. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric/Rational Number Plane
snippet: Let $\Q$ be the set of rational numbers. The Euclidean metric on $\Q^2$ is defined as: $\ds \map {d_2} {x, y} := \sqrt {\paren {x_1 - y_1}^2 + \paren {x_2 - y_2}^2}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2} \in \Q^2$.

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric/Real Number Line
snippet: Consider the Euclidean space $\struct {\R^n, d}$. On the real number line, the Euclidean metric can be seen to degenerate to: $\map d {x, y} := \sqrt {\paren {x - y}^2} = \size {x - y}$ where $\size {x - y}$ denotes the absolute value of $x - y$.

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric/Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be an $n$-dimensional real vector space. The Euclidean metric on $\R^n$ is defined as: $\ds \map {d_2} {x, y} := \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {x_i - y_i}^2}^{1 / 2}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n} \in \R^n$.

label: Definition:Euclidean Metric/Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $x \in \R^n$ be a point. Let $\tuple {x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ be the standard coordinates. Let $T_x \R^n$ be the tangent space of $\R^n$ at $x$. Let $T_x \R^n$ be identified with $\R^n$: $T_x \R^n \cong \R^n$ Let $v, w \in T_x \R^n$ be vectors such that: $\ds v = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n v^i \valueat {\partial_i} x$ $\ds w = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n w^i \valueat {\partial_i} x$ Let $g$ be a Riemannian metric such that: $\ds g_x = \innerprod v w_x = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n v^i w^i$ Then $g$ is called the Euclidean metric.

label: Definition:Euclidean Number
snippet: A Euclidean number is a perfect number which is even.

label: Definition:Euclidean Number/Also known as
snippet: == Euclidean Numbers: Also known as == A Euclidean number is also known by some sources as a Euclid number. However, the latter term is also used to denote a completely different concept. To reduce confusion, many sources merely refer to an even perfect number.

label: Definition:Euclidean Number Theory
snippet: Euclidean number theory concerns aspects of number theory and real analysis as presented in . Particular attention is paid to certain properties of the irrational numbers.

label: Definition:Euclidean Plane
snippet: For any real number $a$ let: $L_a = \set {\tuple {x, y} \in \R^2: x = a}$ Furthermore, define: $L_A = \set {L_a: a \in \R}$ For any two real numbers $m$ and $b$ let: $L_{m, b} = \set {\tuple {x, y} \in \R^2: y = m x + b}$ Furthermore, define: $L_{M, B} = \set {L_{m, b}: m, b \in \R}$ Finally let: $L_E = L_A \cup L_{M, B}$ The abstract geometry $\struct {\R^2, L_E}$ is called the Euclidean plane.

label: Definition:Euclidean Plus Metric
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $\set {r_i}$ be an enumeration of the rational numbers $\Q$. The Euclidean plus metric $d: \R \times \R \to \R$ is the metric defined as: $\map d {x, y} := \size {x - y} + \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty 2^{-i} \map \inf {1, \size {\max_{j \mathop \le i} \frac 1 {\size {x - r_j} } - \max_{j \mathop \le i} \frac 1 {\size {y - r_j} } } }$ Thus $d$ adds to the Euclidean metric between $x$ and $y$ a contribution which measures the relative distances of $x$ and $y$ from $\Q$.

label: Definition:Euclidean Relation/Source of Name
snippet: == Source of Name of Euclidean Relation == The concept of a Euclidean relation was named for . It derives ultimately from the first of Euclid's common notions. However, did not delve deeply into the field of relation theory. The concept of equivalence relations was a much later development. Category:Definitions/Relation Theory

label: Definition:Euclidean Space
snippet: Let $S$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q$, $\R$, $\C$. Let $S^n$ be a cartesian space for $n \in \N_{\ge 1}$. Let $d: S^n \times S^n \to \R$ be the usual (Euclidean) metric on $S^n$. Then $\tuple {S^n, d}$ is a Euclidean space.

label: Definition:Euclidean Space/Euclidean Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q$, $\R$, $\C$. Let $S^n$ be a cartesian space for $n \in \N_{\ge 1}$. Let $M = \struct {S^n, d}$ be a Euclidean space. The topology $\tau_d$ induced by the Euclidean metric $d$ is called the Euclidean topology.

label: Definition:Euclidean Space/Euclidean Topology/Real Number Line
snippet: Let $\R$ denote the real number line. Let $d: \R \times \R \to \R$ denote the Euclidean metric on $\R$. Let $\tau_d$ denote the topology on $\R$ induced by $d$. The topology $\tau_d$ induced by $d$ is called the Euclidean topology. Hence $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ is referred to as the real number line with the Euclidean topology.

label: Definition:Euclidean Space/Euclidean Topology/Real Number Plane
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be an $n$-dimensional real vector space. Let $M = \struct {\R^2, d}$ be a real Euclidean space of $2$ dimensions. The topology $\tau_d$ induced by the Euclidean metric $d$ is called the Euclidean topology. The space $\struct {\R^2, \tau_d}$ is known as the (real) Euclidean plane.

label: Definition:Euclidean Space/Real
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be an $n$-dimensional real vector space. Let the Euclidean metric $d$ be applied to $\R^n$. Then $\struct {\R^n, d}$ is a (real) Euclidean $n$-space.

label: Definition:Euclidean Space/Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold where $M = \R^n$ for some $n \in \N_{> 0}$ and $g$ is the Euclidean metric. Then $\struct {M, g}$ is known as the ($n$-dimensional) Euclidean space.

label: Definition:Euclidean Valuation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euclidean Valuation == A Euclidean valuation is so named because it is central to the definition of a Euclidean domain. In turn, a Euclidean domain is so named because, as an algebraic structure, it sustains the concept of the Euclidean Algorithm. himself made no mention of the concept, which is an abstract algebraic concept defined in (mathematically speaking) modern times. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Euler's Equation for Vanishing Variation
snippet: Let $\map y x$ be a real function. Let $\map F {x, y, z}$ be a real function belonging to $C^2$ all its variables. Let $J \sqbrk y$ be a functional of the form: $\ds \int_a^b \map F {x, y, y'} \rd x$ Then Euler's equation for vanishing variation is defined a differential equation, resulting from condition: $\ds \delta \int_a^b \map F {x, y, y'} \rd x = 0$ In other words: $F_y - \dfrac \d {\d x} F_{y'} = 0$

label: Definition:Euler's Equations of Fluid Dynamics
snippet: Let $F$ be an inviscid and incompressible fluid of constant density $\rho$. Let the velocity of flow of $F$ be $\mathbf u$. Then Euler's equations of fluid dynamics state: {{eqn | l = \operatorname {div} \mathbf u | r = 0 }} {{eqn | l = \dfrac {\mathrm D \mathbf u} {\mathrm D t} | r = -\dfrac 1 \rho \nabla p + \mathbf g }} where: $\operatorname {div} \mathbf u$ denotes the divergence of $\mathbf u$ $p$ denotes the pressure $\mathbf g$ denotes acceleration due to gravity $\dfrac {\mathrm D} {\mathrm D t}$ denotes the convective derivative.

label: Definition:Euler's Number/Also known as
snippet: == Euler's Number: Also known as == Euler's number is also known as Napier's constant for . Some sources give it as the Euler number, but this is not endorsed on in order not to confuse this with the Euler numbers.

label: Definition:Euler's Number/Base of Exponential
snippet: There is a number $x \in \R$ such that: $\ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \frac {x^h - 1} h = 1$ This number is called Euler's number and is denoted $e$.

label: Definition:Euler's Number/Base of Logarithm
snippet: Euler's number $e$ can be defined as the number satisfied by: {{eqn | l = \ln e | r = \int_1^e \dfrac {\d x} x}} where $\ln e$ denotes the natural logarithm of $e$. That $e$ is unique follows from Logarithm is Strictly Increasing.

label: Definition:Euler's Number/Exponential Function
snippet: Euler's number $e$ can be defined as the number satisfied by: $e := \exp 1 = e^1$ where $\exp 1$ denotes the exponential function of $1$.

label: Definition:Euler's Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euler's Number == Euler's number was named $e$ by himself. He originally defined it as the limit of the sequence $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {1 + \dfrac 1 n}^n$

label: Definition:Euler's Number/Limit of Sequence
snippet: The sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ defined as $x_n = \paren {1 + \dfrac 1 n}^n$ converges to a limit as $n$ increases without bound. That limit is called Euler's number and is denoted $e$.

label: Definition:Euler's Number/Limit of Series
snippet: The series $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac 1 {n!}$ converges to a limit. This limit is Euler's number $e$.

label: Definition:Euler's Number as Limit of Sequence/Also presented as
snippet: == Euler's Number as the Limit of a Sequence: Also presented as == The sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ defining Euler's number can also be presented in the form: $e := \ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \paren {1 + h}^{1 / h}$

label: Definition:Euler's Number as Limit of Series/Also known as
snippet: == Euler's Number as Limit of Series: Also known as == The expression for Euler's number $e$ as the limit of the series: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac 1 {n!}$ is known as the factorial series.

label: Definition:Euler-Gompertz Constant/Continued Fraction
snippet: The Euler-Gompertz constant is the real number $G$ defined as: $G = \cfrac 1 {2 - \cfrac {1^2} {4 - \cfrac {2^2} {6 - \cfrac {3^2} {8 - \cfrac {4^2} {10 - \dotsb} } } } }$

label: Definition:Euler-Gompertz Constant/Integral Form
snippet: The Euler-Gompertz constant is the real number $G$ defined as: $G = \ds \int_0^\infty \dfrac {e^{-u} } {1 + u} \rd u$

label: Definition:Euler-Lagrange Equation
snippet: The Euler–Lagrange equation is an equation satisfied by a mapping $\mathbf q$ of a real variable $t$ which is a stationary point of the functional: $\forall t \in \R: \ds \map S {\mathbf q} = \int_a^b \map L {t, \map {\mathbf q} t, \map {\mathbf q'} t} \rd t$ where: $\mathbf q$ is the function to be found: $\mathbf q: \closedint a b \subset \R \to X : t \mapsto x = \map {\mathbf q} t$ such that: $\mathbf q$ is differentiable $\map {\mathbf q} a = \mathbf x_a$ $\map {\mathbf q} b = \mathbf x_b$ $\mathbf q'$ is the derivative of $\mathbf q$: $\mathbf q': \closedint a b \to T_{\map {\mathbf q}…

label: Definition:Euler-Lagrange Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Euler-Lagrange Equation: Also known as == The Euler-Lagrange equation is often taken in the plural: Euler-Lagrange equations, as it actually defines a system of differential equations. They are sometimes referred to as Lagrange's equations (of motion). Some sources refer to this as Euler's equation, but that name is fraught with ambiguity.

label: Definition:Euler-Lagrange Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euler-Lagrange Equation == The Euler-Lagrange equation was developed in the $1750$s by and in connection with their studies of the Tautochrone Problem. solved it in $1755$ and sent the solution to . They further developed 's method and applied it to mechanics. This led to the formulation of Lagrangian mechanics. Their correspondence ultimately led to the calculus of variations.

label: Definition:Euler-Mascheroni Constant
snippet: The Euler-Mascheroni constant $\gamma$ is the real number that is defined as: {{eqn | l = \gamma | o = := | r = \lim_{n \mathop \to +\infty} \paren {\sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \frac 1 k - \int_1^n \frac 1 x \rd x} }} {{eqn | r = \lim_{n \mathop \to +\infty} \paren {H_n - \ln n} }} where $\sequence {H_n}$ are the harmonic numbers and $\ln$ is the natural logarithm.

label: Definition:Euler-Mascheroni Constant/Also known as
snippet: == Euler-Mascheroni Constant: Also known as == The Euler-Mascheroni constant $\gamma$ is also known as Euler's constant. However, this allows it to be confused with Euler's number, so its use is not endorsed by . It is also sometimes known as Mascheroni's constant. Some sources denote it by the symbol $\mathrm C$.

label: Definition:Euler-Mascheroni Constant/Decimal Expansion
snippet: == Decimal Expansion == The decimal expansion of the Euler-Mascheroni constant $\gamma$ starts: $\gamma \approx 0 \cdotp 57721 \, 56649 \, 01532 \, 86060 \, 65120 \, 90082 \, 40243 \, 1 \ldots$

label: Definition:Euler-Mascheroni Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euler-Mascheroni Constant == The Euler-Mascheroni Constant was presented by to the St. Petersburg Academy on $11$ March $1734$. It was published in $1738$, calculated to $6$ decimal places, as $0 \cdotp 577218$ (although only the first $5$ were correct, as himself surmised). He subsequently calculated it to $16$ places in $1781$, and published this in $1785$. published a calculation to $32$ places of the value of this constant. Only the first $19$ places were accurate. The remaining ones were corrected in $1809$ by .

label: Definition:Euler-Poincaré Characteristic/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euler-Poincaré Characteristic == The concept of the Euler-Poincaré characteristic originated with , who first noted that $\map \chi K = 2$ when $K$ is a regular polyhedron in Cartesian $3$-space. His original definition was extended by in $1813$ and then in $1895$.

label: Definition:Euler Characteristic/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Euler characteristic

label: Definition:Euler Diagram
snippet: An Euler diagram is a graphical technique for illustrating the relationships between sets. It differs from a Venn diagram in that whereas the latter illustrates all possible intersections between a number of general sets, an Euler diagram depicts only those which are relevant for the situation being depicted.

label: Definition:Euler Line
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle which is not equilateral. The Euler line of $\triangle ABC$ is the straight line through the orthocenter, centroid and circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$. 700px In the above, the line $OGK$ is the Euler line of $\triangle ABC$.

label: Definition:Euler Lucky Number/Definition 1
snippet: The Euler lucky numbers are the prime numbers $p$ such that: $n^2 + n + p$ is prime for $0 \le n < p - 1$.

label: Definition:Euler Lucky Number/Definition 2
snippet: The Euler lucky numbers are the prime numbers $p$ such that: $n^2 - n + p$ is prime for $1 \le n < p$.

label: Definition:Euler Numbers
snippet: The Euler Numbers $E_n$ are a sequence of integers defined by the exponential generating function: $\ds \sech x = \frac {2 e^x} {e^{2 x} + 1} = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {E_n x^n} {n!}$ where $\size x < \dfrac \pi 2$.

label: Definition:Euler Numbers/Alternative Form/Definition 1
snippet: The alternative form Euler numbers ${E_n}^*$ are a sequence of rational numbers defined as: {{eqn | l = \sech x | r = 1 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {-1}^n \frac { {E_n}^* x^{2 n} } {\paren {2 n}!} | c = }} {{eqn | r = 1 - \frac { {E_1}^* x^2} {2!} + \frac { {E_2}^* x^4} {4!} - \frac { {E_3}^* x^6} {6!} + \cdots | c = }} where $\size x < \dfrac \pi 2 $.

label: Definition:Euler Numbers/Alternative Form/Definition 2
snippet: The alternative form Euler numbers ${E_n}^*$ are a sequence of rational numbers defined as: {{eqn | l = \sec x | r = 1 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac { {E_n}^* x^{2 n} } {\paren {2 n}!} | c = }} {{eqn | r = 1 + \frac { {E_1}^* x^2} {2!} + \frac { {E_2}^* x^4} {4!} + \frac { {E_3}^* x^6} {6!} + \cdots | c = }} where $\size x < \dfrac \pi 2$.

label: Definition:Euler Numbers/Recurrence Relation
snippet: The Euler numbers $E_n$ are a sequence of rational numbers defined by the recurrence relation: $E_n = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 0 \\ \\ 0 & : n > 0, n = 2 r + 1 \\ \\ \ds -\sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \binom {2 n} {2 k} E_{2 k} & : n > 0, n = 2 r \end {cases}$

label: Definition:Euler Phi Function
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$, that is, a strictly positive integer. The Euler $\phi$ (phi) function is the arithmetic function $\phi: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ defined as: $\map \phi n = $ the number of strictly positive integers less than or equal to $n$ which are prime to $n$ That is: $\map \phi n = \card {S_n}: S_n = \set {k: 1 \le k \le n, k \perp n}$ That is, the number of totitives to $n$.

label: Definition:Euler Phi Function/Also known as
snippet: == Euler Phi Function: Also known as == The Euler $\phi$ function is also known as: the totient function the Euler totient function. It is also variously rendered: with a hyphen: Euler $\phi$-function in the possessive form: Euler's $\phi$ function merely as Euler's function the $\phi$ function The symbol $\map \varphi n$ can sometimes be seen. Some sources use the term indicator function, but this has more than one use, and so is discouraged on .

label: Definition:Euler Phi Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euler $\phi$ Function == The Euler $\phi$ function was invented by in $1760$ in order to generalise Fermat's Little Theorem to non-prime indices.

label: Definition:Euler Phi Function/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == Euler's phi function

label: Definition:Euler Product
snippet: Let $a_n : \N \to \C$ be an arithmetic function. Let $\ds \map f s = \sum_{n \mathop \in \N} a_n n^{-s}$ be its Dirichlet series. Let $\sigma_a$ be its abscissa of absolute convergence. From Product Form of Sum on Completely Multiplicative Function, for $\map \Re s > \sigma_a$ we have: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty a_n n^{-s} = \prod_p \frac 1 {1 - a_p p^{-s} }$ where $p$ ranges over the primes. This representation for $f$ is called an Euler product for the Dirichlet series. {{stub|Completely multiplicative hypothesis not mentioned.

label: Definition:Euler Substitution/Third
snippet: == Proof Technique == Euler's third substitution is a technique for evaluating primitives of the form: $\ds \map R {x, \sqrt {a x^2 + b x + c} } \rd x$ where $R$ is a rational function of $x$ and $\sqrt {a x^2 + b x + c}$. Let $a x^2 + b x + c$ have real roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Euler's third substitution is the substitution: $\ds \sqrt {a x^2 + b x + c} = \sqrt {a \paren {x - \alpha} \paren {x - \beta} } = \paren {x - \alpha} t$ Then: $x = \dfrac {a \beta - \alpha t^2} {a - t^2}$ and hence $\d x$ is expressible as a rational function of $x$.

label: Definition:Eulerian Circuit
snippet: An Eulerian circuit is a circuit that passes through every vertex of a graph and uses every edge exactly once.

label: Definition:Eulerian Graph
snippet: A loop-multigraph or loop-multidigraph is called Eulerian it contains an Eulerian circuit.

label: Definition:Evaluation Mapping
snippet: Let $S, T$ be sets, and let $S^T$ be the set of all mappings from $T$ to $S$. The evaluation mapping for $S^T$ is the mapping $\operatorname{ev}: S^T \times T \to S$ defined by: $\map {\operatorname{ev} } {f, t} := \map f t$

label: Definition:Evaluation Mapping (Topology)
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\family {Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces for some indexing set $I$. Let $\family {f_i : X \to Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of continuous mappings. Let $\ds Y = \prod_{i \mathop \in I} Y_i$ be the product space of $\family {Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$. Let $f : X \to Y$ be the mapping defined by: $\forall x \in X : \map f x = \family{\map {f_i} x}_{i \mathop \in I}$ Then $f$ is said to be the evaluation mapping induced by the family $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$

label: Definition:Eve/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Eve == Eve, in the context of cryptography, is short for eavesdropper.

label: Definition:Even Cover
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\UU$ be a cover of $S$. Let $S \times S$ denote the cartesian product of $S$ with itself. Let $\tau_{S \times S}$ denote the product topology on $S \times S$. Let $T \times T$ denote the product space $\struct {S \times S, \tau_{S \times S} }$. Then $\UU$ is an even cover of $T$ there exists a neighborhood $V$ of the diagonal $\Delta_S$ of $S \times S$ in $T \times T$: $\set{\map V x : x \in S}$ is a refinement of $\UU$ where: $V$ is seen as a relation on $S \times S$ $\map V x$ denotes the image of $x$ under $V$.

label: Definition:Even Integer/Definition 1
snippet: An integer $n \in \Z$ is even it is divisible by $2$.

label: Definition:Even Integer/Definition 2
snippet: An integer $n \in \Z$ is even it is of the form: $n = 2 r$ where $r \in \Z$ is an integer.

label: Definition:Even Integer/Definition 3
snippet: An integer $n \in \Z$ is even : $x \equiv 0 \pmod 2$ where the notation denotes congruence modulo $2$.

label: Definition:Even Integer/Even-Times Even
snippet: Let $n$ be an integer. Then $n$ is even-times even it has $4$ as a divisor. The first few non-negative even-times even numbers are: $0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, \ldots$

label: Definition:Even Integer/Even-Times Odd
snippet: Let $n$ be an integer. Then $n$ is even-times odd it has $2$ as a divisor and also an odd number. The first few non-negative even-times odd numbers are: $2, 6, 10, 12, 14, 18, \ldots$

label: Definition:Even Integer/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Even Integer == The concept of classifying numbers as odd or even appears to have originated with the Pythagoreans. It was their belief that even numbers are female, and odd numbers are male. A commentator on used the term isosceles number for an even number, in correspondence with the concept of an isosceles triangle. In a similar way an odd number was described as scalene.

label: Definition:Even Parity/Also defined as
snippet: == Even Parity: Also known as == Some sources refer to even parity as a property of a pair of integers $\set {z_1, z_2}$: $\set {z_1, z_2}$ are of even parity $z_1$ and $z_2$ are either both even or both odd. That is, the same as the definition of such a pair of integers as being of the same parity

label: Definition:Evenly Covered
snippet: Let $E$ and $B$ be topological spaces. Let $p: E \to B$ be a continuous surjection. An open set $U \subset B$ is evenly covered by $p$ if its preimage is a disjoint union of open sets such that the restriction of $p$ to each of them is a homeomorphism to $U$.

label: Definition:Evenly Spaced Integer Topology
snippet: Let $\Z$ denote the set of integers. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets defined as: $\BB = \set {a + k \Z: a, k \in \Z, k \ne 0}$ where $a + k \Z := \set {a + k \lambda: \lambda \in \Z}$. Then $\BB$ is the basis for a topology $\tau$ on $S$. Then $\tau$ is referred to as the evenly spaced integer topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the evenly spaced integer space.

label: Definition:Event/Also defined as
snippet: == Event: Also defined as == Some sources define an event as a (measurable) subset of the sample space $\Omega$. However, while this is technically consistent with the definition as given here, it misses the nuance that it is an element of a specified set of such subsets of $\Omega$ that comprise the event space.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events, so that $A \subseteq \Omega$ and $B \subseteq \Omega$. Let the outcome of the experiment be $\omega \in \Omega$. Then the following real-world interpretations of the occurrence of events can be determined: If $\omega \in A$, then $A$ occurs. If $\omega \notin A$, that is $\omega \in \Omega \setminus A$, then $A$ does not occur.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Certainty
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A \in \Sigma$ be an event of $\EE$ whose probability of occurring is equal to $1$. Then $A$ is described as certain. That is, it is a certainty that $A$ occurs.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Difference
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events, so that $A \subseteq \Omega$ and $B \subseteq \Omega$. Let the outcome of the experiment be $\omega \in \Omega$. Let $\omega \in A \setminus B$, where $A \setminus B$ denotes the difference of $A$ and $B$. Then $A$ occurs but $B$ does not occur.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Equality
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events of $\EE$ such that $A = B$. Then: the occurrence of $A$ inevitably brings about the occurrence of $B$ and: the occurrence of $B$ inevitably brings about the occurrence of $A$.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Impossibility
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A \in \Sigma$ be an event of $\EE$ whose probability of occurring is equal to $0$. Then $A$ is described as impossible. That is, it is an impossibility for $A$ to occur.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Intersection
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events, so that $A \subseteq \Omega$ and $B \subseteq \Omega$. Let the outcome of the experiment be $\omega \in \Omega$. Let $\omega \in A \cap B$, where $A \cap B$ denotes the intersection of $A$ and $B$. Then both $A$ and $B$ occur. This can be referred to as the intersection of $A$ and $B$.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Symmetric Difference
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events, so that $A \subseteq \Omega$ and $B \subseteq \Omega$. Let the outcome of the experiment be $\omega \in \Omega$. Let $\omega \in A \symdif B$, where $A \symdif B$ denotes the symmetric difference of $A$ and $B$. Then either $A$ occurs or $B$ occurs, but not both.

label: Definition:Event/Occurrence/Union
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events, so that $A \subseteq \Omega$ and $B \subseteq \Omega$. Let the outcome of the experiment be $\omega \in \Omega$. Let $\omega \in A \cup B$, where $A \cup B$ denotes the union of $A$ and $B$. Then either $A$ or $B$ occur. This is known as the union of the events $A$ and $B$.

label: Definition:Event/Simple Event
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment. A simple event in $\EE$ is an event in $\EE$ which consists of exactly $1$ elementary event. That is, it is a singleton subset of the sample space $\Omega$ of $\EE$.

label: Definition:Event Space
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment whose probability space is $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The event space of $\EE$ is usually denoted $\Sigma$ (Greek capital sigma), and is the set of all outcomes of $\EE$ which are interesting. By definition, $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma}$ is a measurable space. Hence the event space $\Sigma$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$.

label: Definition:Event Space/Also denoted as
snippet: == Event Space: Also denoted as == Some sources use $\FF$ or $\mathscr F$ to denote an event space. In the field of decision theory, the symbol $\Xi$ can often be seen.

label: Definition:Event Space/Discrete
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment. Let $\Omega$ be a discrete sample space of $\EE$. Then it is commonplace to take $\Sigma$ to be the power set $\powerset \Omega$ of $\Omega$, that is, the set of all possible subsets of $\Omega$.

label: Definition:Eventually (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {E_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of events in $\Sigma$. We define: {{eqn | l = \set {E_n \text { eventually} } | r = \set {\omega \in \Omega : \text {there exists } N \in \N \text { such that } \omega \in E_n \text { for } n \ge N} }} {{eqn | r = \liminf_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n }} where $\ds \liminf_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n$ is the limit inferior of $\sequence {E_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$.

label: Definition:Eventually Constant Sequence
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a convergent sequence in $S$. Then $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is eventually constant : $\exists m \in \R: \forall n \in \N, n \ge m: x_{n + 1} = x_n$

label: Definition:Eventually Periodic P-adic Expansion
snippet: Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers for some prime $p$. Let $x \in \Q_p$. Let $\ldots d_n \ldots d_2 d_1 d_0 . d_{-1} d_{-2} \ldots d_{-m}$ be the canonical expansion of $x$. Let there be a finite sequence of $k$ digits of $x$: $\tuple {d_{r + k - 1} \ldots d_{r+1} d_r }$ such that $r \ge 0$ and for all $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ and for all $j \in \set {0, 2, \ldots, k - 1}$: $d_{r + j + n k} = d_{r + j}$ where $k$ is the smallest $k$ to have this property.

label: Definition:Everywhere Dense
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset.

label: Definition:Everywhere Dense/Also known as
snippet: == Everywhere Dense: Also known as == Some authors refer to an everywhere dense subset merely as a dense set or a dense subset. However, this can be confused with dense-in-itself.

label: Definition:Everywhere Dense/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset. The subset $H$ is (everywhere) dense in $T$ : $H^- = S$ where $H^-$ is the closure of $H$. That is, every point in $S$ is a point or a limit point of $H$.

label: Definition:Everywhere Dense/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset. The subset $H$ is (everywhere) dense in $T$ the intersection of $H$ with every non-empty open set of $T$ is non-empty: $\forall U \in \tau \setminus \set \O: H \cap U \ne \O$

label: Definition:Everywhere Dense/Definition 3
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset. The subset $H$ is (everywhere) dense in $T$ every neighborhood of every point of $S$ contains at least one point of $H$.

label: Definition:Everywhere Dense/Informal Definition
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset. Informally, the subset $H$ is (everywhere) dense in $T$ every element of $S$ is either an element of $H$ or arbitrarily close to an element of $H$.

label: Definition:Everywhere Dense/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $B \subseteq A$ be a subset of $A$. Then $B$ is (everywhere) dense in $M$ every point of $A$ is a limit point of a sequence of points of $B$.

label: Definition:Everywhere Dense/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $Y \subseteq X$ be a subset of $X$. Suppose: $\forall x \in X: \forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists y \in Y: \norm {x - y} < \epsilon$ Then $Y$ is (everywhere) dense in $X$.

label: Definition:Everywhere Dense/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $S$ be a subset of the real numbers. Then $S$ is (everywhere) dense in $\R$ : $\forall x \in \R: \forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists s \in S: x - \epsilon < s < x + \epsilon$. That is, in every neighborhood of every real number lies an element of $S$.

label: Definition:Evolute
snippet: Consider a curve $\CC$ embedded in a plane.

label: Definition:Evolute/Definition 1
snippet: Consider a curve $\CC$ embedded in a plane. The evolute of $\CC$ is the locus of the centers of curvature of each point on $\CC$.

label: Definition:Evolute/Definition 2
snippet: Consider a curve $\CC$ embedded in a plane. The evolute of $\CC$ is the envelope of the normals to $\CC$ at each point of $\CC$.

label: Definition:Evolute/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Evolute == The concept of the evolute of a curve in the plane was first introduced by in his . However, the first detailed study of the evolute was undertaken by during his analysis of the cycloid in his $1673$ treatise . Some sources fail to register 's interest.

label: Definition:Exact Chain Complex
snippet: Let $\AA$ be an abelian category. Let $\family {d_i : C_i \to C_{i - 1} }_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ be a chain complex in $\AA$. Then $\family {d_i : C_i \to C_{i - 1} }_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ is exact it is exact at $C_i$ for all $i \mathop \in \Z$.

label: Definition:Exact Differential Equation/Definition 2
snippet: Let a first order ordinary differential equation be expressible in this form: $\map M {x, y} + \map N {x, y} \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = 0$ such that $M$ and $N$ are not homogeneous functions of the same degree. However, suppose there happens to exist a function $\map f {x, y}$ such that: $\dfrac {\partial f} {\partial x} = M, \dfrac {\partial f} {\partial y} = N$ such that the second partial derivatives of $f$ exist and are continuous. Then the expression $M \rd x + N \rd y$ is called an exact differential, and the differential equation is called an exact differential equation.

label: Definition:Exact Division/Divisor
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$ be integers such that: $a \div b = q \rem 0$ where $\div$ denotes integer division. Then $b$ is known as an exact divisor of $a$.

label: Definition:Exact Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be categories. Let $F : \mathbf A \to \mathbf B$ be a functor. Then $F$ is an exact functor $F$ is both a left exact and a right exact functor.

label: Definition:Exact Normal Series
snippet: Let $\sequence {H_i}_{i \mathop \in I \mathop \subseteq \Z}$ be a normal series: $\cdots \stackrel {\phi_{i - 1} } {\longrightarrow} H_{i - 1} \stackrel {\phi_i} {\longrightarrow} H_i \stackrel {\phi_{i + 1} } {\longrightarrow} H_{i + 1} \stackrel {\phi_{i + 2} } {\longrightarrow} \cdots$ Suppose that, for some $i \in I$: $\Img {\phi_i} = \map \ker {\phi_{i + 1} }$ That is, the image of one homomorphism is the kernel of the next. Then $\sequence {H_i}$ is referred to as exact at $H_i$. If $\sequence {H_i}$ is exact for all $i \in I$, then $\sequence {H_i}$ itself is an exact normal series.

label: Definition:Exact P-Value
snippet: Let $\tau$ be a parametric test. Let all the conditions for $\tau$ to hold be fulfilled. The exact $p$-value of $\tau$ is the probability that a statistic takes a value as extreme or more extreme than all of those observed in the appropriate tests.

label: Definition:Exact Sequence of Groups
snippet: Let $\left({G, \circ}\right)$ be a group. Consider the sequence of groups $\left\langle{G_i}\right\rangle$ and group homomorphisms $\phi_i$: $\ds \cdots \stackrel{\phi_{i-2}}{\longrightarrow} G_{i-1} \stackrel{\phi_{i-1}}{\longrightarrow} G_i \stackrel{\phi_i}{\longrightarrow} G_{i+1} \stackrel{\phi_{i+1}}{\longrightarrow} \cdots$ $\left\langle{G_i}\right\rangle$ is exact : $\forall i: \map {\operatorname{Im}} {\phi_i} = \map \ker {\phi_{i+1}}$ where: $\map {\operatorname{Im}} {\phi_i}$ denotes the image of $\phi_i$ $\map \ker {\phi_{i+1}}$ denotes the kernel of $\phi_{i+1}$.

label: Definition:Exact Sequence of Modules
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \cdot}$ be a ring. Let: $(1): \quad \cdots \longrightarrow M_i \stackrel {d_i} {\longrightarrow} M_{i + 1} \stackrel {d_{i + 1} } {\longrightarrow} M_{i + 2} \stackrel {d_{i + 2} } {\longrightarrow} \cdots$ be a sequence of $R$-modules $M_i$ and $R$-module homomorphisms $d_i$. Then the sequence $(1)$ is exact : $\forall i: \Img {d_i} = \map \ker {d_{i + 1} }$ where $\Img {d_i}$ and $\map \ker {d_{i + 1} }$ denote the image and kernel of homomorphisms respectively.

label: Definition:Exactness of Chain Complex at Object
snippet: Let $\AA$ be an abelian category. Let $\family {d_i : C_i \to C_{i - 1} }_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ be a chain complex in $\AA$. Then $\family {d_i : C_i \to C_{i - 1} }_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ is exact at $C_j$ the canonical map $\Img {d_{i + 1} } \to \ker \paren {d_i}$ is an isomorphism. The canonical map is induced by Homomorphisms Theorem for Categories with Zero Object since by definition $d_{j} \circ d_{j+1} = 0$.

label: Definition:Excess Kurtosis
snippet: Excess kurtosis is defined as the difference between the kurtosis of a particular probability distribution and that of the normal distribution. Let $X$ be a random variable with kurtosis $\alpha_4$. By Kurtosis of Normal Distribution, the kurtosis of a normal distribution is equal to $3$. So the excess kurtosis of $X$, usually denoted $\gamma_2$, is given by: $\gamma_2 = \alpha_4 - 3$

label: Definition:Excircle of Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle whose sides are $a$, $b$ and $c$ opposite vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ respectively. Let sides $b$ and $c$ be produced beyond the vertices $C$ and $B$ respectively. Let a circle be constructed tangent to both of these extensions to $b$ and $c$ lines and also to $a$. The circle so constructed is called the excircle of $\triangle ABC$ $a$. 490px There are three excircles for every triangle.

label: Definition:Excircle of Triangle/Excenter
snippet: 490px The center of an excircle of a triangle is called an excenter of the triangle. In the above diagram, $I_a$ is the excenter of $\triangle ABC$ $a$.

label: Definition:Excircle of Triangle/Exradius
snippet: 490px A radius of an excircle of a triangle is called an exradius of the triangle. In the above diagram, $r_a$ is the exradius of $\triangle ABC$ $a$.

label: Definition:Excluded Point Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be some particular point of $S$. We define a subset $\tau_{\bar p}$ of the power set $\powerset S$ as: $\tau_{\bar p} = \set {A \subseteq S: p \notin A} \cup \set S$ That is, all the subsets of $S$ which do not include $p$, along with the set $S$. Then $\tau_{\bar p}$ is a topology called the excluded point topology on $S$ by $p$, or just an excluded point topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ is called the excluded point space on $S$ by $p$, or just an excluded point space.

label: Definition:Excluded Point Topology/Countable
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be some particular point of $S$. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ be the excluded point space on $S$ by $p$. Let $S$ be a countably infinite set. Then $\tau_{\bar p}$ is a countable excluded point topology, and $\struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ is a countable excluded point space.

label: Definition:Excluded Point Topology/Finite
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be some particular point of $S$. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ be the excluded point space on $S$ by $p$. Let $S$ be a finite set. Then $\tau_{\bar p}$ is a finite excluded point topology, and $\struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ is a finite excluded point space.

label: Definition:Excluded Point Topology/Infinite
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be some particular point of $S$. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ be the excluded point space on $S$ by $p$. Let $S$ be an infinite set. Then $\tau_{\bar p}$ is an infinite excluded point topology, and $\struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ is a infinite excluded point space.

label: Definition:Excluded Point Topology/Uncountable
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $p \in S$ be some particular point of $S$. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ be the excluded point space on $S$ by $p$. Let $S$ be an uncountable set. Then $\tau_{\bar p}$ is an uncountable excluded point topology, and $\struct {S, \tau_{\bar p} }$ is an uncountable excluded point space.

label: Definition:Excluded Point Topology on Three-Point Set
snippet: == Example of Finite Excluded Point Topology == Let $S = \set {0, 1, 2}$ be an instance of an arbitrary set with $3$ points. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau_{\overline 0} }$ be the excluded point space on $S$ with excluded point $p = 0$. Then $\tau_{\overline 0}$ is the excluded point topology on a $3$-point set. The topological space $T$ itself is hence referred to as the excluded $3$-point space.

label: Definition:Excluded Set Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-empty. Let $H \subseteq S$ be some subset of $S$. We define a subset $\tau_{\bar H}$ of the power set $\powerset S$ as: $\tau_{\bar H} = \set {A \subseteq S: A \cap H = \O} \cup \set S$ that is, all the subsets of $S$ which are disjoint from $H$, along with the set $S$. Then $\tau_{\bar H}$ is a topology called the excluded set topology on $S$ by $H$, or just an excluded set topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau_{\bar H} }$ is called the excluded set space on $S$ by $H$, or just an excluded set space.

label: Definition:Exhausting Sequence of Sets
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\SS = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\sequence {S_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ be a nested sequence of subsets of $S$ such that: $(1): \quad \forall k \in \N: S_k \subseteq S_{k + 1}$ $(2): \quad \ds \bigcup_{k \mathop \in \N} S_k = S$ Then $\sequence {S_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ is an exhausting sequence of sets (in $\SS$). That is, it is an increasing sequence of subsets of $S$, whose union is $S$. It is common to write $\sequence {S_k}_{k \mathop \in \N} \uparrow S$ to indicate an exhausting sequence of sets.

label: Definition:Exhaustive Set of Events
snippet: Let the probability space of an experiment $\EE$ be $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of events in $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Then $\family {A_i}$ is exhaustive : $\ds \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} A_i = \Omega$ That is, a set of events is exhaustive their union is the whole probability space.

label: Definition:Exhaustive Set of Sets
snippet: Let $\mathbb U$ be a universal set. Let $\SS$ be a set of sets in $\mathbb U$. Then $\SS$ is exhaustive : $\ds \bigcup_{s \mathop \in \SS} s = \mathbb U$ That is, a set of sets is exhaustive their union is the universal set.

label: Definition:Existential Quantifier
snippet: The symbol $\exists$ is called the existential quantifier. It expresses the fact that, in a particular universe of discourse, there exists (at least one) object having a particular property. That is: $\exists x:$ means: There exists at least one object $x$ such that ... In the language of set theory, this can be formally defined: $\exists x \in S: \map P x := \set {x \in S: \map P x} \ne \O$ where $S$ is some set and $\map P x$ is a propositional function on $S$.

label: Definition:Exogenous Variable
snippet: In an economic model, an exogenous variable is a variable which models a phenomenon which impinges upon the system from outside.

label: Definition:Expanded Number
snippet: Let $x$ be a number expressed in base $b$ for some $b \in \Z_{>1}$. Let $x$ be written as a sum of multiples of powers of $b$. Then $x$ is said to be expressed as an expanded number.

label: Definition:Expansion
snippet: Topology: Expansion of Topology Number Theory and Arithmetic: Decimal Expansion and, in general, Basis Expansion Algebra: Algebraic Expansion: for example: $\paren {x + y}^2 = x^2 + 2 x y + y^2$ Number Theory: Continued Fraction Expansion Set Theory: Finite Expansion Propositional Logic: Propositional Expansion Physics: Expansion

label: Definition:Expansion of Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ be topologies on $S$ such that $\tau_1 \subseteq \tau_2$. Then $\tau_2$ is an expansion of $\tau_1$.

label: Definition:Expectation/Absolutely Continuous
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be an absolutely continuous random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $f_X$ be the probability density function of $X$. The expectation of $X$, written $\expect X$, is defined by: $\ds \expect X = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x \map {f_X} x \rd x$ whenever: $\ds \int_{-\infty}^\infty \size x \map {f_X} x \rd x < \infty$

label: Definition:Expectation/Also known as
snippet: == Expectation: Also known as == The expectation of a random variable $X$ is also called the expected value of $X$ or the mean value of $X$. For a given random variable, the expectation is often denoted $\mu$. The terminology is appropriate, as it can be seen that an expectation is an example of a normalized weighted mean. This follows from the fact that a probability mass function is a normalized weight function. Various forms of $E$ can be seen to denote expectation: $\map E X$ $\map {\mathrm E} X$ $E \sqbrk X$ $\mathop {\mathbb E} \sqbrk X$ and so on.

label: Definition:Expectation/Continuous
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The expectation of $X$ is defined and denoted by: $\ds \expect X = \int_\R x \map f x \rd x$ where $f$ is the probability density function of $X$.

label: Definition:Expectation/Definition 1
snippet: The expectation of a random variable is the arithmetic mean of its values.

label: Definition:Expectation/Definition 2
snippet: The expectation of a random variable $X$ is the first moment about the origin of $X$.

label: Definition:Expectation/Discrete
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a real-valued discrete random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The expectation of $X$, written $\expect X$, is defined as: $\expect X := \ds \sum_{x \mathop \in \image X} x \map \Pr {X = x}$ whenever the sum is absolutely convergent, that is, when: $\ds \sum_{x \mathop \in \image X} \size {x \map \Pr {X = x} } < \infty$ where $\map \Pr {X = x}$ is the probability mass function of $X$.

label: Definition:Expectation/General Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be an integrable real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. The expectation of $X$, written $\expect X$, is defined by: $\ds \expect X = \int X \rd \Pr$ where the integral sign denotes the $\Pr$-integral of $X$.

label: Definition:Expectation of Matrix Game
snippet: Let $\GG$ be a matrix game given by the matrix $\mathbf A = \sqbrk {a_{i j} }$ of order $m \times n$. The expectation of $\GG$ can be described as the mean payoff each time when $\GG$ is played repeatedly with both players using mixed strategies. Let $\mathbf x = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m}$ and $\mathbf y = \tuple {y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n}$ be the mixed strategies for players $A$ and $B$.

label: Definition:Expectation of Random Vector
snippet: Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be random variables on a probability space $\tuple {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\mathbf X = \tuple {X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n}$ be a random vector. Then the expected value of $\mathbf X$, $\expect {\mathbf X}$, is defined by: $\expect {\mathbf X} = \tuple {\expect {X_1}, \expect {X_2}, \ldots, \expect {X_n} }$ Category:Definitions/Random Variables Category:Definitions/Probability Theory

label: Definition:Expected Monetary Value
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let the payoff from $G$ be dependent upon probabilistic outcomes. Let $P$ be a player of $G$. The expected monetary value to $P$ is the expectation of the gain $P$ would obtain from $G$ in the long run. It is calculated as the sum of each payoff multiplied by the probability of occurrence of that payoff.

label: Definition:Experiment
snippet: An experiment can be defined in natural language as a test to see what happens.

label: Definition:Experiment/Also defined as
snippet: == Experiment: Also defined as == An experiment can also be defined in the context of statistics, along the lines of: a statistical study in which the researchers make an intervention and measure its effect on some outcome of interest which is compatible with the definition of experiment in the probability theoretical context.

label: Definition:Experiment/Formal Definition
snippet: An experiment, which can conveniently be denoted $\EE$, is a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$.

label: Definition:Experimental Design
snippet: Let us want to set up a series of comparative experiments to compare the effects of administering $2$ or more treatments of some kind, for example: different medicines for patients different fertilizers for plots of land different lubricants for machines to a number of experimental units. An experimental design is a crafted system of experiments defined by a set of rules which defines how experimental units are grouped, in order to maximise the efficiency and precision of the experiments.

label: Definition:Experimental Group
snippet: An experimental group is a set of experimental units in an experimental design which are given a treatment whose effects are being investigated. This is in apposition to the control group, which are the experimental units specifically not given that treatment.

label: Definition:Exploratory Data Analysis
snippet: Exploratory data analysis is the process of performing preliminary examination of raw data in order to gain insight into their general structure and characteristics, and often identify outliers. Tools used in this activity include: box-and-whisker diagrams Five-number summaries Histograms For multivariate data or particularly large data sets, kernel density estimation methods can be used. Having performed an exploratory data analysis, the data engineer may be better placed to make a decision as to what formal statistical methods may then be appropriate.

label: Definition:Exponent of Convergence
snippet: Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence of nonzero complex numbers. The exponent of convergence of $\sequence {a_n}$ is the infimum of $\tau \ge 0$ for which the series $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \size {a_n}^{-\tau}$ converges. The exponent of convergence of a finite sequence is $0$.

label: Definition:Exponential (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory with binary products. Let $B$ and $C$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. An exponential of $C$ by $B$ consists of an object $C^B$ of $\mathbf C$ and a morphism: $\epsilon: C^B \times B \to C$ subject to the following (exponential) universal mapping property(or UMP):

label: Definition:Exponential (Category Theory)/Evaluation
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory with binary products. Let $B$ and $C$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $C^B$ be an exponential of $C$ by $B$. The morphism: $\epsilon: C^B \times B \to C$ associated to $C^B$ is called the evaluation morphism.

label: Definition:Exponential (Category Theory)/Transpose
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory with binary products. Let $B$ and $C$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. Let $C^B$ be an exponential of $C$ by $B$, with evaluation morphism $\epsilon: C^B \times B \to C$. For a morphism $f: A \times B \to C$, the unique: $\tilde f: A \to C^B$ provided by the universal mapping property for $C^B$ is called the exponential transpose of $f$. For a morphism $g: A \to C^B$, the morphism $\bar g: A \times B \to C$ defined by: $\bar g = \epsilon \circ \paren {g \times \operatorname{id}_B}$ is also called the exponential transpose of $g$.

label: Definition:Exponential Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Then $X$ has the exponential distribution with parameter $\beta$ : $\map X \Omega = \R_{\ge 0}$ $\map \Pr {X < x} = 1 - e^{-\frac x \beta}$ where $0 < \beta$. It is written: $X \sim \Exponential \beta$

label: Definition:Exponential Family of Distributions
snippet: Let $P$ be a probability distribution. $P$ is a member of the exponential family of distributions it has a probability density function of the form: $\map f {x, h} = \map \exp {\map a x \map b h + \map c h + \map d x}$ where $h$ is a parameter whose value is to be determined.

label: Definition:Exponential Form of Complex Number/Also known as
snippet: == Exponential Form of Complex Number: Also known as == Some sources refer to the exponential form $r e^{i \theta}$ of a complex number $z$ as polar form, and do not feel the need to treat it as a different representation from the $z = r \paren {\cos \theta + i \sin \theta}$ form.

label: Definition:Exponential Function
snippet: The exponential function is denoted $\exp$ and can be defined in several ways, as described below.

label: Definition:Exponential Function/Complex
snippet: For all definitions of the complex exponential function: The domain of $\exp$ is $\C$. The image of $\exp$ is $\C \setminus \set 0$, as shown in Image of Complex Exponential Function. For $z \in \C$, the complex number $\exp z$ is called the exponential of $z$.

label: Definition:Exponential Function/Complex/Differential Equation
snippet: Let $\exp: \C \to \C \setminus \set 0$ denote the (complex) exponential function. The exponential function can be defined as the unique particular solution $y = \map f z$ to the first order ODE: $\dfrac {\d y} {\d z} = y$ satisfying the initial condition $\map f 0 = 1$. That is, the defining property of $\exp$ is that it is its own derivative. The complex number $\exp z$ is called the exponential of $z$.

label: Definition:Exponential Function/Complex/Limit of Sequence
snippet: Let $\exp: \C \to \C \setminus \set 0$ denote the (complex) exponential function. The exponential function can be defined as a limit of a sequence: $\ds \exp z := \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \paren {1 + \dfrac z n}^n$ The complex number $\exp z$ is called the exponential of $z$.

label: Definition:Exponential Function/Complex/Power Series Expansion
snippet: Let $\exp: \C \to \C \setminus \set 0$ denote the (complex) exponential function. The exponential function can be defined as a (complex) power series: {{eqn | q = \forall z \in \C | l = \exp z | r = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {z^n} {n!} | c = }} {{eqn | r = 1 + \frac z {1!} + \frac {z^2} {2!} + \frac {z^3} {3!} + \cdots + \frac {z^n} {n!} + \cdots | c = }} The complex number $\exp z$ is called the exponential of $z$.

label: Definition:Exponential Function/Complex/Real Functions
snippet: Let $\exp: \C \to \C \setminus \set 0$ denote the (complex) exponential function. The exponential function can be defined by the real exponential, sine and cosine functions: $\exp z := e^x \paren {\cos y + i \sin y}$ where $z = x + i y$ with $x, y \in \R$. Here, $e^x$ denotes the real exponential function, which must be defined first. The complex number $\exp z$ is called the exponential of $z$.

label: Definition:Exponential Function/Real
snippet: For all definitions of the real exponential function: {{item||the codomain of $\exp$ is $\R_{>0}$.}} For $x \in \R$, the real number $\exp x$ or $e^x$ is called the exponential of $x$.

label: Definition:Exponential Function/Real/Differential Equation
snippet: Let $\exp: \R \to \R_{>0}$ denote the (real) exponential function. The exponential function can be defined as the unique solution $y = \map f x$ to the first order ODE: $\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = y$ satisfying the initial condition $\map f 0 = 1$. That is, the defining property of $\exp$ is that it is its own derivative. The number $\exp x$ is called the exponential of $x$.

label: Definition:Exponential Function/Real/Extension of Rational Exponential
snippet: Let $e$ denote Euler's number. Let $f: \Q \to \R$ denote the real-valued function defined as: $\map f x = e^x$ That is, let $\map f x$ denote $e$ to the power of $x$, for rational $x$. Then $\exp : \R \to \R$ is defined to be the unique continuous extension of $f$ to $\R$. $\map \exp x$ is called the exponential of $x$.

label: Definition:Exponential Generating Function
snippet: Let $A = \sequence {a_n}$ be a sequence in $\R$. Then $\ds \map {G_A} z = \sum_{n \mathop \ge 0} \frac {a_n} {n!} z^n$ is called the exponential generating function for the sequence $A$. The mapping $\map {G_A} z$ is defined for all $z$ for which the power series $\ds \sum_{n \mathop \ge 0} \frac {a_n} {n!} z^n$ is convergent. The definition can be modified so that the lower limit of the summation is $b$ where $b > 0$ by assigning $a_k = 0$ where $0 \le k < b$.

label: Definition:Exponential Map
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g, \nabla}$ be a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold without boundary endowed with the Levi-Civita connection. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $v \in T_p M$. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be an open real interval. Let $\gamma_v : I \to M$ be the unique maximal geodesic such that: $\map {\gamma '} 0 = v$ where $\gamma'$ is the velocity of $\gamma$. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$.

label: Definition:Exponential Order/Real Index
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \mathbb F$ be a function, where $\mathbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $f$ be continuous on the real interval $\hointr 0 \to$, except possibly for some finite number of discontinuities of the first kind in every finite subinterval of $\hointr 0 \to$. Let $\size {\, \cdot \,}$ be the absolute value if $f$ is real-valued, or the modulus if $f$ is complex-valued. Let $e^{a t}$ be the exponential function, where $a \in \R$ is constant.

label: Definition:Exponential Time
snippet: Exponential time is a measure of algorithmic complexity. An algorithm runs in exponential time it does not run in polynomial time. That is, there do not exist integers $A$ and $k$ such that, for $n$ inputs, the algorithm terminates in no more than $A n^k$ steps.

label: Definition:Exponential UMP
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory with binary products. Let $B$ and $C$ be objects of $\mathbf C$. An object $C^B$ of $\mathbf C$ and a morphism: $\epsilon: C^B \times B \to C$ is said to satisfy the (exponential) universal mapping property(or UMP) :

label: Definition:Exponential UMP/Property
snippet: == Property for Exponential UMP == For all objects $A$ and morphisms $f: A \times B \to C$, there exists a unique morphism: $\tilde f: A \to C^B$ such that: $\epsilon \circ \paren {\tilde f \times \operatorname{id}_B} = f$. That is: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+1em@L+3px{ C^B \times B \ar[r]^*+{\epsilon} & C \\ A \times B \ar[u]^*+{\tilde f \times \operatorname{id}_B} \ar[ur]_*+{f} }\end{xy}$ is a commutative diagram.

label: Definition:Exponentiation
snippet: Exponentiation is the process of raising a number to a power.

label: Definition:Exponentiation Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a Cartesian closed metacategory. Let $A$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Then exponentiation by $A$, denoted $\paren -^A: \mathbf C \to \mathbf C$, is the functor defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = $C^A := C^A$ $C^A$ is the exponential of $C$ by $A$ |mor = $f^A := \widetilde {\paren {f \circ \epsilon} }$ $f: B \to C$ is a morphism of $\mathbf C$ }} Here $\epsilon: B^A \times A \to B$ denotes the evaluation morphism, and $\widetilde {\paren {f \circ \epsilon} }: B^A \to C^A$ is the exponential transpose of $f \circ \epsilon$.

label: Definition:Exponentiation of Cardinals
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be the cardinals associated respectively with $A$ and $B$. Then the exponentiation of $\mathbf a$ to $\mathbf b$ is defined as: $\mathbf a^{\mathbf b} := \map \Card {A^B}$ where: $A^B$ denotes the set of all mappings from $B$ to $A$ $\map \Card {A^B}$ denotes the cardinal associated with $A^B$.

label: Definition:Expression
snippet: An expression is a well-formed word of mathematical symbols which together can be considered as a single object.

label: Definition:Expression/Algebraic
snippet: An algebraic expression is a formula obtained by combining symbols together with the arithmetic operations $+$, $-$, $\times$, $\div$, and possibly powers and roots.

label: Definition:Extended Absolute Value
snippet: Let $\overline \R$ denote the extended real numbers. Extend the absolute value $\size {\, \cdot \,}$ on $\R$ to $\overline \R$ by defining: $\size {-\infty} = \size {+\infty} = +\infty$ Thus, the extended absolute value is a mapping $\size{\, \cdot \,}: \overline \R \to \overline \R$.

label: Definition:Extended Complex Plane
snippet: The extended complex plane $\overline \C$ is defined as: $\overline \C := \C \cup \set \infty$ that is, the set of complex numbers together with the point at infinity.

label: Definition:Extended Long Line
snippet: Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let $\closedint 0 \Omega$ denote the closed ordinal space on $\Omega$. Let $L^*$ be the set constructed as follows. Between each ordinal $\alpha \in \closedint 0 \Omega$ and its successor $\alpha + 1$, let a copy of the open (real) unit interval $\openint 0 1$ be inserted. Let a total ordering $\preccurlyeq$ be applied to $L^*$ according to the betweenness described above. Let the order topology $\tau$ be applied to the ordered structure $\struct {L^*, \preccurlyeq}$.

label: Definition:Extended Metric
snippet: When defining a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$, it is sometimes convenient to allow the metric $d$ to be infinite. That is, such that: $\Rng d = \R_{\ge 0} \cup \set \infty$ In such a case, $d$ is referred to as an extended metric.

label: Definition:Extended Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $S$ be a set, and let $\overline \R$ denote the extended real numbers. A mapping $f: S \to \overline \R$ is said to be an extended real-valued function.

label: Definition:Extended Real Addition
snippet: Let $\overline \R$ denote the extended real numbers. Define extended real addition or addition on $\overline \R$, denoted $+_{\overline \R}: \overline \R \times \overline \R \to \overline \R$, by: {{eqn | q = \forall x, y \in \R | l = x +_{\overline \R} y | o = := | r = x +_\R y | c = where $+_\R$ denotes real addition }} {{eqn | q = \forall x \in \R | l = x +_{\overline \R} \paren {+\infty} | o = := | r = +\infty }} {{eqn | q = \forall x \in \R | l = \paren {+\infty} +_{\overline \R} x | o = := | r = +\infty }} {{eqn | q = \forall x \in \R | l = x +_{\overline \R} \paren {-\infty} | o = := |…

label: Definition:Extended Real Multiplication
snippet: Let $\overline \R$ denote the extended real numbers. Define extended real multiplication or multiplication on $\overline \R$, denoted $\times_{\overline \R}: \overline \R \times \overline \R \to \overline \R$, by: $\forall x \in \overline \R: x \times_{\overline \R} 0 = 0 \times_{\overline \R} x = 0$ $\forall x, y \in \R: x \times_{\overline \R} y := x \times_\R y$ where $\times_\R$ denotes real multiplication $\forall x \in \R_{>0}: x \times_{\overline \R} \paren {+\infty} = \paren {+\infty} \times_{\overline \R} x := +\infty$ $\forall x \in \R_{0}: x \times_{\overline \R} \paren {-\infty} =…

label: Definition:Extended Real Number Line/Also defined as
snippet: == Extended Real Number Line: Also defined as == Some sources define the extended real number line $\overline \R$ as $\R \cup \set \infty$, that is, without the negative infinity $-\infty$. This is the Alexandroff extension of $\R$. This is isomorphic to the topological group of complex numbers with norm $1$ under multiplication. This has the benefit that extended real addition is defined on all of $\overline \R$. A drawback is that not all suprema and infima exist. Depending on the context one may decide which form is most suitable. Category:Definitions/Extended Real Numbers

label: Definition:Extended Real Number Line/Definition 1
snippet: The extended real number line $\overline \R$ is defined as: $\overline \R := \R \cup \set {+\infty, -\infty}$ that is, the set of real numbers together with two auxiliary symbols: $+\infty$, positive infinity $-\infty$, negative infinity such that: $\forall x \in \R: x < +\infty$ $\forall x \in \R: -\infty < x$

label: Definition:Extended Real Number Line/Definition 2
snippet: The extended real number line $\overline \R$ is the order completion of the set of real numbers $\R$. The greatest element of $\overline \R$ is often denoted by $+\infty$ and its least element by $-\infty$.

label: Definition:Extended Real Sequence
snippet: An extended real sequence is a sequence (usually infinite) whose codomain is the extended real number line.

label: Definition:Extended Real Subtraction
snippet: Let $\overline \R$ denote the extended real numbers. Define extended real subtraction or subtraction on $\overline \R$, denoted $-_{\overline \R}: \overline \R \times \overline \R \to \overline \R$, by: $\forall x, y \in \R: x -_{\overline \R} y := x -_{\R} y$ where $-_\R$ denotes real subtraction $\forall x \in \R: x -_{\overline \R} \paren {+\infty} = \paren {-\infty} -_{\overline \R} x := -\infty$ $\forall x \in \R: x -_{\overline \R} \paren {-\infty} = \paren {+\infty} -_{\overline \R} x := +\infty$ $\paren {-\infty} -_{\overline \R} \paren {+\infty} := -\infty$ $\paren {+\infty}…

label: Definition:Extended Topologist's Sine Curve
snippet: 420px Let $G = \set {\tuple {x, \sin \dfrac 1 x} : 0 < x}$, considered as a subset of the real number plane with the usual (Euclidean) topology $\struct {\R^2, \tau_d}$. Let $J$ be the line segment joining the points $\tuple {0, 1}$ and $\tuple {1, 1}$ in $\R^2$. Then the set $G \cup J$ is called the extended topologist's sine curve.

label: Definition:Extended Weight Function
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\mathscr F$ be the set of all finite subsets of $S$. Let $w: S \to \R$ be a weight function. The extended weight function of $w$ is the function $w^+: \mathscr F \to \R$ defined by: $\forall A \in \mathscr F : \map {w^+} A = \ds \sum_{a \mathop \in A} \map w a$

label: Definition:Extension
snippet: In set theory: Definition:Extension of Relation Definition:Extension of Mapping Definition:Extension of Operation Definition:Extension of Sequence In class theory: Definition:Extension of Class Definition:Immediate Extension of Class In abstract algebra: Definition:Field Extension Definition:Ring Extension Definition:Extension of Ideal Definition:Extension of Scalars In model theory: Definition:Extension of Structure In propositional logic: Definition:Extension of Propositional Tableau In physics: Definition:Extension of Elastic Material Definition:Extension of Spring

label: Definition:Extension Problem
snippet: Let $H$ and $K$ be groups. The extension problem is to determine all groups $G$ such that: $K \trianglelefteq G$ $G / K \cong H$ where: $K \trianglelefteq G$ denotes that $K$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ $G / K$ denotes the quotient group of $G$ by $K$ $\cong$ denotes group isomorphism.

label: Definition:Extension of Mapping
snippet: As a mapping is, by definition, also a relation, the definition of an extension of a mapping is the same as that for an extension of a relation: Let: $f_1 \subseteq X \times Y$ be a mapping on $X \times Y$ $f_2 \subseteq S \times T$ be a mapping on $S \times T$ $X \subseteq S$ $Y \subseteq T$ $f_2 \restriction_{X \times Y}$ be the restriction of $f_2$ to $X \times Y$. Let $f_2 \restriction_{X \times Y} = f_1$. That is, let $f_1$ be a subset of $f_2$. Then $f_2$ extends or is an extension of $f_1$.

label: Definition:Extension of Sequence
snippet: As a sequence is, by definition, also a mapping, the definition of an extension of a sequence is the same as that for an extension of a mapping: Let: $\sequence {a_k}_{k \mathop \in A}$ be a sequence on $A$, where $A \subseteq \N$ $\sequence {b_k}_{k \mathop \in B}$ be a sequence on $B$, where $B \subseteq \N$ $A \subseteq B$ $\forall k \in A: b_k = a_k$ Then $\sequence {b_k}_{k \mathop \in B}$ extends or is an extension of $\sequence {a_k}_{k \mathop \in A}$.

label: Definition:Extension of Sequence/Negative Integers
snippet: A sequence on $\N$ can be extended to the negative integers. Let $\sequence {a_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ and $\sequence {b_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ be sequences on $\N$. Let $a_0 = b_0$. Let $c_k$ be defined as: $\quad \forall k \in \Z: c_k = \begin {cases} a_k & : k \ge 0 \\ b_{-k} : & k \le 0 \end {cases}$ Then $\sequence {c_k}_{k \mathop \in \Z}$ extends (or is an extension of) $\sequence {a_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ to the negative integers.

label: Definition:Exterior
snippet: Topology and metric spaces: The exterior of a subset of a topological space: The interior of the complement. Exterior Derivative Plane Geometry: Exterior Angle of Polygon Exterior Angle of Transversal Complex Analysis: Exterior Point (Complex Analysis) Exterior of Jordan Curve

label: Definition:Exterior (Topology)
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq T$.

label: Definition:Exterior (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The exterior of $H$ in $T$ is the complement of the closure of $H$ in $T$.

label: Definition:Exterior (Topology)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq T$. The exterior of $H$ in $T$ is the interior of the complement of $H$ in $T$.

label: Definition:Exterior (Topology)/Notation
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The exterior of $H$ in $T$ can be denoted: $\map {\mathrm {Ext} } H$ $H^e$ The first is regarded by some as cumbersome, but has the advantage of being clear. $H^e$ is neat and compact, but has the disadvantage of being less intuitive. On , the notation of choice is $H^e$.

label: Definition:Exterior Derivative
snippet: Let an exact $n$-form $\omega$ be given on an $m$-manifold, with local coordinates $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_m$. Let a local coordinate expression for $\omega$ be given: $\omega = \map f {x_1, \ldots, x_m} \rd x_{\map \phi 1} \wedge \d x_{\map \phi 2} \wedge \cdots \wedge \d x_{\map \phi n}$ where: $\phi: \set {1, \ldots, n} \to \set {1, \ldots, m}$ is an injection which determines which coordinate vectors $\omega$ acts on. $\wedge$ denotes the wedge product.

label: Definition:Exterior Point (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the complex plane. Let $z_0 \in \C$.

label: Definition:Exterior Point (Complex Analysis)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the complex plane. Let $z_0 \in \C$. $z_0$ is an exterior point of $S$ $z_0$ has an $\epsilon$-neighborhood which is disjoint from $S$.

label: Definition:Exterior Point (Complex Analysis)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the complex plane. Let $z_0 \in \C$. $z_0$ is an exterior point of $S$ : $z_0$ is not an interior point of $S$ and: $z_0$ is not a boundary point of $S$.

label: Definition:Exterior of Circle
