snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle embedded in the plane whose radius is $r$ and whose center is at $O$. The exterior of $\CC$ is the set of points in the plane whose distance from $O$ is (strictly) greater than $r$.

label: Definition:External Angle Bisector/Also defined as
snippet: == External Angle Bisector: Also defined as == Some sources define an external (angle) bisector the exterior angle of a triangle or other polygon.

label: Definition:External Direct Product
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {T, \circ_2}$ be algebraic structures. The (external) direct product $\struct {S \times T, \circ}$ of $\struct {S, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {T, \circ_2}$ is the set of ordered pairs: $\struct {S \times T, \circ} = \set {\tuple {s, t}: s \in S, t \in T}$ where the operation $\circ$ is defined as: $\tuple {s_1, t_1} \circ \tuple {s_2, t_2} = \tuple {s_1 \circ_1 s_2, t_1 \circ_2 t_2}$

label: Definition:Extraordinary Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Then $S$ is an extraordinary set : $S \in S$ That is, $S$ is an element of itself.

label: Definition:Extremal Embedding in Field of Functional
snippet: Let $J$ be a functional such that: $\ds J \sqbrk {\mathbf y} = \int_a^b \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'} \rd x$ Let $\gamma$ be an extremal of $J$. Let $R$ be a simply connected open region which contains $\gamma$ as a subset. Let a field of functional $J$ be defined at every point of $R$. Let one of the trajectories of the field be $\gamma$. Then $\gamma$ can be embedded in a field of functional $J$.

label: Definition:Extremal Length
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a set of rectifiable curves in the complex plane $\C$. We consider conformal metrics of the form $\map \rho z \cmod {\d z}$, where: $\rho: \C \to \hointr 0 \to$ is Borel measurable and: the area $\ds \map A \rho := \iint \rho^2 \paren {x + i y} \rd x \rd y$ is finite and positive. Every $\gamma \in \Gamma$ has a distance function with respect to such a metric, defined by: $\ds \map L {\gamma, \rho} := \int_\gamma \map \rho z \size {\d z}$ We define: $\ds \map L {\Gamma, \rho} := \inf_{\gamma \mathop \in \Gamma} \map L {\gamma, \rho}$ and: $\ds \map \lambda \Gamma := \sup_\rho…

label: Definition:Extremally Disconnected Hausdorff Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is an extremally disconnected Hausdorff space : {{item||$\struct {S, \tau}$ is an extremally disconnected space}} {{item||$\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space.}}

label: Definition:Extremally Disconnected Hausdorff Space/Also known as
snippet: == Extremally Disconnected Hausdorff Space: Also known as == An extremally disconnected Hausdorff space is referred to by some sources as an extremally disconnected space. Such sources generally do not consider the concept of such a space not being $T_2$ (Hausdorff). However, follows such authorities that allow for the latter.

label: Definition:Extremally Disconnected Space/Also defined as
snippet: == Extremally Disconnected Space: Also defined as == Some sources, in their definition of an extremally disconnected space, impose the condition that such a space must also be $T_2$ (Hausdorff). prefers to maintain the distinction, and raises the concept of an extremally disconnected Hausdorff space.

label: Definition:Extremally Disconnected Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is extremally disconnected the closure of every open set of $T$ is open.

label: Definition:Extremally Disconnected Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is extremally disconnected the interior of every closed set of $T$ is closed.

label: Definition:Extremally Disconnected Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is extremally disconnected the closures of every pair of open sets which are disjoint are also disjoint.

label: Definition:Extreme Point of Convex Set
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $K$ be a convex subset of $X$.

label: Definition:Extreme Point of Convex Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $K$ be a convex subset of $X$. We say that $a$ is an extreme point of $K$ : whenever $a = t x + \paren {1 - t} y$ for $t \in \openint 0 1$, we have $x = y = a$.

label: Definition:Extreme Point of Convex Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $K$ be a convex subset of $X$. We say that $a$ is an extreme point of $K$ : $K \setminus \set a$ is convex.

label: Definition:Extreme Set
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $K$ be a convex subset of $X$. Let $M \subseteq K$ be a non-empty closed set. We say that $M$ is an extreme set in $K$ : whenever $x, y \in K$ and $t \in \openint 0 1$ have $t x + \paren {1 - t} y \in M$ we have $x, y \in M$.

label: Definition:Extreme Value/Series
snippet: Let $s$ be a series: $\ds s := \sum_{n \mathop \ge 1} a_n = a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + \cdots$ for some sequence $\sequence {a_n}$. An extreme value of $s$ is either: the first term of $s$ or: the last term of $s$.

label: Definition:Extremum/Functional
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of mappings. Let $J \sqbrk y: S \to \R$ be a functional. Let $y, \hat y: \R \to \R$ be real functions. Suppose for $y = \hat y \paren x$ there exists a neighbourhood of the curve $y = \hat y \paren x$ such that the difference $J \sqbrk y - J \sqbrk {\hat y}$ does not change its sign in this neighbourhood. Then $y = \hat y$ is called a (relative) extremum of the functional $J$.

label: Definition:Extremum of Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $x \in S$ be such that $\map f x$ is an extremum of $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq}$. Then $x$ is known as an extremum of $f$.

label: Definition:F-Homomorphism
snippet: Let $R, S$ be rings with unity. Let $F$ be a subfield of both $R$ and $S$. Then a ring homomorphism $\varphi: R \to S$ is called an $F$-homomorphism if: $\forall a \in F: \map \phi a = a$ That is, $\phi \restriction_F = I_F$ where: $\phi \restriction_F$ is the restriction of $\phi$ to $F$ $I_F$ is the identity mapping on $F$.

label: Definition:F-Sigma Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. An $F_\sigma$ set ($F$-sigma set) is a set which can be written as a countable union of closed sets of $T$.

label: Definition:F-Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $K$. We say that $\struct {X, \tau}$ is an $F$-space there exits a metric $d$ on $X$ such that: $(1): \quad$ $\tau$ is induced by $d$ $(2): \quad$ $d$ is an invariant metric $(3): \quad$ $\struct {X, d}$ is a complete metric space. With $d$ as above, we may also say $\struct {X, d}$ is an $F$-space.

label: Definition:F-Test
snippet: The $F$-test is a coefficient whose purpose is to check for equality of variances of $2$ populations. In an analysis of variance: the null hypothesis is that two components estimate the same variance the alternative hypothesis is that the numerator component estimates a greater variance. The latter occurrence is indicated by a high $F$ value. It can also be used to test the acceptance of the hypothesis that two samples are from normal distributions with the same variance.

label: Definition:FPS/Volume/Cubic Foot
snippet: == Cubic Inch == The cubic foot is the FPS base unit of volume. It is defined as the volume contained by a cube whose edges are $1$ foot long.

label: Definition:FPS/Volume/Cubic Inch
snippet: == Cubic Inch == The cubic inch is an FPS and imperial unit of volume. It is defined as the volume contained by a cube whose edges are $1$ inch long.

label: Definition:Face
snippet: Graph Theory: The faces of a planar graph are the areas which are surrounded by edges. Solid Geometry: The faces of a polyhedron or the faces of another solid figure are the surfaces that form its extremities. The faces of a polyhedral angle: each of the planes bounded by its defining half-lines.

label: Definition:Face-Centered Cubic Lattice
snippet: 300px A face-centered cubic lattice is a set of points in Cartesian $3$-space whose coordinates are of the form: $\tuple {\dfrac 1 2 a x, \dfrac 1 2 a y, \dfrac 1 2 a z}$ such that: $a$ is a positive real constant $x$, $y$ and $z$ are all integers $x + y + z$ is an even integer.

label: Definition:Face of Simplex
snippet: Let $\sigma$ be a $k$-simplex. Let $\sigma_k$ denote the set of $k + 1$ vertices of $\sigma$. Let $r \in \Z_{>0}$ such that $r < k$. A face of $\sigma$ is an $r$-simplex consisting of a subset of $r + 1$ elements of $\sigma_k$ .

label: Definition:Factor Analysis
snippet: Factor analysis is a technique used in statistics which aims to express: $p$ observed random variables as linear functions of $m$ factors, where $m < p$ plus a term representing error or residual variation. There exist several specifications of the basic problem. Estimation requires a knowledge of the covariance matrix of the observations.

label: Definition:Factorable Polynomial
snippet: A factorable polynomial is a polynomial which can be expressed as the product of $2$ or more factors, other than itself and a constant.

label: Definition:Factorial
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer.

label: Definition:Factorial/Also known as
snippet: == Factorial: Also known as == While the canonical vocalisation of $n!$ is $n$ factorial, it can often be found referred to as $n$ bang or (usually by schoolchildren) $n$ shriek. Some mathematicians prefer $n$ gosh. Some early sources favour factorial $n$.

label: Definition:Factorial/Definition 1
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. The factorial of $n$ is defined inductively as: $n! = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 0 \\ n \paren {n - 1}! & : n > 0 \end {cases}$

label: Definition:Factorial/Definition 2
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. The factorial of $n$ is defined as: {{eqn | l = n! | r = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n k | c = }} {{eqn | r = 1 \times 2 \times \cdots \times \paren {n - 1} \times n | c = }} where $\ds \prod$ denotes continued product.

label: Definition:Factorial/Historical Note
snippet: The symbol $!$ used on for the factorial, which is now universal, was introduced by in his $1808$ work . Before that, various symbols were used whose existence is now of less importance. Notations for $n!$ in history include the following: $\sqbrk n$ as used by $\mathop{\Pi} n$ as used by $\left\lvert {\kern-1pt \underline n} \right.$ and $\left. {\underline n \kern-1pt} \right\rvert$, once popular in England and Italy. In fact, was using $\left\lvert {\kern-1pt \underline n} \right.$ as recently as the $1920$s. It can sometimes be seen rendered as $\lfloor n$.

label: Definition:Factorial/Multiindices
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be a multiindex, indexed by a set $J$ such that for each $j \in J$, $\alpha_j \ge 0$. Then we define: $\ds \alpha! = \prod_{j \mathop \in J} \alpha_j!$ where the factorial on the right is a factorial of natural numbers. Note that by definition, all but finitely many of the $\alpha_j$ are zero, so the product over $J$ is convergent.

label: Definition:Factorial Number System/Also known as
snippet: == Factorial Number System: Also known as == The factorial number system is also known as factoradic. Some sources use the misnomer factorial base, despite the fact that the factorials do not act as a number base. Category:Definitions/Factorial Number System

label: Definition:Factorion
snippet: A factorion (base $b$) is a positive integer which, when expressed in base $b$, equals the sum of the factorials of its digits. When the number base is not given, base $10$ is assumed.

label: Definition:Factorization of Matrix
snippet: Factorization of a matrix $\mathbf A$ is the representation of $\mathbf A$ as the product of $2$ or more matrices.

label: Definition:Fair/Coin
snippet: A fair coin is a coin which has an equal probability of landing heads or tails, that is, $\dfrac 1 2$.

label: Definition:Fair/Die
snippet: A fair die is a die whose physical properties are such that the probabilities of showing each of its faces are equal. That is, for a conventional $6$-sided die, the probabilities are all $\dfrac 1 6$.

label: Definition:Faithful Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is faithful for all objects $C_1, C_2$ of $\mathbf C$: $F: \map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {C_1, C_2} \to \map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D} } {F C_1, F C_2}, \ f \mapsto F f$ is an injection. Here $\operatorname{Hom}$ signifies a hom class.

label: Definition:Faithful Group Action
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\phi: G \times X \to X$ be a group action: $\forall \tuple {g, x} \in G \times X: g * x := \map \phi {g, x} \in X$

label: Definition:Faithful Group Action/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\phi: G \times X \to X$ be a group action: $\forall \tuple {g, x} \in G \times X: g * x := \map \phi {g, x} \in X$ $\phi$ is faithful $e$ is the only element if $G$ which acts trivially: $\forall g \in G: \paren {\forall x \in X: g * x = x \implies g = e}$

label: Definition:Faithful Group Action/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$. Let $X$ be a set. Let $\phi: G \times X \to X$ be a group action. $\phi$ is faithful its permutation representation is injective.

label: Definition:Faithful Linear Representation of Group
snippet: Let $ \struct {K, +, \circ}$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$ of finite dimension. Let $\GL V$ be the general linear group of $V$. Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a finite group. Let $\rho : G \to \GL V$ be a linear representation of $G$ on $V$. Then $\rho$ is faithful the kernel of $\rho$ is trivial.

label: Definition:Fallacy
snippet: A (logical) fallacy is a mistake caused by an application of an invalid argument. Logical fallacies abound. Most of the documented fallacies that can be found in the literature arise from linguistic imprecision or deliberately misleading statements, or both. Frequently the commission of fallacies is as deliberate as the telling of lies.

label: Definition:Falling Factorial
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number (but usually an integer). Let $n$ be a positive integer. Then $x$ to the (power of) $n$ falling is: $\ds x^{\underline n} := \prod_{j \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {x - j} = x \paren {x - 1} \cdots \paren {x - n + 1}$

label: Definition:False
snippet: A statement has a truth value of false what it says does not match the way that things are.

label: Definition:Family of Curves
snippet: A family of curves is a set of curves which are described with a common equation, in such a way that all such curves can be generated by varying one or more parameters.

label: Definition:Family of Curves/One-Parameter
snippet: Consider the implicit function $\map f {x, y, c} = 0$ in the cartesian $\tuple {x, y}$-plane where $c$ is a constant. For each value of $c$, we have that $\map f {x, y, z, c} = 0$ defines a relation between $x$ and $y$ which can be graphed in the cartesian plane. Thus, each value of $c$ defines a particular curve. The complete set of all these curve for each value of $c$ is called a one-parameter family of curves.

label: Definition:Family of Curves/Parameter
snippet: The parameters of a family of curves $\FF$ is a set of real numbers which, when varied, generate all the elements of $\FF$.

label: Definition:Family of Probability Distributions
snippet: A family of probability distributions is a set of probability distributions with the same general probability density function, differing by one or more parameters.

label: Definition:Family of Probability Distributions/Parameter
snippet: Let $\PP$ be a probability distribution of a particular family. A parameter of $\PP$ is a constant that determines the specific properties of $\PP$.

label: Definition:Family of Surfaces
snippet: A family of surfaces is a set of surfaces which are described with a common equation, in such a way that all such surfaces can be generated by varying one or more parameters.

label: Definition:Family of Surfaces/One-Parameter
snippet: Consider the implicit function $\map f {x, y, z, c} = 0$ in the Cartesian $3$-space where $c$ is a constant. For each value of $c$, we have that $\map f {x, y, z, c} = 0$ defines a relation between $x$, $y$ and $z$ which can be graphed in cartesian $3$-space. Thus, each value of $c$ defines a particular surface. The complete set of all these surfaces for each value of $c$ is called a one-parameter family of surfaces.

label: Definition:Family of Surfaces/Parameter
snippet: The parameters of a family of surfaces $\FF$ is a set of real numbers which, when varied, generate all the elements of $\FF$.

label: Definition:Fano Plane
snippet: The Fano plane is the finite projective plane of order $2$. It can be denoted: $\operatorname {PG} \left({2, 2}\right)$ where: $\operatorname {PG}$ stands for projective geometry the first parameter $2$ specifies the dimension the second parameter $2$ specifies the order. $\operatorname {PG} \left({2, 2}\right)$ has the following properties: It has $7$ points It has $7$ lines There are $3$ points on each line There are $3$ lines through each point. 400px

label: Definition:Farey Sequence
snippet: A Farey sequence is a chain of subsets of the reduced rational numbers lying in $\Q \cap \closedint 0 1$. For $Q \in \Z_{>0}$, the Farey set $F_Q$ is the set of all reduced rational numbers with denominators not larger than $Q$: $F_Q = \set {\dfrac p q: p = 0, \ldots, Q,\ q = 1, \ldots, Q,\ p \perp q}$ where $p \perp q$ denotes that $p$ and $q$ are coprime.

label: Definition:Farey Sequence/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Farey Sequence == The Farey sequence was first exploited by in $1801$ in creating tables of the decimal expansions for all vulgar fractions whose denominators are less than $100$. In order to make sure he captured them all, he used a technique exploiting the properties of the mediant that originated with . Some $15$ years later, rediscovered this property, and published a paper on the subject. This was subsequently picked up on by , who reproved the results of while crediting with the technique.

label: Definition:Farey Sequence/Order
snippet: Let $F_Q$ denote the Farey sequence of all reduced rational numbers with denominators not larger than $Q$: $F_Q = \set {\dfrac p q: p = 0, \ldots, Q,\ q = 1, \ldots, Q,\ p \perp q}$ The index $Q$ is called the order of $F_Q$.

label: Definition:Farthest Point
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $H \subseteq A$ be a subset of $A$. Let $p \in A \setminus H$ be a point of $M$ outside $H$ such that: the distance from $p$ to the nearest point in $A$ is greater than for any other point in $A \setminus H$. Then $p$ is the farthest point from $A$.

label: Definition:Fast Fourier Transform
snippet: The fast Fourier transform is a way of evaluating the discrete Fourier transform in a number of operations proportional to $n \ln n$ for a sequence of $n$ points.

label: Definition:Feasible Region
snippet: The feasible region of a linear programming exercise is an area of a graphical presentation in which the points represent solution which fulfil the constraints.

label: Definition:Feasible Solution
snippet: A feasible solution to a linear programming exercise is a point within the feasible region.

label: Definition:Feigenbaum Constants
snippet: The Feigenbaum constants are a pair of real constants which arise in bifurcation theory.

label: Definition:Fermat-Torricelli Point
snippet: Let $ABC$ be a triangle. The Fermat-Torricelli Point is defined to be the point $P$ which minimizes the following quantity: $AP + BP + CP$ which is the total distance from the three vertices to point $P$.

label: Definition:Fermat Number
snippet: A Fermat number is a natural number of the form $2^{\paren {2^n} } + 1$, where $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$. The number $2^{\paren {2^n} } + 1$ is, in this context, often denoted $F_n$.

label: Definition:Fermat Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fermat Number == In $1640$, wrote to that $2^n + 1$ is composite if $n$ is divisible by an odd prime. He also observed that the first $5$ numbers of the form $2^{2^n} + 1$ are all prime. This led him to propose the Fermat Prime Conjecture: that all numbers of this form are prime. On being unable to prove it, he sent the problem to , with the note: I wouldn't ask you to work at it if I had been successful. Pascal unfortunately did not take up the challenge.

label: Definition:Fermat Prime
snippet: A Fermat prime is a Fermat number, that is a number of the form $2^{\paren {2^n} } + 1$, which happens to be prime. In fact, $2^{\paren {2^n} } + 1$ is prime for $n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$. However, $2^{\paren {2^5} } + 1 = 2^{32} + 1$ is divisible by $641$, as was proved by . No Fermat prime for $n > 4$ has ever been discovered.

label: Definition:Fermat Prime/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Fermat Primes == The sequence of Fermat primes begins: {{eqn | l = 2^{\paren {2^0} } + 1 | r = 3 }} {{eqn | l = 2^{\paren {2^1} } + 1 | r = 5 }} {{eqn | l = 2^{\paren {2^2} } + 1 | r = 17 }} {{eqn | l = 2^{\paren {2^3} } + 1 | r = 257 }} {{eqn | l = 2^{\paren {2^4} } + 1 | r = 65 \, 537 }} No other Fermat primes are known.

label: Definition:Fermat Pseudoprime
snippet: Let $q$ be a composite number such that $\exists n \in N: n^q \equiv n \pmod q$. Then $q$ is a Fermat pseudoprime to base $n$.

label: Definition:Fermat Pseudoprime/Base 4/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == The Dictionary $217$

label: Definition:Fermat Pseudoprime/Base 5
snippet: Let $q$ be a composite number such that $5^q \equiv 5 \pmod q$. Then $q$ is a Fermat pseudoprime to base $5$.

label: Definition:Fermat Pseudoprime/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fermat Pseudoprime == From as far back as the ancient Chinese, right up until the time of , it was thought that $n$ had to be prime in order for $2^n - 2$ to be divisible by $n$. This used to be used as a test for primality. But it was discovered that $2^{341} \equiv 2 \pmod {341}$, and $341 = 31 \times 11$ and so is composite.

label: Definition:Fermat Set
snippet: The Fermat set is the set of integers: $\left\{ {1, 3, 8, 120}\right\}$ It has the property of being a Diophantine quadruple.

label: Definition:Fermi Coordinates
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $P \subseteq M$ an embedded $p$-dimensional submanifold. Let $\pi : NP \to P$ be the normal bundle of $P$ in $M$. Let $V \subseteq NP$ be an open subset. Let $E$ be the normal exponential map. Let $U \subseteq M$ be the normal neighborhood such that $U = \map E V$. Let $\struct {W_0, \psi}$ be a smooth coordinate chart for $P$. Let $\tuple {E_1, \ldots, E_{n - p}}$ be a local orthonormal frame for $NP$. Let $\hat W_0 = \map \psi {W_0} \subseteq \R^p$.

label: Definition:Ferrier's Prime/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Ferrier's Prime == Ferrier's prime was discovered in $1951$ by using a manual desk calculator. It is generally considered to have been the highest known prime at the time, having $44$ digits. However, it was eclipsed by $180 \times \paren {2^{127} - 1} + 1$ ($79$ digits), discovered in the same month by and of Cambridge University. Exactly which was discovered first is debated, but 's is traditionally determined as being earlier. Both were then well and truly superseded in $1952$, when discovered the prime nature of $2^{521} - 1$ and a number of others.

label: Definition:Feuerbach Circle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. The Feuerbach circle of $\triangle ABC$ is the circle which passes through each of the $9$ points: the feet of the altitudes of $\triangle ABC$ the midpoints of the sides of $\triangle ABC$ the midpoints of the lines from the vertices of $\triangle ABC$ to the orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$. 500px

label: Definition:Feuerbach Circle/Also known as
snippet: == Feuerbach Circle: Also known as == The Feuerbach circle of a triangle is also known as the nine point circle or nine-point circle.

label: Definition:Fiber Bundle
snippet: Let $M, E, F$ be topological spaces. Let $\pi: E \to M$ be a continuous surjection. Let $\UU := \set {U_\alpha \subseteq M: \alpha \in I}$ be an open cover of $M$ with index set $I$. Let $\pr_{1, \alpha}: U_\alpha \times F \to U_\alpha$ be the first projection on $U_\alpha \times F$. Let there exist homeomorphisms: $\chi_\alpha: \map {\pi^{-1} } {U_\alpha} \to U_\alpha \times F$ such that for all $\alpha \in I$: $\pi {\restriction}_{U_\alpha} = \pr_{1, \alpha} \circ \chi_\alpha$ where $\pi {\restriction}_{U_\alpha}$ is the restriction of $\pi$ to $U_\alpha \in \UU$.

label: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Also known as
snippet: == Fiber Bundle: Also known as == Some sources refer to a fiber bundle just as a bundle. Some sources use the term twisted product. By an abuse of language, it is common to say that $E$ is a fiber bundle over $M$. One also finds the formulation Let $E \overset \pi \to M$ be a fiber bundle in the literature.

label: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Base Point
snippet: Let $M$ be the base space of a fiber bundle $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$. A point $m \in M$ is called a base point of $B$.

label: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Base Space
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. The topological space $M$ is called the base space of $B$.

label: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Bundle Projection
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. The continuous surjection $\pi: E \to M$ is called the bundle projection of $B$.

label: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Fiber Bundle == In British English, the word fibre is used instead of fiber. Category:Linguistic Notes

label: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Model Fiber
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. The topological space $F$ is called the model fiber of $B$.

label: Definition:Fiber Bundle/System of Local Trivializations
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. Let $\UU = \set {U_\alpha \subseteq M: \alpha \in I}$ be an open cover of $M$ with index set $I$. Let $\struct {U_\alpha, \chi_\alpha}$ be local trivializations for all $\alpha \in I$. The set $\set {\struct {U_\alpha, \chi_\alpha}: \alpha \in I}$ is called a system of local trivializations of $E$ on $M$.

label: Definition:Fiber Bundle/Total Space
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. The topological space $E$ is called the total space of $B$.

label: Definition:Fiber of Truth/Also known as
snippet: == Fiber of Truth: Also known as == The fiber of truth is often referred to also as the solution set for $P$. This is particularly the case in algebraic contexts. Some sources denote the fiber of truth under $P$ as $\sqbrk {\size P}$.

label: Definition:Fiber of Truth/Solution
snippet: Let $P: X \to \set {\T, \F}$ be a propositional function defined on a domain $X$. Let $P$ be in the form of an equation in the context of algebra. Let $S = \map {P^{-1} } \T$ be the fiber of truth (under $P$). Then an element of $S$ is known as a solution of $P$.

label: Definition:Fibonacci-Like Sequence
snippet: Let $A = \tuple {a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n - 1} }$ be an ordered tuple of numbers. The Fibonacci-like sequence formed from $A$ is defined as: $\map {F_A} k = \begin {cases} \qquad \qquad a_k & : 0 \le k < n \\ & \\ \ds \sum_{k - n \mathop \le j \mathop < k} a_j & : k \ge n \end {cases}$ That is, apart from the first $n$ terms, every term is the sum of the previous $n$ terms. The main term can also be expressed as: $\map {F_A} k = 2 \map {F_A} {k - 1} - \map {F_A} {k - n}$

label: Definition:Fibonacci Multiplication
snippet: Fibonacci multiplication is an operation on the positive integers using Zeckendorf representation, also known as the Fibonacci number system. Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers expressed in Zeckendorf representation as: {{eqn | l = a | o = := | r = \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^k F_{c_i} | c = where $c_i \ge 2$ for all $i$ }} {{eqn | l = b | o = := | r = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^l F_{d_j} | c = where $d_j \ge 2$ for all $j$ }} where $F_n$ denotes the $n$th Fibonacci number.

label: Definition:Fibonacci Number
snippet: The Fibonacci numbers are a sequence $\sequence {F_n}$ of integers which is formally defined recursively as: $F_n = \begin {cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ 1 & : n = 1 \\ F_{n - 1} + F_{n - 2} & : \text {otherwise} \end {cases}$ for all $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$. That is, the next integer in the sequence is found by adding together the two previous ones.

label: Definition:Fibonacci Number/Also known as
snippet: == Fibonacci Numbers: Also known as == According to some sources, the Fibonacci sequence is also known as Lamé's Sequence, after . However, this suggestion is difficult to corroborate. The notation for the $n$th Fibonacci number is not universally standardised. In much professional literature, $u_n$ is used. $F_n$ tends to appear more in amateur publications, but $F_n$ is rapidly taking over as standard. $F_n$ is the notation used in . Category:Definitions/Fibonacci Numbers

label: Definition:Fibonacci Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fibonacci Numbers == famously discussed this sequence in his , in the context of breeding pairs of rabbits. Hence the name Fibonacci numbers, which was given to this sequence by , who studied them in detail. The sequence $\sequence {F_n}$ was known to Indian mathematicians as long ago as the $7$th century C.E. It was also studied by before $1135$, and by in about $1150$. Hence some sources refer to these numbers as the Gopala-Hemachandra numbers. They are also discussed by in his work of $1611$ De Nive Sexangula (On the Six-Cornered Snowflake).

label: Definition:Fibonacci Number/Negative
snippet: The definition of Fibonacci numbers for negative integers is an extension of the definition for positive integers: $F_n = \begin{cases} 0 & : n = 0 \\ 1 & : n = 1 \\ F_{n + 2} - F_{n + 1} & : n for all $n \in \Z$.

label: Definition:Fibonacci Prime
snippet: A Fibonacci prime is a Fibonacci number which happens to be prime.

label: Definition:Fibonacci Prime Pair
snippet: A Fibonacci prime pair is a pair of Fibonacci numbers $F_p$ and $F_{p + 2}$ such that: $p$ and $p + 2$ are both prime numbers $F_p$ and $F_{p + 2}$ are both prime numbers.

label: Definition:Fibonacci String
snippet: Consider the alphabet $\set {\text a, \text b}$. For all $n \in \Z_{>0}$, let $S_n$ be the (finite) string formed as: $S_n = \begin {cases} \text a & : n = 1 \\ \text b & : n = 2 \\ S_{n - 1} S_{n - 2} & : n > 2 \end{cases}$ where $S_{n - 1} S_{n - 2}$ denotes that $S_{n - 1}$ and $S_{n - 2}$ are concatenated. The terms of the sequence $\sequence {S_n}$ are Fibonacci strings.

label: Definition:Fibonacci String/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fibonacci String == The sequence of Fibonacci strings was first studied by in the $18$th century. It was later studied by in the $19$th century, and by many mathematicians since then.

label: Definition:Fibonomial Coefficient
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ and $k \in \Z$. Then the Fibonomial coefficient $\dbinom n k$ is defined as: $\dbinom n k_\FF = \begin{cases} 0 & : n k \\ 1 & : n \ge 0, k = 0 \\ \dfrac {F_n F_{n - 1} \cdots F_{n - k + 1} } {F_k F_{k - 1} \cdots F_1} = \ds \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^k \dfrac {F_{n - k + j} } {F_j} & : \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ where $F_n$ denotes the $n$th Fibonacci number.

label: Definition:Fiducial Theory
snippet: Fiducial theory is a branch of statistics which studies the effectiveness of fiducial inference.

label: Definition:Field
snippet: Abstract Algebra: Field (Abstract Algebra): A non-trivial division ring whose ring product is commutative. Relation Theory: Field of Relation The union of the domain of a relation with its image. Calculus: Field of Integration: The set of values over which a multiple integral is defined. Physics: Field (Physics): A physical quantity associated with every point of spacetime. Linear Algebra: Vector Field

label: Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be an algebraic structure.

label: Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be an algebraic structure. $\struct {F, +, \times}$ is a field : $(1): \quad$ the algebraic structure $\struct {F, +}$ is an abelian group $(2): \quad$ the algebraic structure $\struct {F^*, \times}$ is an abelian group where $F^* = F \setminus \set {0_F}$ $(3): \quad$ the operation $\times$ distributes over $+$.

label: Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)/Product
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a field. The distributive operation $\times$ in $\struct {F, +, \times}$ is known as the (field) product.

label: Definition:Field (Physics)
snippet: A field, in the context of physics, is a region of space which is acted on by a point-function. That is, in which a physical quantity is associated with every point of spacetime. The physical quantity in question may be either in vector or scalar form.

label: Definition:Field Automorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \circ}$ be a field. Let $\phi: F \to F$ be a (field) isomorphism from $F$ to itself. Then $\phi$ is a field automorphism.

label: Definition:Field Epimorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {K, \oplus, *}$ be fields. Let $\phi: R \to S$ be a (field) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a field epimorphism $\phi$ is a surjection.

label: Definition:Field Extension
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. A field extension over $F$ is a field $E$ where $F \subseteq E$. That is, such that $F$ is a subfield of $E$. This can be expressed: $E$ is a field extension over a field $F$ or: $E$ over $F$ is a field extension as: $E / F$ is a field extension. $E / F$ can be voiced as $E$ over $F$.

label: Definition:Field Extension/Complex
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a subfield of $\struct {\C, +, \times}$, the field of complex numbers. Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be complex numbers, in or not in $F$. Then $\map F {X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n}$ is the smallest field extension over $F$ containing $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$. Category:Definitions/Field Extensions

label: Definition:Field Extension/Degree
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension of a field $F$. The degree of $E / F$, denoted $\index E F$, is the dimension of $E / F$ when $E$ is viewed as a vector space over $F$.

label: Definition:Field Extension/Degree/Finite
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension of a field $F$. $E / F$ is a finite field extension its degree $\index E F$ is finite.

label: Definition:Field Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ and $\struct {K, \oplus, \otimes}$ be fields. Let $\phi: F \to K$ be a mapping such that both $+$ and $\times$ have the morphism property under $\phi$. That is, $\forall a, b \in F$: {{eqn | n = 1 | l = \map \phi {a + b} | r = \map \phi a \oplus \map \phi b }} {{eqn | n = 2 | l = \map \phi {a \times b} | r = \map \phi a \otimes \map \phi b }} Then $\phi: \struct {F, +, \times} \to \struct {K, \oplus, \otimes}$ is a field homomorphism.

label: Definition:Field Norm/Definition 1
snippet: Let $K$ be a field and $L / K$ a finite field extension of $K$. Let $\alpha \in L$. By Vector Space on Field Extension is Vector Space, $L$ is naturally a finite dimensional vector space over $K$. Let $\theta_\alpha$ be the linear operator: $\theta_\alpha: L \to L: \beta \mapsto \alpha \beta$ The field norm $\map {N_{L/K} }\alpha$ of $\alpha$ is the determinant of $\theta_\alpha$.

label: Definition:Field Norm/Definition 2
snippet: Let $K$ be a field and $L / K$ a finite field extension of $K$. Let $\alpha \in L$. Let $L / K$ be Galois. By Finite Field Extension has Finite Galois Group, the Galois group $\Gal {L / K}$ is finite. The field norm $\map {N_{L / K}} \alpha$ of $\alpha$ is $\ds \prod_{\sigma \mathop \in \Gal {L / K}} \map \sigma \alpha$.

label: Definition:Field Norm of Complex Number
snippet: Let $z = a + i b$ be a complex number, where $a, b \in \R$. Then the field norm of $z$ is written $\map N z$ and is defined as: $\map N z := \cmod \alpha^2 = a^2 + b^2$ where $\cmod \alpha$ denotes the complex modulus of $\alpha$.

label: Definition:Field Norm of Quaternion
snippet: Let $\mathbf x = a \mathbf 1 + b \mathbf i + c \mathbf j + d \mathbf k$ be a quaternion. Let $\overline {\mathbf x}$ be the conjugate of $\mathbf x$. The (field) norm of $\mathbf x$ is the real number defined as: $\map n {\mathbf x} := \size {\mathbf x \overline {\mathbf x} } = \size {\overline {\mathbf x} \mathbf x} = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2$

label: Definition:Field Strength
snippet: Let $P$ be a point in a conservative field $V$. The field strength $\map {\mathbf g} {\mathbf r}$ of $V$ at $P$ is given by: {{eqn | l = \map {\mathbf g} {\mathbf r} | o = := | r = \pm \map \nabla \phi | c = $\pm$ according to sign convention adopted }} {{eqn | r = \dfrac {\partial \phi} {\partial x} \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial \phi} {\partial y} \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial \phi} {\partial z} \mathbf k | c = }} where: $\phi$ denotes the potential at $P$ $\mathbf r$ denotes the position vector of $P$: $\mathbf r = \tuple {x, y, z}$ $\map \nabla \phi$ denotes the gradient of $\phi$ $\tuple…

label: Definition:Field Theory
snippet: Field theory is a branch of abstract algebra which studies fields and other related algebraic structures.

label: Definition:Field of Complex Numbers
snippet: The field of complex numbers $\struct {\C, +, \times}$ is the set of complex numbers under the two operations of addition and multiplication.

label: Definition:Field of Integers Modulo Prime
snippet: Let $p \in \Bbb P$ be a prime number. Let $\Z_p$ be the set of integers modulo $p$. Let $+_p$ and $\times_p$ denote addition modulo $p$ and multiplication modulo $p$ respectively. The algebraic structure $\struct {\Z_p, +_p, \times_p}$ is the field of integers modulo $p$.

label: Definition:Field of Integration
snippet: A field of integration is a set of values over which a multiple integral is defined.

label: Definition:Field of P-adic Numbers
snippet:
Let $p$ be any prime number. Let $
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p$ be the $p$-adic norm on the rationals $\Q$. Let $\CC$ be the commutative ring of Cauchy sequences over $\struct {\Q, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$. Let $\NN$ be the set of null sequences in $\struct {\Q, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$. Let $\Q_p$ denote the quotient ring $\CC \,  ig / \NN$. The field of $p$-adic numbers is the field $\Q_p$. For any Cauchy sequence $\sequence{x_n}$ in $\struct{\Q, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$, let $\eqclass{x_n}{}$ denote the left coset of $\sequence{x_n}$ in $\Q_p$.

label: Definition:Field of Quotients/Also known as
snippet: == Field of Quotients: Also known as == Since the construction of the field of quotients $F$ from an integral domain $D$ mirrors the construction of the rationals from $\Z$, $F$ is sometimes called the field of fractions or fraction field of $D$. Some sources prefer the term quotient field, but this can cause confusion with similarly named but unrelated concepts. Common notations include $\map {\operatorname {Frac} } D$, $\map Q D$ and $\map {\operatorname {Quot} } D$.

label: Definition:Field of Rational Fractions
snippet: Let $R$ be an integral domain.

label: Definition:Field of Rational Numbers
snippet: The field of rational numbers $\struct {\Q, + \times, \le}$ is the set of rational numbers under the two operations of addition and multiplication, with an ordering $\le$ compatible with the ring structure of $\Q$. When the ordering $\le$ is subordinate or irrelevant in the context in which it is used, $\struct {\Q, +, \times}$ is usually seen.

label: Definition:Field of Real Numbers
snippet: The field of real numbers $\struct {\R, +, \times, \le}$ is the set of real numbers under the two operations of addition and multiplication, with an ordering $\le$ compatible with the ring structure of $\R$. When the ordering $\le$ is subordinate or irrelevant in the context in which it is used, $\struct {\R, +, \times}$ is usually seen.

label: Definition:Field of Relation
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. The field of $\RR$ is defined as: $\Field \RR := \set {x \in S: \exists t \in T: \tuple {x, t} \in \RR} \cup \set {x \in T: \exists s \in S: \tuple {s, x} \in \RR}$ That is, it is the union of the domain of $\RR$ with its image.

label: Definition:Fields Medal
snippet: The Fields Medal is the highest award of the , for "oustanding achievement in mathematics". It is a gold medal, awarded once every $4$ years at its , using the funds remaining after the financing of the in in $1924$. It is awarded to no fewer than $2$ and no more than $4$ mathematicians, usually under $40$ years of age. The medals stem from a bequest by , who wanted to provide an award comparable to the in stature. It was his intention to stress the international nature of mathematics, and stated that there should not be attached to the medals: the name of any country, institution or person.

label: Definition:Fifth Power
snippet: A fifth power is an integer which can be expressed as the $5$th power of an integer. The sequence of fifth powers begins: $0, 1, 32, 243, 1024, 3125, 7776, 16807, 32768, 59049, 100000, 161051, \ldots$

label: Definition:Fifth Root/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R_{\ge 0}$ be a positive real number. The fifth root of $x$ is the real number defined as: $x^{\paren {1 / 5} } := \set {y \in \R: y^5 = x}$ where $x^{\paren {1 / 5} }$ is the $5$th root of $x$. The notation: $y = \sqrt [5] x$ is usually encountered.

label: Definition:Figurate Number
snippet: A figurate number is loosely defined as a (natural) number corresponding to a set of objects which can be arranged in a geometric pattern (in an arbitrary number of dimensions, but usually $2$ or $3$).

label: Definition:Figure (Number)
snippet: A figure is a symbol or combination of symbols representing a number.

label: Definition:Filter
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. A subset $\FF \subseteq S$ is called a filter of $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ (or a filter on $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$) $\FF$ satisfies the filter axioms:

label: Definition:Filter Basis
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ denote the power set of $S$.

label: Definition:Filter Basis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\BB \subset \powerset S$ such that $\O \notin \BB$ and $\BB \ne \O$. Then $\FF := \set {V \subseteq S: \exists U \in \BB: U \subseteq V}$ is a filter on $S$ : $\forall V_1, V_2 \in \BB: \exists U \in \BB: U \subseteq V_1 \cap V_2$ Such a $\BB$ is called a filter basis of $\FF$.

label: Definition:Filter Basis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\BB$ be a subset of a filter $\FF$ on $S$ such that $\BB \ne \O$. Then $\BB$ is a filter basis of $\FF$ : $\forall U \in \FF: \exists V \in \BB: V \subseteq U$

label: Definition:Filter Basis/Generated Filter
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\BB \subset \powerset S$ be a filter basis of a filter $\FF$ on $S$. $\FF$ is said to be generated by $\BB$.

label: Definition:Filter Generated by Net
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\struct {\Lambda, \preceq}$ be a directed set. Let $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ be a net. For each $\lambda_0 \in \Lambda$, let $B_{\lambda_0} = \set {x_\lambda : \lambda \succeq \lambda_0}$. Let $\BB = \set {B_{\lambda_0} : \lambda_0 \in \Lambda}$. We define the filter generated by $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ as the filter generated by $\BB$.

label: Definition:Filter Sub-Basis
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ denote the power set of $S$. Let $\BB \subset \powerset S$ be a set of subsets of $\powerset S$ which satisfies the finite intersection property. That is, the intersection of any finite number of sets in $\BB$ is not empty. Then $\BB$, together with the finite intersections of all its elements, is a basis for a filter $\FF$ on $S$. Thus $\BB$ is known as a sub-basis for $\FF$.

label: Definition:Filter Theory
snippet: Filter theory is a branch of topology which studies filters.

label: Definition:Filter in Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a preordered set. Let $F$ be a subset of $S$. $F$ is a filter in $\struct {S, \preceq}$ : $F$ is non-empty, filtered and upper.

label: Definition:Filter on Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ denote the power set of $S$.

label: Definition:Filter on Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ denote the power set of $S$. A set $\FF \subset \powerset S$ is a filter on $S$ $\FF$ satisfies the filter on set axioms:

label: Definition:Filter on Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ denote the power set of $S$. A set $\FF \subset \powerset S$ is a filter on $S$ $\FF$ satisfies the filter on set axioms:

label: Definition:Filter on Set/Filtered Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\FF$ be a filter on $S$. Then $S$ is said to be a set filtered by $\FF$.

label: Definition:Filter on Set/Trivial Filter
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A filter $\FF$ on $S$ by definition specifically does not include the empty set $\O$. If a filter $\FF$ were to include $\O$, then from Empty Set is Subset of All Sets it would follow that every subset of $S$ would have to be in $\FF$, and so $\FF = \powerset S$. Such a "filter" is called the trivial filter on $S$.

label: Definition:Filtered Category
snippet: Let $\mathbf I$ be a category. $\mathbf I$ is filtered, when: $\mathbf I$ is not empty For every two objects $i$ and $i'$ of $\mathbf I$, there exists an object $k$ and morphisms $f: i \to k$ and $f' : i' \to k$ For every two objects $i$ and $j$ of $\mathbf I$ and every two morphisms $u : i \to j$ and $v : i \to j$, there exists an object $k$ a morphism $w : j \to k$, such that $w \circ u = w \circ v$.

label: Definition:Filtered Probability Space/Continuous Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {\mathcal F_t}_{t \ge 0}$ be a continuous-time filtration of $\Sigma$. We say that $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\mathcal F_t}_{t \ge 0}, \Pr}$ is a filtered probability space.

label: Definition:Filtered Probability Space/Discrete Time
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {\mathcal F_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a discrete-time filtration of $\Sigma$. We say that $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \sequence {\mathcal F_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}, \Pr}$ is a filtered probability space.

label: Definition:Filtered Subset
snippet: Let $\left({S, \precsim}\right)$ be a preordered set. Let $H$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. Then $H$ is a filtered subset of $S$ : $\forall x, y \in H: \exists z \in H: z \precsim x$ and $z \precsim y$

label: Definition:Final Topology
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {\struct{Y_i, \tau_i}}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of topological spaces. Let $\family {f_i: Y_i \to X}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of mappings.

label: Definition:Final Topology/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {\struct{Y_i, \tau_i}}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of topological spaces. Let $\family {f_i: Y_i \to X}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of mappings. The final topology on $X$ with respect to $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is defined as: $\tau = \set{U \subseteq X: \forall i \in I: \map {f_i^{-1}} U \in \tau_i} \subseteq \powerset X$

label: Definition:Final Topology/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {\struct{Y_i, \tau_i}}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of topological spaces. Let $\family {f_i: Y_i \to X}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed family of mappings. Let $\tau$ be the finest topology on $X$ such that each $f_i: Y_i \to X$ is $\tuple{\tau_i, \tau}$-continuous. Then $\tau$ is known as the final topology on $X$ with respect to $\family{f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$.

label: Definition:Financial Mathematics
snippet: Financial mathematics is the branch of mathematics which seeks to model financial markets valuing stock derivatives, especially stock options. It mainly uses the methods of stochastic calculus.

label: Definition:Financial Mathematics/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Financial Mathematics == The credibility of the models underlying the discipline of financial mathematics was seriously damaged in $2008$ as a result of the financial crisis. However, criticism of the subject dates back to .

label: Definition:Finer Equivalence Relation
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\equiv$ and $\sim$ be equivalence relations on $X$. Then $\equiv$ is finer than $\sim$ : $\forall x, y \in X : x \equiv y \implies x \sim y$

label: Definition:Finer Filter on Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\FF, \FF' \subset \powerset S$ be two filters on $S$. Let $\FF \subseteq \FF'$. Then $\FF'$ is finer than $\FF$.

label: Definition:Finer Filter on Set/Strictly Finer
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\FF, \FF' \subset \powerset S$ be two filters on $S$. Let $\FF \subset \FF'$, that is, $\FF \subseteq \FF'$ but $\FF \ne \FF'$. Then $\FF'$ is strictly finer than $\FF$.

label: Definition:Finer Subset (Order Theory)
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be a preordered set. Let $X, Y$ be subsets of $S$. Then $X$ is finer (subset) than $Y$ $\forall x \in X: \exists y \in Y: x \preceq y$

label: Definition:Finer Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ be topologies on $S$.

label: Definition:Finer Topology/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ be topologies on $S$. $\tau_1$ is finer than $\tau_2$ $\tau_1 \supseteq \tau_2$.

label: Definition:Finer Topology/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ be topologies on $S$. $\tau_1$ is finer than $\tau_2$ the identity mapping $\struct {S, \tau_1} \to \struct {S, \tau_2}$ is continuous.

label: Definition:Finer Topology/Strictly Finer
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ be topologies on $S$. Let $\tau_1 \supsetneq \tau_2$. $\tau_1$ is said to be strictly finer than $\tau_2$. This can be expressed as: $\tau_1 > \tau_2 := \tau_1 \supsetneq \tau_2$

label: Definition:Finite Cardinal
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be a cardinal. Then $\mathbf a$ is described as finite : $\mathbf a < \mathbf a + \mathbf 1$ where $\mathbf 1$ is (cardinal) one. That is, such that $\mathbf a \ne \mathbf a + \mathbf 1$.

label: Definition:Finite Category
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Then $\mathbf C$ is said to be a finite category both the collection of its objects $\mathbf C_0$ and the collection of its morphisms $\mathbf C_1$ are finite sets.

label: Definition:Finite Character
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $A$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $A$ has finite character for each $x \subseteq S$: $x \in A$ every finite subset of $x$ is in $A$.

label: Definition:Finite Character/Also see
snippet: == Finite Character: Also see == Tukey's Lemma, an equivalent of the Axiom of Choice Restricted Tukey's Theorem, an equivalent of the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem. Category:Definitions/Finite Character

label: Definition:Finite Character/Mappings
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\FF$ be a set of mappings from subsets of $S$ to $T$. That is, let $\FF$ be a set of partial mappings from $S$ to $T$. Then $\FF$ has finite character for each partial mapping $f \subseteq S \times T$: $f \in \FF$ for each finite subset $K$ of the domain of $f$, the restriction of $f$ to $K$ is in $\FF$.

label: Definition:Finite Character/Property of Sets
snippet: Let $P$ be a property of sets. Then $P$ has finite character for every set $x$: $x$ has property $P$ every finite subset of $x$ has property $P$.

label: Definition:Finite Complement Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set whose cardinality is usually specified as being infinite. Let $\tau$ be the set of subsets of $S$ defined as: $H \in \tau \iff \relcomp S H \text { is finite, or } H = \O$ where $\relcomp S H$ denotes the complement of $H$ relative to $S$. Then $\tau$ is the finite complement topology on $S$, and the topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a finite complement space.

label: Definition:Finite Complement Topology/Also known as
snippet: == Finite Complement Topology: Also known as == The finite complement topology is also called the cofinite topology. Some sources are more explicit about the nature of this topology, and call it the topology of finite complements. The finite complement topology can also be referred to as the minimal $T_1$ topology (on a given set). This is justified by Finite Complement Topology is Minimal $T_1$ Topology. This topology is also given by some sources as the Zariski topology, for . However, this is not recommended as there is another so named Zariski topology which is unrelated to this one.

label: Definition:Finite Complement Topology/Finite
snippet: It is possible to define the finite complement topology on a finite set $S$, but as every subset of a finite set has a finite complement, it is clear that this is trivially equal to the discrete space. This is why the finite complement topology is usually understood to apply to infinite sets only.

label: Definition:Finite Complement Topology/Uncountable
snippet: Let $S$ be an uncountable set. Let $\tau$ be the finite complement topology on $S$. Then $\tau$ is a finite complement topology on an uncountable space, and $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a uncountable finite complement space.

label: Definition:Finite Cyclic Group/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a cyclic group. Then $\struct {G, \circ}$ is a finite cyclic group it is a finite group.

label: Definition:Finite Cyclic Group/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a cyclic group generated by $a \in G$. Then $\struct {G, \circ}$ is a finite cyclic group : $\exists n \in \N: a^n = e$

label: Definition:Finite Difference Table
snippet: A finite difference table is an array which displays sequences of finite differences in an easily comprehended form.

label: Definition:Finite Dimensional Vector Space/Notation
snippet: == Finite Dimensional Vector Space: Notation == The dimension of a finite dimensional $K$-vector space $V$ is denoted $\map {\dim_K} V$, or just $\map \dim V$. Some sources use the notation $K^{\dim V}$.

label: Definition:Finite Element Method
snippet: The finite element method is a technique for approximating the solution to a partial differential equation with boundary conditions over a given domain $D$. $D$ is partitioned into elements, typically: triangles for a $2$-dimensional domain tetrahedra for a $3$-dimensional domain. On each element the solution is approximated by an appropriate function, usually a polynomial of small degree. The coefficients that define the polynomials are chosen to satisfy a best approximation criterion.

label: Definition:Finite Extended Real Number
snippet: An extended real number is defined as finite it is a real number. Category:Definitions/Real Numbers

label: Definition:Finite Game
snippet: A finite game is a game in which the set $A_i$ of moves available to player $i$ is finite for each player $i$.

label: Definition:Finite Group
snippet: A finite group is a group of finite order. That is, a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ is a finite group its underlying set $G$ is finite. That is, a finite group is a group with a finite number of elements.

label: Definition:Finite Group/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Finite Group == The theory of finite groups was effectively originated by . Some sources refer to him as the father of finite groups.

label: Definition:Finite Infima Set
snippet: Let $P = \struct{S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then finite infima set of $X$, denoted $\map {\operatorname{fininfs}} X$, is defined by $\leftset {\inf A: A \in \map {\mathit{Fin}} X \land A}$ admits an infimum$\rightset{}$ where $\map {\mathit{Fin}} X$ denotes the set of all finite subsets of $X$.

label: Definition:Finite Intersection Axiom
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $T$ be such that: Every set $V_\alpha$ of closed sets of $T$ such that $\ds \bigcap V_\alpha = \O$ contains a finite subset $V_\beta \subseteq V_\alpha$ such that $\ds \bigcap V_\beta = \O$. Then $T$ satisfies the finite intersection axiom.

label: Definition:Finite Intersection Axiom/Also presented as
snippet: == Finite Intersection Axiom: Also presented as == The finite intersection axiom can also be seen presented in the following form: Let $T$ be such that: Every set $V_\alpha$ of closed sets of $T$ for which every finite subset $V_\beta \subseteq V_\alpha$ has the property that $\ds \bigcap V_\beta \ne \O$, then $\ds \bigcap V_\alpha \ne \O$. Then $T$ satisfies the finite intersection axiom.

label: Definition:Finite Intersection Property
snippet: Let $\Bbb S$ be a non-empty set of sets. Let $\Bbb S$ have the property that: the intersection of any finite number of sets in $\Bbb S$ is not empty. Then $\Bbb S$ satisfies the finite intersection property.

label: Definition:Finite Join Preserving Mapping
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \vee_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \vee_2, \preceq_2}$ be join semilattices with smallest elements $\bot_1$ and $\bot_2$ respectively. Let $\phi: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping between the underlying sets of $L_1$ and $L_2$. Then: $\phi$ is finite join preserving, denoted $\phi:L_1 \to L_2$ $\forall$ finite $A \subseteq S_1 : \map \phi {\sup A} = \sup \set{\map \phi a : a \in A}$

label: Definition:Finite Measure
snippet: Let $\mu$ be a measure on a measurable space $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Then $\mu$ is said to be a finite measure : $\map \mu X < \infty$

label: Definition:Finite Meet Preserving Mapping
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct{S_1, \wedge_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct{S_2, \wedge_2, \preceq_2}$ be meet semilattices with greatest elements $\top_1$ and $\top_2$ respectively. Let $\phi: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping between the underlying sets of $L_1$ and $L_2$. Then: $\phi$ is finite meet preserving, denoted $\phi:L_1 \to L_2$ $\forall$ finite $A \subseteq S_1 : \map \phi {\inf A} = \inf \set{\map \phi a : a \in A}$

label: Definition:Finite Monoid
snippet: A finite monoid is a monoid whose underlying set is finite. Category:Definitions/Monoids

label: Definition:Finite Order
snippet: Abstract algebra: Finite Order of Algebraic Structure Finite Group: a group of finite order Group theory: Finite Order of Group Element

label: Definition:Finite Ordinal
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be an ordinal. Then $\alpha$ is said to be finite one of the following holds: $\alpha = \O$ $\alpha = \beta^+$ for some finite ordinal $\beta$ where $\O$ denotes the empty set, and $\beta^+$ is the successor ordinal of $\beta$.

label: Definition:Finite Partition (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\xi$ be a partition of $\Omega$. Then, $\xi$ said to be a finite partition : $\exists A_1, \ldots, A_n \in \Sigma \setminus \set \O : \xi = \set {A_1, \ldots, A_n}$

label: Definition:Finite Partition Generated by Finite Sub-Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\AA \subseteq \Sigma$ be a finite sub-$\sigma$-algebra. The finite partition generated by $\AA$ is defined as: $\ds \map \xi \AA := \set {\bigcap_{i \mathop = 1}^n B_i : B_i \in \set {A_i, \Omega \setminus A_i} } \setminus \set \O$ where $\AA = \set {A_1, \ldots, A_n}$.

label: Definition:Finite Projective Plane/Order 4
snippet: The finite projective plane of order $4$. It can be denoted: $\operatorname {PG} \left({4, 4}\right)$ where: $\operatorname {PG}$ stands for projective geometry the first parameter $2$ specifies the dimension the second parameter $2$ specifies the order. $\operatorname {PG} \left({4, 4}\right)$ has the following properties: It has $21$ points It has $21$ lines There are $5$ points on each line There are $5$ lines through each point.

label: Definition:Finite Rank Operator
snippet: Let $H, K$ be Hilbert spaces. Let $T: H \to K$ be a linear transformation. Then $T$ is said to be a finite rank operator, or of finite rank, its range, $\Rng T$, is finite dimensional. Note that a finite rank operator is not necessarily bounded.

label: Definition:Finite Real Number
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number. Then $x$ is a finite real number there exists another real number $y$ such that $\size x < \size y$.

label: Definition:Finite Ring
snippet: A finite ring is a ring $\left({R, +, \circ}\right)$ such that $R$ is a finite set. Category:Definitions/Ring Theory

label: Definition:Finite Sequence
snippet: A finite sequence is a sequence with a finite number of terms.

label: Definition:Finite Set
snippet: A set $S$ is defined as finite : $\exists n \in \N: S \sim \N_{<n}$ where $\sim$ denotes set equivalence. That is, if there exists an element $n$ of the set of natural numbers $\N$ such that the set of all elements of $\N$ less than $n$ is equivalent to $S$. Equivalently, a finite set is a set with a count.

label: Definition:Finite Set Coding
snippet: Let $A \subset \N$ be a finite subset of the natural numbers. Let $\ds n = \sum_{a \mathop \in A} 2^a$. Then $n$ codes the finite set $A$, or $n$ is the code number for the finite set $A$.

label: Definition:Finite State Machine
snippet: A finite state machine is an ordered tuple: $F = \left({ S, A, I, \Sigma, T }\right)$ where: $S$ is the (finite) set of states $A \subseteq S$ is the set of accepting states $I \in S$ is the initial state $\Sigma$ is the alphabet of symbols that can be fed into the machine $T : \left({ S \times \Sigma }\right) \rightarrow S$ is the transition function. A finite state machine operates as follows: $(1): \quad$ At the beginning, the current state $s$ of the finite state machine is $I$. $(2): \quad$ One by one, the input (a sequence of symbols from $\Sigma$) is fed into the machine.

label: Definition:Finite Sub-Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\AA \subseteq \Sigma$ be a sub-$\sigma$-algebra. Then, $\AA$ is said to be a finite sub-$\sigma$-algebra : $\exists A_1, \ldots, A_n \in \Sigma : \AA = \set {A_1, \ldots, A_n}$

label: Definition:Finite Subset
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $T$ be a subset of $S$ which is a finite set. Then $T$ is a finite subset of $S$. Category:Definitions/Subsets

label: Definition:Finite Suprema Set
snippet: Let $P = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then the finite suprema set of $X$, denoted $\map {\mathrm {finsups} } X$, is defined as: $\leftset {\sup A: A \in \map {\mathit {Fin} } X \land A}$ admits a supremum$\rightset{}$ where $\map {\mathit {Fin} } X$ denotes the set of all finite subsets of $X$.

label: Definition:Finite Topological Space
snippet: A finite topological space is a topological space whose underlying set is finite.

label: Definition:Finitely Branching
snippet: Let $T$ be a tree. Then $T$ is finitely branching $T$ is locally finite.

label: Definition:Finitely Generated Field Extension
snippet: Let $E / F$ be a field extension. Then $E$ is said to be finitely generated over $F$ , for some $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in E$: $E = F \left({\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n}\right)$ where $F \left({\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n}\right)$ is the field in $E$ generated by $F \cup \left\{{\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n}\right\}$.

label: Definition:Finitely Generated Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be a module over $R$. Then $M$ is finitely generated there is a generator for $M$ which is finite.

label: Definition:First-Countable Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a first-countable space every point in $S$ has a countable local basis.

label: Definition:First-Fit Decreasing Packing Algorithm
snippet: The first-fit decreasing packing algorithm is a refinement of the first-fit packing algorithm for solving the bin packing problem. The algorithm proceeds as follows: $(1): \quad$ Sort the boxes into decreasing height $(2): \quad$ Apply the first-fit packing algorithm. Hence the largest boxes are packed first, and it is more likely to produce an optimal solution than the first-fit packing algorithm.

label: Definition:First-Fit Packing Algorithm
snippet: The first-fit packing algorithm is an algorithm for solving the bin packing problem. The algorithm proceeds as follows: $(1): \quad$ Number the bins into arbitrary order $(2): \quad$ Select the boxes in arbitrary order $(3): \quad$ For each box, place it into the lowest-numbered bin it will fit into.

label: Definition:First-Order Property of Sets
snippet: A first-order property of sets is a property defined by a logical formula whose domain is entirely over sets. Thus the quantifiers $\forall x$ and $\exists x$ are valid when $x$ is a set, but $\forall A$ and $\exists A$ are not valid when $A$ is a class. Hence we allow, for example: $\map \phi {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n, x}$ to be a logical formula whose variables $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ represent classes, and are all free, and $x$ is the only free variable representing a set.

label: Definition:First Chebyshev Function
snippet: The first Chebyshev function is defined and denoted: $\ds \map \vartheta x := \sum_{p \mathop \le x} \ln p$ where the summation extends over all prime numbers $p$ such that $p \le x$.

label: Definition:First Fundamental Form
snippet: Let $S$ be a surface of a $3$-dimensional Euclidean space. Let $p$ be a point of $S$. Let $T_pS$ be the tangent space to $S$ at the point $p$. The first fundamental form is the bilinear form: $\operatorname I: T_p S \times T_p S \longrightarrow \R$ induced from the dot product of $\R^3$: $\map {\operatorname I} {x, y} = \innerprod x y$ The first fundamental form is a way to calculate the length of a given line $C \subset S$ or the area of a given bounded region $R \subset S$.

label: Definition:First Order Logic with Identity
snippet: A system of first order logic with identity is a system of predicate logic with the following elements in its alphabet:

label: Definition:First Order Ordinary Differential Equation
snippet: A first order ordinary differential equation is an ordinary differential equation in which any derivatives with respect to the independent variable have order no greater than $1$. The general first order ODE can be written as: $\map F {x, y, \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} }$ or, using prime notation: $\map F {x, y, y'}$ If it is possible to do so, then it is often convenient to present such an equation in the form: $\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = \map f {x, y}$ that is: $y' = \map f {x, y}$ It can also be seen presented in the form: $\map \phi {x, y, y'} = 0$

label: Definition:First Order Ordinary Differential Equation/Also known as
snippet: == First Order Ordinary Differential Equation: Also known as == A first order ordinary differential equation is often seen referred to just as a first order differential equation by sources which are not concerned about partial differential equations. Some sources hyphenate: first-order differential equation. The abbreviation ODE is frequently seen, hence first order ODE for first order ordinary differential equation.

label: Definition:First Principles
snippet: A proof is constructed from first principles when no reliance is made on other established theorems.

label: Definition:Fischer-Griess Monster
snippet: The Fischer-Griess monster $\mathrm M$ is the automorphism group of the Griess algebra.

label: Definition:Fit
snippet: Consider a mathematical model $\MM$, often in the context of statistics. The fit of $\MM$ is the degree of correspondence between observations in the real world and the behaviour predicted by $\MM$.

label: Definition:Five-Number Summary
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of observations of a quantitative variable. The five-number summary of $S$ consists of:

label: Definition:Fixed-Point Representation
snippet: Fixed-point representation is a technique for representing an approximation to a real number $x$ in a given number base $\beta$ by presenting it by means of a fixed number of digits with: a fixed number of digits before the radix point to hold the integer part of $x$ a fixed number of digits after the radix point to hold the fractional part of $x$.

label: Definition:Fixed Element under Permutation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\pi: S \to S$ be a permutation on $S$. Let $x \in S$. $x$ is fixed under $\pi$ : $\map \pi x = x$

label: Definition:Fixed Element under Permutation/Moved
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\pi: S \to S$ be a permutation on $S$. Let $x \in S$. $x$ moved by $\pi$ : $\map \pi x \ne x$

label: Definition:Fixed Element under Permutation/Set of Fixed Elements
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\pi: S \to S$ be a permutation on $S$. The set of elements of $S$ which are fixed by $\pi$ can be denoted $\Fix \pi$. Note that: $x \notin S \implies x \in \Fix \pi$

label: Definition:Fixed Field
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. Let $G \le \Aut F$ be a subgroup of the automorphism group of $F$. The fixed field of $G$ is the set: $\Fix G = \set {f \in F : \forall \sigma \in G : \map \sigma f = f}$

label: Definition:Fixed Point
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Then a fixed point of $S$ under $f$ is an element $x \in S$ such that $\map f x = x$.

label: Definition:Fixed Point (Physics)
snippet: A fixed point is a point in space which is constrained to be stationary some specified frame of reference. Category:Definitions/Physics Category:Definitions/Mechanics

label: Definition:Fixed Point Theorem
snippet: A fixed point theorem is a theorem that gives conditions under which a continuous mapping $f: S \to S$ is guaranteed to have at least one fixed point, that is: $\exists x \in S: \map f x = x$ The following are examples:

label: Definition:Fixed Point Theorem/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fixed Point Theorem == Fixed point theorems have shown themselves to have considerable importance in the development of the mathematics of economics.

label: Definition:Flasque Sheaf of Sets on Topological Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\FF : \map {\mathbf {Ouv} } X^{\mathrm {op} } \to \mathbf {Set}$ be a sheaf of sets on $X$. $\FF$ is flasque for all open subsets $V \subset U \subset X$, the restriction map $\map{\FF}{U} \to \map{\FF}{V}$ is surjective. Category:Definitions/Sheaf Theory

label: Definition:Flat (Matroid)
snippet: Let $M = \struct{S, \mathscr I}$ be a matroid. Let $\rho : \powerset S \to \Z$ be the rank function of $M$. A subset $A \subseteq S$ is a flat of $M$ : $\forall x \in S \setminus A : \map \rho {A \cup \set x} = \map \rho A + 1$

label: Definition:Flat Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. $M$ is called the flat Riemannian manifold it is locally isometric to an Euclidean Space. That is, for every point $p \in M$ there is a neighborhood that is isometric to an open set in $\R^n$ with the Euclidean metric.

label: Definition:Fleenor-Heronian Triangle
snippet: A Fleenor-Heronian triangle is a Heronian triangle whose sides have lengths form a set of $3$ consecutive integers.

label: Definition:Fleenor-Heronian Triangle/Sequence
snippet: The sequence of Fleenor-Heronian triangles begins: $\paren {1, 2, 3}$ $\paren {3, 4, 5}$ $\paren {13, 14, 15}$ $\paren {51, 52, 53}$ $\paren {193, 194, 195}$ $\paren {723, 724, 725}$ $\paren {2701, 2702, 2703}$ $\paren {10 \, 083, 10 \, 084, 10 \, 085}$ $\paren {37 \, 633, 37 \, 634, 37 \, 635}$ Category:Definitions/Fleenor-Heronian Triangles

label: Definition:Flexible
snippet: Abstract Algebra: Definition:Flexible Operation Physics: Definition:Flexible Chain

label: Definition:Floating-Point Operation
snippet: A floating-point operation is an arithmetic operation (addition, subtraction, multiplication or division) performed on floating-point numbers.

label: Definition:Floating-Point Representation
snippet: Floating-point representation is a technique for representing a real number $x$ in a given number base $\beta$ by presenting it uniquely in the form: $x = f \times \beta^e$ where: $f$ is a real number such that $\dfrac 1 \beta \le \size f < 1$, expressed in decimal notation $e$ is an integer.

label: Definition:Floating-Point Representation/Base
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number expressed in floating-point representation as: $x = f \times \beta^e$ where: $f$ is a real number such that $\dfrac 1 \beta \le \size f < 1$, expressed in decimal notation $e$ is an integer. The number $\beta$ is known as the base of the floating-point representation.

label: Definition:Floating-Point Representation/Computer Implementation
snippet: == Floating-Point Representation: Computer Implementation == Implementation of floating-point representation of a real number: $x = f \times \beta^e$ is subject to the following considerations. Both the mantissa $f$ and the exponent $e$ have a limited range: $f$ is a number with $t$ digits base $\beta$ $e$ lies in an interval $\closedint L U$.

label: Definition:Floating-Point Representation/Exponent
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number expressed in floating-point representation as: $x = f \times \beta^e$ where: $f$ is a real number such that $\dfrac 1 \beta \le \size f < 1$, expressed in decimal notation $e$ is an integer. The integer $e$ is known as the exponent of the floating-point representation.

label: Definition:Floating-Point Representation/Mantissa
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number expressed in floating-point representation as: $x = f \times \beta^e$ where: $f$ is a real number such that $\dfrac 1 \beta \le \size f < 1$, expressed in decimal notation $e$ is an integer. The real number $f$ is known as the mantissa of the floating-point representation.

label: Definition:Floating-Point Representation/Normalized
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number implemented in floating-point representation as: $x = f \times \beta^e$ such that: $x = \pm \sqbrk {0.f_1 f_2 \ldots f_t} \times \beta^e$ This representation is said to be normalized $f_1 \ne 0$.

label: Definition:Floating Point Representation
snippet: Floating point representation is a technique whereby numbers are held in a digital computer in standard scientific notation.

label: Definition:Floating Point Representation/Examples/CRAY-1
snippet: == Example of Floating Point Representation == In the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cray-1 CRAY-1] supercomputer, a number is held in floating point representation in a total of $64$ bits, of which $15$ bits hold the exponent.

label: Definition:Floor Function
snippet: right Let $x$ be a real number. Informally, the floor function of $x$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$.

label: Definition:Floor Function/Also known as
snippet: == Floor Function: Also known as == The floor function of a real number $x$ is usually just referred to as the floor of $x$. The floor function is sometimes called the entier function, from the French for integer. The floor of $x$ is also often referred to as the integer part or integral part of $x$, particularly in older treatments of number theory. Some sources give it as the greatest integer function.

label: Definition:Floor Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number. The floor function of $x$ is defined as the supremum of the set of integers no greater than $x$: $\floor x := \sup \set {m \in \Z: m \le x}$ where $\le$ is the usual ordering on the real numbers.

label: Definition:Floor Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The floor function of $x$, denoted $\floor x$, is defined as the greatest element of the set of integers: $\set {m \in \Z: m \le x}$ where $\le$ is the usual ordering on the real numbers.

label: Definition:Floor Function/Definition 3
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number. The floor function of $x$ is the unique integer $\floor x$ such that: $\floor x \le x < \floor x + 1$

label: Definition:Floor Function/Notation
snippet: Before around $1970$, the usual symbol for the floor function was $\sqbrk x$. The notation $\floor x$ for the floor function is a relatively recent development. Compare the notation for the corresponding ceiling function, $\ceiling x$, which in the context of discrete mathematics is used almost as much. Some sources use $\map {\mathrm {fl} } x$ for the floor function of $x$. However, this notation is clumsy, and will not be used on .

label: Definition:Flow Chart
snippet: A flow chart is a graphical depiction of an algorithm in which the steps are depicted in the form of boxes connected together by arrows. Let $F$ and $P$ be sets. Let $C = \struct {V, E}$ be a finite digraph. Let $V$ be divided into pairwise disjoint sets $\tuple {V_F, V_P, V_J, V_I, V_O}$. These are assigned specific terms: $V_F$ are the functional boxes $V_P$ are the predicative boxes $V_J$ are the junctions $V_I$ are the entry points $V_O$ are the exit points Let each $b \in V_F$ be assigned a unique $F_b \in F$, and each $b \in V_P$ be assigned a unique $P_b \in P$.

label: Definition:Flow Chart/Graphical Representation
snippet: == Flow Chart: Graphical Representation == Conventionally, the shape of the box representing a step is dependent upon the type of operation encapsulated within the step: Rectangular for an action, represented by a functional box. A different shape, conventionally a diamond, for a condition, represented by a predicative box. On , the preferred shape for condition boxes is rectangular with rounded corners. This is to maximise ease and neatness of presentation: configuring a description inside a diamond shaped boxes in order for it to be aesthetically pleasing can be challenging and tedious.

label: Definition:Flow Chart/Interpretation
snippet: Let $C = \struct {F, P, V, E}$ be a flow chart. Let $X$ be a set. For each $g \in F$, let $f_g : X \to X$ be a partial mapping on $X$. For each $q \in P$, let $p_q \subseteq X_q \subseteq X$ be a unary relation defined on a subset $X_q$ of $X$. Then, $\struct {X, \set {f_g}, \set {p_q}}$ is an interpretation for $C$.

label: Definition:Fluid/Ideal
snippet: An ideal fluid is a fluid which delivers a damping force whose magnitude is proportional to the velocity of a body passing through it.

label: Definition:Fluid Mechanics
snippet: Fluid mechanics is the branch of mechanics concerned with the behaviour of fluids.

label: Definition:Fluid Mechanics/Also defined as
snippet: == Fluid Mechanics: Also defined as == Some sources define fluid mechanics to be specifically the branch of mechanics concerned with the behaviour of fluids in motion. That is, what on is defined as being hydrodynamics.

label: Definition:Flux
snippet: Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field which acts on a region of space $R$. Let $S$ be a surface embedded in $R$. The flux through $S$ is the dot product of $\mathbf V$ with the vector area of $S$. Hence flux is a scalar quantity.

label: Definition:Flux/Informal Definition
snippet: Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field which acts on a region of space $R$. Let $S$ be a surface embedded in $R$. The concept of flux is most easily pictured in the context of the flow of fluids. Let there be a fluid whose flow is defined by the vector $\mathbf v$. Imagine a small loop of wire enclosing an area element $\delta S$ placed in the fluid, perpendicular to the direction of $\mathbf v$. The flux $F$ of fluid through $\delta S$ is the rate of flow of fluid through the loop.

label: Definition:Flux/Total
