snippet: Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field which acts on a region of space $R$. Let $S$ be a surface embedded in $R$. The total flux through $S$ is the surface integral over $S$ of the dot product of $\mathbf V$ with the vector area of $S$: $F = \ds \int_S \mathbf V \cdot \rd S$ where $\d S$ is an infinitesimal area element of $S$.

label: Definition:Focal Chord
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a conic section. A focal chord of $\KK$ is a chord of $\KK$ which passes through a focus of $\KK$.

label: Definition:Focal Radius
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a conic section. Let $P$ be a point on $\KK$. A line segment between $P$ and a focus of $\KK$ is called a focal radius of $\KK$.

label: Definition:Focus
snippet: Geometry: Focus of Conic Section Focus of Ellipse Focus of Parabola Focus of Hyperbola

label: Definition:Focus/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Focus == The word focus is of Latin origin, hence its irregular plural form foci. It was introduced into geometry by when he established his First Law of Planetary Motion. The word in Latin means fireplace or hearth, which is appropriate, considering the position of the sun. The pronunciation of foci has a hard c, and is rendered approximately as foke-eye. Beware the solecism of pronouncing it fo-sigh, which is incorrect. The form of focus is focal.

label: Definition:Foiaș Constant/Second
snippet: Let $x_1 \in \R_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive real number. Let: $x_{n + 1} = \paren {1 + \dfrac 1 {x_n} }^n$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ The second Foiaș constant is defined as the unique real number $\alpha$ such that if $x_1 = \alpha$ then the sequence $\sequence {x_{n + 1} }$ diverges to infinity. No closed-form expression is known.

label: Definition:Following Term
snippet: Let $P = a \circ b$ be an expression. The term $b$ is known as the following term of $P$.

label: Definition:Foot per Second Squared/Also known as
snippet: == Foot per Second Squared: Also known as == The foot per second squared is also seen referred to as the foot per second per second. This logically arises as its definition as the acceleration that causes a change in velocity of $1$ foot per second over the course of $1$ second. Category:Definitions/Foot per Second Squared

label: Definition:Force
snippet: A force is an influence which causes a body to undergo a change in velocity. Force is a vector quantity.

label: Definition:Force/Also known as
snippet: == Force: Also known as == Some writers and thinkers subdivide the idea of a force into a push or a pull, but such a dichotomy can serve to confuse the fact that they are in fact both forces. Some treatments of physics and applied mathematics refer to a force as an action, and refer to the opposite force as the reaction to that action.

label: Definition:Force Field
snippet: A force field is a vector field in which the physical quantity associated with every point is a non-contact force which applies to a body placed at that point.

label: Definition:Force Polygon
snippet: Let a system of forces $\SS$ act at a point. Let $\SS$ consist of the forces $\mathbf F_1, \mathbf F_2, \ldots, \mathbf F_n$, represented by directed line segments $A_0 A_1, A_1 A_2, \ldots, A_{n - 1} A_n$. The polygon $A_0 A_1 \ldots A_n A_0$ is called the force polygon representing $\SS$. The resultant of $\SS$ is represented by the directed line segment $A_0 A_n$.

label: Definition:Forecast Function
snippet: Let $T$ be a time series. Let $S$ denote the range of $T$. Let $L$ denote the set of lead times of $T$. Let $t$ denote the origin of $T$. A forecast function $\hat z_t : L \to S$ is a function which provides forecasts of the future values of $T$ at the lead times $L$. The objective is to make the mean squares of the deviations $z_{t + l} - \map {\hat z_t} l$ as small as possible for each lead time $l$. In the above: $\map {\hat z_t} l$ denotes the forecast value of the observation at the timestamp of lead time $l$ $z_{t + l}$ denotes the actual value of the observation at the timestamp of $l$.

label: Definition:Forest/Also defined as
snippet: == Forest: Also known as == Some sources demand that a forest cannot consist of just one tree: that is, that a forest is always disconnected.

label: Definition:Forest/Definition 1
snippet: A forest is a simple graph whose components are all trees.

label: Definition:Fork
snippet: Let $T$ be a complete $\LL$-theory. Let $\mathfrak C$ be a monster model for $T$. Let $A$ be a subset of the universe of $\mathfrak C$. Let $\map \pi {\bar x, \bar b}$ be a set of $\LL$-formulas with free variables $\bar x$ and parameters $\bar b$ from the universe of $\mathfrak C$. $\map \pi {\bar x, \bar b}$ forks over $A$ it implies some disjunction $\map {\phi_1} {\bar x, \bar c_1} \vee \cdots \vee \map {\phi_n} {\bar x, \bar c_n}$ where each $\map {\phi_i} {\bar x, \bar c_i}$ divides over $A$.

label: Definition:Forking Extension
snippet: Let $T$ be a complete $\LL$-theory. Let $\mathfrak C$ be a monster model for $T$. Let $A\subseteq B$ be subsets of the universe of $\mathfrak C$. Let $\map p {\bar x}$ be a complete $n$-type over $B$. Denote by $p \restriction A$ the subset of $p$ consisting of those formulas which involve only parameters from $A$. $p$ is a forking extension of $p \restriction A$ $\map p {\bar x}$ forks over $A$. Category:Definitions/Model Theory for Predicate Logic

label: Definition:Form
snippet: A form is a homogeneous polynomial in $2$ or more variables.

label: Definition:Form/Order
snippet: The order of a form is the number of sets of variables it has.

label: Definition:Formal Calculation
snippet: Formal calculation is a calculation, often involving power series, which is purely algebraic in nature, such that questions of convergence is not considered.

label: Definition:Formal Derivative of Polynomial
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $R \sqbrk X$ be the polynomial ring over $R$. Let $f = a_0 + a_1 X + \cdots + a_n X^n \in R \sqbrk X$. The formal derivative $f'$ of $f$ is the polynomial: $\map {f'} X = a_1 + 2 a_2 X + \cdots + n a_n X^{n - 1}$ Category:Definitions/Polynomial Theory

label: Definition:Formal Fallacy
snippet: A formal fallacy is a logical argument which is rendered invalid by a flaw that can be expressed in the propositional calculus.

label: Definition:Formal Language
snippet: A formal language is a structure $\LL$ which comprises: A set of symbols $\AA$ called the alphabet of $\LL$ A collation system with the unique readability property for $\AA$ A formal grammar that determines which collations belong to the formal language and which do not. Often, the collation system is left implicit, and taken simply to match the formal grammar.

label: Definition:Formal Language/Alphabet
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language. The alphabet $\AA$ of $\LL$ is a set of symbols from which collations in $\LL$ may be constructed. An alphabet consists of the following parts: The letters The signs. Depending on the specific nature of any particular formal language, these too may be subcategorized.

label: Definition:Formal Language/Also defined as
snippet: == Formal Language: Also defined as == Some sources state that: the alphabet $\AA$ must be a finite set for $\LL$ to be classified as a formal language the formal language can consist of any arbitrary set of strings from $\AA$.

label: Definition:Formal Semantics
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language. A formal semantics for $\LL$ comprises: A collection of objects called structures; A notion of validity of $\LL$-WFFs in these structures. Often, a formal semantics provides these by using a lot of auxiliary definitions.

label: Definition:Formal Semantics/Structure
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language. Part of specifying a formal semantics $\mathscr M$ for $\LL$ is to specify structures $\MM$ for $\mathscr M$. A structure can in principle be any object one can think of. However, to get a useful formal semantics, the structures should support a meaningful definition of validity for the WFFs of $\LL$. It is common that structures are sets, often endowed with a number of relations or functions.

label: Definition:Formal System
snippet: A formal system is a formal language $\LL$ together with a deductive apparatus for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be a formal system consisting of a formal language with deductive apparatus $\DD$. By applying the formal grammar of $\LL$, one constructs well-formed formulae in $\LL$. Of such a well-formed formula, one can then use the deductive apparatus $\DD$ to determine whether or not it is a theorem in $\FF$.

label: Definition:Formal System/Also known as
snippet: == Formal System: Also known as == A formal system is also known as: A formal theory A logical system A logical calculus A logic particularly in sources where the main application of formal systems lies in symbolic logic. On , these terms are discouraged because they provoke false conclusions about the scope of the term formal system. Some sources use the term axiomatic system, particularly when applying this technique to specific fields of mathematics. Some sources use the term logistic system, but this strictly speaking is a formal system which contains only axioms of logic.

label: Definition:Formalism
snippet: Formalism is the philosophical position that mathematics can be considered as manipulation of symbols independently of their meaning or interpretation. Hence, to a formalist, the truth value of a statement in mathematics does not depend upon whether or how it describes an independent reality. Instead, it is a game played according to a set of rules that allow the construction of sequences of symbols from other sequences of symbols. Hence the concern of a formalist is to provide proofs of consistency that prevent contradictions from being made.

label: Definition:Formation of Ordinary Differential Equation by Elimination
snippet: Let $\map f {x, y, C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_n} = 0$ be an equation: whose dependent variable is $y$ whose independent variable is $x$ $C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_n$ are constants which are deemed to be arbitrary. A differential equation may be formed from $f$ by: differentiating $n$ times $x$ to obtain $n$ equations in $x$ and $\dfrac {\d^k y} {\d x^k}$, for $k \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$ eliminating $C_k$ from these $n$ equations, for $k \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$.

label: Definition:Fort Space
snippet: Let $S$ be an infinite set. Let $p \in S$ be a particular point of $S$. Let $\tau_p \subseteq \powerset S$ be a subset of the power set of $S$ defined as: $\tau_p = \leftset {U \subseteq S: p \in \relcomp S U} \text { or } \set {U \subseteq S: \relcomp S U}$ is finite$\rightset{}$ That is, $\tau_p$ is the set of all subsets of $S$ whose complement in $S$ either contains $p$ or is finite. Then $\tau_p$ is a Fort topology on $S$, and the topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau_p}$ is a Fort space.

label: Definition:Fortissimo Space
snippet: Let $S$ be an uncountably infinite set. Let $p \in S$ be a particular point of $S$. Let $\tau_p \subseteq \powerset S$ be a subset of the power set of $S$ defined as: $\tau_p = \leftset {U \subseteq S: p \in \relcomp S U}$ or $\set {U \subseteq S: \relcomp S U}$ is countable (either finitely or infinitely)$\rightset {}$ That is, $\tau_p$ is the set of all subsets of $S$ whose complement in $S$ either contains $p$ or is countable. Then $\tau_p$ is a Fortissimo topology on $S$, and the topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau_p}$ is a Fortissimo space.

label: Definition:Forward Reparametrization of Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $I, I' \subseteq \R$ be real intervals. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Let $\phi : I' \to I$ be a diffeomorphism. Let $\tilde \gamma$ be a curve defined by: $\tilde \gamma := \gamma \circ \phi : I' \to M$ where $\circ$ denotes the composition of mappings $\gamma$ and $\phi$. Suppose $\phi$ is increasing. Then $\tilde \gamma$ is called the forward reparametrization of $\gamma$.

label: Definition:Foucault's Pendulum
snippet: Foucault's pendulum is an experiment for demonstrating the rotation of Earth about its axis. It consists of a long pendulum (of the order of tens of metres) with a heavy bob (of the order of tens of kilograms). Such a pendulum is set in motion with a small (of the order of tens of centimetres) and left to swing. It is seen that the bob swings in a plane, tracing a straight line on the floor beneath. As Earth rotates about its axis, the plane of swing remains constant. Hence the plane of swing appears to slowly rotate in the opposite direction to that of Earth.

label: Definition:Foundations of Mathematics
snippet: Foundations of mathematics is the study of the logical basis for mathematics. In particular it attempts to construct an axiomatic basis upon which mathematics can be built.

label: Definition:Foundations of Mathematics/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Foundations of Mathematics == In the early $20$th century, tried without success to establish a set of axioms that would unify the whole of mathematics.

label: Definition:Fourier Analysis
snippet: Fourier analysis is a branch of analysis which seeks to express functions (usually periodic) by means of series of sines and cosines.

label: Definition:Fourier Series/Formulation 1
snippet: Let $\alpha \in \R$ be a real number. Let $\lambda \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a function such that $\ds \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \lambda} \map f x \rd x$ converges absolutely. Let: {{eqn | l = a_n | r = \dfrac 1 \lambda \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \lambda} \map f x \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x }} {{eqn | l = b_n | r = \dfrac 1 \lambda \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \lambda} \map f x \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda \rd x }} Then: $\ds \frac {a_0} 2 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda + b_n \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda}$ is…

label: Definition:Fourier Series/Formulation 2
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R$ be real numbers. Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a function such that $\ds \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$ converges absolutely. Let: {{eqn | l = A_m | r = \dfrac 2 {b - a} \int_a^b \map f x \cos \frac {2 m \pi \paren {x - a} } {b - a} \rd x }} {{eqn | l = B_m | r = \dfrac 2 {b - a} \int_a^b \map f x \sin \frac {2 m \pi \paren {x - a} } {b - a} \rd x }} Then: $\ds \frac {A_0} 2 + \sum_{m \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {A_m \cos \frac {2 m \pi \paren {x - a} } {b - a} + B_m \sin \frac {2 m \pi \paren {x - a} } {b - a} }$ is the Fourier series for $f$.

label: Definition:Fourier Series/Fourier Coefficient
snippet: Let $\alpha \in \R$ be a real number. Let $\lambda \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a function such that $\ds \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \lambda} \map f x \rd x$ converges absolutely. Let: $\ds \frac {a_0} 2 + \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos \frac {n \pi x} \lambda + b_n \sin \frac {n \pi x} \lambda}$ be the Fourier series for $f$. The constants: $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n, \ldots; b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n, \ldots$ are the Fourier coefficients of $f$.

label: Definition:Fourier Series/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fourier Series == Despite the fact that the Fourier series bears the name of , they were first studied by . himself made considerable use of this series during the course of his analysis of the behaviour of heat. The first person to feel the need for a careful study of its convergence was . In $1829$, gave the first satisfactory proof about the sums of Fourier series for certain types of function. The criteria set by were extended and generalized by in his $1854$ paper .

label: Definition:Fourier Series/Range 2 Pi
snippet: Let $\alpha \in \R$ be a real number. Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a function such that $\ds \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \pi} \map f x \rd x$ converges absolutely. Let: {{eqn | l = a_n | r = \dfrac 1 \pi \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \pi} \map f x \cos n x \rd x }} {{eqn | l = b_n | r = \dfrac 1 \pi \int_\alpha^{\alpha + 2 \pi} \map f x \sin n x \rd x }} Then: $\dfrac {a_0} 2 + \ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {a_n \cos n x + b_n \sin n x}$ is called the Fourier series for $f$.

label: Definition:Fourier Transform of Tempered Distribution
snippet: Let $T \in \map {\SS'} \R$ be a tempered distribution. Let $\map \SS \R$ be the Schwartz space. The Fourier transform $\hat T$ of (the tempered distribution) $T$: $\hat T \in \map {\SS'} \R$ is defined as: $\forall \phi \in \map \SS \R: \map {\hat T} \phi := \map T {\hat \phi}$

label: Definition:Fourth Power
snippet: A fourth power is an integer which can be expressed as the $4$th power of an integer. The sequence of fourth powers begins: $1, 16, 81, 256, 625, 1296, 2401, 4096, 6561, 10 \, 000, 14 \, 641, \ldots$

label: Definition:Fractal
snippet: A fractal is a geometric object whose dimension is not an integer, but is instead fractional. A fractal is often generated by an infinitely repeated process It also has the property of self-similarity on all scales.

label: Definition:Fractal/Definition 1
snippet: A fractal is a set of points which has a similarity dimension or Hausdorff dimension which is not an integer.

label: Definition:Fractal/Definition 2
snippet: A fractal is a set of points whose topological dimension is strictly less than its fractal dimension.

label: Definition:Fractal Dimension
snippet: A fractal dimension is one of the extensions of the concept of dimension for which the conventional concept of (topological) dimension cannot be applied. It is often the case that the fractal dimension is not an integer.

label: Definition:Fraction
snippet: A fraction is an expression representing a quotient of one number (or expression) by another number (or expression). It is usually expressed in the form: $\dfrac a b$ or: $a / b$ where $a$ and $b$ are either numbers or expressions. The term fraction is usually encountered when $a$ and $b$ are integers. In this case, the fraction $\dfrac a b$ represents a rational number.

label: Definition:Fraction/Also defined as
snippet: == Fraction: Also defined as == Many sources define a fraction solely in the context of numbers. Specifically, a fraction in such a context will be used to denote a rational number $\dfrac a b$ such that both $a$ and $b$ are integers. Such sources will typically also demand that the fraction specifically represent a non-integer. Thus $\dfrac 3 1$ and $\dfrac 4 2$ will not be considered as actual fractions, as they represent the integers $3$ and $2$ respectively.

label: Definition:Fraction/Also known as
snippet: == Fraction: Also known as == Some sources introduce the more unwieldy term fractional number for fraction. This will be the case only when such a fraction denotes a rational number.

label: Definition:Fraction/Denominator
snippet: Let $\dfrac a b$ be a fraction. The term $b$ is known as the denominator of $\dfrac a b$.

label: Definition:Fraction/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fraction == The consideration of fraction was the next development of the concept of a number after the natural numbers. They arose as a matter of course from the need to understand the process of measurement. Hence the fraction $\dfrac p q$ was found by taking a unit length, dividing it into $q$ parts, and taking $p$ of them. The convention where a bar is placed between the numerator and denominator was introduced to the West by , following the work of the Arabic mathematicians. Previous to this, fractions were written by the Hindu mathematicians without the bar.

label: Definition:Fraction/Improper
snippet: An improper fraction is a fraction representing a rational number whose absolute value is greater than $1$. Specifically, when expressed in the form $r = \dfrac p q$, where $p$ and $q$ are integers such that (the absolute value of) the numerator is greater than (the absolute value of) the denominator: $\size p > \size q$.

label: Definition:Fraction/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Fraction == The word fraction derives from the Latin fractus meaning broken. This is in [http://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/antithesis antithesis] to the concept of integer, which derives from the Latin for untouched, in the sense of whole, or unbroken. Colloquially, informally and rhetorically, the word fraction is typically used to mean a (small) part of a whole, and not in the sense of improper fraction. Category:Linguistic Notes

label: Definition:Fraction/Mixed
snippet: A mixed fraction is a representation of a rational number whose absolute value is greater than $1$, expressed in the form $r = n \frac p q$ where: $n$ is an integer $\dfrac p q$ is a proper fraction, that is, $p$ and $q$ are integers such that $p < q$. Hence $n \frac p q$ is interpreted as $n + \dfrac p q$.

label: Definition:Fraction/Numerator
snippet: Let $\dfrac a b$ be a fraction. The term $a$ is known as the numerator of $\dfrac a b$.

label: Definition:Fraction/Proper
snippet: A proper fraction is a fraction representing a rational number whose absolute value is less than $1$, expressed in the form $r = \dfrac p q$, where $p$ and $q$ are integers. That is, such that $p < q$.

label: Definition:Fraction/Vulgar
snippet: A vulgar fraction is a fraction representing a rational number whose numerator and denominator are both integers.

label: Definition:Fractional Calculus
snippet: Fractional calculus is the branch of calculus which considers the concept of derivatives of fractional order.

label: Definition:Fractional Calculus/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fractional Calculus == The field of fractional calculus was initiated by when he assigned meaning to the concept of the derivative $\dfrac {\d^n} {\d x^n}$ for $n$ not a positive integer.

label: Definition:Fractional Ideal
snippet: Let $R$ be an integral domain with field of fractions $K$. A fractional ideal of $R$ is a subset of $K$ that is a product of an ideal $I$ with the inverse $\lambda^{-1}$ of an element of $R$: $\lambda^{-1} I = \left\{ {\lambda^{-1} a : a \in I}\right\}$

label: Definition:Fractional Part
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The fractional part of $x$ is the difference: $\fractpart x := x - \floor x$ where $\floor x$ denotes the floor of $x$. Beware, of course, not to get $\fractpart x$ confused with the singleton set containing $x$.

label: Definition:Fractional Part/Also known as
snippet: == Fractional Part: Also known as == Some sources, particularly those aimed for the grade-school and muggle market, refer to this as the decimal part, or (even worse) just the decimal. This misnomer arises from the fact that it is the part of the number after the decimal point. Burn it with fire. Category:Definitions/Fractional Parts

label: Definition:Fractional Part/Basis Expansion
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \ge 0$. Let $x$ be expressed in the number base $b$, where $b \in \N_{>1}$. In the basis expansion: $x = \sqbrk {r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0 . d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ the part $.d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots$ is known as the fractional part.

label: Definition:Frame
snippet: Lattice theory: Frame: a complete lattice that satisfies the infinite join distributive law Statistics: Sampling frame: a specification of all units in a population in sufficient detail in order that a random sample may be selected.

label: Definition:Frame-Homogeneous Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\map O M$ be the set of the disjoint union of all orthonormal frames for all tangent spaces of $M$: $\ds \map O M = \bigsqcup_{p \mathop \in M} \set {\text{all orthonormal bases for } T_p M}$ Let $\map {\operatorname {Iso}} {M, g}$ be the set of all isometries from $M$ to itself. Let $\phi$ be an isometry.

label: Definition:Frame (Lattice Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {L, \preceq}$ be a complete lattice. $\struct {L, \preceq}$ is a frame $\struct {L, \preceq}$ satisfies the infinite join distributive law:

label: Definition:Frame Adapted to Submanifold
snippet: Let $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be an $m$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $M : M \subseteq \tilde M$ be an $n$-dimensional submanifold. Let $\tilde U \subseteq \tilde M$ be an open subset. Let $E = \tuple {E_1, \ldots E_n}$ be a local frame for $\tilde M$ on $\tilde U$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at the point $p \in M$. Suppose the first $n$ vector fields of $E$ are tangent to $M$: $\forall p \in \tilde U : E_1, \ldots E_n \in T_p M$ Then $E$ is called the frame adapted to $M$.

label: Definition:Frame Homomorphism
snippet: Let $L_1 = \struct {S_1, \preceq_1}$ and $L_2 = \struct {S_2, \preceq_2}$ be frames. Let $\phi: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping between the underlying sets of $L_1$ and $L_2$. Then: $\phi$ is a frame homomorphism, denoted $\phi: L_1 \to L_2$ $\phi$ is finite meet preserving and arbitrary join preserving

label: Definition:Frame Homomorphism of Continuous Mapping
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct{S_1, \tau_1}, T_2 = \struct{S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f : T_1 \to T_2$ be a continuous mapping. Let $\map \Omega {T_1} = \struct{\tau_1, \subseteq}$ and $\map \Omega {T_2} = \struct{\tau_2, \subseteq}$ denote the frames of $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively. The frame homomorphism of $f$, denoted $\map \Omega f : \map \Omega {T_2} \to \map \Omega {T_1}$, is the inverse image mapping $f^\gets : \powerset {S_2} \to \powerset{S_1}$ restricted to $\tau_2 \times \tau_1$.

label: Definition:Frame of Reference
snippet: A frame of reference is a coordinate system which is more or less arbitrarily or conveniently disposed in a model of the physical universe. A frame of reference need not necessarily be spatial.

label: Definition:Frame of Reference/Point of Reference
snippet: A point of reference is a distinct point in a frame of reference.

label: Definition:Frame of Topological Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct{S, \tau}$ be a topological space. The frame of $T$, denoted $\map \Omega T$, is the ordered set $\struct{\tau, \subseteq}$ where $\subseteq$ denotes the subset relation on $\tau$.

label: Definition:Fredholm Operator
snippet: Let $U, V$ be vector spaces. Let $T: U \to V$ be a linear transformation. $T$ is a Fredholm operator : $(1): \quad \map \ker T$ is finite-dimensional $(2): \quad$ the quotient space $V / \Img T$ is finite-dimensional where: $\map \ker T$ denotes the kernel of $T$ $\Img T$ denotes the image of $T$.

label: Definition:Free
snippet: Abstract Algebra Definition:Free Monoid Definition:Free Commutative Monoid Definition:Free Group Definition:Free Group on Set Definition:Free Abelian Group Definition:Free Abelian Group on Set Definition:Free Module over Ring Definition:Free Module on Set Definition:Free Group Action Topology Definition:Free Loop Definition:Free Object on Set

label: Definition:Free Abelian Group
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group. $G$ is a free abelian group the $\Z$-module associated with $G$ is a free $\Z$-module. That is, $G$ is a free abelian group it has a basis over $\Z$.

label: Definition:Free Abelian Group on Set
snippet: Let $\Z$ be the additive group of integers. Let $S$ be a set. The free abelian group on $S$ is the pair $\struct {\Z^{\paren S}, \iota}$ where: $\Z^{\paren S}$ is the direct sum of $S$ copies of $\Z$. That is, of the indexed family $S \to \set {\Z}$ $\iota : S \to \Z^{\paren S}$ is the canonical mapping, which sends $s$ to the mapping $\delta_{st} \in \Z^{\paren S}$, where $\delta$ denotes Kronecker delta.

label: Definition:Free Category
snippet: Let $G$ be a digraph. The free category on $G$, denoted $\map {\mathbf C} G$, is the category with: {{DefineCategory | ob = The vertices of $G$ | mor = The walks in $G$ | comp = concatenation of walks | id = $\operatorname{id}_v$ is the empty walk at $v$ }}

label: Definition:Free Commutative Monoid
snippet: The free commutative monoid on an indexed set $X = \family {X_j: j \in J}$ is the set $M$ of all monomials under the standard multiplication. That is, it is the set $M$ of all finite sequences of $X$.

label: Definition:Free Group/Definition 1
snippet: A group $G$ is a free group it is isomorphic to the free group on some set.

label: Definition:Free Group/Definition 2
snippet: A group $G$ is a free group it has a presentation of the form $\gen S$, where $S$ is a set. That is, it has a presentation without relators.

label: Definition:Free Group/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Free Group == A free group is so called because it is free of non-trivial relations.

label: Definition:Free Group Action
snippet: Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$ acting on a set $X$. The group action is free : $\forall g \in G: \forall x \in X : g * x = x \implies g = e$

label: Definition:Free Group on Set
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. A free group on $X$ is a certain $X$-pointed group, that is, a pair $\struct {F, \iota}$ where: $F$ is a group $\iota : X \to F$ is a mapping that can be defined as follows:

label: Definition:Free Group on Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. A free group on $X$ is an $X$-pointed group $\struct {F, \iota}$ that satisfies the following universal property: For every $X$-pointed group $\struct {G, \kappa}$ there exists a unique group homomorphism $\phi : F \to G$ such that: $\phi \circ \iota = \kappa$ that is, a morphism of pointed groups $F \to G$.

label: Definition:Free Group on Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. The free group on $X$ is the pair $\struct {F, \iota}$ such that: $F$ is the group of reduced group words on $X$ $\iota : X \to F$ is the canonical injection.

label: Definition:Free Homotopy/Also known as
snippet: == Free Homotopy: Also known as == When relative homotopy is not under consideration, free homotopy is usually referred to as simply homotopy.

label: Definition:Free Idempotent Monoid
snippet: Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be a monoid which is generated by a set of elements, and such that: $\forall x \in S: x = x \circ x$ Then $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ is a free idempotent monoid. Category:Definitions/Monoids

label: Definition:Free Matroid
snippet: Let $S$ be a finite set. Let $\mathscr I = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. That is, let $\mathscr I$ be the set of all subsets of $S$: $\mathscr I := \set {X: X \subseteq S}$ Then the ordered pair $\struct {S, \mathscr I}$ is called the free matroid of $S$.

label: Definition:Free Module over Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $G$ be a unitary $R$-module. Then $G$ is described as free there exists a basis of $G$.

label: Definition:Free Monoid
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A free monoid over $S$ is a monoid $M$ together with a mapping $i: S \to M$, subject to the universal mapping property (or UMP)

label: Definition:Free Monoid/Category Theoretic Formulation
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Mon}$ be the category of monoids, and let $\mathbf{Set}$ be the category of sets. Let $\size {\cdot}$ be the underlying set functor on $\mathbf{Mon}$. Let $M \in \mathbf{Mon}_0$ be a monoid, and let $i: S \to \size {M}$ be a mapping. Then $\struct {M, i}$ is said to be a free monoid over $S$ $\struct {M, i}$ satisfies the universal mapping property:

label: Definition:Free Monoid UMP
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A monoid $M$ together with a mapping $i: S \to M$ is said to satisfy the universal mapping property (or UMP)

label: Definition:Free Monoid UMP/Property
snippet: == Property for Free Monoid UMP == For all monoids $N$, for all mappings $f: S \to N$, there is a unique monoid homomorphism $\bar f: M \to N$, such that: $\bar f \circ i = f$ Category:Definitions/Monoids

label: Definition:Free Monoid UMP (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Mon}$ be the category of monoids, and let $\mathbf{Set}$ be the category of sets. Let $\size {\cdot}$ be the underlying set functor on $\mathbf{Mon}$. Let $M \in \mathbf{Mon}_0$ be a monoid, and let $i: S \to \size {M}$ be a mapping. Then $\struct {M, i}$ is said to satisfy the universal mapping property

label: Definition:Free Monoid UMP (Category Theory)/Property
snippet: == Property for Free Monoid UMP (Category Theory) == For all $N \in \mathbf{Mon}_0$ and $f: S \to \size {N} \in \mathbf{Set}_1$, a unique $\bar f \in \mathbf{Mon}_1$ makes the following diagram commute: $\begin{xy} {\mathbf{Mon} :}, {\mathbf{Set} :}, +{M} = "M", +{N} = "N", "M";"N" **@{.} ?>*@{>} ?*!/_1em/{\bar f}, +{\size M} = "MM", +{\size N} = "NN", +{S} = "S", "MM";"NN" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/_1em/{\size {\bar f}}, "S";"MM" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/_1em/{i}, "S";"NN" **@{-} ?>*@{>} ?*!/^1em/{f} \end{xy}$ Category:Category of Monoids

label: Definition:Free Set of Sets
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a set of sets. Then $\SS$ is a free set of sets the intersection of $\SS$ is empty. That is: $\bigcap \SS = \O$

label: Definition:Free Variable
snippet: Let $x$ be a variable in an expression $E$. $x$ is a free variable in $E$ it is not a bound variable.

label: Definition:Free Variable/Also known as
snippet: == Free Variable: Also known as == A free variable is often referred to as an unknown, particularly in mathematical contexts. In the field of logic, a free variable can also be referred to as a real variable. However, this can be confused with a variable whose domain is the set of real numbers, so its use on is discouraged. The name arises in apposition to the name apparent variable, which is another name for bound variable.

label: Definition:Free Variable/Predicate Logic
snippet: In predicate logic, a free variable is a variable which exists in a WFF only as free occurrences.

label: Definition:Frege Set Theory
snippet: The Frege system of set theory is a system of axiomatic set theory which has as its sole axiom the : In support of this, the various logical axioms supporting predicate logic also hold. It is accepted that the above statement lacks clarity, but the field of symbolic logic was less well understood when this system was first defined.

label: Definition:Frequency
snippet: Physics: Frequency of Periodic Process Frequency of Simple Harmonic Motion Analysis: Frequency of Periodic Real Function Statistics Frequency (Descriptive Statistics): Absolute Frequency Relative Frequency Cumulative Frequency

label: Definition:Frequency (Physics)
snippet: Let $\map f t$ be a periodic function of time $t$. The frequency of $f$ is the number of periods of $f$ that occur during a unit time interval.

label: Definition:Frequency Analysis/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Frequency Analysis == The technique of frequency analysis was first developed in the $9$th century by Arabic mathematicians. Modern methods of cryptography, while still essentially working on ciphers, are not susceptible to frequency analysis.

label: Definition:Frequency Curve (Statistics)
snippet: A frequency curve is a smooth curve approximating a frequency polygon for a large data set.

label: Definition:Frequency Distribution
snippet: A frequency distribution is a specification of the frequencies with which values of a random variable occur. This may take the form of a frequency table. For a continuous random variable, the data will need to be grouped. It is usually presented in the form of: a table a bar chart a stem-and-leaf plot.

label: Definition:Frequency Table
snippet: A frequency table is a table which contains a summary of the absolute or relative frequencies or both for a set of observations.

label: Definition:Frequential Inference
snippet: Frequential inference is statistical inference based on the frequential theory of probability. In hypothesis testing, this leads to tests, such as the $t$-test, as to whether data provide evidence for the hull hypothesis that it comes from a population with a parameter $\theta$, for example, having some predefined fixed value $\theta_0$. The question posed and answered by this approach is: "What is the probability, given by a $p$-value, of obtaining this or a more extreme (that is, unlikely) value of a relevant statistic obtained from the observed data when the hull hypothesis holds?"

label: Definition:Frequential Theory of Probability
snippet: The frequential theory of probability regards the probability of an event as the limit of the frequency of occurrence of that event in a sequence of $n$ trials as $n \to \infty$

label: Definition:Frequentist Statistics
snippet: Frequentist statistics is a type of statistics in which the parameters of the probability distributions themselves are considered as constants.

label: Definition:Fresnel Cosine Integral Function/Also defined as
snippet: == Fresnel Cosine Integral Function: Also defined as == The Fresnel cosine integral function can also be seen defined as: $\ds \map {\operatorname C} x = \int_0^x \cos u^2 \rd u$ In the context of physics, the Fresnel cosine integral function is most often defined as: $\ds \map {\operatorname C} x = \int_0^x \map \cos {\dfrac {\pi u^2} 2} \rd u$

label: Definition:Fresnel Sine Integral Function/Also defined as
snippet: == Fresnel Sine Integral Function: Also defined as == The Fresnel sine integral function can also be seen defined as: $\ds \map {\operatorname S} x = \int_0^x \sin u^2 \rd u$ In the context of physics, the Fresnel sine integral function is most often defined as: $\ds \map {\operatorname S} x = \int_0^x \map \sin {\dfrac {\pi u^2} 2} \rd u$

label: Definition:Friction
snippet: Friction is a force whose tendency is to reduce the velocity of a body relative to its surroundings. It is caused by interaction of the matter in the body with that of the environment in which it is traveling. Friction is (at a fundamental level) an electromagnetic force. That is, bits of the medium in or on which the body is traveling get in the way (on a molecular level) of bits of the body itself. The less friction, the less the reduction in velocity. If there were no friction, then motion would continue for ever.

label: Definition:Friction/Coefficient
snippet: Let $B$ be a body at rest on a plane surface $S$ on which friction acts. Let $N$ be the normal reaction of $S$ on $B$. Let a force be applied to $B$ parallel to $S$.

label: Definition:Friction/Coefficient/Kinetic
snippet: Let $B$ be a body at rest on a plane surface $S$ on which friction acts. Let $N$ be the normal reaction of $S$ on $B$. Let a force be applied to $B$ parallel to $S$. Let $F$ be the magnitude of that force needed to keep $B$ moving at a constant velocity. Then the coefficient of kinetic friction is defined and denoted: $\mu_k = \dfrac F N$

label: Definition:Friction/Coefficient/Static
snippet: Let $B$ be a body at rest on a plane surface $S$ on which friction acts. Let $N$ be the normal reaction of $S$ on $B$. Let a force be applied to $B$ parallel to $S$. Let $F$ be the magnitude of that force in the limiting case when $B$ is just about to move. Then the coefficient of static friction is defined and denoted: $\mu_s = \dfrac F N$

label: Definition:Frobenius Endomorphism
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity of characteristic $p$. The Frobenius endomorphism on $R$ is the ring endomorphism $\Frob: R \to R$ defined as: $\forall x \in R: \map \Frob x = x^p$

label: Definition:Frobenius Endomorphism/Also defined as
snippet: == Frobenius Endomorphism: Also defined as == Some sources restrict their definition of a Frobenius endomorphism to a field with (prime) characteristic $p$.

label: Definition:Frobenius Norm
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. Let $\map \MM {m, n}$ denote the vector space of matrices of order $m \times n$ over the complex numbers $\C$.

label: Definition:Frobenius Norm/Definition 1
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. Let $\map \MM {m, n}$ denote the vector space of matrices of order $m \times n$ over the complex numbers $\C$. The Frobenius norm on $\map \MM {m, n}$ is defined and denoted as: $\forall \mathbf A \in \map \MM {m, n}: \norm {\mathbf A}_F := \sqrt {\map \tr {\mathbf A^\dagger \mathbf A} }$ where: $\tr$ denotes the trace of a matrix $\mathbf A^\dagger$ denotes the Hermitian conjugate of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Frobenius Norm/Definition 2
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. Let $\map \MM {m, n}$ denote the vector space of matrices of order $m \times n$ over the complex numbers $\C$. The Frobenius norm on $\map \MM {m, n}$ is defined and denoted as: $\forall \mathbf A \in \map \MM {m, n}: \norm {\mathbf A}_F := \sqrt {\map \tr {\mathbf A \mathbf A^\dagger} }$ where: $\tr$ denotes the trace of a matrix $\mathbf A^\dagger$ denotes the Hermitian conjugate of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Frobenius Norm/Definition 3
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. Let $\map \MM {m, n}$ denote the vector space of matrices of order $m \times n$ over the complex numbers $\C$. The Frobenius norm on $\map \MM {m, n}$ is defined and denoted as: $\forall \mathbf A \in \map \MM {m, n}: \norm {\mathbf A}_F := \ds \sqrt {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^m \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \cmod {a_{i j} }^2}$ where $a_{i j}$ denotes the $\tuple {i, j}$th element of $\mathbf A$. That is, the Frobenius norm is the square root of the sum of the squares of the moduli of all the elements of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Frobenius Number/Also defined as
snippet: == Frobenius Number: Also defined as == In their definition of a Frobenius number, some sources fail to note that $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ should be (setwise) coprime. If this is not the case, then $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ has no Frobenius number, as arbitrarily large integers which are not multiples of $\gcd \set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ exist. Category:Definitions/Frobenius Numbers

label: Definition:Fréchet Filter
snippet: Let $S$ be an infinite set. Let $\FF$ be the set of all $A \subset S$ such that $A$ is cofinite in $S$. Then $\FF$ is the Fréchet filter on $S$.

label: Definition:Fréchet Product Space
snippet: Let $\R^\omega$ denote the countable-dimensional real Cartesian space. Let: $x := \family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in \N} = \tuple {x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots}$ and: $y := \family {y_i}_{i \mathop \in \N} = \tuple {y_0, y_1, y_2, \ldots}$ denote arbitrary elements of $\R^\omega$. Let the metric $d: \R^\omega \times \R^\omega \to \R$ be applied to $\R^\omega$ as: $\forall x, y \in \R^\omega: \map d {x, y} = \ds \sum_{i \mathop \in \N} \dfrac {2^{-i} \size {x_i - y_i} } {1 + \size {x_i - y_i} }$ The metric $d$ is referred to as the Fréchet (product) metric.

label: Definition:Fréchet Space
snippet: Definition:Fréchet Space (Topology): a topological space with the property that all points are closed Definition:Fréchet Product Space: the countable-dimensional real Cartesian space with the Fréchet product metric applied. Both are concepts in the field of topology. Category:Definitions/Topology

label: Definition:Full Angle
snippet: A full angle is an angle equivalent to one full rotation.

label: Definition:Full Embedding Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $F : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. The functor $F$ is a full embedding it is: full an embedding

label: Definition:Full Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu: \Sigma \to \overline \R$ be a measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $E \in \Sigma$ be a set such that: $\map \mu {\relcomp X E} := 0$ where: $\overline \R$ denotes the extended real numbers $\relcomp X E$ denotes the complement of $E$ relative to $X$. That is, such that the measure of the complement of $E$ is a null set. Then the measure of $E$ is a full measure

label: Definition:Full Rank
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$. $\mathbf A$ is said to be of full rank its rank equals the minimum of $m$ and $n$.

label: Definition:Full Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subset S$ be a compact subspace of $T$. Then $H$ is a full set the complement of $H$ $S$ is connected in $T$.

label: Definition:Fully Faithful Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $F : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a covariant functor. $F$ is fully faithful it is both full and faithful.

label: Definition:Fully Normal Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a fully normal space :

label: Definition:Fully Normal Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a fully normal space :

label: Definition:Fully T4 Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a fully $T_4$ space every open cover of $S$ has a barycentric refinement.

label: Definition:Function
snippet: The process which is symbolised by an operation is called a function. The operand(s) of the operation can be considered to be the input(s). The output of the function is whatever the operation is defined as doing with the operand(s). A function is in fact another name for a mapping, but while the latter term is used in the general context of set theory and abstract algebra, the term function is generally reserved for mappings between sets of numbers.

label: Definition:Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Function == The term function, as used in the modern sense, was first used by in $1694$. The notation $\map f x$ itself appears to have originated with . He used it in two particular contexts: particular conventional examples like trigonometric function and powers and the like $\map y x$ for an arbitrary curve in the plane. Up until the time of , it was accepted that a function was limited to various classes of expression: a polynomial, a finite combination of elementary functions, a power series or a trigonometric series.

label: Definition:Function Space
snippet: A function space is a general concept relating to an abstract space of functions between two sets.

label: Definition:Functional
snippet: A functional is a mapping: whose domain is a set of mappings whose codomain is another set of mappings.

label: Definition:Functional/Real
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of mappings. Let $J: S \to \R$ be a mapping from $S$ to the real numbers $\R$: $\forall y \in S: \exists x \in \R: J \sqbrk y = x$ Then $J: S \to \R$ is known as a (real) functional, denoted by $J \sqbrk y$. That is, a (real) functional is a real-valued function whose arguments are themselves mappings.

label: Definition:Functional Analysis
snippet: Functional analysis is a branch of analysis, which studies vector spaces endowed a structure such as inner product, norm or topology. It can be understood as the study of analysis, including calculus, both differential and integral, to Banach spaces.

label: Definition:Functional Series/Region of Convergence
snippet: Let $S$ be a functional series of an independent variable $x$. The region of convergence of $S$ is the set of values of $x$ for which $S$ is convergent.

label: Definition:Functionally Complete
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of truth functions. Then $S$ is functionally complete all possible truth functions are definable from $S$.

label: Definition:Functor
snippet: Informally, a functor is a morphism of categories. It may be described as what one must define in order to define a natural transformation. This is formalized by defining the category of categories.

label: Definition:Functor/Co- and Contravariance
snippet: == Functor: Co- and Contravariance == Both covariant and contravariant functors are paramount in all of contemporary mathematics. The intention behind defining a functor is to formalise and abstract the intuitive notion of "preserving structure". Functors thus can be understood as a generalisation of the concept of homomorphism in all its instances. This explains why one would be led to contemplate covariant functors. However, certain "natural" operations like transposing a matrix do not preserve the structure as rigidly as a homomorphism (we do have Transpose of Matrix Product, however).

label: Definition:Functor/Covariant
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. A covariant functor $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ consists of: An object functor $F_0$ that assigns to each object $X$ of $\mathbf C$ an object $F X$ of $\mathbf D$. An arrow functor $F_1$ that assigns to each arrow $f: X \to Y$ of $\mathbf C$ an arrow $F f : F X \to F Y$ of $\mathbf D$.

label: Definition:Functor Category
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. The functor category $\map {\operatorname{Funct} } {\mathbf C, \mathbf D}$ is the category with:

label: Definition:Functor Evaluation Bifunctor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $\map {\operatorname{Funct}} {\mathbf C, \mathbf D}$ be their covariant functor category. Let $\map {\operatorname{Funct}} {\mathbf C, \mathbf D} \times \mathbf C$ be the product category. The evaluation bifunctor $\operatorname{ev}: \map {\operatorname{Funct}} {\mathbf C, \mathbf D} \times \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ is the covariant functor that sends: {{DefineFunctor |ob = an object $\tuple {F, a}$ to $\map F a$ |mor = a morphism $\tuple {\eta, f}: \tuple {F, a} \to \tuple {G, b}$ to $\map G f \circ \eta_a = \eta_b \circ \map F f$ }}

label: Definition:Fundamental Group/Also known as
snippet: == Fundamental Group: Also known as == The fundamental group of a topological space $T$ is also known more explicitly as the fundamental homotopy group of $T$. The fundamental group of $T$ is also known as the Poincaré group of $T$, for .

label: Definition:Fundamental Group/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, x_0}$ be a pointed topological space with base point $x_0$. The fundamental group $\map {\pi_1} {X, x_0}$ of $X$ at the base point $x_0$ is the set of homotopy classes of loops with base point $x_0$ with multiplication of homotopy classes of paths.

label: Definition:Fundamental Group/Definition 2
snippet: Let $* : \map {\pi_n} {X, x_0} \times \map {\pi_n} {X, x_0} \to \map {\pi_n} {X, x_0}$ denote the concatenation of homotopy classes of paths. That is, if $\overline {c_1}, \overline {c_2}$ are two elements of $\map {\pi_n} {X, x_0}$, then: $\overline {c_1} * \overline {c_2} = \overline {c_1 \cdot c_2}$ where $\cdot$ denotes the usual concatenation of paths. Then $\struct {\map {\pi_n} {X, x_0}, *}$ is the $n$th fundamental group of $X$. The first homotopy group is usually called the fundamental group when higher homotopy groups are not in sight.

label: Definition:Fundamental Group/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Fundamental Group == The concept of the fundamental group was defined by in $1895$. The definition was extended to $n > 1$ by in $1932$ and in $1935$.

label: Definition:Fundamental Group Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf{Top}^*$ be the category of pointed topological spaces. Let $\mathbf{Grp}$ be the category of groups. The fundamental group functor is the covariant functor $\pi_1 : \mathbf{Top}^* \to \mathbf{Grp}$ with:

label: Definition:Fundamental Solution
snippet: Let $\delta$ be the Dirac delta distribution. Let $D$ be a differential operator with constant coefficients. A fundamental solution is a Schwartz distribution $E \in \map {\DD'} {\R^d}$ such that: $DE = \delta$

label: Definition:Fundamental Unit (Physics)
snippet: A fundamental unit is a unit of measurement for a measurable physical property from which every other unit for that quantity can be derived. The fundamental unit for a particular measurable quantity is chosen by convention. They are the units of the fundamental dimensions of physics.

label: Definition:Furstenberg Topology
snippet: Let $\Z$ be the set of integers. Let: $\BB := \set {a \Z + b : a,b \in \Z, a \ne 0}$ where: $a \Z + b := \set {a k + b : k \in \Z}$ Let: $\tau := \set {\bigcup \AA : \AA \subseteq \BB}$ Then $\tau$ is called Furstenberg topology on $\Z$.

label: Definition:Fuzzy Logic/Historical Note/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == fuzzy logic

label: Definition:Fuzzy Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\closedint 0 1$ denote the closed unit interval. Let $\mu: S \to \closedint 0 1$ be a mapping. Then $\struct {S, \mu}$ is a fuzzy set.

label: Definition:Fuzzy Set Theory
snippet: Fuzzy set theory is a version of set theory in which the membership relation is not precisely defined. Hence the membership relation is represented by a real number between $0$ and $1$: $0$ meaning definitely not an element $1$ meaning definitely an element.

label: Definition:G-Delta Set
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A $G_\delta$ set ($G$-delta set) is a set which can be written as a countable intersection of open sets of $T$.

label: Definition:G-Module Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a group. Let $\struct {V, \phi}$ and $\struct {W, \mu}$ be $G$-modules. Then a linear transformation $f: V \to W$ is called a $G$-module homomorphism : $\forall g \in G: \forall v \in V: \map f {\map \phi {g, v} } = \map \mu {g, \map f v}$

label: Definition:G-Ordered Class
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $g$ be a progressing mapping. Let $A$ be well-ordered by the subset relation such that: Then $A$ is said to be $g$-ordered.

label: Definition:G-Statistics
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of observations of a quantitative variable. The $g$-statistics on $S$ are the statistical coefficients $g_1$ and $g_2$, defined as: $g_1$ is the skewness $\gamma_1$ of the elements of $S$ $g_2$ is the kurtosis $\gamma_2$ of the elements of $S$.

label: Definition:G-Submodule
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \cdot}$ be a finite group. Let $\struct {V, \phi}$ be a $G$-module. Let $W$ be a vector subspace of $V$. Let $\phi$ be a linear group action when restricted to $G \times W \subseteq G \times V$. Let $\phi_W$ be the restriction of $\phi$ to $G \times W$. Then $\struct {W, \phi_W}$ is called a $G$-submodule of $\struct {V, \phi}$.

label: Definition:Gal/Also known as
snippet: == Gal: Also known as == The gal is also known as the centimetre per second squared. It is also seen referred to as the centimetre per second per second. This logically arises as its definition as the acceleration that causes a change in velocity of $1$ centimetre per second over the course of $1$ second. Category:Definitions/Gal

label: Definition:Galactic Center
snippet: The galactic center is the point on the galactic equator which is taken to be the center of the (Milky Way) galaxy. It is used as the origin of the galactic coordinate system. Its agreed position in equatorial coordinates is: Right ascension: $17 \, \mathrm h \, 46 \, \mathrm {min}$ Declination: $-28 \degrees \, 56 '$

label: Definition:Galactic Coordinate System
snippet: The galactic coordinate system is an astronomical coordinate system in which measurements are based on the galactic equator. Hence a point on the celestial sphere is located by means of $2$ angular measurements: the galactic longitude $l$, which is the angular distance measured eastwards along the galactic equator from the galactic center the galactic latitude $b$, which is the angular distance measured north or south of the galactic equator.

label: Definition:Galactic Equator
snippet: The galactic equator is the great circle that is the intersection of the plane of the Milky Way with the celestial sphere.

label: Definition:Galilean Relativity
snippet: Let $O$ and $O'$ be two observers moving in ordinary $3$-dimensional space. According to Galilean relativity, $O$ and $O'$ will have coordinate systems related by: $\begin {bmatrix} t \\ \mathbf r \end {bmatrix} = \begin {bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \mathbf v & \mathbf M \end {bmatrix} \begin {bmatrix} t' \\ \mathbf r' \end {bmatrix} + \mathbf c$ where: $t$ and $t'$ are the time coordinates for $O$ and $O'$ respectively $\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf r'$ are the space coordinates for $O$ and $O'$ respectively $\mathbf v$ is the velocity of $O$ $O'$ $\mathbf M$ is a order $3$ square matrix with determinant…

label: Definition:Galilean Transformation
snippet: A Galilean transformation is a transformation between inertial frames of reference which adhere to the postulates of classical mechanics.

label: Definition:Galois Connection/Also known as
snippet: In some sources the upper adjoint is called the right adjoint and the lower adjoint is called the left adjoint. The terminology right adjoint and left adjoint is also used to denote the functors of an adjuntion in the context of category theory. So the use of the terms upper adjoint and lower adjoint for a Galois connection serves to differentiate the context of order theory from the context of category theory. The mappings are named for the position that each mapping has with respect to the orderings involved in the defining condition of Galois connection.

label: Definition:Galois Extension
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a finite field extension.

label: Definition:Galois Extension/Arbitrary
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a finite field extension. $L / K$ is a Galois extension it is normal and separable.

label: Definition:Galois Extension/Finite
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a finite field extension.

label: Definition:Galois Extension/Finite/Definition 1
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a finite field extension. $L / K$ is a (finite) Galois extension the fixed field of its automorphism group is $K$: $\map {\operatorname{Fix}_L} {\Gal {L / K} } = K$

label: Definition:Galois Extension/Finite/Definition 3
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a finite field extension $L / K$ is a (finite) Galois extension the order of the automorphism group $\Aut {L / K}$ equals the degree $\index L K$: $\order {\Aut {L / K} } = \index L K$

label: Definition:Galois Field
snippet: A Galois field $\struct {\GF, +, \circ}$ is a field such that $\GF$ is a finite set. The symbol conventionally used to denote a Galois field of $q$ elements is $\map \GF q$.

label: Definition:Galois Group of Field Extension
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. The Galois group of $L / K$ is the subgroup of the automorphism group of $L$ consisting of field automorphisms that fix $K$ point-wise: $\Gal {L / K} = \set {\sigma \in \Aut L: \forall k \in K: \map \sigma k = k}$

label: Definition:Galois Group of Field Extension/Also defined as
snippet: == Galois Group: Also defined as == More generally, we can abandon the condition that $L / K$ be Galois if we choose an algebraic closure $\overline K$ such that $L \subseteq \overline K$ and define: $\Gal {L / K} = \leftset {\sigma: L \to \overline K: \sigma}$ is an embedding of $L$ such that $\sigma$ fixes $K$ point-wise$\rightset {}$ This set will form a group $L / K$ is normal.

label: Definition:Galois Group of Field Extension/Also denoted as
snippet: == Galois Group: Also denoted as == The Galois group of $L / K$ can also be denoted $\map G {L / K}$.

label: Definition:Galois Group of Field Extension/Also known as
snippet: == Galois Group: Also known as == The Galois group of $L / K$ is also known as its automorphism group and denoted $\Aut {L / K}$. Some authors refer to $\Aut {L / K}$ as a Galois group only when $L / K$ is a Galois extension. Some sources use the notation $\map G {L \mid K}$.

label: Definition:Galois Group of Field Extension/Topological Group
snippet: The notation $\Gal {L / K}$ is also a shorthand for the topological group: $\struct {\Gal {L / K}, \tau}$ where $\tau$ is the Krull topology.

label: Definition:Galois Group of Polynomial
snippet: Let $P$ be a polynomial. The Galois group of $P$ is the symmetry group of the roots of $P$.

label: Definition:Galois Theory
snippet: Galois theory is a subfield of abstract algebra which reduces the study of field extensions to the study of the associated Galois groups. Hence it provides a connection between field theory and group theory.

label: Definition:Galois Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Galois Theory == The discipline of Galois theory dates back as far as $1600$ BCE, when the mathematicians of ancient Babylon worked out how to solve the quadratic equation. In the $16$th century, the technique leaked out into the public that the cubic equation was also soluble. Soon after that, extended this method to show how to solve the quartic. The quintic remained unsolved until the early $19$th century, at which point and proved it insoluble.

label: Definition:Gambler's Ruin
snippet: Gambler's ruin is the classic problem to determine the probability that a gambler $G$ with an initial capital of $C$ units becomes bankrupt in a sequence of games in which: $G$ gains $1$ unit of capital with probability $p$ $G$ loses $1$ unit of capital with probability $q = 1 - p$. $G$ is ruined he loses all $C$ units. There is usually a condition that $G$ stops on attaining a total fortune of $N$ units, where $N > C$.

label: Definition:Game
snippet: In the context of game theory, a game is a social situation which involves more than one person. More specifically, a game is a problem of strategy between two or more parties in which all parties involved seek (usually) to maximise their outcome. A game $G$ can be specified by: its players the moves available to each player the preference relation for each player: that is: $G = \stratgame N {A_i} {\succsim_i}$ $G$ can also be specified by: its players the moves available to each player the payoff function for each player: that is: $G = \stratgame N {A_i} {u_i}$

label: Definition:Game/Payoff
snippet: The payoff of a game is the reward or punishment made to a player at the end of the game as a result of combination of the various strategies employed. Let $G$ be a game. Let $N$ be the set of players of $G$. Let $A$ be the set of moves available to player $i \in N$. Let $u_i: A \to \R$ be a the payoff function on $A$. A payoff is the value of $u_i$ for a given $a \in A$.

label: Definition:Game/Player
snippet: Each of the parties involved in a game are called players. In the context of game theory, a player may not necessarily be a person acting alone. A group of people who are collaborating in a game, for example, the members of a football team, can be considered to be a single player.

label: Definition:Game Theory
snippet: Game theory is the branch of discrete mathematics which studies mathematical models of conflict and cooperation between intelligent rational decision-makers. Problems in game theory are a special case of those of linear programming.

label: Definition:Game Theory/Also known as
snippet: == Game Theory: Also known as == Game theory can also be seen with the name theory of games. suggests that conflict analysis or interactive decision theory might be better names, but accepts that game theory is what it is called.

label: Definition:Game Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Game Theory == The origins of the mathematical discipline of game theory can be traced to 's . Another early landmark was 's . He also stated, but failed to prove, a special case of the Fundamental Theorem of Games in his paper of . The proof was given in a lecture by , documented as . The field was properly established by and in their of $1944$, as a result of their observation that certain problems in economics were identical with those of games of strategy.

label: Definition:Gamma Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \R_{\ge 0}$. $X$ is said to have a gamma distribution if it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac {\beta^\alpha x^{\alpha - 1} e^{-\beta x} } {\map \Gamma \alpha}$ for $\alpha, \beta > 0$, where $\Gamma$ is the gamma function. This is written: $X \sim \map \Gamma {\alpha, \beta}$ {{questionable|In my Oxford dictionary, the parameters are the other way round.

label: Definition:Gamma Function/Euler Form/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Euler Form of Gamma Function == was the first to find this extension of the factorial to the real numbers. He actually specified it in the form: $\ds n! = \lim_{m \mathop \to \infty} \frac {m^n m!} {\paren{n + 1} \paren{n + 2} \cdots \paren{n + m}}$ He wrote to about it in a letter dated $13$th October $1729$.

label: Definition:Gamma Function/Graph
snippet: The graph of the gamma function is illustrated here for real arguments. The gamma function: $\map \Gamma z$ ( solid line) and $\dfrac 1 {\map \Gamma z}$ ( broken line) The gamma function: $\map \Gamma z$ ( solid line) $\dfrac 1 {\map \Gamma z}$ ( broken line)

label: Definition:Gamma Function/Weierstrass Form
snippet: The form of the gamma function is: $\ds \frac 1 {\map \Gamma z} = z e^{\gamma z} \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \paren {\paren {1 + \frac z n} e^{-z / n} }$ where $\gamma$ is the Euler-Mascheroni constant. The Weierstrass form is valid for all $\C$.

label: Definition:Gauge Theory
snippet: A gauge theory is a theory of fields in the context of physics in which the Lagrangian is invariant under local transformations according to Lie groups. The theory is a modern form of 's theory of electromagnetism.

label: Definition:Gauge Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gauge Theory == The ideas behind gauge theory have been used by to study the geometric and topological properties of $4$-dimensional spaces. He has shown that their properties are fundamentally different from spaces of lower or higher dimension.

label: Definition:Gauge Transformation
snippet: A gauge transformation is a mathematical reformulation of a physical theory that does not change the physical interpretation.

label: Definition:Gauss-Jordan Elimination
snippet: Gauss-Jordan elimination is a variant of Gaussian elimination whose effect is to reduce a given matrix $\mathbf A$ to diagonal form.

label: Definition:Gauss-Jordan Elimination/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gauss-Jordan Elimination == Gauss-Jordan elimination was invented by as a variant of Gaussian elimination. As a means of solving a system of simultaneous equations $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \mathbf b$, Gaussian elimination is preferred, as it requires much less work. When used to calculate the inverse of a square matrix, Gauss-Jordan elimination is sometimes used instead of Gaussian elimination, as they take the same amount of work.

label: Definition:Gauss Error Function
snippet: The Gauss error function is the following improper integral, considered as a real function $\erf : \R \to \R$: $\map {\erf} x = \ds \dfrac 2 {\sqrt \pi} \int_0^x \map \exp {-t^2} \rd t$ where $\exp$ is the real exponential function.

label: Definition:Gaussian Curvature
snippet: The Gaussian curvature $\Kappa$ of a surface at a point is the product of the principal curvatures, $\kappa_1$ and $\kappa_2$, at the given point: $\Kappa = \kappa_1 \kappa_2$

label: Definition:Gaussian Curvature/Also known as
snippet: == Gaussian Curvature: Also known as == The Gaussian curvature of a surface at a point is also known as the Gauss curvature. Some sources refer to it as the total curvature. Some sources refer to it as just the curvature of a surface.

label: Definition:Gaussian Curvature/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gaussian Curvature == The concept of Gaussian curvature was developed by in his $1827$ work .

label: Definition:Gaussian Elimination
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix over a field $K$. Let $\mathbf E$ be a reduced echelon matrix which is row equivalent to $\mathbf A$. The Gaussian elimination method is a technique for converting $\mathbf A$ into $\mathbf E$ by means of a sequence of elementary row operations.

label: Definition:Gaussian Elimination/Procedure
snippet: == Gaussian Elimination: Procedure == The procedure for Gaussian elimination is as follows: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix over a field $F$. Let $\mathbf E$ be a reduced echelon matrix which is row equivalent to $\mathbf A$. Let the first column of $\mathbf A$ containing a non-zero element be column $j$. Let a non-zero element in row $i$ be distinguished. This element $a_{i j} \ne 0$ is called the pivot element. Perform the elementary row operation: $(1): \quad r_1 \leftrightarrow r_i$ This moves the pivot element to $a_{1 j}$.

label: Definition:Gaussian Field
snippet: The Gaussian field is the field of Gaussian rationals under the operations of complex addition and complex multiplication.

label: Definition:Gaussian Hypergeometric Function/Also denoted as
snippet: == Gaussian Hypergeometric Function: Also denoted as == Using the notation of the generalized hypergeometric function, the Gaussian hypergeometric function can be denoted as: $\ds \map { {}_2 F_1} {a, b; c; z}$ or if necessary to draw particular attention to where it came from: $\ds \map { {}_2 F_1} { { {a, b} \atop c} \, \middle \vert \, z}$ Category:Definitions/Gaussian Hypergeometric Function

label: Definition:Gaussian Hypergeometric Function/Also known as
snippet: == Gaussian Hypergeometric Function: Also known as == The Gaussian hypergeometric function is also known as the ordinary hypergeometric function, or just the hypergeometric function Some sources refer to this as Gauss's hypergeometric function or (grammatically inaccurately) Gauss' hypergeometric function.

label: Definition:Gaussian Integer
snippet: A Gaussian integer is a complex number whose real and imaginary parts are both integers. That is, a Gaussian integer is a number in the form: $a + b i: a, b \in \Z$ The set of all Gaussian integers can be denoted $\Z \sqbrk i$, and hence can be defined as: $\Z \sqbrk i = \set {a + b i: a, b \in \Z}$ Some sources use the symbol $J$ for the set $\Z \sqbrk i$.

label: Definition:Gaussian Integer/Also known as
snippet: == Gaussian Integer: Also known as == A Gaussian integer can also be referred to as a complex integer. Some sources render the eponym in lowercase: gaussian integer.

label: Definition:Gaussian Integer/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gaussian Integer == The concept of a Gaussian integer was introduced by in his papers of $1828$ and $1832$.

label: Definition:Gaussian Integration Rule
snippet: A Gaussian integration rule is a numerical integration rule of the form: $\ds \int_a^b \map w x \map f x \rd x \approx \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n w_i \map f {x_i}$ where $\map w x$ is a non-negative weight function on the interval $\closedint a b$ such that both: the $n$ nodes $x_i$ the weights $w_i$ are chosen to make the approximation exact when $f$ is a polynomial of degree less than or equal to $2 n - 1$. The purpose of the weight function is to build into the rule any special behaviour of the integrand.

label: Definition:Gaussian Prime/Definition 1
snippet: Let $x \in \Z \sqbrk i$ be a Gaussian integer. $x$ is a Gaussian prime : it cannot be expressed as the product of two Gaussian integers, neither of which is a unit of $\Z \sqbrk i$ (that is, $\pm 1$ or $\pm i$) it is not itself a unit of $\Z \sqbrk i$.

label: Definition:Gaussian Prime/Definition 2
snippet: A Gaussian prime is a Gaussian integer which has exactly $8$ divisors which are themselves Gaussian integers.

label: Definition:Gaussian Rational/Definition 1
snippet: A Gaussian rational is a complex number whose real and imaginary parts are both rational numbers. That is, a Gaussian rational is a number in the form: $a + b i: a, b \in \Q$

label: Definition:Gaussian Rational/Definition 2
snippet: The field $\struct {\Q \sqbrk i, +, \times}$ of Gaussian rationals is the field of quotients of the integral domain $\struct {\Z \sqbrk i, +, \times}$ of Gaussian integers. This is shown to exist in Existence of Field of Quotients. In view of Field of Quotients is Unique, we construct the field of quotients of $\Z \sqbrk i$, give it a label $\Q \sqbrk i$ and call its elements Gaussian rationals.

label: Definition:Gaussian Rational/Notation
snippet: The set of all Gaussian rationals can be denoted $\Q \sqbrk i$, and hence we have: $\Q \sqbrk i = \set {z \in \C: z = a + b i: a, b \in \Q}$ Category:Definitions/Gaussian Rationals

label: Definition:Gelfand Transform
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a commutative Banach algebra over $\C$ such that: the spectrum $\Phi_A$ of $A$ is non-empty. Define $\hat a : \Phi_A \to \C$ by: $\map {\hat a} \phi = \map \phi a$ for each $\phi \in \Phi_A$. We say that $\hat a$ is the Gelfand transform of $a$.

label: Definition:Gelfond's Constant
snippet: Gelfond's constant is the number obtained by raising Euler's number $e$ to the power of $\pi$ (pi): $e^\pi$ Its decimal expansion gives its value to be approximately: $e^\pi \approx 23 \cdotp 14069 \, 26327 \, 79269 \, 00572 \, 90863 \, 67948 \, 54738 \ldots$

label: Definition:Gelfond's Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gelfond's Constant == Gelfond's constant arises in the context of the $7$th problem of the Hilbert $23$. It was proved to be transcendental in $1929$ by . It was since determined to be a special case of the Gelfond-Schneider Theorem, established .

label: Definition:Gelfond-Schneider Constant
snippet: The Gelfond-Schneider constant is defined as $2$ raised to the power of the square root of $2$: $2^{\sqrt 2}$ Its decimal expansion begins: $2^{\sqrt 2} \approx 2 \cdotp 66514 \, 4$

label: Definition:Gelfond-Schneider Constant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Gelfond-Schneider Constant == The Gelfond-Schneider constant arises in the context of the $7$th problem of the Hilbert $23$. It had been proved transcendental in $1930$ by . However, as a result of the work done by and in , it could be shown to be a trivial application of the Gelfond-Schneider Theorem. Hence the name of this constant.

label: Definition:General Fibonacci Sequence
snippet: Let $r, s, t, u$ be numbers, usually integers but not necessarily so limited. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be the sequence defined as: $a_n = \begin{cases} r & : n = 0 \\ s & : n = 1 \\ t a_{n - 2} + u a_{n - 1} & : n > 1 \end{cases}$ Then $\sequence {a_n}$ is a general Fibonacci sequence.

label: Definition:General Fibonacci Sequence/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on General Fibonacci Sequence == The general Fibonacci sequences were first investigated by , who used what are now known Fibonacci numbers and Lucas numbers to investigate the primality of Mersenne numbers.

label: Definition:General Linear Group
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. The set of all nonsingular order-$n$ square matrices over $K$ is a group under (conventional) matrix multiplication. This group is called the general linear group (of degree $n$) and is denoted $\GL {n, K}$, or $\GL n$ if the field is implicit. The field itself is usually $\R$, $\Q$ or $\C$, but can be any field.

label: Definition:General Linear Group/Also denoted as
snippet: == General Linear Group: Also denoted as == Some sources use the notation $\map {\mathrm {GL}_n} K$ for the general linear group instead of $\GL {n, K}$. If $K$ is a Galois field of order $q$, the notations $\map {\mathrm {GL}_n} q$ and $\GL {n, q}$ are also seen. Some sources use $\map {\mathrm {Gl} } {n, r}$ for $\GL {n, \R}$.

label: Definition:General Linear Group/Vector Space
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. The general linear group over $\GL V$ is the group of all invertible linear transformations of $V$.

label: Definition:General Logarithm/Binary
snippet: Logarithms base $2$ are becoming increasingly important in computer science. They are often referred to as binary logarithms.

label: Definition:General Logarithm/Common/Characteristic
snippet: Let $n \in \R$ be a positive real number such that $0 < n < 1$. Let $n$ be presented (possibly approximated) in scientific notation as: $a \times 10^d$ where $d \in \Z$ is an integer. Let $\log_{10} n$ be expressed in the form: $\log_{10} n = \begin {cases} c \cdotp m & : d \ge 0 \\ \overline c \cdotp m & : d < 0 \end {cases}$ where: $c = \size d$ is the absolute value of $d$ $m := \log_{10} a$ $c$ is the characteristic of $\log_{10} n$.

label: Definition:General Logarithm/Common/Mantissa
snippet: Let $n \in \R$ be a positive real number such that $0 < n < 1$. Let $n$ be presented (possibly approximated) in scientific notation as: $a \times 10^d$ where $d \in \Z$ is an integer. Let $\log_{10} n$ be expressed in the form: $\log_{10} n = \begin {cases} c \cdotp m & : d \ge 0 \\ \overline c \cdotp m & : d < 0 \end {cases}$ where: $c = \size d$ is the absolute value of $d$ $m := \log_{10} a$ $\log_{10} a$ is the mantissa of $\log_{10} n$.

label: Definition:General Logarithm/Common/Notation for Negative Logarithm
snippet: Let $n \in \R$ be a real number such that $0 0}$ is a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\log_{10} n$ denote the common logarithm of $n$. Then it is the standard convention to express $\log_{10} n$ in the form: $\log_{10} n = \overline d \cdotp m$ where $m := \log_{10} a$ is the mantissa of $\log_{10} n$. The overline notation is commonly read as bar, that is: $\overline 2$ is read as bar two.

label: Definition:General Logarithm/Complex
snippet: Let $z \in \C_{\ne 0}$ be a non-zero complex number. Let $a \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number such that $a \ne 1$. The logarithm to the base $a$ of $z$ is defined as: $\log_a z := \set {y \in \C: a^y = z}$ where $a^y = e^{y \ln a}$ as defined in Powers of Complex Numbers. The act of performing the $\log_a$ function is colloquially known as taking logs.

label: Definition:General Solution
snippet: Let $E$ be an equation in which $x$ is the independent variable. The general solution of $E$ is the set of all $x$ that make $E$ a true statement.

label: Definition:General Solution to Differential Equation/Also known as
snippet: == General Solution to Differential Equation: Also known as == The general solution to a differential equation $\Phi$ can also be referred to as the solution of $\Phi$, but beware of confusing this with the concept of a solution to $\Phi$. The general solution to a differential equation can also be referred to as the general solution of a differential equation. Some sources refer to this general solution as a general integral. Some sources use the terminology complete solution. The term solution set is sometimes encountered.

label: Definition:General Theory of Relativity/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on General Theory of Relativity == The general theory of relativity was published by in $1916$.

label: Definition:Generalized Continued Fraction
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Informally, a generalized continued fraction in $k$ is an expression of the form: $b_0 + \cfrac {a_1} {b_1 + \cfrac {a_2} {b_2 + \cfrac {a_3} {\ddots \cfrac {} {b_{n - 1} + \cfrac {a_n} {b_n + \cfrac {a_{n + 1} } \ddots } } } } }$ Formally, a generalized continued fraction in $k$ is a pair of sequences $\tuple {\sequence {b_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}, \sequence {a_n}_{n \mathop \ge 1} }$ in $k$, called the sequence of partial denominators and sequence of partial numerators respectively.

label: Definition:Generalized Coordinates
snippet: A set of coordinates: $\set {q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_n}$ sufficient to specify the configuration of a mechanical system can be referred to as generalized coordinates.

label: Definition:Generalized Eigenvalue
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be square matrices of the same order. Let $\lambda$ be a number such that: $\mathbf A \mathbf x = \lambda \mathbf B \mathbf x$ for some non-zero vector $\mathbf x$. Then $\lambda$ is a generalized eigenvalue of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Generalized Hilbert Sequence Space
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be an infinite cardinal. Let $I$ be an indexed set of cardinality $\alpha$. Let $A$ be the set of all real-valued functions $x : I \to \R$ such that: $(1)\quad \set{i \in I: x_i \ne 0}$ is countable $(2)\quad$ the generalized sum $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \in I} x_i^2$ is a convergent net. Let $d_2: A \times A \to \R$ be the real-valued function defined as: $\ds \forall x = \family {x_i}, y = \family {y_i} \in A: \map {d_2} {x, y} := \paren {\sum_{i \mathop \in I} \paren {x_i- y_i}^2}^{\frac 1 2}$ The metric space $\struct {A, d_2}$ is the generalized Hilbert sequence space on $\R$ of…

label: Definition:Generalized Inverse Gaussian Distribution
