label: Definition:Ideal (Order Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $I \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. Then $I$ is an ideal of $S$ $I$ satisifies the ideal axioms:

label: Definition:Ideal Point
snippet: An ideal point is a point at infinity.

label: Definition:Ideal Quotient
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathfrak a, \mathfrak b \subseteq A$ be ideals of $A$. Their ideal quotient is the ideal consisting of elements whose product with $\mathfrak b$ is a subset of $\mathfrak a$: $\ideal {\mathfrak a : \mathfrak b} := \set {x \in A : x \mathfrak b \subseteq \mathfrak a}$

label: Definition:Ideal Theory
snippet: Ideal theory is a branch of abstract algebra which studies ideals of rings.

label: Definition:Ideal in Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a preordered set. Let $I$ be a subset of $S$. $I$ is ideal in $\struct {S, \preceq}$ : $I$ is non-empty directed and lower.

label: Definition:Ideal of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {J, +}$ be a subgroup of $\struct {R, +}$. Then $J$ is an ideal of $R$ : $\forall j \in J: \forall r \in R: j \circ r \in J \land r \circ j \in J$ that is, : $\forall r \in R: J \circ r \subseteq J \land r \circ J \subseteq J$ The letter $J$ is frequently used to denote an ideal.

label: Definition:Ideal of Ring/Also known as
snippet: == Ideal of Ring: Also known as == An ideal can also be referred to as a two-sided ideal to distinguish it from a left ideal and a right ideal. Some sources use $I$ to denote an ideal, but on this can be too easily conflated with an identity mapping. Some sources refer to such a two-sided ideal as a normal subring, in apposition with the concept of a normal subgroup.

label: Definition:Ideal of Ring/Proper Ideal
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. A proper ideal $J$ of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is an ideal of $R$ such that $J$ is a proper subset of $R$. That is, such that $J \subseteq R$ and $J \ne R$.

label: Definition:Idempotence
snippet: Idempotence is a property of an algebraic system, or an element of an algebraic system such that: $E \circledcirc E = E$ for an object $E$ and an operation $\circledcirc$. Let $S$ be a set.

label: Definition:Idempotence/Element
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\circ: S \times S \to S$ be a binary operation on $S$. Let $x \in S$ have the property that $x \circ x = x$. Then $x \in S$ is described as idempotent under the operation $\circ$.

label: Definition:Idempotence/Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to S$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is idempotent : $\forall x \in S: \map f {\map f x} = \map f x$ That is, applying the same mapping a second time to an argument gives the same result as applying it once. And of course, that means the same as applying it as many times as you want. The condition for idempotence can also be written: $f \circ f = f$ where $\circ$ denotes composition of mappings.

label: Definition:Idempotence/Operation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\circ: S \times S \to S$ be a binary operation on $S$. If all the elements of $S$ are idempotent under $\circ$, then the term can be applied to the operation itself: The binary operation $\circ$ is idempotent : $\forall x \in S: x \circ x = x$

label: Definition:Idempotence/Relation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation on $S$. Then $\RR$ is idempotent : $\RR \circ \RR = \RR$ where $\circ$ denotes composition of relations.

label: Definition:Idempotent Operator
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A \in \map B \HH$ be a bounded linear operator. Then $A$ is said to be (an) idempotent (operator) $A^2 = A$.

label: Definition:Idempotent Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. $R$ is an idempotent ring its ring product $\circ$ is an idempotent operation.

label: Definition:Identically Zero
snippet: Let $f$ be a mapping whose codomain is a subset of one of the standard number systems $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$ or $\C$. Let $f$ be such that: $\forall x \in \Dom f: \map f x = 0$ That is, $f$ is the constant mapping $f_0$. Then $f$ is described as being identically zero on its domain. Category:Definitions/Analysis

label: Definition:Identification Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Let $S_2$ be a set. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping. The identification topology on $S_2$ $f$ and $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ is defined as: $\tau_2 = \set {V \in \powerset {S_2}: f^{-1} \sqbrk V \in \tau_1}$ That is, it is the set of all subsets of $S_2$ whose preimages under $f$ are elements of $\tau_1$. The identification topology is seen to depend both on $f$ and $\tau_1$.

label: Definition:Identification Topology/Identification Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Let $S_2$ be a set. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping. Let $\tau_2$ be the identification topology on $S_2$ with respect to $f$ and $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$. The mapping $f: S_1 \to S_2$ in this context is called the identification mapping.

label: Definition:Identity
snippet: Equations Identity: an equation which is true for all values of the variables it contains. Abstract algebra: Identity: an element of an algebraic structure with certain properties. Category:Definitions/Identities Category:Definitions/Language Definitions

label: Definition:Identity (Abstract Algebra)/Two-Sided Identity
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. An element $e \in S$ is called an identity (element) it is both a left identity and a right identity: $\forall x \in S: x \circ e = x = e \circ x$ In Identity is Unique it is established that an identity element, if it exists, is unique within $\struct {S, \circ}$. Thus it is justified to refer to it as the identity (of a given algebraic structure). This identity is often denoted $e_S$, or $e$ if it is clearly understood what structure is being discussed.

label: Definition:Identity Arithmetic Function
snippet: The identity arithmetic function $\iota: S \to \Z$ is defined for $n \ge 1$ by: $\forall n \in S: \map \iota n = \delta_{n 1}$ where: $S$ is (in theory) any set, but in this context is usually one of the standard number sets $\Z, \Q, \R, \C$ $\delta$ is the Kronecker delta. That is: $\forall n \in S: \map \iota n = \begin {cases} 1 & : n = 1\\ 0 & : n \ne 1 \end {cases}$

label: Definition:Identity Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. The identity functor on $\mathbf C$ is the functor $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}: \mathbf C \to \mathbf C$ defined by: {{axiom | lc= For all objects $C$ of $\mathbf C$: | ml = \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C} C | mo = := | mr = C }} {{axiom | lc= For all morphisms $f: C_1 \to C_2$ of $\mathbf C$: | ml = \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C} f | mo = := | mr = f }} That $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}$ constitutes a functor is shown on Identity Functor is Functor.

label: Definition:Identity Mapping
snippet: The identity mapping of a set $S$ is the self-map $I_S: S \to S$ defined as: $I_S = \set {\tuple {x, y} \in S \times S: x = y}$ or alternatively: $I_S = \set {\tuple {x, x}: x \in S}$ That is: $I_S: S \to S: \forall x \in S: \map {I_S} x = x$ That is, it is a mapping in which every element is a fixed element.

label: Definition:Identity Morphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $X$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. The identity morphism of $X$, denoted $\operatorname{id}_X$, is a morphism of $\mathbf C$ subject to: $\operatorname{dom} \operatorname{id}_X = \operatorname{cod} \operatorname{id}_X = X$ $f \circ \operatorname{id}_X = f$ $\operatorname{id}_X \circ g = g$ whenever $X$ is the domain of $f$ or the codomain of $g$, respectively. In most metacategories, the identity morphisms can be viewed as a representation of "doing nothing", in a sense suitable to the metacategory under consideration.

label: Definition:Identity Natural Transformation
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be categories. Let $F : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a covariant functor. The identity natural transformation $\operatorname{id}_F$ from $F$ to $F$, denoted $\operatorname{id}_F: F \to F$, is defined as: $\forall X \in \mathbf C : \paren{\operatorname{id}_F}_X = \operatorname{id}_{FX}$ where $\operatorname{id}_{FX}$ is the identity morphism of $FX$ in $\mathbf D$.

label: Definition:Image/Also denoted as
snippet: The notation $\Img f$ to denote the image of a mapping $f$ is specific to . The usual notation is $\map {\mathrm {Im} } f$ or a variant, but this is too easily confused with $\map \Im z$, the imaginary part of a complex number. Hence the non-standard usage $\Img f$. Some sources use $f \sqbrk S$, where $S$ is the domain of $f$. Others just use $\map f S$, but that notation is deprecated on so as not to confuse it with the notation for the image of an element.

label: Definition:Image (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a locally small category. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a morphism in $\CC$. An image of $f$ consists of an object $I$ and a monomorphism $m: I \to Y$ such that: $(1): \quad$ There exists a morphism $e : X \to I$ such that $f = m \circ e$. $(2): \quad$ For any object $I'$ with a morphism $e' : X \to I'$ and a monomorphism $m' : I' \to Y$ such that $f = m' \circ e'$, there exists a unique morphism $v : I \to I'$ such that $m = m' \circ v$.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)
snippet: The definition of a relation as a subset of the Cartesian product of two sets gives a "static" sort of feel to the concept. However, we can also consider a relation as being an operation, where you feed an element $s \in S$ (or a subset $S_1 \subseteq S$) in at one end, and you get a set of elements $T_s \subseteq T$ out of the other. Thus we arrive at the following definition.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Mapping/Element
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $s \in S$. The image of $s$ (under $f$) is defined as: $\Img s = \map f s = \ds \bigcup \set {t \in T: \tuple {s, t} \in f}$ That is, $\map f s$ is the element of the codomain of $f$ related to $s$ by $f$. By the nature of a mapping, $\map f s$ is guaranteed to exist and to be unique for any given $s$ in the domain of $f$.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Mapping/Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Mapping/Subset
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $X \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Relation/Element
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. Let $s \in S$. The image of $s$ by (or under) $\RR$ is defined as: $\map \RR s := \set {t \in T: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR}$ That is, $\map \RR s$ is the set of all elements of the codomain of $\RR$ related to $s$ by $\RR$. Thus: $\map \RR s$ is another way to write: $\RR \sqbrk {\set s}$ where $\RR \sqbrk {\set s}$ denotes the image of a subset of $\RR$.

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Relation/Relation/General Definition
snippet: Let $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ be the cartesian product of sets $S_1$ to $S_n$. Let $\ds \RR \subseteq \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ be an $n$-ary relation on $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$. The image of $\RR$ is the set defined as: $\Img \RR := \set {s_n \in S_n: \exists \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n - 1} } \in \ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^{n - 1} S_i: \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in \RR}$ The concept is usually encountered when $\RR$ is an endorelation on $S$: $\Img \RR := \set {s_n \in S: \exists \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n - 1} } \in S^{n - 1}: \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n}…

label: Definition:Image (Set Theory)/Relation/Subset
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation. Let $X \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then the image set (of $X$ by $\RR$) is defined as: $\RR \sqbrk X := \set {t \in T: \exists s \in X: \tuple {s, t} \in \RR}$

label: Definition:Image Filter
snippet: Let $S_1, S_2$ be sets. Let $\powerset {S_1}$ and $\powerset {S_2}$ be the power sets of $S_1$ and $S_2$ respectively. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ a mapping. Let $\FF \subset \powerset {S_1}$ be a filter on $S_1$. Then $f \sqbrk \FF := \set {U \subseteq S_2: f^{-1} \sqbrk U \in \FF}$ is the image filter of $\FF$ (on $S_2$) with respect to $f$.

label: Definition:Image of Class under Mapping/Warning
snippet: == Image of Class under Mapping: Warning == Let $V$ be a basic universe Let $f: V \to V$ be a mapping. Let $A$ be a class. Let $x \in A$ be a set of sets Then: $f \sqbrk x$ is not necessarily the same as $\map f x$ where: $f \sqbrk x$ denotes the image of $x$ under $f$ where $x$ is treated as a class $\map f x$ denotes the image of $x$ under $f$ where $x$ is treated as an element of the class $A$. Thus: $\map f x$ is what you get by applying $f$ to $x$ $f \sqbrk x$ is what you get by applying $f$ to each of the elements of $x$ (but not $x$ itself) and then gathering the results into a set.

label: Definition:Image of Element under Mapping/Also known as
snippet: The image of an element $s$ under a mapping $f$ is also called the functional value, or value, of $f$ at $s$. The terminology: $f$ maps $s$ to $\map f s$ $f$ assigns the value $\map f s$ to $s$ $f$ carries $s$ into $\map f s$ can be found. The modifier by $f$ can also be used for under $f$. Thus, for example, the image of $s$ by $f$ means the same as the image of $s$ under $f$. In the context of computability theory, the following terms are frequently found: If $\tuple {x, y} \in f$, then $y$ is often called the output of $f$ for input $x$, or simply, the output of $f$ at $x$.

label: Definition:Image of Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Image of Mapping: Also known as == Some sources refer to this as the direct image of a mapping, in order to differentiate it from an inverse image. Rather than apply a mapping $f$ directly to a subset $A$, those sources often prefer to define the direct image mapping of $f$ as a separate concept in its own right. In the context of set theory, the term image set for $\Img f$ can often be seen. Category:Definitions/Images

label: Definition:Image of Mapping/Definition 1
snippet: The image of a mapping $f: S \to T$ is the set: $\Img f = \set {t \in T: \exists s \in S: \map f s = t}$ That is, it is the set of values taken by $f$.

label: Definition:Image of Relation/Also known as
snippet: The image of a relation $\RR$, when in the context of set theory, is often seen referred to as the image set of $\RR$. Some sources refer to this as the direct image of a relation, in order to differentiate it from an inverse image. Rather than apply a relation $\RR$ directly to a subset $A$, those sources often prefer to define the direct image mapping of $\RR$ as a separate concept in its own right. Other sources call the image of $\RR$ its range, but this convention is discouraged because of potential confusion.

label: Definition:Image of Subset under Mapping/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $X \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. The image of $X$ (under $f$) is defined and denoted as: $f \sqbrk X := \set {t \in T: \exists s \in X: \map f s = t}$

label: Definition:Image of Subset under Mapping/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $X \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. The image of $X$ under $f$ is the element of the codomain of the direct image mapping $f^\to: \powerset S \to \powerset T$ of $f$: $\forall X \in \powerset S: \map {f^\to} X := \set {t \in T: \exists s \in X: \map f s = t}$

label: Definition:Image of Subset under Mapping/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Image of Subset under Mapping == In parallel with the notation $f \sqbrk X$ for the direct image mapping of $f$, also employs the notation $\map {f^\to} X$. This latter notation is used in, for example, , and is referred to as the mapping induced by $f$: It should be noted that most mathematicians write $\map f X$ for $\map {f^\to} X$. Now it is quite clear that the mappings $f$ and $f^\to$ are not the same, so we shall retain the notation $f^\to$ to avoid confusion. ...

label: Definition:Image of Topological Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ and $Q = \struct {X, \tau'}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S \to X$ be a mapping. The image (of the topological space $T$) of $f$ is defined as: $\Img f := Q_{f \sqbrk S} = \struct {f \sqbrk S, \tau'_{f \sqbrk S} }$ where $\tau'_{f \sqbrk S}$ denotes the subspace topology on $f \sqbrk S$.

label: Definition:Imaginary Circle
snippet: An imaginary circle is the locus of imaginary points defined by the equation: $\paren {x - a}^2 + \paren {y - b}^2 = -r^2$

label: Definition:Imaginary Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Imaginary Number == was one of the first to accept negative numbers, and possibly the first to consider their square roots, which he did in his . When considering the roots of $x^2 + 40 = 10 x$, and determining that they are $5 \pm \sqrt {-15}$, he concluded: These quantities are "truly sophisticated" and that to continue working with them would be "as subtle as it would be useless". As negative numbers were even then considered "false" and "fictitious", no wonder the square roots of negative numbers would be named imaginary.

label: Definition:Imaginary Part/Also denoted as
snippet: == Imaginary Part: Also denoted as == Variants of $\map \Im z$ for the imaginary part of a complex number $z$ are: $\map {\mathrm {Im} } z$ $\mathrm {Im} \set z$ $\map {\mathscr I} z$ $\map {\mathrm {im} } z$ $\map {\mathfrak I} z$ $\map {\mathbf I} z$ or $\mathbf I z$ While the fraktur font is falling out of fashion, because of its cumbersome appearance and difficulty to render in longhand, its use for this application is conveniently unambiguous.

label: Definition:Imaginary Part/Polar Form
snippet: Let $z$ be a complex number expressed in polar form: $z = \polar {r, \theta}$ The imaginary part of $z$ is: $\map \Im z = r \sin \theta$

label: Definition:Imaginary Part (Linear Operator)
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $A \in \map B \HH$ be a bounded linear operator. Then the imaginary part of $A$ is the Hermitian operator: $\Im A := \dfrac 1 {2 i} \paren {A - A^*}$

label: Definition:Imaginary Straight Line
snippet: An imaginary straight line in the Cartesian plane is a straight line whose equation includes the imaginary unit $i$ somewhere in its definition.

label: Definition:Imaginary Unit/Also denoted as
snippet: == Imaginary Unit: Also denoted as == The non-italicized $\mathrm i$ can also be seen. Using the formal definition of complex numbers, the imaginary unit is the ordered pair $\tuple {0, 1}$. When mathematics is applied to engineering, in particular electrical and electronic engineering, the symbol $j$ is usually used This is because $i$ is the standard symbol used to denote the flow of electric current, and to use it also for $\sqrt {-1}$ would cause untold confusion. In some mathematical traditions, the Greek symbol $\iota$ (iota) is used for $i$.

label: Definition:Imaginary Unit/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on the Imaginary Unit == The symbol $i$ that is in widespread use for the imaginary unit was at least partly due to 's influence.

label: Definition:Immediate Successor Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. Then $a$ is an immediate successor (element) to $b$ $b$ is an immediate predecessor (element) to $a$. That is, : $(1): \quad b \prec a$ $(2): \quad \nexists c \in S: b \prec c \prec a$ That is, there exists no element strictly between $b$ and $a$ in the ordering $\preceq$. That is: $a \prec b$ and $\openint a b = \O$ where $\openint a b$ denotes the open interval from $a$ to $b$. We say that $a$ immediately succeeds $b$.

label: Definition:Impedance of Free Space
snippet: Impedance of free space is a physical constant relating the magnitudes of the electric and magnetic fields of electromagnetic radiation travelling through a vacuum. It is defined as: the quotient of the magnitudes of the electric field and magnetic fields of electromagnetic radiation travelling through a vacuum: $\dfrac {\size {\mathbf E} } {\size {\mathbf H} }$ the vacuum permeability multiplied by the speed of light: $\mu_0 c$ the square root of the quotient of the vacuum permeability by the vacuum permittivity: $\sqrt {\dfrac {\mu_0} {\varepsilon_0} }$

label: Definition:Impedance of Free Space/Dimension
snippet: The impedance of free space has the dimension $\mathsf {M L^2 T^{-3} I^{-2} }$. This arises from its definition as: electric field strength per unit magnetic field strength: $\dfrac {\mathsf {M L T^{-3} I^{-1} } } {\mathsf {I L^{-1} } }$ vacuum permeability multiplied by the speed of light: $\mathsf {M L T^{-2} I^{-2} } \times \mathsf {L T^{-1} }$ the square root of the quotient of the vacuum permeability by the vacuum permittivity: $\sqrt {\dfrac {\mathsf {M L T^{-2} I^{-2} } } {\mathsf {M^{-1} L^{-3} T^4 I^2} } } = \sqrt {\mathsf {M^2 L^4 T^{-6} I^{-4} } }$ Category:Definitions/Dimensions…

label: Definition:Imperial/Area/Acre/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Acre == The acre is a traditional measure of land arising from the days of ploughing in mediaeval times and earlier. It was defined as the area of land that could be ploughed by $1$ ploughman with $1$ ox in $1$ day. It is noted that an acre is not actually defined as a square area, but as an oblong strip $10$ times as long as it is wide. The reason is readily apparent: its length is, as is apparent from its definition, one furlong, that is, furrow-long. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Chain
snippet: The square chain is an imperial unit of area. One square chain is equal to a square of side $1$ chain in length. Category:Definitions/Imperial Category:Definitions/Area

label: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Foot
snippet: The square foot is an imperial unit of area. One square foot is equal to a square of side $1$ foot in length.

label: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Inch
snippet: The square inch is an imperial unit of area. One square inch is equal to a square of side $1$ inch in length. The definition is exact.

label: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Mile
snippet: The square mile is an imperial unit of area. One square mile is equal to a square whose side measures $1$ mile.

label: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Rod, Pole or Perch
snippet: The square rod, pole or perch is an imperial unit of area. One square rod, pole or perch is equal to a square of side $1$ rod, pole or perch in length. {{eqn | r = 30 \tfrac 1 4 | rr= = \paren {5 \tfrac 1 2}^2 | c = square yards }} {{eqn | r = 272 \tfrac 1 4 | rr= = \paren {16 \tfrac 1 2}^2 | c = square feet }}

label: Definition:Imperial/Area/Square Yard
snippet: The square yard is an imperial unit of area. One square yard is equal to a square of side $1$ yard in length.

label: Definition:Imperial/Volume
snippet: The imperial units of volume are based on a binary system, in which each unit is a factor of $2$ larger than the next smaller unit.

label: Definition:Imperial/Volume/Example
snippet: == Examples of Use of Imperial Volume Measure == As the imperial volume measure are related by powers of two, it is possible to use them to express a volume as a binary number of gills. Thus a volume equal to $3815$ gills is: $1$ gill $1$ chopin $1$ pint $0$ quarts $0$ pottles $1$ gallon $0$ pecks $1$ demi-bushel $1$ bushel $1$ kilderkin $0$ barrels $0$ hogsheads $1$ pipe Thus $3815$ gills can be expressed as: $1001110100111$ gills in binary.

label: Definition:Implicit Function
snippet: Consider a (real) function of two independent variables $z = \map f {x, y}$. Let a relation between $x$ and $y$ be expressed in the form $\map f {x, y} = 0$ defined on some subset of $\R^2$. If there exists a function: $y = \map g x$ defined on some real interval $\mathbb I$ such that: $\forall x \in \mathbb I: \map f {x, \map g x} = 0$ then the relation $\map f {x, y} = 0$ defines $y$ as an implicit function of $x$.

label: Definition:Implicit Function/General
snippet: Let: $f: \R^{n + 1} \to \R, \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, z} \mapsto \map f {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, z}$ be a real-valued function on $\R^{n + 1}$, where: $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} \in \R^n, z \in \R$ Let a relation between $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ and $z$ be expressed in the form: $\map f {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, z} = 0$ defined on some subset $S \subseteq \R^n$.

label: Definition:Impredicative Definition
snippet: An impredicative definition is a definition in which an element of a set is defined by reference to the totality of the elements of the set .

label: Definition:Improper Subset/Also defined as
snippet: == Improper Subset: Also defined as == Let us consider treatments of set theory which categorise the empty set $\O$ as a proper subset. Then an improper subset $S$ of a set $T$ is such that: $S = T$ As this is merely a matter of nomenclature, this distinction should not be of great importance. However, it is wise to make sure which usage is intended when it is encountered.

label: Definition:In-Order Traversal of Labeled Tree
snippet: Let $T$ be a binary labeled tree. In-order traversal of $T$ is an algorithm designed to obtain a string representation of $T$. The steps are as follows:

label: Definition:In-Order Traversal of Labeled Tree/Variant 1
snippet: Let $T$ be a binary labeled tree. In-order traversal of $T$ is an algorithm designed to obtain a string representation of $T$. The steps are as follows: $\mathtt{Inorder} (T):$ $n \gets t$, where $t$ is the root node of $T$. If $n$ is a leaf node, output the label of $n$, and stop. Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be the left and right subtrees of $T$. If $n$ has only one child, skip this step. Output $\mathtt{Inorder} (T_1)$. Output the label of $n$. Output $\mathtt{Inorder} (T_2)$. Stop.

label: Definition:In-Order Traversal of Labeled Tree/Variant 2
snippet: Let $T$ be a binary labeled tree. In-order traversal of $T$ is an algorithm designed to obtain a string representation of $T$. The steps are as follows: $\mathtt{Inorder} (T):$ $n \gets t$, where $t$ is the root node of $T$. If $n$ is a leaf node, output the label of $n$, and stop. Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be the left and right subtrees of $T$. Output a left bracket $($. If $n$ has only one child, skip this step. Output $\mathtt{Inorder} (T_1)$. Output the label of $n$. Output $\mathtt{Inorder} (T_2)$. Output a right bracket $)$. Stop.

label: Definition:Inaccessible by Directed Suprema
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be an up-complete ordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then $X$ is inaccessible by directed suprema : for all directed subsets $D$ of $S$: $\sup D \in X \implies X \cap D \ne \O$

label: Definition:Incenter of Polygon
snippet: 300px The center of an incircle of a polygon is called an incenter of the polygon.

label: Definition:Incident (Graph Theory)/Also known as
snippet: == Incident in the context of Graph Theory: Also known as == It is common to see incident to being used for incident with. For undirected graphs this is appropriate; for digraph the situation is more complicated. Some sources use incident on. Some sources use the term adjacent for incident.

label: Definition:Incident (Graph Theory)/Planar Graph
snippet: 220px Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a planar graph: Then a face of $G$ is incident to an edge $e$ of $G$ if $e$ is one of those which surrounds the face. Similarly, a face of $G$ is incident to a vertex $v$ of $G$ if $v$ is at the end of one of those incident edges. In the above graph, for example, the face $BCEF$ is incident to: the edges $BC, CE, EF, FB$ the vertices $B, C, E, F$.

label: Definition:Incident (Graph Theory)/Undirected Graph
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be an undirected graph. Let $u, v \in V$ be vertices of $G$. Let $e = \set {u, v} \in E$ be an edge of $G$: 320px Then: $u$ and $v$ are each incident with $e$ $e$ is incident with $u$ and incident with $v$.

label: Definition:Incircle
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. Let $C$ be a circle which is inscribed within $P$. 300px Then $C$ is an incircle of $P$.

label: Definition:Incircle/Inradius
snippet: 300px A radius of an incircle of a polygon is called an inradius of the polygon. In the above diagram, $OG$ is an inradius of the polygon $ABCDEF$.

label: Definition:Incircle of Triangle
snippet: The incircle of a triangle is the circle tangent to each side of the triangle. This circle is said to be inscribed in the triangle. 410px

label: Definition:Incircle of Triangle/Incenter
snippet: 410px The center of an incircle of a triangle is called an incenter of the triangle.

label: Definition:Incircle of Triangle/Inradius
snippet: 410px A radius of an incircle of a triangle is called an inradius of the triangle. In the above diagram, $r$ is an inradius.

label: Definition:Inclination/Straight Line to Plane
snippet: 500px Let $P$ be a plane. Let $L$ be a straight line which intersects $P$ at the point $A$. Let $Q$ be the perpendicular from a point $B$ on $L$. Let $C$ be the point where $Q$ intersects $P$. The inclination of $L$ to $P$ is defined as the angle $BAC$. In the above diagram, this has been marked as $\theta$.

label: Definition:Inclination between Planes/Definition 1
snippet: The inclination between two intersecting planes is the smaller of the dihedral angles between them.

label: Definition:Inclination between Planes/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\PP_1$ and $\PP_2$ be planes. Let $\mathbf n_1$ and $\mathbf n_2$ be normal vectors to $\PP_1$ and $\PP_2$ respectively, oriented such that the angle $\theta$ between them is such that: $0 \le \theta \le \dfrac \pi 2$ that is: $0 \degrees \le \theta \le 90 \degrees$ The inclination between $\PP_1$ and $\PP_2$ is defined as that $\theta$.

label: Definition:Inclined Plane
snippet: An inclined plane is a plane surface which is neither horizontal nor vertical.

label: Definition:Included Set Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set which is non-null. Let $H \subseteq S$ be some subset of $S$. We define a subset $\tau_H$ of the power set $\powerset S$ as: $\tau_H = \set {A \subseteq S: H \subseteq A} \cup \set \O$ that is, all the subsets of $S$ which are supersets of $H$, along with the empty set $\O$. Then $\tau_H$ is a topology called the included set topology on $S$ by $H$, or just an included set topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau_H}$ is called the included set space on $S$ by $H$, or just an included set space.

label: Definition:Inclusion-Preserving Mapping
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $f : A \to B$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is inclusion-preserving for every two sets $a_1, a_2 \in A$: $a_1 \subseteq a_2 \implies f(a_1) \subseteq f(a_2)$

label: Definition:Inclusion-Reversing Mapping
snippet: Let $A, B$ be sets of sets and $\phi: A \to B$ be a mapping. Then $\phi$ is inclusion-reversing : for every pair of sets $a_1, a_2 \in A$ such that $a_1 \subseteq a_2$: $\map \phi {a_2} \subseteq \map \phi {a_1}$

label: Definition:Inclusion Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf D$ be a metacategory, and let $\mathbf C$ be a subcategory of $\mathbf D$. The inclusion functor on $\mathbf C$ is the functor $\Iota_{\mathbf C}: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ defined by: {{DefineFunctor |ob = For all objects $C$ of $\mathbf C$: $\Iota_{\mathbf C} C := C$ |mor = For all morphisms $f: C_1 \to C_2$ of $\mathbf C$: $\Iota_{\mathbf C} f := f$ }}

label: Definition:Inclusion Mapping
snippet: Let $T$ be a set. Let $S\subseteq T$ be a subset. The inclusion mapping $i_S: S \to T$ is the mapping defined as: $i_S: S \to T: \forall x \in S: \map {i_S} x = x$

label: Definition:Inclusion Relation on Subobject Classes
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. The inclusion relation $\subseteq$ on subobject classes of $C$ is defined as follows: $\eqclass m {} \subseteq \eqclass {m'} {}$ there exists a morphism $\eqclass f {}: \eqclass m {} \to \eqclass {m'} {}$

label: Definition:Inclusion Relation on Subobjects
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Let $\map {\mathbf{Sub}_{\mathbf C} } C$ be the category of subobjects of $C$. The inclusion relation $\subseteq$ on subobjects of $C$ is defined as follows: $m \subseteq m'$ there exists a morphism $f: m \to m'$

label: Definition:Inconsistent
snippet: Logic Definition:Inconsistent (Logic) Algebra and Linear Algebra Definition:Inconsistent Simultaneous Equations

label: Definition:Inconsistent (Logic)
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL$.

label: Definition:Inconsistent (Logic)/Also known as
snippet: Inconsistent sets of logical formulas are often called contradictory. Likewise, a logical formula which is inconsistent by itself is often called a contradiction. Since these terms are also often used to describe unsatisfiability in the context of a formal semantics, they are discouraged as synonyms of inconsistent on . Category:Definitions/Inconsistent (Logic)

label: Definition:Inconsistent (Logic)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL$. A set $\FF$ of logical formulas is inconsistent for $\mathscr P$ : For every logical formula $\phi$, $\FF \vdash_{\mathscr P} \phi$. That is, every logical formula $\phi$ is a provable consequence of $\FF$.

label: Definition:Inconsistent (Logic)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL$. A set $\FF$ of logical formulas is inconsistent for $\mathscr P$ : There exists a logical formula $\phi$ such that both $\FF \vdash_{\mathscr P} \paren {\phi \land \neg \phi}$

label: Definition:Increasing/Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a mapping. Then $\phi$ is increasing : $\forall x, y \in S: x \preceq_1 y \implies \map \phi x \preceq_2 \map \phi y$ Note that this definition also holds if $S = T$.

label: Definition:Increasing/Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $A$ be a subset of the natural numbers $\N$. Then a sequence $\sequence {a_k}_{k \mathop \in A}$ of terms of $S$ is increasing : $\forall j, k \in A: j < k \implies a_j \preceq a_k$

label: Definition:Increasing Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Increasing Mapping: Also known as == An increasing mapping is also referred to as an increasing function. An increasing mapping is also known as isotone or non-decreasing. In contexts where the ordering in question is more general than in the context of numbers, the term order-preserving mapping is often more appropriate than increasing mapping. Some authors refer to this concept as a monotone mapping, but that term has a different meaning on ProofWiki. Beware that some authors who use the term order-preserving mapping use it to define what on is referred to as an order embedding.

label: Definition:Increasing Sequence of Events
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {A_n}$ be a sequence of events in $\Sigma$. Then $\sequence {A_n}$ is described as increasing : $\forall i \in \N: A_i \subseteq A_{i + 1}$

label: Definition:Increasing Sequence of Extended Real-Valued Functions
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}, f_n: S \to \overline{\R}$ be a sequence of extended real-valued functions. Then $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is said to be an increasing sequence (of extended real-valued functions) : $\forall s \in S: \forall m, n \in \N: m \le n \implies \map {f_m} s \le \map {f_n} s$ That is, $m \le n \implies f_m \le f_n$, where the second $\le$ denotes pointwise inequality.

label: Definition:Increasing Sequence of Mappings
snippet: Let $S$ be a set, and let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}, f_n: S \to T$ be a sequence of mappings. Then $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is said to be an increasing sequence (of mappings) : $\forall s \in S: \forall m, n \in \N: m \le n \implies \map {f_m} s \preceq \map {f_n} s$ That is, $m \le n \implies f_m \preceq f_n$, where $\preceq$ denotes pointwise inequality.

label: Definition:Increasing Sequence of Real-Valued Functions
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}, f_n: S \to \R$ be a sequence of real-valued functions. Then $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is said to be an increasing sequence (of real-valued functions) : $\forall s \in S: \forall m, n \in \N: m \le n \implies \map {f_m} s \le \map {f_n} s$ That is, $m \le n \implies f_m \le f_n$, where the second $\le$ denotes pointwise inequality.

label: Definition:Increasing Sequence of Sets
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\SS = \powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\sequence {S_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ be a nested sequence of subsets of $S$ such that: $\forall k \in \N: S_k \subseteq S_{k + 1}$ Then $\sequence {S_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ is an increasing sequence of sets (in $\SS$).

label: Definition:Increasing Union
snippet: Let $S_0, S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_i, \ldots$ be a nested sequence of sets, that is: $S_0 \subseteq S_1 \subseteq S_2 \subseteq \ldots \subseteq S_i \subseteq \ldots$ Let $S$ be the set: $\ds S = \bigcup_{i \mathop \in \N} S_i$ where $\bigcup$ denotes set union. Then $S$ is called the increasing union of $S_0, S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_i, \ldots$

label: Definition:Increment/Functional
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of mappings. Let $y, h: \R \to \R$ be real functions. Let $J \sqbrk y: S \to \R$ be a functional defined on a normed vector space. Consider the following difference: $ \Delta J \sqbrk {y; h} = J \sqbrk {y + h} - J \sqbrk y$ Then $\Delta J \sqbrk {y; h}$ is known as the increment of the functional $J$.

label: Definition:Indecomposable Continuum
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a continuum in $T$. Then $H$ is indecomposable it is not the union of two distinct nondegenerate proper subcontinua.

label: Definition:Indeed
snippet: The adverb indeed is used in mathematics in the following manner. Let $P$ be an assertion which is about to be proven in the next step of the exposition. That next step is then frequently prefaced by the word indeed. The philosophy is that: $(1): \quad$ The assertion is presented as a true statement. $(2): \quad$ The writer is sure of what has been stated, and will indeed back up this assertion with the logical argument which is immediately to follow. Category:Definitions/Language Definitions

label: Definition:Independence System
snippet: Let $S$ be a finite set. Let $\mathscr F$ be a set of subsets of $S$ satisfying the independence system axioms: The ordered pair $I = \struct {S, \mathscr F}$ is called an independence system on $S$.

label: Definition:Independent
snippet: Analysis: Independent Variable Probability Theory: Independent Events Independent Random Variables Group Theory: Independent Subgroups Field Theory: Algebraically Independent Linear Algebra: Linearly Independent Affine Geometry: Affinely Independent Logic: Independent Statements Matroid Theory: Independent Subset

label: Definition:Independent Equations
snippet: A set of simultaneous equations is independent it contains no dependent equations.

label: Definition:Independent Events
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events of $\EE$ such that $\map \Pr A > 0$ and $\map \Pr B > 0$.

label: Definition:Independent Events/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events of $\EE$ such that $\map \Pr A > 0$ and $\map \Pr B > 0$. The events $A$ and $B$ are defined as independent (of each other) the occurrence of one of them does not affect the probability of the occurrence of the other one. Formally, $A$ is independent of $B$ : $\condprob A B = \map \Pr A$ where $\condprob A B$ denotes the conditional probability of $A$ given $B$.

label: Definition:Independent Events/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events of $\EE$ such that $\map \Pr A > 0$ and $\map \Pr B > 0$. The events $A$ and $B$ are defined as independent (of each other) the occurrence of both of them together has the same probability as the product of the probabilities of each of them occurring on their own. Formally, $A$ and $B$ are independent : $\map \Pr {A \cap B} = \map \Pr A \map \Pr B$

label: Definition:Independent Events/Dependent
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be events of $\EE$ such that $\map \Pr A > 0$ and $\map \Pr B > 0$. If $A$ and $B$ are not independent, then they are dependent (on each other), and vice versa.

label: Definition:Independent Events/General Definition
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\AA = \family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of events of $\EE$. Then $\AA$ is independent , for all finite subsets $J$ of $I$: $\ds \map \Pr {\bigcap_{i \mathop \in J} A_i} = \prod_{i \mathop \in J} \map \Pr {A_i}$ That is, the occurrence of any finite collection of $\AA$ has the same probability as the product of each of those sets occurring individually.

label: Definition:Independent Events/Pairwise Independent
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\AA = \family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of events of $\EE$. Then $\AA$ is pairwise independent : $\forall j, k \in I: \map \Pr {A_j \cap A_k} = \map \Pr {A_j} \map \Pr {A_k}$ That is, every pair of events of $\EE$ are independent of each other. That is, $\AA$ is pairwise independent the condition for general independence: $\ds \map \Pr {\bigcap_{i \mathop \in J} A_i} = \prod_{i \mathop \in J} \map \Pr {A_i}$ holds whenever $\card J = 2$.

label: Definition:Independent Random Variables/Dependent
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are defined as dependent (on each other) $X$ and $Y$ are not independent (of each other).

label: Definition:Independent Random Variables/Discrete
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be discrete random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are defined as independent (of each other) : $\map \Pr {X = x, Y = y} = \map \Pr {X = x} \map \Pr {Y = y}$ where $\map \Pr {X = x, Y = y}$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y$.

label: Definition:Independent Random Variables/Discrete/General Definition
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X = \tuple {X_1, X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ be an ordered tuple of discrete random variables.

label: Definition:Independent Random Variables/Discrete/General Definition/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X = \tuple {X_1, X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ be an ordered tuple of random variables. $X$ is independent : $\ds \map \Pr {X_1 = x_1, X_2 = x_2, \ldots, X_n = x_n} = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n \map \Pr {X_k = x_k}$ for all $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} \in \R^n$.

label: Definition:Independent Random Variables/Discrete/General Definition/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X = \tuple {X_1, X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ be an ordered tuple of random variables. $X$ is independent : $\ds \map {p_X} x = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n \map {p_{X_k} } {x^k}$ for all $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n} \in \R^n$.

label: Definition:Independent Random Variables/Discrete/Pairwise Independent
snippet: Let $\EE$ be an experiment with probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X = \tuple {X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n}$ be an ordered tuple of discrete random variables. Then $X$ is pairwise independent $X_i$ and $X_j$ are independent (of each other) whenever $i \ne j$.

label: Definition:Independent Random Variables/General Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ be a measurable space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of random variables on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$. For each $i \in \N$, let $\map \sigma {X_i}$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $X_i$. We say that $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a sequence of independent random variable : $\sequence {\map \sigma {X_n} }_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a sequence of independent $\sigma$-algebras.

label: Definition:Independent Set of Truth Functions
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of truth functions. Then $S$ is independent the elements of $S$ cannot be expressed from a proper subset of $S$.

label: Definition:Independent Shocks
snippet: Let $M$ be a stochastic model which describes a time series in which adjacent observations are highly dependent. Then $M$ may be able to be modelled by a time series whose elements are of the form: $\map z t = \map {z_d} t + \map {z_r} t$ where: $\map {z_d} t$ has a deterministic model $\map {z_r} t$ has a stochastic model which consists of a sequence of independent random variables from a specified probability distribution (usually a white noise process). The terms of the sequence $\sequence {z_r}$ are known as independent shocks.

label: Definition:Independent Sigma-Algebras/Binary Case
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\GG_1$ and $\GG_2$ be sub-$\sigma$-algebras of $\EE$. Then $\GG_1$ and $\GG_2$ are said to be ($\Pr$-)independent : $\forall E_1 \in \GG_1, E_2 \in \GG_2: \map \Pr {E_1 \cap E_2} = \map \Pr {E_1} \map \Pr {E_2}$

label: Definition:Independent Sigma-Algebras/Countable Case
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {\GG_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of sub-$\sigma$-algebras of $\Sigma$. We say that $\sequence {\GG_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a sequence of ($\Pr$-)independent $\sigma$-algebras : for each $n \in \N$ and distinct natural numbers $i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_n$, we have: $\ds \map \Pr {\bigcap_{k \mathop = 1}^n G_{i_k} } = \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n \map \Pr {G_{i_k} }$ for all $G_{i_1}, G_{i_2}, \ldots, G_{i_n}$ with $G_{i_k} \in \GG_{i_k}$ for each $k$.

label: Definition:Independent Statements
snippet: Let $p$ and $q$ be statements. Let it be the case that: $(1): \quad p$ and $q$ are not contrary $(2): \quad p$ and $q$ are not subcontrary $(3): \quad p$ is not superimplicant to $q$ $(4): \quad p$ is not subimplicant to $q$ $(5): \quad p$ and $q$ are not equivalent $(6): \quad p$ and $q$ are not contradictory. Then $p$ and $q$ are independent statements.

label: Definition:Independent Subgroups
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e$. Let $\sequence {H_n}$ be a sequence of subgroups of $G$.

label: Definition:Independent Subgroups/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e$. Let $\sequence {H_n}$ be a sequence of subgroups of $G$. The subgroups $H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_n$ are independent : $\ds \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n h_k = e \iff \forall k \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}: h_k = e$ where $h_k \in H_k$ for all $k \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$. That is, the product of any elements from different $H_k$ instances forms the identity all of those elements are the identity.

label: Definition:Independent Subgroups/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e$. Let $\sequence {H_n}$ be a sequence of subgroups of $G$. The subgroups $H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_n$ are independent : $\ds \forall k \in \set {2, 3, \ldots, n}: \paren {\prod_{j \mathop = 1}^{k - 1} H_j} \cap H_k = \set e$ That is, the product of any elements from different $H_k$ instances forms the identity all of those elements are the identity.

label: Definition:Independent Vertex Set
snippet: Let $G$ be a graph. Let $U \subseteq \map V G$ be a subset of the vertex set of $G$. $U$ is an independent vertex set of $G$ no pair of elements of $U$ is adjacent.

label: Definition:Index
snippet: Set Theory: Index: an element of an indexing set Index set, set of indices: other names for an indexing set Sequences: Index: the index of a term $x_k$ of a sequence $\sequence {x_n}$ is $k$ Group Theory: Index of Subgroup: order of coset space Index of Group Element: another term for discrete logarithm Matrix Theory: Index of Matrix Element: one of the two parameters which specifies an element of a matrix Arithmetic: Index notation: another word for scientific notation Algebra and Analysis: Index (Algebra): the $y$ term in expressions such as $x^y$, more commonly known as the exponent of $x$…

label: Definition:Index Lowering
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\tuple {E_i}$ and $\tuple {\epsilon^i}$ be a smooth local frame and its dual coframe. Let $g = g_{ij} \epsilon^i \epsilon^j$ be the local expression of $g$. Let $X = X^i E_i$ be a smooth vector field. Let $\hat g : TM \to T^* M$ be the Riemannian metric mapping. Let $\map {\hat g} X = g_{ij} X^i \epsilon^j$ be the covector field. Index lowering of $X$, denoted by $X^\flat$, is an isomorphism $\flat : TM \to T^*M$ such that: $X^\flat := \map {\hat g} X$

label: Definition:Index Lowering for Tensor
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\hat g : TM \to T^* M$ be the Riemannian metric mapping. Let $F$ be a $\tuple {k, l}$-tensor. Let $i \in \tuple {1, \ldots, k + l}$ be a covariant index position. label: Definition:Index Number
snippet: An index number in the context of statistics and economics is a measure of a change in some business activity over time. It is constructed based on reliable information on relevant components, usually weighted according to importance. An index number is usually defined relative to a specific base year, at which time the value of the index number would be assigned a round number, usually $100$ but sometimes $1000$.

label: Definition:Index Raising
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\hat g : TM \to T^* M$ be the Riemannian metric mapping. Let $\tuple {E_i}$ and $\tuple {\epsilon^i}$ be a smooth local frame and its dual coframe. Let $g = g_{ij} \epsilon^i \epsilon^j$ be the local expression of $g$. Let $g^{ij}$ be the inverse matrix of $g_{ij}$. Let $\omega$ be a smooth covector field. Let $\map {\hat g^{-1}} \omega = \omega_i g^{ij} E_j$ be the vector field. Index raising of $\omega$, denoted by $\omega^\sharp$, is an isomorphism $\sharp : T^*M \to TM$ such that: $\omega^\sharp := \map {\hat g^{-1}} \omega$

label: Definition:Index Raising for Tensor
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\hat g : TM \to T^* M$ be the Riemannian metric mapping. Let $F$ be a $\tuple {k, l}$-tensor. Let $i \in \tuple {1, \ldots, k + l}$ be a covariant index position. Index raising of $F$, denoted by $F^\sharp$, is an isomorphism $\sharp : \underbrace{V \times \ldots \times V}_{\text{$k$ times}} \times \underbrace{{T_p^*M} \times \ldots \times {T_p^*M}}_{\text{$l$ times}} \to \underbrace{T_p M \times \ldots \times T_p M}_{\text{$k + 1$ times}} \times \underbrace{{T_p^*M} \times \ldots \times {T_p^*M}}_{\text{$l - 1$ times}}$ such that: $\map…

label: Definition:Index of Fredholm Operator
snippet: Let $U, V$ be vector spaces. Let $T: U \to V$ be a Fredholm operator. The index of $T$ is defined as: $\map {\mathrm{ind} } T := \map \dim {\map \ker T} - \map {\mathrm {codim}} {\Img T}$ where: $\map \dim {\map \ker T}$ denotes the dimension of the kernel of $T$ $\map {\mathrm {codim} } {\Img T}$ denotes the codimension of the image of $T$

label: Definition:Index of Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. The index of $H$ (in $G$), denoted $\index G H$, is the cardinality of the left (or right) coset space $G / H$.

label: Definition:Index of Subgroup/Also defined as
snippet: == Index of Subgroup: Also defined as == Some sources define the index $\index G H$ of a subgroup only for the case where $G$ is finite. Some, while developing the groundwork of the subject, refer to the left index and right index, according to whether the cardinality of the left coset space or right coset space is under consideration. However, from Left and Right Coset Spaces are Equivalent, it follows that the left index and right index are in fact the same thing, and such a distinction is of minimal relevance.

label: Definition:Indexing Set
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be a mapping. Let $x_i$ denote the image of an element $i \in I$ of the domain $I$ of $x$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the set of the images of all the elements $i \in I$ under $x$. When a mapping is used in this context, the domain $I$ of $x$ is called the indexing set of the terms $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Family
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be an indexing function for $S$. Let $x_i$ denote the image of an element $i \in I$ of the domain $I$ of $x$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the set of the images of all the elements $i \in I$ under $x$. The image $\Img x$, consisting of the terms $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$, along with the indexing function $x$ itself, is called a family of elements of $S$ indexed by $I$.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Family of Distinct Elements
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be an indexing function for $S$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the family of elements of $S$ indexed by $x$. Let $x$ be an injection, that is: $\forall \alpha, \beta \in I: \alpha \ne \beta \implies x_\alpha \ne x_\beta$ Then $\family {x_i} _{i \mathop \in I}$ is called a family of distinct elements of $S$.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Family of Sets
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a set of sets. Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of elements of $\SS$ indexed by $I$. Then $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is referred to as an indexed family of sets.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Family of Subsets
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $I$ be an indexing set. For each $i \in I$, let $S_i$ be a corresponding subset of $S$. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of subsets of $S$ indexed by $I$. Then $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is referred to as an indexed family of subsets (of $S$ by $I$).

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Function
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be a mapping. Let $x_i$ denote the image of an element $i \in I$ of the domain $I$ of $x$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the set of the images of all the element $i \in I$ under $x$. When used in this context, the mapping $x$ is referred to as an indexing function for $S$.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Index
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be a mapping. Let $x_i$ denote the image of an element $i \in I$ of the domain $I$ of $x$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the set of the images of all the element $i \in I$ under $x$. An element of the domain $I$ of $x$ is called an index.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Indexed Set
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be a mapping. Let $x_i$ denote the image of an element $i \in I$ of the domain $I$ of $x$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the set of the images of all the elements $i \in I$ under $x$. The image of $x$, that is, $x \sqbrk I$ or $\Img x$, is called an indexed set. That is, it is the set indexed by $I$.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Note on Terminology
snippet: It is a common approach to blur the distinction between an indexing function $x: I \to S$ and the indexed family $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ itself, and refer to the mapping as the indexed family. This approach is in accordance with the definition of a mapping as a relation defined as an as ordered triple $\tuple {I, S, x}$, where the mapping is understood as being defined to include its domain and codomain.

label: Definition:Indexing Set/Term
snippet: Let $I$ and $S$ be sets. Let $x: I \to S$ be a mapping. Let $x_i$ denote the image of an element $i \in I$ of the domain $I$ of $x$. Let $\family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ denote the set of the images of all the element $i \in I$ under $x$. The image of $x$ at an index $i$ is referred to as a term of the (indexed) family, and is denoted $x_i$.

label: Definition:Indicator
snippet: Definition:Indicator of Group Element Definition:Indicator Function Definition:Characteristic Function of Subset Definition:Euler Phi Function

label: Definition:Indicator Function
snippet: Another name for the characteristic function of a set. Another name for the Euler $\phi$ function.

label: Definition:Indicator of Group Element
snippet: Let $G$ be a finite group. Let $a \in G$. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. The indicator of $a$ in $H$ is the least strictly positive integer $n$ such that $a^n \in H$.

label: Definition:Indiscrete Extension of Reals
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $D$ be an everywhere dense subset of $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ with an everywhere dense complement in $\R$. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets: $\BB := \set {H: \exists U \in \tau_d: H = U \cap D}$ Let $\tau^*$ be the topology generated from $\tau_d$ by the addition of all sets of $\BB$. $\tau^* = \tau_d \cup \BB$ $\tau^*$ is then referred to as an indiscrete extension of $\R$.

label: Definition:Indiscrete Extension of Reals/Rational
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $\Q$ denote the set of rational numbers. Let $\tau^*$ be the indiscrete extension of $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$: $\tau^* = \tau_d \cup \set {H: \exists U \in \tau_d: H = U \cap \Q}$ $\tau^*$ is then referred to as the indiscrete rational extension of $\R$.

label: Definition:Indiscrete Topology
snippet: Let $S \ne \O$ be a set. Let $\tau = \set {S, \O}$. Then $\tau$ is called the indiscrete topology on $S$. A topological space $\struct {S, \set {S, \O} }$ is known as an indiscrete space.

label: Definition:Indiscrete Topology/Also defined as
snippet: == Indiscrete Topology: Also defined as == Some sources, on defining the indiscrete topology on a set $S$, make the assumption that $S$ has at least $2$ elements. It is noted that a singleton with the indiscrete topology on it is in fact a trivial topological space.

label: Definition:Indiscrete Topology on Two-Point Set
snippet: == Example of Indiscrete Space == Let $S = \set {0, 1} = 2$ be an instance of an arbitrary doubleton. Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be the topological space on $S$ where $\tau = \set {\O, S}$. Then $\tau$ is the indiscrete topology on a two-point space. The topological space $T$ itself is hence referred to as the indiscrete two-point space.

label: Definition:Induced Homomorphism Between Fundamental Groups
snippet: Let $X,Y$ be topological spaces. Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map. Let $x_0\in X$ and $y_0=f(x_0)\in Y$. Let $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ and $\pi_1(Y,y_0)$ be their fundamental groups. The homomorphism induced by $f$ is the group homomorphism $f_* : \pi_1(X,x_0) \to \pi_1(Y,y_0)$ defined by: $f_*([\gamma]) = [f\circ\gamma]$

label: Definition:Induced Homomorphism between Localizations of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $S, T \subseteq A$ be multiplicatively closed subsets. Let $S$ be a subset of the saturation of $T$. The induced homomorphism between localizations $A_S \to A_T$ is the unique $A$-algebra homomorphism between them.

label: Definition:Induced Mapping on Maximal Spectra
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Let $A$ and $B$ be finitely generated $k$-algebras. Let $f : A \to B$ be a $k$-algebra homomorphism. The induced mapping on spectra by $f$ is the mapping $f^* : \operatorname{Max} B \to \operatorname{Max} A$ between their maximal spectra with: $f^* (\mathfrak m) = f^{-1}(\mathfrak m)$, the preimage of a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m \in \operatorname{Max} B$.

label: Definition:Induced Mapping on Spectra of Rings
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be commutative rings with unity. Let $f : A \to B$ be a ring homomorphism. The induced mapping on spectra by $f$ is the mapping $f^* : \Spec B \to \Spec A$ between their spectra with: $\map {f^*} {\mathfrak p} = \map {f^{-1} } {\mathfrak p}$, the preimage of a prime ideal $\mathfrak p \in \Spec B$.

label: Definition:Induced Metric on Submanifold
snippet: Let $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be a Riemannian manifold with or without a boundary. Let $M : M \subseteq \tilde M$ be a submanifold immersed in $\tilde M$. Let $i : M \to \tilde M$ be the inclusion mapping. Let $g$ be a Riemannian metric such that $g = i^* \tilde g$. Then $g$ is called the induced metric on $M$.

label: Definition:Induced Norm on Quotient of Cauchy Sequences
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\CC$ be the ring of Cauchy sequences over $R$ Let $\NN$ be the set of null sequences. For all $\sequence {x_n} \in \CC$, let $\eqclass {x_n} {}$ denote the left coset $\sequence {x_n} + \NN$ Let $
orm {\, \cdot \,}_1: \CC \, ig / \NN 	o \R_{\ge 0}$ be defined by: $\ds  orall \eqclass {x_n} {} \in \CC \, ig / \NN: 
orm {\eqclass {x_n} {} }_1 = \lim_{n \mathop 	o \infty} 
orm {x_n}$ $
orm {\, \cdot \,}_1$ is called the induced norm on the quotient ring of Cauchy sequences.

label: Definition:Induced Operation
snippet: Operation Induced by Restriction: Where $\struct {T, \circ} \subseteq \struct {S, \circ}$, the restriction of $\circ$ to $T$, namely $\circ \restriction_T$, is called the operation induced on $T$ by $\circ$. Operation Induced on Power Set: Where $\struct {S, \circ}$ is an algebraic structure, the operation $\circ_\PP$ defined on the power set $\powerset S$ as: $A \circ_\PP B = \set {a \circ b: a \in A, b \in B}$ Operation Induced on Quotient Set: Where $\struct {S, \circ}$ is an algebraic structure and $\RR$ is a congruence relation on $\struct {S, \circ}$, the operation $\circ_\RR$ defined…

label: Definition:Induced Outer Measure
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a collection of subsets of a set $X$, and suppose that $\O \in \SS$. Let $\mu$ be a pre-measure on $\SS$. The outer measure induced by the pre-measure $\mu$ is the mapping $\mu^* : \powerset X \to \overline \R_{\ge 0}$ defined as: $\ds \map {\mu^*} S = \inf \set {\sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \map \mu {A_n}: \forall n \in \N: A_n \in \SS, \ S \subseteq \bigcup_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty A_n}$ Here, $\powerset X$ denotes the power set of $X$, and $\overline \R_{\ge 0}$ denotes the set of positive extended real numbers. The infimum of the empty set is taken to be $+\infty$.

label: Definition:Induced Subgraph
snippet: Let $G = \struct {\map V G, \map E G}$ be a graph. Let $V' \subseteq V$ be a subset of vertices of $G$. The subgraph of $G$ induced by $V'$ is the subgraph $G' = \struct {\map {V'} {G'}, \map {E'} {G'} }$ of $G$ such that: $G'$ has the vertex set $V'$ For all $u, v \in V'$, $e = u v \in \map E G$ $e \in \map {E'} {G'}$. That is, it contains all the edges of $G$ that connect elements of the given subset of the vertex set of $G$, and only those edges.

label: Definition:Induction
snippet: Definition:Mathematical Induction, a proof technique. Definition:Induced Representation

label: Definition:Induction Hypothesis
snippet: == Terminology of Mathematical Induction == Consider a proof by mathematical induction: The assumption that $Q$ is true for $w_p$ is called the induction hypothesis. Expressed in the various contexts of mathematical induction:

label: Definition:Induction Step
snippet: == Terminology of Mathematical Induction == Consider a proof by mathematical induction: The proof that the truth of $Q$ for $w_p$ implies the truth of $Q$ for $w_{p^+}$is called the induction step. Expressed in the various contexts of mathematical induction:

label: Definition:Inductive Argument
snippet: An inductive argument is a form of argument in which, if all the premises are true, the conclusion is probably true, but might not be. Such lines of reasoning are ubiquitous in everyday life and in most human endeavors. However, inductive arguments are only conjectures in the field of mathematics. Such arguments are not truth preserving and therefore they are not proofs.

label: Definition:Inductive Class
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Then $A$ is inductive : {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= $A$ is closed under the successor mapping: | q = \forall x | m = \paren {x \in A \implies x^+ \in A} | rc= where $x^+$ is the successor of $x$ }}

label: Definition:Inductive Class/General
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $g: A \to A$ be a mapping on $A$. Then $A$ is inductive under $g$ : {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= $A$ is closed under $g$: | q = \forall x | m = \paren {x \in A \implies \map g x \in A} }}

label: Definition:Inductive Ordered Set
snippet: An inductive ordered set is an ordered set in which every chain has an upper bound.

label: Definition:Inductive Semigroup
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a semigroup. Let there exist $\alpha, \beta \in S$ such that the only subset of $S$ containing both $\alpha$ and $x \circ \beta$ whenever it contains $x$ is $S$ itself. That is: $\exists \alpha, \beta \in S: \forall A \subseteq S: \paren {\alpha \in A \land \paren {\forall x \in A: x \circ \beta \in A} } \implies A = S$ Then $\struct {S, \circ}$ is an inductive semigroup.

label: Definition:Inductive Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of sets. Then $S$ is inductive : {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= $S$ is closed under the successor mapping: | q = \forall x | m = \paren {x \in S \implies x^+ \in S} | rc= where $x^+$ is the successor of $x$ }}

label: Definition:Inductive Set/Axiomatic Set Theory
snippet: The concept of an inductive set is axiomatised in the Axiom of Infinity in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory: $\exists x: \paren {\paren {\exists y: y \in x \land \forall z: \neg \paren {z \in y} } \land \forall u: u \in x \implies \paren {u \cup \set u \in x} }$

label: Definition:Inductive Set/Subset of Real Numbers
snippet: Let $I$ be a subset of the real numbers $\R$. Then $I$ is an inductive set : $1 \in I$ and $x \in I \implies \paren {x + 1} \in I$

label: Definition:Inductive Statistics
snippet: Inductive statistics is the phase of statistics which is concerned with the conditions under which conclusions about populations can be drawn from analysis of particular samples. The inferences drawn by inductive statistics are generally couched in the language of probability theory.

label: Definition:Inelastic Collision
snippet: An inelastic collision is a collision in which the total kinetic energy of the interacting bodies is not the same after the collision as it was before.

label: Definition:Inequality
snippet: An inequality is a mathematical statement that two expressions relate in one of several conventional ways: $a b$ $a \ge b$

label: Definition:Inequality/Also defined as
snippet: == Inequality: Also defined as == A statement of the form: $a \ne b$ may or may not be classified as an inequality, depending on the source work inspected.

label: Definition:Inequality/Member
snippet: Let $\RR$ be an inequality. Let $a \mathrel \RR b$. Then both $a$ and $b$ are referred to as members of the inequality $\RR$.

label: Definition:Inequality/Opposite Sense
snippet: Two inequalities are of opposite sense the direction of the ordering which the inequality is different. That is, whether it is: a greater than relation: $a > b$ or: a less than relation: $a < b$ These two are of opposite sense.

label: Definition:Inequality/Strict
snippet: A strict inequality is an inequality which does not permit the possibility of equality. That is, an inequality of the form: $a b$

label: Definition:Inequality/Weak
snippet: A weak inequality is an inequality which permits the possibility of equality. That is, an inequality of the form: $a \le b$ $a \ge b$

label: Definition:Inertia (Physics)
snippet: Inertia is the tendency of a body to maintain the same velocity in the absence of an external force, in accordance with Newton's First Law of Motion. Equivalently put, inertia is the resistance of a body to a change in its motion. Inertia is equivalent to mass.

label: Definition:Inertia Matrix
snippet: Let $B$ be a rigid body in ordinary $3$-dimensional space. Let $P$ be a fixed point, which may be arbitrary, and can be the center of mass of $B$. Let $\bsomega$ be the column vector which represents the angular velocity of $B$ about $P$. Let $\mathbf L$ be the column vector which represents the angular momentum of $B$ about $P$. Let $\mathbf I$ be the square matrix of order $3$ such that: $\mathbf L = \mathbf I \bsomega$ Then $\mathbf I$ is the inertia matrix for $B$ about $P$, and involves: the moments of inertia the products of inertia of $B$ relative to axes through $P$.

label: Definition:Inertia of Hermitian Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf H$ be a Hermitian matrix. The inertia of $\mathbf H$ is an ordered triple of integers comprising: the number of positive eigenvalues of $\mathbf H$ the number of negative eigenvalues of $\mathbf H$ the number of zero eigenvalues of $\mathbf H$ in that order.

label: Definition:Inertial Coordinate System
snippet: An inertial coordinate system is a set of coordinate axes which are moving at a constant velocity a set of coordinate axes that are fixed in space relative to the positions of distant stars. These are coordinate axes of an inertial frame of reference.

label: Definition:Inertial Frame of Reference
snippet: An inertial frame of reference is a frame of reference in which a body moves at constant velocity in the absence of an external force. That is, it is a frame of reference in which Newton's First Law of Motion holds.

label: Definition:Inessential Mapping
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a continuous mapping. $f$ is an inessential mapping if it is homotopic to a continuous mapping whose image consists of a single point of $Y$.

label: Definition:Infima Inheriting
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $R = \struct {T, \preceq'}$ be an ordered subset of $L$. Then $R$ inherits infima of $L$ for all subsets $X$ of $T$ if $X$ admits an infimum of $L$, then $X$ admits an infimum of $R$ and $\inf_R X = \inf_L X$

label: Definition:Infimum/Also known as
snippet: Particularly in the field of analysis, the infimum of a set $T$ is often referred to as the greatest lower bound of $T$ and denoted $\map {\mathrm {glb} } T$ or $\map {\mathrm {g.l.b.} } T$. Some sources refer to the infimum of a set as the infimum on a set. Some sources refer to the infimum of a set as the meet of the set and use the notation $\bigwedge T$ or $\ds \bigwedge_{y \mathop \in T} y$. Some sources introduce the notation $\ds \inf_{y \mathop \in T} y$, which may improve clarity in some circumstances.

label: Definition:Infimum of Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping from $S$ to $T$. Let $f \sqbrk S$, the image of $f$, admit an infimum. Then the infimum of $f$ (on $S$) is defined by: $\ds \inf_{x \mathop \in S} \map f x = \inf f \sqbrk S$

label: Definition:Infimum of Mapping/Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $f$ be bounded below on $S$.

label: Definition:Infimum of Sequence
snippet: A special case of an infimum of a mapping is an infimum of a sequence, where the domain of the mapping is $\N$. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Let $\set {x_n: n \in \N}$ admit an infimum. Then the infimum of $\sequence {x_n}$) is defined as: $\map \inf {\sequence {x_n} } = \map \inf {\set {x_n: n \in \N} }$

label: Definition:Infimum of Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T \subseteq S$. An element $c \in S$ is the infimum of $T$ in $S$ : $(1): \quad c$ is a lower bound of $T$ in $S$ $(2): \quad d \preccurlyeq c$ for all lower bounds $d$ of $T$ in $S$. If there exists an infimum of $T$ (in $S$), we say that: $T$ admits an infimum (in $S$) or $T$ has an infimum (in $S$).

label: Definition:Infimum of Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $T \subseteq \R$. A real number $c \in \R$ is the infimum of $T$ in $\R$ : $(1): \quad c$ is a lower bound of $T$ in $\R$ $(2): \quad d \le c$ for all lower bounds $d$ of $T$ in $\R$. If there exists an infimum of $T$ (in $\R$), we say that $T$ admits an infimum (in $\R$). The infimum of $T$ is denoted $\inf T$ or $\map \inf T$.

label: Definition:Infinite/Also known as
snippet: == Infinite: Also known as == When did his original work on his development of set theory, the concepts were considered alien and difficult to accept. To sweeten the pill slightly, he coined the word transfinite, which he used instead of infinite, so as not to scare mathematicians who already had a conception of the meaning of infinite, and were having difficulty accepting the challenge to their notions. Hence the concept of a transfinite set, which is exactly the same as an infinite set.

label: Definition:Infinite Cardinal
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ be a cardinal. Then $\mathbf a$ is described as infinite : $\mathbf a = \mathbf a + \mathbf 1$ where $\mathbf 1$ is (cardinal) one.

label: Definition:Infinite Cyclic Group/Also known as
snippet: == Infinite Cyclic Group: Also known as == An infinite cyclic group is also known as a free group on one generator. From Integers under Addition form Infinite Cyclic Group, the additive group of integers $\struct {\Z, +}$ forms an infinite cyclic group. Thus the notation $\Z$ is often used for the infinite cyclic group. This is justified as, from Cyclic Groups of Same Order are Isomorphic, $\Z$ is isomorphic to $\gen a$. Category:Definitions/Infinite Cyclic Group

label: Definition:Infinite Cyclic Group/Definition 1
snippet: An infinite cyclic group is a cyclic group $G$ such that: $\forall n \in \Z_{> 0}: n > 0 \implies \nexists a \in G, a \ne e: a^n = e$

label: Definition:Infinite Cyclic Group/Definition 2
snippet:
An infinite cyclic group is a cyclic group $G$ such that: $ orall a \in G, a 
e e:  orall m, n \in \Z: m 
e n \implies a^m 
e a^n$ where $e$ is the identity element of $G$. That is, such that all the powers of $a$ are distinct.

label: Definition:Infinite Cyclic Group/Group Presentation
snippet: == Group Presentation of Infinite Cyclic Group: Also known as == The presentation of an infinite cyclic group is: $G = \gen a$ This specifies $G$ as being generated by a single element of infinite order.

label: Definition:Infinite Field
snippet: An infinite field $\struct {F, +, \cdot}$ is a field such that $F$ is a infinite set.

label: Definition:Infinite Group
snippet: A group which is not finite is an infinite group. That is, an infinite group is a group of infinite order. That is, a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ is an infinite group its underlying set $G$ is infinite. That is, an infinite group is a group with an infinite number of elements.

label: Definition:Infinite Group/Countable
snippet: An infinite group whose underlying set $G$ is countable is a countably infinite group.

label: Definition:Infinite Limit Operator
snippet: Let $c$ be the space of convergent sequences. Let $\mathbf x := \sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} \in c$. Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. The infinite limit operator, denoted by $L$, is the mapping $L : c \to \R$ such that: $\ds \map L {\mathbf x} := \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n$

label: Definition:Infinite Matrix
snippet: An infinite matrix is a matrix whose order is infinite.

label: Definition:Infinite Order
snippet: Abstract algebra: Infinite Order of Algebraic Structure Infinite Group: a group of infinite order Group theory: Infinite Order of Group Element

label: Definition:Infinite Sequence/Also known as
snippet: == Infinite Sequence: Also known as == Treatments of infinite sequences which approach the definition of a sequence from the direction of ordered tuples offer the term $\omega$-tuple for the concept of a tuple whose domain is (countably) infinite. Some sources use the term denumerable sequence.

label: Definition:Infinite Set
snippet: A set which is not finite is called infinite. That is, it is a set for which there is no bijection between it and any $\N_n$, where $\N_n$ is the the set of all elements of $n$ less than $n$, no matter how big we make $n$.

label: Definition:Infinite Topological Space
snippet: An infinite topological space is a topological space whose underlying set is infinite.

label: Definition:Infinitely Often (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {E_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $\Sigma$. We define: {{eqn | l = \set {E_n \text { infinitely often} } | r = \set {\omega \in \Omega : \omega \in E_n \text { for infinitely many } n} }} {{eqn | r = \limsup_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n }} where $\ds \limsup_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n$ is the limit superior of $\sequence {E_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$.

label: Definition:Infinitesimal/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Infinitesimal == The concept of an infinitesimal was initially proposed by when inventing calculus. The logical inconsistencies of this approach, famously criticised by , caused it to be abandoned. However, the concept has been revived in recent years with the invention of nonstandard analysis.

label: Definition:Infinitesimal/Informal Definition
snippet: An infinitesimal is a mathematical object $\delta$ resembling a (real) number such that: $(1): \quad \delta > 0$ $(2): \quad \forall x \in \R_{>0}: \delta < x$ That is, an infinitesimal is a (strictly) positive real number which is smaller than every other (strictly) positive real number.

label: Definition:Infinitesimal Generator of Semigroup
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $\family {\map T t}_{t \ge 0}$ be a $\hointr 0 \infty$-indexed family of bounded linear transformations $\map T t : X \to X$. Define: $\ds \map D A = \set {x \in X : \lim_{t \mathop \to 0^+} \frac {\map T t x - x} t \text { exists} }$ Define $A : \map D A \to X$ by: $\ds A x = \lim_{t \mathop \to 0^+} \frac {\map T t x - x} t$ for $x \in \map D A$. We say that $\struct {\map D A, A}$ is the infinitesimal generator of $\family {\map T t}_{t \ge 0}$.

label: Definition:Infinity
snippet: Informally, the term infinity is used to mean some infinite number, but this concept falls very far short of a usable definition. The symbol $\infty$ (supposedly invented by ) is often used in this context to mean an infinite number. However, outside of its formal use in the definition of limits its use is strongly discouraged until you know what you're talking about.

label: Definition:Inflationary Mapping/Also known as
snippet: == Inflationary Mapping: Also known as == An inflationary mapping is also known as a progressive mapping or progressing mapping, particularly in the context of class theory, where the ordering on the underlying ordered set is the subset relation. The term extensive mapping can also occasionally be seen, but this is not endorsed on because of its possible confusion with the concept of the . Sources which prefer the term function to mapping will tend to use such here: inflationary function, progressing function, and so on. Category:Definitions/Inflationary Mappings

label: Definition:Information Model
snippet: An information model is a mathematical model constructed to investigate a question in the field of information theory.
