It is usual for it to consist of: $(1): \quad$ a source of information $(2): \quad$ an encoder to convert the information into a form suitable for transmission $(3): \quad$ a channel along which the information is transmitted $(4): \quad$ a decoder to convert the information back into a readable form $(5): \quad$ a destination, or user, which receives the information.

label: Definition:Information Theory
snippet: Information theory is that branch of mathematics concerned with the flow of information. It is mainly concerned with the handling of uncertainty in communication media. It can also be considered as also encompassing coding theory.

label: Definition:Initial Condition
snippet: Let $\Phi = \map F {x, y, y', y, \ldots, y^{\paren n} }$ be an ordinary differential equation. An initial condition is an ordered pair $\tuple {x_0, y_0}$ which any solution of $\Phi$ must satisfy. That is, an initial condition is the additional imposition that a solution $y = \map y x$ of $\Phi$ satisfy: $\map y {x_0} = y_0$

label: Definition:Initial Homomorphism from Integers to Ring with Unity
snippet: Let $\Z$ be the ring of integers. Let $R$ be a ring with unity. The initial homomorphism $\Z \to R$ is the unital ring homomorphism that sends $n \in \Z$ to the $n$th power of $1$ in $R$: $ n \mapsto n \cdot 1$.

label: Definition:Initial Object
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. An initial object of $\mathbf C$ is an object $0 \in \mathbf C_0$ of $\mathbf C$ such that: For all $C \in \mathbf C_0$, there is a unique morphism $0 \to C$.

label: Definition:Initial Segment
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a well-ordered set. Let $a \in S$. The initial segment (of $S$) determined by $a$ is defined as: $S_a := \set {b \in S: b \preceq a \land b \ne a}$ which can also be rendered as: $S_a := \set {b \in S: b \prec a}$ That is, $S_a$ is the set of all elements of $S$ that strictly precede $a$. That is, $S_a$ is the strict lower closure of $a$ (in $S$). By extension, $S_a$ is described as an initial segment (of $S$).

label: Definition:Initial Segment/Also defined as
snippet: == Initial Segment: Also defined as == Some sources use the term initial segment to refer to sets with a certain property a relation. Terminology for such sets is currently not fixed on . It is also worth noting that the concept of defining the set of all elements which are related to another element crops up throughout the fields of mapping theory and relation theory. However, defining that set as a segment is usually done only in the context of order theory. Category:Definitions/Initial Segments

label: Definition:Initial Segment/Also known as
snippet: The concept of an initial segment is often (and usually more clearly) referred to by its mundane description: the set of strictly preceding elements. Some sources refer to this concept as a segment. Some sources refer to this concept as a section. When it is necessary to distinguish between this and a weak initial segment, this is called a strict initial segment. Some sources use the term strict lower closure, but prefers to reserve that term for when the ordering in question is not necessarily a well-ordering. There is no standard notation or convention for this concept.

label: Definition:Initial Segment/Class Theory
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $\preceq$ be a well-ordering on $A$. Let $a \in A$. The initial segment (of $A$) determined by $a$ is defined as: $A_a := \set {b \in S: b \preceq a \land b \ne a}$ which can also be rendered as: $A_a := \set {b \in S: b \prec a}$

label: Definition:Initial Segment of Natural Numbers/One-Based
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. The initial segment of the non-zero natural numbers determined by $n$: $\set {1, 2, 3, \ldots, n}$ is denoted $\N^*_{\le n}$.

label: Definition:Initial Segment of Natural Numbers/Zero-Based
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. The initial segment of the natural numbers determined by $n$: $\set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1}$ is denoted $\N_{<n}$.

label: Definition:Initial Topology
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {\struct {Y_i, \tau_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces indexed by $I$. Let $\family {f_i: X \to Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of mappings indexed by $I$.

label: Definition:Initial Topology/Also known as
snippet: == Initial Topology: Also known as == The initial topology is also known as: the projective topology the weak topology on $X$ with respect to $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ If only a single topological space $\struct {Y, \tau_Y}$ and a single mapping $f: X \to Y$ are under consideration, the initial topology on $X$ with respect to $f$ is additionally known as: the pullback topology on $X$ under $f$ the topology on $X$ induced by $f$ (but this is ambiguous) the inverse image of $\tau_Y$ under $f$ and is often denoted by $\map {f^*} {\tau_Y}$ or $\map {f^{-1} } {\tau_Y}$.

label: Definition:Initial Topology/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {\struct {Y_i, \tau_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces indexed by $I$. Let $\family {f_i: X \to Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of mappings indexed by $I$. Let: $\SS = \set {f_i^{-1} \sqbrk U: i \in I, U \in \tau_i}$ where $f_i^{-1} \sqbrk U$ denotes the preimage of $U$ under $f_i$. The topology $\tau$ on $X$ generated by $\SS$ is called the initial topology on $X$ with respect to $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$.

label: Definition:Initial Topology/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $I$ be an indexing set. Let $\family {\struct {Y_i, \tau_i} }_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of topological spaces indexed by $I$. Let $\family {f_i: X \to Y_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of mappings indexed by $I$. Let $\tau$ be the coarsest topology on $X$ such that each $f_i: X \to Y_i$ is $\tuple {\tau, \tau_i}$-continuous. Then $\tau$ is known as the initial topology on $X$ with respect to $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$.

label: Definition:Initial Value Problem
snippet: Let $\map y x$ be a solution to the first order ordinary differential equation: $\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = \map f {x, y}$ which is subject to an initial condition: $\tuple {a, b}$. That is, it is required that $y = b$ when $x = a$, that is $\map y a = b$. The finding of the resulting particular solution is known as an initial value problem.

label: Definition:Injection/Definition 4
snippet: Let $f$ be a mapping. $f$ is an injection : $\forall y \in \Img f: \card {\map {f^{-1} } y} = \card {\set {f^{-1} \sqbrk {\set y} } } = 1$ where: $\Img f$ denotes the image set of $f$ $\card {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the cardinality of a set $\map {f^{-1} } y$ is the preimage of $y$ $f^{-1} \sqbrk {\set y}$ is the preimage of the subset $\set y \subseteq \Img f$. That is, the preimage of $y$ is a singleton for all $y$ in the image set of $f$.

label: Definition:Injection/Definition 6
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping where $S \ne \O$. Then $f$ is an injection $f$ is left cancellable: $\forall X: \forall g_1, g_2: X \to S: f \circ g_1 = f \circ g_2 \implies g_1 = g_2$ where $g_1$ and $g_2$ are arbitrary mappings from an arbitrary set $X$ to the domain $S$ of $f$.

label: Definition:Injective
snippet: Definition:Injection Definition:Injective Object Definition:Injective Module Definition:Injective Morphism

label: Definition:Injective Banach Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {Y, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. We say that $Y$ is injective : for each Banach space $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ with closed linear subspace $E$ and bounded linear transformation $T : E \to Y$: there exists a bounded linear transformation $\widetilde T : X \to Y$ extending $T$.

label: Definition:Injective Module
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. A left $R$-module is injective it is an injective object in the category of left $R$-modules.

label: Definition:Injective Object
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $I$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. $I$ is an injective object : for every monomorphism $i: X \to Y$ in $\mathbf C$ and: for every morphism $f : X \to I$ there exists a morphism $g : Y \to I$, such that: $g \circ i = f$

label: Definition:Injective Path
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbb I \subset \R$ be the closed unit interval $\closedint 0 1$. Let $a, b \in T$. An injective path from $a$ to $b$ is a path $f: \mathbb I \to T$ such that $f$ is injective. That is, an injective path from $a$ to $b$ is a continuous injection $f: \mathbb I \to T$ such that $\map f 0 = a$ and $\map f 1 = b$. The mapping $f$ can be described as an injective path (in $T$) joining $a$ and $b$.

label: Definition:Injective Path Component
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let us define the relation $\sim$ on $T$ as follows: $x \sim y \iff x$ and $y$ are injectively path-connected. We have that $\sim $ is an equivalence relation, so from the Fundamental Theorem on Equivalence Relations, the points in $T$ can be partitioned into equivalence classes. These equivalence classes are called the injective path components of $T$. If $x \in T$, then the injective path component of $T$ containing $x$ (that is, the set of points $y \in T$ with $x \sim y$) can be denoted by $\map {\operatorname {IPC}_x} T$.

label: Definition:Injective Resolution
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an abelian category. Let $X$ be an object in $\mathbf A$. An injective resolution of $X$ is a cochain complex $P := \family {d^i : I^i \to I^{i + 1} }_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ in $\mathbf A$, such that: $(1): \quad \forall i < 0 : I^i = 0$ $(2): \quad I^i$ is injective for all $i \ge 0$ together with a morphism $\varepsilon : X \to I^0$, such that the cochain complex: $\begin{xy} \xymatrix{ \dots \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & 0 \ar[r] & X \ar[r]^{\varepsilon} & I^0 \ar[r]^{d^0} & I^1 \ar[r]^{d^1} & I^2 \ar[r]^{d^2} & \dots } \end{xy}$ is exact.

label: Definition:Injective Space
snippet: Let $Z = \struct {S, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Then $Z$ is (an) injective (space) for all topological spaces $X = \struct {H, \tau_2}$ and for all continuous mappings $f: H \to S$ and for all topological spaces $Y = \struct {T, \tau_3}$ such that $X$ is topological subspace of $Y$: there exists a continuous mapping $g: T \to S$: $g \restriction H = f$

label: Definition:Injective on Morphisms
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to be injective on morphisms for all morphisms $f, g$ of $\mathbf C$: $F f = F g$ implies $f = g$ Note that it is not required that $f$ and $g$ have equal domains or codomains.

label: Definition:Injective on Objects
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to be injective on objects for all objects $C_1, C_2$ of $\mathbf C$: $F C_1 = F C_2$ implies $C_1 = C_2$

label: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected
snippet: Injective path-connectedness is a property of a topological space $T$ which relates to the existence of certain continuous injections from a closed real interval (in practice, usually just the closed unit interval) into $T$.

label: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected/Points
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $a, b \in S$ be such that there exists an injective path from $a$ to $b$. That is, there exists a continuous injection $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that: Then $a$ and $b$ are injectively path-connected in $T$. It is also declared that any point $a$ is injectively path-connected to itself.

label: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected/Subset
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $U \subseteq S$ be a subset of $T$. Let $T' = \struct {U, \tau_U}$ be the subspace of $T$ induced by $U$. Then $T'$ is injectively path-connected in $T$ every two points in $U$ are injectively path-connected in $T'$. That is, $T'$ is injectively path-connected : for every $x, y \in U$, there exists a continuous injection $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that $\map f 0 = x$ and $\map f 1 = y$.

label: Definition:Injectively Path-Connected/Topological Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is injectively path-connected every two points in $T$ are injectively path-connected in $T$. That is, $T$ is injectively path-connected : $\forall x, y \in S: \exists$ a continuous injection $f: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ such that $\map f 0 = x$ and $\map f 1 = y$.

label: Definition:Injectivity Radius at Point of Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold without boundary. Let $T_ p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $\exp_p$ be the restricted exponential map at $p \in M$. Let $\map {B_a} 0 \in T_p M$ be an open ball. Suppose $A_p$ is the set of all $a \in \R_{> 0}$ for which $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism from $\map {B_a} 0 \subseteq T_p M$ onto its image. Then the supremum of $A_p$ is called the injectivity radius of $M$ at $p$ and is denoted by $\map {\operatorname{inj} } p$: $\map {\operatorname{inj} } p = \sup {A_p}$

label: Definition:Injectivity Radius of Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold without boundary. Let $\map {\operatorname {inj} } p$ be the injectivity radius at $p \in M$. Suppose $\map {\operatorname {inj} } p = \infty$. Then the infimum of $\map {\operatorname {inj} } p$ over $p \in M$ is called the injectivity radius of $M$ and is denoted by $\map {\operatorname{inj} } M$: $\ds \map {\operatorname{inj} } M = \inf_{p \mathop \in M} {\map {\operatorname {inj} } p}$

label: Definition:Inner Automorphism
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $x \in G$. Let the mapping $\kappa_x: G \to G$ be defined such that: $\forall g \in G: \map {\kappa_x} g = x g x^{-1}$ $\kappa_x$ is called the inner automorphism of $G$ (given) by $x$. The set of inner automorphisms of $G$ is denoted on as $\Inn G$.

label: Definition:Inner Automorphism Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. The inner automorphism group of $G$ is the algebraic structure: $\struct {\Inn G, \circ}$ where: $\Inn G$ is the set of inner automorphisms of $G$ $\circ$ denotes composition of mappings.

label: Definition:Inner Jordan Content
snippet: Let $M \subseteq \R^n$ be a bounded subspace of Euclidean $n$-space. Let: $\ds \RR = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \closedint {a_i} {b_i}$ be a closed $n$-rectangle that contains $M$. The inner Jordan content of $M$ is defined and denoted as: $\map {m_*} M = \map V \RR - \map {m^*} {\RR \setminus M}$ where: $\map {m^*} {\RR \setminus M}$ denotes the outer Jordan content of $R \setminus M$ That is, the inner Jordan content of $M$ is defined to be the outer Jordan content of the complement of $M$, relative to some fixed $\RR \supseteq M$.

label: Definition:Inner Limit
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) topological space. Let $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of sets in $X$. The inner limit of $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is defined as: $\ds \liminf_{n \mathop \to \infty} \ C_n := \set {x \in X: \exists N \text { cofinite set of } \N, \exists x_v \in C_v \paren {v \in N} \text { such that } x_v \to x}$ where $x_v \to x$ denotes convergence in the topology $\tau$.

label: Definition:Inner Model Theory
snippet: Inner model theory is a branch of set theory and model theory which studies certain models of ZFC.

label: Definition:Inner Product/Also defined as
snippet: == Also defined as == Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $\GF$ that is a subfield of $\R$ or $\C$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \GF$ be an inner product on $\GF$. Some texts define an inner product only for vector spaces over $\R$ or $\C$. This ensures that for all $v \in V$, the inner product norm: $\norm v = \sqrt {\innerprod v v}$ is a scalar. prefers the more general definition, and lists additional requirement on $\GF$ in theorems where it is needed, such as the Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization theorem.

label: Definition:Inner Product/Also denoted as
snippet: == Also denoted as == The inner product $\innerprod x y$ can also be denoted as $\left \langle {x; y} \right \rangle$. If there is more than one vector space under consideration, then the notation $\innerprod x y_V$ for a vector space $V$ is commonplace.

label: Definition:Inner Product/Complex Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a complex subfield $\GF$. A (complex) inner product is a mapping $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \GF$ that satisfies the complex inner product axioms: That is, a (complex) inner product is a complex semi-inner product with the additional condition $(4)$.

label: Definition:Inner Product/Real Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a real subfield $\GF$. A (real) inner product is a mapping $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \GF$ that satisfies the real inner product axioms: That is, a (real) inner product is a real semi-inner product with the additional condition $(4)$.

label: Definition:Inner Product Induced by Positive Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a positive linear operator on $\HH$. Define a mapping $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_T : \map D T \times \map D T \to \C$ by: $\innerprod \phi \psi_T = \innerprod {\paren {T + I} \phi} \psi$ for each $\tuple {\phi, \psi} \in \map D T \times \map D T$. We say that $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_T$ is the inner product on $\map D T$ induced by $T$.

label: Definition:Inner Product Norm
snippet: Let $\Bbb F$ be a subfield of $\C$. Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be an inner product space over $\Bbb F$. Then the inner product norm on $V$ is the mapping $\norm {\, \cdot \,} : V \to \R_{\ge 0}$ given by: $\norm x = \sqrt {\innerprod x x}$ for each $x \in V$.

label: Definition:Inner Product Space
snippet: An inner product space is a vector space together with an associated inner product.

label: Definition:Inner Product Space/Complex Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a complex subfield $\GF$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot : V \times V \to \GF$ be an complex inner product on $V$. We say that $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ is a (complex) inner product space. That is, a (complex) inner product space is a complex vector space together with an associated complex inner product.

label: Definition:Inner Product Space/Real Field
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a real subfield $\GF$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot : V \times V \to \GF$ be an real inner product on $V$. We say that $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ is a (real) inner product space. That is, an (real) inner product space is a real vector space together with an associated real inner product.

label: Definition:Inner Product on Cotangent Space
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $x \in M$ be a base point. Let ${T_x}^* M$ be the cotangent space of $M$ at $x$. Let $\omega, \eta \in {T_x}^* M$ be covector fields. The inner product on the cotangent space is defined by: $\innerprod \omega \eta_g := \innerprod {\omega^\sharp} {\eta^\sharp}_g$ where $\sharp$ denotes the sharp operator. Locally this reads: $\innerprod \omega \eta = g^{ij} \omega_i \eta_j$

label: Definition:Inscribe
snippet: Let a geometric figure $A$ be constructed in the interior of another geometric figure $B$ such that: $(1): \quad$ $A$ and $B$ have points in common $(2): \quad$ No part of $A$ is outside $B$. Then $A$ is inscribed inside $B$.

label: Definition:Inscribe/Circle in Polygon
snippet: A circle is inscribed in a polygon when it is tangent to each of the sides of that polygon: 300px '

label: Definition:Inscribe/Polygon in Circle
snippet: A polygon is inscribed in a circle when each of its vertices lies on the circumference of the circle: 300px That is, the vertices are concyclic. '

label: Definition:Inscribe/Polygon in Polygon
snippet: A polygon is inscribed in another polygon when each of its vertices lies on the corresponding side of the other polygon. '

label: Definition:Insertion of Generators
snippet: Let $S$ be a set, and let $S^*$ be its Kleene closure. The insertion of generators (into $S^*$) is the mapping $i: S \to S^*$ defined by: $i \left({s}\right) := \left\langle{s}\right\rangle$ that is, it sends any element $s$ of $S$ to the one-term sequence containing only $s$.

label: Definition:Instant of Time
snippet: An instant is a specific point in time. Category:Definitions/Time

label: Definition:Instantaneous/Acceleration
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion. Let $\Bbb I = \closedint t {t + h}$ be a time interval. Let $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ be the velocity of $B$ at $t$ and $t + h$ respectively. Let $\overline {\mathbf a}$ denote the average acceleration of $B$ over $\Bbb I$. The instantaneous acceleration $\mathbf a$ of $B$ at time $t$ is defined as the limit of $\overline {\mathbf a}$ as $h \to 0$: $\mathbf a := \ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \dfrac {\mathbf v_2 - \mathbf v_1} h$

label: Definition:Instantaneous/Center of Rotation
snippet: Let $B$ be a body undergoing rotation. The instantaneous center of rotation of $B$ is the point about which $B$ is rotating at a particular time instant.

label: Definition:Instantaneous/Velocity
snippet: Let $B$ be a body in motion. Let $\Bbb I = \closedint t {t + h}$ be a time interval. Let $\mathbf s_1$ and $\mathbf s_2$ be the displacement of $B$ at $t$ and $t + h$ respectively. Let $\overline {\mathbf v}$ denote the average velocity of $B$ over $\Bbb I$. The instantaneous velocity $\mathbf v$ of $B$ at time $t$ is defined as the limit of $\overline {\mathbf v}$ as $h \to 0$: $\mathbf v := \ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \dfrac {\mathbf s_2 - \mathbf s_1} h$

label: Definition:Instanton
snippet: An instanton is a solution to a certain kind of equation in gauge theories.

label: Definition:Integer
snippet: The numbers $\set {\ldots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ are called the integers. This set is usually denoted $\Z$. An individual element of $\Z$ is called an integer.

label: Definition:Integer-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a function. Let $S_1 \subseteq S$ such that $f \left({S_1}\right) \subseteq \Z$. Then $f$ is said to be integer-valued on $S_1$. That is, $f$ is defined as integer-valued on $S_1$ the image of $S_1$ under $f$ lies entirely within the set of integers $\Z$. An integer-valued function is a function $f: S \to \Z$ whose codomain is the set of integers $\Z$. That is, $f$ is integer-valued it is integer-valued over its entire domain. Category:Definitions/Integers

label: Definition:Integer/Also known as
snippet: == Integer: Also known as == The integers are also referred to as whole numbers, so as to distinguish them from fractions. However, use of this term is discouraged because it is ambiguous: it can refer to the integers, the positive integers, or the negative integers, depending on the preference of the author. Some sources refer to the integers as rational integers, to clearly distinguish them from the algebraic integers. Some sources use the term directed numbers or signed numbers for integers, so as to distinguish them from the natural numbers which are, by definition defined without a sign.

label: Definition:Integer/Formal Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {\N, +}$ be the commutative semigroup of natural numbers under addition. From Inverse Completion of Natural Numbers, we can create $\struct {\N', +'}$, an inverse completion of $\struct {\N, +}$. From Construction of Inverse Completion, this is done as follows: Let $\boxtimes$ be the cross-relation defined on $\N \times \N$ by: $\tuple {x_1, y_1} \boxtimes \tuple {x_2, y_2} \iff x_1 + y_2 = x_2 + y_1$ From Cross-Relation is Congruence Relation, $\boxtimes$ is a congruence relation.

label: Definition:Integer/Formal Definition/Notation
snippet: Let $\Z$ be the integers defined as a set of ordered pairs of natural numbers. We have that $\eqclass {\tuple {a, b} } \boxminus$ is an equivalence class of ordered pairs of natural numbers under the congruence relation $\boxminus$. As this notation is cumbersome, it is commonplace though technically incorrect to streamline it to $\eqclass {a, b} \boxminus$, or $\eqclass {a, b} {}$. This is generally considered acceptable, as long as it is made explicit as to the precise meaning of $\eqclass {a, b} {}$ at the start of any exposition. Category:Definitions/Integers

label: Definition:Integer/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Integer == The use of $Z$ to denote the set of integers appears to have originated with . Earlier, the symbol $\overline{\mathfrak Z}$ had been used by .

label: Definition:Integer/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Integer == The word integer is pronounced with the stress on the first syllable, and the g is soft (i.e. sounds like j): in-te-jer. This is inconsistent with the pronunciation of its for integral (pertaining to an integer), where the g is hard (as in get): in-te-gral. Also note the use of the word integral as an adjective, which in natural language means necessary or inherent, usually encountered in rhetoric. For further confusion, this is pronounced in-teg-ral, the stress being on the second syllable.

label: Definition:Integer/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Integers == Variants on $\Z$ are often seen, for example $\mathbf Z$, $\ZZ$ and $\mathfrak Z$, or even just $Z$. Some sources use $I$, while others use $\mathbf J$ or a variant.

label: Definition:Integer Coding
snippet: Computability Theory: Code Number for Integer

label: Definition:Integer Combination
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$. An integer $n$ of the form: $n = p a + q b: p, q \in \Z$ is an integer combination of $a$ and $b$.

label: Definition:Integer Division
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$ be integers such that $b \ne 0$. From the Division Theorem: $\exists_1 q, r \in \Z: a = q b + r, 0 \le r < \size b$ where $q$ is the quotient and $r$ is the remainder. The process of finding $q$ and $r$ is known as (integer) division of $a$ by $b$, and we write: $a \div b = q \rem r$

label: Definition:Integer Division/Exact
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$ be integers such that $b \ne 0$. Let: $a \div b = q \rem 0$ where $\div$ denotes integer division. This is an instance of exact division.

label: Definition:Integer Heronian Triangle
snippet: An integer Heronian triangle is a Heronian triangle whose sides are integers.

label: Definition:Integer Interval/Also denoted as
snippet: == Integer Interval: Also known as == Some authorities consider $\closedint m n$ to be an abuse of notation, as there is nothing in it intrinsically to distinguish it from the closed real interval $\set {x \in \R: m \le x \le n}$. Such sources prefer to use the more conventional $\set {m, m + 1, \ldots, n}$, but then again it relies upon the implicit understanding that the domain is the set of integers.

label: Definition:Integer Lattice
snippet: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Let $\R^n$ be the $n$-dimensional real Euclidean space. Let $\CC$ be the Cartesian coordinate system of $n$ dimensions embedded in $\R^n$. The integer lattice in $\R^n$ is the set of points in $\R^n$ which can be defined using coordinates of $\CC$ which are integers. Thus it is the point lattice on $\R^n$ whose basis is the standard ordered basis over $\R^n$: $\BB = \set {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ where: $\mathbf e_k := \tuple {\delta_{1 k}, \delta_{2 k}, \ldots, \delta_{n k} }$ $\delta_{j k}$ is the Kronecker delta.

label: Definition:Integer Partition
snippet: A partition of a (strictly) positive integer $n$ is a way of writing $n$ as a sum of (strictly) positive integers.

label: Definition:Integer Partition/Partition Function
snippet: The partition function $p: \Z_{>0} \to \Z_{>0}$ is defined as: $\forall n \in \Z_{>0}: \map p n =$ the number of partitions of the (strictly) positive integer $n$.

label: Definition:Integer Reciprocal Space
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line $\R$ under the usual (Euclidean) topology $\tau_d$. Let $A \subseteq \R$ be the set of all points on $\R$ defined as: $A := \set {\dfrac 1 n : n \in \Z_{>0} }$ That is: $A := \set {1, \dfrac 1 2, \dfrac 1 3, \dfrac 1 4, \ldots}$ Then $\struct {A, \tau_d}$ is the integer reciprocal space.

label: Definition:Integer Sequence
snippet: An integer sequence is a sequence (usually infinite) whose codomain is the set of integers $\Z$.

label: Definition:Integer Square
snippet: An integer square is a square whose sides are integers.

label: Definition:Integers Modulo m
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. The integers modulo $m$ are the set of least positive residues of the set of residue classes modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$

label: Definition:Integrable Function/Complex
snippet: Let $\mathbb I := \closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $f: \mathbb I \to \C$ be a bounded complex-valued function. Define the real function $x: \mathbb I \to \R$ by: $\forall t \in \mathbb I: \map x t = \map \Re {\map f t}$ Define the real function $y: \mathbb I \to \R$ by: $\forall t \in \mathbb I: \map y t = \map \Im {\map f t}$ where: $\map \Re {\map f t}$ denotes the real part of the complex number $\map f t$ $\map \Im {\map f t}$ denotes the imaginary part of $\map f t$. Suppose that both $x$ and $y$ are Riemann integrable over $\mathbb I$.

label: Definition:Integrable Function/Lebesgue
snippet: Let $\lambda^n$ be a Lebesgue measure on $\R^n$ for some $n > 0$. Let $f: \R^n \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. Then $f$ is said to be Lebesgue integrable it is $\lambda^n$-integrable. Similarly, for all real numbers $p \ge 1$, $f$ is said to be Lebesgue $p$-integrable it is $p$-integrable under $\lambda^n$.

label: Definition:Integrable Function/Measure Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\MM_{\overline \R}$ denote the space of $\Sigma$-measurable, extended real-valued functions . Let $f \in \MM_{\overline \R}, f: X \to \overline \R$ be a measurable function. Then $f$ is said to be $\mu$-integrable : $\ds \int f^+ \rd \mu < +\infty$ and $\ds \int f^- \rd \mu < +\infty$ where $f^+$, $f^-$ are the positive and negative parts of $f$, respectively. The integral signs denote $\mu$-integration of positive measurable functions.

label: Definition:Integrable Function/Measure Space/Complex Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\struct {\C, \map \BB \C}$ be the complex numbers made into a measurable space with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Let $f : X \to \C$ be a $\Sigma/\map \BB C$-measurable function. Let $\map \Re f : X \to \R$ and $\map \Im f : X \to \R$ be the real part and imaginary part of $f$ respectively. We say that $f$ is $\mu$-integrable $\map \Re f$ and $\map \Im f$ are (real) $\mu$-integrable.

label: Definition:Integrable Function/p-Integrable
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f \in \MM_{\overline \R}, f: X \to \overline \R$ be a measurable function. Let $p \ge 1$ be a real number. Then $f$ is said to be $p$-integrable $\mu$ : $\ds \int \size f^p \rd \mu < +\infty$ is $\mu$-integrable.

label: Definition:Integrable Random Variable
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. We say that $X$ is integrable $X$ is $\Pr$-integrable.

label: Definition:Integrable System
snippet: An integrable system is a system of one or more nonlinear partial differential equations whose solutions have special properties.

label: Definition:Integrable System/Also defined as
snippet: == Integrable System: Also known as == An integrable system can also be seen defined as a system of differential equations that can be solved by explicit integration.

label: Definition:Integral
snippet: Commutative algebra: Integral Closure Integrally Closed Integral Element of Ring Extension Integral Ring Extension Ring theory: Integral Domain Integral Polynomial Number theory: Integral Multiple Integral Part Analysis: Integral Calculus Integral: Definite Integral Indefinite Integral Integral: As a synonym for the term solution to a differential equation.

label: Definition:Integral/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Integral == The word integral has the following meanings in mathematics: From the term integral calculus, where it is defined as the subfield of calculus concerned with the rates at which quantities accumulate The form of the word integer, which is in generally deprecated on as much as practical in favour of using the word integer itself as an In abstract algebra, where it arises in the concept of an integral domain. In all of the above, the word is pronounced in-te-gral. In natural language, the integral, meaning necessary or inherent, usually encountered in rhetoric.

label: Definition:Integral Basis
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct {G, +, \circ}$ be the $\Z$-module associated with $G$. An integral basis for $G$ is a basis of $G$ over $\Z$.

label: Definition:Integral Curvature
snippet: Let $ABC$ be a geodesic triangle on a surface $S$. The integral curvature of $ABC$ is given by: $\ds \int_{ABC} \Kappa \rd a$ where $\Kappa$ is the Gaussian curvature at each point on $ABC$.

label: Definition:Integral Curve
snippet: Let $\map f {x, y}$ be a continuous real function within a rectangular region $R$ of the Cartesian plane. Consider the first order ODE: $(1): \quad \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = \map f {x, y}$ 500px Let $P_0 = \tuple {x_0, y_0}$ be a point in $R$. The number: $\paren {\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} }_{P_0} = \map f {x_0, y_0}$ determines the slope of a straight line passing through $P_0$. Let $P_1 = \tuple {x_1, y_1}$ be a point in $R$ close to $P_0$. Then: $\paren {\dfrac {\d y} {\d x} }_{P_1} = \map f {x_1, y_1}$ determines the slope of a straight line passing through $P_1$.

label: Definition:Integral Equation/Parameter
snippet: Consider the integral equation: of the first kind: $\map f x = \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ of the second kind: $\map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ of the third kind: $\map u x \map g x = \map f x + \lambda \ds \int_{\map a x}^{\map b x} \map K {x, y} \map g y \rd x$ The number $\lambda$ is known as the parameter of the integral equation.

label: Definition:Integral Ideal
snippet: Let $J \subseteq \Z$ be a non-empty subset of the set of integers. Let $J$ fulfil the following conditions: Then $J$ is an integral ideal.

label: Definition:Integral Multiple/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Then $x$ is an integral multiple of $y$ $x$ is congruent to $0$ modulo $y$: $x \equiv 0 \pmod y$ That is: $\exists k \in \Z: x = 0 + k y$

label: Definition:Integral Multiple/Rings and Fields
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a ring or a field whose zero is $0_F$. Let $a \in F$. Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Then $n \cdot a$ is an integral multiple of $a$ where $n \cdot a$ is defined as: $n \cdot a := \begin {cases} 0_F & : n = 0 \\ \paren {\paren {n - 1} \cdot a} + a & : n > 1 \\ \size n \cdot \paren {-a} & : n where $\size n$ is the absolute value of $n$. Using sum notation: $\ds n \cdot a := \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n a$

label: Definition:Integral Operator
snippet: Let $X, Y$ be sets of mappings, real or complex numbers. Let $A : X \to Y$ be a mapping such that $A$ is expressible as an integral of elements of $X$ (possibly involving weight functions and kernels). Then $A$ is known as an integral operator. Category:Definitions/Operator Theory

label: Definition:Integral Transform
snippet: Let $p$ be a variable whose domain is a subset of the set of real numbers $\R$. Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed real interval for some $a, b \in \R: a \le b$. Let $f: \closedint a b \to \R$ be a real function defined on the domain $\closedint a b$. Let $\map K {p, x}$ be a real-valued function defined for all $p$ in its domain and all $x \in \closedint a b$. Let $\map f x \map K {p, x}$ be integrable $x$ for all $p$ in its domain and all $x \in \closedint a b$.

label: Definition:Integral Transform/Operator
snippet: Let $\map F p$ be an integral transform: $\map F p = \ds \int_a^b \map f x \map K {p, x} \rd x$ This can be written in the form: $F = \map T f$ where $T$ is interpreted as the (unitary) operator meaning: Multiply this by $\map K {p, x}$ and integrate $x$ between the limits $a$ and $b$. Thus $T$ transforms the function $\map f x$ into its image $\map F p$, which is itself another real function.

label: Definition:Integral of Continuous Function wrt Arc Length
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $\gamma : \closedint a b \to M$ be a smooth curve segment. Let $f : \closedint a b \to \R$ be a continuous real function. Let $\size {\, \cdot \,}_g$ be the Riemannian inner product norm. Then the integral of $f$ $\gamma$ is defined as: $\ds \int_\gamma f \rd s = \int_a^b \map f t \size {\map {\gamma'} t}_g \rd t$

label: Definition:Integral of Measure-Integrable Function/Complex Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\struct {\C, \map \BB \C}$ be the complex numbers made into a measurable space with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Let $f : X \to \C$ be a $\mu$-integrable function. Let $\map \Re f : X \to \R$ and $\map \Im f : X \to \R$ be the real part and imaginary part of $f$ respectively. We define the integral of $f$ by: $\ds \int f \rd \mu = \int \map \Re f \rd \mu + i \int \map \Im f \rd \mu$

label: Definition:Integral on L-1 Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\map {\mathcal L^1} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be the Lebesgue $1$-space of $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$. Let $\map {L^1} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be the $L^1$ space of $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$. We define the integral $I_\mu : \map {L^1} {X, \Sigma, \mu} \to \R$ by: $\ds \map {I_\mu} {\eqclass f \sim} = \int f \rd \mu$ where: $\eqclass f \sim \in \map {L^1} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$, where $\eqclass f \sim$ is the equivalence class of $f \in \map {\LL^1} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ under the $\mu$-almost everywhere equality relation.

label: Definition:Integrating Factor
snippet: Consider the first order ordinary differential equation: $(1): \quad \map M {x, y} + \map N {x, y} \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} = 0$ such that $M$ and $N$ are real functions of two variables which are not homogeneous functions of the same degree. Suppose also that: $\dfrac {\partial M} {\partial y} \ne \dfrac {\partial N} {\partial x}$ Then from Solution to Exact Differential Equation, $(1)$ is not exact, and that method can not be used to solve it.

label: Definition:Integrating Factor/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Integrating Factor == The technique of using an integrating factor to solve a differential equation appears to have been invented by , in $1734$. It was also independently invented by both and . Some sources attribute it to .

label: Definition:Integration/Integrand
snippet: In the expression for the definite integral: $\ds \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$ or primitive (that is, indefinite integral: $\ds \int \map f x \rd x$ the function $f$ is called the integrand.

label: Definition:Intelligent Player
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $P$ be a player in $G$. Then $P$ is described as intelligent $P$ knows everything about $G$ that there is to know, and can use that knowledge to make informed decisions about what move to make. In game theory, all players are assumed to be intelligent.

label: Definition:Intercept
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a line, a curve or a surface. An intercept of $\CC$ is the intersection of $\CC$ with another line, a curve or a surface. In particular:

label: Definition:Intercept/X-Intercept
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve embedded in a cartesian plane. An $x$-intercept of $\CC$ is a point where $\CC$ intersects the $x$-axis. Hence it can also be used for the length of the line segment between that point and the origin.

label: Definition:Intercept/Y-Intercept
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve embedded in a cartesian plane. A $y$-intercept of $\CC$ is a point where $\CC$ intersects the $y$-axis. Hence it can also be used for the length of the line segment between that point and the origin.

label: Definition:Interior
snippet: Topology and metric spaces: The interior of a subset $H$ of a topological space: The largest open set contained in $H$. The interior of a subset $H$ of the complex plane $\C$: The set of all interior points of $H$ The interior of a topological manifold with boundary. Plane Geometry: Interior of a Region Interior of an Angle Interior Angle of a Transversal Interior Angle of a Polygon Complex Analysis: Interior of Jordan Curve

label: Definition:Interior (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $H \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the complex plane. The interior of $H$ is the subset of $H$ which consists of the interior points of $H$.

label: Definition:Interior (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Interior (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The interior of $H$ is the union of all subsets of $H$ which are open in $T$. That is, the interior of $H$ is defined as: $\ds H^\circ := \bigcup_{K \mathop \in \mathbb K} K$ where $\mathbb K = \set {K \in \tau: K \subseteq H}$.

label: Definition:Interior (Topology)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The interior of $H$ is defined as the largest open set of $T$ which is contained in $H$.

label: Definition:Interior (Topology)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The interior of $H$ is the set of all interior points of $H$.

label: Definition:Interior (Topology)/Notation
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. The interior of $H$ can be denoted: $\map {\mathrm {Int} } H$ $H^\circ$ The first is regarded by some as cumbersome, but has the advantage of being clear. $H^\circ$ is neat and compact, but has the disadvantage of being less intuitive. On , $H^\circ$ is the notation of choice.

label: Definition:Interior Multiplication
snippet: Let $V$ and $V^*$ be a vector space and its algebraic dual. Let $\omega \in \map {\Lambda^k} {V^*}$ be an alternating $k$-tensor. Let $v \in V$ be a vector. Let $v \mathop \lrcorner \omega$ be an alternating $\paren {k - 1}$-tensor such that: $\map {\paren {v \mathop \lrcorner \omega}} {w_1, \ldots, w_{k - 1}} := \map \omega {v, w_1, \ldots, w_{k - 1}}$ Then the mapping $\omega \mapsto v \mathop \lrcorner \omega$ is known as the interior multiplication by $v$. If $\omega$ is a $0$-tensor then: $v \mathop \lrcorner \omega := 0$

label: Definition:Interior Node
snippet: Let $v$ be a node of a tree $T$. Then $v$ is an interior node of a $T$ $v$ not a leaf node.

label: Definition:Interior Point
snippet: Topology and metric spaces: An Interior point of a subset $H$ of a topological space: A point of the interior of $H$. An interior point of a subspace $H$ of a metric space: A point which has an open ball completely contained in $H$. An interior point of a subset $H$ of the complex plane $\C$: A complex number which has a neighborhood completely contained in $H$. Geometry: An interior point of a region is one of the points intuitively understood as being inside the region.

label: Definition:Interior Point (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the complex plane. Let $z \in S$. $z$ is an interior point of $S$ $z$ has an $\epsilon$-neighborhood $\map {N_\epsilon} z$ such that $\map {N_\epsilon} z \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Interior Point (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Interior Point (Topology)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. Let $h \in H$. Then $h$ is an interior point of $H$ : $h \in H^\circ$ where $H^\circ$ denotes the interior of $H$.

label: Definition:Interior Point (Topology)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. Let $h \in H$. $h$ is an interior point of $H$ $h$ has an open neighborhood $N_h$ such that $N_h \subseteq H$.

label: Definition:Interior Point (Topology)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. Let $h \in H$. $h$ is an interior point of $H$ $h$ is an element of an open set of the subspace topology of $H$.

label: Definition:Interior of Circle
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle embedded in the plane whose radius is $r$ and whose center is at $O$. The interior of $\CC$ is the set of points in the plane whose distance from $O$ is (strictly) less than $r$.

label: Definition:Interior of Simple Closed Contour
snippet: Let $C$ be a simple closed contour in the complex plane. Let $f : \closedint 0 1 \to \R^2$ be a Jordan curve. Let $\phi : \R^2 \to \C$ be defined by: $\map \phi {x, y} = x + i y$ Let $\Img C = \map \phi {\Img f}$, where $\Img C$ denotes the image of $C$, and $\Img f$ denotes the image of $f$. Then the interior of $C$ is denoted $\Int C$ and defined as: $\Int C = \map \phi {\Int f}$ where $\Int f$ denotes the interior of $f$.

label: Definition:Interlocking Interval Topology
snippet: Let $S = \R_{>0} \setminus \Z_{>0}$ denote the set of (strictly) positive real numbers excluding the positive integers. Let $\BB$ be the family of sets $\family {S_n}_{n \mathop \in \Z_{>0} }$ defined as: $S_n = \set {\openint 0 {\dfrac 1 n} \cup \openint n {n + 1} }$ Then $\BB$ is the basis for a topology $\tau$ on $S$. $\tau$ is referred to as the interlocking interval topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the interlocking interval space.

label: Definition:Intermediate Field
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. Let $F$ be a field such that: $K \subset F \subset L$ Then $F$ is an intermediate field. Category:Definitions/Field Extensions

label: Definition:Internal Direct Product/Also known as
snippet: == Internal Direct Product: Also known as == Some sources refer to the internal direct product simply as the direct product. Others call it the direct composite. It is also commonplace for sources which evolve their expositions on abstract algebra purely from an arithmetical perspective to refer to the direct sum when the operation is, or derives from, addition.

label: Definition:Internal Direct Product/Decomposition
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \circ {\restriction_{S_1} } }, \struct {S_2, \circ {\restriction_{S_2} } }, \ldots, \struct {S_n, \circ {\restriction_{S_n} } }$ be closed algebraic substructures of an algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_{S_1} }, \circ {\restriction_{S_2} }, \ldots, \circ {\restriction_{S_n} }$ are the operations induced by the restrictions of $\circ$ to $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$ respectively. Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be the internal direct product of $S_1$, $S_2, \ldots, S_n$.

label: Definition:Internal Direct Sum of Rings/Direct Summand
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$ be a sequence of subrings of $R$. Let $\ds S = \prod_{j \mathop = 1}^n S_j$ be the ring direct sum of $S_1$ to $S_n$. In Conditions for Internal Ring Direct Sum it is proved that for this to be the case, then $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$ must be ideals of $R$. Such ideals are known as direct summands of $R$.

label: Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/Definition by Subset Product
snippet: Let $\struct {H, \circ {\restriction_H} }$ and $\struct {K, \circ {\restriction_K} }$ be subgroups of a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_H}$ and $\circ {\restriction_K}$ are the restrictions of $\circ$ to $H, K$ respectively. The group $\struct {G, \circ}$ is the internal group direct product of $H$ and $K$ : $(1): \quad \struct {H, \circ {\restriction_H} }$ and $\struct {K, \circ {\restriction_K} }$ are both normal subgroups of $\struct {G, \circ}$ $(2): \quad G$ is the subset product of $H$ and $K$, that is: $G = H \circ K$ $(3): \quad$ $H \cap K = \set e$ where $e$ is…

label: Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/Definition by Unique Expression
snippet: Let $\struct {H, \circ {\restriction_H} }$ and $\struct {K, \circ {\restriction_K} }$ be subgroups of a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_H}$ and $\circ {\restriction_K}$ are the restrictions of $\circ$ to $H, K$ respectively. The group $\struct {G, \circ}$ is the internal group direct product of $H$ and $K$ : $(1): \quad \struct {H, \circ {\restriction_H} }$ and $\struct {K, \circ {\restriction_K} }$ are both normal subgroups of $\struct {G, \circ}$ $(2): \quad$ every element of $G$ can be expressed uniquely in the form: $g = h \circ k$ where $h \in H$ and $k \in K$.

label: Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/General Definition/Definition by Subset Product
snippet: Let $\sequence {H_n} = \struct {H_1, \circ {\restriction_{H_1} } }, \ldots, \struct {H_n, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} } }$ be a (finite) sequence of subgroups of a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_{H_1} }, \ldots, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} }$ are the restrictions of $\circ$ to $H_1, \ldots, H_n$ respectively.

label: Definition:Internal Group Direct Product/General Definition/Definition by Unique Expression
snippet: Let $\sequence {H_n} = \struct {H_1, \circ {\restriction_{H_1} } }, \ldots, \struct {H_n, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} } }$ be a (finite) sequence of subgroups of a group $\struct {G, \circ}$ where $\circ {\restriction_{H_1} }, \ldots, \circ {\restriction_{H_n} }$ are the restrictions of $\circ$ to $H_1, \ldots, H_n$ respectively.

label: Definition:Internal Hilbert Space Direct Sum
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\family {M_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an $I$-indexed set of pairwise orthogonal subspaces of $\HH$. Then the internal (Hilbert space) direct sum of the $M_i$ is their closed linear span $\vee_i M_i$. It is denoted by $\bigoplus_i M_i$, or $\ds \bigoplus_{i \mathop \in I} M_i$ if the set $I$ is to be stressed. When $I$ is finite, by Closed Linear Subspaces Closed under Setwise Addition, have that: $\ds \bigoplus_{i \mathop \in I} M_i = \sum_{i \mathop \in I} M_i$, where $\ds \sum$ signifies setwise addition.

label: Definition:Internal Point of Subset of Vector Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $B \subseteq X$. Let $x \in B$. We say that $x$ is an internal point of $B$ there exists an absorbing set $A$ such that: $x + A \subseteq B$

label: Definition:International Standard Book Number/ISBN-10
snippet: An International Standard Book Number is a codeword used to uniquely identify a published . The ISBN-$10$ format consists of a string of $9$ digits followed by a check digit in the set $\set {0, 1, \ldots, 9, X}$. The check digit $d$ is calculated as follows. Let $c$ be calculated as: $c = \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^9 k d_k \pmod {11}$ where $d_k$ denotes the $k$th digit in the ISBN-$10$. Then the check digit $d$ is defined as: $d = \begin {cases} c & : c \le 9 \\ X &: c = 10 \end {cases}$ Hyphens may be included in the string to separate out the sections for lexicographical convenience.

label: Definition:Interpretation
snippet: Let $S$ be the codomain of a mapping $f$ whose domain consists of the set of expressions of a formal language $\FF$. Then $S$ together with $f$ are known as an interpretation.

label: Definition:Interpretation/Semantic Rule
snippet: Let $\struct {S, f}$ be an interpretation such that $S$ is the codomain of a mapping $f$ whose domain is a set of expressions of a formal language $\FF$. The mapping $f$ is known as a semantic rule.

label: Definition:Interpretation/Semantic Value
snippet: Let $\struct {S, f}$ be an interpretation such that $S$ is the codomain of a semantic rule $f$ whose domain is a set of expressions $\EE$ of a formal language $\FF$. The image $s \in S$ of an expression $e \in \EE$ under $f$ is known as the semantic value of $e$.

label: Definition:Interquartile Range
snippet: The interquartile range is a measure of dispersion in statistics. Let $Q_1$ and $Q_3$ be first quartile and third quartile respectively. The interquartile range is defined and denoted as: $\operatorname {IQR} := Q_3 - Q_1$

label: Definition:Intersecting Sets
snippet: Two sets $S$ and $T$ intersect : $S \cap T \ne \O$ That is, intersecting sets are such that their intersection is a non-empty set -- they have at least one element in common.

label: Definition:Intersection
snippet: Set theory: Set intersection: the elements common to two or more sets. Geometry: Geometrical intersection: the points common to two or more geometric figures. Definition:Intersection Product

label: Definition:Intersection (Geometry)
snippet: The intersection of two lines $AB$ and $CD$ is denoted by $AB \cap CD$. The intersection of two geometric figures is the set of points shared by both figures. Note that this use of $\cap$ is consistent with that of its more usual context of set intersection. When two lines intersect, they are said to cut each other.

label: Definition:Intersection of Family/Also denoted as
snippet: == Intersection of Family: Also denoted as == The set $\ds \bigcap_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ can also be seen denoted as: $\ds \bigcap_I S_i$ or, if the indexing set is clear from context: $\ds \bigcap_i S_i$ Some sources use the form: $\bigcap \set {S_i: i \in I}$

label: Definition:Intersection of Relations
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\RR_1$ and $\RR_2$ be relations on $S \times T$. The intersection of $\RR_1$ and $\RR_2$ is the relation $\QQ$ defined by: $\QQ := \RR_1 \cap \RR_2$ where $\cap$ denotes set intersection. Explicitly, for $s \in S$ and $t \in T$, we have: $s \mathrel \QQ t$ both $s \mathrel{\RR_1} t$ and $s \mathrel{\RR_2} t$

label: Definition:Intersection of Relations/General Definition
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\mathscr R$ be a collection of relations on $S \times T$. The intersection of $\mathscr R$ is the relation $\RR$ defined by: $\ds \RR = \bigcap \mathscr R$ where $\bigcap$ denotes set intersection. Explicitly, for $s \in S$ and $t \in T$: $s \mathrel \RR t$ : $\forall \QQ \in \mathscr R: s \mathrel \QQ t$

label: Definition:Intersection of Special Subsets
snippet: Let $g$ be a progressing mapping. Let $x$ be a set. Let $\powerset x$ denote the power set of $x$. Let $A$ be the class of all $x$-special subsets of $\powerset x$ $g$. We denote by $M_x$ the intersection of $A$: $M_x = \bigcap A$

label: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Closed
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The closed interval between $a$ and $b$ is the set: $\closedint a b := a^\succcurlyeq \cap b^\preccurlyeq = \set {s \in S: \paren {a \preccurlyeq s} \land \paren {s \preccurlyeq b} }$ where: $a^\succcurlyeq$ denotes the upper closure of $a$ $b^\preccurlyeq$ denotes the lower closure of $b$.

label: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Left Half-Open
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The left half-open interval between $a$ and $b$ is the set: $\hointl a b := a^\succ \cap b^\preccurlyeq = \set {s \in S: \paren {a \prec s} \land \paren {s \preccurlyeq b} }$ where: $a^\succ$ denotes the strict upper closure of $a$ $b^\preccurlyeq$ denotes the lower closure of $b$.

label: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Open
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The open interval between $a$ and $b$ is the set: $\openint a b := a^\succ \cap b^\prec = \set {s \in S: \paren {a \prec s} \land \paren {s \prec b} }$ where: $a^\succ$ denotes the strict upper closure of $a$ $b^\prec$ denotes the strict lower closure of $b$.

label: Definition:Interval/Ordered Set/Right Half-Open
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a, b \in S$. The right half-open interval between $a$ and $b$ is the set: $\hointr a b := a^\succcurlyeq \cap b^\prec = \set {s \in S: \paren {a \preccurlyeq s} \land \paren {s \prec b} }$ where: $a^\succcurlyeq$ denotes the upper closure of $a$ $b^\prec$ denotes the strict lower closure of $b$.

label: Definition:Interval Estimate
snippet: An interval estimate is a numerical value of an estimator calculated from a confidence interval.

label: Definition:Interval of Convergence
snippet: Let $\xi \in \R$ be a real number. Let $\ds \map S x = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a_n \paren {x - \xi}^n$ be a power series in $x$ about $\xi$. The set of values of $x$ for which $\map S x$ converges is called the interval of convergence of $S$.

label: Definition:Intransitive Dice
snippet: Intransitive dice are a set of dice with different, non-standard, numbering such that the relation: die $p$ beats die $q$ is a non-transitive relation.

label: Definition:Intuitionistic Propositional Logic
snippet: The intuitionist school of mathematics is one which adopts the following philosophical position: "Although we may know that it is not the case that a statement $p$ is (provably) false, we don't necessarily know that it is (provably) true either." Thus the intuitionist school rejects the Law of the Excluded Middle. The classical school, by affirming that if a statement is not true it must be false, and if it is not false it must be true, accepts as an axiom that "not not-true" must mean "true".

label: Definition:Intuitionistic Propositional Logic/Also known as
snippet: == Intuitionistic Propositional Logic: Also known as == Some prefer to address this logic by its practitioners, calling it intuitionist (propositional) logic. This field of logic is also (more intuitively) (no pun intended) known as constructive logic or constructivist logic. That is, a mathematical object can not be deduced to exist based on the Law of Excluded Middle -- it specifically needs to be constructed.

label: Definition:Invalid/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Invalid == The word invalid, as used in the logical context, has the stress on the second syllable: in-val-id. Pronounced in-val-id, with the stress on the first syllable, the word means a person who is being treated for an illness. There are plenty of apocryphal tales on the internet where furious users have called the helpdesk to tell the staff that their computer is calling them bad, and an invalid. So let's be careful out there. Category:Linguistic Notes

label: Definition:Invariant/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Invariant == Invariants were investigated by , who proved important general results about the set of all algebraic invariants of certain groups of transformations. It is noted that the problem of calculation and full description of all possible invariants can be difficult, if not intractable.

label: Definition:Invariant Functional under Transformation
snippet: Let $y_i$, $F$, $\Phi$, $\Psi$ be real functions. Let $\mathbf y = \sequence {y_i}_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n}$. Let $\ds J \sqbrk {\mathbf y} = \int_{x_0}^{x_1} \map F {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'} \rd x$ be a functional. Let: $X = \map \Phi {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'}$ $\mathbf Y = \map {\mathbf \Psi} {x, \mathbf y, \mathbf y'}$ Let curve $\gamma$ defined by: $\mathbf y = \map {\mathbf y} x, \quad x_0 \le x \le x_1$ be transformed into a curve $\Gamma$ defined by: $\mathbf Y = \map {\mathbf Y} X, \quad X_0 \le X \le X_1$ Then the functional $J \sqbrk {\mathbf y}$ is invariant under the…

label: Definition:Invariant Mapping Under Equivalence Relation
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\RR$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is invariant under $\RR$ : $x \mathrel \RR y \implies \map f x = \map f y$

label: Definition:Invariant Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\theta: X \to X$ be a $\Sigma / \Sigma$-measurable mapping. Then $\mu$ is said to be a $\theta$-invariant measure or to be invariant under $\theta$ : $\forall E \in \Sigma: \map \mu {\theta^{-1} \sqbrk E} = \map \mu E$ where $\theta^{-1} \sqbrk E$ denotes the preimage of $E$ under $\theta$. In terms of a pushforward measure, this can be concisely formulated as: $\theta_* \mu = \mu$

label: Definition:Invariant Metric on Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $d$ be a metric on $X$. We say that $d$ is invariant : $\map d {x, y} = \map d {x + z, y + z}$ for each $x, y, z \in X$.

label: Definition:Invariant Pseudometric on Vector Space
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $X$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $d$ be a pseudometric on $X$. We say that $d$ is invariant : $\map d {x, y} = \map d {x + z, y + z}$ for each $x, y, z \in X$.

label: Definition:Invariant Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to S$ be a self-map on $S$. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then $T$ is an invariant set of $f$ : $f \sqbrk Y = Y$

label: Definition:Invariant Set/Also known as
snippet: == Invariant Set: Also known as == An invariant set of a mapping is also known as an invariant subset of a set under a mapping if it is important to attach more emphasis to the set than to the mapping.

label: Definition:Invariant Set/Negatively Invariant
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to S$ be a self-map on $S$. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$ such that: $f^{-1} \sqbrk T \subseteq T$ Then $T$ is a negatively invariant set of $f$.

label: Definition:Invariant Set/Positively Invariant
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to S$ be a self-map on $S$. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$ such that: $f \sqbrk T \subseteq T$ Then $T$ is a positively invariant set of $f$.

label: Definition:Invariant Subspace
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A \in \map B H$ be a bounded linear operator. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of $H$. Then $M$ is said to be an invariant subspace for $A$ $h \in M \implies A h \in M$. That is, $AM \subseteq M$.

label: Definition:Invariant Theory
snippet: Invariant theory is the subfield of abstract algebra which studies the actions of groups on mathematical objects to investigate those aspects which are invariant.

label: Definition:Inverse
snippet: Logic: The inverse of a conditional $p \implies q$ is $\neg p \implies \neg q$ Abstract Algebra: Inverse Element Ring Product Inverse Definition:Inverse Semigroup Definition:Inverse in Inverse Semigroup Linear Algebra Definition:Inverse Linear Transformation Definition:Inverse Linear Operator Relation Theory: Inverse Relation Inverse Image (also known as Preimage) Mapping Theory: Inverse Mapping Inverse of a Mapping Matrix Algebra: Inverse Matrix

label: Definition:Inverse (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity is $e_S$.

label: Definition:Inverse (Abstract Algebra)/Left Inverse
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity is $e_S$. An element $x_L \in S$ is called a left inverse of $x$ : $x_L \circ x = e_S$

label: Definition:Inverse (Abstract Algebra)/Right Inverse
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity is $e_S$. An element $x_R \in S$ is called a right inverse of $x$ : $x \circ x_R = e_S$

label: Definition:Inverse Cosecant/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $z \in \C_{\ne 0}$ be a non-zero complex number. The inverse cosecant of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\csc^{-1} \left({z}\right) := \left\{{w \in \C: \csc \left({w}\right) = z}\right\}$ where $\csc \left({w}\right)$ is the cosecant of $w$.

label: Definition:Inverse Cosecant/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $z \in \C_{\ne 0}$ be a non-zero complex number. The inverse cosecant of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\csc^{-1} \left({z}\right) := \left\{{\dfrac 1 i \ln \left({\dfrac {i + \sqrt{\left|{z^2 - 1}\right|} e^{\left({i / 2}\right) \arg \left({z^2 - 1}\right)}} z}\right) + 2 k \pi: k \in \Z}\right\}$ where: $\sqrt{\left|{z^2 - 1}\right|}$ denotes the positive square root of the complex modulus of $z^2 - 1$ $\arg \left({z^2 - 1}\right)$ denotes the argument of $z^2 - 1$ $\ln$ denotes the complex natural logarithm considered as a multifunction.

label: Definition:Inverse Cosecant/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \le -1$ or $x \ge 1$. The inverse cosecant of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \csc x := \set {y \in \R: \map \csc y = x}$ where $\map \csc y$ is the cosecant of $y$.

label: Definition:Inverse Cosine/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. The inverse cosine of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\cos^{-1} \left({z}\right) := \left\{{w \in \C: \cos \left({w}\right) = z}\right\}$ where $\cos \left({w}\right)$ is the cosine of $w$.

label: Definition:Inverse Cosine/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. The inverse cosine of $z$ is the multifunction defined as: $\cos^{-1} \left({z}\right) := \left\{{\dfrac 1 i \ln \left({z + \sqrt{\left|{z^2 - 1}\right|} e^{\left({i / 2}\right) \arg \left({z^2 - 1}\right)} }\right) + 2 k \pi: k \in \Z}\right\}$ where: $\sqrt{\left|{z^2 - 1}\right|}$ denotes the positive square root of the complex modulus of $z^2 - 1$ $\arg \left({z^2 - 1}\right)$ denotes the argument of $z^2 - 1$ $\ln$ denotes the complex natural logarithm considered as a multifunction.

label: Definition:Inverse Cosine/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $-1 \le x \le 1$. The inverse cosine of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \cos x := \set {y \in \R: \map \cos y = x}$ where $\map \cos y$ is the cosine of $y$.

label: Definition:Inverse Cosine/Real/Arccosine
snippet: From Shape of Cosine Function, we have that $\cos x$ is continuous and strictly decreasing on the interval $\closedint 0 \pi$. From Cosine of Multiple of Pi, $\cos \pi = -1$ and $\cos 0 = 1$. Therefore, let $g: \closedint 0 \pi \to \closedint {-1} 1$ be the restriction of $\cos x$ to $\closedint 0 \pi$. Thus from Inverse of Strictly Monotone Function, $\map g x$ admits an inverse function, which will be continuous and strictly decreasing on $\closedint {-1} 1$. This function is called the arccosine of $x$.

label: Definition:Inverse Cotangent/Complex
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \left\{{0 + i, 0 - i}\right\}$

label: Definition:Inverse Cotangent/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \left\{{0 + i, 0 - i}\right\}$ The inverse cotangent is a multifunction defined on $S$ as: $\forall z \in S: \cot^{-1} \left({z}\right) := \left\{{w \in \C: \cot \left({w}\right) = z}\right\}$ where $\cot \left({w}\right)$ is the cotangent of $w$.

label: Definition:Inverse Cotangent/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \left\{{0 + i, 0 - i}\right\}$ The inverse cotangent is a multifunction defined on $S$ as: $\forall z \in S: \cot^{-1} \left({z}\right) := \left\{{\dfrac 1 {2 i} \ln \left({\dfrac {z + i} {z - i}}\right) + k \pi: k \in \Z}\right\}$ where $\ln$ denotes the complex natural logarithm as a multifunction.

label: Definition:Inverse Cotangent/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $-1 \le x \le 1$. The inverse cotangent of $x$ is the multifunction defined as: $\inv \cot x := \set {y \in \R: \map \cot y = x}$ where $\map \cot y$ is the cotangent of $y$.

label: Definition:Inverse Element/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Element: Also known as == An inverse of $x$ is also known as a two-sided inverse of $x$, symmetric element or negative of $x$. Some sources refer to it as a reciprocal element, which terminology is borrowed from the real numbers under multiplication. The notation used to represent an inverse of an element is often understood to depend on the set and binary operation under consideration. Various symbols are seen for a general inverse, for example $\hat x$, $x'$ and $x^*$. In multiplicative notation: If $s \in S$ has an inverse, it is denoted $s^{-1}$.

label: Definition:Inverse Entourage
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\UU$ be a quasiuniformity on $S$. Let $u \in \UU$ be an entourage of $\UU$. Then the inverse entourage $u^{-1}$ is defined as: $u^{-1} := \set {\tuple {y, x}: \tuple {x, y} \in u}$

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cosecant/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Hyperbolic Cosecant: Also known as == The principal branch of the inverse hyperbolic cosecant is also known as the area hyperbolic cosecant, as it can be used, among other things, for evaluating areas of regions bounded by hyperbolas. Some sources refer to it as hyperbolic arccosecant, but this is strictly a misnomer, as there is nothing arc related about an inverse hyperbolic cosecant. Category:Definitions/Inverse Hyperbolic Cosecant

Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine: Also known as == The principal branch of the inverse hyperbolic cosine is known as the area hyperbolic cosine, as it can be used, among other things, for evaluating areas of regions bounded by hyperbolas. Some sources refer to it as hyperbolic arccosine, but this is strictly a misnomer, as there is nothing arc related about an inverse hyperbolic cosine. Category:Definitions/Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine/Real
snippet: Let $S$ denote the subset of the real numbers: $S = \set {x \in \R: x \ge 1}$

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine/Real/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ denote the subset of the real numbers: $S = \set {x \in \R: x \ge 1}$ The inverse hyperbolic cosine $\cosh^{-1}: S \to \R$ is a real multifunction defined on $S$ as: $\forall x \in S: \map {\cosh^{-1} } x := \set {y \in \R: x = \map \cosh y}$ where $\map \cosh y$ denotes the hyperbolic cosine function. Hence for $x > 1$, $\map {\cosh^{-1} } x$ has $2$ values. For $x < 1$, $\map {\cosh^{-1} } x$ is not defined.

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine/Real/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ denote the subset of the real numbers: $S = \set {x \in \R: x \ge 1}$ The inverse hyperbolic cosine $\cosh^{-1}: S \to \R$ is a real multifunction defined on $S$ as: $\forall x \in S: \map {\cosh^{-1} } x := \map \ln {x \pm \sqrt {x^2 - 1} }$ where: $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm of a (strictly positive) real number. $\sqrt {x^2 - 1}$ denotes the square root of $x^2 - 1$ Hence for $x > 1$, $\map {\cosh^{-1} } x$ has $2$ values. For $x < 1$, $\map {\cosh^{-1} } x$ is not defined.

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine/Real/Principal Branch
snippet: Let $S$ denote the subset of the real numbers: $S = \set {x \in \R: x \ge 1}$ The principal branch of the real inverse hyperbolic cosine function is defined as: $\forall x \in S: \map \arcosh x := \map \ln {x + \sqrt {x^2 - 1} }$ where: $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm of a (strictly positive) real number. $\sqrt {x^2 - 1}$ specifically denotes the positive square root of $x^2 - 1$ That is, where $\map \arcosh x \ge 0$.

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent: Also known as == The principal branch of the inverse hyperbolic cotangent is also known as the area hyperbolic cotangent, as it can be used, among other things, for evaluating areas of regions bounded by hyperbolas. Some sources refer to it as hyperbolic arccotangent, but this is strictly a misnomer, as there is nothing arc related about an inverse hyperbolic cotangent. Category:Definitions/Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent/Complex
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \set {-1 + 0 i, 1 + 0 i}$

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \set {-1 + 0 i, 1 + 0 i}$ The inverse hyperbolic cotangent is a multifunction defined on $S$ as: $\forall z \in S: \map {\coth^{-1} } z := \set {w \in \C: z = \map \coth w}$ where $\map \coth w$ is the hyperbolic cotangent function.

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \set {-1 + 0 i, 1 + 0 i}$ The inverse hyperbolic cotangent is a multifunction defined on $S$ as: $\forall z \in S: \map {\coth^{-1} } z := \set {\dfrac 1 2 \map \ln {\dfrac {z + 1} {z - 1} } + k \pi i: k \in \Z}$ where $\ln$ denotes the complex natural logarithm considered as a multifunction.

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Function/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Hyperbolic Function: Also known as == The inverse hyperbolic functions are also known as the area hyperbolic functions, as they can be used, among other things, for evaluating areas of regions bounded by hyperbolas. On , the term area hyperbolic function is specifically reserved for the principal branch of those inverse hyperbolic functions which are multifunctions. Some sources refer to them as hyperbolic arc functions, but this is strictly a misnomer, as there is nothing arc related about an inverse hyperbolic function. Category:Definitions/Inverse Hyperbolic Functions

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Function/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Inverse Hyperbolic Function == In general, the inverse hyperbolic functions are multifunctions. When used in their multifunction form, the notation of choice on for the inverse of a hyperbolic function $\operatorname h$ is $\operatorname h^{-1}$. When the area hyperbolic function is specifically required, the following prefixes are used: $\text {ar}$ for the real inverse hyperbolic functions $\text {Ar}$ for the complex inverse hyperbolic functions where $\text{ar}$ is an abbreviation for area.

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Secant/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Hyperbolic Secant: Also known as == The principal branch of the inverse hyperbolic secant is also known as the area hyperbolic secant, as it can be used, among other things, for evaluating areas of regions bounded by hyperbolas. Some sources refer to it as hyperbolic arcsecant, but this is strictly a misnomer, as there is nothing arc related about an inverse hyperbolic secant. Category:Definitions/Inverse Hyperbolic Secant

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Secant/Real/Principal Branch
snippet: Let $S$ denote the subset of the real numbers: $S := \hointl 0 1$ The principal branch of the real inverse hyperbolic secant function is defined as: $\forall x \in S: \map \arsech x := \map \ln {\dfrac {1 + \sqrt {1 - x^2} } x}$ where: $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm of a (strictly positive) real number. $\sqrt {1 - x^2}$ specifically denotes the positive square root of $x^2 - 1$ That is, where $\map \arsech x \ge 0$.

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Sine/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Hyperbolic Sine: Also known as == The principal branch of the inverse hyperbolic sine is also known as the area hyperbolic sine, as it can be used, among other things, for evaluating areas of regions bounded by hyperbolas. Some sources refer to it as hyperbolic arcsine, but this is strictly a misnomer, as there is nothing arc related about an inverse hyperbolic sine. Category:Definitions/Inverse Hyperbolic Sine

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent/Also known as
snippet: == Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent: Also known as == The inverse hyperbolic tangent is also known as the area hyperbolic tangent, as it can be used, among other things, for evaluating areas of regions bounded by hyperbolas. Some sources refer to it as hyperbolic arctangent, but this is strictly a misnomer, as there is nothing arc related about an inverse hyperbolic tangent. Category:Definitions/Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent/Complex
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \set {-1 + 0 i, 1 + 0 i}$

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \set {-1 + 0 i, 1 + 0 i}$ The inverse hyperbolic tangent is a multifunction defined on $S$ as: $\forall z \in S: \map {\tanh^{-1} } z := \set {w \in \C: z = \map \tanh w}$ where $\map \tanh w$ is the hyperbolic tangent function.

label: Definition:Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent/Complex/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be the subset of the complex plane: $S = \C \setminus \set {-1 + 0 i, 1 + 0 i}$ The inverse hyperbolic tangent is a multifunction defined on $S$ as: $\forall z \in S: \map {\tanh^{-1} } z := \set {\dfrac 1 2 \map \ln {\dfrac {1 + z} {1 - z} } + k \pi i: k \in \Z}$ where $\ln$ denotes the complex natural logarithm considered as a multifunction.

label: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets.

label: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping.

label: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Mapping/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. The inverse image mapping of $f$ is the mapping $f^\gets: \powerset T \to \powerset S$ that sends a subset $Y \subseteq T$ to its preimage $f^{-1} \sqbrk T$ under $f$: $\forall Y \in \powerset T: \map {f^\gets} Y = \begin {cases} \set {s \in S: \exists t \in Y: \map f s = t} & : \Img f \cap Y \ne \O \\ \O & : \Img f \cap Y = \O \end {cases}$

label: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Mapping/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. The inverse image mapping of $f$ is the direct image mapping of the inverse $f^{-1}$ of $f$: $f^\gets = \paren {f^{-1} }^\to: \powerset T \to \powerset S$: That is: $\forall Y \in \powerset T: \map {f^\gets} Y = \set {s \in S: \exists t \in Y: \map f s = t}$

label: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Relation
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation on $S \times T$.

label: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Relation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation on $S \times T$. The inverse image mapping of $\RR$ is the mapping $\RR^\gets: \powerset T \to \powerset S$ that sends a subset $Y \subseteq T$ to its preimage $\map {\RR^{-1} } Y$ under $\RR$: $\forall Y \in \powerset T: \map {\RR^\gets} Y = \begin {cases} \set {s \in S: \exists t \in Y: \tuple {t, s} \in \RR^{-1} } & : \Img \RR \cap Y \ne \O \\ \O & : \Img \RR \cap Y = \O \end {cases}$

label: Definition:Inverse Image Mapping/Relation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\powerset S$ and $\powerset T$ be their power sets. Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation on $S \times T$. The inverse image mapping of $\RR$ is the direct image mapping of the inverse $\RR^{-1}$ of $\RR$: $\RR^\gets = \paren {\RR^{-1} }^\to: \powerset T \to \powerset S$ That is: $\forall Y \in \powerset T: \map {\RR^\gets} Y = \set {s \in S: \exists t \in Y: \tuple {t, s} \in \RR^{-1} }$
