snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\cl: \powerset S \to \powerset S$ be a mapping from the power set of $S$ to itself. Then $\cl$ is a Kuratowski closure operator it satisfies the following axioms for all $A, B \subseteq X$: {{axiom | n = 2 | t = $\map \cl {A \cup B} = \map \cl A \cup \map \cl B$ | rc= $\cl$ preserves binary unions }} Note that axioms $(2)$ and $(3)$ may be replaced by the single axiom that for any finite subset $\FF$ of $powerset S$: $\ds \map \cl {\bigcup \FF} = \map {\bigcup_{F \mathop \in \FF} } {\map \cl F}$ That is, the axiom that $\cl$ preserves finite unions.

label: Definition:Kurtosis
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The kurtosis of $X$ is a measure of the concentration of $X$ about its expectation.

label: Definition:Kurtosis/Coefficient
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The coefficient of kurtosis of $X$ is the coefficient: $\gamma_2 = \dfrac {\mu_4} { {\mu_2}^2} - 3$ where $\mu_i$ denotes the $i$th central moment of $X$.

label: Definition:Kurtosis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The kurtosis of $X$ is a measure of the concentration of $X$ about its expectation. The kurtosis of $X$ is the fourth standardized moment of $X$: $\alpha_4 = \expect {\paren {\dfrac {X - \mu} \sigma}^4}$ where $\expect {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes expectation.

label: Definition:Kurtosis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The kurtosis of $X$ is a measure of the concentration of $X$ about its expectation. The kurtosis of $X$ is defined as: $\alpha_4 = \dfrac {\mu_4} {\paren {\mu_2}^2}$ where $\mu_i$ denotes the $i$th central moment of $X$.

label: Definition:Kurtosis/Incorrect Definition
snippet: The kurtosis of a random variable is often seen described as a measure of how steep the peak is at the mean or the mode. However, this is incorrect. It is more accurate to describe it as a measure of how heavy or fat the tails are.

label: Definition:Kurtosis/Notation
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. The kurtosis of $X$ is usually denoted $\alpha_4$. Some sources denote the kurtosis by the symbol $\Beta_2$ or $\beta_2$.

label: Definition:L-2 Inner Product
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $\map {\LL^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be the Lebesgue $2$-space of $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$. Let $\map {L^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be the $L^2$ space of $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$. We define the $L^2$ inner product $\innerprod \cdot \cdot : \map {L^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu} \times \map {L^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu} \to \R$ by: $\ds \innerprod {\eqclass f \sim} {\eqclass g \sim} = \int \paren {f \cdot g} \rd \mu$ where: $\eqclass f \sim, \eqclass g \sim \in \map {L^2} {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ where $\eqclass f \sim$ and $\eqclass g \sim$ are the equivalence class of…

label: Definition:L1 Metric/Closed Real Interval
snippet: Let $S$ be the set of all real functions which are continuous on the closed interval $\closedint a b$. Let the real-valued function $d: S \times S \to \R$ be defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in S: \map {d_1} {f, g} := \int_a^b \size {\map f t - \map g t} \rd t$ Then $d_1$ is the $L^1$ metric on $\closedint a b$.

label: Definition:L2 Metric/Closed Real Interval
snippet: Let $S$ be the set of all real functions which are continuous on the closed interval $\closedint a b$. Let the real-valued function $d: S \times S \to \R$ be defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in S: \map d {f, g} := \paren {\int_a^b \paren {\map f t - \map g t}^2 \rd t}^{\frac 1 2}$ Then $d$ is the $L^2$ metric on $\closedint a b$.

label: Definition:LAST
snippet: LAST stands for LAnguage of Set Theory. It is a formal system designed for the description of sets.

label: Definition:Labeled Graph
snippet: A labeled graph is a graph whose vertices are each assigned an element from a set of symbols (letters, usually, but this is unimportant). The important thing to note is that the vertices can be distinguished one from another. Note that it is not necessary for all the vertices to be assigned different labels.

label: Definition:Labeled Tree
snippet: A labeled tree is a finite tree (which may or may not be rooted) in which each node has attached to it a label. These labels may be any symbol or other object that one can think of, but usually consist of one letter or symbol. The parent function is usually depicted by placing the ancestor above the child and connecting them with a line. The various children of a node may also be considered to be in a particular order. This is usually depicted by placing them in a left-to-right order.

label: Definition:Labeled Tree for Propositional Logic
snippet: A labeled tree for propositional logic is a system containing: A rooted tree $T$; A countable set $\mathbf H$ of WFFs of propositional logic; A WFF $\map \Phi t$ attached to each non-root node $t$ of $T$. Such a structure can be denoted $\struct {T, \mathbf H, \Phi}$.

label: Definition:Labeled Tree for Propositional Logic/Hypothesis Set
snippet: Let $\struct {T, \mathbf H, \Phi}$ be a labeled tree for propositional logic. The countable set $\mathbf H$ of WFFs of propositional logic is called the hypothesis set. The elements of $\mathbf H$ are known as hypothesis WFFs. The hypothesis set $\mathbf H$ is considered to be attached to the root node of $T$.

label: Definition:Lagrange Basis Polynomial
snippet: Let $x_0, \ldots, x_n \in \R$ be real numbers. The Lagrange basis polynomials associated to the $x_i$ are the polynomials: $\ds \map {L_j} X := \prod_{\substack {0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n \\ i \mathop \ne j} } \frac {X - x_i} {x_j - x_i} \in \R \sqbrk X$

label: Definition:Lagrange Number
snippet: Let $\xi$ be an irrational number. Consider a real number $L_n$ such that there are infinitely many relatively prime integers $p, q \in \Z$ such that: $\size {\xi - \dfrac p q} < \dfrac 1 {L_n q^2}$ We define the Lagrange number of $\xi$ to be $\map L \xi = \map \sup L$ over all $L$ satisfying the inequality above.

label: Definition:Lagrangian Derivative
snippet: Consider a fluid flow $\FF$. The Lagrangian derivative of $\FF$ is the partial derivative $\dfrac \partial {\partial t}$ which measures the rate of change at a fixed point of $\FF$ as different material flows through that point. The rate of change of the quantity $q$ is given by: $\dfrac {\rD q} {\rD t} = \dfrac {\partial q} {\partial t} + \mathbf u \cdot \nabla q$ where $\mathbf u$ is the velocity of $q$.

label: Definition:Lambert W Function
snippet: Let $e^z: \C \to \C$ be the complex exponential function. Then $\map W z$ is defined to be the multifunction that satisfies: $\map W z e^{\map W z} = z$

label: Definition:Lambert W Function/Lower Branch
snippet: The lower branch of the Lambert W function is the real function $W_{-1}: \hointr {-\dfrac 1 e} 0 \to \hointl \gets {-1}$ such that: $x = \map {W_{-1} } x e^{\map {W_{-1} } x}$

label: Definition:Lambert W Function/Principal Branch/Real Valued
snippet: The principal branch of the Lambert W function is the real function $W_0: \hointr {-\dfrac 1 e} \to \to \hointr {-1} \to$ such that: $x = \map {W_0} x e^{\map {W_0} x}$

label: Definition:Lambert W Function/Real Valued/Graphs
snippet: == Graphs == There are two real-valued branches of the Lambert $W$ Function: The real valued principal branch, $W_0$ The lower branch, $W_{-1}$ 600px Category:Definitions/Lambert W Function

label: Definition:Lanczos Method
snippet: The Lanczos method is an iterative technique for computing the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix. It is most often used when the matrix is large and sparse, because each iteration involves a single product between the matrix and a vector.

label: Definition:Language
snippet: A language is a tool for the transmission and communication of information.

label: Definition:Language of Arithmetic
snippet: A language of arithmetic is a signature for predicate logic consisting of: the binary operation symbols: $+$ and $\times$ the unary function symbol: $s$ the binary relation symbol: $<$ the constant symbol: $0$

label: Definition:Language of Predicate Logic
snippet: There are a lot of different formal systems expressing predicate logic. Although they vary wildly in complexity and even disagree (to some extent) on what expressions are valid, generally all of these use a compatible formal language. This page defines the formal language of choice on . We will use $\LL_1$ to represent the formal language of predicate logic in what follows. In order to define $\LL_1$, it is necessary to specify: An alphabet $\AA$ A collation system with the unique readability property for $\AA$ A formal grammar (which determines the WFFs of $\LL_1$)

label: Definition:Language of Propositional Logic
snippet: There are a lot of different formal systems expressing propositional logic. Although they vary wildly in complexity and even disagree (to some extent) on what expressions are valid, generally all of these use a compatible formal language. This page defines the formal language of choice on . We will use $\LL_0$ to represent the formal language of propositional logic in what follows. label: Definition:Language of Propositional Logic/Alphabet/Letter
snippet: Part of specifying the language of propositional logic $\LL_0$ is to specify its letters. The letters of $\LL_0$, called propositional symbols, is an arbitrary collection $\PP_0$ of symbols which has no limit on its extent. It is usual to specify them as a limited subset of the English alphabet with appropriate subscripts. A typical set of propositional symbols would be, for example: $\PP_0 = \set {p_1, p_2, p_3, \ldots, p_n, \ldots}$

label: Definition:Language of Propositional Logic/Alphabet/Sign/Bracket
snippet: The signs of the language of propositional logic include the brackets: These are used as parenthesis signs.

label: Definition:Language of Propositional Logic/Also defined as
snippet: == Language of Propositional Logic: Also defined as == Since most authors concern themselves only with one formal system for propositional logic, they tend to refer to the whole formal system as propositional logic or propositional calculus. In correspondence, a particular author may decide to use only a subset of the signs. Generally, the other signs then are considered definitional abbreviations. At we aim to incorporate all these different approaches, and thus we have come to separately define the formal language.

label: Definition:Language of Propositional Logic/Formal Grammar/WFF
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be approved of by the formal grammar of propositional logic. Then $\mathbf A$ is called a well-formed formula of propositional logic. Often, one abbreviates well-formed formula, speaking of a WFF of propositional logic instead. More informally, a WFF of propositional logic is any sequence of symbols containing statement variables, such that when statements are substituted for the statement variables (the same statement for any given statement variable throughout), the result is a statement.

label: Definition:Laplace's Equation
snippet: == Equation == Laplace's equation is a second order PDE of the form: $\dfrac {\partial^2 \psi} {\partial x^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \psi} {\partial y^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \psi} {\partial z^2} = 0$ or: $\nabla^2 \psi = 0$ where $\nabla^2$ denotes the Laplacian operator.

label: Definition:Laplace's Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Laplace's Equation: Also known as == Laplace's equation is also known as the equation of continuity, but that term usually has a wider definition. Some sources render it as (the) Laplace equation.

label: Definition:Laplace's Equation/Complex Plane
snippet: == Equation == Let $D \subseteq \C$ be an open subset of the set of complex numbers $\C$. Let $f: D \to \C$ be a complex function on $D$. Let $u, v: \set {\tuple {x, y} \in \R^2: x + i y = z \in D} \to \R$ be the two real-valued functions defined as: {{eqn | l = \map u {x, y} | r = \map \Re {\map f z} }} {{eqn | l = \map v {x, y} | r = \map \Im {\map f z} }} where: $\map \Re {\map f z}$ denotes the real part of $\map f z$ $\map \Im {\map f z}$ denotes the imaginary part of $\map f z$.

label: Definition:Laplace's Equation/Complex Plane/Polar Form
snippet: == Equation == Let $D \subseteq \C$ be an open subset of the set of complex numbers $\C$. Let $f: D \to \C$ be a complex function on $D$. Let $u, v: \set {\tuple {x, y} \in \R^2: x + i y = z \in D} \to \R$ be the two real-valued functions defined as: {{eqn | l = \map u {x, y} | r = \map \Re {\map f z} }} {{eqn | l = \map v {x, y} | r = \map \Im {\map f z} }} where: $\map \Re {\map f z}$ denotes the real part of $\map f z$ $\map \Im {\map f z}$ denotes the imaginary part of $\map f z$.

label: Definition:Laplace Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \R$. Let $\mu$ be a real number. Let $b$ be a strictly positive real number. $X$ is said to have a Laplace distribution with parameters $\mu$ and $b$ it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} x = \dfrac 1 {2 b} \map \exp {- \dfrac {\size {x - \mu} } b}$ This is written: $X \sim \map {\operatorname {Laplace} } {\mu, b}$

label: Definition:Laplace Transform/Applications in Physics
snippet: == Applications of Laplace Transforms in Physics == Signal Processing: The domain of $f$ is the time domain The domain of $\laptrans f$ is the frequency domain.

label: Definition:Laplace Transform/Graphical Interpretation
snippet: Define $\gamma$ as the integrand of $\ds \int_0^{\to +\infty} e^{-s t} \map f t \rd t$ as a function of $\map f t$, $s$, and $t$: $\map \gamma {\map f t, t; s} = \map f t \, e^{-s t}$ For any particular function $f$, holding $s$ fixed, the integrand of the Laplace Transform $\kappa$ can be interpreted as a contour. That is, for a given function $f$ and a particular complex number $s_0$ held constant: $\map \kappa t: \R_{\ge 0} \to \C$ $\map \kappa t = \map \gamma {\map f t, t; s_0}$ is a parameterization of a contour.

label: Definition:Laplace Transform/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Laplace Transform == Despite the fact that the Laplace transform bears the name of , they were first used by to solve differential equations. Also during the course of solutions of differential equations, advanced sophisticated applications of Laplace transforms.

label: Definition:Laplace Transform/Restriction to Reals
snippet: Although the definition of the Laplace transform has $s$ be a complex variable, sometimes the restriction of $\map {\laptrans f} s$ to wholly real $s$ is sufficient to solve a particular differential equation. Therefore, elementary textbooks introducing the Laplace transform will often write something like the following: ... where we assume at present that the parameter $s$ is real. Later it will be found useful to consider $s$ complex.

label: Definition:Laplacian/Also known as
snippet: == Laplacian: Also known as == The Laplacian is also known as the Laplace operator, Laplace's operator or Laplace-Beltrami operator. The last name is usually used in the context of submanifolds in Euclidean space and on (pseudo-)Riemannian manifolds. Category:Definitions/Laplacian

label: Definition:Laplacian/Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $f \in \map {C^\infty} M : M \to \R$ be a smooth mapping on $M$. Let $\grad$ be the gradient operator. Let $\operatorname {div}$ be the divergence operator. The Laplace-Beltrami operator of $f$ is defined as: $\nabla^2 f := \map {\operatorname {div} } {\grad f}$

label: Definition:Laplacian/Riemannian Manifold/Also denoted as
snippet: == Laplacian: Also denoted as == In the context of Riemannian manifolds, the Laplacian can be seen as $\Delta f$, particularly in older texts. The $\nabla^2$ form is to be used on as it allows less opportunity for ambiguity and misunderstanding. Category:Definitions/Laplacian

label: Definition:Laplacian/Scalar Field
snippet: Let $\R^n$ denote the real Cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $\map U {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a scalar field over $\R^n$. Let the partial derivatives of $U$ exist throughout $\R^n$. The Laplacian of $U$ is defined as: $\ds \nabla^2 U := \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \dfrac {\partial^2 U} {\partial {x_k}^2}$

label: Definition:Laplacian/Scalar Field/Cartesian 3-Space
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of Cartesian $3$-space $\R^3$. Let $\map U {x, y, z}$ be a scalar field acting over $R$. The Laplacian of $U$ is defined as: $\nabla^2 U := \dfrac {\partial^2 U} {\partial x^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 U} {\partial y^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 U} {\partial z^2}$ where $\nabla$ denotes the del operator.

label: Definition:Laplacian/Vector Field
snippet: Let $\map {\R^n} {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ denote the real Cartesian space of $n$ dimensions. Let $\tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ be the standard ordered basis on $\R^n$. Let $\mathbf V: \R^n \to \R^n$ be a vector field on $\R^n$: $\forall \mathbf x \in \R^n: \map {\mathbf V} {\mathbf x} := \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n \map {V_k} {\mathbf x} \mathbf e_k$ where each of $V_k: \R^n \to \R$ are real-valued functions on $\R^n$.

label: Definition:Laplacian/Vector Field/Cartesian 3-Space
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of Cartesian $3$-space $\R^3$. Let $\map {\mathbf V} {x, y, z}$ be a vector field acting over $R$.

label: Definition:Laplacian/Vector Field/Cartesian 3-Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of Cartesian $3$-space $\R^3$. Let $\map {\mathbf V} {x, y, z}$ be a vector field acting over $R$. The Laplacian on $\mathbf V$ is defined as: $\nabla^2 \mathbf V = \dfrac {\partial^2 \mathbf V} {\partial x^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \mathbf V} {\partial y^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \mathbf V} {\partial z^2}$

label: Definition:Laplacian/Vector Field/Cartesian 3-Space/Definition 2
snippet:
Let $R$ be a region of Cartesian $3$-space $\R^3$. Let $\map {\mathbf V} {x, y, z}$ be a vector field acting over $R$. Let $	uple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ be the standard ordered basis on $\R^3$. Let $\mathbf V$ be expressed as vector-valued function: $\mathbf V := V_x \mathbf i + V_y \mathbf j + V_z \mathbf k$ The Laplacian on $\mathbf V$ is defined as: $
abla^2 \mathbf V = 
abla^2 V_x \mathbf i + 
abla^2 V_x \mathbf j + 
abla^2 V_y \mathbf k$ where $
abla^2 V_x$ and so on are the laplacians of $V_x$, $V_y$ and $V_z$ as scalar fields.

label: Definition:Larger Set
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. $S$ is defined as being larger than $T$ there exists a bijection from $T$ to a subset of $S$. $S$ is larger than $T$ can be denoted: $S \ge T$

label: Definition:Laspeyres Index
snippet: Let the prices of a set of $k$ commodities in the base year be $p_{0 1}, p_{0 2}, \ldots, p_{0 k}$. Let the quantities sold of each of those $k$ commodities in the base year be $q_{0 1}, q_{0 2}, \ldots, q_{0 k}$. Let the corresponding prices and quantities of those $k$ commodities in the $n$th year after the base year be $p_{n 1}, p_{n 2}, \ldots, p_{n k}$ and $q_{n 1}, q_{n 2}, \ldots, q_{n k}$. The Laspeyres index is the index number calculated as: $L_{0 n} = \dfrac {\ds \sum_j p_{n j} \, q_{0 j} } {\ds \sum_j p_{0 j} \, q_{0 j} }$

label: Definition:Latitude/Celestial
snippet: Let $P$ be a point on the celestial sphere. The celestial latitude of $P$ is the angle subtended by the the arc of the vertical circle through $P$ between $P$ and the ecliptic. If $P$ is closer to the north ecliptic pole, the celestial latitude is defined as latitude $\beta \degrees$ north, where $\beta \degrees$ denotes $\beta$ degrees (of angle), written $\beta \degrees \, \mathrm N$. If $P$ is closer to the south ecliptic pole, the celestial latitude is defined as latitude $\beta \degrees$ south, written $\beta \degrees \, \mathrm S$.

label: Definition:Latitude/Galactic
snippet: Let $P$ be a point on the celestial sphere. The galactic latitude of $P$ is the angular distance measured north or south of the galactic equator. It ranges from: $0 \degrees$ to $90 \degrees$ north $0 \degrees$ to $90 \degrees$ south where $0 \degrees$ is the galactic latitude of the galactic equator itself. This is denoted $l$.

label: Definition:Latitude/Terrestrial
snippet: Let $J$ be a point on Earth's surface that is not one of the two poles $N$ and $S$. Let $\bigcirc NJS$ be a meridian passing through $J$, whose endpoints are by definition $N$ and $S$. Let $\bigcirc NJS$ pass through the equator at $L$. The (terrestrial) latitude of $J$ is the (spherical) angle $\sphericalangle LOJ$ , where $O$ is the center of Earth. 500px If $J$ is in the northern hemisphere of Earth, the latitude is defined as latitude $n \degrees$ north, where $n \degrees$ denotes $n$ degrees (of angle), written $n \degrees \, \mathrm N$.

label: Definition:Latitude Circle of Surface of Revolution
snippet: Let $S_C$ be a surface of revolution. Let its smooth local parametrization be of the form: $\map X {t, \theta} = \tuple {\map y t \cos \theta, \map y t \sin \theta, \map x t}$ Then the $\theta$-coordinate curves $\theta \mapsto \map X {t_0, \theta}$ are called the latitude circles.

label: Definition:Lattice
snippet: Lattice (Order Theory), also known as an order lattice Point Lattice

label: Definition:Lattice (Order Theory)/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee}$ and $\struct {S, \wedge}$ be semilattices on a set $S$. Suppose that $\vee$ and $\wedge$ satisfy the absorption laws, that is, for all $a, b \in S$: $a \vee \paren {a \wedge b} = a$ $a \wedge \paren {a \vee b} = a$ Let $\preceq$ be the ordering on $S$ defined by: $\forall a, b \in S: a \preceq b$ $a \vee b = b$ as on Semilattice Induces Ordering. Then the ordered structure $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ is called a lattice. Thus $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ is called a lattice the lattice axioms are satisfied and $\preceq$ is defined as above:

label: Definition:Lattice (Ordered Set)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is a lattice : for all $x, y \in S$, the subset $\set {x, y}$ admits both a supremum and an infimum.

label: Definition:Lattice Filter
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preccurlyeq}$ be a lattice. Let $F \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$.

snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preccurlyeq}$ be a lattice. Let $F \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. $F$ is a lattice filter of $S$ $F$ satisifes the lattice filter axioms:

label: Definition:Lattice Filter/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preccurlyeq}$ be a lattice. Let $F \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. $F$ is a lattice filter of $S$ $F$ is a meet semilattice filter.

label: Definition:Lattice Ideal
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $I \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$.

label: Definition:Lattice Ideal/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $I \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. $I$ is a lattice ideal of $S$ $I$ satisifes the lattice ideal axioms:

label: Definition:Lattice Ideal/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \vee, \wedge, \preceq}$ be a lattice. Let $I \subseteq S$ be a non-empty subset of $S$. $I$ is a lattice ideal of $S$ $I$ is a join semilattice ideal

label: Definition:Lattice Point
snippet: Let $\R^m$ be the $m$-dimensional real Euclidean space. Let $\BB = \set {\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2, \ldots, \mathbf v_n}$ be a linearly independent set of vectors of $\R^m$. Let $\LL$ be the point lattice in $\R^m$ whose basis is $\BB$. Let $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ be an ordered $n$-tuple of integers. Let: {{eqn | l = P | r = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n a_i \mathbf v_i | c = }} Then $P$ is a lattice point of $\LL$.

label: Definition:Lattice Point/Cartesian Coordinate System
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a cartesian coordinate system of $n$ dimensions. Let $P = \tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ be a point in $\CC$. Then $P$ is a lattice point of $\CC$ $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ are all integers.

label: Definition:Lattice Point/Rational
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a cartesian coordinate system of $n$ dimensions. Let $P = \tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ be a point in $\CC$. $P$ is a rational lattice point of $\CC$ $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ are all rational numbers.

label: Definition:Lattice Theory
snippet: Lattice theory is the branch of abstract algebra concerned with the structure and properties of lattices in the specific context of order theory.

label: Definition:Lattice of Bounded Continuous Real-Valued Functions
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau_{_S} }$ be a topological space. Let $\R$ denote the real number line. Let $\struct {\map C {S, \R}, \vee, \wedge}$ be the lattice of continuous real-valued functions from $S$. The lattice of bounded continuous real-valued functions from $S$, denoted $\map {C^*} {S, \R}$, is the set of all bounded continuous mappings in $\map C {S, \R}$ with (pointwise) lattice operations $\vee$ and $\wedge$ restricted to $\map {C^*} {S, R}$.

label: Definition:Lattice of Continuous Real-Valued Functions
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau_{_S} }$ be a topological space. Let $\R$ denote the real number line. Let $\struct {\R^S, \vee, \wedge}$ be the lattice of real-valued functions from $S$ to $\R$. The lattice of continuous real-valued functions from $S$, denoted $\map C {S, \R}$, is the set of all continuous mappings in $\R^S$ with (pointwise) lattice operations $\vee$ and $\wedge$ restricted to $\map C {S, \R}$.

label: Definition:Lattice of Real-Valued Functions
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau_{_S} }$ be a topological space. Let $\R$ denote the real number line. Let $\R^S$ be the set of mappings from $S$ to $\R$. The lattice of real-valued mappings from $S$, denoted $\struct{\R^S, \vee, \wedge, \le}$, is the set of all mappings $\R^S$ with (pointwise) lattice operations $\vee$ and $\wedge$ defined by: $\forall f, g \in \R^S : f \vee g : S \to \R$ is defined by: $\forall s \in S : \map {\paren{f \vee g}} s = \max \set{\map f s, \map g s}$ $\forall f, g \in \R^S : f \wedge g : S \to \R$ is defined by: $\forall s \in S : \map {\paren{f \wedge g}} s = \min…

label: Definition:Latus Rectum/Circle
snippet: The circle, being a degenerate ellipse whose foci coincide, properly has no latus rectum, as a circle has neither a directrix nor a major axis. However, there is a case to make that, in a sense, a diameter of a circle $C$ can be considered as a latus rectum of $C$.

label: Definition:Latus Rectum/Definition 1
snippet: A latus rectum of a conic section $K$ is a chord of $K$ passing through a focus of $K$ perpendicular to the major axis of $K$.

label: Definition:Latus Rectum/Definition 2
snippet: A latus rectum of a conic section $K$ is a chord of $K$ passing through a focus of $K$ parallel to the directrix of $K$.

label: Definition:Latus Rectum/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Latus Rectum == The term latus rectum is a compound of the Latin: latus, meaning side rectum, meaning straight or right, as in straight line or right angle. Hence it literally means right side or straight side. Its plural is latera recta.

label: Definition:Latus Rectum of Ellipse/Definition 1
snippet: A latus rectum of an ellipse $K$ is a chord of $K$ passing through a focus of $K$ perpendicular to the major axis of $K$.

label: Definition:Latus Rectum of Ellipse/Definition 2
snippet: A latus rectum of an ellipse $K$ is a chord of $K$ passing through a focus of $K$ parallel to the directrix of $K$.

label: Definition:Latus Rectum of Hyperbola/Definition 1
snippet: A latus rectum of a hyperbola $K$ is a chord of $K$ passing through a focus of $K$ perpendicular to the major axis of $K$.

label: Definition:Latus Rectum of Hyperbola/Definition 2
snippet: A latus rectum of a hyperbola $K$ is a chord of $K$ passing through a focus of $K$ parallel to the directrix of $K$.

label: Definition:Laurent Series
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $z_0 \in \C$ such that: $f$ is analytic in $U := \set {z \in \C: r_1 \le \cmod {z - z_0} \le r_2}$ where $r_1, r_2 \in \overline \R$ are points in the extended real numbers. A Laurent series is a summation: $\forall z \in \C: r_1 < \cmod {z - z_0} < r_2: \map f z = \ds \sum_{n \mathop \in \Z} a_n \paren {z - z_0}^n$ where: $a_n = \dfrac 1 {2 \pi i} \ds \int_C \map f z \paren {z - z_0}^{n + 1} \rd z$ $C$ is a circle with center $z_0$ and radius $r$ for $r_1 < r < r_2$ $\ds \int_C \map f z \paren {z - z_0}^{n + 1} \rd z$ is the contour integral over…

label: Definition:Laurent Series/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Laurent series == The Laurent series expansion of an analytic function was established by in $1843$, but he never got round to publishing this work. independently discovered it during his work to rebuild the theory of complex analysis.

label: Definition:Laws of Conservation
snippet: The laws of conservation are laws of physics that states that certain particular measurable properties of isolated physical systems do not change as the system evolves over time.

label: Definition:Leading Coefficient of Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix. The leading coefficient of each row of $\mathbf A$ is the leftmost non-zero element of that row. A zero row has no leading coefficient.

label: Definition:Leading Term
snippet: Let $P = a \circ b$ be an expression. The term $a$ is known as the leading term of $P$.

label: Definition:Leaf Node/Also known as
snippet: == Leaf Node: Also known as == A leaf node is also known as just a leaf. In the context of rooted trees, a leaf node is often referred to as a terminal node. In the context of more general graphs which are not trees, a degree $1$ vertex is known as a pendant vertex or an end vertex.

label: Definition:Leap Year
snippet: The number of days in a year is not an integer, but lies somewhere between $365$ and $366$. However, it is convenient to assign an integer number of days to any given year. It is also desirable to ensure that a particular day of the year occurs at approximately the same time each year. In the Julian and Gregorian calendars: some years are assigned $365$ days and: some years are assigned $366$ days. The years which have $366$ days are called leap years.

label: Definition:Least Significant Digit
snippet: Let $b \in \Z: b \ge 2$ be a number base Let $n$ be a number which is reported to $r$ significant figures, to base $b$, that is: $n = d_1 \times b^k + d_2 \times b^{k - 1} + \dotsb + d_{r - 1} \times b^{k - r + 2} + d_r \times b^{k - r + 1}$ where: $d_1, d_2, \dotsc, d_r$ are the significant figures of $n$ $b^k$ is the largest power of $b$ less than or equal to $n$. Then the digit $d_r$ is known as the least significant digit of $n$. Note that the usual situation is when $b = 10$, but in the field of computer science, binary is usual.

label: Definition:Least Significant Digit/Also known as
snippet: == Least Significant Digit: Also known as == The least significant digit can also sometimes be seen as least significant figure. When $n$ is expressed in binary notation, the least significant digit is often referred to as the least significant bit and abbreviated lsb or l.s.b. Category:Definitions/Significant Figures

label: Definition:Lebesgue Decomposition/Finite Borel Measure
snippet: Let $\map \BB \R$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of the real number line $\R$. Let $\lambda$ be the Lebesgue measure on $\struct {\R, \map \BB \R}$. Let $\mu$ be a finite Borel measure on $\struct {\R, \map \BB \R}$. Let $\mu_{pp}$, $\mu_{sc}$ and $\mu_{ac}$ be measures on $\struct {\R, \map \BB \R}$. We say that $\tuple {\mu_{pp}, \mu_{sc}, \mu_{ac} }$ is the Lebesgue decomposition of $\mu$ : $\mu_{pp}$ is discrete measure $\mu_{sc}$ is continuous and mutually singular with respect to $\lambda$ $\mu_{ac}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\lambda$ $\mu = \mu_{pp} + \mu_{sc} +…

label: Definition:Lebesgue Integral
snippet: Let $\lambda^n$ be a Lebesgue measure on $\R^n$. Let $f: \R^n \to \overline \R$ be a Lebesgue integrable function, where $\overline \R$ denote the set of extended real numbers. Then the $\lambda^n$-integral of $f$: $\ds \int f \rd \lambda^n$ is called the Lebesgue integral of $f$. The definition proceeds in several steps.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Integral/Simple Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $E$ be a measurable subset of $X$. Let $\phi: E \to \overline \R$ be a $\Sigma$-measurable simple function which vanishes outside a set of finite measure. Then the Lebesgue integral of $\phi$ on $E$ is defined as: $\ds \int_E \map \phi x \rd \mu = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n a_i \map \mu {A_i}$ where $\ds \map \phi x = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n a_i \chi_{A_i}$. If the term $0 \cdot \infty$ appears in the sum, the term is defined to be zero.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Measure
snippet: Let $\JJ_{ho}^n$ be the set of half-open $n$-rectangles. Let $\map \BB {\R^n}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R^n$. Let $\lambda^n$ be the $n$-dimensional Lebesgue pre-measure on $\JJ_{ho}^n$. A measure $\mu$ extending $\lambda^n$ to $\map \BB {\R^n}$ is called $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. That is, $\mu$ is an $n$-dimensional Lebesgue measure it satisfies: $\mu \restriction_{\JJ_{ho}^n} = \lambda^n$ where $\restriction$ denotes restriction. Usually, this measure is also denoted by $\lambda^n$, even though this may be considered abuse of notation.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Measure/Real Number Line
snippet: For a given set $S \subseteq \R$, let $\set {I_n}$ be a countable set of open intervals such that: $S \subseteq \bigcup \set {I_n}$ For the power set $\powerset \R$ of the real numbers $\R$, construct a function $\mu^*: \powerset \R \to \R_{>0}$ as: $\ds \map {\mu^*} S = \inf \set {\sum_{n \mathop \in \N} \map l {I_n} : \set {I_n} : S \subseteq \bigcup_{n \mathop \in \N} I_n}$ where: the infimum ranges over all such sets $\set {I_n}$ $\map l {I_n}$ is the length of the interval $I_n$. Then $\mu^*$ is known as the Lebesgue outer measure and can be shown to be an outer measure.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Number
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\UU$ be an open cover of $M$. A fixed strictly positive real number $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ is called a Lebesgue number for $\UU$ : $\forall x \in A: \exists \map U x \in \UU: \map {B_\epsilon} x \subseteq \map U x$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} x$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ in $M$.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Outer Measure/Also known as
snippet: == Lebesgue Outer Measure: Also known as == When the domain of a Lebesgue outer measure $\mu^*$ is restricted to the set $\mathfrak M$ of Lebesgue-measurable sets, $\mu^*$ is instead written as $\mu$ and is simply referred to as the Lebesgue measure.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Pre-Measure
snippet: Let $\JJ_{ho}$ be the collection of half-open $n$-rectangles. $n$-dimensional Lebesgue pre-measure is the mapping $\lambda^n: \JJ_{ho} \to \overline \R_{\ge 0}$ given by: $\ds \map {\lambda^n} {\horectr {\mathbf a} {\mathbf b} } = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {b_i - a_i}$ where $\overline \R_{\ge 0}$ denotes the set of positive extended real numbers.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space, and let $p \in \R$, $p \ge 1$. The (real) Lebesgue $p$-space of $\mu$ is defined as: $\map {\LL^p} \mu := \set {f: X \to \R: f \in \map \MM \Sigma, \ds \int \size f^p \rd \mu < \infty}$ where $\map \MM \Sigma$ denotes the space of $\Sigma$-measurable functions.

label: Definition:Lebesgue Space/L-Infinity
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. The Lebesgue $\infty$-space for $\mu$, denoted $\map {\LL^\infty} \mu$, is defined as: $\map {\LL^\infty} \mu := \set {f \in \map \MM \Sigma: f \text{ is essentially bounded} }$ and so consists of all $\Sigma$-measurable $f: X \to \R$ that are essentially bounded.

label: Definition:Lebombo Bone
snippet: The Lebombo bone is a baboon's leg bone bearing $29$ notches which were carved into it between $33 \ 000$ B.C.E. and $42 \ 000$ B.C.E. It is the earliest known instance of a system of tally marks. It was found in in in the , near the border with . Various untestable hypotheses have been raised concerning this artefact, notably that it was created by an early African woman to count the days between her menses. However, as the bone appears to be broken at one end, it is possible that the count of $29$ is not the complete set of notches that were originally carved.

label: Definition:Left-Hand Derivative
snippet: Let $B$ be a Banach space over the set of real numbers $\R$. Let $f: \R \to B$ be a mapping from $\R$ to $B$. The left-hand derivative of $f$ is defined as the left-hand limit: $\ds \map {f'_-} x = \lim_{h \mathop \to 0^-} \frac {\map f {x + h} - \map f x} h$ If the left-hand derivative exists, then $f$ is said to be left-hand differentiable at $x$.

label: Definition:Left-Invariant Riemannian Metric
snippet: Let $G$ be a Lie group. Let $\struct {G, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $L_\phi : G \to G$ be a left translation. Suppose $g$ is invariant under all left translations: $\forall \phi \in G : {L_\phi}^* g = g$ where $*$ denotes the pullback of $g$ by $L_\phi$. Then $g$ is said to be left-invariant.

label: Definition:Left-Total Relation/Multifunction
snippet: A multifunction is a left-total relation $\RR$ which is specifically not many-to-one or one-to-one. That is, for each element $s$ of the domain of $\RR$, there exists more than one $t$ in the codomain of $\RR$ such that $\tuple {s, t} \in \RR$. Hence a multifunction is not strictly speaking a mapping. However, if $\RR$ is regarded as a mapping from $S$ to the power set of $T$, then left-totality of $\RR$ is the same as totality of this lifted function. See the definition of a direct image mapping.

label: Definition:Left-Truncatable Prime
snippet: A left-truncatable prime is a prime number which remains prime when any number of digits are removed from the left hand end. Zeroes are excluded, in order to eliminate, for example, prime numbers of the form $10^n + 3$ for arbitrarily large $n$.

label: Definition:Left Adjoint Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ be locally small categories. Let $F : \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ and $G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be functors. $F$ is a left adjoint functor of $G$ there exists an adjunction $\struct {F, G, \alpha}$.

label: Definition:Left Cancellable Mapping
snippet: A mapping $f: Y \to Z$ is left cancellable (or left-cancellable) : $\forall X: \forall \struct {g_1, g_2: X \to Y}: f \circ g_1 = f \circ g_2 \implies g_1 = g_2$ That is, for any set $X$, if $g_1$ and $g_2$ are mappings from $X$ to $Y$: If $f \circ g_1 = f \circ g_2$ then $g_1 = g_2$.

label: Definition:Left Exact Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be categories. Let $F : \mathbf A \to \mathbf B$ be a functor. Then $F$ is left exact $F$ preserves finite limits.

label: Definition:Left Haar Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ be a locally compact topological group. Let $\BB$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. A measure $m$ on $\BB$ is called a left Haar measure : $(1): \quad \forall U \in \tau : U \ne \O \implies \map m U > 0$ $(2): \quad$ $m$ is left translation invariant, that is: $\forall g \in G, \forall E \in \BB : \map m {g \odot E} = \map m E$ where: $ g \odot E := \set {g \odot h : h \in E}$

label: Definition:Left Inverse
snippet: Mapping Theory: Left Inverse Mapping Abstract Algebra: Left Inverse Element Matrix Theory: Left Inverse Matrix

label: Definition:Left Inverse Mapping
snippet: Let $S, T$ be sets where $S \ne \O$, that is, $S$ is not empty. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $g: T \to S$ be a mapping such that: $g \circ f = I_S$ where: $g \circ f$ denotes the composite mapping $f$ followed by $g$; $I_S$ is the identity mapping on $S$. Then $g: T \to S$ is called a left inverse (mapping).

label: Definition:Left Linear Ring Action/Also known as
snippet: == Left Linear Ring Action: Also known as == In expositions which start with the definition of a left module as the basic starting point, the linearity of the left linear ring action is often taken for granted. Hence the name left ring action is often found as a synonym. Similarly, expositions which do not consider the concept of a right module may simply refer to a linear ring action, or even just ring action. However, all of those terms have wider scope than the specific case of a scalar ring acting on an abelian group in this specific manner. Category:Definitions/Left Linear Ring Actions

label: Definition:Left Module over Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. A left module over $R$ is an $R$-algebraic structure $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ with one operation $\ast: R \times G \to G$, the (left) ring action, which satisfies the left module axioms:

label: Definition:Left Null Space
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix in the matrix space $\map {\MM_{m, n} } R$. Let $\mathbf A^\intercal$ be the transpose of $\mathbf A$. The left null space $\mathbf A$ is defined as the null space of $\mathbf A^\intercal$.

label: Definition:Left Operation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. For any $x, y \in S$, the left operation on $S$ is the binary operation defined as: $\forall x, y \in S: x \gets y = x$

label: Definition:Left Order Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $\tau$ be the topology on $S$ generated by the basis sets of the form: $S_a = \set {x: x \prec a}$ for $a \in S$. Then the topological space $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq, \tau}$ is known as the left order topology on $S$.

label: Definition:Left Singular Vector of Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$. Let $\mathbf A = \mathbf U \mathbf D \mathbf V$ be a singular value decomposition of $\mathbf A$. The columns of $\mathbf U$ are known as the left singular vectors of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Left Vector Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. A left vector space over $R$ is an $R$-algebraic structure $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ with one operation $\ast: R \times G \to G$, which satisfies the left vector space axioms:

label: Definition:Legendre's Associated Differential Equation
snippet: Legendre's associated differential equation is a second order ODE of the form: $\ds \paren {1 - x^2} \frac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} - 2 x \frac {\d y} {\d x} + \paren {n \paren {n + 1} - \frac {m^2} {1 - x^2} } y = 0$ where $m$ and $n$ are complex numbers. Solutions to Legendre's associated differential equation are called associated Legendre functions.

label: Definition:Legendre's Constant
snippet: Legendre's constant is a mathematical constant conjectured by to specify the prime-counting function $\map \pi n$. conjectured in $1796$ that $\map \pi n$ satisfies: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \map \pi n - \frac n {\map \ln n} = B$ where $B$ is what is now known as Legendre's constant. If such a number $B$ exists, then this implies the Prime Number Theorem. 's guess for $B$ was about $1 \cdotp 08366$. Later, looked at this problem and thought that $B$ might actually be lower. In $1896$, and independently proved the Prime Number Theorem and showed that $B$ is in fact equal to $1$.

label: Definition:Legendre's Differential Equation
snippet: Legendre's differential equation is a second order ODE of the form: $\paren {1 - x^2} \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} - 2 x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + p \paren {p + 1} y = 0$ The parameter $p$ may be any arbitrary real or complex number. Solutions to Legendre's differential equation for $p \in \N$ are called Legendre polynomials of order $p$.

label: Definition:Legendre Polynomial
snippet: Consider the Legendre's differential equation: $(1): \quad \paren {1 - x^2} \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} - 2 x \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} + n \paren {n + 1} y = 0$ for $n \in \N$. The solutions to $(1)$ are called the Legendre polynomials of order $n$ and denoted $\map {P_n} x$. These solutions form a polynomial sequence of orthogonal polynomials on the interval $\closedint {-1} 1$.

label: Definition:Legendre Symbol
snippet: Let $p$ be an odd prime. Let $a \in \Z$ be an integer.

label: Definition:Legendre Symbol/Also known as
snippet: == Legendre Symbol: Also known as == The Legendre symbol for fixed prime $p$ is also known as the quadratic character modulo $p$. However, that term is defined on from this as simply whether an integer $a$ is a quadratic residue of $p$ or not, without assigning the result to an integer variable. Hence Legendre symbol will be used throughout. Category:Definitions/Legendre Symbol

label: Definition:Lehmer's Constant
snippet: Let the sequence $\sequence {b_k}_{k \mathop \in \N}$ be defined by the recurrence relation: {{eqn | l = b_k | r = \begin {cases} 0 & : k = 0 \\ {b_{k - 1} }^2 + b_{k - 1} + 1 & : \text {otherwise} \end{cases} }} {{eqn | r = \sequence {0, 1, 3, 13, 183, 33973 \ldots} }} Lehmer's constant is the real number $\xi$ defined as: {{eqn | l = \xi | r = \map \cot {\sum_{k \mathop = 0}^\infty \paren {-1}^k \arccot b_k} }} {{eqn | r = \map \cot {\arccot 0 - \arccot 1 + \arccot 3 - \arccot 13 + \arccot 183 - \arccot 33973 + \dotsb} }}

label: Definition:Lehmer's Electromechanical Sieve
snippet: Lehmer's Electromechanical Sieve Lehmer's electromechanical sieve is a device which was invented for the purpose of solving number theory problems, such as: determining the prime decomposition of integers determining whether an integer is prime. It consists of: a mechanical assemblage of gearwheels photo detector an electronic amplifier. It is currently located at the [http://www.computerhistory.org/ Computer History Museum], where its lot number is $\text X 85.82$.

label: Definition:Leibniz Harmonic Triangle
snippet: The Leibniz Harmonic Triangle is a triangular array where: the zeroth element in the $n$th row, counting from $0$, is $\dfrac 1 {n + 1}$ subsequent elements in the $n$th row are the zeroth element divided by the corresponding element of Pascal's triangle: $\begin{array}{r|rrrrrr} n & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline 0 & \frac 1 1 \\ 1 & \frac 1 2 & \frac 1 2 \\ 2 & \frac 1 3 & \frac 1 6 & \frac 1 3 \\ 3 & \frac 1 4 & \frac 1 {12} & \frac 1 {12} & \frac 1 4 \\ 4 & \frac 1 5 & \frac 1 {20} & \frac 1 {30} & \frac 1 {20} & \frac 1 5 \\ 5 & \frac 1 6 & \frac 1 {30} & \frac 1 {60} & \frac 1 {60} &…

label: Definition:Lemma
snippet: A lemma is a statement which is proven during the course of reaching the proof of a theorem. Logically there is no qualitative difference between a lemma and a theorem. They are both statements whose value is either true or false. However, a lemma is seen more as a stepping-stone than a theorem in itself (and frequently takes a lot more work to prove than the theorem to which it leads).

label: Definition:Lemma/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Lemma == The plural of lemma is either lemmas or lemmata. The form lemmata is preferred on . Category:Linguistic Notes

label: Definition:Lemniscate of Bernoulli/Geometric Definition
snippet: Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be points in the plane such that $P_1 P_2 = 2 a$ for some constant $a$. The lemniscate of Bernoulli is the locus of points $M$ in the plane such that: $P_1 M \times P_2 M = a^2$ 630px

label: Definition:Length
snippet: Geometry: Length (Linear Measure): a formal comparison between the spatial extent of a geometric figure in a specified direction against a reference quantity (often tacitly understood). Length of a line: a formal measure of the spatial extent of a line segment. Analysis: Length of a (real) interval: the difference between the endpoints of a real interval. Length of a curve: the limit of the length of a polygonal line inscribed within the curve as the maximum length of the chords which form that polygonal line tends to zero.

label: Definition:Length (Linear Measure)/Vector
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be points in a real Euclidean space $\R^n$. Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ respectively. The length of the straight line $AB$ is given by: $\map L {AB} := \size {\mathbf a - \mathbf b}$ where: $\mathbf a - \mathbf b$ denotes the vector subtraction operation $\size {\mathbf a - \mathbf b}$ denotes the magnitude of $\mathbf a - \mathbf b$.

label: Definition:Length of Group
snippet: Let $G$ be a finite group. The length of $G$ is the length of a composition series for $G$. That is, the length of $G$ is the number of factors in a composition series for $G$ (not including $G$ itself). The length of $G$ can be denoted $\map l G$. By the Jordan-Hölder Theorem, all composition series for $G$ have the same length. Therefore, the length of a finite group $G$ is well-defined.

label: Definition:Length of Normal
snippet: right Let $\CC$ be a curve in a Cartesian plane. Let $\NN$ be the normal to $\CC$ at a point $P$ on $\CC$. Let $Q$ be the $x$-intercept of $\NN$. The length of $\NN$ is defined as the length of the line segment $PQ$.

label: Definition:Length of Tangent
snippet: right Let $\CC$ be a curve in a Cartesian plane. Let $\TT$ be a tangent to $\CC$ through a point $P$ on $\CC$. Let $Q$ be the $x$-intercept of $\TT$. The length of $\TT$ is defined as the length of the line segment $PQ$.

label: Definition:Leptokurtic
snippet: A random variable with kurtosis greater than $3$ is described as leptokurtic.

label: Definition:Lerch Transcendent
snippet: The Lerch transcendent $\map \Phi {z, s, a}$ is defined on $\set {z \in \C: 0 \le \cmod z 1, a \ne 0, -1, -2, \cdots}$ as the series: $\ds \map \Phi {z, s, a} = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {z^n} {\paren {n + a}^s}$

label: Definition:Less Than
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \le}$ be one of the sets of numbers: $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$ under the usual ordering. Let $a, b \in S$ such that $a < b$. Then $a$ is described as being less than $b$.

label: Definition:Lever
snippet: A lever is a simple machine consisting of: a rigid bar $M$ pivoted at a point $F$, called the fulcrum so that: an effort applied at one point $E$ of $M$ is transferred to: a load at another point $L$ of $M$ so as to generate a mechanical advantage.

label: Definition:Lever/Fulcrum
snippet: The fulcrum of a lever is the pivot about which the lever turns. It is the point about which the moments of the applied effort and load are calculated.

label: Definition:Levi-Civita Connection
snippet:
Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold with or without boundary. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $
abla$ be a connection on $TM$. Suppose $
abla$ is compatible with $g$ and symmetric. Then $
abla$ is called Levi-Civita connection. This is exactly a least-model construction in logic programming. levi_civita(Nabla, G) :- connection(Nabla), metric(G), torsion_free(Nabla), metric_compatible(Nabla, G). torsion_free(Nabla) :- forall(indices(I,J,K), ( gamma(Nabla,K,I,J,G1), gamma(Nabla,K,J,I,G2), G1 = G2 ) ).

label: Definition:Lexicographic Order/General Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. For $n \in \N: n > 0$, we define $T_n$ as the set of all ordered $n$-tuples: $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ of elements $x_j \in S$. Let $\ds T = \bigcup_{n \mathop \ge 1} T_n$. The lexicographic order on $T$ is the relation $\preccurlyeq_l$ defined on $T$ as: $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m} \preccurlyeq_l \tuple {y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n}$ : $\exists k: 1 \le k \le \map \min {m, n}: \paren {\forall j: 1 \le j < k: x_j = y_j} \land x_k \prec y_k$ or: $m \le n$ and $\forall j: 1 \le j \le m: x_j = y_j$.

label: Definition:Lexicographic Order/Ordinals
snippet: The lexicographic order is a relation on ordered pairs of ordinals denoted $\preccurlyeq_l$. $\preccurlyeq_l$ is the set of all ordered pairs $\tuple {\tuple {\alpha, \beta}, \tuple {\gamma, \delta} }$ such that: $(1): \quad$ Each $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ is a member of the class of all ordinals $(2): \quad$ $\alpha \in \gamma$ or $\alpha = \gamma \land \beta \in \delta$

snippet: Let $L$ be an algebra over a ring. Then $L$ is a Lie algebra it satisfies the Lie algebra axioms:

label: Definition:Lie Algebra/Bracket
snippet: Let $L$ be a Lie algebra. The bilinear mapping $\sqbrk {\, \cdot, \cdot \,}$ on $L$ which defines the underlying algebra of $L$ is referred to as the bracket operator.

label: Definition:Lie Group
snippet: A Lie group is a group which is also a smooth manifold.

label: Definition:Lie Group/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Lie Group == When the concept of a Lie group was originally researched, it did not appear to have any immediate practical application. In more recently times, they have been used: to describe pseudo-Riemannian locally homogeneous symmetric spaces, to be used in geometric theory of gravitation to model phenomena in quantum mechanics, from $1925$ to $1926$, via Hermitian matrix representations of observations

label: Definition:Lie Theory
snippet: Lie theory is the study of Lie groups and Lie algebras.

label: Definition:Lie Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Lie Theory == The branch of mathematics now known as Lie theory emerged from the research by , started in $1873$, into the structure of what are now known as Lie groups. The results of this research appeared in the publication of $3$ books by and between $1888$ and $1893$, and $4$ papers by between $1888$ and $1890$. The work built on the concepts of groups and matrices by , and , dating back to the years between $1850$ and $1859$. More recently, Lie groups have shown they have a practical application in modern physics.

label: Definition:Lift (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ and $C = \struct {X, \phi}$ be topological spaces. Let $\pi: C \to T$ be a (topological) covering mapping for $T$ by $C$. Let $\gamma$ be a path in $T$. The unique path $\Gamma$ in $C$ such that $\gamma = \pi \circ \Gamma$ is called the lift of $\gamma$.

label: Definition:Light Framework
snippet: A light framework is a set of light rods joined together so as to form a structure that is rigid. Because of the approximation to zero mass, the forces acting in the rods can be worked out by considering the forces acting at the points where they are connected together.

label: Definition:Limaçon of Pascal
snippet: Let $C$ be a circle of diameter $a$ with a distinguished point $O$ on the circumference. Let $OQ$ be a chord of $C$. The limaçons of Pascal are the loci of points $P$ in the plane such that: $PQ = b$ where: $OPQ$ is a straight line $b$ is a real constant.

label: Definition:Limit (Category Theory)/Notation
snippet: == Limit: Notation == By definition the limit is technically a cone $\paren {\varprojlim_j D_j, \sequence {p_j}_j }$ in $\map {\mathbf{Cone} } D$ where $\varprojlim_j D_j$ is an object in $\mathbf C$ with morphisms: $p_j: \varprojlim_j D_j \to D_j$ such that for each morphism $\alpha: i \to j$ of $\mathbf J$: $p_j = D_{\alpha} \circ p_i$ In practice, the object $\varprojlim_j D_j$ in $\mathbf C$ is thought of as being the limit and the associated morphisms $p_i: \varprojlim_j D_j \to D_i$ are left implicit.

label: Definition:Limit Inferior/Also known as
snippet: == Limit Inferior: Also known as == The limit inferior is also called the lower limit, or just liminf. However, note that the term lower limit has a subtly different meaning in the context of topology, so to avoid ambiguity its use here is not recommended. Some sources use the term lower bound, but that term has a wider application and is not recommended in this context. Category:Definitions/Limits Inferior

label: Definition:Limit Inferior/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a bounded sequence in $\R$. Let $L$ be the set of all real numbers which are the limit of some subsequence of $\sequence {x_n}$. From Existence of Maximum and Minimum of Bounded Sequence, $L$ has a minimum. This minimum is called the limit inferior. It can be denoted: $\ds \map {\liminf_{n \mathop \to \infty} } {x_n} = \underline l$

label: Definition:Limit Inferior of Net
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a directed set. Let $L = \struct {T, \precsim}$ be a complete lattice. Let $N: S \to T$ be a net in $T$. Then limit inferior of $N$ is defined as follows: $\liminf N := \sup_L \set { {\map {\inf_L} {N \sqbrk {\map \preceq j} } : j \in S} }$ where $\map \preceq j$ denotes the image of $j$ by $\preceq$ $N \sqbrk {\map \preceq j}$ denotes the image of $\map \preceq j$ under $N$.

label: Definition:Limit Inferior of Sequence of Sets/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\sequence {E_n : n \in \N}$ be a sequence of sets. Then the limit inferior of $\sequence {E_n : n \in \N}$, denoted $\ds \liminf_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n$, is defined as: {{eqn | l = \liminf_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n | o = := | r = \bigcup_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \bigcap_{i \mathop = n}^\infty E_i }} {{eqn | r = \paren {E_0 \cap E_1 \cap E_2 \cap \ldots} \cup \paren {E_1 \cap E_2 \cap E_3 \cap \ldots} \cup \cdots }}

label: Definition:Limit Inferior of Sequence of Sets/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\sequence {E_n : n \in \N}$ be a sequence of sets. Then the limit inferior of $\sequence {E_n : n \in \N}$, denoted $\ds \liminf_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n$, is defined as: $\ds \liminf_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n := \set {x: x \in E_i \text { for all but finitely many } i}$

snippet: Let $\set {E_n: n \in \N}$ be a sequence of sets. The limit inferior of $E_n$ can also be seen denoted as: $\ds \underset {n \mathop \to \infty} {\underline \lim} E_n$ but this notation is not used on . Some sources merely present this as: $\ds \underline \lim E_n$ The abbreviated notation $E_*$ can also be seen.

label: Definition:Limit Ordinal/Definition 1
snippet: An ordinal $\lambda$ is a limit ordinal it is a limit element in the well-ordering on the class of all ordinals $\On$ that is the subset relation.

label: Definition:Limit Ordinal/Definition 2
snippet: An ordinal $\lambda$ is a limit ordinal it is neither the zero ordinal nor a successor ordinal.

label: Definition:Limit Point/Filter
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a filter on $S$. A point $x \in S$ is called a limit point of $\FF$ $\FF$ is finer than the neighborhood filter of $x$.

label: Definition:Limit Point/Filter Basis
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a filter on the underlying set $S$ of $T$. Let $\BB$ be a filter basis of $\FF$.

label: Definition:Limit Point/Filter Basis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a filter on the underlying set $S$ of $T$. Let $\BB$ be a filter basis of $\FF$. A point $x \in S$ is called a limit point of $\BB$ $\FF$ converges on $x$. $\BB$ is likewise said to converge on $x$.

label: Definition:Limit Point/Filter Basis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a filter on the underlying set $S$ of $T$. Let $\BB$ be a filter basis of $\FF$. A point $x \in S$ is called a limit point of $\BB$ every neighborhood of $x$ contains a set of $\BB$.

label: Definition:Limit Point/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {S, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\tau$ be the topology induced by the metric $d$. Let $A \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Let $\alpha \in S$.

label: Definition:Limit Point/Metric Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M = \struct {S, d}$ be a metric space. Let $A \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Let $\alpha \in S$. $\alpha$ is a limit point of $A$ every deleted $\epsilon$-neighborhood $\map {B_\epsilon} \alpha \setminus \set \alpha$ of $\alpha$ contains a point in $A$: $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \paren {\map {B_\epsilon} \alpha \setminus \set \alpha} \cap A \ne \O$ that is: $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \set {x \in A: 0 < \map d {x, \alpha} < \epsilon} \ne \O$ Note that $\alpha$ does not have to be an element of $A$ to be a limit point.

label: Definition:Limit Point/Metric Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M = \struct {S, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\tau$ be the topology induced by the metric $d$. Let $A \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Let $\alpha \in S$. $\alpha$ is a limit point of $A$ there is a sequence $\sequence{\alpha_n}$ in $A \setminus \set \alpha$ such that $\sequence{\alpha_n}$ converges to $\alpha$, that is, $\alpha$ is a limit of the sequence $\sequence{\alpha_n}$ in $S$.

label: Definition:Limit Point/Metric Space/Definition 3
snippet: Let $M = \struct {S, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\tau$ be the topology induced by the metric $d$. Let $A \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Let $\alpha \in S$. $\alpha$ is a limit point of $A$ $\alpha$ is a limit point in the topological space $\struct{S, \tau}$.

label: Definition:Limit Point/Real Analysis
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. Let $\xi \in \R$ and let $S_\xi$ be the set defined as: $S_\xi := \set {x: x \in S, x \ne \xi}$ Then $\xi$ is a limit point of $S$ $\xi$ is at zero distance from $S_\xi$.

label: Definition:Limit Point/Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space.

label: Definition:Limit Point/Topology/Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $a \in S$. A point $x \in S, x \ne a$ is a limit point of $a$ every open neighborhood of $x$ contains $a$. That is, it is a limit point of the singleton $\set a$.

label: Definition:Limit Point of Set/Definition from Adherent Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. A point $x \in S$ is a limit point of $H$ $x$ is an adherent point of $H$ but is not an isolated point of $H$.

label: Definition:Limit Point of Set/Definition from Closure
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. A point $x \in S$ is a limit point of $H$ : $x$ belongs to the closure of $H$ but is not an isolated point of $H$.

label: Definition:Limit Point of Set/Definition from Open Neighborhood
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. A point $x \in S$ is a limit point of $H$ every open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ satisfies: $H \cap \paren {U \setminus \set x} \ne \O$ That is, every open set $U \in \tau$ such that $x \in U$ contains some point of $H$ distinct from $x$.

label: Definition:Limit Point of Set/Definition from Relative Complement
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. A point $x \in S$ is a limit point of $H$ $\paren {S \setminus H} \cup \set x$ is not a neighborhood of $x$.

label: Definition:Limit Superior
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a bounded sequence in $\R$.

label: Definition:Limit Superior/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a bounded sequence in $\R$. Let $L$ be the set of all real numbers which are the limit of some subsequence of $\sequence {x_n}$. From Existence of Maximum and Minimum of Bounded Sequence, $L$ has a maximum. This maximum is called the limit superior. It can be denoted: $\ds \map {\limsup_{n \mathop \to \infty} } {x_n} = \overline l$

snippet: Let $\sequence {E_n: n \in \N}$ be a sequence of sets. Then the limit superior of $\sequence {E_n: n \in \N}$, denoted $\ds \limsup_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n$, is defined as: $\ds \limsup_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n = \set {x : x \in E_i \text { for infinitely many } i}$

label: Definition:Limit of Net
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\struct {\Lambda, \preceq}$ be a directed set. Let $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \mathop \in \Lambda}$ be a net. $x \in X$ is called a limit (point) of $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$ $\family {x_\lambda}_{\lambda \in \Lambda}$ converges to $x$.

label: Definition:Limit of Real Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\openint a b$ be an open real interval. Let $c \in \openint a b$. Let $f: \openint a b \setminus \set c \to \R$ be a real function. Let $L \in \R$. $\map f x$ tends to the limit $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: x \in \map {N_\delta} c \setminus \set c \implies \map f x \in \map {N_\epsilon} L$ where: $\map {N_\epsilon} L$ denotes the $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $L$ $\map {N_\delta} c \setminus \set c$ denotes the deleted $\delta$-neighborhood of $c$ $\R_{>0}$ denotes the set of strictly positive real numbers.

label: Definition:Limit of Real Function/Intuition
snippet: Though the founders of Calculus viewed the limit: $\ds \lim_{x \mathop \to c} \map f x$ as the behavior of $f$ as it gets infinitely close to $x = c$, the real number system as defined in modern mathematics does not allow for the existence of infinitely small distances. But: $\exists L: \forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: 0 < \size {x - c} < \delta \implies \size {\map f x - L} < \epsilon$ can be interpreted this way: You want to get very close to the value $c$ on the $\map f x$ axis. This degree of closeness is the positive real number $\epsilon$.

label: Definition:Limit of Real Function/Left
snippet: Let $\openint a b$ be an open real interval. Let $f: \openint a b \to \R$ be a real function. Let $L \in \R$. Suppose that: $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \forall x \in \R: b - \delta 0}$ denotes the set of strictly positive real numbers. That is, for every real strictly positive $\epsilon$ there exists a real strictly positive $\delta$ such that every real number in the domain of $f$, less than $b$ but within $\delta$ of $b$, has an image within $\epsilon$ of $L$.

label: Definition:Limit of Real Function/Right
snippet: Let $\Bbb I = \openint a b$ be an open real interval. Let $f: \Bbb I \to \R$ be a real function. Let $L \in \R$. Suppose that: $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \forall x \in \Bbb I: a 0}$ denotes the set of strictly positive real numbers. That is, for every real strictly positive $\epsilon$ there exists a real strictly positive $\delta$ such that every real number in the domain of $f$, greater than $a$ but within $\delta$ of $a$, has an image within $\epsilon$ of $L$.

snippet: Let $f: \R \times \R \to \R$ be a real function of $2$ variables. Then $\map f {x, y}$ tends to the limit $A$ as $x$ approaches $a$ and $y$ approaches $b$: $\ds \lim_{\substack {x \mathop \to a \\ y \mathop \to b} } \map f {x, y} = A$ for each positive real number $\epsilon$ there exists another positive real number $\delta$ such that: whenever $\size {x - a} < \delta$ and $\size {y - b} < \delta$ such that $0 < \paren {x - a}^2 + \paren {y - b}^2$, we have: $\size {\map f {x, y} - A} < \epsilon$ That is, when $\tuple {x, y}$ is at any point inside a square somewhere (except for its center)…

label: Definition:Limit of Sequence/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or pseudometric space. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $M$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ converge to a value $l \in A$. Then $l$ is a limit of $\sequence {x_n}$ as $n$ tends to infinity. If $M$ is a metric space, this is usually written: $\ds l = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n$

label: Definition:Limit of Sequence/Normed Division Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $R$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ converge to $x \in R$. Then $x$ is a limit of $\sequence {x_n}$ as $n$ tends to infinity which is usually written: $\ds x = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n$

label: Definition:Limit of Sequence/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}}$ be a normed vector space. Let $L \in X$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converge to $L$. Then $L$ is a limit of $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ as $n$ tends to infinity which is usually written: $\ds L = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n$

label: Definition:Limit of Sequence/P-adic Numbers
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\sequence {x_n} $ be a sequence in $\Q_p$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ converge to $x \in \Q_p$ Then $x$ is a limit of $\sequence {x_n}$ as $n$ tends to infinity which is usually written: $\ds x = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n$

label: Definition:Limit of Sequence/Rational Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $\Q$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ converge to a value $l \in \R$, where $\R$ denotes the set of real numbers. Then $l$ is a limit of $\sequence {x_n}$ as $n$ tends to infinity. This is usually written: $\ds l = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n$

label: Definition:Limit of Sequence/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $\R$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ converge to a value $l \in \R$. Then $l$ is a limit of $\sequence {x_n}$ as $n$ tends to infinity. This is usually written: $\ds l = \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} x_n$

label: Definition:Limit of Sequence/Test Function Space
snippet: Let $\map \DD {\R^d}$ be the test function space. Let $\phi \in \map \DD {\R^d}$ be a test function. Let $\sequence {\phi_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of test functions in $\map \DD {\R^d}$. Let $\sequence {\phi_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converge to $\phi$ in $\map \DD {\R^d}$. Then $\phi$ is a limit of $\sequence {\phi_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $\map \DD {\R^d}$ as $n$ tends to infinity which is usually written: $\phi_n \stackrel \DD {\longrightarrow} \phi$

label: Definition:Limit of Sequence/Topological Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $A$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ converge to a value $\alpha \in S$. Then $\alpha$ is known as a limit point of $\sequence {x_n}$ (as $n$ tends to infinity).

label: Definition:Limit of Sequence of Events
snippet: Let $\left({\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}\right)$ be a probability space.

label: Definition:Limit of Sequence of Events/Decreasing
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {A_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an decreasing sequence of events. Then the intersection: $\ds A = \bigcap_{i \mathop \in \N} A_i$ of such a sequence is called the limit of the sequence $\sequence {A_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. From the Elementary Properties of Event Space we have that such a $\ds \bigcap_{i \mathop \in \N} A_i$ is itself an event.

label: Definition:Limit of Sequence of Events/Increasing
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\sequence {A_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an increasing sequence of events. Then the union: $\ds A = \bigcup_{i \mathop \in \N} A_i$ of such a sequence is called the limit of the sequence $\sequence {A_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. From the definition of event space we have that such a $\ds \bigcup_{i \mathop \in \N} A_i$ is itself an event.

label: Definition:Limit of Sets
snippet: Let $\Bbb S = \set {E_n : n \in \N}$ be a sequence of sets. Let the limit superior of $\Bbb S$ be equal to the limit inferior of $\Bbb S$. Then the limit of $\Bbb S$, denoted $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n$, is defined as: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n := \limsup_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n$ and so also: $\ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n := \liminf_{n \mathop \to \infty} E_n$ and $\Bbb S$ converges to the limit.

label: Definition:Limit of Topological Spaces
snippet: Let $\II$ be a small category. Let $D : \II \to \mathbf {Top}$ be a diagram in the category of topological spaces $\mathbf {Top}$. The limit of topological spaces of $D$ is defined as the limit of sets of $D$ equipped with the limit topology. The corresponding projections $\pi_j : \lim D \to \map D j$ are defined by: $\forall j \in \II: \map {\pi_j} {\family {a_i}_{i \mathop \in \II}} := a_j$ By Equivalence of Definitions of Initial Topology the projections are continuous and thus define morphisms in $\mathbf {Top}$.

label: Definition:Lindelöf Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a Lindelöf space every open cover of $S$ has a countable subcover.

label: Definition:Line
snippet: ' This can be interpreted to mean that a line is a construct that has no thickness. This mathematical abstraction can not of course be actualised in reality because however thin you make your line, it will have some finite width. It can be considered as a continuous succession of points. The word line is frequently used to mean infinite straight line. The context ought to make it clear if this is the case.

label: Definition:Line/Curve
snippet: A curve is a line which may or may not be straight.

label: Definition:Line/Curve/Plane
snippet: A plane curve is a curve which can be embedded in the plane.

label: Definition:Line/Endpoint
snippet: Each of the points at either end of a line segment is called an endpoint of that line segment. Similarly, the point at which an infinite half-line terminates is called the endpoint of that line. '

label: Definition:Line/Infinite
snippet: An infinite line is a line which has no endpoints. Category:Definitions/Lines

label: Definition:Line/Infinite Half-Line
snippet: An infinite half-line is a line which terminates at an endpoint at one end, but has no such endpoint at the other.

label: Definition:Line/Infinite Straight Line
snippet: An infinite straight line is a straight line which has no endpoints, or equally, a straight line which is infinite. Category:Definitions/Straight Lines

label: Definition:Line/Midpoint
snippet: Let $L = AB$ be a line segment whose endpoints are $A$ and $B$. Let $M$ be a point on $L$ such that the line segment $AM$ is equal to the line segment $MB$. That is, let $M$ be the bisector of $L$. Then $M$ is the midpoint of $L$.

label: Definition:Line/Segment
snippet: A line segment is any line (straight or not) which terminates at two points.

label: Definition:Line/Straight Line Segment
snippet: A straight line segment is a line segment which is straight. A straight line segment can be drawn joining any two points. Thus a definition for straight line which is frequently encountered is: A straight line is the shortest distance between two points. This is all very well but it assumes that the line in question terminates at two particular endpoints.

label: Definition:Line of Action
snippet: Let a force $\mathbf F$ act on a rigid body $B$. In order to completely specify how $\mathbf F$ acts on $B$, it is necessary to know the point $P$ on $B$ at which $\mathbf F$ is applied. 400px The (straight) line $L$ passing through $P$ in the direction of $\mathbf F$ is known as the line of action of $\mathbf F$ on $B$.

label: Definition:Line of Best Fit
