This logically arises as its definition as the acceleration that causes a change in velocity of $1$ metre per second over the course of $1$ second. Category:Definitions/Metre per Second Squared

label: Definition:Metric/Also defined as
snippet: == Metric: Also defined as == If $\struct {A, d}$ is a pseudometric space or quasimetric space, this definition still applies. We also find that a pseudometric and a quasimetric are also both found to be categorised in the literature as metrics and distance functions.

label: Definition:Metric/Also known as
snippet: == Metric: Also known as == The metric $d$ in a metric space $\struct {A, d}$ is frequently referred to as a distance function on $A$. The two terms are used interchangeably on this website, although metric is preferred. Some sources call a metric just a distance, but that is a general term with a number of interpretations.

label: Definition:Metric Compatible Connection
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold with or without boundary. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $\map {\mathfrak X} M$ be the space of smooth vector fields on $M$. Let $\nabla$ be a connection in $TM$. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$ be the Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian scalar product.

snippet:

label: Definition:Metric Induced by Smooth Immersion
snippet: Let $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$, $\struct {M, g}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $F : M \to \tilde M$ be a smooth immersion. Suppose, the metric $g$ is such that $g = F^* \tilde g$. Then $g$ is called the metric induced by $F$.

label: Definition:Metric Invariant under Group Action
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $G$ be a group. Suppose $\forall \phi \in G$ the mapping $x \mapsto \phi \cdot x$ is an isometry. Then the metric $g$ is said to be invariant under $G$.

orm {\, \cdot \,}_\HH$ be the inner product norm. Let $C \subseteq \HH$ be a non-empty closed convex set. For each $x \in \HH$, let $\map {\pi_C} x$ be the unique point in $C$ such that: $\ds

label: Definition:Metric Space/Definition 1
snippet: A metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is an ordered pair consisting of: $(1): \quad$ a non-empty set $A$ together with: $(2): \quad$ a real-valued function $d: A \times A \to \R$ which acts on $A$, satisfying the metric space axioms:

label: Definition:Metric Space/Definition 2
snippet: A metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ is a topological space together with a metric $d$ which induces its topology.

label: Definition:Metric Space/Metric
snippet: Let $\struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. The mapping $d: A \times A \to \R$ is referred to as a metric on $A$. Here, $d: A \times A \to \R$ is a real-valued function satisfying the metric space axioms:

label: Definition:Metric Space/Notation
snippet: == Metric Space: Notation == Some authors use the suboptimal $M = \set {A, d}$, which leaves it conceptually unclear as to which is the set and which the metric. This adds unnecessary complexity to the underlying axiomatic justification for the existence of the very object that is being defined. The notation $M = \eqclass {A, \rho} {}$ can also be found.

label: Definition:Metric Space/Point
snippet: The elements of a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ are called the points of the space. Category:Definitions/Metric Spaces

label: Definition:Metric Spaces (Mathematical Branch)
snippet: Metric spaces is the branch of mathematics in which the topology on a topological space is derived from a notion of distance or metric. The notion of a metric gives rise to the treatment of convergent sequences and limits, as well as continuity of mappings. It is closely aligned with the branch of analysis.

label: Definition:Metric Subspace
snippet: Let $\struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $H \subseteq A$. Let $d_H: H \times H \to \R$ be the restriction $d \restriction_{H \times H}$ of $d$ to $H$. That is, let $\forall x, y \in H: \map {d_H} {x, y} = \map d {x, y}$. Then $d_H$ is the metric induced on $H$ by $d$ or the subspace metric of $d$ (with respect to $H$). The metric space $\struct {H, d_H}$ is called a metric subspace of $\struct {A, d}$.

label: Definition:Metric System
snippet: The metric system is the colloquial term for the system of measurement based on the metre. Its main characteristic is that its units are constructed on a decimal system.

label: Definition:Metric System/Length/Centimetre
snippet: == Centimetre == The centimetre is the CGS base unit of length.

label: Definition:Metric System/Length/Metre
snippet: == Metre == The metre is the SI base unit of length. It is defined as the distance travelled by light in vacuum in $\dfrac 1 {299 \ 792 \ 458}$ of a second.

label: Definition:Metrical Geometry
snippet: Metrical geometry is the study of points, lines, surfaces and volumes in real space, and is based on the concepts of distance and angle. It is what is usually understood in the everyday world as geometry proper.

label: Definition:Metrically Complete Connected Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a connected Riemannian manifold. Let $d_g$ be the Riemannian distance. Then $M$ is called the (metrically) complete manifold if every Cauchy sequence in $M$ converges with respect to the distance function $d_g$.

label: Definition:Metrizable Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is metrizable there exists a metric $d: S \times S \to \R_{\gt 0}$ on $S$ such that: $\tau$ is the topology induced by $d$ on $S$.

label: Definition:Metrizable Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is metrizable there exists a metric space $M = \struct{A, d}$ such that: $T$ is homeomorphic to the topological space $\struct{A, \tau_d}$ where $\tau_d$ is the topology induced by $d$ on $A$.

label: Definition:Metrizable Tangent Disc Topology
snippet: Let $A$ be a countable subset of the $x$-axis in the Cartesian plane $\R^2$. Let $P$ denote the open upper half-plane in $\R^2$. Let $S := A \cup P$. Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be the topological subspace of the Niemytzki plane. $\struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the metrizable tangent disc topology.

label: Definition:Metrizable Uniformity
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\UU$ be the uniformity on $X$ defined as: $\UU := \set {u_\epsilon: \epsilon \in \R_{>0} }$ where: $\R_{>0}$ is the set of strictly positive real numbers $u_\epsilon$ is defined as: $u_\epsilon := \set {\paren {x, y}: \map d {x, y} < \epsilon}$ Then $\UU$ is defined as metrizable.

label: Definition:Michael's Product Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ be the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $\Bbb I := \R \setminus \Q$ denote the set of irrational numbers. Let $\struct {S, \sigma} := \struct {\R, \tau^*} \times \struct {\Bbb I, \tau'}$, where: $\tau^*$ is the discrete irrational extension of $\tau_d$ by $\Bbb I$ $\tau'$ is the subspace topology on $\Bbb I$ induced by $\tau_d$. $\struct {S, \sigma}$ is referred to as Michael's product topology.

label: Definition:Midline
snippet: In the context of triangles in geometry: Definition:Median of Triangle: a straight line segment joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side Definition:Midline of Triangle: a straight line segment joining the midpoints of two sides. Category:Definitions/Triangles

label: Definition:Midline of Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. Let $D$ and $E$ be the midpoints of any two of the sides of $\triangle ABC$. The line $DE$ is a midline of $\triangle ABC$. 400px

label: Definition:Midpoint
snippet: Geometry: The midpoint of a line segment. Analysis: The midpoint of a real interval. The concepts are related in the real number line, which is a one-to-one correspondence between an infinite straight line and the set of real numbers.

label: Definition:Mile per Hour
snippet: The mile per hour is an imperial unit of speed or velocity. $1$ mile per hour is the speed at which it takes $1$ hour to travel $1$ mile.

label: Definition:Millennium Problems
snippet: The Millennium problems are a collection of seven mathematical problems stated by the on $24$ May $2000$. Each carries a prize of $\$1 \, 000 \, 000$ (US dollars). Six of them remain unsolved. They are as follows:

label: Definition:Miller's Biconnected Set
snippet: Let $C$ be a nowhere dense perfect subset of the closed unit interval $\I = \closedint 0 1$. Let $W$ be the set defined as: $W = C \times \I \subseteq \R^2$ Let $K$ be an indecomposable continuum such that: $K \cap \I^2 = W$ Let us define the space $T = \struct {X, \tau}$ using the as follows: Let $\CC$ be the set of composants of $K$. Let $\BB$ be the set of continua which separate $K$.

label: Definition:Millin Series
snippet: The Millin series is the series defined as: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac 1 {F_{2^n} }$ where $F_k$ is the $k$th Fibonacci number.

label: Definition:Minimal/Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a relational structure. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$.

label: Definition:Minimal/Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\TT \subseteq \powerset S$ be a subset of $\powerset S$. Let $\struct {\TT, \subseteq}$ be the ordered set formed on $\TT$ by $\subseteq$ considered as an ordering. Then $T \in \TT$ is a minimal set of $\TT$ $T$ is a minimal element of $\struct {\TT, \subseteq}$. That is: $\forall X \in \TT: X \subseteq T \implies X = T$

label: Definition:Minimal (Model Theory)
snippet: Let $\MM$ be an $\LL$-structure. Let $M$ be the universe of $\MM$. Let $A$ be a subset of $M$. Let $D \subseteq M^n$ be an infinite $A$-definable set. Let $\phi \left({\bar x, \bar a}\right)$ be an $\LL$-formula with parameters $\bar a$ from $A\subseteq M$ and free variables $\bar x$ which defines $D$. $D$ is minimal in $\MM$ every definable subset of $D$ is either finite or cofinite. $\phi$ is minimal in $\MM$ if $D$ is minimal in $\MM$. $D$ and $\phi$ are strongly minimal in $\MM$ $\phi$ is minimal in any elementary extension $\NN$ of $\MM$.

label: Definition:Minimal Condition/Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Then $S$ satisfies the minimal condition $\preccurlyeq$ is well-founded: Every non-empty subset has a minimal element.

label: Definition:Minimal Condition/Submodule Ordering
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be an $A$-module. Let $\struct {D, \supseteq}$ be the set of submodules of $M$ ordered by the subset relation. Then the hypothesis: Every non-empty subset of $D$ has a minimal element is called the minimal condition on submodules.

label: Definition:Minimal Condition/Subset Ordering
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $F$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Let $F$ be ordered by the subset relation. Then $S$ satisfies the minimal condition on $F$ $F$ satisfies the minimal condition.

label: Definition:Minimal Element/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a relational structure. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. An element $x \in T$ is a minimal element (under $\RR$) of $T$ : $\forall y \in T: y \mathrel \RR x \implies x = y$

snippet:

eg \exists y \in T: y \mathrel {\RR^
e} x$ where $y \mathrel {\RR^
e} x$ denotes that $y \mathrel \RR x$ but $y 
e x$.

label: Definition:Minimal Hausdorff Topology
snippet: neighborhood bases of $a$ and $-a$]] Let $\omega$ be the first transfinite ordinal. Let $\struct {A, \tau_1}$ denote the totally ordered set defined as: $A := \set {1, 2, 3, \ldots, \omega, \ldots, -3, -2, -1}$ with the interval topology $\tau_1$. Let $\struct {\Z_{>0}, \tau_2}$ denote the (strictly) positive integers with the discrete topology $\tau_2$. Let $S$ be defined as: $S = A \times \Z_{>0} \cup \set {a, -a}$ where $a$ and $-a$ are new elements of $S$.

label: Definition:Minimal Length Path
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a simple graph. Let $u, v \in V$ be vertices of $G$. Let $W$ be the set of all open paths between $u$ and $v$. An open path $p \in W$ is a minimal length path from $u$ to $v$ : there exists no path $q$ beginning at $u$ and ending at $v$ such that the length of $q$ is (strictly) less than the length of $p$.

label: Definition:Minimal Polynomial
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. Let $\alpha \in L$ be algebraic over $K$.

label: Definition:Minimal Polynomial of Square Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix of order $n$. The minimal polynomial $m$ of $\mathbf A$ is the monic polynomial of smallest degree such that: $\map m {\mathbf A} = \mathbf 0$ where $\mathbf 0$ is the zero matrix of order $n$.

label: Definition:Minimal Prime
snippet: Let $b \in \N_{>1}$ be a natural number. A minimal prime base $b$ is a prime number whose base-$b$ representation has no proper subsequence which is also a prime number. If $b$ is not specified, then decimal notation (that is, base $10$) is assumed.

label: Definition:Minimal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $M \le G$ be a non-trivial subgroup of $G$. Then $M$ is a minimal subgroup of $G$ : For every subgroup $H$ of $G$, $H \subseteq M$ means $H = M$ or $H = \set e$. That is, there is no subgroup of $M$, except $M$ and $\set e$ itself, which is a subset of $M$.

label: Definition:Minimal Topology
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\powerset S$ be the power set of $S$. Let $\Theta_S$ be the set of all topologies on $S$: $\Theta_S = \leftset {\tau \in \powerset S: \tau}$ is a topology on $\rightset S$ Let $\Phi: \Theta_S \to \set {\T, \F}$ be a propositional function on $\Theta_S$. Let $\vartheta \in \Theta_S$ have the property that $\map \Phi \vartheta$ and: $\forall \tau \in \Theta_S: \map \Phi \tau \implies \vartheta \subseteq \tau$ That is, $\vartheta$ is the coarsest topology on $S$ which satisfies the propositional function $\Phi$. Then $\vartheta$ is the minimal topology satisfying $\Phi$.

label: Definition:Minimal Uncountable Well-Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\Omega$ be an uncountable well-ordered set. Then $\Omega$ is the minimal uncountable well-ordered set every initial segment in $\Omega$ is countable.

label: Definition:Minimally Inductive Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be an inductive set. The minimally inductive set $\omega$ is the inductive set given by: $\ds \omega := \bigcap \set {S' \subseteq S: S' \text{ is an inductive set} }$ that is, $\omega$ is the intersection of every inductive set which is a subset of $S$.

label: Definition:Minimally Inductive Set/Definition 2
snippet: The minimally inductive set $\omega$ is defined as the set of all finite ordinals: $\omega := \set {\alpha: \alpha \text{ is a finite ordinal} }$

label: Definition:Minimally Inductive Set/Definition 3
snippet: The minimally inductive set $\omega$ is defined as: $\omega := \set {x \in \On: \paren {x \cup \set x} \subseteq K_I}$ where: $K_I$ is the class of all non-limit ordinals $\On$ is the class of all ordinals.

label: Definition:Minimizing Curve on Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $L_g$ be the Riemannian length. Let $S$ be the set of all admissible curves in $M$ with same endpoints $p_i, p_f \in M$. Let $\gamma_{min} \in S$ be such that: $\forall \tilde \gamma \in S : \map {L_g} {\gamma_{min}} \le \map {L_g} {\tilde \gamma}$. Then $\gamma_{min}$ is called the minimizing curve.

label: Definition:Minimum Value of Functional
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of mappings. Let $y, \hat y \in S: \R \to \R$ be real functions. Let $J \sqbrk y: S \to \R$ be a functional. Let $J$ have a (relative) extremum for $y = \hat y$. Let $J \sqbrk y - J \sqbrk {\hat y} \ge 0$ in the neighbourhood of $y = \hat y$. Then this extremum is called the minimum of the functional $J$.

label: Definition:Minimum Value of Real Function/Absolute
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Let $f$ be bounded below by an infimum $B$. It may or may not be the case that $\exists x \in \R: \map f x = B$. If such a value exists, it is called the (absolute) minimum of $f$ on $S$, and this absolute minimum is attained at $x$.

label: Definition:Minimum Value of Real Function/Local
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function defined on an open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi \in \openint a b$. Then $f$ has a local minimum at $\xi$ : $\exists \openint c d \subseteq \openint a b: \forall x \in \openint c d: \map f x \ge \map f \xi$ That is, there is some subinterval on which $f$ attains a minimum within that interval.

label: Definition:Minkowski Functional
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a vector space over $\GF$. Let $A \subseteq X$ be a convex absorbing subset of $X$. The Minkowski functional of $A$ is the real-valued function $\mu_A : X \to \closedint 0 \infty$ defined as: $\forall x \in X: \map {\mu_A} x = \inf \set {t > 0 : \dfrac x t \in A}$

label: Definition:Minkowski Functional/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $C$ be an open convex subset of $X$ with $0 \in C$. The Minkowski functional of $C$ is the mapping $p_C : X \to \hointr 0 \infty$ defined as: $\forall x \in X: \map {p_C} x = \inf \set {t > 0 : \dfrac x t \in C}$

label: Definition:Minkowski Spacetime/Also known as
snippet: == Minkowski Spacetime: Also known as == Minkowski spacetime can also be seen rendered hyphenated, that is, as Minkowski space-time. Other terms that can be found for the same concept: Minkowskian space-time Minkowski space Minkowski world Minkowski universe $\paren {r + 1}$-dimensional Minkowski space

label: Definition:Minkowski Spacetime/Definition 1
snippet: Minkowski spacetime is the pseudo-Euclidean space $\R^{r, 1}$.

label: Definition:Minkowski Spacetime/Definition 2
snippet: Minkowski spacetime is a $4$-dimensional model of physical space and time: $3$ of those dimensions correspond to the position of an event in space the remaining dimension represents the time of that event.

label: Definition:Minkowski Spacetime/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Minkowski Spacetime == realised that the two postulates of the Special Theory of Relativity require space and time to be treated not as separate entitiies, but as a unified $4$-dimensional concept, referred to as spacetime. Hence (Minkowski) spacetime became the frame of all later extensions of the theory of relativity.

label: Definition:Minkowski Sum
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. Let $A, B$ be two subsets of $V$. Then the Minkowski sum of $A$ and $B$, denoted as $A + B$, is defined as: $A + B := \set {a + b: a \in A, b \in B}$ where the operation $+$ is vector addition. The Minkowski sum is therefore a relation in the power set of $V$ in the sense that it is a mapping: $+: \powerset V^2 \to \powerset V$ Category:Definitions/Linear Algebra

label: Definition:Minor
snippet: Euclidean Number Theory: Minor (Euclidean) Geometry: Minor Axis of Ellipse Semiminor Axis of Ellipse Minor Axis of Hyperbola Categorical Syllogisms: Minor Premise of Syllogism Linear Algebra Minor of Determinant

label: Definition:Minor (Euclidean)
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ in the forms: $a = \dfrac \rho {\sqrt 2} \sqrt {1 + \dfrac k {\sqrt {1 + k^2} } }$ $b = \dfrac \rho {\sqrt 2} \sqrt {1 - \dfrac k {\sqrt {1 + k^2} } }$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a - b$ is a minor.

label: Definition:Minor Arc
snippet: Let $a$ and $b$ be points on the boundary $\BB$ of a simple closed curve $\CC$ in the plane. Let $a$ and $b$ divide $\BB$ into unequal parts. The shorter of the arcs described by $a$ and $b$ is referred to as the minor arc of $\BB$.

label: Definition:Minor Arc/Also known as
snippet: == Minor Arc: Also known as == The minor arc of a simple closed curve two points is also known as the short arc.

label: Definition:Minor Axis of Ellipse/Definition 1
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$ whose foci are $F_1$ and $F_2$. The minor axis of $K$ is the line segment through the center of $K$ perpendicular to the major axis of $K$ such that its endpoints are the points of intersection with $K$. In the above diagram, $C_1 C_2$ is the minor axis of $K$.

label: Definition:Minor Axis of Ellipse/Definition 2
snippet: 500px Consider an ellipse $K$ whose foci are $F_1$ and $F_2$. The minor axis of $K$ is the diameter of $K$ which has the smallest length. In the above diagram, $C_1 C_2$ is the minor axis of $K$.

label: Definition:Minor of Determinant
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_n$ be a square matrix of order $n$. Consider the order $k$ square submatrix $\mathbf B$ obtained by deleting $n - k$ rows and $n - k$ columns from $\mathbf A$. Let $\map \det {\mathbf B}$ denote the determinant of $\mathbf B$. Then $\map \det {\mathbf B}$ is an order-$k$ minor of $\map \det {\mathbf A}$. Thus a minor is a determinant formed from the elements (in the same relative order) of $k$ specified rows and columns.

label: Definition:Mirror Property of Primes
snippet: Let $p_n$ denote the $n$th prime number. Let $\map {\operatorname {rev} } {p_n}$ denote the reversal of $p_n$. $p_n$ satisfies the mirror property : $(1): \quad \map {\operatorname {rev} } {p_n}$ is also a prime number $(2): \quad$ the product of the digits of the base $10$ representation of $\map {\operatorname {rev} } {p_n}$ equals $\map {\operatorname {rev} } n$.

label: Definition:Miscellaneous Volume Measure/Cord
snippet: The cord is a unit of volume traditionally used for or . Thus a cord is a quantity of wood that can be stacked in a woodpile $4$ feet long, $8$ feet wide, and $4$ feet high. Category:Definitions/Volume

label: Definition:Mixed Decimal
snippet: A mixed decimal is a number consisting of a non-zero integer together with a decimal fraction.

label: Definition:Mixed Tensor
snippet: Let $V$ and $V^*$ be a vector space and its algebraic dual. Then a (mixed) tensor $F$ of type $\tuple {k, l}$ is a multilinear map such that: $F : \underbrace {V \times \ldots \times V}_{\text {$k$ times} } \times \underbrace { {V^*} \times \ldots \times {V^*} }_{\text {$l$ times} } \to \R$

label: Definition:Modal Class
snippet: Let $\mathsf C_1, \mathsf C_2, \cdots, \mathsf C_n$ be class intervals of data. Let $N_1, N_2, \ldots, N_n$ denote the frequency of each of $\mathsf C_1, \mathsf C_2, \cdots, \mathsf C_n$ respectively. The modal class is the class interval $\mathsf C_j$ for which $N_j$ is the greatest. The modal class is not necessarily unique for a given set of data.

label: Definition:Modal Logic
snippet: Modal logic is a branch of logic in which truth values are more complex than being merely true or false, and which distinguishes between different "modes" of truth. There are two operators in classical modal logic, defined for some proposition $P$ dependent on some world $w$: $(1): \quad$ Necessity, represented by $\nec$, defined by: $\nec P : \iff \forall w: \map P w$ $(2): \quad$ Possibility, represented by $\pos$, defined by: $\pos P: \iff \exists w: \map P w$ Modal logic may also have other operators, including: Temporal logic, which uses several operators including present and future…

label: Definition:Modal Operator
snippet: The modal operators are the operators in modal logic defined as follows:

label: Definition:Modal Operator/Necessity
snippet: The necessity operator $\nec$ is the unary modal operator defined for some proposition $P$ dependent on some world $w$: $\nec P : \iff \forall w: \map P w$

label: Definition:Modal Operator/Possibility
snippet: The possibility operator $\pos$ is the unary modal operator defined for some proposition $P$ dependent on some world $w$: $\pos P : \iff \exists w: \map P w$

label: Definition:Modal Proposition
snippet: A modal proposition is a statement in modal logic: It is possible that $A$ is true.

label: Definition:Mode
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of quantitative data. The mode of $S$ is the element of $S$ which occurs most often in $S$. If there is more than one such element of $S$ which occurs equally most often, it is then understood that each of these is a mode. If there is no element of $S$ which occurs more often (in the extreme case, all elements are equal) then $S$ has no mode.

label: Definition:Mode of Continuous Random Variable
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $X$ have probability density function $f_X$. We call $M$ a mode of $X$ if $f_X$ attains its (global) maximum at $M$. Category:Definitions/Probability Theory Category:Definitions/Modes

label: Definition:Model
snippet: Logic: Model (Logic) Model (Predicate Logic) Applied Mathematics: Mathematical Model

label: Definition:Model (Logic)/Set of Logical Formulas
snippet: Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for a logical language $\LL$. Let $\MM$ be a structure of $\mathscr M$. Let $\FF$ be a set of logical formulas of $\LL$. Then $\MM$ is a model of $\FF$ : $\MM \models_{\mathscr M} \phi$ for every $\phi \in \FF$ that is, it is a model of every logical formula $\phi \in \FF$.

label: Definition:Model (Predicate Logic)
snippet: Let $\LL_1$ be the language of predicate logic. Let $\AA$ be a structure for predicate logic. Then $\AA$ models a sentence $\mathbf A$ : $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\mathbf A} = \T$ where $\map {\operatorname{val}_\AA} {\mathbf A}$ denotes the value of $\mathbf A$ in $\AA$. This relationship is denoted: $\AA \models_{\mathrm{PL} } \mathbf A$ When pertaining to a collection of sentences $\FF$, one says $\AA$ models $\FF$ : $\forall \mathbf A \in \FF: \AA \models_{\mathrm{PL} } \mathbf A$ that is, it models all elements of $\FF$.

label: Definition:Model Theory
snippet: Model theory is a sub-branch of mathematical logic which studies mathematical structures by means of formal semantics for formal languages.

label: Definition:Model Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Model Theory == Historically, the greatest amount of research in model theory has focused on model theory for predicate logic. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Model Theory for Predicate Logic
snippet: Model theory for predicate logic is the sub-branch of model theory that focuses on predicate logic. In particular, the formal semantics of structures for predicate logic is studied.

label: Definition:Model of Class-Set Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a collection of objects. Then $V$ is a model of class-set theory it satisfies the axioms of Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel set theory. Thus: The elements of $V$ are then known as sets The subcollections of $V$ are known as classes.

label: Definition:Model of Rational Choice
snippet: A model of rational choice for a player in a game consists of: $(1): \quad$ A set $A$ of moves from which the player may choose $(2): \quad$ A set $C$ of consequences of each of those moves $(3): \quad$ A consequence function $g: A \to C$ which maps a consequence to each action $(4): \quad$ A preference relation $\succsim$, which is a total ordering on $C$.

label: Definition:Modification of Stochastic Process
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {E, \mathcal E}$ be a measurable space. Let $\sequence {X_i}_{i \in I}$ and $\sequence {\widetilde X_i}_{i \in I}$ be $E$-valued stochastic processes. We say that $\sequence {\widetilde X_i}_{i \in I}$ is a modification of $\sequence {X_i}_{i \in I}$ : $\widetilde X_i = X_i$ almost surely for each $i \in I$.

label: Definition:Modified Fort Space
snippet: Let $N$ be an infinite set. Let $\set a$ and $\set b$ be singleton sets such that $a \ne b$ and $a, b \notin N$. Let $S = N \cup \set a \cup \set b$. Let $\tau_{a, b}$ be the set of subsets of $S$ defined as: $\tau_{a, b} = \set {H \subseteq N} \cup \set {H \subseteq S: \paren {a \in H \lor b \in H} \land N \setminus H \text { is finite} }$ That is, a subset $H$ of $S$ is in $\tau_{a, b}$ either of the following hold: Then $\tau_{a, b}$ is a modified Fort topology on $a$ and $b$, and the topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau_{a, b} }$ is a modified Fort space.

label: Definition:Module Defined by Ring Homomorphism
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be a rings. Let $f: A \to B$ be a ring homomorphism.

label: Definition:Module Endomorphism
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. A module endomorphism of $M$ is a module homomorphism from $M$ to itself.

label: Definition:Module Theory
snippet: Module theory is the branch of abstract algebra which studies modules.

label: Definition:Module of All Mappings
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {M, +_M, \ast}_R$ be an $R$-module. Let $S$ be a set. Let $M^S$ be the set of all mappings from $S$ to $M$. Let: $+$ be the operation induced on $M^S$ by $+_M$ $\forall \lambda \in R: \forall f \in M^S: \forall x \in S: \map {\paren {\lambda \ast f} } x = \lambda \ast \paren {\map f x}$ Then $\struct {M^S, +, \ast}_R$ is the module of all mappings from $S$ to $M$.

label: Definition:Module over Group
snippet: Let $\struct {V, +, \cdot}$ be a vector space over a field $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$. Let $G$ be a group. Let $\phi : G \times V \to V$ be a linear group action of $G$ on $V$, either: a left linear group action: $\phi : G \times V \to V$ or a right linear group action: $\phi : V \times G \to V$ Then $\struct {V, \phi}$ is called a module over $G$, either a left module or a right module respectively.

label: Definition:Module over Group/Left
snippet: Let $\struct {V, +, \cdot}$ be a vector space over a field $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$. Let $G$ be a group. Let $\phi : G \times V \to V$ be a left linear group action of $G$ on $V$. Then $\struct {V, \phi}$ is called a left module over $G$.

label: Definition:Module over Group/Right
snippet: Let $\struct {V, +, \cdot}$ be a vector space over a field $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$. Let $G$ be a group. Let $\phi : V \times G \to V$ be a right linear group action of $G$ on $V$. Then $\struct {V, \phi}$ is called a right module over $G$.

label: Definition:Module over Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. A module over $R$ is an $R$-algebraic structure $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ with one operation $\ast$ which is either a left module or a right module, depending upon whether $\ast$ is defined as: $\ast: R \times G \to G$ or: $\ast: G \times R \to G$ respectively. As follows:

label: Definition:Module over Ring/Also defined as
snippet: == Module over Ring: Also defined as == Sources which deal only with rings with unity often define a module as what on is called a unitary module. Sometimes no distinction is made between the module and the associated ring representation. The word module can also be seen in some older works to mean vector magnitude or vector length. Category:Definitions/Modules over Rings

label: Definition:Module over Ring/Left and Right Modules
snippet: == Left Modules and Right Modules == In the case where the scalar ring is a commutative ring, the difference between a left module and a right module is little more than a notational difference. See: Left Module over Commutative Ring induces Right Module Right Module over Commutative Ring induces Left Module. But this is not the case for a scalar ring that is not commutative.

label: Definition:Moduli Space
snippet: A moduli space is a set of all solutions to certain nonlinear differential equations.

label: Definition:Modulo Addition/Definition 1
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {\eqclass 0 m, \eqclass 1 m, \ldots, \eqclass {m - 1} m}$ where $\eqclass x m$ is the residue class of $x$ modulo $m$. The operation of addition modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $\eqclass a m +_m \eqclass b m = \eqclass {a + b} m$

label: Definition:Modulo Addition/Definition 2
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ The operation of addition modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $\forall a, b \in \Z_m: a +_m b$ equals the remainder after $a + b$ has been divided by $m$

label: Definition:Modulo Addition/Definition 3
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ The operation of addition modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $a +_m b := a + b - k m$ where $k$ is the largest integer such that $k m \le a + b$.

label: Definition:Modulo Arithmetic
snippet: Modulo arithmetic is the branch of abstract algebra which studies the residue class of integers under a modulus. As such it can also be considered to be a branch of number theory.

label: Definition:Modulo Division
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ The operation of division modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $a \div_m b$ equals the integer $q \in \Z_m$ such that $b \times_m q \equiv a \pmod m$ and is possible only if $q$ is unique modulo $m$. This happens $a$ and $m$ are coprime.

label: Definition:Modulo Division/Divisor
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ For all $a, b \in \Z_m$, let $a \div_m b$ denote the operation of division modulo $m$: $a \div_m b$ equals the integer $q \in \Z_m$ such that $b \times_m q \equiv a \pmod m$ The integers $b$ and $q$ are divisors of $a$ modulo $m$.

label: Definition:Modulo Division/Polynomials
snippet: Let $\map f x$ and $\map g x$ be integral polynomials. The operation of polynomial division modulo $m$ is defined as: $\map f x \div_m \map g x$ equals the integral polynomial $\map h x$ such that: $\map g x \times_m \map h x \equiv \map f x \pmod m$ where: $m \in \Z$ is an integer $\equiv$ means that the respective coefficients are congruent modulo $m$ provided such a polynomial exists.

label: Definition:Modulo Multiplication/Also denoted as
snippet: == Modulo Multiplication: Also denoted as == Although the operation of multiplication modulo $m$ is denoted by the symbol $\times_m$, if there is no danger of confusion, the conventional multiplication symbols $\times, \cdot$ etc. are often used instead. The notation for multiplication of two integers modulo $m$ is not usually $\eqclass a m \times_m \eqclass b m$. What is more normally seen is $a b \pmod m$. Category:Definitions/Modulo Multiplication

label: Definition:Modulo Multiplication/Definition 1
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {\eqclass 0 m, \eqclass 1 m, \ldots, \eqclass {m - 1} m}$ where $\eqclass x m$ is the residue class of $x$ modulo $m$. The operation of multiplication modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $\eqclass a m \times_m \eqclass b m = \eqclass {a b} m$

label: Definition:Modulo Multiplication/Definition 2
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ The operation of multiplication modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $a \times_m b$ equals the remainder after $a b$ has been divided by $m$.

label: Definition:Modulo Multiplication/Definition 3
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {0, 1, \ldots, m - 1}$ The operation of multiplication modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $a \times_m b := a b - k m$ where $k$ is the largest integer such that $k m \le a b$.

label: Definition:Modulo Operation
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Then the modulo operation is defined and denoted as: $x \bmod y := \begin{cases} x - y \floor {\dfrac x y} & : y \ne 0 \\ x & : y = 0 \end{cases}$ where $\floor {\, \cdot \,}$ denotes the floor function.

label: Definition:Modulo Operation/Modulo One
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Let the modulo operation $\bmod$ be defined as: $x \bmod y := \begin{cases} x - y \floor {\dfrac x y} & : y \ne 0 \\ x & : y = 0 \end{cases}$ Then: $x \bmod 1 = x - \floor x$ from which it follows directly that: $x = \floor x + \paren {x \bmod 1}$

label: Definition:Modulo Operation/Modulo Zero
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers. Let the modulo operation $\bmod$ be defined as: $x \bmod y := \begin {cases} x - y \floor {\dfrac x y} & : y \ne 0 \\ x & : y = 0 \end {cases}$ Then: $\forall x \in \R: x \bmod 0 = x$ This can be considered as a special case of the modulo operation, but it is interesting to note that most of the results concerning the modulo operation still hold.

label: Definition:Modulo Polynomial Division/Divisor
snippet: Let $\map f x$ and $\map g x$ be integral polynomials. Let $\map f x \div_m \map g x$ denote the operation of polynomial division modulo $m$: $\map f x \div_m \map g x$ equals the integral polynomial $\map h x$ such that: $\map g x \times_m \map h x \equiv \map f x \pmod m$ The polynomials $\map g x$ and $\map h x$ are (polynomial) divisors of $\map f x$ modulo $m$.

label: Definition:Modulo Subtraction
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$: $\Z_m = \set {\eqclass 0 m, \eqclass 1 m, \ldots, \eqclass {m - 1} m}$ where $\eqclass x m$ is the residue class of $x$ modulo $m$. The operation of subtraction modulo $m$ is defined on $\Z_m$ as: $\eqclass a m -_m \eqclass b m = \eqclass {a - b} m$

label: Definition:Modulus
snippet: Algebra and Real Analysis: The absolute value $\size x$ of a real number $x$. Modulus of a Multiindex: The modulus of a multiindex $k = \sequence {k_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ is defined as $\ds \size k = \sum_{j \mathop \in J} k_j$ Complex Analysis: Modulus of Complex Number: the length of a complex number when drawn as a vector on the complex plane. Modulus of Complex-Valued Function: The real-valued function $\size f$ obtained by taking the (complex) modulus of all the values of the complex-valued function $f$.

label: Definition:Modulus (Geometric Function Theory)
snippet: In geometric function theory, the term modulus is used to denote certain conformal invariants of configurations or curve families. More precisely, the modulus of a curve family $\Gamma$ is the reciprocal of its extremal length: $\mod \Gamma := \dfrac 1 {\map \lambda \Gamma}$

label: Definition:Modulus of Element of C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $a \in A$. From Product of Element of C*-Algebra with its Star is Positive, $a^\ast a$ is positive. Hence we can consider the square root $\paren {a^\ast a}^{1/2}$. We define the modulus $\cmod a$ of $a$ by: $\cmod a = \paren {a^\ast a}^{1/2}$

label: Definition:Moment (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable on some probability space. Let $a$ be a real number. Then the $n$th moment of $X$ about $a$, usually denoted $\map {\mu_n} a$, is defined as: $\map {\mu_n} a = \expect {\paren {X - a}^n}$ where $\expect X$ denotes the expectation of $X$.

label: Definition:Moment Generating Function
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable. Then the moment generating function of $X$ is defined and denoted as: $\map {M_X} t = \expect {e^{t X} }$ for all $t$ such that this expectation exists.

label: Definition:Moment of Couple
snippet: Let $C$ be a couple composed of the forces $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2$. The moment of $C$ is a vector given by: $\mathbf M = \mathbf F_1 \times \mathbf d$ where: $\mathbf F_1$ is one of the forces that compose $C$ $\mathbf d$ is the displacement from $\mathbf F_1$ to $\mathbf F_2$. Hence: the line of action of $\mathbf M$ is perpendicular to the plane containing $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2$ the magnitude of $\mathbf M$ is equal to $F d$, where: $F$ is the magnitude of $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2$ $d$ is the magnitude of $\mathbf d$.

label: Definition:Moment of Inertia/Continuous
snippet: Let $B$ be a rigid body which is rotating in space about some axis $\LL$. Let each point in $B$ have: a position vector $\mathbf r$ a given frame of reference. a density $\map \rho {\mathbf r}$ a perpendicular distance $\map p {\mathbf r}$ from $\LL$ The moment of inertia of $B$ about $\LL$ is given by: $I := \ds \int_B \paren {\map p {\mathbf r} }^2 \map \rho {\mathbf r} \rd V$ where $\d V$ is an infinitesimal volume element of $B$.

label: Definition:Moment of Inertia/Discrete
snippet: Let $B$ be a rigid body which is rotating in space about some axis $\LL$. Let $B$ be composed of a countable number of particles $P_1, P_2, \ldots$ such that: each $P_i$ has mass $m_i$ each $P_i$ has perpendicular distance $r_i$ from $\LL$. The moment of inertia of $B$ about $\LL$ is given by: $I := \ds \sum m_i {r_i}^2$

label: Definition:Moment of Mass
snippet: Let $B$ be a particle Let $\PP$ be a point, a straight line or a plane. The moment of mass of $B$ $\PP$ is defined as the mass of $B$ multiplied by the distance from $B$ to $\PP$.

label: Definition:Monic Polynomial
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$. Let $f \in R \sqbrk x$ be a polynomial in one variable over $R$. Then $f$ is monic $f$ is nonzero and its leading coefficient is $1_R$. Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {S, +, \circ}$ be a subring of $R$. Let $\ds f = \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n a_k \circ x^k$ be a polynomial in $x$ over $S$. Then $f$ is a monic polynomial its leading coefficient $a_n$ is $1_R$.

label: Definition:Monochromatic Graph
snippet: A monochromatic graph is a colored graph (either vertex-colored or edge-colored, depending on the context) in which each of the vertices or edges is assigned the same color. Category:Definitions/Graph Colorings Category:Definitions/Ramsey Theory

label: Definition:Monoid
snippet: A monoid is a semigroup with an identity element.

label: Definition:Monoid/Also known as
snippet: == Monoid: Also known as == Some treatments of group theory and abstract algebra do not introduce the term monoid, but simply discuss semigroups which happen to have an identity element. Some sources present the monoid as $\struct {S, \circ, e_S}$ in order to place emphasis on the identity element, but this approach is not endorsed on as it complicates notation to little advantage. Category:Definitions/Monoids

label: Definition:Monoid Automorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid. Let $\phi: S \to S$ be a (monoid) isomorphism from $S$ to itself. Then $\phi$ is a monoid automorphism.

label: Definition:Monoid Category
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid with identity $e_S$. One can interpret $\struct {S, \circ}$ as being a category, with: {{DefineCategory | ob = Only one, say $*$ | mor = $a: * \to *$, for all $a \in S$ | comp = $a \circ b: * \to *$ is defined using the operation $\circ$ of the monoid $S$ | id = $\operatorname{id}_* := e_S: * \to *$ }} The category that so arises is called a monoid category.

label: Definition:Monoid Endomorphism
snippet: Let $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ be a monoid. Let $\phi: S \to S$ be a (monoid) homomorphism from $S$ to itself. Then $\phi$ is a monoid endomorphism.

label: Definition:Monoid Epimorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {T, *}$ be monoids. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a (monoid) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a monoid epimorphism $\phi$ is a surjection.

label: Definition:Monoid Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {T, *}$ be monoids. Let $\phi: S \to T$ be a mapping such that $\circ$ has the morphism property under $\phi$. That is, $\forall a, b \in S$: $\map \phi {a \circ b} = \map \phi a * \map \phi b$ Suppose further that $\phi$ preserves identities, that is: $\map \phi {e_S} = e_T$ Then $\phi: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, *}$ is a monoid homomorphism.

label: Definition:Monoid Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\struct {G, *}$ be a monoid. Let $R^{\paren G}$ be the free $R$-module on $G$. Let $\set {e_g: g \in G}$ be its canonical basis. By Multilinear Mapping from Free Modules is Determined by Bases, there exists a unique bilinear map: $\circ: R^{\paren G} \times R^{\paren G} \to R^{\paren G}$ which satisfies: $e_g \circ e_h = e_{g \mathop * h}$ Then $R \sqbrk G = \struct {R^{\paren G}, +, \circ}$ is called the monoid ring of $G$ over $R$.

label: Definition:Monoid Ring/Canonical Mapping
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $\struct {G, *}$ be a monoid with identity element $1$. Let $R \sqbrk G$ be the monoid ring of $G$ over $R$. Let $e_1$ be the canonical basis element. The canonical mapping to $R \sqbrk G$ is the mapping $R \to R \sqbrk G$ which sends $r$ to $r * e_1$.

label: Definition:Monomial/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Monomial == Because the word monomial derives ultimately from the late Latin word binomium (binomial), by changing the prefix bi (two in Latin), it should theoretically be mononomial. Monomial is a syncope by haplology of mononomial. The word [https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mononomial mononomial] does exist in English: it means having a single name. Category:Linguistic Notes

label: Definition:Monomial of Free Commutative Monoid
snippet: A monomial in the indexed set $\family {X_j: j \in J}$ is a possibly infinite product: $\ds \prod_{j \mathop \in J} X_j^{k_j}$ with integer exponents $k_j \ge 0$ such that $k_j = 0$ for all but finitely many $j$. Let $\mathbf X = \family {X_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ and for a multiindex $k = \paren {k_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ over $J$ define: $\ds \mathbf X^k = \prod_{j \mathop \in J} X_j^{k_j}$ Then a monomial is an object of the form $\mathbf X^k$, where $k$ is a multiindex.

label: Definition:Monomial of Polynomial Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity.

label: Definition:Monomial of Polynomial Ring/Multiple Variables
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be a set. Let $R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$ be a polynomial ring in $I$ variables $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$. Let $y \in R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$. A monomial of $R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$ is an element that is a product of variables; specifically:

label: Definition:Monomial of Polynomial Ring/Multiple Variables/Definition 1
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be a set. Let $R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$ be a polynomial ring in $I$ variables $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$. Let $y \in R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$. The element $y$ is a monomial of $R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$ there exists a mapping $a: I \to \N$ with finite support such that: $y = \ds \prod_{i \mathop \in I} X_i^{a_i}$ where: $\prod$ denotes the product with finite support over $I$ $X_i^{a_i}$ denotes the $a_i$th power of $X_i$.

label: Definition:Monomial of Polynomial Ring/Multiple Variables/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be a set. Let $R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$ be a polynomial ring in $I$ variables $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$. Let $y \in R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$. The element $y$ is a monomial of $R \sqbrk {\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I} }$ there exists a finite set $S$ and a mapping $f: S \to \set {X_i : i \in I}$ such that it equals $y = \ds \prod_{s \mathop \in S} \map f s$ where $\prod$ denotes the product over the finite set $S$.

label: Definition:Monomino
snippet: A monomino is a $1$-omino: 100px That is, it is a polyomino consisting of exactly $1$ unit square.

label: Definition:Monomorphism (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: A homomorphism which is an injection is descibed as monic, or called a monomorphism.

label: Definition:Monomorphism (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. A monomorphism is a morphism $f \in \mathbf C_1$ such that: $f \circ g = f \circ h \implies g = h$ for all morphisms $g, h \in \mathbf C_1$ for which these compositions are defined. That is, a monomorphism is a morphism which is left cancellable. One writes $f: C \rightarrowtail D$ to denote that $f$ is a monomorphism.

label: Definition:Monotone
snippet: Mappings: Monotone (Order Theory): A mapping from one ordered set to another is monotone it is either increasing or decreasing. Monotone (Measure Theory): A mapping $f: \SS \to \R$ on an algebra of sets $\SS$ is monotone $A \subseteq B \iff \map f A \le \map f B$. Monotone class: A collection of subsets closed under countable intersections and unions. Monotone Galois connection In all cases, the sense is one of changing always in the same direction.

label: Definition:Monotone (Order Theory)/Sequence
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a totally ordered set. A sequence $\sequence {a_k}_{k \mathop \in A}$ of elements of $S$ is monotone it is either increasing or decreasing.

label: Definition:Monotone Basis
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a Schauder basis for $X$. We say that $\sequence {e_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a monotone basis its basis constant is $1$.

label: Definition:Monotone Class
snippet: Let $X$ be a set, and let $\powerset X$ be its power set. Let $\MM \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Then $\MM$ is said to be a monotone class (on $X$) for every countable, nonempty, index set $I$, it holds that: $\ds \family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I} \in \MM \implies \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} A_i \in \MM$ $\ds \family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I} \in \MM \implies \bigcap_{i \mathop \in I} A_i \in \MM$ that is, $\MM$ is closed under countable unions and countable intersections.

label: Definition:Monotone Class Generated by Collection of Subsets
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\GG \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. Then the monotone class generated by $\GG$, $\map {\mathfrak m} \GG$, is the smallest monotone class on $X$ that contains $\GG$. That is, $\map {\mathfrak m} \GG$ is subject to: $(1): \quad \GG \subseteq \map {\mathfrak m} \GG$ $(2): \quad \GG \subseteq \MM \implies \map {\mathfrak m} \GG \subseteq \MM$ for any monotone class $\MM$ on $X$

label: Definition:Monotone Sequence of Sets
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\SS \subseteq \powerset X$ be a collection of subsets of $X$. A monotone sequence of sets (in $\SS$) is a sequence $\sequence {A_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $\SS$, such that either: $\forall n \in \N: A_n \subseteq A_{n + 1}$ or: $\forall n \in \N: A_n \supseteq A_{n + 1}$ That is, such that $\sequence {A_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is either increasing or decreasing

label: Definition:Monte Carlo Method
snippet: A Monte Carlo method is a technique in statistics for investigating mathematical properties by repeated experiments a large number of times. This is useful when an analytic solution is difficult to obtain.

label: Definition:Moon
snippet: The moon is the single natural satellite of Earth.

label: Definition:Moore-Penrose Conditions
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$ over the complex numbers $\C$. The Moore-Penrose conditions are a set of criteria to determine whether a matrix $\mathbf X$ of order $n \times m$ is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $\mathbf A$: {{axiom | n = 3 | ml= \mathbf A \mathbf X | mo= = | mr= \paren {\mathbf A \mathbf X}^* }} {{axiom | n = 4 | ml= \mathbf X \mathbf A | mo= = | mr= \paren {\mathbf X \mathbf A}^* }} where $\mathbf A^*$ denotes the Hermitian conjugate of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$ over the complex numbers $\C$.

label: Definition:Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$ where $m \ne n$ over the complex numbers $\C$. The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $\mathbf A$ is the unique $n \times m$ matrix $\mathbf A^+$ defined as: $\mathbf A^+ = \begin {cases} \paren {\mathbf A^\intercal \mathbf A}^{-1} \mathbf A^\intercal & : m > n \\ \mathbf A^\intercal \paren {\mathbf A \mathbf A^\intercal}^{-1} & : n < m \end {cases}$ where $\mathbf A^\intercal$ denotes the transpose of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Moore-Penrose Pseudoinverse/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$ over the complex numbers $\C$. The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse of $\mathbf A$ is the unique $n \times m$ matrix $A^+$ which satisfies the four Moore-Penrose conditions: where $\mathbf A^*$ denotes the Hermitian conjugate of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Moore Method
snippet: The Moore method is a deductive manner of instruction used in some advanced mathematics courses. Instead of using a textbook, the students are given a list of definitions. Based on these, the students are also given a list of theorems to prove and present in class. This leads the students through the subject material. The Moore method typically limits the amount of material that a class is able to cover, but this is countered by the depth of understanding that listening to lectures cannot give. Category:Definitions/Schools

label: Definition:Morphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. A morphism of $\mathbf C$ is an object $f$, together with: A domain $\operatorname {dom} f$, which is an object of $\mathbf C$ A codomain $\operatorname {cod} f$, also an object of $\mathbf C$ The collection of all morphisms of $\mathbf C$ is denoted $\mathbf C_1$. If $A$ is the domain of $f$ and $B$ is its codomain, this is mostly represented by writing: $f: A \to B$ or $A \stackrel f \longrightarrow B$

label: Definition:Morphism/Also known as
snippet: == Morphism: Also known as == A morphism is also known as: an arrow an edge. Category:Definitions/Morphisms

label: Definition:Morphism/Motivation
snippet: == Morphism: Motivation == A morphism is one of the two basic concepts of a metacategory, and therefore of category theory. The other one is the notion of an object. Thus in order to discuss a particular metacategory, it is necessary to specify what exactly its morphisms are. Note that a morphism is defined to be an object. This should not be confused with an object of $\mathbf C$. Usually, the morphisms of a metacategory $\mathbf C$ are not also objects of $\mathbf C$. Category:Definitions/Morphisms

label: Definition:Morphism Category
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Its morphism category, denoted $\mathbf C^\to$, is defined as follows: {{DefineCategory |ob = The morphisms $\mathbf C_1$ of $\mathbf C$ |mor = $g: f \to f'$ is a pair $\tuple {g_1, g_2}$ of morphisms of $\mathbf C$ such that $g_2 \circ f = f' \circ g_1$ |comp = $\tuple {h_1, h_2} \circ \tuple {g_1, g_2} := \tuple {h_1 \circ g_1, h_2 \circ g_2}$, whenever this is defined |id = $\operatorname{id}_f := \tuple {\operatorname{id}_C, \operatorname{id}_D}$ for $f: C \to D$ }} The morphisms of $\mathbf C^\to$ can be made more intuitive by the following diagram:…

label: Definition:Morphism Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. A morphism functor $F$ assigns to each morphism $f$ of $\mathbf C$ a morphism $F f$ of $\mathbf D$.

label: Definition:Morphism Property
snippet: Let $\phi: \struct {S, \circ} \to \struct {T, *}$ be a mapping from one algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ to another $\struct {T, *}$. Then $\circ$ has the morphism property under $\phi$ : $\forall x, y \in S: \map \phi {x \circ y} = \map \phi x * \map \phi y$

label: Definition:Morphism of Chain Complexes
snippet: Let $\AA$ be an abelian category. Let $\family {C_i, d_i}_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ and $\family {C_i', d_i'}_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ be chain complexes in $\AA$. A morphism of chain complexes from $\family {C_i}_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ to $\family {D_i}_{i \mathop \in \Z}$ is a family of morphisms $\family {f_i: C_i \to C_i'}_{i \mathop \in \Z}$, such that: $\forall i \in \Z: f_{i-1} \circ d_i = d_i' \circ f_i$

label: Definition:Morphism of Cocones
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $D: \mathbf J \to \mathbf C$ be a $\mathbf J$-diagram in $\mathbf C$. Let $\struct {C, c_j}$ and $\struct {C', c'_j}$ be cocones from $D$. Let $f: C \to C'$ be a morphism of $\mathbf C$. Then $f$ is a morphism of cones , for all objects $j$ of $\mathbf J$: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+0.5em@L+3px{ D_j \ar[d]_*+{c_j} \ar[dr]^*+{c'_j} \\ C \ar[r]_*+{f} & C' }\end{xy}$ is a commutative diagram.

label: Definition:Morphism of Cones
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $D: \mathbf J \to \mathbf C$ be a $\mathbf J$-diagram in $\mathbf C$. Let $\struct {C, c_j}$ and $\struct {C', c'_j}$ be cones to $D$. Let $f: C \to C'$ be a morphism of $\mathbf C$. Then $f$ is a morphism of cones , for all objects $j$ of $\mathbf J$: $\begin{xy}\xymatrix@+0.5em@L+2px{ C \ar[r]^*+{f} \ar[dr]_*+{c_j} & C' \ar[d]^*+{c'_j} \\ & D_j }\end{xy}$ is a commutative diagram.

label: Definition:Morphism of Presheaves on Topological Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $\FF$ and $\GG$ be $\mathbf C$-valued presheaves on $X$.

label: Definition:Morphism of Schemes
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be schemes. A morphism of schemes from $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ is a morphism of locally ringed spaces from $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$.

label: Definition:Morphism of Schemes Locally of Finite Type
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be schemes. Let $f : \struct {X, \OO_X} \to \struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be a morphism of schemes. $f$ is locally of finite type for all affine open subsets $U \subset Y$, there is an open cover $\family {V_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ of $\map {f^{-1} } U$ by affine open subsets $V_i \subset \map {f^{-1} } U$, such that the ring homomorphism $\map {\OO_Y} U \to \map {\OO_X} {V_i}$ makes $\map {\OO_X} {V_i}$ a finitely generated commutative $\map {\OO_Y} U$-algebra.

label: Definition:Morphism of Schemes of Finite Type
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be schemes. Let $f : \struct {X, \OO_X} \to \struct {Y, \OO_Y}$ be a morphism of schemes. $f$ is of finite type $f$ is locally of finite type and quasi-compact.

label: Definition:Morphism of Sheaves
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $\FF$ and $\GG$ be $\mathbf C$-valued sheaves on $X$. A sheaf morphism from $\FF$ to $\GG$ is a presheaf morphism $\FF \to \GG$.

label: Definition:Morse-Kelley Set Theory
snippet: Morse-Kelley set theory is a system of axiomatic set theory. It is a stronger form of Zermelo-Fraenkel-Skolem set theory which allows not only for first order formulas to specify the existence of properties of sets, but also defines properties by quantifying over properties as well as over sets.

label: Definition:Morse Theory
snippet: Morse theory is an approach to topology whereby the topological properties of a manifold $M$ can be described in terms of the singularities of a mapping defined on $M$.

label: Definition:Most Significant Digit
snippet: Let $b \in \Z: b \ge 2$ be a number base Let $n$ be a number which is reported to $r$ significant figures, to base $b$, that is: $n = d_1 \times b^k + d_2 \times b^{k - 1} + \dotsb + d_{r - 1} \times b^{k - r + 2} + d_r \times b^{k - r + 1}$ where: $d_1, d_2, \dotsc, d_r$ are the significant figures of $n$ $b^k$ is the largest power of $b$ less than or equal to $n$. Then the digit $d_1$ is known as the most significant digit of $n$. Note that the usual situation is when $b = 10$, but in the field of computer science, binary is usual.

label: Definition:Motion
snippet: A particle or a body is defined as being in motion it is not stationary with respect to the given frame of reference. Thus motion is the state of changing position.

label: Definition:Move/Also known as
snippet: == Move: Also known as == Some texts refer to a move as an action, but the latter word already has several uses in mathematics.

snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process based on an equispaced time series. Let the values of $S$ at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ be $z_t, z_{t - 1}, z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ Let $\tilde z_t$ be the deviation from a constant mean level $\mu$: $\tilde z_t = z_t - \mu$ Let $a_t, a_{t - 1}, a_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be a sequence of independent shocks at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ Let $M$ be a moving average model on $S$ of order $q$: $\tilde z_t = a_t - \theta_1 a_{t - 1} - \theta_2 a_{t - 2} - \dotsb - \theta_q a_{t - q}$ Let $\map \theta B$ be defined as: $\map \theta B = 1 - \theta_1 B -…

label: Definition:Moving Average Model/Parameter
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process based on an equispaced time series. Let the values of $S$ at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ be $z_t, z_{t - 1}, z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ Let $\tilde z_t$ be the deviation from a constant mean level $\mu$: $\tilde z_t = z_t - \mu$ Let $a_t, a_{t - 1}, a_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be a sequence of independent shocks at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ Let $M$ be an moving average model on $S$ of order $q$: $\tilde z_t = a_t - \theta_1 a_{t - 1} - \theta_2 a_{t - 2} - \dotsb - \theta_q a_{t - q}$ The parameters of $M$ consist of: the constant mean level $\mu$ the…

label: Definition:Muggle
snippet: A muggle is a person who is mathematically illiterate. Specifically, it refers to those who do not realise that they are indeed embarrassingly mathematically unsophisticated, and insist on peppering their speech with mathematical-sounding phrases, like Q.E.D (on believing they have won an argument) or I had $n$ pints of beer last night (being under the impression that $n$ means "a big unspecified number").

label: Definition:Multi-Digit Integer
snippet: Let $b \in \N_{>1}$ be a natural number greater than $1$. An $n$-digit integer base $b$ is an integer which has no more than $n$ digits when expressed in base $b$. That is, it is strictly less than $b^n$.

label: Definition:Multi-Value Logic
snippet: Multi-value logic is a branch of logic in which it is admissible for a statements to have a truth value other than just true or false.

label: Definition:Multibrot Set
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer such that $n > 2$ The multibrot $n$ set $M_n$ is the subset of the complex plane defined as follows: Let $c \in \C$ be a complex number. Let $T_c: \C \to \C$ be the complex function defined as: $\forall z \in \C: \map {T_c} z = z^n + c$ Then $c \in M_n$ the sequence: $\tuple {0, \map {T_c} 0, \map { {T_c}^2} 0, \ldots}$ is bounded.

label: Definition:Multifunction/Branch
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $f: A \to B$ be a multifunction on $A$. Let $\family {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a partitioning of the codomain of $f$ such that: $\forall i \in I: f \restriction_{A \times S_i}$ is a mapping. Then each $f \restriction_{A \times S_i}$ is a branch of $f$.

label: Definition:Multifunction/Principal Branch
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $f: A \to B$ be a multifunction on $A$. Let $\sequence {S_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a partitioning of the codomain of $f$ into branches. It is usual to distinguish one such branch of $f$ from the others, and label it the principal branch of $f$.

label: Definition:Multifunction/Principal Value
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $f: A \to B$ be a multifunction on $A$. Let $x \in A$ be an element of the domain of $f$. The principal value of $x$ is the element $y$ of the principal branch of $f$ such that $\map f x = y$.

label: Definition:Multigraph
snippet: A multigraph is a graph that can have more than one edge between a pair of vertices. That is, $G = \struct {V, E}$ is a multigraph if $V$ is a set and $E$ is a multiset of doubleton subsets of $V$. 400px The graph above is a multigraph because of the double edge between $v_2$ and $v_3$ and the triple edge between $v_5$ and $v_6$.

label: Definition:Multiindex Power Notation
snippet: Let $M$ be a commutative monoid. Let $I$ be a set. Let $\mathbf x = \family {x_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of elements of $M$. Let $\mathbf a = \family {a_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of natural numbers of finite support. We denote $\ds \mathbf x^{\mathbf a} = \prod_{i \mathop \in I} x_i^{a_i}$ where: $x_i^{a_i}$ is the $a_i$th power of $x_i$ $\prod$ denotes product with finite support Category:Definitions/Polynomial Theory

label: Definition:Multilateral Polygon/Also known as
snippet: == Multilateral Polygon: Also known as == The term multilateral polygon can also be seen hyphenated: multi-lateral polygon. A polygon with $n$ sides is known as an $n$-gon.

label: Definition:Multinomial Coefficient
snippet: Let $k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_m \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be positive integers. The multinomial coefficient of $k_1, \ldots, k_m$ is defined as: $\dbinom {k_1 + k_2 + \cdots + k_m} {k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_m} := \dfrac {\paren {k_1 + k_2 + \cdots + k_m}!} {k_1! \, k_2! \, \ldots k_m!}$

label: Definition:Multinomial Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. At each of $n$ trials, let $X$ have $r$ possible outcomes with probabilities $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ such that $\sum p_i = 1$. Then $X$ has the multinomial distribution. The probabilities of the various outcomes are given by the terms of the expansion of: $\paren {p_1 + p_2 + \cdots + p_r}^n$

label: Definition:Multiple/Integer
snippet: Let $\Z$ denote the set of integers. Let $x, y \in \Z$. Let $x$ be a divisor of $y$. Then $y$ is a multiple of $x$.

label: Definition:Multiple Correlation Coefficient
snippet: Context: multiple regression. Let the expectation of a random variable $Y$ be given by: $\expect y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 \cdots$ Let the least-squares regression estimators of $y$ corresponding to the observed $y_i$ be denoted $\hat y_i$. Then the multiple correlation coefficient is the product moment correlation coefficient between the $y_i$ and $\hat y_i$, and is denoted $R$.

label: Definition:Multiple Linear Regression/General
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be a random variable. Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p$ also be random variables for $p \in \N_{>1}$ Let $\mathbb x$ be a vector of $p$ explanatory variables from $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p$. Let $\bstheta$ be a vector of $q$ unknown parameters Let the regression of $Y$ on $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be expressible in the form: $\expect {Y \mid \mathbf x} = \map f {\mathbf x, \bstheta}$ Then $\expect {Y \mid \mathbf x}$ is known as general multiple linear regression.

label: Definition:Multiple Pointed Algebra
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be a set. An $I$-pointed algebra over $R$ is an ordered pair $(A, f)$ where: $A$ is an algebra over $R$ $f : I \to A$ is a mapping

label: Definition:Multiple Pointed Set
snippet: Let $I$ be a set. An $I$-pointed set is an ordered pair $\struct {A, f}$ where: $A$ is a set $f : I \to A$ is a mapping

label: Definition:Multiple Pointed Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be a finite set whose cardinality is greater than $1$. Let $D = \struct {A, \set {\O, A} }$ be the indiscrete space on $A$. Let $T \times D$ be the product space of $T$ and $D$. Then $T \times D$ is known as the multiple pointed topology on $T$. It is seen that $T \times D$ is conceptually equivalent to taking the space $T$ and replacing each point with a finite set of topologically indistinguishable points.

label: Definition:Multiple Regression/Linear
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be a random variable. Let $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_p$ also be random variables for $p \in \N_{>1}$ Let the regression of $Y$ on $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ be expressible in the form: $\expect {Y \mid x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_p} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_2 + \beta_2 x_2 + \ldots + \beta_n x_n$ Then $\expect {Y \mid x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_p}$ is known as multiple linear regression.

label: Definition:Multiplicand/Also known as
snippet: == Multiplicand: Also known as == In algebraic systems where multiplication is commutative, it is commonplace to treat both the multiplier and multiplicand as the same sort of object, and refer to them both as factors. Category:Definitions/Multiplication

label: Definition:Multiplication
snippet: Multiplication is the basic operation $\times$ everyone is familiar with. For example:

label: Definition:Multiplication/Complex Numbers
snippet: The multiplication operation in the domain of complex numbers $\C$ is written $\times$. Let $z = a + i b, w = c + i d$ where $a, b, c, d \in \R$. Then $z \times w$ is defined as: $\paren {a + i b} \times \paren {c + i d} = \paren {a c - b d} + i \paren {a d + b c}$ This follows by the facts that: Real Numbers form Field and thus real multiplication is distributive over real addition the entity $i$ is such that $i^2 = -1$.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Multiplication == The symbol $\times$ for multiplication was invented by . However, he was criticized by , as it was in his view too similar to the letter $x$. himself preferred the symbol $\cdot$.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Integers
snippet: The multiplication operation in the domain of integers $\Z$ is written $\times$. Let us define $\eqclass {\tuple {a, b} } \boxtimes$ as in the formal definition of integers. That is, $\eqclass {\tuple {a, b} } \boxtimes$ is an equivalence class of ordered pairs of natural numbers under the congruence relation $\boxtimes$. $\boxtimes$ is the congruence relation defined on $\N \times \N$ by $\tuple {x_1, y_1} \boxtimes \tuple {x_2, y_2} \iff x_1 + y_2 = x_2 + y_1$. In order to streamline the notation, we will use $\eqclass {a, b} {}$ to mean $\eqclass {\tuple {a, b} } \boxtimes$, as suggested.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Multiplicand
snippet: Let $a \times b$ denote the operation of multiplication on two objects. The object $b$ is known as the multiplicand of $a$. That is, it is the object which is to be multiplied by the multiplier. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Multiplier
snippet: Let $a \times b$ denote the operation of multiplication on two objects. The object $a$ is known as the multiplier of $b$. That is, it is the object which is to multiply the multiplicand. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Natural Numbers/Addition
snippet: Let $\N$ be the natural numbers. Let $+$ denote addition. The binary operation $\times$ is recursively defined on $\N$ as follows: $\forall m, n \in \N: \begin {cases} m \times 0 & = 0 \\ m \times \paren {n + 1} & = m \times n + m \end {cases}$ This operation is called multiplication. Equivalently, multiplication can be defined as: $\forall m, n \in \N: m \times n := \mathop {+^n} m$ where $\mathop {+^n} m$ denotes the $n$th power of $m$ under $+$.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Notation
snippet: There are several variants of the notation for multiplication: $n \times m$ This is usually used when numbers are under consideration, for example: $3 \times 5 = 15$. However, it can be used in the context of algebra where extra clarity is needed. $n m$ This is most common in algebra, but not with numbers, as it is difficult to make it obvious where one number ends and the next number begins. $\paren n \paren m$ This form can be used for either symbols denoting variables or numbers, for example: $\paren 3 \paren 4 = 12$. $n \cdot m$ or $n .

label: Definition:Multiplication/Product
snippet: Let $a \times b$ denote the operation of multiplication on two objects $a$ and $b$. Then the result $a \times b$ is referred to as the product of $a$ and $b$. Note that the nature of $a$ and $b$ has deliberately been left unspecified. They could be, for example, numbers, matrices or more complex expressions constructed from such elements.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Rational Numbers
snippet: The multiplication operation in the domain of rational numbers $\Q$ is written $\times$. Let $a = \dfrac p q, b = \dfrac r s$ where $p, q \in \Z, r, s \in \Z \setminus \set 0$. Then $a \times b$ is defined as $\dfrac p q \times \dfrac r s = \dfrac {p \times r} {q \times s}$. This definition follows from the definition of and proof of existence of the field of quotients of any integral domain, of which the set of integers is one.

label: Definition:Multiplication/Real Numbers
snippet: The multiplication operation in the domain of real numbers $\R$ is written $\times$. From the definition, the real numbers are the set of all equivalence classes $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers. Let $x = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}, y = \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$, where $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ and $\eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {}$ are such equivalence classes. Then $x \times y$ is defined as: $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {} \times \eqclass {\sequence {y_n} } {} = \eqclass {\sequence {x_n \times y_n} } {}$

label: Definition:Multiplication of Homotopy Classes of Paths
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\alpha, \beta$ be homotopy classes of paths in $T$. Let $f, g: \closedint 0 1 \to S$ be representative paths for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ respectively. Let $\map f 1 = \map g 0$. The product of the homotopy classes $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is the homotopy class of the concatenated path $f * g$.

label: Definition:Multiplication of Positive Cuts
snippet: Let $0^*$ denote the rational cut associated with the (rational) number $0$. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be positive cuts, that is, cuts such that $\alpha \ge 0^*$ and $\beta \ge 0^*$, where $\ge$ denotes the ordering on cuts. Let the operation of multiplication be defined on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ as: $\gamma := \alpha \beta$ where $\gamma$ is the set of all rational numbers $r$ such that either: $r < 0$ or $\exists p \in \alpha, q \in \beta: r = p q$ where $p \ge 0$ and $q \ge 0$. In this context, $\gamma$ is known as the product of $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Function
snippet: Number Theory: Definition:Multiplicative Arithmetic Function Definition:Completely Multiplicative Function Ring Theory: Definition:Multiplicative Function on Ring Definition:Multiplicative Function on UFD

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \times}$ be a field. Let $F^* := F \setminus \set 0$ be the set $F$ less its zero. The group $\struct {F^*, \times}$ is known as the multiplicative group of $F$.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group/Also defined as
snippet: == Multiplicative Group: Also defined as == A multiplicative group is also defined as a group $G$ such that: the elements of $G$ are numbers the operation is multiplication and denoted by concatenation: $a b$ the identity is $1$.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Complex Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of complex numbers $\struct {\C_{\ne 0}, \times}$ is the set of complex numbers without zero under the operation of multiplication.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Complex Roots of Unity
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer such that $n > 0$. Let $U_n := \set {z \in \C: z^n = 1}$ denote the set of complex $n$th roots of unity. Let $\struct {U_n, \times}$ be the algebraic structure formed by $U_n$ under complex multiplication. Then $\struct {U_n, \times}$ is the multiplicative group of complex $n$th roots of unity.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Positive Rational Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of positive rational numbers $\struct {\Q_{> 0}, \times}$ is the set of (strictly) positive rational numbers under the operation of multiplication.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Positive Real Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of positive real numbers $\left({\R_{> 0}, \times}\right)$ is the set of (strictly) positive real numbers under the operation of multiplication. Thus real multiplication is: Well-defined on $\R_{> 0}$ Closed on $\R_{> 0}$ Associative on $\R_{> 0}$ Commutative on $\R_{> 0}$ The identity of $\left({\R_{> 0}, \times}\right)$ is $1$ Each element of $\left({\R_{> 0}, \times}\right)$ has an inverse.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Rational Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of rational numbers $\struct {\Q_{\ne 0}, \times}$ is the set of rational numbers without zero under the operation of multiplication.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Real Numbers
snippet: The multiplicative group of real numbers $\struct {\R_{\ne 0}, \times}$ is the set of real numbers without zero under the operation of multiplication.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Group of Reduced Residues
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\Z'_m$ denote the reduced residue system modulo $m$. Consider the algebraic structure: $\struct {\Z'_m, \times_m}$ where $\times_m$ denotes multiplication modulo $m$. Then $\struct {\Z'_m, \times_m}$ is referred to as the multiplicative group of reduced residues modulo $m$.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Inverse/Number
snippet: Let $\Bbb F$ be one of the standard number fields: $\Q$, $\R$, $\C$. Let $a \in \Bbb F$ be any arbitrary number. The multiplicative inverse of $a$ is its inverse under multiplication and can be denoted: $a^{-1}$, $\dfrac 1 a$, $1 / a$, and so on. $a \times a^{-1} = 1$

label: Definition:Multiplicative Magic Square
snippet: A multiplicative magic square is an arrangement of $n^2$ distinct numbers into an $n \times n$ square array such that: the product of the elements of each row the product of the elements in each column the product of the elements along each diagonal are the same.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Magic Square/Magic Constant
snippet: The magic constant of a multiplicative magic square is the number that each of the rows and columns multiplies up to.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Monoid of Integers Modulo m
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$ such that $m > 1$. The multiplicative monoid of integers modulo $m$ $\struct {\Z_m, \times_m}$ is the set of integers modulo $m$ under the operation of multiplication modulo $m$.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Notation
snippet: Multiplicative notation, also called product notation, is a convention for representing a binary operation of an algebraic structure. Let $S$ be such an algebraic structure, and let $x, y \in S$. $x y$ is used to indicate the result of the operation on $x$ and $y$. There is no symbol used to define the operation itself. $e$ or $1$ is used for the identity element. $x^{-1}$ is used for the inverse element. $x^n$ is used to indicate the $n$th power of $x$. This notation is usual in group theory when discussing the general group.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Order of Integer
snippet: Let $a$ and $n$ be integers. Let there exist a positive integer $c$ such that: $a^c \equiv 1 \pmod n$ Then the least such integer is called the (multiplicative) order of $a$ modulo $n$.

label: Definition:Multiplicative Semigroup of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. The semigroup $\struct {R, \circ}$ is known as the multiplicative semigroup of $R$.

label: Definition:Multiplicatively Closed Subset of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {A, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity $1_A$ and zero $0_A$. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a subset. Then $S$ is multiplicatively closed : $(1): \quad 1_A \in S$ $(2): \quad x, y \in S \implies x \circ y \in S$
