snippet: There are various number-naming systems for naming large numbers (that is: greater than $1 \, 000 \, 000$).

label: Definition:Number/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Number == The word number comes from an Indo-European word meaning share or portion. It appears to have been originally associated with the division of land. Hence we have the derived terms: nimble: descriptive of one who is quick to take his share nemesis: your share of fate numb: originally meaning seized or taken nomad: a person who wanders in search of some pasture he can take a share of Supernumerary, which means redundant, but originally had the sense of meaning over and above the numbers stated by the rules The root nom can be found in the following examples of…

label: Definition:Number Base/Integer Part
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \ge 0$. Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. In the basis expansion: $x = \left[{r_m r_{m-1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0 . d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}\right]_b$ the part $r_m r_{m-1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0$ is known as the integer part.

label: Definition:Number Base/Integers
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $b \in \Z$ be an integer such that $b > 1$. By the Basis Representation Theorem, $n$ can be expressed uniquely in the form: $\ds n = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^m r_j b^j$ where: $m$ is such that $b^m \le n < b^{m + 1}$ all the $r_j$ are such that $0 \le r_j < b$. The number $b$ is known as the number base to which $n$ is represented. $n$ is thus described as being (written) in base $b$. Thus we can write $\ds n = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^m {r_j b^j}$ as: $\sqbrk {r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0}_b$ or, if the context is clear: ${r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0}_b$

label: Definition:Number Base/Radix Point
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \ge 0$. Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. In the basis expansion: $x = \sqbrk {r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0 \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ the dot that separates the integer part from the fractional part is called the radix point.

label: Definition:Number Base/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number such that $x \ge 0$. Let $b \in \N: b \ge 2$. See the definition of Basis Expansion for how we can express $x$ in the form: $x = \sqbrk {s \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ Then we express $m$ as for integers, and arrive at: $x = \sqbrk {r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0 \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots}_b$ or, if the context is clear: $r_m r_{m - 1} \ldots r_2 r_1 r_0 \cdotp d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots_b$

label: Definition:Number Field
snippet: A number field is a subfield of the field of complex numbers.

label: Definition:Number Names
snippet: This page gathers together instances of names of numbers in various languages and contexts.

label: Definition:Number Prefix
snippet: A number prefix is a prefix which determines a number, usually a natural number.

label: Definition:Number Prefixes
snippet: This page documents some of the more common prefixes that are used to indicate specific numbers.

label: Definition:Number Prefixes/6/Hect-/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Use of Hect- in the context of $6$ == The prefix hect- denoting $6$ can be found in the following contexts: hectad: possibly erroneously as a synonym for hexad, meaning a set or tuple with exactly $6$ elements hectic equation: a synonym for a sextic equation

label: Definition:Number Sieve
snippet: A number sieve is a numerical process for finding divisors of large integers.

label: Definition:Number System
snippet: A number system is a technique for representing numbers.

label: Definition:Number Theory
snippet: Number theory is the branch of mathematics which studies the properties of the integers, and by extension the rational numbers and related number systems.

label: Definition:Number Theory/Also defined as
snippet: == Number Theory: Also defined as== Some sources allow that number theory studies the properties of just the natural numbers.

label: Definition:Number Theory/Also known as
snippet: == Number Theory: Also known as== Older sources refer to number theory variously as: theory of numbers higher arithmetic or the higher arithmetic arithmetic. himself used the term arithmetic, after the manner of the ancient Greeks. Number theory can also be seen described by the fanciful name the Queen of Mathematics for various whimsical reasons.

label: Definition:Number Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Number Theory == The field of number theory is considered by some to be one of the oldest branches of mathematics in history. At the time of , there existed a mass of unstructured information on the subject dating back to the Babylonians, ancient Egyptians and the Chinese. and his followers believed that all the phenomena in the Universe could be explained by the study of the natural numbers. Some of the first serious results are found in , thinly disguised as geometry. developed the ideas into a distinct branch of mathematics.

label: Definition:Numeral
snippet: A numeral is a symbol which is used to identify a particular number (usually a natural number). A numeral is one of a small subset of the numbers. Other numbers can be created by combining numeral using specific well-defined rules.

label: Definition:Numeral System
snippet: A numeral system is: a set of symbols that is used to represent a specific subset of the set of numbers (usually natural numbers), referred to as numerals a set of rules which define how to combine the numerals so as to be able to express other numbers.

label: Definition:Numerators and Denominators of Continued Fraction
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. Let $n \in \N \cup \set \infty$ be an extended natural number. Let $C = \sqbrk {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ be a continued fraction in $F$ of length $n$.

label: Definition:Numerical Analysis
snippet: Numerical analysis is the branch of applied mathematics concerned with the processes by which certain kinds of numerical solutions to problems in (mainly) physics.

label: Definition:Numerical Analysis/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Numerical Analysis == As a result of the development since the middle of the $20$th century of the electronic computer, the discipline of numerical analysis has greatly increased in importance. It is now possible to directly model the behaviour of an artefact by simulation to a high level of accuracy.

label: Definition:Numerical Analysis/Motivation
snippet: == Numerical Analysis: Motivation == It is impossible to write down an exact decimal representation of a solution to certain equations, as they may be irrational. Certain other problems are defined by equations which cannot be solved using analytical methods. Hence: The aim of numerical methods is to provide practical procedures for calculating the solutions of problems in applied mathematics to a specified degree of accuracy. -- To produce a number which answers a problem is only one aspect of the topic of numerical analysis.

label: Definition:Numerical Equation
snippet: A numerical equation is an equation in which the coefficients and constants are actual numbers as opposed to symbols representing numerical values.

label: Definition:Numerical Integration Rule
snippet: A numerical integration rule is a formula for implementing a technique of using numerical integration.

label: Definition:Numerical Range
snippet: Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\norm {\, \cdot \,}$ be the inner product norm on $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a densely-defined linear operator on $\HH$. We define the numerical range $\map W T$ of $T$ by: $\map W T = \set {\innerprod {T u} u : u \in \map D T, \, \norm u = 1}$

label: Definition:Numerology
snippet: Numerology is a philosophical belief structure, borrowed from the Pythagoreans, that considers numbers to possess mystical properties. At its heart is the pseudo-science of gematria or arithmology: the process of translating linguistic text (in particular a name) into numerical form, and thence to interpret the significance of that text from the mystical power of that particular number.

label: Definition:O Notation
snippet: $\OO$ notation is a type of order notation, typically used in computer science for comparing 'run-times' of algorithms, or in analysis for comparing growth rates between two growth functions.

label: Definition:Object
snippet: An object is a thing. Everything that can be talked about in mathematics and logic can be referred to as an object.

label: Definition:Object (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. An object of $\mathbf C$ is an object which is considered to be atomic from a category theoretic perspective.

label: Definition:Object (Category Theory)/Motivation
snippet: An object is a conceptual device introduced mainly to make the discussion of morphisms more convenient. That objects do not play an important role in category theory is apparent from the fact that the notion of a metacategory can be described while avoiding to mention objects altogether. Nonetheless the notion of object is one of the two basic concepts of metacategories and as such of category theory.

label: Definition:Object Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. An object functor $F$ assigns to each object $X$ of $\mathbf C$ an object $F X$ of $\mathbf D$.

label: Definition:Objective Function/Standard Form
snippet: Let $P$ be an objective function. Then $P$ is in standard form when it is in the form: $P - a_1 x_1 - a_2 x_2 - \cdots - a_m x_m + 0 \times s_1 + 0 \times s_2 + \cdots + 0 \times s_n = 0$ where: $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_m$ are the initial variables defining $P$ $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_m$ are the coefficients of those initial variables $s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n$ are the slack variables introduced to enable the inequalities to be expressed as equations.

label: Definition:Objective Unknown
snippet: An objective unknown is an event which has a well-defined objective probability of occurring. Two objective unknowns with the same probability are equivalent in the field of decision theory. An objective unknown is appropriately modelled by means of a probability model.

label: Definition:Oblique Angle
snippet: A (plane) angle is an oblique angle is not an integer multiple of a right angle.

label: Definition:Oblique Coordinate System
snippet: An oblique coordinate system is a coordinate system in which the position of a point is determined by its relation to a set of straight coordinate axes which are oblique. 400px

label: Definition:Oblique Spherical Triangle
snippet: An oblique Spherical triangle is a spherical triangle in which none of the angles nor sides are right angles. That is, it is a spherical triangle which is neither a right spherical triangle nor a quadrantal spherical triangle.

label: Definition:Oblong/Also known as
snippet: == Oblong: Also known as == The word oblong is rarely seen nowadays. Rectangle is the term usually used instead, unless it is essential to emphasise that such a quadrilateral is not a square. Category:Definitions/Oblongs

label: Definition:Observation
snippet: An observation is an item of raw data that has been obtained as the result of measurement or counting. Hence it is a particular value taken by a variable in statistics.

label: Definition:Obstinate Number
snippet: An obstinate number is a positive odd integer which cannot be expressed as the sum of a power of $2$ and a prime.

label: Definition:Obtuse Angle
snippet: An obtuse angle is an angle which has a measurement between those of a right angle and a straight angle. Note that did not consider the concept of reflex angles.

label: Definition:Oct-/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Use of Oct- == The prefix oct- can be found in the following contexts: octad: a set or ordered tuple with $8$ elements octagon or octangle: a polygon with $8$ sides and hence $8$ vertices octahedron: a polyhedron with $8$ faces

label: Definition:Octad
snippet: An octad is a set or tuple which has exactly $8$ elements.

label: Definition:Octagon/Regular
snippet: A regular octagon is an octagon which is both equilateral and equiangular. That is, a regular polygon with $8$ sides. That is, an octagon in which all the sides are the same length, and all the vertices have the same angle: 300px

label: Definition:Octagonal Number
snippet: Octagonal numbers are those denumerating a collection of objects which can be arranged in the form of a regular octagon. They can be denoted: $O_1, O_2, O_3, \ldots$

label: Definition:Octahedron/Regular
snippet: 300px A regular octahedron is an octahedron whose $8$ faces are all congruent equilateral triangles. It has: $6$ vertices $12$ edges $8$ faces The regular octahedron is an example of a deltahedron.

label: Definition:Octal Notation
snippet: Octal notation is the positional number system whose base is $8$. That is, every number $x \in \R$ is expressed in the form: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z} r_j 8^j$ where: $\forall j \in \Z: r_j \in \set {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}$

label: Definition:Octal Notation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Octal Notation == Octal notation was advocated by . Octal notation used to be important in the field of computer science, but is less so nowadays, as hexadecimal has proved itself more convenient in general.

label: Definition:Octal Notation/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == octal system

label: Definition:Octonion
snippet: The set of octonions, usually denoted $\Bbb O$, can be defined by using the Cayley-Dickson construction from the quaternions $\H$ as follows: From Quaternions form Algebra, $\H$ forms a nicely normed $*$-algebra. Let $a, b \in \H$. Then $\tuple {a, b} \in \Bbb O$, where: $\tuple {a, b} \tuple {c, d} = \tuple {a c - d \overline b, \overline a d + c b}$ $\overline {\tuple {a, b} } = \tuple {\overline a, -b}$ where: $\overline a$ is the conjugate of $a$ and $\overline {\tuple {a, b} }$ is the conjugation operation on $\Bbb O$.

label: Definition:Octonion/Addition
snippet: Let $x = \tuple {a, b}$ and $y = \tuple {c, d}$ be octonions, where $a, b, c, d \in \H$ are quaternions. The sum of $x$ and $y$ is defined as: $x + y = \tuple {a, b} + \tuple {c, d} = \tuple {a + c, b + d}$ Category:Definitions/Octonions

label: Definition:Octonion/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Octonions == The octonions were discovered by in December $1843$, in the wake of the work he did with on the quaternions. However, he never made it into print, and it was who published his own work on octonions in $1845$, hence claiming the credit. precedent was discovered in $1847$ on the evidence of a letter he had written to on the occasion of his initial discovery of them. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Odd-Even Topology
snippet: Let $\Z_{>0}$ denote the set of strictly positive integers: $\Z_{>0} = \set {x \in \Z: x > 0}$ Let $\PP$ be the partition on $\Z_{>0}$ defined as: $\PP = \set {\set {2 k - 1, 2 k}: k \in \Z_{>0} }$ That is: $\PP = \set {\set {1, 2}, \set {3, 4}, \set {5, 6}, \ldots}$ Then the topology whose basis is $\PP$ is called the odd-even topology, and its topological space is the odd-even space.

label: Definition:Odd Integer/Definition 1
snippet: An integer $n \in \Z$ is odd it is not divisible by $2$. That is, it is not even.

label: Definition:Odd Integer/Definition 2
snippet: An integer $n \in \Z$ is odd : $\exists m \in \Z: n = 2 m + 1$

label: Definition:Odd Integer/Definition 3
snippet: An integer $n \in \Z$ is odd : $x \equiv 1 \pmod 2$ where the notation denotes congruence modulo $2$.

label: Definition:Odd Integer/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Odd Integer == The concept of classifying numbers as odd or even appears to have originated with the Pythagoreans. It was their belief that odd numbers (except $1$) are male, and even numbers are female. A commentator on used the term scalene number for an odd number, in correspondence with the concept of a scalene triangle. In a similar way an even number was described as isosceles.

label: Definition:Odd Integer/Odd-Times Odd
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$, i.e. let $n$ be an integer.

label: Definition:Odd Integer/Odd-Times Odd/Definition 1
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. $n$ is odd-times odd it is an odd number greater than $1$ which is not prime.

label: Definition:Odd Integer/Odd-Times Odd/Definition 2
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. $n$ is odd-times odd there exist odd numbers $x, y > 1$ such that $n = x y$.

label: Definition:Odd Parity/Also defined as
snippet: == Odd Parity: Also known as == Some sources refer to odd parity as a property of a pair of integers $\set {z_1, z_2}$: $\set {z_1, z_2}$ are of odd parity one of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is even and the other is odd. That is, the same as the definition of such a pair of integers as being of opposite parity

label: Definition:Odd Prime
snippet: Every even integer is divisible by $2$ (because this is the definition of even). Therefore, apart from $2$ itself, all primes are odd. So, referring to an odd prime is a convenient way of specifying that a number is a prime number, but not equal to $2$.

label: Definition:Odds
snippet: Let $A$ be an event. Let the probability of $A$ occurring be $p$.

label: Definition:Odds/Against
snippet: Let $A$ be an event. Let the probability of $A$ occurring be $p$. The odds against $A$ is defined as: $\dfrac {1 - p} p$ where $1 - p$ is the probability of $A$ not occurring.

label: Definition:Odds/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Odds == While the concept of odds is in everyday use in gambling, it is rarely used in the context of statistical statements. The concept of probability preferred instead, except while discussing the odds ratio.

label: Definition:Odds/On
snippet: Let $A$ be an event. Let the probability of $A$ occurring be $p$. The odds on $A$ is defined as: $\dfrac p {1 - p}$ where $1 - p$ is the probability of $A$ not occurring.

label: Definition:Odds Ratio
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be events. Let the probability of $A$ occurring be $p_A$ and the probability of $B$ occurring be $p_B$. The odds ratio of $A$ to $B$ is given by: $\theta = \dfrac {\theta_A} {\theta_B}$ where: $\theta_A$ is the odds on $A$: $\theta_A = \dfrac {p_A} {1 - p_A}$ $\theta_B$ is the odds on $B$: $\theta_B = \dfrac {p_B} {1 - p_B}$

label: Definition:Odds Ratio/Empirical
snippet: Let $P$ be a population partitioned into $P_1$ and $P_2$. Let $Q$ be a property that the members of $P$ may or may not have. Let the number of the members of $P_1$ having $Q$ be $A$. Let the number of the members of $P_2$ having $Q$ be $B$. The empirical odds ratio of $A$ to $B$ is the ratio $\theta^*$ defined as: $\theta^* = \dfrac {A : \paren {P_1 - A} } {B : \paren {P_2 - B} }$ It is often more convenient to work with $\theta^*$, which is symmetrically distributed about $0$.

label: Definition:Off-Diagonal Element
snippet: Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix. The off-diagonal elements of $A$ are the elements of $\mathbf A$ which do not lie on the main diagonal of $\mathbf A$. That is, the elements $\map a {r, s}$ where $r \ne s$. That is, the elements of $\mathbf A$ which are not diagonal elements.

label: Definition:Ohm
snippet: The ohm is the SI unit of electrical resistance. It is defined as being the electrical resistance between two points of an electrical conductor when a constant electric potential of $1$ volt, applied to these points, produces in the conductor an electric current of $1$ ampere, the conductor not being the seat of any electromotive force.

label: Definition:Omega-Accumulation Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$. An $\omega$-accumulation point of $A$ is a limit point $x$ of $A$ such that every open set containing $x$ also contains an infinite number of points of $A$.

label: Definition:Omega Constant
snippet: The omega constant $\Omega$ is the constant as the value of the principal branch of the Lambert W function at $1$: $\Omega \, e^ \Omega = 1$ That is, it is the root of the equation: $x e^x = 1$ where $e$ denotes Euler's number.

label: Definition:One
snippet: The immediate successor element of zero in the set of natural numbers $\N$ is called one and has the symbol $1$.

label: Definition:One-Parameter Family of Curves on Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I, J \subseteq \R$ be real intervals. Let $\Gamma : I \times J \to M$ be a continuous map, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product. Then $\Gamma$ is called the one-parameter family of curves on $M$.

label: Definition:One-Sided Alternative
snippet: Let $\delta$ be a hypothesis test. Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be the null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis of $\delta$ respectively. Let $\theta$ be the test statistic which is being used to determine whether $H_0$ or $H_1$ holds. Let $H_1$ be such that the critical region of $\delta$ is governed by a single inequality, for example: $H_1: \theta > x$ where $x$ is the critical value of $\delta$. Then $H_1$ is known as a one-sided alternative.

label: Definition:One-Sided Inverse
snippet: Let $S, T$ be sets where $S \ne \O$, that is, $S$ is not empty. A one-sided inverse (mapping) from $S$ to $T$ is a mapping which is either: a left inverse mapping or: a right inverse mapping but (specifically) not both.

label: Definition:One-Sided Shift of Finite Type
snippet: Let $k \in \Z_{\ge 2}$. Let $\mathbf A = \sqbrk a_{kk}$ be a logical matrix. Let $\Sigma = \set {1, 2, \ldots, k}$. Let: $X_\mathbf A ^+ = \set {x = \sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} : x_n \in \Sigma, a_{x_n, x_{n + 1} } = 1}$ Let $\sigma : X_\mathbf A ^+ \to X_\mathbf A ^+$ be the forward shift operator. Then the pair $\struct {X _\mathbf A ^+, \sigma}$ is called a one-sided shift of finite type.

label: Definition:One-to-One Relation
snippet: A relation $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ is one-to-one if it is both many-to-one and one-to-many. That is, every element of the domain of $\RR$ relates to no more than one element of its codomain, and every element of the image is related to by exactly one element of its domain.

label: Definition:One (Cardinal)
snippet: The cardinal associated with the singleton $\set \O$ is called one, and is denoted $1$. More informally, this means that one is defined as being the number of elements in a singleton set.

label: Definition:One (Category)
snippet: The category one $\mathbf 1$, is the category with: {{DefineCategory |ob = One object: $*$ |mor = One morphism: the identity morphism $\operatorname{id}_*$. }}

label: Definition:One (Ordinal)
snippet: The ordinal $1$ is defined as: $1 = 0^+$ where $0^+$ denotes the successor of the ordinal $0$.

label: Definition:Ones Matrix
snippet: A ones matrix is a matrix all of whose elements are $1$.

label: Definition:Open
snippet: Predicate Logic: an open statement is a statement which contains at least one free occurrence of a variable. Topology: Open set: A set $U$ in a topological space $\left({S, \tau}\right)$ such that $U \in \tau$. Open mapping: A mapping $f: T_1 \to T_2$ from a topological space $T_1$ to another $T_2$ which maps open sets in $T_1$ to open sets in $T_2$. Open cover: A cover consisting of open sets. Open neighborhood: A neighborhood which is an open set.

label: Definition:Open Ball
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or pseudometric space. Let $a \in A$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$ in $M$ is defined as: $\map {B_\epsilon} a := \set {x \in A: \map d {x, a} < \epsilon}$ where $d$ is the distance function on $M$. If it is necessary to show the distance function itself, then the notation $\map {B_\epsilon} {a; d}$ can be used.

label: Definition:Open Ball/Center
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or pseudometric space. Let $a \in A$. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $a$ is referred to as the center of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

label: Definition:Open Ball/Normed Vector Space
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $x \in X$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$ in $\struct {X, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ is defined as: $\map {B_\epsilon} x = \set {y \in X: 
orm{x - y} < \epsilon}$

label: Definition:Open Ball/P-adic Numbers
snippet:
Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $a \in R$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$ in $\struct {\Q_p, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ is defined as: $\map {B_\epsilon} a = \set {x \in \Q_p: 
orm{x - a}_p < \epsilon}$

label: Definition:Open Ball/P-adic Numbers/Center
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $a \in R$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $a$ is referred to as the center of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

label: Definition:Open Ball/P-adic Numbers/Radius
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $a \in R$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $\epsilon$ is referred to as the radius of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

label: Definition:Open Ball/Radius
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space or pseudometric space. Let $a \in A$. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} a$ be the open $\epsilon$-ball of $a$. In $\map {B_\epsilon} a$, the value $\epsilon$ is referred to as the radius of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

label: Definition:Open Ball/Real Analysis
snippet: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $\R^n$ denote the real Euclidean space of dimension $n$. Let $\norm {\, \cdot \,}$ denote the Euclidean norm. Let $a \in \R^n$. Let $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. The open (Euclidean) ball of center $a$ and radius $\epsilon$ is the subset: $\map {B_\epsilon} a = \set {x \in \R^n : \norm {x - a} < \epsilon}$

label: Definition:Open Cover
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\CC$ be a cover for $S$. Then $\CC$ is an open cover (of $T$) : $\CC \subseteq \tau$ That is, all the elements of $\CC$ are open sets.

label: Definition:Open Cover/Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H$ be a subset of $S$. Let $\CC$ be a cover of $H$. Then $\CC$ is an open cover for $H$ : $\CC \subseteq \tau$ That is, all the elements of $\CC$ are open sets.

label: Definition:Open Discrete Set of Subsets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\UU$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $\UU$ is open discrete : $(1) \quad \UU \subseteq \tau$, that is, for all $U \in \UU: U$ is open in $T$ $(2) \quad \UU$ is discrete

label: Definition:Open Extension Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $p$ be a new element which is not in $S$. Let $S^*_p = S \cup \set p$. Let $\tau^*_p$ be the set defined as: $\tau^*_{\bar p} = \set {U: U \in \tau} \cup \set {S^*_p}$ That is, $\tau^*_{\bar p}$ is the set of all sets formed by taking all the open sets of $\tau$ and adding to them the set $S^*_p$. Then: $\tau^*_{\bar p}$ is the open extension topology of $\tau$ and: $T^*_{\bar p} = \struct {S^*_p, \tau^*_{\bar p} }$ is the open extension space of $T = \struct {S, \tau}$.

label: Definition:Open Geodesic Ball in Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p \in M$. Let $\exp_p$ be the restricted exponential map. Let $\map {B_\epsilon} 0 \subseteq T_p M$ be the open ball in $T_p M$ with $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$ such that $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism from $\map {B_\epsilon} 0$ to its image. Then the image set $\map {\exp_p} {\map {B_\epsilon} 0 }$ is called the open geodesic ball in $M$.

label: Definition:Open Invariant
snippet: Let $P$ be a property whose domain is the set of all topological spaces. Suppose that whenever $\map P T$ holds, then so does $\map P {T'}$, where: $T$ and $T'$ are topological spaces $\phi: T \to T'$ is a mapping from $T$ to $T'$ $\phi \sqbrk T = T'$, where $\phi \sqbrk T$ denotes the image of $\phi$ $T'$ is an open set. Then $P$ is an open invariant. Loosely, an open invariant is a property which is preserved in the open image of a mapping.

label: Definition:Open Locally Finite Set of Subsets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\UU$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $\UU$ is open locally finite :

label: Definition:Open Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $\struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is said to be an open mapping : $\forall U \in \tau_1: f \sqbrk U \in \tau_2$ where $f \sqbrk U$ denotes the image of $U$ under $f$.

label: Definition:Open Neighborhood
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Let $N_A$ be a neighborhood of $A$. Let: $N_A \in \tau$ That is, let $N_A$ itself be an open set of $T$. Then $N_A$ is called an open neighborhood of $A$ in $T$.

label: Definition:Open Neighborhood/Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$ be a point of $S$. Let $N_x$ be a neighborhood of $x$ in $T$. Let: $N_x \in \tau$ That is, let $N_x$ itself be an open set of $T$. Then $N_x$ is called an open neighborhood of $x$ in $T$.

label: Definition:Open Neighborhood/Real Analysis/Real Euclidean Space
snippet: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $x \in \R^n$. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a subset. Then $I$ is an open neighborhood of $x$ $I$ is open and $I$ is a neighborhood of $x$. Category:Definitions/Open Neighborhoods Category:Definitions/Real Euclidean Spaces

label: Definition:Open Neighborhood/Real Analysis/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a subset. Then $I$ is an open neighborhood of $x$ $I$ is open and $I$ is a neighborhood of $x$. Category:Definitions/Open Neighborhoods Category:Definitions/Real Numbers

label: Definition:Open Point
snippet: Let $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ be a topological space. Let $p \in S$ such that $\left\{{p}\right\} \in \tau$. That is, let $\left\{{p}\right\}$ be an open set of $T$. Then $p$ is an open point of $T$.

label: Definition:Open Rectangle
snippet: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $a_1, \ldots, a_n, b_1, \ldots, b_n$ be real numbers. The Cartesian product: $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \openint {a_i} {b_i} = \openint {a_1} {b_1} \times \cdots \times \openint {a_n} {b_n} \subseteq \R^n$ is called an open rectangle in $\R^n$ or open $n$-rectangle. The collection of all open $n$-rectangles is denoted $\JJ_o$, or $\JJ_o^n$ if the dimension $n$ is to be emphasized.

label: Definition:Open Rectangle/Degenerate Case
snippet: In the case where $a_i \ge b_i$ for some $i$, the open rectangle $\ds \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n \openint {a_i} {b_i}$ degenerates to the empty set $\O$. This is in accordance with the result Cartesian Product is Empty iff Factor is Empty for general Cartesian products. Category:Definitions/Open Rectangles

label: Definition:Open Refinement
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\UU$ and $\VV$ be covers of $S$. Then $\VV$ is an open refinement of $\UU$ : That is:

label: Definition:Open Region/Complex
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers. $D$ is an open region of $\C$ $D$ is: $(1): \quad$ An open set and $(2): \quad$ connected.

label: Definition:Open Set/Complex Analysis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers. Let: $\forall z_0 \in S: \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map {N_{\epsilon} } {z_0} \subseteq S$ where $\map {N_{\epsilon} } {z_0}$ is the $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $z_0$ for $\epsilon$. Then $S$ is an open set (of $\C$), or open (in $\C$). Note that $\epsilon$ may depend on $z_0$.

label: Definition:Open Set/Complex Analysis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers. Then $S$ is an open set (of $\C$), or open (in $\C$) every point of $S$ is an interior point.

label: Definition:Open Set/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $U \subseteq A$. Then $U$ is an open set in $M$ it is a neighborhood of each of its elements. That is: $\forall y \in U: \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map {B_\epsilon} y \subseteq U$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} y$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $y$. That is, for every point $y$ in $U$, we can find an $\epsilon \in \R_{>0}$, dependent on that $y$, such that the open $\epsilon$-ball of $y$ lies entirely inside $U$. Another way of saying the same thing is that one can not get out of $U$ by moving an arbitrarily small distance from any point in $U$.

label: Definition:Open Set/Normed Vector Space
snippet: Let $V = \struct {X, \norm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a normed vector space. Let $U \subseteq X$. Then $U$ is an open set in $V$ : $\forall x \in U: \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \map {B_\epsilon} x \subseteq U$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} x$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $x$.

label: Definition:Open Set/Pseudometric Space
snippet: Let $P = \struct {A, d}$ be a pseudometric space. An open set in $P$ is defined in exactly the same way as for a metric space: $U$ is an open set in $P$ : $\forall y \in U: \exists \map \epsilon y > 0: \map {B_\epsilon} y \subseteq U$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} y$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $y$.

label: Definition:Open Set/Real Analysis/Real Euclidean Space
snippet: Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $U \subseteq \R^n$ be a subset. Then $U$ is open (in $\R^n$) : $\forall x \in U : \exists R \in \R_{>0}: \map B {x, R} \subset U$ where $\map B {x, R}$ denotes the open Euclidean ball of radius $R$ centered at $x$.

label: Definition:Open Set/Real Analysis/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the set of real numbers. Then $I$ is open (in $\R$) : $\forall x_0 \in I: \exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \openint {x_0 - \epsilon} {x_0 + \epsilon} \subseteq I$ where $\openint {x_0 - \epsilon} {x_0 + \epsilon}$ is an open interval. Note that $\epsilon$ may depend on $x_0$.

label: Definition:Open Set/Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Then the elements of $\tau$ are called the open sets of $T$. Thus: $U \in \tau$ and: $U$ is open in $T$ are equivalent statements.

label: Definition:Open Set (Metric Space)/Also known as
snippet: == Open Set (Metric Space): Also known as == An open set in a metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ can also be referred to as: an open set of $M$ open in $M$ a $d$-open set $d$-open. An open set in $M$ is sometimes seen written as open subset of $A$.

label: Definition:Open Sigma-Discrete Set of Subsets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\UU$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $\UU$ is open $\sigma$-discrete : $(1) \quad \UU \subseteq \tau$, that is, for all $U \in \UU: U$ is open in $T$ $(2) \quad \UU$ is $\sigma$-discrete.

label: Definition:Open Sigma-Locally Finite Set of Subsets
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\UU$ be a set of subsets of $S$. Then $\UU$ is open sigma-locally finite : $(1) \quad \UU \subseteq \tau$, that is, for all $U \in \UU: U$ is open in $T$ $(2) \quad \UU$ is $\sigma$-locally finite

label: Definition:Open Subscheme
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a scheme. Let $U \subset X$ be an open subset. Then the open subscheme defined by $U$ is the restriction $\struct {U, \OO_X {\restriction_U}}$ of $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $U$.

label: Definition:Open Subset in Strong Operator Topology
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $\map {CL} {X, Y}$ be a continuous linear transformation space. Let $	au$ be the strong operator topology on $\map {CL} {X, Y}$. label: Definition:Operating Characteristic Curve
snippet: An operating characteristic curve is a graph showing the probability of accepting a batch as a function of the proportion of defectives in that batch.

label: Definition:Operation
snippet: An operation is an object, identified by a symbol, which can be interpreted as a process which, from a number of objects, creates a new object.

label: Definition:Operation/Arity/Zero
snippet: It is possible to conceive of an operator which takes no operands. A constant can be considered as an operation which takes no operands. That is, it has an arity of zero. There are circumstances in mathematics and logic in which it is advantageous to do so.

label: Definition:Operation/Binary Operation
snippet: A binary operation is the special case of an operation where the operation has exactly two operands. A binary operation is a mapping $\circ$ from the Cartesian product of two sets $S \times T$ to a universal set $\mathbb U$: $\circ: S \times T \to \mathbb U: \map \circ {s, t} = y \in \mathbb U$ If $S = T$, then $\circ$ can be referred to as a binary operation on $S$.

label: Definition:Operation/Binary Operation/Infix Notation
snippet: == Notation == Let $S, T, U$ be sets. Let $\circ: S \times T \to U$ be a binary operation. When $\map \circ {x, y} = z$, it is common to put the symbol for the operation between the two operands: $z = x \circ y$ This convention is called infix notation.

label: Definition:Operation/Binary Operation/Product
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let $\circ$ be the operation on $\struct {S, \circ}$. Let $z = x \circ y$. Then $z$ is called the product of $x$ and $y$. This is an extension of the normal definition of product that is encountered in conventional arithmetic.

label: Definition:Operation/N-Ary Operation
snippet: Let $S_1, S_2, \dots, S_n$ be sets. Let $\circ: S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n \to \mathbb U$ be a mapping from the cartesian product $S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n$ to a universal set $\mathbb U$: That is, suppose that: $\circ: S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n \to \mathbb U: \forall \tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n: \map \circ {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in \mathbb U$ Then $\circ$ is an $n$-ary operation. Such an $n$-ary operation needs to be defined for all ordered tuples in $S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n$.

label: Definition:Operation/Unary Operation
snippet: A unary operation is the special case of an operation where the operation has exactly one operand. Thus, a unary operation on a set $S$ is a mapping whose domain and codomain are both $S$.

label: Definition:Operation Compatible with Set Equivalence
snippet: Let $F$ be a (unary) operation which can be applied to sets. Then $F$ is compatible with set equivalence : $F \sqbrk A = F \sqbrk B \iff A \sim B$ where: $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary sets $F \sqbrk A$ denotes the image of $A$ under $F$ $\sim$ denotes set equivalence.

label: Definition:Operation Induced by Permutation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure on a set $S$. Let $\sigma: S \to S$ be a permutation on $S$. Let $\circ_\sigma$ be the operation on $S$ defined as: $\forall x, y \in S: x \circ_\sigma y := \map \sigma {x \circ y}$ Then $\circ_\sigma$ is the operation (on $S$) induced by $\sigma$.

label: Definition:Operation Induced by Restriction
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a magma. Let $\struct {T, \circ} \subseteq \struct {S, \circ}$. That is, let $T$ be a subset of $S$ such that $\circ$ is closed in $T$. Then the restriction of $\circ$ to $T$, namely $\circ {\restriction_T}$, is called the (binary) operation induced on $T$ by $\circ$. Note that this definition applies only if $\struct {T, \circ}$ is closed, by which virtue it is a submagma of $\struct {S, \circ}$.

label: Definition:Operations Research
snippet: Operations research is the branch of applied mathematics which studies the management of human organizations.

snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $P \sqbrk R$ be the set of all sequences in $R$: $P \sqbrk R = \set {\sequence {r_0, r_1, r_2, \ldots} }$ such that each $r_i \in R$, and all but a finite number of terms is zero. The operations ring addition $\oplus$, ring negative, and ring product $\odot$ on $P \sqbrk R$ are defined as follows: {{axiom | n = 1 | lc= Ring Addition: | ml= \sequence {r_0, r_1, r_2, \ldots} \oplus \sequence {s_0, s_1, s_2, \ldots} | mo= = | mr= \sequence {r_0 + s_0, r_1 + s_1, r_2 + s_2, \ldots} | c = }} {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= Ring Negative: | ml= -\sequence {r_0, r_1,…

label: Definition:Operator Domain
snippet: An operator domain is a notational tool for indexing a collection of operations on a set. Formally, an operator domain is a set $\Omega$ together with a mapping $a : \Omega \to \N_0$. We also use the notation, for $n \in \N_0$, $\Omega(n) = \{\omega \in \Omega : a(\omega) = n \}$. The elements of $\Omega$ are operators. If $\omega \in \Omega$, then $a(\omega)$ is the arity of the operator $\omega$. The elements of $\Omega(n)$ are the $n$-ary operators of $\Omega$.

label: Definition:Operator Norm
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A: \HH \to \HH$ be a bounded linear operator. Let $\norm A$ be the norm of $A$. Then $\norm A$ is referred to as the operator norm on $A$. Category:Definitions/Hilbert Spaces

label: Definition:Operator Theory
snippet: Operator theory is the study of linear operators on function spaces, beginning with differential operators and integral operators.

label: Definition:Opposite
snippet: Geometry: Opposite (in a Polygon): The opposite side (or angle) to a given side is that side (or angle) which has the same number of sides between it and the side in question. The opposite side (or angle) to a given angle is that side (or angle) which has the same number of sides between it and the angle in question. Opposite (in a Triangle): The side of a triangle which is not one of the sides adjacent to a particular angle is referred to as its opposite. Thus, each angle has an opposite side, and each side has an opposite angle.

label: Definition:Opposite Direction
snippet: Let $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ be vectors in space. We say that $\mathbf v$ is in the opposite direction to $\mathbf w$ : the lines of action of $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ are parallel but at the same time: the lines of action of $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ are not the same. Category:Definitions/Vectors

label: Definition:Opposite Magma
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {S, *}$ be magmas on $S$. $\struct {S, *}$ is the opposite magma of $\struct {S, \circ}$ : $\forall x_1, x_2, x_3 \in S: x_1 \circ x_2 = x_3 \iff x_2 * x_1 = x_3$ The operation $*$ is sometimes referred to as the opposite law of $\circ$.

label: Definition:Opposite Parity/Also known as
snippet: == Opposite Parity: Also known as == Some sources refer to a pair of integers $\set {z_1, z_2}$ having opposite parity as having odd parity. Note the difference between this and the definition of odd parity as being a property of an individual integer as being odd.

label: Definition:Optics
snippet: Optics is the branch of physics which studies the properties of light.

label: Definition:Optimization Theory
snippet: Optimization theory is a branch of mathematics whose aim is to find the "best" solution to a practical problem, often using techniques of numerical analysis. In this context, best is dependent upon the aim of what the solution of the problem is to achieve. Optimization theory encompasses such topics as: the calculus of variations control theory convex optimization theory decision theory game theory linear programming Markov chains network analysis queueing theory and so on.

label: Definition:Optimum Solution
snippet: The optimum solution of a problem in linear programming or optimization theory is the feasible solution which, according to the definition of the problem, is the most desirable.

label: Definition:Oracle Machine
snippet: An oracle machine is an extension of a Turing machine with an additional capability. In addition to manipulating the symbols on its tape (or tapes, in the case of a multitape Turing machine), it can determine if a value belongs to a given language $T$ in a single step.

label: Definition:Orbit
snippet: Group Theory: The orbits of a group action. Physics (and in particular celestial mechanics): The orbit of a body around another body. Dynamical Systems: Orbit of dynamical system: the set of values taken by a variable under an iterated mapping.

label: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$.

label: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$. The orbit of an element $x \in X$ is defined as: $\Orb x := \set {y \in X: \exists g \in G: y = g * x}$ where $*$ denotes the group action. That is, $\Orb x = G * x$. Thus the orbit of an element is all its possible destinations under the group action.

label: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$. Let $\RR$ be the relation on $X$ defined as: $\forall x, y \in X: x \mathrel \RR y \iff \exists g \in G: y = g * x$ where $*$ denotes the group action. From Group Action Induces Equivalence Relation, $\RR$ is an equivalence relation. The orbit of $x$, denoted $\Orb x$, is the equivalence class of $x$ under $\RR$.

label: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)/Length
snippet: Let $G$ be a group acting on a set $X$. Let $x \in X$. Let $\Orb x$ be the orbit of $x$. The length of the orbit $\Orb x$ of $x$ is the number of elements of $X$ it contains: $\size {\Orb x}$ Category:Definitions/Group Actions

label: Definition:Orbit (Group Theory)/Set of Orbits
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $X$ be a set Let $*: G \times S \to S$ be a group action. Let $\Orb x$ denote the orbit of $x \in X$. From Group Action Induces Equivalence Relation, the relation $\RR_G$ defined as: $x \mathrel {\RR_G} y \iff y \in \Orb x$ is an equivalence relation. The quotient set $X / \RR_G$ is called the set of orbits of $X$ under the action of $G$.

label: Definition:Orbit (Physics)
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies in space. The orbit of $A$ around $B$ is the path taken by $A$ as it travels around $B$ under the influence of the force acting between $A$ and $B$.

label: Definition:Orbit (Physics)/Period
snippet: Let body $A$ be in orbit around body $B$. The period of the orbit is the length of time it takes for $A$ to travel once around $B$ and return to its original position.

label: Definition:Order
snippet: Set Theory: Order of Set: Another word for the cardinality of a set. Abstract Algebra: Order of an Algebraic Structure Group Theory: Order of an Element in a Group Matrix Theory and Linear Algebra: Order of a Matrix Order of a Square Matrix Order of a Determinant Tensor Theory: Order of a Tensor: another term for the rank of a tensor. Number Theory: Multiplicative Order of an Integer: the least positive integer $c$ such that $a^c \equiv 1 \pmod n$. Order of a Sociable Chain: the number of members of a sociable chain.

label: Definition:Order-Convex Set/Definition 1
snippet: A subset $A$ of an ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is convex (in $S$) : $\forall x, y \in A: \forall z \in S: x \preceq z \preceq y \implies z \in A$

label: Definition:Order-Convex Set/Definition 2
snippet: A subset $A$ of an ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is order-convex (in $S$) : $\forall x, y \in A: \forall z \in S: x \prec z \prec y \implies z \in A$

label: Definition:Order-Convex Subset of Natural Numbers
snippet: Let $A \subseteq \N$ be a subset of the set of natural numbers. $A$ is defined as being order-convex (in $\N$) : $\forall x, y, z \in \N: \paren {x, z \in A \land x \le y \le z} \implies y \in A$

label: Definition:Order Category/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. One can interpret $\struct {S, \preceq}$ as being a category, with: More formally, we let the morphisms be the elements of the relation ${\preceq} \subseteq S \times S$. Thus, $a \to b$ in fact denotes the ordered pair $\tuple {a, b}$. The category that so arises is called an order category.

label: Definition:Order Category/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Then $\mathbf C$ is an order category : For all objects $C, C'$ of $\mathbf C$, there is at most one morphism $f: C \to C'$ Whenever $f: C \to C'$ is an isomorphism, $C = C'$ Thus, an order category is a skeletal preorder category.

label: Definition:Order Complete Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is order complete : Each non-empty subset $H \subseteq S$ which has an upper bound admits a supremum.

label: Definition:Order Complete Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is order complete : Each non-empty subset $H \subseteq S$ which has a lower bound admits an infimum.

label: Definition:Order Completion
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_S}$ be an ordered set. An ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq_T}$ is an order completion of $S$ : $(1):\quad S \subseteq T$ $(2):\quad {\preceq_T \restriction_S} = {\preceq_S}$, where $\restriction$ denotes restriction $(3):\quad \struct {T, \preceq_T}$ is a complete ordered set $(4):\quad$ For all ordered sets $\struct {T', \preceq_{T'} }$ satisfying $(1), (2)$ and $(3)$, there is a unique increasing injection $\phi: T' \to T$

label: Definition:Order Generating Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a preordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then $X$ is order generating : $\forall x \in S: x^\succeq \cap X$ admits an infimum and $x = \map \inf {x^\succeq \cap X}$

label: Definition:Order Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq_1}$ and $\struct {T, \preceq_2}$ be ordered sets.

label: Definition:Order Notation/Abuse of Notation
snippet: == Order Notation: Abuse of Notation == The concept of order notation is properly defined as sets of real sequences that fulfil certain properties a given real sequence. Some sources state that extending to general real functions is an abuse of notation, although an acceptable one.

label: Definition:Order Sum/Informal Interpretation
snippet: We can consider the order sum $\struct {S \preccurlyeq} := \struct {S_1 \preccurlyeq_1} \oplus \struct {S_2 \preccurlyeq_2}$ as: First the set $S_1$, ordered by $\preccurlyeq_1$ Then the set $S_2$, ordered by $\preccurlyeq_2$ Note that: $\forall x \in S_1, y \in S_2: \tuple {x, 0} \preccurlyeq \tuple {y, 1}$ That is, every element of $S_1$ is comparable with every element of $S_2$. Category:Definitions/Order Sums

label: Definition:Order Type of Rational Numbers
snippet: Consider the ordered set $\struct {\Q, \le}$ consisting of the set of rational numbers under the usual ordering $\le$. The order type of $\struct {\Q, \le}$ is denoted $\eta$ (eta).

label: Definition:Order Type of Rational Numbers/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Order Type of Rational Numbers == The use of $\eta$ to denote the order type of $\struct {\Q, \le}$ dates back to the writings of and . According to and in their of $1996$, this order type, along with that for $\struct {\R, \le}$, has not been greatly studied in recent years. $\eta$ is in fact far more often used to denote a general ordinal.

label: Definition:Order Type of Real Numbers
snippet: Consider the ordered set $\struct {\R, \le}$ consisting of the set of real numbers under the usual ordering $\le$. The order type of $\struct {\R, \le}$ is denoted $\lambda$ (lambda).

label: Definition:Order Unit
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \succeq}$ be a preordered vector space over the real numbers $\R$. Let $e \in X$. We call $e$ an order unit for $\struct {X, \succeq}$ : for each $x \in X$ there exists $n \in \N$ such that: $n e \succeq x \succeq -n e$

label: Definition:Order of Contact
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ and $g: \R \to \R$ be real functions. Then $f$ and $g$ have contact of order $k$ at the point $a \in \R$ : {{eqn | n = 1 | l = \map {f^{\paren i} } a | r = \map {g^{\paren i} } a | c = for $0 \le i \le k$ }} {{eqn | n = 2 | l = \map {f^{\paren {k + 1} } } a | o = \ne | r = \map {g^{\paren {k + 1} } } a }} where $f^{\paren n}$ denotes the $n$th derivative of $f$.

label: Definition:Order of Convergence
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence of numbers or vectors in a normed vector space. Let $\alpha \in \R$. Let $p \in \R_{\ge 1}$. Then $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $\alpha$ with order $p$ there exists a sequence $\sequence {\epsilon_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that: $(1): \quad \size {x_n - \alpha} \le \epsilon_n$ for every $n \in \N$ $(2): \quad \ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \frac {\epsilon_{n + 1} } { {\epsilon_n}^p} = c$ where $c > 0$ If $p = 1$, the constant $c$ is additionally required to be less than $1$.

label: Definition:Order of Convergence/First Order
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence of real numbers. Let $\alpha \in \R$. $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $\alpha$ with order $1$ there exists a sequence $\sequence {\epsilon_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that: $(1): \quad \size {x_n - \alpha} \le \epsilon_n$ for every $n \in \N$ $(2): \quad \ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \frac {\epsilon_{n + 1} } {\epsilon_n} = c$ where $0 < c < 1$.

label: Definition:Order of Convergence/Second Order
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be an infinite sequence of real numbers. Let $\alpha \in \R$. $\sequence {x_n}$ converges to $\alpha$ with order $2$ there exists a sequence $\sequence {\epsilon_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ such that: $\size {x_n - \alpha} \le \epsilon_n$ for every $n \in \N$ $(2): \quad \ds \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \frac {\epsilon_{n + 1} } { {\epsilon_n}^2} = c$ where $0 < c < 1$.

label: Definition:Order of Differential Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Order of Differential Equation: Also known as == Some sources refer to the order of a differential equation as its dimension. Category:Definitions/Order of Differential Equation

label: Definition:Order of Differential Equation/Warning
snippet: == Warning on Order of Differential Equation == Consider the ordinary differential equation: $y' ' - y' ' + y' - y = 0$ At first glance it looks as though it is of the $2$nd order. But after some (fairly obvious) simplification, it is seen that it can be written: $y' - y = 0$ which is of the $1$st order.

label: Definition:Order of Entire Function/Finite Order
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be an entire function. $f$ has finite order its order is a real number. Category:Definitions/Order of Entire Function

label: Definition:Order of Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Order of Matrix: Also known as == The order of a matrix can also be referred to as its dimensions, but the term dimension has a different, deeper meaning in linear algebra and this may be a source of confusion. Some sources refer to the size rather than order, which is acceptable enough. Others use the term type, but this word can have different connotations. Some sources do not bother to give the order an actual name, merely referring to, say, an $n \times m$ matrix.

label: Definition:Order of Pole
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function.

label: Definition:Order of Pole/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $z_0 \in U \subset \C$ be such that $f$ is holomorphic in $U \setminus \set {z_0}$, with a pole at $z_0$. By Existence of Laurent Series there is a series: $\ds \map f z = \sum_{n \mathop \ge n_0}^\infty a_j \paren {z - z_0}^n$ The order of the pole at $z_0$ is defined to be $\size {n_0} > 0$.

label: Definition:Order of Pole/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $z_0 \in U \subset \C$ be such that $f$ is holomorphic in $U \setminus \set {z_0}$, with a pole at $z_0$: By definition $z_0$ is a pole $f$ can be written in the form: $\map f z = \dfrac {\map \phi z} {\paren {z - z_0}^k}$ where: $\phi$ is analytic at $z_0$ $\map \phi {z_0} \ne 0$ $k \in \Z$ such that $k \ge 1$. The order of the pole at $z_0$ is defined to be $k$.

label: Definition:Order of Pole/Simple Pole
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $z_0 \in U \subset \C$ be such that $f$ is holomorphic in $U \setminus \set {z_0}$, with a pole at $z_0$. Let the order of the pole at $z_0$ be $1$. Then $z_0$ is a simple pole.

label: Definition:Order of Structure
snippet: The order of an algebraic structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ is the cardinality of its underlying set, and is denoted $\order S$. Thus, for a finite set $S$, the order of $\struct {S, \circ}$ is the number of elements in $S$.

label: Definition:Order of Structure/Finite Structure
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure. Let the underlying set $S$ of $\struct {S, \circ}$ be finite. Then $\struct {S, \circ}$ a finite structure. That is, $\struct {S, \circ}$ is a finite structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ is not an infinite structure.

label: Definition:Ordered Basis
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $G$ be a free $R$-module. An ordered basis of $G$ is a sequence $\sequence {a_k}_{1 \mathop \le k \mathop \le n}$ of elements of $G$ such that $\set {a_1, \ldots, a_n}$ is a basis of $G$.

label: Definition:Ordered Field Isomorphism
Definition:Ordered Geometry
snippet: Ordered geometry is a sub-branch of geometry which features the concept of betweenness but, like projective geometry, omitting the basic notion of distance.

label: Definition:Ordered Monoid
snippet: An ordered monoid is an ordered structure $\left({S, \circ, \preceq}\right)$ such that $\left({S, \circ}\right)$ is a monoid.

label: Definition:Ordered Pair
snippet: The definition of a set does not take any account of the order in which the elements are listed. That is, $\set {a, b} = \set {b, a}$, and the elements $a$ and $b$ have the same status - neither is distinguished above the other as being more "important".

label: Definition:Ordered Pair/Informal Definition
snippet: The definition of a set does not take any account of the order in which the elements are listed. That is, $\set {a, b} = \set {b, a}$, and the elements $a$ and $b$ have the same status -- neither is distinguished above the other as being more "important". An ordered pair is a two-element set together with an ordering. In other words, one of the elements is distinguished above the other - it comes first. Such a structure is written: $\tuple {a, b}$ and it means: first $a$, then $b$.

label: Definition:Ordered Pair/Kuratowski Formalization
snippet: The definition of a set does not take any account of the order in which the elements are listed. That is, $\set {a, b} = \set {b, a}$, and the elements $a$ and $b$ have the same status - neither is distinguished above the other as being more "important". The concept of an ordered pair can be formalized by the definition: $\tuple {a, b} := \set {\set a, \set {a, b} }$ This formalization justifies the existence of ordered pairs in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory.

label: Definition:Ordered Pair/Notation
snippet: In the field of symbolic logic and modern treatments of set theory, the notation $\sequence {a, b}$ is often seen to denote an ordered pair. In sources where the possibility of confusion is only minor, one can encounter $a \times b$ for $\tuple {a, b}$ on an ad hoc basis. These notations are not used on , where $\tuple {a, b}$ is used exclusively.

label: Definition:Ordered Set
snippet: An ordered set is a relational structure $\struct {S, \preceq}$ such that the relation $\preceq$ is an ordering. Such a structure may be: A partially ordered set (poset) A totally ordered set (toset) A well-ordered set (woset) depending on whether the ordering $\preceq$ is: A partial ordering A total ordering A well-ordering.

label: Definition:Ordered Set of All Mappings
snippet: Let $L = \struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $X$ be a set. The ordered set of all mappings from $X$ to $L$ is defined by: $L^X := \struct {S^X, \precsim}$ where $\forall f, g \in S^X: f \precsim g \iff f \preceq g$ $\preceq$ denotes the ordering on mappings, $S^X$ denotes the set of all mappings from $X$ into $S$.

label: Definition:Ordered Set of Closure Systems
snippet: Let $L$ be an ordered set. The ordered set of closure systems of $L$ is a relational structure $\operatorname{ClSystems}\left({L}\right) = \left({X, \precsim}\right)$ where $X$ is the set of all closure systems of $L$, dor all closure systems $S_1 = \left({T_1, \preceq_1}\right), S_2 = \left({T_2, \preceq_2}\right)$ of $L$: $S_1 \precsim S_2 \iff T_1 \subseteq T_2$

label: Definition:Ordered Set of Subalgebras
snippet: Let $L$ be an ordered set. The ordered set of subalgebras of $L$ is ordered subset of $\operatorname{ClSystems}\left({L}\right)$ and is defined by $\operatorname{Subalgeras}\left({L}\right) := \left({X, \precsim}\right)$ where $X$ is the set of all directed suprema inheriting closure systems on $L$, $\operatorname{ClSystems}\left({L}\right)$ denotes the ordered set of closure systems on $L$.

label: Definition:Ordered Statistic
snippet: Let $X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_N$ be a sequence of $N$ independent random variables chosen from an identical probability space. Let $X_{(1)},X_{(2)},X_{(3)},\ldots,X_{(N)}$ be these measures re-arranged in increasing order. Then $X_{(i)}$ is said to be the $i$th ordered statistic. Category:Definitions/Probability Theory

label: Definition:Ordered Structure Monomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ and $\struct {T, *, \preccurlyeq}$ be ordered structures. An ordered structure monomorphism from $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ to $\struct {T, *, \preccurlyeq}$ is a mapping $\phi: S \to T$ that is both: $(1): \quad$ A monomorphism, i.e. an injective homomorphism, from the structure $\struct {S, \circ}$ to the structure $\struct {T, *}$ $(2): \quad$ An order embedding from the ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$ to the ordered set $\struct {T, \preccurlyeq}$.

label: Definition:Ordered Subsemigroup
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ be an ordered structure. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$ such that: $\struct {T, \circ_T, \preceq_T}$ is an ordered semigroup where: $\circ_T$ denotes the operation induced on $T$ by $\circ$ $\preceq_T$ denotes the restriction of $\preceq$ to $T \times T$. Then $\struct {T, \circ_T, \preceq_T}$ is an ordered subsemigroup of $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$.

So either: (a) $\struct{S, \preceq}$ needs to be ordered; (b) $\struct{S', \preceq'}$ needs to be ordered; or (c) the page needs to be renamed. label: Definition:Ordered Triple/Also known as
snippet: == Ordered Triple: Also known as == An ordered triple is also sometimes seen named an ordered triad. Some sources refer to it as just a triple, but it is usually important to stress that it is in fact ordered, so as not to confuse with a set with $3$ elements. Some sources use the term $3$-tuple.

label: Definition:Ordered Tuple
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $\N^*_n$ be the first $n$ non-zero natural numbers: $\N^*_n := \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$

label: Definition:Ordered Tuple/Also defined as
snippet: == Ordered Tuple: Also defined as == Some treatments take the intuitive approach of regarding an ordered tuple merely as an ordered set, that is, without stressing the fact of it being a mapping from a subset of the natural numbers:

label: Definition:Ordered Tuple/Also known as
snippet: Some sources refer to an ordered tuple as a tuple. The term ordered $n$-tuple or just $n$-tuple can sometimes be seen, particularly for specific instances of $n$. Instead of writing $2$-tuple, $3$-tuple and $4$-tuple, the terms couple, triple and quadruple are usually used. However, beware of couple, as this has a completely different meaning in the context of mechanics. In the context of abstract algebra, the concept is encountered as (associative) word. It is noted that an ordered tuple is in fact a one-dimensional array.

label: Definition:Ordered Tuple/Empty
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. The empty ordered tuple on $S$ is the empty mapping: $\O \to S$ from the empty set $\O$ to $S$. It is justified to call this an ordered tuple because the "first $0$ non-zero natural numbers" form the empty set: $\N^*_0 = \O$

label: Definition:Ordered Tuple/Notation
snippet: Notation for an ordered tuple varies throughout the literature. There are also specialised instances of an ordered tuple where the convention is to use angle brackets. However, it is common for an ordered tuple to be denoted: $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ extending the notation for an ordered pair. For example: $\tuple {6, 3, 3}$ is the ordered triple $f$ defined as: $\map f 1 = 6, \map f 2 = 3, \map f 3 = 3$ The notation: $\sequence {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ is recommended when use of round brackets would be ambiguous.

label: Definition:Ordered Tuple/On Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $s: \N^*_n \to S$ be an ordered tuple. Then $s$ is called an ordered tuple on $S$, its codomain.

label: Definition:Ordered Tuple/Ordered Couples and Ordered Pairs
snippet: Notice the difference between ordered pairs and ordered couples. By definition, an ordered couple $\tuple {a, b}$ is in fact the set $\set {\tuple {1, a}, \tuple {2, b} }$, where each of $\tuple {1, a}$ and $\tuple {2, b}$ are ordered pairs. It is not possible to use the definition of ordered couple as the definition of ordered pair, as the latter is used to define a mapping, which is then used to define an ordered couple.

label: Definition:Ordered Tuple as Ordered Set
snippet: The rigorous definition of an ordered tuple is as a finite sequence whose domain is $\N^*_n$. However, it is possible to treat an ordered tuple as an extension of the concept of an ordered pair.

label: Definition:Ordered Tuple as Ordered Set/Ordered Triple
snippet: The ordered triple $\tuple {a, b, c}$ of elements $a$, $b$ and $c$ can be defined either as the ordered pair: $\tuple {a, \tuple {b, c} }$ or as the ordered pair: $\tuple {\tuple {a, b}, c}$ where $\tuple {a, b}$ and $\tuple {b, c}$ are themselves ordered pairs. Whichever definition is chosen does not matter much, as long as it is understood which is used. And even then, the importance is limited.

label: Definition:Ordering/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\RR$ be a relation $\RR$ on $S$. $\RR$ is an ordering on $S$ $\RR$ satisfies the ordering axioms:

label: Definition:Ordering/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\RR$ be a relation $\RR$ on $S$. $\RR$ is an ordering on $S$ $\RR$ satisfies the ordering axioms:

label: Definition:Ordering/Notation
snippet: Symbols used to denote a general ordering relation are usually variants on $\preceq$, $\le$ and so on. On , to denote a general ordering relation it is recommended to use $\preceq$ and its variants: $\preccurlyeq$ $\curlyeqprec$ To denote the conventional ordering relation in the context of numbers, the symbol $\le$ is to be used, or its variants: $\leqslant$ $\leqq$ $\eqslantless$ The symbol $\subseteq$ is universally reserved for the subset relation. If, for two elements $a, b \in S$, it is not the case that $a \preceq b$, then the symbols $a \npreceq b$ and $b \nsucceq a$ can be used.

label: Definition:Ordering/Size
snippet: An ordering can often be considered to be a comparison of the size of objects, perhaps in some intuitive sense. This is particularly applicable in the context of numbers. Thus the expression $A \preceq B$ can in such contexts be interpreted as: $A$ is smaller than $B$ $A$ is less than $B$ and $B \preceq A$ can similarly be interpreted as: $A$ is larger than $B$ $A$ is greater than $B$ In natural language, such terms are called [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparative comparative adjectives], or just comparatives.

label: Definition:Ordering Induced by Injection
snippet: Let $\left({T, \le}\right)$ be an ordered set, and let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to T$ be an injection. Define $\le_f$ as the ordering induced by $f$ on $S$ by: $\forall s_1, s_2 \in S: s_1 \le_f s_2 \iff f \left({s_1}\right) \le f \left({s_2}\right)$ That $\le_f$ is in fact an ordering is shown on Ordering Induced by Injection is Ordering.

label: Definition:Ordering of Cuts/Strict
snippet: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be cuts. $\alpha$ and $\beta$ conventionally have the following strict ordering imposed on them, as follows: $\alpha$ is less than $\beta$, denoted $\alpha \alpha$.

label: Definition:Ordering on Extended Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\overline \R$ denote the extended real numbers. Extend the natural ordering $\le_\R$ on $\R$ to $\overline \R = \R \cup \set {+\infty, -\infty}$ by imposing: $\forall x \in \overline \R: -\infty \le x$ $\forall x \in \overline \R: x \le +\infty$ That is, considering the relations $\le$ and $\le_\R$ as subsets of $\overline \R \times \overline \R$: ${\le} := {\le_\R} \cup \set {\tuple {x, +\infty}: x \in \overline \R} \cup \set {\tuple {-\infty, x}: x \in \overline \R}$ where $\tuple {x, +\infty}$ and $\tuple {-\infty, x}$ denote ordered pairs in $\overline \R \times \overline \R$.

label: Definition:Ordering on Integers/Definition 1
snippet: The integers are ordered on the relation $\le$ as follows: $\forall x, y \in \Z: x \le y$ $\exists c \in P: x + c = y$ where $P$ is the set of positive integers. That is, $x$ is less than or equal to $y$ $y - x$ is non-negative.

label: Definition:Ordering on Integers/Definition 2
snippet: The integers are ordered on the relation $\le$ as follows: Let $x$ and $y$ be defined as from the formal definition of integers: $x = \eqclass {x_1, x_2} {}$ and $y = \eqclass {y_1, y_2} {}$ where $x_1, x_2, y_1, y_2 \in \N$. Then: $x < y \iff x_1 + y_2 \le x_2 + y_1$ where: $+$ denotes natural number addition $\le$ denotes natural number ordering.

label: Definition:Ordering on Mappings
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\left({T, \preceq}\right)$ be an ordered set. Let $f, g: S \to T$ be mappings. Then ordering on mappings $f$ and $g$ denoted $f \preceq g$ is defined by $\forall s \in S: f\left({s}\right) \preceq g\left({s}\right)$

label: Definition:Ordering on Multiindices
snippet: Let $Z$ be the set of multiindices. We define an ordering on $Z$ as follows. Let: $k = \sequence {k_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ $\ell = \sequence {\ell_j}_{j \mathop \in J}$ be multiindices. Then we write: $k \preceq \ell$ $\paren {\forall j \in J} \paren {k_j \le \ell_j}$ By abuse of notation, it is standard to use $\le$ to denote the ordering on the set of multiindices as well.

label: Definition:Ordinal/Also known as
snippet: == Ordinal: Also known as == An ordinal is also known as an ordinal number. For a given well-ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$, the expression: $\map {\mathrm {Ord} } S$ can be used to denote the unique ordinal which is order isomorphic to $\struct {S, \preceq}$.

label: Definition:Ordinal/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be a set. $\alpha$ is an ordinal it fulfils the following conditions: {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= $\Epsilon {\restriction_\alpha}$ strictly well-orders $\alpha$ }} where $\Epsilon {\restriction_\alpha}$ is the restriction of the epsilon relation to $\alpha$.

label: Definition:Ordinal/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be a set. $\alpha$ is an ordinal it fulfils the following conditions:

label: Definition:Ordinal/Definition 3
snippet: An ordinal is a strictly well-ordered set $\struct {\alpha, \prec}$ such that: $\forall \beta \in \alpha: \alpha_\beta = \beta$ where $\alpha_\beta$ is the initial segment of $\alpha$ determined by $\beta$: $\alpha_\beta = \set {x \in \alpha: x \prec \beta}$

label: Definition:Ordinal/Definition 4
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be a set. $\alpha$ is an ordinal : $\alpha$ is an element of every superinductive class.

label: Definition:Ordinal/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Ordinal == The concept of a ordinal was first introduced by .

label: Definition:Ordinal/Informal Definition
snippet: A natural number considered as an indication of the position in a sequence of objects is referred to as an ordinal number.

label: Definition:Ordinal/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Ordinal == The class of all ordinals can be found denoted $\On$. In order to indicate that a set $S$ is an ordinal, this notation is often seen: $\Ord S$ whose meaning is: $S$ is an ordinal. Thus $\operatorname {Ord}$ can be used as a propositional function whose domain is the class of all sets. A tradition has grown up in set theory to use lowercase Greek letters $\alpha, \ \beta, \ \gamma, \ldots$ as symbols to represent variables over ordinals. It is also customary to denote the ordering relation between ordinals as $\le$ rather than $\subseteq$ or $\preceq$.

snippet: Let $x$ and $y$ be ordinals. The operation of ordinal addition $x + y$ is defined using the Second Principle of Transfinite Recursion on $y$, as follows.

label: Definition:Ordinal Data
snippet: Ordinal data are data which have a natural numerical ordering associated with them.
