label: Definition:Ordinal Function
snippet: Let $A$ be an ordinal (we shall allow $A$ to be a proper class). Then the mapping $G : A \to \On$ is called an ordinal function.

label: Definition:Ordinal Multiplication
snippet: Let $x$ and $y$ be ordinals. The operation of ordinal multiplication $x \times y$ is defined using the Second Principle of Transfinite Recursion as follows:

label: Definition:Ordinal Sequence
snippet: An ordinal sequence is a mapping $\theta$ whose domain is an ordinal $\alpha$. That is, the domain of $\theta$ is the set of all ordinals $\gamma$ such that $\gamma < \alpha$. Such a sequence can be referred to as an $\alpha$-sequence. Hence an $\On$-sequence is a mapping whose domain is the class of all ordinals $\On$.

label: Definition:Ordinal Sequence/Length
snippet: Let $\alpha$ be an ordinal. Let $\theta$ be an ordinal sequence whose domain is $\alpha$. Then $\alpha$ can be referred to as the length of $\theta$. The length of $\theta$ can be denoted $\size \theta$.

label: Definition:Ordinal Space/Closed
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal. The closed ordinal space on $\Gamma$ is the set $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ of all ordinal numbers less than or equal to $\Gamma$, together with the order topology. Particular special cases of a closed ordinal space are as follows:

label: Definition:Ordinal Space/Closed/Countable
snippet: Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal. The countable closed ordinal space on $\Gamma$ is a particular case of a closed ordinal space $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ where $\Gamma < \Omega$. That is, it is the set $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ of all ordinal numbers less than or equal to $\Gamma < \Omega$, together with the order topology.

label: Definition:Ordinal Space/Closed/Uncountable
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal. Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal. The uncountable closed ordinal space on $\Omega$ is the particular case of a closed ordinal space $\closedint 0 \Gamma$ where $\Gamma = \Omega$. That is, it is the set $\closedint 0 \Omega$ of all ordinal numbers less than or equal to $\Omega$, together with the order topology.

label: Definition:Ordinal Space/Open
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal. The open ordinal space on $\Gamma$ is the set $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ of all ordinal numbers (strictly) less than $\Gamma$, together with the order topology. Particular special cases of an open ordinal space are as follows:

label: Definition:Ordinal Space/Open/Countable
snippet: Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal. Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal such that $\Gamma < \Omega$. The countable open ordinal space on $\Gamma$ is a particular case of an open ordinal space $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ where $\Gamma < \Omega$. That is, it is the set $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ of all ordinal numbers (strictly) less than $\Gamma < \Omega$, together with the order topology.

label: Definition:Ordinal Space/Open/Uncountable
snippet: Let $\Gamma$ be a limit ordinal. Let $\Omega$ denote the first uncountable ordinal. The uncountable open ordinal space on $\Omega$ is the particular case of an open ordinal space $\hointr 0 \Gamma$ where $\Gamma = \Omega$. That is, it is the set $\hointr 0 \Omega$ of all ordinal numbers (strictly) less than $\Omega$, together with the order topology.

label: Definition:Ordinal Subtraction
snippet: Let $x$ and $y$ be ordinals such that $x \le y$. Then the operation of ordinal subtraction is defined as: $y - x = \bigcup \set {z: x + z = y}$

label: Definition:Ordinal Sum
snippet: Let $y$ be an ordinal. Let $\sequence {A_x}$ be a sequence of ordinals. The ordinal sum of $A_x$ is denoted $\ds \sum_{x \mathop = 1}^y A_x$ and defined using the Second Principle of Transfinite Recursion on $y$ as follows: $\ds \sum_{x \mathop = 1}^\O A_x = \O$ $\ds \sum_{x \mathop = 1}^{z^+} A_x = \sum_{x \mathop = 1}^z \paren {A_x} + A_{z^+}$ $\ds \sum_{x \mathop = 1}^y A_x = \bigcup_{z \mathop \in y} \paren {\sum_{x \mathop = 1}^z A_x}$ for limit ordinals $y$. Category:Definitions/Ordinal Arithmetic

label: Definition:Ordinal Variable
snippet: An ordinal variable is a categorical variable whose values has a natural ordering.

label: Definition:Ordinary Differential Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Ordinary Differential Equation: Also known as == The term ordinary differential equation is often presented in its abbreviated form ODE or O.D.E.

label: Definition:Ordinary Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Then $S$ is an ordinary set : $S \notin S$ That is, $S$ is not an element of itself.

label: Definition:Ordinary Space
snippet: Ordinary space (or just space) is a word used to mean the universe we live in. The intuitive belief is that space is $3$-dimensional and therefore isomorphic to the real vector space $\R^3$. Hence ordinary space is usually taken as an alternative term for Euclidean $3$-dimensional space.

label: Definition:Ordinate
snippet: Consider the graph $y = \map f x$ of a real function $f$ embedded in a Cartesian plane. 500px The $y$ coordinate of a point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ on $f$ is known as the ordinate of $P$.

label: Definition:Ore Number
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer. $n$ is an Ore number the harmonic mean of its divisors is an integer.

label: Definition:Orientation
snippet: Graph Theory Orientation: a property of digraphs Topology Orientation of Differential Manifold Analytic Geometry Orientation of Coordinate Axes: the general disposition of the coordinate axes relative to each other

label: Definition:Orientation of Contour (Complex Plane)/Negative/Simple Closed
snippet: Let $C$ be a simple closed contour in the complex plane $\C$ with parameterization $\gamma: \closedint a b \to \C$. Set $K := \set { t \in \closedint a b : \textrm{ $\gamma$ is not differentiable at $t$ } }$. Let $\Int C$ denote the interior of $C$ Then $C$ is negatively oriented, for all $t \in \openint a b \setminus K$, there exists $r \in \R_{>0}$ such that: for all $\epsilon \in \openint 0 r$ : $\map \gamma t - \epsilon i \map {\gamma'} t \in \Int C$ Alternatively, we say that $C$ has a negative orientation.

label: Definition:Orientation of Contour (Complex Plane)/Positive/Simple Closed
snippet: Let $C$ be a simple closed contour in the complex plane $\C$ with parameterization $\gamma: \closedint a b \to \C$. Set $K := \set { t \in \closedint a b : \textrm{ $\gamma$ is not differentiable at $t$ } }$. Let $\Int C$ denote the interior of $C$ Then $C$ is positively oriented, for all $t \in \openint a b \setminus K$, there exists $r \in \R_{>0}$ such that: for all $\epsilon \in \openint 0 r$ : $\map \gamma t + \epsilon i \map {\gamma'} t \in \Int C$ Alternatively, we say that $C$ has a positive orientation.

label: Definition:Orientation of Coordinate Axes/Cartesian 3-Space/Left-Handed
snippet: A Cartesian $3$-Space is defined as being left-handed if it has the following property: Let a left hand be placed such that: the thumb and index finger are at right-angles to each other the $3$rd finger is at right-angles to the thumb and index finger, upwards from the palm the thumb points along the $x$-axis in the positive direction the index finger points along the $y$-axis in the positive direction. Then the $3$rd finger is pointed along the $z$-axis in the positive direction. 320px

label: Definition:Orientation of Coordinate Axes/Cartesian 3-Space/Right-Handed
snippet: A Cartesian $3$-Space is defined as being right-handed if it has the following property: Let a right hand be placed such that: the thumb and index finger are at right-angles to each other the $3$rd finger is at right-angles to the thumb and index finger, upwards from the palm the thumb points along the $x$-axis in the positive direction the index finger points along the $y$-axis in the positive direction. Then the $3$rd finger is pointed along the $z$-axis in the positive direction. 450px

label: Definition:Orientation of Coordinate Axes/Cartesian Plane/Left-Handed
snippet: A Cartesian plane is defined as being left-handed if it has the following property: Let a left hand be placed, with palm uppermost, such that the thumb points along the $x$-axis in the positive direction, such that the thumb and index finger are at right-angles to each other. Then the index finger is pointed along the $y$-axis in the positive direction. 320px

label: Definition:Orientation of Coordinate Axes/Cartesian Plane/Right-Handed
snippet: A Cartesian plane is defined as being right-handed if it has the following property: Let a right hand be placed, with palm uppermost, such that the thumb points along the $x$-axis in the positive direction, such that the thumb and index finger are at right-angles to each other. Then the index finger is pointed along the $y$-axis in the positive direction. 320px

label: Definition:Orientation of Differential Manifold
snippet: An orientation of a differential manifold is a continuous choice of orientation for each of its tangent spaces.

label: Definition:Oriented Manifold
snippet: An oriented manifold is a smooth orientable manifold together with a choice of orientation. If $M$ is an oriented $n$-manifold, then a smooth coordinate chart $\left(U,\left(x^i\right)\right)$ is said to be an oriented chart if the coordinate frame $\left(\partial / \partial x^1, \ldots, \partial / \partial x^n\right)$ is positively oriented at each point.

label: Definition:Orthic Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. Let $\triangle DEF$ be the triangle formed by the feet of the altitudes $AD$, $BC$ and $ED$ of $\triangle ABC$. 420px $\triangle DEF$ is known as the orthic triangle of $\triangle ABC$. That is, the orthic triangle of $\triangle ABC$ is the pedal triangle of its orthocenter.

label: Definition:Orthic Triangle/Also known as
snippet: == Orthic Triangle: Also known as == The orthic triangle of a given triangle $\triangle ABC$ is also known as the pedal triangle of $\triangle ABC$. However, as this term is also used for the pedal triangle of an arbitrary point $\triangle ABC$, it is the policy of to use the term orthic triangle consistently.

label: Definition:Orthocenter
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. The orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$ is where its three altitudes meet. 500px

label: Definition:Orthogonal
snippet: Analytic Geometry: Orthogonal (Analytic Geometry) Orthogonal Curves Orthogonal Coordinate System: Orthogonal Curvilinear Coordinates Rectangular Coordinate System Orthogonal Trajectories Linear Algebra: Orthogonal (Linear Algebra) Orthogonal (Bilinear Form) Orthogonal (Quadratic Form) Hilbert Spaces: Orthogonal Difference Matrix Algebra: Orthogonal Matrix Group Theory: Orthogonal Group

label: Definition:Orthogonal/Also known as
snippet: == Orthogonal: Also known as == Two objects that are orthogonal are often seen described as perpendicular. However, the latter usually used where those objects are straight lines or planes. Category:Definitions/Orthogonality (Geometry)

label: Definition:Orthogonal (Bilinear Form)
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $b: V \times V \to \mathbb K$ be a reflexive bilinear form on $V$. Let $v,w\in V$. Then $v$ and $w$ are orthogonal (with respect to $b$) $\map b {v, w} = \map b {w, v} = 0$ This is denoted: $v \perp w$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal (Bilinear Form)/Orthogonal Complement
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $b : V\times V \to \mathbb K$ be a reflexive bilinear form on $V$. Let $S\subset V$ be a subset. The orthogonal complement of $S$ (with respect to $b$) is the set of all $v \in V$ which are orthogonal to all $s \in S$. This is denoted: $S^\perp$. If $S = \set v$ is a singleton, we also write $v^\perp$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal (Bilinear Form)/Radical
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $b : V\times V \to \mathbb K$ be a reflexive bilinear form on $V$. The radical of $V$ is the orthogonal complement of $V$: $\map {\operatorname {rad} } V = V^\perp$

label: Definition:Orthogonal (Bilinear Form)/Subsets
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $b: V \times V \to \mathbb K$ be a reflexive bilinear form on $V$. Let $S, T \subset V$ be subsets. Then $S$ and $T$ are orthogonal for all $s \in S$ and $t \in T$, $s$ and $t$ are orthogonal: $s \perp t$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal (Linear Algebra)/Orthogonal Complement
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be an inner product space. Let $S\subseteq V$ be a subset. We define the orthogonal complement of $S$ (with respect to $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$), written $S^\perp$ as the set of all $v \in V$ which are orthogonal to all $s \in S$. That is: $S^\perp = \set {v \in V : \innerprod v s = 0 \text { for all } s \in S}$ If $S = \set v$ is a singleton, we may write $S^\perp$ as $v^\perp$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal (Linear Algebra)/Orthogonal Complement/Also known as
snippet: == Orthogonal Complement: Also known as == The orthogonal complement of a subset $A$ of an inner product space is also known as its orthocomplement. The operation of assigning the orthogonal complement $A^\perp$ to $A$ is referred to as orthocomplementation.

label: Definition:Orthogonal (Linear Algebra)/Set
snippet: Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be an inner product space. Let $S = \set {u_1, \ldots, u_n}$ be a subset of $V$. Then $S$ is an orthogonal set its elements are pairwise orthogonal: $\forall i \ne j: \innerprod {u_i} {u_j} = 0$

label: Definition:Orthogonal Basis/Bilinear Space
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $\struct {V, f}$ be a bilinear space over $\mathbb K$ of finite dimension $n > 0$. Let $\BB = \tuple {b_1, \ldots, b_n}$ be an ordered basis of $V$. Then $\BB$ is orthogonal : $\map f {b_i, b_j} = 0$ for $i \ne j$. That is, the matrix of $f$ relative to $\BB$ is diagonal.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Basis of Vector Space
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. Let $\BB = \tuple {\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n}$ be a basis of $V$. Then $\BB$ is an orthogonal basis $\mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2, \ldots, \mathbf e_n$ are pairwise perpendicular.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Curves
snippet: Let $C_1$ and $C_2$ be curves that intersect at a point $P$. $C_1$ and $C_2$ are orthogonal at $P$ the tangent line to $C_1$ at $P$ is at right angles to the tangent line to $C_2$ at $P$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Curves/Circles
snippet: Two circles are orthogonal if their angle of intersection is a right angle. 540px

label: Definition:Orthogonal Curvilinear Coordinates/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\KK$ be a curvilinear coordinate system in $3$-space. Let $\QQ_1$, $\QQ_2$ and $\QQ_3$ denote the one-parameter families that define the curvilinear coordinates. Let the relation between those curvilinear coordinates and Cartesian coordinates be expressed as: {{eqn | l = x | r = \map x {q_1, q_2, q_3} }} {{eqn | l = y | r = \map y {q_1, q_2, q_3} }} {{eqn | l = z | r = \map z {q_1, q_2, q_3} }} where: $\tuple {x, y, z}$ denotes the Cartesian coordinates of an arbitrary point $P$ $\tuple {q_1, q_2, q_3}$ denotes the curvilinear coordinates of $P$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Difference
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. Let $M, N$ be closed linear subspaces of $H$. Then the orthogonal difference of $M$ and $N$, denoted $M \ominus N$, is the set $M \cap N^\perp$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Functions
snippet: Let $S = \set {f_1, f_2, \ldots}$ be a set of real functions that are integrable over the closed real interval $\closedint a b$. Let $S$ be such that: $\forall m, n: m \ne n \implies \innerprod {f_m} {f_n} = 0$ where $\innerprod {f_m} {f_n}$ denotes the inner product of $f_m$ and $f_n$: $\innerprod {f_m} {f_n} := \ds \int_a^b \map {f_m} x \map {f_n} x \rd x$ Then $S$ is a set of orthogonal functions.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Group
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. The ($n$th) orthogonal group (on $k$), denoted $\map {\mathrm O} {n, k}$, is the following subset of the general linear group $\GL {n, k}$: $\map {\mathrm O} {n, k} := \set {M \in \GL {n, k}: M^\intercal = M^{-1} }$ where $M^\intercal$ denotes the transpose of $M$. Further, $\map {\mathrm O} {n, k}$ is considered to be endowed with conventional matrix multiplication. That is, the ($n$th) orthogonal group (on $k$) is the set of all orthogonal order-$n$ square matrices over $k$ under (conventional) matrix multiplication.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Group/Bilinear Form
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $\mathbb K$. Let $B: V \times V \to \mathbb K$ be a nondegenerate bilinear form. Its orthogonal group $\map {\mathrm O} B$ is the group of invertible linear transformations $g \in \GL V$ such that: $\forall v, w \in V : \map B {g v, g w} = \map B {v, w}$

label: Definition:Orthogonal Group/Inner Product Space
snippet: Let $V$ be an inner product space. Its orthogonal group $\map {\mathrm O} V$ is the group of invertible linear transformations $g \in \GL V$ such that: $\forall v, w \in V: \innerprod {g v} {g w} = \innerprod v w$ That is, it is the orthogonal group of its inner product.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Latin Squares
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be Latin squares of order $n$. Let $\left[{a}\right]_{i j}$ and $\left[{b}\right]_{i j}$ be the elements of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ respectively whose indices are $i$ and $j$. Then $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ are orthogonal : for all $i$ and $j$, the ordered pairs $\left({\left[{a}\right]_{i j}, \left[{b}\right]_{i j}}\right)$ are distinct. That is, $\left({\left[{a}\right]_{i j}, \left[{b}\right]_{i j}}\right)$ appears no more than once for every ordered pair $\left({i, j}\right)$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Latin Squares/Mutually Orthogonal
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $S$ be a set of Latin squares of order $n$. Then the $S$ is mutually orthogonal every element of $S$ is orthogonal to every other element of $S$. Category:Definitions/Latin Squares

label: Definition:Orthogonal Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf Q$ be a nonsingular square matrix over a field $\GF$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Matrix/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf Q$ be a nonsingular square matrix over a field $\GF$. Then $\mathbf Q$ is orthogonal : $\mathbf Q^{-1} = \mathbf Q^\intercal$ where: $\mathbf Q^{-1}$ is the inverse of $\mathbf Q$ $\mathbf Q^\intercal$ is the transpose of $\mathbf Q$

label: Definition:Orthogonal Matrix/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf Q$ be a nonsingular square matrix over a field $\GF$. Then $\mathbf Q$ is orthogonal : $\mathbf Q^\intercal \mathbf Q = \mathbf I$ where: $\mathbf Q^\intercal$ is the transpose of $\mathbf Q$ $\mathbf I$ is the identity matrix of the same order as $\mathbf Q$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Matrix/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\mathbf Q$ be a nonsingular square matrix over a field $\GF$. Then $\mathbf Q$ is orthogonal : $\mathbf Q = \paren {\mathbf Q^\intercal}^{-1}$ where: $\mathbf Q^\intercal$ is the transpose of $\mathbf Q$ $\paren {\mathbf Q^\intercal}^{-1}$ is the inverse of $\mathbf Q^\intercal$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Polynomials
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of polynomials over the real numbers $\R$: $S = \set {\map {p_0} x, \map {p_1} x, \map {p_2} x, \ldots}$ such that $p_n$ is of degree $n$. The elements of $S$ are orthogonal a closed real interval $\closedint a b$ and a continuous non-negative weight function $\map w x$ on $\closedint a b$ : $\ds \int_a^b \map w x \map {p_i} x \map {p_j} x \rd x = 0$ for all $i \ne j$.

label: Definition:Orthogonal Projection
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. Let $K$ be a closed linear subspace of $H$. Then the orthogonal projection on $K$ is the mapping $P_K: H \to H$ defined by $k = \map {P_K} h \iff k \in K$ and $\map d {h, k} = \map d {h, K}$ where the latter $d$ signifies distance to a set. That $P_K$ is indeed a mapping is proved on Orthogonal Projection is Mapping. The name orthogonal projection stems from the fact that $\paren {h - \map {P_K} h} \perp K$.

label: Definition:Orthonormal Frame
snippet: Let $M$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $U \subseteq M$ be an open set. Let $p \in M$ be a point. Let $T_p M$ be a tangent space of $M$ at $p$. Let $\tuple {E_i}$ be the local frame for $M$ on $U$. Suppose for each $p \in U$ the vectors $\bigvalueat {E_i} p$ are an orthonormal basis for $T_p M$. Then $\tuple {E_i}$ is said to be an orthonormal frame.

label: Definition:Orthonormal Functions
snippet: Let $S = \set {f_1, f_2, \ldots}$ be a set of real functions that are integrable over the closed real interval $\closedint a b$. Let $S$ be a set of orthogonal functions which are also normal functions. Then $S$ is a set of orthonormal functions.

label: Definition:Orthonormal Subset
snippet:
Let $\struct {V, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be an inner product space. Let $S \subseteq V$ be a subset of $V$. Then $S$ is an orthonormal subset (of $V$) : $(1): \quad  orall u \in S: 
orm u = 1$ where $
orm {\, \cdot \,}$ is the inner product norm. $(2): \quad S$ is an orthogonal set: $ orall u, v \in S: u 
e v \implies \innerprod u v = 0$

label: Definition:Oscillating Sequence
snippet: Let $S$ be one of the standard number fields $\Q$, $\R$ or $\C$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $S$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be divergent. Suppose $\sequence {x_n}$ is not unbounded. That is, let: $\neg x_n \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ Then $\sequence {x_n}$ is an oscillating sequence.

label: Definition:Oscillation
snippet: Analysis: Oscillation: a measure of the diameter of the image of a subset under a mapping Physics Oscillation: a regular fluctuation in the magnitude of the displacement of a body

label: Definition:Oscillation/Metric Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\struct {Y, d}$ be a metric space. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a mapping.

label: Definition:Oscillation/Metric Space/Point
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\struct {Y, d}$ be a metric space. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a mapping. Let $x \in X$. Let $\tau$ be a topology on $X$, thus making $\struct {X, \tau}$ a topological space. Denote with $\NN_x$ the set of neighborhoods of $x$ in $\struct {X, \tau}$. The oscillation of $f$ at $x$ with respect to $d$, denoted by $\map {\omega_f} {x; d}$, is defined as: $\ds \map {\omega_f} {x; d} := \inf_{U \mathop \in \NN_x} \map {\omega_f} {U; d}$ where $\map {\omega_f} {U; d}$ denotes the oscillation of $f$ on $U$.

label: Definition:Oscillation/Metric Space/Set
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\struct {Y, d}$ be a metric space. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a mapping. Let $A \subseteq X$ be any non-empty subset $A$ of $X$. The oscillation of $f$ on (or over) $A$ with respect to $d$, denoted $\map {\omega_f} {A; d}$, is defined as the diameter of $f \sqbrk A$: $\ds \map {\omega_f} {A; d} := \map \diam {f \sqbrk A} = \sup_{x, y \mathop \in A} \map d {\map f x, \map f y}$ where the supremum is taken in the extended real numbers $\overline \R$.

label: Definition:Oscillation/Real Space
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be real sets. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function.

label: Definition:Oscillation/Real Space/Oscillation at Point
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be real sets. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function. Let $x \in X$.

label: Definition:Oscillation/Real Space/Oscillation at Point/Epsilon
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be real sets. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function. Let $x \in X$. The oscillation of $f$ at $x$ is defined as: $\ds \map {\omega_f} x := \inf \set {\map {\omega_f} {\openint {x - \epsilon} {x + \epsilon} \cap X}: \epsilon \in \R_{>0} }$ where $\map {\omega_f} {\openint {x - \epsilon} {x + \epsilon} \cap X}$ denotes the oscillation of $f$ on $\openint {x - \epsilon} {x + \epsilon} \cap X$.

label: Definition:Oscillation/Real Space/Oscillation at Point/Infimum
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be real sets. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function. Let $x \in X$. Let $\NN_x$ be the set of neighborhoods of $x$. The oscillation of $f$ at $x$ is defined as: $\ds \map {\omega_f} x := \inf_{U \mathop \in \NN_x} \map {\omega_f} {U \cap X}$ where $\map {\omega_f} {U \cap X}$ denotes the oscillation of $f$ on $U \cap X$.

label: Definition:Oscillation/Real Space/Oscillation at Point/Limit
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be real sets. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function. Let $x \in X$. The oscillation of $f$ at $x$ is defined as: $\ds \map {\omega_f} x := \lim_{h \mathop \to 0^+} \map {\omega_f} {\openint {x - h} {x + h} \cap X}$ where $\map {\omega_f} {\openint {x - h} {x + h} \cap X}$ denotes the oscillation of $f$ on $\openint {x - h} {x + h} \cap X$.

label: Definition:Oscillation/Real Space/Oscillation on Set
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be real sets. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a real function. Let $A \subseteq X$ be any non-empty subset $A$ of $X$. The oscillation of $f$ on (or over) $A$ is defined as: $\ds \map {\omega_f} A := \sup_{x, y \mathop \in A} \size {\map f x - \map f y}$ where the supremum is taken in the extended real numbers $\overline \R$. Category:Definitions/Oscillation

label: Definition:Oscillation (Physics)/Also known as
snippet: == Oscillation in context of Physics: Also known as == Oscillation is also known as vibration. This term is usually restricted to the context of mechanics.

label: Definition:Osculating Circle/Definition 1
snippet: Let $I \subseteq \R$ be an open subset of real numbers. Let $\gamma : I \to \R^2$ be a curve defined by a twice differentiable vector-valued function. Let $P$ be a point on $\gamma$. Let $\kappa_P$ be the curvature of $\gamma$ at $P$. Suppose $C$ is a circle such that: $P \in C$ the tangent to $\gamma$ at $P$ is also a tangent to $C$ at $P$ the radius of $C$ at $P$ is equal to $\dfrac 1 {\size {\kappa_P} }$ the center of $C$ is on the inner (concave) side of $\gamma$. Then $C$ is called the osculating circle of $\gamma$ at $P$.

label: Definition:Osculating Circle/Definition 2
snippet: Let $I, I' \subseteq \R$ be open subsets of real numbers. Let $\gamma : I \to \R^2$ be a curve defined by a twice differentiable vector-valued function. Let $C: I' \to \R$ be a circle. Let both $\gamma$ and $C$ have the unit-speed parameterization. Let $P$ be a point on $\gamma$. Suppose $C$ is such that: $P \in C$ $\map {\gamma'} P = \map {C'} P$ $\map {\gamma' '} P = \map {C' '} P$ Then $C$ is called the osculating circle of $\gamma$ at $P$.

label: Definition:Osculating Plane
snippet: Let $C$ be a twisted curve. Let $P$ be a point on $C$. The osculating plane to $C$ at $P$ is the limiting position of a plane through $P$ and two other points $P'$ and $P' '$ also on $C$, as $P'$ and $P' '$ approach $P$.

label: Definition:Outer Jordan Content
snippet: Let $M \subseteq \R^n$ be a bounded subspace of Euclidean $n$-space. Let $\CC$ be the set of all finite coverings of $M$ by closed $n$-rectangles. The outer Jordan content of $M$ is defined as denoted as: $\ds \map {m^*} M = \inf_{C \mathop \in \CC} \sum_{R \mathop \in C} \map V R$ where: $\ds \inf_{C \mathop \in \CC}$ denotes the greatest lower bound. $\map V R$ denotes the content of the rectangle $R$.

label: Definition:Outer Limit
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) topological space. Let $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of sets in $X$. The outer limit of $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is defined as: $\ds \limsup_{n \mathop \to \infty} \ C_n := \set {x \in X: \exists N \text { cofinal set of } \N, \exists x_v \in C_v \paren {v \in N} \text{ such that } x_v \to x}$ where $x_v \to x$ denotes convergence in the topology $\tau$.

label: Definition:Outer Measure
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\powerset X$ be the power set of $X$. An outer measure (on $X$) is a mapping: $\mu^*: \powerset X \to \overline \R_{\ge 0}$ that satisfies the following conditions: $(1): \quad \map {\mu^*} \O = 0$ $(2): \quad \forall A, B \in \powerset X: A \subseteq B \implies \map {\mu^*} A \le \map {\mu^*} B$ (that is, $\mu^*$ is monotone) $(3): \quad \ds \map {\mu^*} {\bigcup_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty A_i} \le \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^\infty \map {\mu^*} {A_i}$ for all sequences $\sequence {A_i}_{i \mathop \in \N} \in \powerset X$ (that is, $\mu^*$ is countably subadditive) where…

label: Definition:Outlier
snippet: An outlier is an observation which departs significantly from the general shape of a set of data. This may either be: a genuine observation which reflects an abnormality in some measurable property being observed a mistake either in the measurement or its recording.

label: Definition:Oval
snippet: An oval is a geometric figure resembling an elongated circle in some way, but which may not actually be an ellipse.

label: Definition:Ovals of Cassini
snippet: Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be points in the plane such that $P_1 P_2 = 2 a$ for some constant $a$. The ovals of Cassini are the loci of points $M$ in the plane such that: $P_1 M \times P_2 M = b^2$ for a real constant $b$.

label: Definition:Ovals of Cassini/Also known as
snippet: == Ovals of Cassini: Also known as == The ovals of Cassini are also known as: Cassini's ovals the Cassini ovals the Cassini ellipses (despite the fact that they are not actually ellipses).

label: Definition:Ovals of Cassini/Shape
snippet: Let $P_1$ and $P_2$ be points in the plane such that $P_1 P_2 = 2 a$ for some constant $a$. Let the ovals of Cassini be defined as the loci of points $M$ in the plane such that: $P_1 M \times P_2 M = b^2$ for real constant $b$. When $b > a$, $M$ is in one continuous piece, either oval or bone-shaped. When $b < a$, $M$ is in two separate pieces, each surrounding one of the foci of $M$. When $b = a$, $M$ degenerates into the lemniscate of Bernoulli. 630px

label: Definition:Overlapping Interval Topology
snippet: Let $S = \closedint {-1} 1$ denote the open real interval: $\closedint {-1} 1 = \set {x \in \R: -1 \le x \le 1}$ Let $\BB$ be the set: $\BB = \set {\hointl a 1: -1 < a < 0} \cup \set {\hointr {-1} b: 0 < b < 1}$ where: $\hointl a 1$ is the half-open interval $\set {x \in \R: a < x \le 1}$. $\hointr {-1} b$ is the half-open interval $\set {x \in \R: -1 \le x < b}$. Then $\BB$ is the sub-basis for a topology $\tau$ on $\closedint {-1} 1$. $\tau$ is referred to as the overlapping interval topology. The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the overlapping interval space.

label: Definition:P-Closure of Relation
snippet: Let $\RR = \struct {S, T, R}$ be a relation on the sets $S$ and $T$: $R \subseteq S \times T$ Let $P$ be a property of relations. Let $\RR' = \struct {S, T, R'}$ be the relation on $S \times T$ such that: $R \subseteq R'$ $\RR'$ is the smallest relation on $S \times T$ with respect to the subset ordering on $S \times T$ $R'$ has the property $P$. Then $\RR'$ is known as the $P$-closure of $\RR$.

label: Definition:P-Element
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be a group. Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $x \in G$ be an element of $G$. Then $x$ is a $p$-element of $G$ its order is a power of $p$.

label: Definition:P-Group
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime integer. A $p$-group (either finite or infinite) is a group whose elements are all $p$-elements.

label: Definition:P-Norm
snippet: Let $p \ge 1$ be a real number. Let $\BB$ be a Banach space. Let $\ell^p$ denote the $p$-sequence space in $\BB$: $\ds \ell^p := \set {\sequence {s_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} \in \BB^\N: \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \norm {s_n}^p < \infty}$ Let $\mathbf s = \sequence {s_n} \in \ell^p$ be a sequence in $\ell^p$. Then the $p$-norm of $\mathbf s$ is defined as: $\ds \norm {\mathbf s}_p = \paren {\sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \size {s_n}^p}^{1 / p}$ This is often presented in expository treatments either on the real number line or the complex plane:

label: Definition:P-Norm/Complex
snippet: Let $p \ge 1$ be a real number. Let $\C$ denote the complex plane. Let ${\ell^p}_\C$ denote the complex $p$-sequence space: $\ds {\ell^p}_\C := \set {\sequence {z_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} \in \C^\N: \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \cmod {z_n}^p < \infty}$ Let $\mathbf z = \sequence {z_n} \in {\ell^p}_\C$ be a sequence in ${\ell^p}_\C$. Then the $p$-norm of $\mathbf z$ is defined as: $\ds \norm {\mathbf z}_p = \paren {\sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \cmod {z_n}^p}^{1 / p}$

label: Definition:P-Norm/Real
snippet: Let $p \ge 1$ be a real number. Let $\R$ denote the real number line. Let ${\ell^p}_\R$ denote the real $p$-sequence space: $\ds {\ell^p}_\R := \set {\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} \in \R^\N: \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \size {x_n}^p < \infty}$ Let $\mathbf x = \sequence {x_n} \in {\ell^p}_\R$ be a sequence in ${\ell^p}_\R$. Then the $p$-norm of $\mathbf x$ is defined as: $\ds \norm {\mathbf x}_p = \paren {\sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \size {x_n}^p}^{1 / p}$

label: Definition:P-Product Metric
snippet: Let $M_{1'} = \struct {A_{1'}, d_{1'} }$ and $M_{2'} = \struct {A_{2'}, d_{2'} }$ be metric spaces. Let $A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$ be the cartesian product of $A_{1'}$ and $A_{2'}$. Let $p \in \R_{\ge 1}$. The $p$-product metric on $A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$ is defined as: $\map {d_p} {x, y} := \paren {\paren {\map {d_{1'} } {x_1, y_1} }^p + \paren {\map {d_{2'} } {x_2, y_2} }^p}^{1/p}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2} \in A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$. The metric space $\MM_p := \struct {A_{1'} \times A_{2'}, d_p}$ is the $p$-product (space) of $M_{1'}$ and $M_{2'}$.

label: Definition:P-Product Metric/General Definition
snippet: Let $M_{1'} = \struct {A_{1'}, d_{1'} }, M_{2'} = \struct {A_{2'}, d_{2'} }, \ldots, M_{n'} = \struct {A_{n'}, d_{n'} }$ be metric spaces. Let $\ds \AA = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_{i'}$ be the cartesian product of $A_{1'}, A_{2'}, \ldots, A_{n'}$. Let $p \in \R_{\ge 1}$. The $p$-product metric on $\AA$ is defined as: $\ds \map {d_p} {x, y} := \paren {\sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \paren {\map {d_{i'} } {x_i, y_i} }^p}^{\frac 1 p}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n} \in \AA$.

label: Definition:P-Sequence Metric/Real Sequences
snippet: Let $A$ be the set of all real sequences $\sequence {x_i}$ such that the series $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \ge 0} x_i^2$ is convergent. Let $d_p: A \times A: \to \R$ be the real-valued function defined as: $\ds \forall x = \sequence {x_i}, y = \sequence {y_i} \in A: \map {d_p} {x, y} := \paren {\sum_{k \mathop \ge 0} \size {x_k - y_k}^p}^{\frac 1 p}$ The metric space $\struct {A, d_p}$ is the $p$-sequence space on $\R$ and is denoted $\ell^p$.

label: Definition:P-Sequence Space
snippet:
Let $p \in \R$ be a real number such that $p \ge 1$. Let $\BB$ be a Banach space. The $p$-sequence space (in $\BB$), denoted $\ell^p$ or $\map {\ell^p} \N$, is defined as: $\ds \ell^p := \set {\sequence {s_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} \in \BB^\N: \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty 
orm {s_n}^p < \infty}$ where: $\BB^\N$ is the set of all sequences in $\BB$ $
orm {s_n}$ denotes the norm of $s_n$. That is, the $p$-sequence space is the set of all sequences in $\BB$ such that $
orm {s_n}^p$ converges to a limit.

label: Definition:P-Sequence Space/Complex
snippet: Let $p \in \R$ be a real number such that $p \ge 1$. Let $\C$ denote the complex plane. The $p$-sequence space (in $\C$), denoted ${\ell^p}_\C$, is defined as: $\ds {\ell^p}_\C := \set {\sequence {z_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} \in \C^\N: \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \cmod {z_n}^p < \infty}$ where: $\C^\N$ is the set of all sequences in $\C$ $\cmod {z_n}$ denotes the modulus of $z_n$. That is, the $p$-sequence space is the set of all sequences in $\C$ such that $\size {z_n}^p$ converges to a limit. Thus ${\ell^p}_\C$ is a subspace of $\C^\N$, the space of all complex sequences.

label: Definition:P-Sequence Space/Complex/Also denoted as
snippet: == Complex $p$-Sequence Space: Also denoted as == The complex $p$-sequence space ${\ell^p}_\C$ is often denoted just as $\ell^p$ when there is no confusion as to what the underlying set is. Some sources use the form $\map { {\ell^p}_\C} \N$ when it is necessary to bring attention to the fact that the domain of the sequences is the natural numbers. That is, that the sequences in question are infinite. Category:Definitions/P-Sequence Spaces

label: Definition:P-Sequence Space/Real
snippet: Let $p \in \R$ be a real number such that $p \ge 1$. Let $\R$ denote the real number line. The $p$-sequence space (in $\R$), denoted ${\ell^p}_\R$, is defined as: $\ds {\ell^p}_\R := \set {\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N} \in \R^\N: \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \size {x_n}^p < \infty}$ where: $\R^\N$ is the set of all sequences in $\R$ $\size {x_n}$ denotes the absolute value of $x_n$. That is, the $p$-sequence space is the set of all sequences in $\R$ such that $\size {x_n}^p$ converges to a limit.

label: Definition:P-Sequence Space/Real/Also denoted as
snippet: == Real $p$-Sequence Space: Also denoted as == The real $p$-sequence space ${\ell^p}_\R$ is often denoted just as $\ell^p$ when there is no confusion as to what the underlying set is. Some sources use the form $\map { {\ell^p}_\R} \N$ when it is necessary to bring attention to the fact that the domain of the sequences is the natural numbers. That is, that the sequences in question are infinite. Category:Definitions/P-Sequence Spaces

label: Definition:P-Series
snippet: Let $p \in \C$ be a complex number. The series defined as: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {n^p} = 1 + \frac 1 {2^p} + \frac 1 {3^p} + \frac 1 {4^p} + \dotsb$ is known as a $p$-series.

label: Definition:P-Series/Also defined as
snippet: == $p$-Series: Also known as == Authors whose focus is on real analysis define a $p$-series for real $p$ only.

label: Definition:P-Value
snippet: Let $\delta$ be a hypothesis test. Let $H_0$ and $H_1$ be the null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis of $\delta$ respectively. Let $T$ be the test statistic which is being used to determine whether $H_0$ or $H_1$ holds. Let $C$ be the critical region of $\delta$. Let $\alpha$ be the significance level of $\delta$. The $p$-value of $\delta$ is the probability that $T$ takes a value greater than or equal to a calculated value when $H_0$ is true.

label: Definition:P-adic Digit
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. The $p$-adic digits are the natural numbers $\set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, p - 1}$.

label: Definition:P-adic Expansion
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. A $p$-adic expansion is a series in the rational numbers $\Q$ of the form: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = m}^\infty d_n p^n$ where: $m \in \Z_{\le 0}$ $\forall n \in \Z_{\ge m}: d_n$ is a $p$-adic digit $m < 0 \implies d_m \ne 0$

label: Definition:P-adic Integer
snippet: Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers for some prime $p$.

label: Definition:P-adic Integer/Definition 1
snippet:
Let $\struct {\Q_p, 
orm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers for some prime $p$. An element $x \in \Q_p$ is called a $p$-adic integer $
orm x_p \le 1$. The set of all $p$-adic integers is usually denoted $\Z_p$. Thus: $\Z_p = \set {x \in \Q_p: 
orm x_p \le 1}$

label: Definition:P-adic Integer/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers for some prime $p$. An element $x \in \Q_p$ is called a $p$-adic integer the canonical expansion of $x$ contains only positive powers of $p$. The set of all $p$-adic integers is usually denoted $\Z_p$. Thus: $\ds \Z_p = \set {\sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty d_n p^n : \forall n \in \N: 0 \le d_n < p} = \set{\ldots d_n \ldots d_3 d_2 d_1 d_0 : \forall n \in \N: 0 \le d_n < p}$

label: Definition:P-adic Integer/Notation
snippet: == Notation == Let $\Z_p$ denote the $p$-adic integers for some prime $p$. The notation $\Z_p$ is also used for the ring of integers modulo $p$ where $p$ is a prime number. On the context of any page where $\Z_p$ appears will define what is referred to by $\Z_p$. Category:Definitions/P-adic Integers

snippet: == Historical Note on P-adic Number == The $p$-adic numbers were invented by in $1897$ in order to bring the methods of power series to number theoretical problems.

label: Definition:P-adic Number Theory
snippet: P-adic number theory is the branch of mathematics which studies the properties of the $p$-adic numbers.

label: Definition:P-adic Topology
snippet: Let $\Z$ denote the set of integers. Let $p \in \Z$ be a fixed prime number. Let $\BB$ be the set of all sets $\map {U_\alpha} n$ defined as: $\map {U_\alpha} n = \set {n + \lambda p^\alpha: \lambda \in \Z}$ Then $\BB$ is the basis for a topology $\tau$ on $S$. $\tau$ is referred to as the $p$-adic topology (on $\Z$). The topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is referred to as the $p$-adic (topological) space.

label: Definition:P-adic Unit
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$ be the $p$-adic numbers. Let $\Z_p$ denote the $p$-adic integers. The set of $p$-adic units, denoted $\Z_p^\times$, is the set of invertible elements of $\Z_p$.

Definition:P-adically Coherent Sequence
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\sequence {\alpha_n}$ be an integer sequence such that: $(1): \quad \forall n \in \N: 0 \le \alpha_n \le p^{n + 1} - 1$ $(2): \quad \forall n \in \N: \alpha_{n + 1} \equiv \alpha_n \pmod {p^{n + 1}}$ The sequence $\sequence {\alpha_n}$ is said to be a coherent sequence. If it is necessary to emphasize the choice of prime $p$ then the sequence $\sequence {\alpha_n}$ is said to be a $p$-adically coherent sequence.

label: Definition:Paasche Index
snippet: Let the prices of a set of $k$ commodities in the base year be $p_{0 1}, p_{0 2}, \ldots, p_{0 k}$. Let the quantities sold of each of those $k$ commodities in the base year be $q_{0 1}, q_{0 2}, \ldots, q_{0 k}$. Let the corresponding prices and quantities of those $k$ commodities in the $n$th year after the base year be $p_{n 1}, p_{n 2}, \ldots, p_{n k}$ and $q_{n 1}, q_{n 2}, \ldots, q_{n k}$. The Paasche index is the index number calculated as: $L_{0 n} = \dfrac {\ds \sum_j p_{n j} \, q_{n j} } {\ds \sum_j p_{0 j} \, q_{n j} }$

label: Definition:Padé Approximation
snippet: Padé approximation is a technique whereby a function $f$ is approximated by a rational function $f'$ such that the numerator and denominator are: polynomials with specified degree chosen so that the Maclaurin series of $f$ and $f'$ agree to as many terms as possible.

label: Definition:Painlevé-Kuratowski Convergence
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) topological space. Let $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of sets in $T$. Let $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be such that: $\ds \liminf_n C_n = \limsup_n C_n = C$ where: $\ds \liminf_n C_n$ denotes the inner limit of $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ $\ds \limsup_n C_n$ denotes the outer limit of $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ Then $\sequence {C_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is said to be convergent in the sense of Painlevé-Kuratowski.

label: Definition:Pairwise Coprime/Euclidean Domain
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \times}$ be a Euclidean domain. A subset $S \subseteq D$ is pairwise coprime (in $D$) : $\forall x, y \in S: x \ne y \implies x \perp y$ where $x \perp y$ denotes that $x$ and $y$ are coprime.

label: Definition:Pairwise Coprime/GCD Domain
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \times}$ be a GCD domain. A subset $S \subseteq D$ is pairwise coprime (in $D$) : $\forall x, y \in S: x \ne y \implies x \perp y$ where $x \perp y$ denotes that $x$ and $y$ are coprime.

label: Definition:Pairwise Coprime/Integers
snippet: A set of integers $S$ is pairwise coprime : $\forall x, y \in S: x \ne y \implies x \perp y$ where $x \perp y$ denotes that $x$ and $y$ are coprime.

label: Definition:Pairwise Disjoint/Set of Sets
snippet: A set of sets $\Bbb S$ is said to be pairwise disjoint : $\forall X, Y \in \Bbb S: X \ne Y \implies X \cap Y = \O$ Here, $\cap$ denotes intersection, and $\O$ denotes the empty set. Hence we can say that the elements of $\Bbb S$ are pairwise disjoint.

label: Definition:Pairwise Disjoint Events
snippet: Let $\family {A_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of events in a probability space. Then $\family {A_i}$ is pairwise disjoint : $\forall i, j \in I, i \ne j: A_i \cap A_j = \O$ That is, a set of events is pairwise disjoint every pair of them is disjoint.

label: Definition:Pairwise Orthogonal
snippet: Let $\sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$.

label: Definition:Pairwise Orthogonal/Columns
snippet: Let $\sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$. The columns of $\sqbrk a_{m n}$ are described as pairwise orthogonal : $\forall i, j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}, i \ne j: c_i \cdot c_j = 0$ That is, the dot product of each pair of distinct columns of $\sqbrk a_{m n}$, when considered as vectors, is zero.

label: Definition:Pairwise Orthogonal/Rows
snippet: Let $\sqbrk a_{m n}$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$. The rows of $\sqbrk a_{m n}$ are described as pairwise orthogonal : $\forall i, j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, m}, i \ne j: {r_i}^\intercal \cdot {r_j}^\intercal = 0$ That is, the dot product of each pair of distinct rows of $\sqbrk a_{m n}$, when transposed and considered as vectors, is zero.

label: Definition:Pairwise Perpendicular
snippet: Let $S = \set {L_1, L_2, \ldots, L_n}$ be a set of lines in a Euclidean space. Then the elements of $S$ are pairwise perpendicular $\forall i, j \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}, i \ne j:$ $L_i$ and $L_j$ are perpendicular to each other.

label: Definition:Palindromic Number
snippet: A palindromic number (base $b$) is a number which is a palindrome when expressed in number base $b$. That is, it reads the same reversed as it does forwards. When the base is not specified, it is commonplace to understand it as being $10$.

label: Definition:Palindromic Prime
snippet: A palindromic prime is a prime number which is also a palindromic number.

label: Definition:Palindromic Prime/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Palindromic Primes == The sequence of palindromic primes begins: $2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 101, 131, 151, 181, 191, 313, 353, 373, 383, 727, 757, 787, 797, 919, 929, \ldots$

label: Definition:Pandiagonal Magic Square
snippet: A pandiagonal magic square is an arrangement of $n^2$ numbers into an $n \times n$ square array such that: the sum of the elements of each row the sum of the elements in each column the sum of the elements along each diagonal the sum of the elements along each broken diagonal are the same. Hence a pandiagonal magic square is a magic square, with the added property of the broken diagonals.

label: Definition:Pandigital Set
snippet: A set of integers is pandigital it contains exactly $1$ instance of each digit.

label: Definition:Pandigital Set/Also defined as
snippet: == Pandigital Set: Also defined as == Some sources refer to penholodigital sets as pandigital sets which do not contain zero. By extension, the same applies to penholodigital integers. prefers the more esoteric term penholodigital for such sets in order to reduce possible confusion and ambiguity. Category:Definitions/Pandigital Sets

label: Definition:Pandigital Set/Penholodigital
snippet: A set of integers is penholodigital it contains exactly $1$ instance of each digit excluding $0$.

label: Definition:Parabola/Directrix
snippet: 300px Let $K$ be an [Definition:Focus-Directrix Property of Parabola|parabola]] specified in terms of: a given straight line $D$ a given point $F$ where $K$ is the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ equals the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$: $p = q$ The line $D$ is known as the directrix of the parabola.

label: Definition:Parabola/Focus
snippet: 300px Let $K$ be a parabola specified in terms of: a given straight line $D$ a given point $F$ where $K$ is the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ equals the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$: $p = q$ The point $F$ is known as the focus of the parabola.

label: Definition:Parabola/Focus-Directrix
snippet: 300px Let $D$ be a straight line. Let $F$ be a point. Let $K$ be the locus of points $P$ such that the distance $p$ from $P$ to $D$ equals the distance $q$ from $P$ to $F$: $p = q$ Then $K$ is a parabola.

label: Definition:Parabola/Vertex
snippet: 420px Let $P$ be a parabola. The vertex of $P$ is the point where the axis intersects $P$. In the above diagram, $V$ is the vertex of $P$.

label: Definition:Paraboloid
snippet: A paraboloid is a figure whose sections parallel to at least one plane are parabolas.

label: Definition:Paracompact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a paracompact space : every open cover of $T$ has an open refinement which is locally finite.

label: Definition:Paracompactness Property
snippet: A paracompactness property is a property that specifies a form of (topological) compactness of a topological space concerning the concept of a refinement of a cover.

label: Definition:Paradox
snippet: A paradox is a statement or group of statements that leads to one of the following:

label: Definition:Paradox/Logical
snippet: A logical paradox is a paradox which arises from the application of formal techniques of propositional or predicate logic. Hence a logical paradox arises from an inherent contradiction in the set of axioms.

label: Definition:Parallactic Angle
snippet: Let $x$ be a point on the celestial sphere. Let $\SS_1$ be the arc of the great circle between $x$ and the zenith. Let $\SS_2$ be the arc of the great circle between $x$ and the north celestial pole. The parallactic angle is defined as the (spherical) angle between $\SS_1$ and $\SS_2$.

label: Definition:Parallel
snippet: Geometry: Parallel: Parallel Lines Parallel Planes Line Parallel to Plane Matroid Theory: Parallel Elements of Matroid

label: Definition:Parallel (Geometry)/Line to Plane
snippet: Let $L$ be a straight line. Let $P$ be a plane. Then $L$ and $P$ are parallel , when produced indefinitely, they do not intersect at any point.

label: Definition:Parallel (Geometry)/Lines
snippet: ' The contemporary interpretation of the concept of parallelism declares that a straight line is parallel to itself.

label: Definition:Parallel (Geometry)/Planes
snippet: Two planes are parallel , when produced indefinitely, do not intersect at any point. The contemporary interpretation of the concept of parallelism declares that a plane is parallel to itself.

label: Definition:Parallel (Geometry)/Surfaces
snippet: Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be surfaces in ordinary space. Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ have the property that: for every point $P$ on $S_1$, a normal vector passing through $P$ is also a normal vector to $S_2$ and: for every point $Q$ on $S_2$, a normal vector passing through $Q$ is also a normal vector to $S_1$. Then $S_1$ and $S_2$ are parallel.

label: Definition:Parallel Transport Map
snippet: Let $I \subseteq \R$ be an open real interval. Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $v \in T_{\map \gamma {t_0} } M$. Let $V$ be the parallel transport of $v$ along $\gamma$. Then the parallel transport map is defined as the map: $P_{t_0 t_1}^\gamma : T_{\map \gamma {t_0} } M \to T_{\map \gamma {t_1} } M$ such that: $\forall v \in T_{\map \gamma {t_0} } M : \map {P_{t_0 t_1}^\gamma} v = \map V {t_1}$

label: Definition:Parallel of Altitude
snippet: Let $X$ be a point on the celestial sphere. Let $LXM$ be a small circle through $X$ which is parallel to the celestial horizon. Then $LXM$ is a parallel of altitude, and is such that all celestial bodies on it have the same altitude.

label: Definition:Parallel of Declination
snippet: Let $X$ be a point on the celestial sphere. Let $LXM$ be a small circle through $X$ which is parallel to the celestial equator. Then $LXM$ is a parallel of declination, and is such that all celestial bodies on it have the same declination. 500px

label: Definition:Parallel of Latitude
snippet: Let $J$ be a point on Earth's surface that is not one of the two poles $N$ and $S$. Let $C$ be the small circle through $J$ parallel to the plane containing the equator. Then $C$ is known as the parallel of latitude of $J$. Thus $C$ consists of all the points on Earth's surface which have the same latitude as $J$. 500px

label: Definition:Parallelepiped/Height
snippet: 400px The height of a parallelepiped is the length of the perpendicular between the planes of the bases. In the above diagram, $h$ is the height of the parallelepiped one of whose bases is $AB$.

label: Definition:Parallelepiped/Right
snippet: A right parallelepiped is a parallelepiped whose lateral faces are square or rectangular.

label: Definition:Parallelogram/Altitude
snippet: 450px An altitude of a parallelogram is a line drawn perpendicular to its base, through one of its vertices to the side opposite to the base (which is extended if necessary). In the parallelogram above, line $DE$ is an altitude of the parallelogram $ABCD$. The term is also used for the length of such a line.

label: Definition:Parameter
snippet: A parameter is a constant or a variable that distinguishes special cases of a general mathematical expression.

label: Definition:Parameter/Also defined as
snippet: == Parameter: Also defined as == In the context of predicate logic, a parameter is another term for proper name, or constant symbol. Category:Definitions/Parameters

label: Definition:Parameter Space
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some population. The parameter space of $\theta$, typically denoted $\Omega$, is the domain of $\theta$. That is, it is the set of all possible values that $\theta$ can take.

label: Definition:Parameter of Differential Equation
snippet: Let $f$ be a differential equation with general solution $F$. A parameter of $F$ is an arbitrary constant arising from the solving of a primitive during the course of obtaining the solution of $f$.

label: Definition:Parameterization
snippet: A parameterization is an expression of a curve or a surface, and so on, by means of a set of parametric equations.

label: Definition:Parametric Equation
snippet: Let $\map \RR {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a relation on the variables $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$. Let the truth set of $\RR$ be definable as: $\forall k \in \N: 1 \le k \le n: x_k = \map {\phi_k} t$ where: $t$ is a variable whose domain is to be defined each of $\phi_k$ is a mapping whose domain is the domain of $t$ and whose codomain is the domain of $x_k$. Then each of: $x_k = \map {\phi_k} t$ is a parametric equation. The set: $\set {\phi_k: 1 \le k \le n}$ is a set of parametric equations specifying $\RR$.

label: Definition:Parametric Equation/Analytic Geometry
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve. A set of parametric equations for $\CC$ is a set of equations that determine the locus of $\CC$ in terms of a single parameter.

label: Definition:Paranormal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. Then $H$ is a paranormal subgroup in $G$ the subgroup generated by $H$ and any conjugate of $H$ is also generated by $H$ and a conjugate of $H$ within that generated subgroup. That is, $H$ is paranormal in $G$ : $\forall g \in G: \exists k \in \left\langle{H, H^g}\right\rangle: \left\langle{H, H^k}\right\rangle = \left\langle{H, H^g}\right\rangle$ where: $\left\langle{H, H^g}\right\rangle$ is the subgroup generated by $H$ and $H^g$ $H^g$ is the conjugate of $H$ by $g$.

label: Definition:Parastrophe
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ and $\struct {S, *}$ be magmas on $S$.

label: Definition:Parenthesization
snippet: Let $\circ$ be a product defined on a set $S$. Let $a_1 \circ a_2 \circ \cdots a_i \circ \cdots \circ a_n$ denote a word in $S$ for some $n > 2$. To distinguish all possible products of $a_1, a_2, \dotsc, a_n$, parentheses are inserted into the word. A set of parentheses applied on a product is called a parenthesization of that word.

label: Definition:Parenthesization/Equivalent
snippet: Let $\circ$ be a product defined on a set $S$. Let $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ denote elements of $S$. Two parenthesizations of $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ are equivalent the product defined by them yields the same result. Category:Definitions/Parenthesization

label: Definition:Pareto Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X \in \hointr b \infty$. $X$ is said to have a Pareto distribution it has probability density function: $\ds \map {f_X} x = \dfrac {a b^a} {x^{a + 1} }$ for $a, b \in \R_{> 0}$.

label: Definition:Pareto Efficiency
snippet: Let $n \in \N_{>0}$ be a non-zero natural number. Let $X \subseteq \R^n$ be a set. Then $x \in X$ is Pareto efficient there exists no $y \in X \setminus \set x$ for which $x_i \le y_i$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$.

label: Definition:Pareto Efficiency/Also known as
snippet: == Pareto Efficient: Also known as == An element of a set which is Pareto efficient can also be referred to as Pareto maximal. Category:Definitions/Pareto Efficiency

label: Definition:Parity
snippet: Number Theory: The parity of an integer: whether it is even or odd. Group Theory: The parity of a permutation of an element of the symmetric group on $n$ letters. Both concepts have the same origin: parity encapsulates the notions of oddness and evenness.

label: Definition:Parity Check
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a linear $\tuple {n, 2}$-code. Let $\LL'$ be the linear $\tuple {n + 1, 2}$-code formed from $\LL$ by adding an extra bit to the end of each of the codewords of $\LL$ such that the digit sums of each of the codewords of $\LL'$ have the same parity. This extra bit is the check digit of $\LL'$. This method of construction of an error-correcting code is called a parity check.

label: Definition:Parity Check Matrix
snippet: Let $C$ be a linear code. A parity check matrix $\mathbf H$ for $C$ is a matrix whose rows form a basis for the dual code for $\mathbf H$ defined over a Galois field $\GF$.

label: Definition:Parity Group
snippet: This has several forms, all of which are isomorphic: The group $\struct {\Z_2, +_2}$ $C_2$, the cyclic group of order 2 The complex square roots of unity $\struct {\set {1, -1}, \times}$ The quotient group $\dfrac {S_n} {A_n}$ of the symmetric group of order $n$ with the alternating group of order $n$ and so on.

label: Definition:Parity Operator
snippet: The parity operator is a unary operator on the integers defined as: $\forall n \in \Z: \paren {-1}^n$ There is no evolved notation for this, neither is there an accepted name for it.

label: Definition:Parity Operator/Motivation
snippet: == Motivation for == When assembling complicated sequences in which each term is constructed in the form of an algebraic expression, it is commonplace for a factor of the form $\paren {-1}^n$ to appear. {{Neologism|parity operator|in order to provide a compact way to refer to terms of the form $\paren {-1}^n$}} There appears to be no evolved notation for this, neither is there an accepted name for it. Category:Definitions/Parity Operator

label: Definition:Parity Ring
snippet: The parity ring is the ring of two elements which defines the nature of the parity of integers under addition and multiplication: $\struct {\set {\text{even}, \text{odd} }, +, \times}$

label: Definition:Parity of Integer
snippet: Let $z \in \Z$ be an integer. The parity of $z$ is whether it is even or odd.

label: Definition:Parity of Integer/Also defined as
snippet: == Parity of Integer: Also defined as == Some sources define parity as a property of a pair of integers $\set {z_1, z_2}$ thus: If $z_1$ and $z_2$ are either both even or both odd, $z_1$ and $z_2$ have even parity If $z_1$ is even and $z_2$ is odd, then $z_1$ and $z_2$ have odd parity.

label: Definition:Parity of Integer/Even
snippet: An integer $z$ is of even parity : $z = 2 n$ for some $n \in \Z$.

label: Definition:Parity of Integer/Odd
snippet: An integer $z$ is of odd parity : $z = 2 n + 1$ for some $n \in \Z$.

label: Definition:Parity of Integer/Opposite
snippet: Two integers $z_1$ and $z_2$ have opposite parity either: $z_1$ is even and $z_2$ is odd or: $z_2$ is even and $z_1$ is odd.

label: Definition:Parity of Integer/Same
snippet: Two integers $z_1$ and $z_2$ have the same parity either: $z_1$ and $z_2$ are both even or: $z_1$ and $z_2$ are both odd.

label: Definition:Parsing Sequence
snippet: Let $\FF$ be a formal language with alphabet $\AA$. Let $S$ be a collation in $\AA$. A parsing sequence for $S$ in $\FF$ is a sequence of collations in $\FF$ formed by application of rules of formation of $\FF$ from previous collations in this sequence, and ending in the collation $S$. If $S$ has no parsing sequence in $\FF$, then it is not a well-formed formula in $\FF$. A parsing sequence for a given well-formed formula in any formal language is usually not unique.

label: Definition:Partial Correlation Coefficient
snippet: Let $X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots$ be random variables in a conditional distribution. The partial correlation coefficient between $X_i$ and $X_j$ is the correlation coefficient between $X_i$ and $X_j$ while keeping all the other random variables fixed.

label: Definition:Partial Derivative
snippet: A partial derivative is the rate of change of a function of several variables one of those variables while keeping all the other variables constant.

label: Definition:Partial Derivative/Vector Function/Cartesian 3-Space
snippet: Let $\map {\R^3} {x, y, z}$ denote the Cartesian $3$-space. Let $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ be the standard ordered basis on $\R^3$. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field in $\R^3$. Let $\mathbf v: \R^3 \to \mathbf V$ be a vector-valued function on $\R^3$: $\forall P = \tuple {x, y, z} \in \R^3: \map {\mathbf v} P := \map {v_1} P \mathbf i + \map {v_2} P \mathbf j + \map {v_3} P \mathbf k$ Let $v_1, v_2, v_3$ be differentiable at $\mathbf a = \tuple {a_x, a_y, a_z}$.

label: Definition:Partial Differential Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Partial Differential Equation: Also known as == The term partial differential equation is often presented in its abbreviated form PDE or P.D.E.

label: Definition:Partial Differential Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Partial Differential Equation == The first partial differential equation to be recognised as such was the one which defines the form of a vibrating string. It was discussed by and in $1747$. completed the solution of that equation. Between $1772$ and $1785$ he also addressed the partial differential equation of the first order. He established the general solution of the linear equation, and classified the various kinds of non-linear equation. These theories are still being developed. Others who have contributed include and . Other methods were given by and .

label: Definition:Partial Differential Operator
snippet: Let $U \subseteq \R^n$ be a open set. Let $\CC \subseteq \map {\CC^k} {U, \R}$ be a set of $k$-times continuously differentiable functions. Let $\ds \partial_i = \frac {\partial} {\partial x_i}$ denote the partial derivative, $i = 1, \ldots, n$. For a multiindex $\alpha = \tuple {\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n}$ indexed by $\set {1, \ldots, n}$ let $\partial^\alpha = \partial_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots \partial_n^{\alpha_n}$.

label: Definition:Partial Function
snippet: Let $S \subset \N^k$. Let $f: S \to \N$ be a function. Suppose that $\forall x \in \N^k \setminus S$, $f$ is undefined at $x$. Then $f$ is known as a partial function from $\N^k$ to $\N$. Thus we can specify a function that has values for some, but not all, elements of $\N$. It can be seen that the definition of a partial function as given here is compatible with that of a partial mapping.

label: Definition:Partial Isometry
snippet:
Let $\struct {\HH_1, \innerprod \cdot \cdot_1}$ and $\struct {\HH_2, \innerprod \cdot \cdot_2}$ be Hilbert spaces. Let $
