label: Definition:Radical of Ideal of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be an ideal of $A$.

label: Definition:Radical of Integer
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer.

label: Definition:Radical of Integer/Also known as
snippet: == Radical of Integer: Also known as == The radical of an integer $n$ is also known as the square-free kernel of $n$.

label: Definition:Radical of Integer/Definition 1
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. The radical of $n$ is the product of the distinct prime factors of $n$.

label: Definition:Radical of Integer/Definition 2
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. The radical of $n$ is the largest square-free integer which divides $n$.

label: Definition:Radioactive Decay
snippet: Radioactive decay is a first-order reaction in which the atoms of a substance may spontaneously break apart, thereby turning into atoms of a different substance. The probability of an individual atom decaying is an intrinsic property of the given chemical element. Having decayed, that atom is now transformed into an atom of a different type, and so is not subject to any further occurrences of that particular decay process. However, the new atom may have its own particular (different) mode of decay itself.

label: Definition:Radius
snippet: Geometry: Radius of a Circle: a straight line segment whose endpoints are the center and the circumference of the circle. Radius of a Sphere: a straight line segment whose endpoints are the center and the surface of the sphere. Radius of Regular Polygon: Long Radius Short Radius Analytic Geometry: The radial coordinate of a point $P$ in a system of polar coordinates is also known as the radius of $P$.

label: Definition:Radius of Convergence/Complex Domain
snippet: Let $\xi \in \C$ be a complex number. For $z \in \C$, let: $\ds \map f z = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a_n \paren {z - \xi}^n$ be a power series about $\xi$. The radius of convergence is the extended real number $R \in \overline \R$ defined by: $R = \ds \inf \set {\cmod {z - \xi}: z \in \C, \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a_n \paren {z - \xi}^n \text{ is divergent} }$ where a divergent series is a series that is not convergent. As usual, $\inf \O = +\infty$.

label: Definition:Radius of Convergence/Real Domain
snippet: Let $\xi \in \R$ be a real number. Let $\ds \map S x = \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty a_n \paren {x - \xi}^n$ be a power series about $\xi$. Let $I$ be the interval of convergence of $\map S x$. Let the endpoints of $I$ be $\xi - R$ and $\xi + R$. (This follows from the fact that $\xi$ is the midpoint of $I$.) Then $R$ is called the radius of convergence of $\map S x$. If $\map S x$ is convergent over the whole of $\R$, then $I = \R$ and thus the radius of convergence is infinite.

label: Definition:Radius of Curvature
snippet: The radius of curvature of a curve $C$ at a point $P$ is defined as the reciprocal of the absolute value of its curvature: $\rho = \dfrac 1 {\size k}$

label: Definition:Radius of Curvature/Cartesian Coordinates
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve defined by a real function which is twice differentiable. Let $C$ be embedded in a cartesian plane. The radius of curvature of $C$ at a point $P$ can be expressed in cartesian coordinates as: $\rho = \size {\dfrac {\paren {1 + y'^2}^{3/2} } {y' '} }$ where: {{eqn | l = y' | o = := | r = \dfrac {\d y} {\d x} }} {{eqn | l = y' ' | o = := | r = \dfrac {\d^2 y} {\d x^2} }}

label: Definition:Radius of Curvature/Parametric Form/Cartesian
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve defined by a real function which is twice differentiable. Let $C$ be embedded in a cartesian plane and defined by the parametric equations: $\begin{cases} x = \map x t \\ y = \map y t \end{cases}$ The radius of curvature $\rho$ of $C$ at a point $P = \tuple {x, y}$ is given by: $\rho = \dfrac {\paren {x'^2 + y'^2}^{3/2} } {\size {x' y' ' - y' x' '} }$ where: $x' = \dfrac {\d x} {\d t}$ is the derivative of $x$ $t$ at $P$ $y' = \dfrac {\d y} {\d t}$ is the derivative of $y$ $t$ at $P$ $x' '$ and $y' '$ are the second derivatives of $x$ and $y$ $t$ at $P$.

label: Definition:Radius of Gyration
snippet: Let $B$ be a rigid body which is rotating in space about some axis $\LL$. Let $P$ be a point on $B$ at which, or from which, a transfer of energy has the maximum effect. The radius of gyration of $B$ is the distance from $P$ to $\LL$.

label: Definition:Radon-Nikodym Derivative
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\map {\mathcal M^+} {X, \Sigma, \R}$ be the space of positive real-valued measurable functions. Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be $\sigma$-finite measures on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ such that: $\nu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$. Let $\sim$ be the $\mu$-almost everywhere equality relation on $\map {\mathcal M} {X, \Sigma, \R}$ restricted to the space of positive real-valued measurable functions $\map {\mathcal M^+} {X, \Sigma, \R}$.

label: Definition:Radon Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space. Let $\map \BB X$ denote the Borel $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\tau$. Let $\MM$ be a $\sigma$-algebra over $X$ such that $\map \BB X \subseteq \MM$. Let $\mu : \MM \to \overline \R$ be a measure on $\MM$, where $\overline \R$ denotes the set of extended real numbers. Then $\mu$ is called a Radon measure, : $(1): \quad \map \mu K < \infty$ for all compact sets $K \subseteq X$ $(2): \quad \map \mu B = \sup \leftset {\map \mu K : K \subseteq B, K}$ is compact for all $\rightset {B \in \MM}$.

label: Definition:Radon Point
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of $n + 2$ points in a real Euclidean space $\R^n$ of $n$ dimensions. Let $S$ be partitioned into $2$ subsets whose convex hulls have at least one point in their intersection. Such a point of intersection is known as a Radon point of $S$.

label: Definition:Radon Transform
snippet: The Radon transform is a transform which reconstructs a function from the values of its integral over a set of lines in the plane. It is used for measuring data from incomplete observations.

label: Definition:Ramanujan-Nagell Equation
snippet: The Ramanujan-Nagell equation is the Diophantine equation: $x^2 + 7 = 2^n$

label: Definition:Ramanujan-Nagell Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Ramanujan-Nagell Equation == conjectured in $1913$ that the equation $x^2 + 7 = 2^n$ had only $5$ integer solutions. The same conjecture was made independently in $1943$ by . The conjecture was proved in $1948$ by Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Ramanujan-Nagell Number
snippet: A Ramanujan-Nagell number is a positive integer of the form $2^m - 1$ which is also triangular.

label: Definition:Ramsey Theory
snippet: Ramsey theory is a branch of combinatorics that studies the conditions under which order must appear.

label: Definition:Random Error
snippet: A random error is the discrepancy between an observation and a value predicted by a particular model. Such an error represents uncontrolled variation. Random errors are usually assumed to be independent with a normal distribution and zero expectation.

label: Definition:Random Numbers
snippet: Random numbers are a sequence of digits or numbers, usually in a given range, such that each number has an equal probability of occurring for each term. In the ideal, it is impossible to predict which number will occur next.

label: Definition:Random Numbers/Methods of Generation
snippet: == Methods of Generation of Random Numbers == The traditional method of generation of random numbers is to draw from a container of tokens, identical but for the number written on them. Computers can be used to generate pseudo-random numbers, but these are not technically speaking actual random numbers.

label: Definition:Random Sample (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $X_i$ be a random variable with $\Img {X_i} = \Omega$, for all $1 \le i \le n$. Let $F_i$ be the cumulative distribution function of $X_i$ for all $1 \le i \le n$. We say that $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ form a random sample of size $n$ if: $X_i$ and $X_j$ are independent if $i \ne j$ $\map {F_1} x = \map {F_i} x$ for all $x \in \Omega$ for all $1 \le i, j \le n$.

label: Definition:Random Sample (Probability Theory)/Continuous Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with a known probability distribution. Let $\map f X$ be the frequency function of $X$. A random sample of values of $X$ is obtained by selecting values $s$ such that: $\map \Pr {s \in \openint x {x + \delta x} } = \map f x \delta x$ That is, the probability that $s$ is in a given interval is proportional to the length of the interval.

label: Definition:Random Sample (Probability Theory)/Discrete Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with a known probability distribution. Let $\map f X$ be the frequency function of $X$. A random sample of values of $X$ is obtained by selecting values $s$ such that: $\map \Pr {s = x_i} = \map f {x_i}$ That is, the probability that $s$ is a given value is determined completely by the frequency function of $X$ at that value.

label: Definition:Random Sample (Statistics)
snippet: Let $P$ be a population. A sample taken from $P$ is a random sample it is chosen in such a way that every possible sample of the same size has an equal probability of being selected.

label: Definition:Random Selection
snippet: A manner of selecting objects from some larger collection of objects is said to be random if the selection is made according to chance. That is, there is no strict rule or procedure that predictably determines the outcome of the selection. See experiment and random variable for a precise mathematical treatment of randomness.

label: Definition:Random Variable
snippet: == Informal Definition == A random variable is a number whose value is determined unambiguously by an experiment.

label: Definition:Random Variable/Also known as
snippet: == Random Variable: Also known as == Other words used to mean the same thing as random variable are: stochastic variable chance variable variate. The image $\Img X$ of $X$ is often denoted $\Omega_X$.

label: Definition:Random Variable/Continuous
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ such that the domain of $X$ is a continuum. We say that $X$ is a continuous random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ : $\ds \lim_{\delta x \mathop \to 0} \map \Pr {X \in \openint x {x + \delta x} } = \map f x \delta x$ where $f$ is the frequency function on $X$.

label: Definition:Random Variable/General Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$ be a measurable space. A random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$, taking values in $\struct {S, \Sigma'}$, is a $\Sigma \, / \, \Sigma'$-measurable mapping $X : \Omega \to S$.

label: Definition:Random Variable/Real-Valued/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. A real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ is a $\Sigma$-measurable function $X : \Omega \to \R$. That is, a function $X : \Omega \to \R$ is a real-valued random variable : $X^{-1} \sqbrk {\hointl {-\infty} x} = \set {\omega \in \Omega : \map X \omega \le x} \in \Sigma$ for each $x \in \R$, where: $\hointl {-\infty} x$ denotes the unbounded closed interval $\set {y \in \R: y \le x}$ $X^{-1} \sqbrk {\hointl {-\infty} x}$ denotes the preimage of $\hointl {-\infty} x$ under $X$.

label: Definition:Random Variable/Real-Valued/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\map \BB \R$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\R$. Let $X$ be a random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {\R, \map \BB \R}$. Then we say that $X$ is a real-valued random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Category:Definitions/Random Variables

label: Definition:Random Vector
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $n \in \N$. Let $\struct {S_1, \Sigma_1}$, $\struct {S_2, \Sigma_2}$, $\ldots$, $\struct {S_n, \Sigma_n}$ be measurable spaces. Let: $\ds S = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i$ For each integer $1 \le i \le n$, let $X_i$ be a random variable on $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ taking values in $\struct {S_i, \Sigma_i}$. Define a function $\mathbf X : \Omega \to S$ by: $\map {\mathbf X} \omega = \tuple {\map {X_1} \omega, \map {X_2} \omega, \ldots, \map {X_n} \omega}$ for each $\omega \in \Omega$. We call $\mathbf X$ a random vector.

label: Definition:Random Walk/One Dimension
snippet: Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \ge 0}$ be a Markov chain whose state space is the set of integers $\Z$. Let $\sequence {X_n}$ be such that $X_{n + 1}$ is an element of the set $\set {X_n + 1, X_n, X_n - 1}$. Then $\sequence {X_n}$ is a one-dimensional random walk.

label: Definition:Range
snippet: Relation Theory Range of Relation Analysis Range of Real Function Statistics Range Applied Mathematics and Mechanics: Range of Projectile

label: Definition:Range (Statistics)
snippet: Range is a measure of dispersion of a set of observations. Let $S$ be a set of observations of a quantitative variable. The range of $S$ is defined as: $\map R S := \map \max S - \map \min S$ where $\map \max S$ and $\map \min S$ are the greatest value of $S$ and the least value of $S$ respectively.

label: Definition:Range (Statistics)/Infinite
snippet: For certain random variables, it is possible that the range may be infinite, in the sense that it is technically unbounded.

label: Definition:Range of Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ be a relation, or (usually) a mapping (which is, of course, itself a relation). The range of $\RR$, denoted is defined as one of two things, depending on the source. On it is denoted $\Rng \RR$, but this may be non-standard.

label: Definition:Range of Sequence
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in A}$ be a sequence. The range of $\sequence {x_n}$ is the set: $\set {x_n: n \mathop \in A}$

label: Definition:Range of Sequence/Also known as
snippet: == Range of Sequence: Also known as == Other terms for the range of a sequence include: the associated set of the sequence the image of the sequence. Some treatments do not bother to give it a name at all, merely referring to it as the set of its elements.

label: Definition:Rank
snippet: Set Theory: Rank (Set Theory) Linear Algebra: Rank (Linear Algebra) Rank of Matrix Rank of Linear Transformation Rank of Module Complex Analysis: Rank of Entire Function Abstract Algebra: Rank of Free Group Rank of Free Monoid Rank of Free Semigroup Topology: Rank of Submersion Rank of Immersion Statistics: Rank (Statistics) Rank Correlation Coefficient

label: Definition:Rank/Linear Transformation
snippet: Let $\phi$ be a linear transformation from one vector space to another. Let the image of $\phi$ be finite-dimensional. Then its dimension is called the rank of $\phi$ and is denoted $\map \rho \phi$.

label: Definition:Rank/Matrix
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$.

label: Definition:Rank (Set Theory)
snippet: Let $A$ be a set. Let $V$ denote the von Neumann hierarchy. Then the rank of $A$ is the smallest ordinal $x$ such that $A \in \map V {x + 1}$, given that $x$ exists.

label: Definition:Rank (Statistics)
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of sample data which has been assigned a ranking $\RR$. The index of a given $x \in S$ according to $\RR$ is known as its rank.

label: Definition:Rank Correlation Coefficient
snippet: A rank correlation coefficient is a statistical coefficient which measures the degree of agreement of a set of subjective rankings.

label: Definition:Rank Function
snippet: Relation Theory: Rank Function on a relational structure $\struct {S, \RR}$: a mapping $\operatorname {rk}$ from $S$ to a well-ordered set $\struct {T, \prec}$ such that: $\forall x, y \in S: \paren {x \ne y \text { and } \tuple {x, y} \in \RR} \implies \map {\operatorname {rk} } x \prec \map {\operatorname {rk} } y$ Matroid theory: Rank Function of a matroid $M = \struct {S, \mathscr I}$: the mapping from the power set of $S$ into the integers defined by: $\forall A \subseteq S : \map \rho A = \max \set {\size X : X \subseteq A \land X \in \mathscr I}$

label: Definition:Rank Function (Matroid)
snippet: Let $M = \struct {S, \mathscr I}$ be a matroid. The rank function of $M$ is the mapping $\rho : \powerset S \to \Z$ from the power set of $S$ into the integers defined by: $\forall A \subseteq S : \map \rho A = \max \set {\size X : X \subseteq A \land X \in \mathscr I}$ where $\size A$ denotes the cardinality of $A$.

label: Definition:Rank of Entire Function
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be an entire function. Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be the sequence of non-zero zeroes of $f$, repeated according to multiplicity. The rank of $f$ is: the smallest positive integer $p \ge 0$ for which the series $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \size {a_n}^{-p - 1}$ converges or: $\infty$ if there is no such integer. If $f$ has finitely many zeroes, its rank is $0$.

label: Definition:Rank of Free Group
snippet: Let $F$ be a free group. The rank of $F$ is the dimension of its abelianization as a module over $\Z$.

label: Definition:Rank of Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Rank of Matrix: Also known as == The rank of a matrix can also be referred to as: its row rank its column rank. Some sources denote the rank of a matrix $\mathbf A$ as: $\map {\mathrm {rk} } {\mathbf A}$ When defined as the order of the largest non-zero determinant that can be extracted from $\mathbf A$ by selecting rows and columns, it can be seen referred to as the determinantal rank of the matrix.

label: Definition:Rank of Matrix/Definition 1
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$. The rank of $\mathbf A$, denoted $\map \rho {\mathbf A}$, is the dimension of the subspace of $K^m$ generated by the columns of $\mathbf A$. That is, it is the dimension of the column space of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Rank of Matrix/Definition 2
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$. Let $\mathbf A$ be converted to echelon form $\mathbf B$. Let $\mathbf B$ have exactly $k$ non-zero rows. Then the rank of $\mathbf A$, denoted $\map \rho {\mathbf A}$, is $k$.

label: Definition:Rank of Matrix/Definition 3
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$. The rank of $\mathbf A$, denoted $\map \rho {\mathbf A}$, is the largest number of elements in a linearly independent set of rows of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Rank of Matrix/Definition 4
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$. The rank of $\mathbf A$, denoted $\map \rho {\mathbf A}$, is the largest number of elements in a linearly independent set of columns of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Rank of Matrix/Definition 5
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $\mathbf A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $K$. The rank of $\mathbf A$, denoted $\map \rho {\mathbf A}$, is the order of the largest non-zero determinant that can be extracted from $\mathbf A$ by selecting rows and columns.

label: Definition:Ranking
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of discrete data which has been linearly ordered by a total ordering $\QQ$. The ranking of $x \in S$ is the index of $x$ in the sequence induced on $S$ by $\QQ$.

label: Definition:Ranking/Motivation
snippet: It is often possible to generate a ranking on a set $S$ of observations without assigning precise measurements of the data being ordered. For example, objects can often be ranked by height without actually measuring those heights precisely. Many non-parametric tests are based on rankings, and use these even when precise measurements are indeed available.

label: Definition:Rare Number
snippet: A rare number is a non-palindromic integer $n$ which has the property that $n + r$ and $n - r$ are both square, where $r$ is the reversal of $n$.

label: Definition:Rate Function
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\overline \R_\ge$ be the positive extended real number line. Let $I : X \to \overline \R_\ge$ be a function. Then $I$ is a rate function $I$ is lower semicontinuous.

label: Definition:Rate of Change
snippet: The rate of change of a physical quantity is its (first) derivative with respect to an independent variable which is usually, but not exclusively, time. Loosely speaking, it means how fast something changes, with a wider scope than change in physical displacement.

label: Definition:Rate of Change/Time
snippet: When the independent variable of a rate of change is time, it is commonplace to take that fact for granted, and refer merely to its rate of change.

label: Definition:Ratio
snippet: Let $x$ and $y$ be quantities which have the same dimensions. Let $\dfrac x y = \dfrac a b$ for two numbers $a$ and $b$. Then the ratio of $x$ to $y$ is defined as: $x : y = a : b$ It explicitly specifies how many times the first number contains the second. '

label: Definition:Ratio/3 Terms
snippet: Let $a$, $b$ and $c$ be numbers. The ratio of $3$ terms: $a : b : c$ means: The ratios of $a$ to $b$, of $b$ to $c$ and of $a$ to $c$ are equivalent to $a : b$, $b : c$ and $a : c$ respectively.

label: Definition:Ratio/Terms
snippet: The numbers or symbols composing a ratio are known as its terms:

label: Definition:Rational
snippet: Definition:Rational Number Definition:Rational Function

label: Definition:Rational-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a function. Let $S_1 \subseteq S$ such that $f \left({S_1}\right) \subseteq \Q$. Then $f$ is said to be rational-valued on $S_1$. That is, $f$ is defined as rational-valued on $S_1$ iff the image of $S_1$ under $f$ lies entirely within the set of rational numbers $\Q$. A rational-valued function is a function $f: S \to \Q$ whose codomain is the set of rational numbers $\Q$. That is, $f$ is rational-valued it is rational-valued over its entire domain. Category:Definitions/Rational Numbers

label: Definition:Rational Area
snippet: A rational area is a geometric figure whose area is a rational number of units of area. '

label: Definition:Rational Decision-Maker
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $P$ be a player of $G$. Let $A$ be the set of moves available to $P$. Let $C$ be the set $C$ of consequences of the moves available to $P$. Let $g: A \to C$ be the consequence function on $A$. Let $B \subseteq A$ be a the set of moves which are feasible. $P$ is a rational decision-maker $P$ chooses an element $a^* \in B$ such that: $\forall a \in a^*: \map g {a^*} \succsim \map g a$ where $\succsim$ is the preference relation on $C$. That is, that $P$ solves the problem: $\ds \max_{a \mathop \in B} \map U {\map g a}$ where $U$ is the utility function on $C$.

label: Definition:Rational Diagonal
snippet: The number $7$ (seven) was referred to by the ancient Greeks as the rational diagonal of the $5 \times 5$ square. This was on account of the fact that: $5^2 + 5^2 = 50 \approx 7^2 = 49$

label: Definition:Rational Diagonal/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Rational Diagonal == The concept of the rational diagonal was raised by in his ' of c. $380$ BCE. was aware that the actual length of the diagonal of the $5 \times 5$ square is the irrational number $5 \sqrt 2$.

label: Definition:Rational Extension in Plane
snippet: Let $\struct {\R^2, \tau_d}$ be the real number plane with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $D$ denote the set: $D := \set {\tuple {x, y}: x \in \Q, y \in \Q}$ where $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets defined as: $\BB = \set {\set x \cup \paren {U \cap D}: x \in U \in \tau_d}$ Let $\tau'$ be the topology generated from $\BB$. $\tau'$ is referred to as the rational extension in the plane.

label: Definition:Rational Function/Complex
snippet: Let $P: \C \to \C$ and $Q: \C \to \C$ be polynomial functions on the set of complex numbers. Let $S$ be the set $\C$ from which all the roots of $Q$ have been removed. That is: $S = \C \setminus \set {z \in \C: \map Q z = 0}$ Then the equation $y = \dfrac {\map P z} {\map Q z}$ defines a function from $S$ to $\C$. Such a function is a rational (complex) function.

label: Definition:Rational Function/Real
snippet: Let $P: \R \to \R$ and $Q: \R \to \R$ be polynomial functions on the set of real numbers. Let $S$ be the set $\R$ from which all the roots of $Q$ have been removed. That is: $S = \R \setminus \set {x \in \R: \map Q x = 0}$. Then the equation $y = \dfrac {\map P x} {\map Q x}$ defines a function from $S$ to $\R$. Such a function is known as a rational function.

label: Definition:Rational Integer
snippet: Let $K$ be a number field. A rational integer of $K$ is an integer of $K$, that is, an element of $\mathbb Z \subseteq K$.

label: Definition:Rational Line Segment
snippet: A rational line segment is a line segment the square of whose length is a rational number of units of area. In other words, a rational line segment is a line segment whose length belongs to the set $\left\{{x \in \R_{>0} : x^2 \in \Q}\right\}$. '

label: Definition:Rational Number
snippet: A number in the form $\dfrac p q$, where both $p$ and $q$ are integers ($q$ non-zero), is called a rational number. The set of all rational numbers is usually denoted $\Q$. Thus: $\Q = \set {\dfrac p q: p \in \Z, q \in \Z_{\ne 0} }$

label: Definition:Rational Number/Canonical Form
snippet: Let $r \in \Q$ be a rational number. The canonical form of $r$ is the expression $\dfrac p q$, where: $r = \dfrac p q: p \in \Z, q \in \Z_{>0}, p \perp q$ where $p \perp q$ denotes that $p$ and $q$ have no common divisor except $1$. That is, in its canonical form, $r$ is expressed as $\dfrac p q$ where: $p$ is an integer $q$ is a strictly positive integer $p$ and $q$ are coprime.

label: Definition:Rational Number/Formal Definition
snippet: The field $\struct {\Q, +, \times}$ of rational numbers is the field of quotients of the integral domain $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ of integers. This is shown to exist in Existence of Field of Quotients. In view of Field of Quotients is Unique, we construct the field of quotients of $\Z$, give it a label $\Q$ and call its elements rational numbers.

label: Definition:Rational Number/Geometrical Definition
snippet: The definitions of rational numbers and irrational numbers as specified in is different from the contemporary definitions: ' '

label: Definition:Rational Number/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Rational Number == The name rational number has two significances: $(1): \quad$ The construct $\dfrac p q$ can be defined as the ratio between $p$ and $q$. $(2): \quad$ In contrast with the concept irrational number, which can not be so defined. The ancient Greeks had such a term for an irrational number: alogon, which had a feeling of undesirably chaotic and unstructured, or, perhaps more literally: illogical. The proof that there exist such numbers was a shock to their collective national psyche.

label: Definition:Rational Number/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Rational Numbers == Variants on $\Q$ are often seen, for example $\mathbf Q$ and $\QQ$, or even just $Q$. Some sources use $R$, and for the real numbers use $\mathfrak R$.

label: Definition:Rational Number Space
snippet: Let $\Q$ be the set of rational numbers. Let $d: \Q \times \Q \to \R$ be the Euclidean metric on $\Q$. Let $\tau_d$ be the topology on $\Q$ induced by $d$. Then $\struct {\Q, \tau_d}$ is the rational number space.

label: Definition:Rational Operation
snippet: The rational operations are the arithmetic and algebraic operations: Addition Subtraction Multiplication Divison.

label: Definition:Rational Point in Plane
snippet: Consider the Cartesian plane $\R^2$. The points $\tuple {x, y} \in \R^2$ such that $x, y \in \Q$ are called the rational points (of $\R^2$).

label: Definition:Rational Sequence
snippet: A rational sequence is a sequence (usually infinite) whose codomain is the set of rational numbers $\Q$.

label: Definition:Rational Sequence Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {\R, \tau_d}$ denote the real number line with the usual (Euclidean) topology. Let $\Bbb I := \R \setminus \Q$ denote the set of irrational numbers For each $x \in \Bbb I$, let $\sequence {x_i}$ be a sequence of rational numbers which converges to $x$ in $\tau_d$. Let $\tau$ be the topology defined on $\R$ as: $(1): \quad$ All rational numbers are open points in $\R$ $(2): \quad$ The sets $U_n$ of the form: $\map {U_n} x := \sequence {x_i}_n^\infty \cup \set x$ form a basis for the irrational point $x$. $\tau$ is then referred to as the rational sequence topology on $\R$.

label: Definition:Rationalization
snippet: Rationalization is the process of removing radicals from an equation or expession by means of valid algebraic manipulations.

label: Definition:Rationally Expressible Number
snippet: A number is rationally expressible its square is rational. Thus, the set of the rationally expressible numbers is: $\set {x \in \R : x^2 \in \Q}$

label: Definition:Raw Moment
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable on some probability space. The $n$th raw moment of $X$, usually denoted $\mu'_n$, is defined as: $\mu'_n = \expect {X^n}$ where $\expect X$ denotes the expectation of $X$. That is, the $n$th raw moment of $X$ is its $n$th moment about $0$.

label: Definition:Raw Moment/Also known as
snippet: == Raw Moment: Also known as == Some sources refer to the raw moment of a random variable as its moment about the origin.

label: Definition:Raw Moment/First
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable on a probability space. The $1$st raw moment of $X$, usually denoted $\mu$, is defined as: $\mu = \expect X$ that is, the expectation of $X$.

label: Definition:Ray
snippet: Geometry Ray (Geometry): Another name for an infinite half-line. Topology A ray in a topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is an embedding $R_{\ge 0} \to T$. Order Theory A ray is an interval which is unbounded at one end. Physics A ray is an ideal beam of electromagnetic radiation of zero thickness.

label: Definition:Ray (Order Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $\prec$ be the reflexive reduction of $\preccurlyeq$. Let $a \in S$ be any point in $S$.

label: Definition:Ray (Topology)
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. A ray in $T$ is an embedding $R_{>0} \to S$. Category:Definitions/Topology

label: Definition:Re-entrant Angle
snippet: Let $P$ be a polygon. Let $V$ be a vertex of $P$ whose internal angle $A$ is greater than $180 \degrees$. Then $A$ is known as a re-entrant angle.

label: Definition:Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a function. Let $S_1 \subseteq S$ such that $\map f {S_1} \subseteq \R$. Then $f$ is said to be real-valued on $S_1$. That is, $f$ is defined as real-valued on $S_1$ the image of $S_1$ under $f$ lies entirely within the set of real numbers $\R$. A real-valued function is a function $f: S \to \R$ whose codomain is the set of real numbers $\R$. That is, $f$ is real-valued it is real-valued over its entire domain.

label: Definition:Real-Valued Periodic Function Space
snippet: Let $I = \closedint 0 T$ be a closed real interval. Let $\map C I$ be the space of real-valued functions, continuous on $I$. Let the elements of $\map C I$ be real periodic functions with the period $T$: $f \in \map C I: \map f T = \map f 0$ Then the set of all such mappings $f$ is known as real-valued periodic (over $I$) function space and is denoted by $\map {C_{per}} I$: $\map {C_{per}} I:= C_{per} \paren {I, \R} = \set {f : I \to \R : \map f T = \map f 0}$

label: Definition:Real Analysis/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Real Analysis == The discipline of real analysis was finally put on a rigorous footing by , who became noted for what has since been referred to as Weierstrassian rigor.

label: Definition:Real Element in Star-Algebra
snippet: Let $A = \struct {A_F, \oplus}$ be a $*$-algebra. Let $A' = \struct {A_F, \oplus'}$ be constructed from $A$ using the Cayley-Dickson construction. Let $a \in A$ be real. Then $\tuple {a, 0}$ is defined as real in $A'$.

label: Definition:Real Embedding
snippet: Let $K$ be a subfield of the set of complex numbers $\C$. A real embedding of $K$ is an embedding of $K$ into the set of real numbers $\R$. That is, a real embedding is an injective field homomorphism $\sigma: K \to \R$.

label: Definition:Real Function
snippet: A real function is a mapping or function whose domain and codomain are subsets of the set of real numbers $\R$. It is frequently understood in many areas of mathematics that the domain and codomain of any function under discussion are of the set of real numbers. Hence the adjective real is often omitted unless it is an important point to stress. Because the concept of a function has been around for a lot longer than that of a general mapping, there is a lot more terminology that has developed up round the subject, some more vague and reliant upon intuition than others.

label: Definition:Real Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the set of real numbers $\R$. Suppose that, for each value of the independent variable $x$ of $S$, there exists a corresponding value of the dependent variable $y$. Then the dependent variable $y$ is a (real) function of the independent variable $x$.

label: Definition:Real Function/Domain
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \R$. Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real function. The domain of $f$ is the set $S$. It is frequently the case that $S$ is not explicitly specified. If this is so, then it is understood that the domain is to consist of all the values in $\R$ for which the function is defined. This often needs to be determined as a separate exercise in itself, by investigating the nature of the function in question.

label: Definition:Real Function/Range
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \R$. Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real function. The range of $f$ is the set of values that the dependent variable can take. That is, it is the image set of $f$.

label: Definition:Real Function/Two Variables
snippet: Let $S, T \subseteq \R$ be subsets of the set of real numbers $\R$. Let $f: S \times T \to \R$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is defined as a (real) function of two (independent) variables. The expression: $z = \map f {x, y}$ means: (The dependent variable) $z$ is a function of (the independent variables) $x$ and $y$.

label: Definition:Real Function/Two Variables/Substitution for y
snippet: Let $S, T \subseteq \R$ be subsets of the set of real numbers $\R$. Let $f: S \times T \to \R$ be a (real) function of two variables: $z = \map f {x, y}$ Then: $\map f {x, a}$ means the real function of $x$ obtained by replacing the independent variable $y$ with $a$. In this context, $a$ can be: a real constant such that $a \in T$ a real function $\map g x$ whose range is a subset of $T$.

label: Definition:Real Hyperbolic Cosecant/Definition 1
snippet: The real hyperbolic cosecant function is defined on the real numbers as: $\csch: \R_{\ne 0} \to \R$: $\forall x \in \R_{\ne 0}: \csch x := \dfrac 2 {e^x - e^{-x} }$ where it is noted that at $x = 0$: $e^x - e^{-x} = 0$ and so $\csch x$ is not defined at that point.

label: Definition:Real Hyperbolic Cosecant/Definition 2
snippet: The real hyperbolic cosecant function is defined on the real numbers as: $\csch: \R_{\ne 0} \to \C$: $\forall x \in \R_{\ne 0}: \csch x := \dfrac 1 {\sinh x}$ where $\sinh$ is the real hyperbolic sine. It is noted that at $x = 0$ we have that $\sinh x = 0$, and so $\csch x$ is not defined at that point.

label: Definition:Real Hyperbolic Cotangent/Definition 1
snippet: The real hyperbolic cotangent function is defined on the real numbers as: $\coth: \R_{\ne 0} \to \R$: $\forall x \in \R_{\ne 0}: \coth x := \dfrac {e^x + e^{-x} } {e^x - e^{-x} }$ where it is noted that at $x = 0$: $e^x - e^{-x} = 0$ and so $\coth x$ is not defined at that point.

label: Definition:Real Hyperbolic Cotangent/Definition 2
snippet: The real hyperbolic cotangent function is defined on the real numbers as: $\coth: \R_{\ne 0} \to \R$: $\forall x \in \R_{\ne 0}: \coth x := \dfrac {\cosh x} {\sinh x}$ where: $\sinh$ is the real hyperbolic sine $\cosh$ is the real hyperbolic cosine It is noted that at $x = 0$ we have that $\sinh x = 0$, and so $\coth x$ is not defined at that point.

label: Definition:Real Hyperbolic Cotangent/Definition 3
snippet: The real hyperbolic cotangent function is defined on the real numbers as: $\coth: \R_{\ne 0} \to \R$: $\forall x \in \R_{\ne 0}: \coth x := \dfrac 1 {\tanh x}$ where $\tanh$ is the real hyperbolic tangent. It is noted that at $x = 0$ we have that $\tanh x = 0$, and so $\coth x$ is not defined at that point.

label: Definition:Real Hyperbolic Secant/Definition 1
snippet: The real hyperbolic secant function is defined on the real numbers as: $\sech: \R \to \R$: $\forall x \in \R: \sech z := \dfrac 2 {e^x + e^{-x} }$

label: Definition:Real Hyperbolic Secant/Definition 2
snippet: The real hyperbolic secant function is defined on the real numbers as: $\sech: \R \to \R$: $\forall x \in \R: \sech x := \dfrac 1 {\cosh x}$ where $\cosh$ is the real hyperbolic cosine.

label: Definition:Real Hyperbolic Tangent/Definition 1
snippet: The real hyperbolic tangent function is defined on the real numbers as: $\tanh: \R \to \R$: $\forall x \in \R: \tanh x := \dfrac {e^z - e^{-x} } {e^z + e^{-x} }$

label: Definition:Real Hyperbolic Tangent/Definition 2
snippet: The real hyperbolic tangent function is defined on the real numbers as: $\tanh: \R \to \R$: $\forall x \in \R: \tanh x := \dfrac {\sinh x} {\cosh x}$ where: $\sinh$ is the real hyperbolic sine $\cosh$ is the real hyperbolic cosine

label: Definition:Real Interval
snippet: Informally, the set of all real numbers between any two given real numbers $a$ and $b$ is called a (real) interval. There are many kinds of intervals, each more-or-less consistent with this informal definition.

label: Definition:Real Interval/Closed
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R$. The closed (real) interval from $a$ to $b$ is defined as: $\closedint a b = \set {x \in \R: a \le x \le b}$

label: Definition:Real Interval/Definition 1
snippet: == Definition 1 == A (real) interval is a subset $I$ of the real numbers such that: $\forall x, y \in I: \forall z \in \R : \paren {x \le z \le y \implies z \in I}$

label: Definition:Real Interval/Definition 2
snippet: A real interval is a subset of $\R$ that is one of the following real interval types: closed bounded interval open bounded interval left half-open bounded interval right half-open bounded interval closed and bounded on the right, also known as a closed unbounded below real interval open and bounded on the right, also known as an open unbounded below real interval closed and bounded on the left, also known as a closed unbounded above real interval open and bounded on the left, also known as an open unbounded above real interval unbounded interval without endpoints

Let $\left [{a \,.\,.\, b} \right]$, $\left [{a \,.\,.\, b} \right)$, $\left ({a \,.\,.\, b} \right)$ and $\left ({a \,.\,.\, b} \right)$ be real intervals: closed, half-open and open as defined. label: Definition:Real Interval/Endpoints
snippet: Let: $\closedint a b$ or $\hointr a b$ or $\hointl a b$ or $\openint a b$ be a real interval. The numbers $a, b \in \R$ are known as the endpoints of the interval. $a$ is sometimes called the left hand endpoint and $b$ the right hand endpoint of the interval.

label: Definition:Real Interval/Half-Open/Left
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R$ be real numbers. The left half-open (real) interval from $a$ to $b$ is the subset: $\hointl a b := \set {x \in \R: a < x \le b}$

label: Definition:Real Interval/Half-Open/Right
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R$ be real numbers. The right half-open (real) interval from $a$ to $b$ is the subset: $\hointr a b := \set {x \in \R: a \le x < b}$

label: Definition:Real Interval/Notation
snippet: An arbitrary (real) interval is variously denoted: $\mathbb I$ $\mathbf I$, often by sources which use the $\textbf {boldface}$ font $\mathbf N, \mathbf Z, \mathbf Q, \mathbf R, \mathbf C$ for the number sets $\N$, $\Z$, and so on $I$, as used by by preference, although other letters are often found When two intervals are being discussed at the same time, $J$ is a popular choice for the second to come under the spotlight. Note that prefers to reserve $\I$ for the specific case of the closed unit interval $\closedint 0 1$.

label: Definition:Real Interval/Open
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R$. The open (real) interval from $a$ to $b$ is defined as: $\openint a b := \set {x \in \R: a < x < b}$

label: Definition:Real Interval/Unbounded Closed
snippet: There are two unbounded closed intervals involving a real number $a \in \R$, defined as: {{eqn | l = \hointr a \to | o = := | r = \set {x \in \R: a \le x} }} {{eqn | l = \hointl \gets a | o = := | r = \set {x \in \R: x \le a} }}

label: Definition:Real Interval/Unbounded Open
snippet: There are two unbounded open intervals involving a real number $a \in \R$, defined as: {{eqn | l = \openint a \to | o = := | r = \set {x \in \R: a < x} }} {{eqn | l = \openint \gets a | o = := | r = \set {x \in \R: x < a} }}

label: Definition:Real Interval/Unbounded without Endpoints
snippet: The unbounded interval without endpoints is equal to the set of real numbers: $\openint \gets \to = \R$

label: Definition:Real Interval Types
snippet: It is usual to define intervals in terms of inequalities. These are in the form of a pair of brackets, either round or square, enclosing the two endpoints of the interval separated by two dots. Whether the bracket at either end is round or square depends on whether the end point is inside or outside the interval, as specified in the following. Let $a, b \in \R$ be real numbers.

label: Definition:Real Inverse Hyperbolic Cosecant/Also known as
snippet: == Real Inverse Hyperbolic Cosecant: Also known as == The real inverse hyperbolic cosecant is also known as the (real) area hyperbolic cosecant, as it can be used, among other things, for evaluating areas of regions bounded by hyperbolas. Note that as the real hyperbolic cosecant $\csch$ is injective, its inverse is properly a function on its domain. Hence there is no need to make a separate distinction between branches in the same way as for real inverse hyperbolic cosine and real inverse hyperbolic secant.

label: Definition:Real Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine/Also known as
snippet: == Real Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine: Also known as == In the real domain, reserves the term area hyperbolic cosine strictly for the principal branch, that is, for $\map \arcosh x > 0$. Category:Definitions/Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine

label: Definition:Real Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent/Also known as
snippet: == Real Inverse Hyperbolic Cotangent: Also known as == The real inverse hyperbolic cotangent is also known as the (real) area hyperbolic cotangent, as it can be used, among other things, for evaluating areas of regions bounded by hyperbolas. Note that as the real hyperbolic cotangent $\coth$ is injective, its inverse is properly a function on its domain. Hence there is no need to make a separate distinction between branches in the same way as for real inverse hyperbolic cosine and real inverse hyperbolic secant.

label: Definition:Real Inverse Hyperbolic Function
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be one of the hyperbolic functions on the set of real numbers. Certain of the inverse hyperbolic function $f^{-1} \subseteq \R \times \R$ are actually multifunctions, such that for a given $y \in \R$ there may be more than one $x \in \R$ such that $y = \map f x$. As with the inverse trigonometric functions, it is usual to restrict the codomain of the multifunction so as to allow $f^{-1}$ to be single-valued. There are six basic hyperbolic functions, so each of these has its inverse functions:

label: Definition:Real Inverse Hyperbolic Secant/Also known as
snippet: == Real Inverse Hyperbolic Secant: Also known as == In the real domain, reserves the term area hyperbolic secant strictly for the principal branch, that is, for $\map \arsech x > 0$. Category:Definitions/Inverse Hyperbolic Secant

label: Definition:Real Inverse Hyperbolic Sine/Also known as
snippet: == Real Inverse Hyperbolic Sine: Also known as == The real inverse hyperbolic sine is also known as the (real) area hyperbolic sine, as it can be used, among other things, for evaluating areas of regions bounded by hyperbolas. Note that as the real hyperbolic sine $\sinh$ is injective, its inverse is properly a function on its domain. Hence there is no need to make a separate distinction between branches in the same way as for real inverse hyperbolic cosine and real inverse hyperbolic secant.

label: Definition:Real Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent/Also known as
snippet: == Real Inverse Hyperbolic Tangent: Also known as == The real inverse hyperbolic tangent is also known as the (real) area hyperbolic tangent, as it can be used, among other things, for evaluating areas of regions bounded by hyperbolas. Note that as the real hyperbolic tangent $\tanh$ is injective, its inverse is properly a function on its domain. Hence there is no need to make a separate distinction between branches in the same way as for real inverse hyperbolic cosine and real inverse hyperbolic secant.

label: Definition:Real Matrix
snippet: A real matrix is a matrix whose elements are all real numbers.

label: Definition:Real Number
snippet: A working definition of the real numbers is as the set $\R$ which comprises the set of rational numbers $\Q$ together with the set of irrational numbers $\R \setminus \Q$. It is admitted that this is a circular definition, as an irrational number is defined as a real number which is not a rational number. More formal approaches are presented below.

label: Definition:Real Number/Also known as
snippet: When the term number is used in general discourse, it is often tacitly understood as meaning real number. They are sometimes referred to in the pedagogical context as ordinary numbers, so as to distinguish them from complex numbers However, depending on the context, the word number may also be taken to mean integer or natural number. Hence it is wise to be specific.

label: Definition:Real Number/Axiomatic Definition
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \times, \le}$ be a Dedekind complete ordered field. Then $R$ is called the (field of) real numbers.

label: Definition:Real Number/Cauchy Sequences
snippet: Consider the set of rational numbers $\Q$. For any two Cauchy sequences of rational numbers $X = \sequence {x_n}, Y = \sequence {y_n}$, define an equivalence relation between the two as: $X \equiv Y \iff \forall \epsilon \in \Q_{>0}: \exists n \in \N: \forall i, j > n: \size {x_i - y_j} < \epsilon$ A real number is an equivalence class $\eqclass {\sequence {x_n} } {}$ of Cauchy sequences of rational numbers.

label: Definition:Real Number/Dedekind Cuts
snippet: The set of rational numbers are identified with the set of rational cuts. All other cuts are called, and are identified with, irrational numbers.

label: Definition:Real Number/Digit Sequence
snippet: Let $b \in \N_{>1}$ be a given natural number which is greater than $1$. The set of real numbers can be expressed as the set of all sequences of digits: $z = \sqbrk {a_n a_{n - 1} \dotsm a_2 a_1 a_0 \cdotp d_1 d_2 \dotsm d_{m - 1} d_m d_{m + 1} \dotsm}$ such that: $0 \le a_j < b$ and $0 \le d_k < b$ for all $j$ and $k$ $\ds z = \sum_{j \mathop = 0}^n a_j b^j + \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^\infty d_k b^{-k}$ It is usual for $b$ to be $10$.

label: Definition:Real Number/Equality
snippet: Two real numbers are defined as being equal they correspond to the same point on the real number line.

label: Definition:Real Number/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Real Numbers == While the symbol $\R$ is the current standard symbol used to denote the set of real numbers, variants are commonly seen. For example: $\mathbf R$, $\RR$ and $\mathfrak R$, or even just $R$.

label: Definition:Real Number/Number Line Definition
snippet: A real number is defined as a number which is identified with a point on the real number line.

label: Definition:Real Number/Operations on Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. We interpret the following symbols: {{axiom | n = \text R 1 | lc= Negative | q = \forall a \in \R | m = \exists ! \paren {-a} \in \R: a + \paren {-a} = 0 }} {{axiom | n = \text R 2 | lc= Minus | q = \forall a, b \in \R | m = a - b = a + \paren {-b} }} {{axiom | n = \text R 3 | lc= Reciprocal | q = \forall a \in \R \setminus \set 0 | m = \exists ! a^{-1} \in \R: a \times \paren {a^{-1} } = 1 = \paren {a^{-1} } \times a | rc= it is usual to write $1/a$ or $\dfrac 1 a$ for $a^{-1}$ }} {{axiom | n = \text R 4 | lc= Divided by | q = \forall a \in \R \setminus…

label: Definition:Real Number/Real Number Line
snippet: From the Cantor-Dedekind Hypothesis, the set of real numbers is isomorphic to any infinite straight line. The real number line is an arbitrary infinite straight line each of whose points is identified with a real number such that the distance between any two real numbers is consistent with the length of the line between those two points. 800px Thus we can identify any (either physically drawn or imagined) line with the set of real numbers and thereby illustrate truths about the real numbers by means of diagrams.

label: Definition:Real Number Plane
snippet: The points on the plane are in one-to-one correspondence with the (real) Cartesian plane $\R^2$. So from the definition of an ordered $n$-tuple, the general element of $\R^2$ can be defined as an ordered couple $\tuple {x_1, x_2}$ where $x_1, x_2 \in \R$, or, conventionally, $\tuple {x, y}$. Thus, we can identify the elements of $\R^2$ with points in the plane and refer to the point as its coordinates. Thus we can refer to $\R^2$ as the plane.

label: Definition:Real Part/Also denoted as
snippet: == Real Part: Also denoted as == Variants of $\map \Re z$ for the real part of a complex number $z$ are: $\map {\mathrm {Re} } z$ $\mathrm {Re} \set z$ $\map {\mathscr R} z$ $\map {\mathrm {re} } z$ $\map {\mathfrak R} z$ $\map {\mathbf R} z$ or $\mathbf R z$ While the fraktur font is falling out of fashion, because of its cumbersome appearance and difficulty to render in longhand, its use for this application is conveniently unambiguous.

label: Definition:Real Part/Polar Form
snippet: Let $z$ be a complex number expressed in polar form: $z = \polar {r, \theta}$ The real part of $z$ is: $\map \Re z = r \cos \theta$

label: Definition:Real Part (Linear Operator)
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $A \in \map B \HH$ be a bounded linear operator. Then the real part of $A$ is the Hermitian operator: $\Re A := \dfrac 1 2 \paren {A + A^*}$

label: Definition:Real Sequence
snippet: A real sequence is a sequence (usually infinite) whose codomain is the set of real numbers $\R$.

label: Definition:Real Sequence/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Real Sequence == The notation for a real sequence is conventionally of the form $\sequence {a_n}$, where it is understood that: the domain of $\sequence {a_n}$ is the natural numbers: either $\set {0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ or $\set {1, 2, 3, \ldots}$ the range of $\sequence {a_n}$ is the set of real numbers $\R$. However, some sources use the notation of mappings to explicitly interpret a real sequence as a real-valued function: $f: \N \to \R$ Hence the $n$th term can be seen denoted in two ways: $\sequence {a_n}$ $\map f n$ Category:Definitions/Real Sequences

label: Definition:Real Submanifold
snippet: Let $n, k \ge 1$ be natural numbers. Let $M \subset \R^n$ be a subset of the real Cartesian space $\R^n$.

label: Definition:Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Then the $\R$-module $\R^n$ is called the real ($n$-dimensional) vector space.

label: Definition:Realification of Complex Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {X, +, \circ}$ be a vector space over $\C$. Define $\circ_\R : \R \times X$ such that: $\lambda \circ_\R x = \lambda \circ x$ for each $\lambda \in \R$, $x \in X$. We say that the $\R$-vector space $X_\R = \struct {X, +, \circ_\R}$ is the realification of $X$.

label: Definition:Realization
snippet: Time Series Analysis: Realization of stochastic process Inductive Statistics: Realization of random variable Model Theory: Realization of type

label: Definition:Realization of Stochastic Process
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process. Let $T$ be a time series of observations of $S$ which has been acquired as $S$ evolves, according to the underlying probability distribution of $S$. Then $T$ is referred to as a realization of $S$. Thus we can regard the observation $z_t$ at some timestamp $t$, for example $t = 25$, as the realization of a random variable with probability mass function $\map p {z_t}$.

label: Definition:Reciprocal
snippet: Let $X$ be a number or an expression such that $X$ is not equal to, nor evaluates to, zero. Then $\dfrac 1 X$ is called the reciprocal of $X$. The real function $f: \R_{\ne 0} \to \R$ defined as: $\forall x \in \R_{\ne 0}: \map f x = \dfrac 1 x$ is called the reciprocal function.

label: Definition:Reciprocal Curve
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve embedded in a Cartesian plane whose general point $P$ is specified by $\tuple {x, y}$. The reciprocal curve to $\CC$ is the curve generated from $\CC$ by replacing the ordinates of points $P$ by their reciprocals: $\tuple {x, \dfrac 1 y}$.

label: Definition:Recreational Mathematics
snippet: Recreational mathematics is a branch of mathematics which studies interesting mathematical phenomena for no reason but for the amusement and entertainment of the mathematician.

label: Definition:Rectangular Hyperbola
snippet: A rectangular hyperbola is a hyperbola whose transverse axis is equal to its conjugate axis.

label: Definition:Rectangular Matrix
snippet: A matrix which is specifically not a square matrix can be referred to as a rectangular matrix.

label: Definition:Recurrence Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Recurrence Relation: Also known as == A recurrence relation is also known as a recursive relation. A recurrence relation can also be seen referred to as a difference equation, and vice versa. However, a difference equation is in fact a particular type of recurrence relation, and the two are not strictly synonymous.

label: Definition:Recursion Theory
snippet: Recursion theory is a branch of computability theory which concerns itself with recursive structures.

label: Definition:Recursive/Function
snippet: A function is recursive it can be obtained from basic primitive recursive functions using the operations of: substitution primitive recursion, and minimization on a function a finite number of times.

label: Definition:Recursive Sequence
snippet: A recursive sequence is a sequence where each term is defined from earlier terms in the sequence. The equation which defines this sequence is called a recurrence relation.

label: Definition:Recursive Sequence/Initial Terms
snippet: Let $S$ be a recursive sequence. In order for $S$ to be defined, it is necessary to define the initial term (or terms) explicitly. For example, in the Fibonacci sequence, the initial terms are defined as: $F_0 = 0, F_1 = 1$

label: Definition:Recursive Sequence/Recurrence Relation
snippet: The equation which defines a recursive sequence is called a recurrence relation or difference equation.

label: Definition:Recursively Defined Mapping/Minimally Inductive Set
snippet: Let $\omega$ be the minimally inductive set. Let $T$ be a set. Let $a \in T$. Let $g: T \to T$ be a mapping. Let $f: \omega \to T$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall x \in \omega: \map f x = \begin {cases} a & : x = 0 \\ \map g {\map f n} & : x = n^+ \end {cases}$ where $n^+$ is the successor set of $n$. Then $f$ is said to be recursively defined on $\omega$.

label: Definition:Recursively Defined Mapping/Natural Numbers
snippet: Let $p \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $S = \set {x \in \N: p \le x}$. Let $T$ be a set. Let $g: T \to T$ be a mapping. Let $f: S \to T$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall x \in S: \map f x = \begin {cases} a & : x = p \\ \map g {\map f n} & : x = n + 1 \end {cases}$ for $a \in T$. Then $f$ is said to be recursively defined on $S$.

label: Definition:Recursively Defined Mapping/Naturally Ordered Semigroup
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ, \preceq}$ be a naturally ordered semigroup. Let $p \in S$. Let $S' = \set {x \in S: p \preceq x}$. Let $T$ be a set. Let $g: T \to T$ be a mapping. Let $f: S' \to T$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall n \in S': \map f x = \begin {cases} a & : x = p \\ \map g {\map f n} & : x = n \circ 1 \end {cases}$ where $a \in T$. Then $f$ is said to be recursively defined on $S'$.

label: Definition:Recursively Defined Mapping/Peano Structure
snippet: Let $\struct {P, 0, s}$ be a Peano structure. Let $T$ be a set. Let $g: T \to T$ be a mapping. Let $f: P \to T$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall x \in P: \map f x = \begin {cases} a & : x = 0 \\ \map g {\map f n} & : x = \map s n \end {cases}$ where $a \in T$. Then $f$ is said to be recursively defined on $P$.

label: Definition:Reduced Cubic
snippet: A reduced cubic in a variable $x$ is a cubic equation in $x$ in which the term in $x^2$ is zero.

label: Definition:Reduced Form of Ellipse/Also known as
snippet: == Reduced Form of Ellipse: Also known as == The reduced form of an ellipse is also known as the normal form.

label: Definition:Reduced Form of Group Word
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $w$ be a group word on $X$. The reduced form $\map {\operatorname {red} } w$ of $w$ is the unique reduced word for which there exists a reduction: $w = w^{\paren 0} \to w^{\paren 1} \to \cdots \to w^{\paren n} = \map {\operatorname {red} } w$

label: Definition:Reduced Group Word on Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $n \ge 0$ be a natural number. Let $w = w_1 \cdots w_i \cdots w_n$ be a group word on $S$ of length $n$. Then $w$ is reduced : $\forall i \in \set {1, 2, \ldots, n - 1}: w_i \ne {w_{i + 1} }^{-1}$

label: Definition:Reduced Residue System
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{> 0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. The reduced residue system modulo $m$, denoted $\Z'_m$, is the set of all residue classes of $k$ (modulo $m$) which are prime to $m$: $\Z'_m = \set {\eqclass k m \in \Z_m: k \perp m}$ Thus $\Z'_m$ is the set of all coprime residue classes modulo $m$: $\Z'_m = \set {\eqclass {a_1} m, \eqclass {a_2} m, \ldots, \eqclass {a_{\map \phi m} } m}$ where: $\forall k: a_k \perp m$ $\map \phi m$ denotes the Euler phi function of $m$.

label: Definition:Reduced Residue System/Least Positive
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{> 0}$. The least positive reduced residue system modulo $m$ is the set of integers: $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{\map \phi m} }$ with the following properties: $\map \phi m$ is the Euler $\phi$ function $\forall i: 0 < a_i < m$ each of which is prime to $m$ no two of which are congruent modulo $m$.

label: Definition:Reducible Linear Representation
snippet: Let $\rho: G \to \GL V$ be a linear representation. $\rho$ is reducible there exists a non-trivial proper vector subspace $W$ of $V$ such that: $\forall g \in G: \map {\map \rho g} W \subseteq W$ That is, such that $W$ is invariant for every linear operator in the set $\set {\map \rho g: g \in G}$.

label: Definition:Reducible Polynomial/Mistake
snippet: == Source Work == reducible polynomial

label: Definition:Reducing Subspace
snippet: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. Let $A \in \map B H$ be a bounded linear operator. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of $H$; denote by $M^\perp$ its orthocomplement. Then $M$ is said to be a reducing subspace for $A$ both $M$ and $M^\perp$ are invariant subspaces for $A$. That is, $AM \subseteq M$ and $A M^\perp \subseteq M^\perp$.

label: Definition:Reduction Formula (Calculus)
snippet: Let $f: \R \times \Z_{\ge 0}: \R$ be a Darboux integrable real-valued function on $\R \times \N$. Let: $\ds I_n = \int \map f {x, n} \rd x$ for some $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$. A reduction formula is a recurrence relation of the form: $\ds I_k = \map g {I_n}$ such that $k < n$. That is, it is a technique to reduce the integer parameter in the integrand in order to allow evaluation of the integral at, usually, $n = 0$ or $n = 1$. This technique relies upon the supposition that $\map f {x, 0}$ or $\map f {x, 1}$ can be integrated directly.

label: Definition:Reduction Formula (Trigonometry)
snippet: A reduction formula in the context of trigonometry is a formula that gives a trigonometric function of an angle plus or minus one or more right angles.

label: Definition:Reduction of Group Word on Set
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $w$ be a group word on $X$. A reduction of $w$ is a finite sequence of group words $\tuple {w^{\paren 0}, \ldots, w^{\paren n} }$ such that: $w^{\paren 0} = w$ $w_{i + 1}$ is an elementary reduction of $w_i$, for all $i \in \set {0, \ldots, n - 1}$ $w^{\paren n}$ is reduced

label: Definition:Reed-Solomon Code
snippet: Let $\GF_q$ be the finite field whose underlying set is $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_q}$ such that $a_q = 0$. The $k$th Reed-Solomon code $\GF_q$ is the linear code of length $q - 1$ defined as: the set of all $\paren {q - 1}$-tuples $\tuple {\map f {a_1}, \map f {a_2}, \ldots, \map f {a_1} }$ where $f$ ranges over all polynomials of degree at most $k - 1$ with coefficients in $\GF_q$.

label: Definition:Reference Table
snippet: A reference table is a set of pages, arranged usually in book form, containing arrays of (usually) numbers arranged in rows and columns for ease of look-up. They have been generally superseded by computers now, but facility in their use is generally considered advantageous.

label: Definition:Reference Table/Also known as
snippet: == Reference Table: Also known as == A set of reference tables is often known just as the tables. Category:Definitions/Reference Tables

label: Definition:Refinement
snippet: Topology: A refinement of a cover Group Theory: A refinement of a normal series

label: Definition:Refinement of Cover
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\UU = \set {U_\alpha}$ and $\VV = \set {V_\beta}$ be covers of $S$. Then $\VV$ is a refinement of $\UU$ : $\forall V_\beta \in \VV: \exists U_\alpha \in \UU: V_\beta \subseteq U_\alpha$ That is, every element of $\VV$ is the subset of some element of $\UU$.

label: Definition:Refinement of Cover/Also defined as
snippet: == Refinement of Cover: Also known as == Although specified for the cover of a set, a refinement is usually used in the context of a topological space.

label: Definition:Refinement of Cover/Coarser Cover
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\UU = \set {U_\alpha}$ and $\VV = \set {V_\beta}$ be covers of $S$. Let $\VV$ be a refinement of $\UU$. Then $\UU$ is coarser than $\VV$.

label: Definition:Refinement of Cover/Finer Cover
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\UU = \set {U_\alpha}$ and $\VV = \set {V_\beta}$ be covers of $S$. Let $\VV$ be a refinement of $\UU$. Then $\VV$ is finer than $\UU$.

label: Definition:Refinement of Finite Subdivision
snippet: Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed interval. Let $P, Q$ be finite subdivisions of $\closedint a b$. We say that $Q$ is a refinement of $P$, or that $Q$ is finer than $P$ : $P$ is a subset of $Q$.

label: Definition:Refinement of Normal Series
snippet: Let $G$ be a group whose identity is $e$. Let $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n}$ be a normal series for $G$: $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n} = \tuple {\set e = G_0 \lhd G_1 \lhd \cdots \lhd G_{n - 1} \lhd G_n = G}$ Let $\sequence {H_j}_{j \mathop \in \closedint 0 m}$ be another normal series for $G$: $\sequence {H_j}_{j \mathop \in \closedint 0 m} = \tuple {\set e = H_0 \lhd H_1 \lhd \cdots \lhd H_{m - 1} \lhd H_m = G}$ such that $\sequence {G_i}_{i \mathop \in \closedint 0 n} \subseteq \sequence {H_j}_{j \mathop \in \closedint 0 m}$ Then $\sequence {H_j}_{j…

label: Definition:Refinement of Normal Series/Proper Refinement
snippet: A proper refinement of a normal series is a refinement which is not equal to the original normal series. That is, it contains extra (normal) subgroups which are not present in the original normal series.

label: Definition:Refinement of Partition (Probability Theory)
snippet: Let $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$ be a probability space. Let $\xi, \eta$ be partitions of $\Omega$. Then $\xi$ said to be a refinement of $\eta$ : $\ds \forall A \in \eta : A = \bigcup \set {B \in \xi : B \subseteq A}$ It is written as: $\eta \le \xi$

label: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)
snippet: A reflection in the context of Euclidean geometry is an isometry from a Euclidean Space $\R^n$ as follows. A reflection is defined usually for either: $n = 2$, representing the plane or: $n = 3$, representing ordinary space.

label: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Plane
snippet: A reflection $\phi_{AB}$ in the plane is an isometry on the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^2$ as follows. Let $AB$ be a distinguished straight line in $\Gamma$, which has the property that: $\forall P \in AB: \map {\phi_{AB} } P = P$ That is, every point on $AB$ maps to itself. Let $P \in \Gamma$ such that $P \notin AB$. Let a straight line be constructed from $P$ to $O$ on $AB$ such that $OP$ is perpendicular to $AB$. Let $PO$ be produced to $P'$ such that $OP = OP'$. 400px Then: $\map {\phi_{AB} } P = P'$ Thus $\phi_{AB}$ is a reflection (in the plane) in (the axis of reflection) $AB$.

label: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Point
snippet: A point reflection $\psi_O$ in space is an isometry on the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^3$ as follows. Let $O$ be a distinguished point in $\Gamma$, called the inversion point, which has the property that: $\map {r_\alpha} O = O$ That is, $O$ maps to itself. Let $P \in \Gamma$ such that $P \ne O$. Let $OP$ be joined by a straight line. Let $PO$ be produced to $P'$ such that $OP = OP'$. Then: $\map {\psi_O} P = P'$ Thus $\phi_S$ is a point reflection (in space) in (the inversion point) $O$.

label: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Point/Inversion Point
snippet: Let $\psi_O$ be a point reflection in the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^3$. The point $O$ in $\Gamma$ such that: $\map {\psi_O} O = O$ is called the inversion point of $\psi_O$. Category:Definitions/Geometric Reflections

label: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Space
snippet: A reflection $\phi_S$ in space is an isometry on the Euclidean Space $\Gamma = \R^3$ as follows. Let $S$ be a distinguished plane in $\Gamma$, which has the property that: $\forall P \in S: \map {\phi_S} P = P$ That is, every point on $S$ maps to itself. Let $P \in \Gamma$ such that $P \notin S$. Let a straight line be constructed from $P$ to $O$ on $S$ such that $OP$ is perpendicular to $S$. Let $PO$ be produced to $P'$ such that $OP = OP'$. 600px In the above diagram, $ABCD$ is in the plane of $S$.

label: Definition:Reflection (Geometry)/Space/Plane
snippet: Let $\phi_S$ be a reflection in space in the plane $S$. Then $S$ is known as the plane of reflection of $\phi_S$.

label: Definition:Reflexive Bilinear Form
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K$. Let $b$ be a bilinear form on $V$. Then $b$ is reflexive : $\forall v, w \in V: \map b {v, w} = 0 \implies \map b {w, v} = 0$

label: Definition:Reflexive Closure/Intersection of Reflexive Supersets
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. Let $\QQ$ be the set of all reflexive relations on $S$ that contain $\RR$. The reflexive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^=$, and is defined as: $\RR^= := \bigcap \QQ$ That is: $\RR^=$ is the intersection of all reflexive relations on $S$ containing $\RR$.

label: Definition:Reflexive Closure/Smallest Reflexive Superset
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The reflexive closure of $\RR$ is defined as the smallest reflexive relation on $S$ that contains $\RR$ as a subset. The reflexive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^=$.

label: Definition:Reflexive Closure/Union with Diagonal
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The reflexive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^=$, and is defined as: $\RR^= := \RR \cup \set {\tuple {x, x}: x \in S}$ That is: $\RR^= := \RR \cup \Delta_S$ where $\Delta_S$ is the diagonal relation on $S$.

label: Definition:Reflexive Reduction
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The reflexive reduction of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^\ne$, and is defined as: $\RR^\ne := \RR \setminus \set {\tuple {x, x}: x \in S}$

label: Definition:Reflexive Transitive Closure
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$.

label: Definition:Reflexive Transitive Closure/Reflexive Closure of Transitive Closure
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The reflexive transitive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^*$, and is defined as the reflexive closure of the transitive closure of $\RR$: $\RR^* = \paren {\RR^+}^=$

label: Definition:Reflexive Transitive Closure/Smallest Reflexive Transitive Superset
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The reflexive transitive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^*$, and is defined as the smallest reflexive and transitive relation on $S$ which contains $\RR$.

label: Definition:Reflexive Transitive Closure/Transitive Closure of Reflexive Closure
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The reflexive transitive closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^*$, and is defined as the transitive closure of the reflexive closure of $\RR$: $\RR^* = \paren {\RR^=}^+$

label: Definition:Region/Complex
snippet: Let $D \subseteq \C$ be a subset of the set of complex numbers. $D$ is a region of $\C$ : $(1): \quad$ $D$ is non-empty $(2): \quad$ $D$ is path-connected.

label: Definition:Region/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. A region of $M$ is a subset $U$ of $M$ such that $U$ is: $(1): \quad$ non-empty $(2): \quad$ path-connected.

label: Definition:Region/Plane
snippet: A point set $R$ in the plane is a region : $(1): \quad$ Each point of $R$ is the center of a circle all of whose elements consist of points of $R$ $(2): \quad$ Each point of $R$ can be joined by a curve consisting entirely of points of $R$.

label: Definition:Regression
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. The regression of $Y$ on $X$ for a given value of $x$ is the mapping defined and denoted as: $\forall x \in X: \map f {Y, x} := \expect {Y \mid x}$ where $\expect {Y \mid x}$ denotes the expectation of $Y$ conditional upon $x$.

label: Definition:Regression/Cause Variable
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Let $\map f {Y, x}$ denote the regression of $Y$ on $X$ for a given value of $x$. The variable $x$ is known as the cause variable.

label: Definition:Regression/Effect Variable
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Let $\map f {Y, x}$ denote the regression of $Y$ on $X$. The random variable $Y$ is known as the effect variable.

label: Definition:Regression/Informal Definition
snippet: A regression is a model which describes how the expectation of one random variable depends on one or more other random variables.

label: Definition:Regression Coefficient
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Let the regression of $Y$ on $x$, for a given value of $x$, be expressible in the form: $\expect {Y \mid x} = \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n \beta_i x^i$ The coefficients $\beta_i$ are known as the regression coefficients, and are usually unknown.

label: Definition:Regression Model
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process based on an equispaced time series. Let the values of $S$ at timestamps $t, t - 1, t - 2, \dotsc$ be $z_t, z_{t - 1}, z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ Let $\tilde z_t, \tilde z_{t - 1}, \tilde z_{t - 2}, \dotsc$ be deviations from a constant mean level $\mu$: $\tilde z_t = z_t - \mu$ Let $M$ be a linear filter model defined as $\tilde z_t = \phi_1 \tilde x_1 + \phi_2 \tilde x_2 + \dotsb + \phi_p \tilde x_p + a$ which relates a dependent variable $z$ to a set of independent variables $x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_p$ plus an error term $a$. $M$ is known as a regression model.

label: Definition:Regular
snippet: Set Theory: Regular Cardinal Complex Analysis: Regular Function: another term for a analytic complex function Matrix Algebra: Regular Matrix: another term for a nonsingular matrix, that is, an invertible matrix Abstract Algebra: Regular Representations: Left Regular Representation Right Regular Representation Regular Element: another term for a cancellable element Regular Element of Ring: an element of a ring which is not a zero divisor Geometry: Regular Polygon, for example: Regular Pentagon Regular Hexagon Regular Polyhedron: also see: Platonic Solid Topology: Regular Open Set Regular…

label: Definition:Regular Cardinal
snippet: Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal. Then $\kappa$ is a regular cardinal : $\map {\mathrm {cf} } \kappa = \kappa$ That is, the cofinality of $\kappa$ is equal to itself.

label: Definition:Regular Closed Set
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq T$. Then $A$ is regular closed in $T$ : $A = A^{\circ -}$ That is, $A$ equals the closure of its interior.

label: Definition:Regular Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a real interval. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. For all $t \in I$ let $T_{\map \gamma t} M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at the point $\map \gamma t$. Then $\gamma$ is called a regular curve : $\forall t \in I : \map {\gamma'} t \ne 0$

label: Definition:Regular Dodecahedron/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Dodecahedron: Also known as == It is commonplace for authors to refer to a regular dodecahedron as just an dodecahedron, glossing over the fact of its regularity.

label: Definition:Regular Graph
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be an simple graph whose vertices all have the same degree $r$. Then $G$ is called regular of degree $r$, or $r$-regular.

label: Definition:Regular Greek Cross
snippet: A regular Greek cross is a dodecagon which is formed by placing $5$ squares all of the same size so that $4$ of them abut the central $5$th square: 300px

label: Definition:Regular Icosahedron/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Icosahedron: Also known as == Occasionally an author may refer to a regular icosahedron as just an icosahedron, glossing over the fact of its regularity. It is wise to make sure of what is meant.

label: Definition:Regular Level Set
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $f \in \map {C^\infty} M : M \to \R$ be a smooth real-valued function. Let $p \in M$ be a base point in $M$. Let $\d f_p$ be the differential of $f$ at $p$. Let $c \in \R$. Let $\inv f c$ be a level set. Suppose every point of $\inv f c$ is a regular point of $f$: $\forall p \in \inv f c : \d f_p \ne 0$ Then $\inv f c$ is called a regular level set.

label: Definition:Regular Octahedron/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Octahedron: Also known as == It is commonplace for authors to refer to a regular octahedron as just an octahedron, glossing over the fact of its regularity.

label: Definition:Regular Open Set
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq T$. Then $A$ is regular open in $T$ : $A = A^{-\circ}$ That is, $A$ equals the interior of its closure.

label: Definition:Regular Polygon/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Polygon: Also known as == In , a regular polygon is referred to as an equilateral and equiangular polygon. Some sources use the word perfect or symmetrical instead of regular. The term regular $n$-gon is usually used nowadays to specify a regular polygon with a specific number, that is $n$, sides. The specific name is usually invoked only in order to draw attention to the fact that such a regular polygon has a particularly interesting set of properties.

label: Definition:Regular Polygon/Apothem
snippet: The apothem of a regular polygon $P$ is defined as the perpendicular distance from the center of $P$ to one of its sides. 300px In the above, the length of $OM$ is the apothem of the regular polygon.

label: Definition:Regular Polygon/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Regular Polygons == Specific instances of regular polygons with specific numbers of sides are as follows: $3$ sides: Equilateral Triangle $4$ sides: Square $5$ sides: Regular Pentagon $6$ sides: Regular Hexagon $7$ sides: Regular Heptagon $8$ sides: Regular Octagon $9$ sides: Regular Nonagon or Regular Enneagon $10$ sides: Regular Decagon $11$ sides: Regular Hendecagon or Regular Undecagon $12$ sides: Regular Dodecagon $17$ sides: Regular Heptadecagon Category:Definitions/Examples of Regular Polygons

label: Definition:Regular Polyhedron
snippet: A regular polyhedron is a polyhedron: $(1): \quad$ whose faces are congruent regular polygons $(2): \quad$ each of whose vertices is the common vertex of the same number of faces.

label: Definition:Regular Prime
snippet: A regular prime is a prime number $p$ that is not a divisor of the class number of the field obtained by adjoining to the rational numbers a primitive $p$th root of unity.

label: Definition:Regular Prism
snippet: A regular prism is a right prism whose bases are regular polygons.

label: Definition:Regular Prism/Also defined as
snippet: == Regular Prism Also defined as == Some sources define a regular prism such that, in addition, each of the lateral faces are squares. refers to such a regular prism as a uniform prism. Please do not confuse with the concept of square prism, because that is a prism with a square base. Category:Definitions/Regular Prisms

label: Definition:Regular Prism/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Prism: Also known as == A regular prism is also known as a right-regular prism. There appears not to be a standard term for an oblique prism whose bases are regular polygons.

label: Definition:Regular Representations/Also defined as
snippet: Some treatments of abstract algebra and group theory define the regular representations for semigroups. Some define it only for groups. Category:Definitions/Regular Representations

label: Definition:Regular Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a regular space : {{item||$\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_3$ space}} {{item||$\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_0$ space.}} That is:

label: Definition:Regular Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a regular space : {{item||$\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_3$ space}} {{item||$\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_1$ space.}} That is:

label: Definition:Regular Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a regular space : {{item||$\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_3$ space}} {{item||$\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_2$ space.}} That is:

label: Definition:Regular Star Polygon
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number such that $n \ge 3$. Let $m \in \N$ such that $m < n$ and such that $m$ and $n$ are coprime. Let $\CC$ be a circle whose circumference has been divided into $n$ equal arcs by $n$ points equally spaced. A regular star polygon is a plane figure formed by constructing a line segment joining every $m$th point of those $n$ equally spaced points. Such a regular star polygon can be denoted $\set {n / m}$.

label: Definition:Regular Surface
snippet: A subset $S \subseteq \R^3$ is a regular surface for each $p \in S$ there exist: a neighborhood $V \subseteq \R^3$ of $p$ an open set $U \subseteq \R^2$ a surjective mapping $\mathbf x : U \to V \cap S$, written as: $\map {\mathbf x} {u, v} := \struct {\map x {u, v}, \map y {u, v}, \map z {u, v} }$ such that: $(1): \quad \map x {u, v}, \map y {u, v}, \map z {u, v}$ are smooth $(2): \quad \mathbf x: U \to V \cap S$ is a homeomorphism $(3): \quad$ For each $q \in U$, the differential $\d_q \mathbf x: \R^2 \to \R^3$ of $\mathbf x$ at $q$ is one-to-one

label: Definition:Regular Tessellation
