snippet: A regular tessellation is a tessellation such that: Its tiles consist of congruent regular polygons No vertex of one tile may lie against the side of another tile.

label: Definition:Regular Tetrahedron/Also known as
snippet: == Regular Tetrahedron: Also known as == It is commonplace for authors to refer to a regular tetrahedron as just a tetrahedron, glossing over the fact of its regularity.

label: Definition:Related Angles
snippet: Related angles are angles which have the same absolute values for their trigonometric functions.

label: Definition:Relation
snippet: Let $S \times T$ be the cartesian product of two sets $S$ and $T$. A relation on $S \times T$ is an ordered triple: $\RR = \tuple {S, T, R}$ where $R \subseteq S \times T$ is a subset of the Cartesian product of $S$ and $T$. What this means is that a relation relates (certain) elements of one set or class $S$ with (certain) elements of another, $T$. Not all elements of $S$ need to be related to every (or even any) element of $T$ (but see Trivial Relation).

label: Definition:Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Relation: Also known as == In this context, technically speaking, what has been defined as a relation can actually be referred to as a binary relation. In the field of predicate logic, a relation can be seen referred to as a relational property. Some sources use the term correspondence for what is defined here as relation, reserving the term relation for what on is defined as endorelation, that is, a relation on $S \times S$ for some set $S$.

label: Definition:Relation/General Definition
snippet: Let $\ds \Bbb S = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n S_i = S_1 \times S_2 \times \ldots \times S_n$ be the cartesian product of $n$ sets $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n$. An $n$-ary relation on $\Bbb S$ is an ordered $n + 1$-tuple $\RR$ defined as: $\RR := \struct {S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n, R}$ where $R$ is an arbitrary subset $R \subseteq \Bbb S$. To indicate that $\tuple {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n} \in R$, we write: $\map \RR {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n}$

label: Definition:Relation/Graph
snippet: Let $S \times T$ be the cartesian product of two sets $S$ and $T$. Let $\RR$ be a relation on $S \times T$. The graph of $\RR$ is the set of all ordered pairs $\tuple {s, t}$ of $S \times T$ such that $s \mathrel \RR t$: $\map \TT \RR = \set {\tuple {s, t}: s \mathrel \RR t}$

label: Definition:Relation/Relation as Ordered Pair
snippet: Some sources define a relation between $S$ and $T$ as an ordered pair: $\struct {S \times T, \map P {s, t} }$ where: $S \times T$ is the Cartesian product of $S$ and $T$ $\map P {s, t}$ is a propositional function on ordered pairs $\tuple {s, t}$ of $S \times T$. Note that this approach leaves the domain and codomain inadequately defined. This situation arises in the case that $S$ or $T$ are empty, whence it follows that $S \times T$ is empty, but $T$ or $S$ are not themselves uniquely determined.

label: Definition:Relation/Relation as Subset of Cartesian Product
snippet: Most treatments of set theory and relation theory define a relation on $S \times T$ to refer to just the truth set itself: $\RR \subseteq S \times T$ where: $S \times T$ is the Cartesian product of $S$ and $T$. Thus under this treatment, $\RR$ is a set of ordered pairs, the first coordinate from $S$ and the second coordinate from $T$. This approach leaves the precise nature of $S$ and $T$ undefined.

label: Definition:Relation/Unary Relation
snippet: As a special case of an $n$-ary relation on $S$, note that when $n = 1$ we define a unary relation on $S$ as: $\RR \subseteq S$ That is, a unary relation is a subset of $S$.

label: Definition:Relation Segment
snippet: Let $X$ be a set. Let $\RR$ be a relation on $X$. Let $x \in X$. Then the $\RR$-segment of $x$, denoted by $x^\RR$, is defined by: $x^\RR := \set {y \in X: \tuple {y, x} \in \RR}$

label: Definition:Relation Theory
snippet: Relation theory is the subfield of set theory concerned with the properties of relations and relational structures. As a relation has the same conceptual definition as a (graph-theoretical) graph, it follows that there is considerable overlap between the fields of relation theory and graph theory.

label: Definition:Relation of Group Presentation/Also known as
snippet: == Relation of Group Presentation: Also known as == A relation in a group presentation is also known as a defining relation. It is also known as a relator.

label: Definition:Relational Loop
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots a_n$ be elements of $S$. A relational loop on $S$ takes the form: $\tuple {a_1 \mathrel \RR a_2 \land a_2 \mathrel \RR a_3 \dots \land a_{n - 1} \mathrel \RR a_n \land a_n \mathrel \RR a_1}$ That is, it is a subset of $\RR$ of the form: $\set {\tuple {a_1, a_2}, \tuple {a_2, a_3}, \ldots, \tuple {a_{n - 1}, a_n}, \tuple {a_n, a_1} }$

label: Definition:Relational Structure
snippet: A relational structure is an ordered pair $\struct {S, \RR}$, where: $S$ is a set $\RR$ is an endorelation on $S$.

label: Definition:Relational Structure/Warning
snippet: == Warning concerning Relational Structures == In the context of class theory, it is common to abuse notation by writing $\struct {C, \RR}$ when $C$ is a class and $\RR$ is a relation on $C$, and to call this a relational structure. One must take care, as if $C$ is a proper class then it cannot be a member of any class. By the set-theoretic definitions for ordered pairs, if $\struct {C, \RR}$ is an ordered pair then $C$ is a member of some class, which is a contradiction.

label: Definition:Relative Algebraic Closure
snippet: Let $L / K$ be a field extension. The relative algebraic closure of $K$ contained in $L$ is the set of all elements of $L$ that are algebraic over $K$.

label: Definition:Relative Complement
snippet: Let $S$ be a set, and let $T \subseteq S$, that is: let $T$ be a subset of $S$. Then the set difference $S \setminus T$ can be written $\relcomp S T$, and is called the relative complement of $T$ in $S$, or the complement of $T$ relative to $S$. Thus: $\relcomp S T = \set {x \in S : x \notin T}$

label: Definition:Relative Complement/Venn Diagram
snippet: == Venn Diagram for Relative Complement == The relative complement $\relcomp S T$ of the set $T$ $S$ is illustrated in the following Venn diagram by the red area: 300px

label: Definition:Relative Frequency
snippet: Let $S$ be a sample or a finite population. Let $\omega$ be a qualitative variable, or a class interval of a quantitative variable. The relative frequency of $\omega$ is defined as: $\map {\operatorname {RF} } \omega := \dfrac {f_\omega} n$ where: $f_\omega$ is the (absolute) frequency of $\omega$ $n$ is the number of individuals in $S$.

label: Definition:Relative Frequency Model
snippet: The relative frequency model is a mathematical model that defines the probability of an event occurring as follows: $\map \Pr {\text {event occurring} } := \dfrac {\paren {\text {observed number of times event has occurred in the past} } } {\paren {\text {observed number of times event has occurred or not occurred} } }$ That is, the probability of an event happening is defined as the relative frequency of a finite number of events of a particular type in some finite reference class of events.

label: Definition:Relative Matrix of Bilinear Form
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $M$ be a free $R$-module of finite dimension $n>0$. Let $\BB = \sequence {b_m}$ be an ordered basis of $M$. Let $f : M \times M \to R$ be a bilinear form. The matrix of $f$ relative to $\BB$ is the $n \times n$ matrix $\mathbf M_{f, \BB}$ where: $\forall \tuple {i, j} \in \closedint 1 n \times \closedint 1 n: \sqbrk {\mathbf M_{f, \BB} }_{i j} = \map f {b_i, b_j}$

label: Definition:Relative Matrix of Linear Transformation
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity. Let $G$ be a free $R$-module of finite dimension $n > 0$ Let $H$ be a free $R$-module of finite dimension $m > 0$ Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be an ordered basis of $G$. Let $\sequence {b_m}$ be an ordered basis of $H$. Let $u : G \to H$ be a linear transformation.

label: Definition:Relative Matrix of Linear Transformation/Warning
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity. Let $G$ be a free $R$-module of finite dimension $n>0$ Let $H$ be a free $R$-module of finite dimension $m>0$ Let $\sequence {a_n}$ be an ordered basis of $G$. Let $\sequence {b_m}$ be an ordered basis of $H$. Let $u : G \to H$ be a linear transformation. Consider the matrix of $u$ relative to $\sequence {a_n}$ and $\sequence {b_m}$: $\sqbrk {u; \sequence {b_m}, \sequence {a_n} }$ Note the order in which the bases are presented in this expression $\sqbrk {u; \sequence {b_m}, \sequence {a_n} }$.

label: Definition:Relative Matrix of Quadratic Form
snippet: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $\Char K \ne 2$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $K$ of finite dimension $n > 0$. Let $\BB$ be an ordered basis of $V$. Let $q$ be a quadratic form on $V$. Its matrix relative to $\BB$ is the matrix of its associated bilinear form relative to $\BB$, denoted $\mathbf M_{q, \BB}$.

label: Definition:Relative Risk
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be a events. Let the probability of $A$ occurring be $p_A$ and the probability of $B$ occurring be $p_B$. The relative risk of $A$ to $B$ is defined as $\dfrac {p_A} {p_B}$.

label: Definition:Relative Scheme
snippet: Let $S$ be a scheme. A (relative) scheme over $S$ is a morphism of schemes $p : X \to S$ for some scheme $X$.

label: Definition:Relative Uncertainty
snippet: Relative uncertainty is a measure of the uncertainty of a measurement relative to the measured value itself. Relative uncertainty is typically expressed as a percentage of the measured value.

label: Definition:Relative Velocity
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies in ordinary space.

label: Definition:Relative Velocity/Definition 1
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies in ordinary space. Let the frame of reference $\RR$ be such that $B$ is stationary $\RR$. Let $\mathbf v_{AB}$ be the velocity of $A$ $\RR$. Then $\mathbf v_{AB}$ is the velocity of $A$ relative to $B$.

label: Definition:Relative Velocity/Definition 2
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be bodies in ordinary space. Let $\mathbf v_A$ and $\mathbf v_B$ be the velocities of $A$ and $B$ in some frame of reference $\RR$. The velocity $\mathbf v_{AB}$ of $A$ relative to $B$ is defined as: $\mathbf v_{AB} := \mathbf v_A - \mathbf v_B$

label: Definition:Relatively Closed Set
snippet: Let $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq B \subseteq S$.

label: Definition:Relatively Closed Set/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq B \subseteq S$. $A$ is relatively closed in $B$ $A$ is closed in the relative topology of $B$.

label: Definition:Relatively Closed Set/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \left({S, \tau}\right)$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq B \subseteq S$. $A$ is relatively closed in $B$ there is a closed set $C \subseteq S$ with $C \cap B = A$.

label: Definition:Relatively Compact Subspace
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $T_H = \struct {H, \tau_H}$ be a subspace of $T$. Let $\map \cl H$ be the closure of $H$ in $T$. Then $T_H$ is relatively compact in $T$ $\map \cl H$ is compact.

label: Definition:Relatively Prime Integer Topology
snippet: Let $\Z_{>0}$ denote the set of (strictly) positive integers. Let $\BB$ be the set of sets $\set {\map {U_a} b: a, b \in \Z_{>0} }$ where: $\map {U_a} b = \set {b + n a \in \Z_{>0}: \gcd \set {a, b} = 1}$ where $\gcd \set {a, b}$ denotes the greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$. Then $\BB$ is the basis for a topology $\tau$ on $\Z_{>0}$. $\tau$ is then referred to as the relatively prime integer topology. The topological space $T = \struct {\Z_{>0}, \tau}$ is referred to as the relatively prime integer space.

label: Definition:Relativistic Mechanics
snippet: Relativistic mechanics is the study of the physical laws describing the motion of and forces on bodies whose velocities are approaching the speed of light.

label: Definition:Relativity Theory
snippet: Relativity theory is the branch of physics concerned with: the behaviour of matter travelling at speeds that are an appreciable fraction of the speed of light the structure of spacetime the theory of gravitation. The theory was developed in two stages:

label: Definition:Relativity Theory/Also known as
snippet: == Relativity Theory: Also known as == Relativity theory can also be referred to as the theory of relativity. Category:Definitions/Relativity Theory

label: Definition:Relativity Theory/General
snippet: The general theory of relativity extends the special theory of relativity by considering observers in non-inertial frames of reference.

label: Definition:Relativity Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Relativity Theory == Relativity theory was conceived by in the early $20$th century. The two theories that it comprises led to a re-analysis of the concepts of space and time, and of the interrelationship between measurement and observer.

label: Definition:Relativity Theory/Special
snippet: The special theory of relativity is concerned with the phenomena of physics as experience by two observers moving relative to one another at constant velocity. Hence it is restricted to inertial frames of reference.

label: Definition:Reliability
snippet: The reliability of a device $D$ is the probability $\map {\mathrm R} t$ that $D$ will not fail in the time interval $\openint 0 t$.

label: Definition:Remainder
snippet: Let $a, b \in \Z$ be integers such that $b \ne 0$. From the Division Theorem, we have that: $\forall a, b \in \Z, b \ne 0: \exists_1 q, r \in \Z: a = q b + r, 0 \le r < \size b$ The value $r$ is defined as the remainder of $a$ on division by $b$, or the remainder of $\dfrac a b$.

label: Definition:Remainder/Real
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R$ be real numbers such that $y \ne 0$. The remainder of $x$ on division by $y$ is defined as the value of $r$ in the expression: $\forall x, y \in \R, y \ne 0: \exists! q \in \Z, r \in \R: x = q y + r, 0 \le r < \size y$ From the definition of the Modulo Operation: $x \bmod y := x - y \floor {\dfrac x y}$ it can be seen that the remainder of $x$ on division by $y$ is defined as: $r = x \bmod y$

label: Definition:Reparametrization of Admissible Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $\closedint a b, \closedint c d$ be closed real intervals. Let $\gamma : \closedint a b \to M$ be an admissible curve. Let $\phi : \closedint c d \to \closedint a b$ be a homeomorphism. Let $\tuple {c_0, \ldots, c_k}$ be a finite subdivision of $\closedint c d$. Suppose $\tuple {c_0, \ldots, c_k}$ is such that for all $i \in \N : 1 \le i \le k$ the restriction of $\phi$ to each subinterval $\closedint {c_{i - 1}} {c_i}$ is a diffeomorphism onto its image.

label: Definition:Reparametrization of Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $I, I' \subseteq \R$ be real intervals. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Let $\phi : I' \to I$ be a diffeomorphism. Let $\tilde \gamma$ be a curve defined by: $\tilde \gamma := \gamma \circ \phi : I' \to M$ where $\circ$ denotes the composition of mappings $\gamma$ and $\phi$. Then $\tilde \gamma$ is called the reparametrization of $\gamma$.

label: Definition:Repdigit Number
snippet: Let $b \in \Z_{>1}$ be an integer greater than $1$. Let a (positive) integer $n$, greater than $b$, be expressed in base $b$. $n$ is a repdigit base $b$ all of the digits of $n$ are the same digit. For example: $55555$ or: $3333_4$ that second one being in base 4.

label: Definition:Representable Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a locally small category. Let $\mathbf{Set}$ be the category of sets. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf{Set}$ be a covariant functor. Then $F$ is representable there exists an object $C \in \mathbf C$ such that $F$ is naturally isomorphic to the covariant hom functor $\map {\operatorname{Hom} } {C, \cdot}$. That is, $F$ is representable $F$ has a representation.

label: Definition:Representation Theorem
snippet: A representation theorem is a theorem that states that every abstract structure with certain properties is isomorphic to another (abstract or concrete) structure.

label: Definition:Representation Theory
snippet: Representation theory is a branch of abstract algebra which studies algebraic structures (usually finite groups) by representing their elements as linear transformations of vector spaces.

label: Definition:Representation Theory/Also known as
snippet: == Representation Theory: Also known as == Representation theory is also known as character theory.

label: Definition:Representation of C*-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\map B \HH$ be the space of linear operators on $\HH$, considered as a $\text C^\ast$-algebra. Let $\pi : A \to \map B \HH$ be a $\ast$-algebra homomorphism. In the case of $A$ unital with identity element ${\mathbf 1}_A$, take $\map \pi { {\mathbf 1}_A} = I_{\map B \HH}$. We call $\tuple {\pi, \HH}$ a representation of $\struct {A, \ast, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$.

label: Definition:Repunit
snippet: Let $b \in \Z_{>1}$ be an integer greater than $1$. Let a (positive) integer $n$, greater than $b$ be expressed in base $b$. $n$ is a repunit base $b$ $n$ is a repdigit number base $b$ whose digits are $1$. That is, $n$ is a repunit base $b$ all of the digits of $n$ are $1$. When $b$ is the usual base $10$, $n$ is merely referred to as a repunit.

label: Definition:Repunit Prime
snippet: Let $b \in \Z_{>1}$ be an integer greater than $1$. A repunit prime base $b$ is a repunit base $b$ which is prime. When $b$ is the usual base $10$, such a prime is merely referred to as a repunit prime.

label: Definition:Repunit Prime/Index
snippet: The index of a repunit prime is the number of digits it has. Thus $R_n$ denotes a repunit prime with $n$ digits.

label: Definition:Residual
snippet: Residuals are the differences $e_i$ between the observed values $y_i$ and values $\hat y_i$ predicted by a model: $e_i = y_i - \hat y_i$

label: Definition:Residual Spectrum of Densely-Defined Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a densely-defined linear operator. We define the residual spectrum $\map {\sigma_r} T$ as the set of $\lambda \in \C$ such that: $T - \lambda I$ is injective but $\map {\paren {T - \lambda I} } {\map D T}$ is not everywhere dense in $\HH$.

label: Definition:Residual Variation
snippet: The residual variation is the variation which is not accounted for by a model fitted to data and which is determined by the residuals.

label: Definition:Residue
snippet: Complex Analysis Residue: the coefficient of $\paren {z - z_0}^{-1}$ in the Laurent series of a complex function Number Theory Residue: an integer $a$ is a residue of $m$ of order $n$ $\exists x \in \Z: x^n \equiv a \pmod m$ for $m, n \in \N$ where $a \perp m$. Modulo Arithmetic Residue: an integer congruent to $a$ modulo $m$. Field Theory Residue Field the quotient ring $R / m$ of a commutative local ring $R$ by its maximal ideal $m$.

label: Definition:Residue (Complex Analysis)
snippet: Let $f: \C \to \C$ be a complex function. Let $z_0 \in U \subset \C$ such that $f$ is analytic in $U \setminus \set {z_0}$. Then by Existence of Laurent Series, there is a Laurent series: $\ds \sum_{j \mathop = -\infty}^\infty a_j \paren {z - z_0}^j$ such that the sum converges to $f$ in $U - \set {z_0}$. The residue at a point $z = z_0$ of $f$ is defined as $a_{-1}$ in that Laurent series. It is denoted $\Res f {z_0}$ or just $\map {\mathrm {Res} } {z_0}$ when $f$ is understood.

label: Definition:Residue (Number Theory)
snippet: Let $m, n \in \N$ be natural numbers. Let $a \in \Z$ be an integer such that $a$ is not divisible by $m$. Then $a$ is a residue of $m$ of order $n$ : $\exists x \in \Z: x^n \equiv a \pmod m$ where $\equiv$ denotes modulo congruence.

label: Definition:Residue (Number Theory)/Nonresidue
snippet: Let $m, n \in \N$ be natural numbers. Let $a \in \Z$ be an integer such that $a$ is not divisible by $m$. $a$ is a nonresidue of $m$ of order $n$ there does not exist $x \in \Z$ such that: $x^n \equiv a \pmod m$ where $\equiv$ denotes modulo congruence.

label: Definition:Residue Class
snippet: Let $m \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\RR_m$ be the congruence relation modulo $m$ on the set of all $a, b \in \Z$: $\RR_m = \set {\tuple {a, b} \in \Z \times \Z: \exists k \in \Z: a = b + k m}$ We have that congruence modulo $m$ is an equivalence relation. So for any $m \in \Z$, we denote the equivalence class of any $a \in \Z$ by $\eqclass a m$, such that: {{eqn | l = \eqclass a m | r = \set {x \in \Z: a \equiv x \pmod m} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \set {x \in \Z: \exists k \in \Z: x = a + k m} | c = }} {{eqn | r = \set {\ldots, a - 2 m, a - m, a, a + m, a + 2 m, \ldots} | c…

label: Definition:Residue Field of Local Ring
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative local ring. Let $m$ be its maximal ideal. The residue field of $R$ is the quotient ring $R / m$.

label: Definition:Resolution of the Identity
snippet: Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\map \BB X$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $X$. Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\map B {\HH}$ be the space of bounded linear transformations on $\HH$. Let $\EE : \map \BB X \to \map B {\HH}$ be a function. For each $x, y \in \HH$, define $\EE_{x, y} : \map \BB X \to \C$ by: $\map {\EE_{x, y} } A = \innerprod {\map \EE A x} y$ for each $A \in \map \BB X$.

label: Definition:Resolvent Set/Bounded Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$ be a Banach space over $\C$. Let $A : X \to X$ be a bounded linear operator. Let $I : X \to X$ be the identity mapping on $X$. Let $\map \rho A$ be the set of $\lambda \in \C$ such that $A - \lambda I$ is invertible as a bounded linear transformation We call $\map \rho A$ the resolvent set of $A$.

label: Definition:Resolvent Set/Densely-Defined Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a closed densely-defined linear operator. We define the resolvent set of $T$, $\map \rho T$, as the set of $\lambda \in \C$ for which: $T - \lambda I$ is injective, $\map {\paren {T - \lambda I} } {\map D T}$ is everywhere dense in $\HH$, and $\paren {T - \lambda I}^{-1}$ is bounded. Note that if $\map D T = \HH$ and $T$ is bounded, we realise we may have a conflict with the definition of its resolvent set as a bounded linear operator.

label: Definition:Rest Mass
snippet: The rest mass of a body is its mass when it is at rest.

label: Definition:Rest Mass/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Rest Mass == Classical mechanics makes no distinction between the mass of a body and its rest mass. However, when the body moves, its effective mass increases. When the speed of the body becomes an appreciable fraction of the speed of light, this increase becomes significant. This mass caused by the body's motion then referred to as its relativistic mass. The famous Einstein's Mass-Energy Equation $E = m c^2$ connects the two concepts together.

label: Definition:Restricted Dipper Operation
snippet: Let $m, n \in \N_{>0}$ be non-zero natural numbers. Let $\N_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} }$ denote the initial segment of the natural numbers: $\N_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} } := \set {0, 1, \ldots, m + n - 1}$ Let $\N^*_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} }$ denote the set defined as $\N_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} } \setminus \set 0$: $\N^*_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} } := \set {1, 2, \ldots, m + n - 1}$ The restricted dipper operation $+^*_{m, n}$ is the binary operation on $\N^*_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} }$ defined as: $\forall a, b \in \N^*_{< \paren {m \mathop + n} }: a +^*_{m, n} b = \begin{cases} a + b…

label: Definition:Restricted Exponential Map
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g, \nabla}$ be a Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifold without boundary endowed with the Levi-Civita connection. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $\EE \subseteq TM$ be the domain of the exponential map. Let $\EE_p = \EE \cap T_p M$. Then the restricted exponential map, denoted by $\exp_p$, is the mapping $\exp : \EE_p \to M$.

label: Definition:Restricted P-adic Metric/Definition 2
snippet: Let $p \in \N$ be a prime. Let $d: \Z^2 \to \R_{\ge 0}$ be the mapping defined as: $\forall x, y \in \Z: \map d {x, y} = \begin {cases} 0 & : x = y \\ \dfrac 1 r & : x - y = p^{r - 1} k: r, k \in \Z, p \nmid k \end {cases}$ Then $d$ is known as the restricted $p$-adic metric on $\Z$.

label: Definition:Restriction/Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $X \subseteq S$. Let $f \sqbrk X \subseteq Y \subseteq T$. The restriction of $f$ to $X \times Y$ is the mapping $f {\restriction_{X \times Y} }: X \to Y$ defined as: $f {\restriction_{X \times Y} } = f \cap \paren {X \times Y}$ If $Y = T$, then we simply call this the restriction of $f$ to $X$, and denote it as $f {\restriction_X}$.

label: Definition:Restriction/Relation
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on $S \times T$. Let $X \subseteq S$, $Y \subseteq T$. The restriction of $\RR$ to $X \times Y$ is the relation on $X \times Y$ defined as: $\RR {\restriction_{X \times Y} }: = R \cap \paren {X \times Y}$ where $R \subseteq S \times T$ is the subset of the Cartesian product of $S$ and $T$ which defines the relation $\RR$. If $Y = T$, then we simply call this the restriction of $\RR$ to $X$, and denote it as $\RR {\restriction_X}$.

label: Definition:Restriction of Measure to Trace Sigma-Algebra of Measurable Set
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $A \in \Sigma$. Let $\Sigma_A$ be the trace $\sigma$-algebra of $A$ in $\Sigma$. We define the restriction of $\mu$ to $\Sigma_A$, written $\mu \restriction_{\Sigma_A}$, as the restriction of $\mu$ to $\Sigma_A$ as a mapping.

label: Definition:Restriction of Ordering
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Then the restriction of $\preceq$ to $T$, denoted $\preceq \restriction_T$, is defined as: ${\preceq \restriction_T} := {\preceq} \cap \paren {T \times T}$ viewing ${\preceq} \subseteq S \times S$ as a relation on $S$. Here, $\times$ denotes Cartesian product. Thence the restriction of $\preceq$ to $T$ is an instance of a restriction of a relation.

label: Definition:Restriction of Presheaf to Open Set
snippet: Let $C$ be a category. Let $X$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a $C$-valued presheaf on $X$. Let $U \subset X$ be open. The restriction of $\FF$ to $U$ is the restriction of the contravariant functor $\FF$ to the subcategory $U$.

label: Definition:Restriction of Ringed Space to Open Set
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ be a ringed space. Let $U \subset X$ be an open subset. Let $\OO_X {\restriction_U}$ denote the restriction of $\OO_X$ to $U$. The restriction of $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ to $U$ is the pair $\struct {U, \OO_X {\restriction_U} }$.

label: Definition:Restriction of Scalars of Module
snippet: Let $R$ and $S$ be commutative rings with unity. Let $f : R \to S$ be a ring homomorphism. Let $M$ be an $S$-module with ring representation $\rho$. The restriction of scalars of $M$ to $R$ via $f$ is the $R$-module with ring representation $\rho \circ f$.

label: Definition:Retract (Topology)
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Let $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be a topological subspace of $T_1$. Then $T_2$ is a retract of $T_1$ there exists a continuous retraction $f: S_1 \to S_2$ of $T_1$.

label: Definition:Retract (Topology)/Absolute
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Let $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be a topological subspace of $T_1$. Let $T_2$ be a retract of $T_1$. $T_2$ is an absolute retract of $T_1$ : for every closed subspace $B$ of a $T_4$ space $T$ such that $B$ is homeomorphic to $A$, then $B$ is a retract of $T$.

label: Definition:Retraction (Category Theory)
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $f: C \to D$ be a morphism of $\mathbf C$. A retraction of $f$ is a morphism $g: D \to C$ such that: $g \circ f = \operatorname{id}_C$ where $\operatorname{id}_C$ denotes the identity morphism on $C$.

label: Definition:Retraction (Category Theory)/Retract
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. Let $f: C \to D$ be a morphism. Let $g: D \to C$ be a retraction of $f$. Then $D$ is said to be a retract of $C$.

label: Definition:Retraction (Topology)
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ be a topological space. Let $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be a topological subspace of $T_1$. That is: $S_2 \subseteq S_1$ Let $f: S_1 \to S_2$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a retraction of $T_1$ : $\forall s \in S_2: \map f s = s$

label: Definition:Reversal
snippet: Let $m = \sqbrk {a_n a_{n - 1} a_{n - 2} \ldots a_2 a_1 a_0}$ be an integer expressed in base $10$. That is: $m = \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n a_k 10^k$ Its reversal $m'$ is the integer created by writing the digits of $m$ in the opposite order: $m' = \sqbrk {a_0 a_1 a_2 \ldots a_{n - 2} a_{n - 1} a_n}$ That is: $m' = \ds \sum_{k \mathop = 0}^n a_{n - k} 10^k$

label: Definition:Reversed Contour/Complex Plane
snippet: Let $C$ be a contour in the complex plane $\C$. Then $C$ is defined as a concatenation of a finite sequence $\sequence {C_1, \ldots, C_n}$ of directed smooth curves in $\C$. The reversed contour of $C$ is denoted $-C$ and is defined as the concatenation of the finite sequence: $-C_n, -C_{n-1}, \ldots, -C_1$ where $-C_k$ is the reversed directed smooth curve of $C_k$ for all $i \in \set {1, \ldots, n}$.

label: Definition:Riccati Equation
snippet: The Riccati equation is the first order ordinary differential equation: $y' = p \left({x}\right) + q \left({x}\right) y + r \left({x}\right) y^2$

label: Definition:Ricci Flow
snippet: Ricci flow is a technique that uses properties of solutions to certain partial differential equations.

label: Definition:Ricci Flow/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Ricci Flow == Using Ricci flow techniques, finally proved the Poincaré Conjecture for $n = 3$ in $2003$ (or $2004$; sources are not consistent).

label: Definition:Riemann-Christoffel Tensor
snippet:
A Riemann-Christoffel tensor is a tensor field which expresses the curvature of a Riemannian manifold. The Riemann-Christoffel tensor is given in terms of the Levi-Civita connection $
abla$ by: $\map R {u, v} w = 
abla_u 
abla_v w - 
abla_v 
abla_u w - 
abla_{\sqbrk {u, v} } w$ where $\sqbrk {u, v}$ is the Lie bracket of vector fields. It measures the extent to which the metric tensor is not locally isometric to that of Euclidean space.

label: Definition:Riemann-Christoffel Tensor/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riemann-Christoffel Tensor == The concept of a Riemann-Christoffel tensor was originated by in his application of a Riemannian manifold to the question of heat conduction.

label: Definition:Riemann-Stieltjes Integral
snippet: Let $\Bbb I = \closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $f, \alpha : \Bbb I \to \R$ be real functions that are bounded on $\Bbb I$. Then, $f$ is Riemann-Stieltjes integrable with respect to $\alpha$ on $\closedint a b$ : there exists some $A \in \R$ such that, for every $\epsilon > 0$, there is a finite subdivision $P_\epsilon$ of $\Bbb I$ such that: for every Riemann-Stieltjes sum $\map S {P, f, \alpha}$ of $f$ with respect to $\alpha$ for a subdivision $P$, where $P$ is finer than $P_\epsilon$: $\size {\map S {P, f, \alpha} - A} < \epsilon$ The real number $A$ is called the…

label: Definition:Riemann Integral/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riemann Integral == Consider the Riemann sum: $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map f {c_i} \Delta x_i$ Historically, the definite integral was an extension of this type of summation such that: The finite difference $\Delta x$ is instead the infinitely small difference $\rd x$ The finite sum $\ds \Sigma$ is instead of the sum of an infinite number of infinitely small quantities: $\ds \int$ Hence the similarity in notation: The notion of "infinitely small" does not exist in the modern formulation of real numbers.

label: Definition:Riemann Surface
snippet: A Riemann surface is a connected complex manifold of dimension $1$.

label: Definition:Riemann Surface/Also defined as
snippet: == Riemann Surface: Also defined as == Some authors do not require a Riemann surface to be connected or second-countable. Note that by Radó's Theorem, a connected Riemann surface is automatically second-countable. Category:Definitions/Riemann Surfaces

label: Definition:Riemann Surface/Elliptic/Definition 1
snippet: A Riemann surface is elliptic its universal cover is the Riemann sphere.

label: Definition:Riemann Surface/Elliptic/Definition 2
snippet: A Riemann surface is elliptic it admits a metric of constant positive curvature.

label: Definition:Riemann Surface/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riemann Surface == The Riemann surface was invented by as a device for clarifying the nature of multiple-valued functions in the complex plane. This invention led directly to the Riemann Mapping Theorem.

label: Definition:Riemann Surface/Hyperbolic/Definition 1
snippet: A Riemann surface is hyperbolic its universal cover is the unit disk.

label: Definition:Riemann Surface/Hyperbolic/Definition 2
snippet: A Riemann surface is hyperbolic it admits a metric of constant negative curvature.

label: Definition:Riemann Surface/Motivation
snippet: == Riemann Surface: Motivation == A Riemann surface allows a holomorphic function to be defined as a single-valued function without branches.

label: Definition:Riemann Surface/Parabolic/Definition 1
snippet: A Riemann surface is parabolic its universal cover is the complex plane.

label: Definition:Riemann Surface/Parabolic/Definition 2
snippet: A Riemann surface is parabolic it admits a metric of zero curvature.

label: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function
snippet: The Riemann $\zeta$ (zeta) function is the complex function defined on the half-plane $\map \Re s > 1$ as the series: $\ds \map \zeta s = \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {n^s}$

label: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Also known as
snippet: == Riemann Zeta Function: Also known as == The Riemann zeta function is also often known as just the zeta function. Some sources use hyphens: Riemann zeta-function or zeta-function Some sources style it as Riemann's zeta function.

label: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Critical Line
snippet: Consider the Riemann zeta function $\map \zeta s$. Let $s = \sigma + i t$. The line defined by the equation $\sigma = \dfrac 1 2$ is known as the critical line. Hence the popular form of the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis: All the nontrivial zeroes of the Riemann zeta function lie on the critical line. 520px

label: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Critical Strip
snippet: == Riemann Hypothesis == Consider the Riemann zeta function $\map \zeta s$. Let $s = \sigma + i t$. The region defined by the equation $0 < \sigma < 1$ is known as the critical strip. 520px

label: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riemann Zeta Function == Investigation of what is now known as the Riemann zeta function goes back as far as , who showed in $1744$ that $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \frac 1 {n^s} = \prod_{\text {$p$ prime} } \frac 1 {1 - p^{-s} }$. The Riemann zeta function was discussed by in his $1859$ article . In that paper he made several statements about that function. Studying it led to his proof of the Prime Number Theorem. All of the statements made in that paper have now been proved except for one.

label: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Zero
snippet: The zeroes of the Riemann $\zeta$ function are, according to the conventional definition of the zero of a (complex) function, the points $s \in \C$ such that: $\map \zeta s = 0$

label: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Zero/Nontrivial
snippet: The nontrivial zeroes of the Riemann $\zeta$ function are the zeroes of $\zeta$ that are not trivial.

label: Definition:Riemann Zeta Function/Zero/Trivial
snippet: The trivial zeroes of the Riemann $\zeta$ function are the strictly negative even integers : $\set {n \in \Z: n = -2 \times k: k \in \N_{\ne 0} } = \set {-2, -4, -6, \ldots}$

label: Definition:Riemannian Arc Length Function of Admissible Curve
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\closedint a b \subseteq \R$ be a closed real interval. Let $\gamma : \closedint a b \to M$ be an admissible curve. The (Riemannian) arc length function of $\gamma$ is the real function $s : \closedint a b \to \R$ defined by: $\ds \map s t := \map {L_g} {\valueat \gamma {\closedint a t} } = \int_a^t \size {\gamma}_g \rd t$ where $L_g$ is the Riemannian length of $\gamma$, and $\size {\, \cdot \,}_g$ is the Riemannian inner product norm.

label: Definition:Riemannian Covering
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ and $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $\pi : \tilde M \to M$ be a smooth covering map. Suppose $\pi$ is a local isometry. Then $\pi$ is called a Riemannian covering.

label: Definition:Riemannian Density
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $\tuple {E_i}$ be an local orthonormal frame. Let $\mu$ be a positive smooth density such that: $\forall \tuple {E_i} : \map \mu {E_1, \ldots, E_n} = 1$ Then $\mu$ is known as the Riemannian density.

label: Definition:Riemannian Distance
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a connected Riemannian manifold. Let $p,q \in M$ be points. Let $\gamma_{pq} : \closedint 0 1 \to M$ be an admissible curve such that $\map \gamma 0 = p$ and $\map \gamma 1 = q$. Let $\map {L_g} {\gamma_{pq}}$ be the Riemannian length of $\gamma_{pq}$. Then the Riemannian distance between $p$ and $q$, denoted by $\map {d_g} {p, q}$, is the infimum of all such curves $\gamma_{pq}$: $\ds \map {d_g} {p, q} := \inf_{\gamma_{pq} \mathop \in M} \map {L_g} {\gamma_{pq}}$

label: Definition:Riemannian Geometry
snippet: Riemannian geometry is the branch of differential geometry that studies Riemannian manifolds.

label: Definition:Riemannian Inner Product Norm
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $p \in M$ be a point. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p$. Let $v \in T_p M$ be a vector. Then the Riemannian inner product norm of $v$ is: $\ds \size {v}_g := \sqrt {g_p \innerprod v v}$ where $g_p$ is the Riemannian metric at $p$.

label: Definition:Riemannian Length of Admissible Curve
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $\gamma : \closedint a b \to M$ be an admissible curve. Then the (Riemannian) length of $\gamma$, denoted by $\map {L_g} \gamma$, is defined by: $\ds \map {L_g} \gamma := \int_a^b \size {\map \gamma t}_g \rd t$ where $\size {\map \gamma t}_g$ is the Riemannian inner product norm.

label: Definition:Riemannian Manifold
snippet: A $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold is a pair $\struct {M, g}$ where $M$ is a $n$-dimensional smooth manifold and $g$ is a Riemannian metric on $M$.

label: Definition:Riemannian Manifold/Also known as
snippet: == Riemannian Manifold: Also known as == A Riemannian manifold is also known as a Riemannian space, or Riemann space. Some sources use the term Riemannian geometry, although on the term is used to refer to the mathematical branch that studies Riemannian manifolds.

label: Definition:Riemannian Manifold/Dimension
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. The dimension of $M$ is $n$.

label: Definition:Riemannian Manifold/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Riemannian Manifold == The concept of a Riemannian manifold was originated by in his trial lecture (published as Ueber die Hypothesen, welche der Geometrie zu Grande liegen) to apply for position of Privatdozent (unpaid lecturer) at Göttingen.

label: Definition:Riemannian Manifold Isotropic at Point
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I_p$ be the isotropy representation at $p \in M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $S_p \subseteq T_p M$ be the set of unit vectors in $T_p M$. Suppose $I_p$ acts transitively on $S_p$. Then $M$ is said to be isotropic at $p$.

label: Definition:Riemannian Metric
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $p \in M$ be a point in $M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p$ with the inner product $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_p$. Let $g \in \map {\TT^2} M$ be a smooth covariant 2-tensor field such that for all $p$ its value at $p$ is equal to $\innerprod \cdot \cdot_p$: $\forall p \in M : g_p = \innerprod \cdot \cdot_p$ Then $g$ is known as a Riemannian metric on $M$.

label: Definition:Riemannian Metric/Interpretation
snippet: == Riemannian Metric: Interpretation == Consider a smooth manifold $\MM$ on the real space $\R^n$. A Riemannian metric on $\MM$ is a metric $\d s$ between nearby points $\tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ and $\tuple {x_1 + \d x_1, x_2 + \d x_2, \ldots, x_n + \d x_n}$ by means of the quadratic differential form: $\ds \d s^2 = \sum_{i, j \mathop = 1}^n \map {g_{i j} } x \rd x_i \rd x_j$ where each $g_{i j}$ is a suitable real-valued function of $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. Usually the $g_{i j}$ are taken so as to form a non-zero determinant.

label: Definition:Riemannian Metric Mapping
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $TM$ and $T^*M$ be tangent and cotangent bundles of $M$. Let $p \in M$ be a base point. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space of $M$ at $p$. Let $v, w \in T_p M$ be tangent vectors. Then the bundle homomorphism is the mapping $\hat g : T M \to T^* M$ such that: $\forall p \in M : \forall v, w \in T_p M : \map {\map {\hat g} v} w = \map {g_p} {v, w}$

label: Definition:Riemannian Submanifold
snippet: Let $M$ be an immersed submanifold with or without a boundary. Let $g$ be a metric induced on $M$. Then $\struct {M, g}$ is called the Riemannian submanifold.

label: Definition:Riemannian Submersion
snippet: Let $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$, $\struct {M, g}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $\pi : \tilde M \to M$ be a smooth submersion. Let $x \in \tilde M$, $p \in M$ be points in $\tilde M$ and $M$. Let $H_x$ be a horizontal tangent space at $x$. Let $T_p M$ be a tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$. Let $g_p$ be a Riemannian metric at $p$.

label: Definition:Riemannian Volume Form/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an oriented $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $T^* M$ be the cotangent bundle of $M$. Let $\tuple {\epsilon^1, \ldots, \epsilon^n}$ be a local oriented orthonormal coframe of $T^* M$. The Riemannian volume form, denoted by $\rd V_g$, is an $n$-form such that: $\rd V_g = \epsilon^1 \wedge \ldots \wedge \epsilon^n$

label: Definition:Riemannian Volume Form/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an oriented $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $T M$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $\tuple {E_1, \ldots, E_n}$ be a local oriented orthonormal frame of $T M$. The Riemannian volume form, denoted by $\rd V_g$, is an $n$-form such that: $\map {\rd V_g} {E_1, \ldots, E_n} = 1$

label: Definition:Riemannian Volume Form/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be an oriented $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Let $\tuple {x_1, \ldots, x_n}$ be a set of local oriented coordinates. Let $g_{i j}$ be a local form of metric $g$. The Riemannian volume form, denoted by $\d V_g$, is an $n$-form such that: $\d V_g = \sqrt {\map \det {g_{i j} } } \rd x^1 \wedge \ldots \wedge \rd x^n$

label: Definition:Rig
snippet: A rig is an additive semiring $\struct {S, *, \circ}$ in which $\struct {S, *}$ is a monoid. Alternatively, this is a semiring in which $\struct {S, *}$ is a commutative monoid. That is, $\struct {S, *, \circ}$ is a rig $\struct {S, *, \circ}$ satisfies the rig axioms: Note that the zero element needs to be specified here as an axiom: $\text M 2$. By Ring Product with Zero, in a ring, the property $\text M 2$ of the zero element follows as a consequence of the ring axioms.

label: Definition:Right-Hand Derivative
snippet: Let $B$ be a Banach space over the set of real numbers $\R$. Let $f: \R \to B$ be a mapping from $\R$ to $B$. The right-hand derivative of $f$ is defined as the right-hand limit: $\ds \map {f'_+} x = \lim_{h \mathop \to 0^+} \frac {\map f {x + h} - \map f x} h$ If the right-hand derivative exists, then $f$ is said to be right-hand differentiable at $x$.

snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vector quantities. The right-hand rule for the vector cross product $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b$ is a consequence of the determinant definition: $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k\\ a_i & a_j & a_k \\ b_i & b_j & b_k \\ \end{vmatrix}$ when embedded in the conventional right-hand Cartesian $3$-space: 450px Let a right hand be placed such that: the $3$rd finger is at right-angles to both the thumb and index finger, upwards from the palm the thumb points along the direction of $\mathbf a$ the index finger points…

label: Definition:Right-Invariant Riemannian Metric
snippet: Let $G$ be a Lie group. Let $\struct {G, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Suppose $g$ is invariant under all right translations $R_\phi : G \to G$: $\forall \phi \in G : {R_\phi}^* g = g$ where $*$ denotes the pullback of $g$ by $R_\phi$. Then $g$ is said to be right-invariant.

label: Definition:Right-Regular Antiprism
snippet: A right-regular antiprism is an antiprism such that: its bases are regular polygons its lateral faces are isosceles triangles.

label: Definition:Right-Regular Antiprism/Also defined as
snippet: == Right-Regular Antiprism: Also known as == Some sources define a right-regular antiprism as an antiprism whose bases are regular polygons, making no restriction of the nature of the lateral faces.

label: Definition:Right-Truncatable Prime
snippet: A right-truncatable prime is a prime number which remains prime when any number of digits are removed from the right hand end.

snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ be locally small categories. Let $F : \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ and $G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be functors. $G$ is a right adjoint functor of $F$ there exists an adjunction $\struct {F, G, \alpha}$.

label: Definition:Right Angle
snippet: A right angle is an angle that is equal to one quarter of a full angle. That is, equal to one half of a straight angle.

label: Definition:Right Ascension
snippet: Let $P$ be a point on the celestial sphere. The right ascension of $P$ is the angular distance measured eastwards along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox. This is denoted $\alpha$ or $\mathrm {RA}$. Conventionally, right ascension is measured in units of time rather than angle. Hence $24$ hours corresponds to $360$ degrees.

label: Definition:Right Cancellable Mapping
snippet: A mapping $f: X \to Y$ is right cancellable (or right-cancellable) : $\forall Z: \forall \paren {h_1, h_2: Y \to Z}: h_1 \circ f = h_2 \circ f \implies h_1 = h_2$ That is, for any set $Z$: If $h_1$ and $h_2$ are mappings from $Y$ to $Z$ then $h_1 \circ f = h_2 \circ f$ implies $h_1 = h_2$.

label: Definition:Right Circular Cone/Axis

snippet: 300px Let $\triangle AOB$ be a right-angled triangle such that $\angle AOB$ is the right angle. Let $K$ be the right circular cone formed by the rotation of $\triangle AOB$ around $OB$. Let $BC$ be the circle described by $B$. The base of $K$ is the plane surface enclosed by the circle $BC$. '

label: Definition:Right Circular Cone/Generatrix
snippet: 300px Let $K$ be a right circular cone. Let $A$ be the apex of $K$. Let $B$ be the base of $K$. Then a line joining the apex of $K$ to its directrix is a generatrix of $K$.

snippet: Let $K$ be a right circular cone. Then $K$ is right-angled the opening angle of $K$ is a right angle. ' Category:Definitions/Right Circular Cones

label: Definition:Right Derived Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be an abelian category with enough injectives. Let $\mathbf B$ be an abelian category. Let $F: \mathbf A \to \mathbf B$ be a left exact functor. Let $X$ and $Y$ be objects of $\mathbf A$. Let $f: X \to Y$ be a morphism of $\mathbf A$. Let $I$ be an arbitrary injective resolution of $X$. Let $J$ be an arbitrary injective resolution of $Y$. Let $\tilde f : I \to J$ be a morphism of cochain complexes induced by $f$. Let $\map F I$ denote the cochain complex defined by applying the functor on cochains induced by $F$ to $I$. Let $i \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a non-negative integer.

label: Definition:Right Elliptical Cylinder
snippet: A right elliptical cylinder is an elliptical cylinder which is also a right cylinder. That is, it is a cylinder with bases are: ellipses perpendicular to the generatrices.

label: Definition:Right Exact Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be categories. Let $F : \mathbf A \to \mathbf B$ be a functor. Then $F$ is right exact $F$ preserves finite colimits.

label: Definition:Right Inverse
snippet: Mapping Theory: Right Inverse Mapping Abstract Algebra: Right Inverse Element Matrix Theory: Right Inverse Matrix

label: Definition:Right Inverse Mapping
snippet: Let $S, T$ be sets where $S \ne \O$, that is, $S$ is not empty. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $g: T \to S$ be a mapping such that: $f \circ g = I_T$ where: $f \circ g$ denotes the composite mapping $g$ followed by $f$ $I_T$ is the identity mapping on $T$. Then $g: T \to S$ is called a right inverse (mapping) of $f$.

label: Definition:Right Module over Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. A right module over $R$ is an $R$-algebraic structure $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ with one operation $\ast: G \times R \to G$, the (right) ring action, which satisfies the right module axioms:

label: Definition:Right Operation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. For any $x, y \in S$, the right operation on $S$ is the binary operation defined as: $\forall x, y \in S: x \to y = y$

label: Definition:Right Order Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be a totally ordered set. Let $\tau$ be the topology on $S$ generated by the basis sets of the form: $S_a = \set {x: a \prec x}$ for $a \in S$. Then the topological space $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq, \tau}$ is known as the right order topology on $S$.

label: Definition:Right Order Topology on Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\tau$ be the subset of the power set $\powerset {\R}$ be defined as: $\tau := \O \cup \set {\openint a \infty: a \in \R} \cup \R$ Then $\tau$ is the right order topology on $\R$. Hence the topological space $T = \struct {\R, \tau}$ can be referred to as the right order space on $\R$.

label: Definition:Right Order Topology on Strictly Positive Integers
snippet: Let $\Z_{>0}$ be the set of strictly positive integers. For $n \in \Z_{>0}$, let $O_n$ denote the set defined as: $O_n := \set {x \in \Z_{>0}: x \ge n}$ Let $\tau$ be the subset of the power set $\powerset {\Z_{>0} }$ be defined as: $\tau := \O \cup \set {O_n: n \in \Z_{>0} }$ Then $\tau$ is the right order topology on $\Z_{>0}$. Hence the topological space $T = \struct {\Z_{>0}, \tau}$ can be referred to as the right order space on $\Z_{>0}$.

label: Definition:Right Ring Action Defined by Ring Antirepresentation
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an abelian group. Let $\rho: R \to \map {\operatorname {End} } M$ be a ring antirepresentation. The associated right ring action is the right linear ring action: $M \times R \to M$: $\tuple {m, r} \mapsto \map \rho r \paren m$

label: Definition:Right Singular Vector of Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a matrix of order $m \times n$. Let $\mathbf A = \mathbf U \mathbf D \mathbf V$ be a singular value decomposition of $\mathbf A$. The columns of $\mathbf V$ are known as the right singular vectors of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Right Spherical Triangle
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a spherical triangle. Let one of the angles of $\triangle ABC$ be a right angle: $\dfrac \pi 2$. 500px Then $\triangle ABC$ is known as a right spherical triangle.

label: Definition:Ring
snippet: Abstract Algebra: Ring Boolean Ring Set Theory: Ring of Sets Topology: Topological Ring Geometry: Ring, also known as an annulus

label: Definition:Ring (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: A ring $\struct {R, *, \circ}$ is a semiring in which $\struct {R, *}$ forms an abelian group. That is, in addition to $\struct {R, *}$ being closed, associative and commutative under $*$, it also has an identity, and each element has an inverse.

label: Definition:Ring (Abstract Algebra)/Also defined as
snippet: == Ring: Also known as == Some sources insist on another criterion which a semiring $\struct {S, *, \circ}$ must satisfy to be classified as a ring: Such sources then use the term rng (pronounced rung): for a ring without an identity. However, defines a ring as any structure fulfilling axioms $\text A 0$ - $\text A 4$, $\text M 0$ - $\text M 1$ and $\text D$, whether or not it has a unity. The more specific structure which does have a unity is termed a ring with unity.

label: Definition:Ring (Abstract Algebra)/Ring Less Zero
snippet: Let $\struct {R, *, \circ}$ be a ring whose zero is $0$. It is convenient to have a symbol for $R \setminus \set 0$, that is, the set of all elements of the ring without the zero. Thus we usually use: $R_{\ne 0} = R \setminus \set 0$

label: Definition:Ring Action Defined by Ring Representation
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an abelian group. Let $\rho : R \to \map {\operatorname {End} } M$ be a ring representation. The associated (left) ring action is the linear ring action: $R \times M \to M$: $\tuple {r, m} \mapsto \map {\map \rho r} m$

label: Definition:Ring Antirepresentation
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an abelian group. A ring antirepresentation of $R$ on $M$ is a ring antihomomorphism to the endomorphism ring of $M$.

label: Definition:Ring Automorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\phi: R \to R$ be a (ring) isomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a ring automorphism. That is, a ring automorphism is a (ring) isomorphism from a ring to itself.

label: Definition:Ring Endomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\phi: R \to R$ be a (ring) homomorphism from $R$ to itself. Then $\phi$ is a ring endomorphism.

label: Definition:Ring Epimorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {S, \oplus, *}$ be rings. Let $\phi: R \to S$ be a (ring) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a ring epimorphism $\phi$ is a surjection.

label: Definition:Ring Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {S, \oplus, *}$ be rings. Let $\phi: R \to S$ be a mapping such that both $+$ and $\circ$ have the morphism property under $\phi$. That is, $\forall a, b \in R$: {{eqn | n = 1 | l = \map \phi {a + b} | r = \map \phi a \oplus \map \phi b }} {{eqn | n = 2 | l = \map \phi {a \circ b} | r = \map \phi a * \map \phi b }} Then $\phi: \struct {R, +, \circ} \to \struct {S, \oplus, *}$ is a ring homomorphism.

label: Definition:Ring Homomorphism/Also defined as
snippet: == Ring Homomorphism: Also defined as == Sources dealing only with rings with unity may define a ring homomorphism as a unital ring homomorphism.

label: Definition:Ring Homomorphism/Also known as
snippet: == Ring Homomorphism: Also known as == A ring homomorphism is also known as a (ring) representation, but that is reserved on for a more specialised definition. Some sources hyphenate: ring-homomorphism.

label: Definition:Ring Less Zero/Also denoted as
snippet: == Ring Less Zero: Also denoted as == Most sources use $R^*$ to denote the set of elements of a ring without the zero. However, this is also used by some sources to mean the group of units of such a ring $R$. Hence prefers the more explicit notation $\R_{\ne 0}$.

label: Definition:Ring Monomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {S, \oplus, *}$ be rings. Let $\phi: R \to S$ be a (ring) homomorphism. Then $\phi$ is a ring monomorphism $\phi$ is an injection.

label: Definition:Ring Product/Also known as
snippet: == Ring Product: Also known as == The operation of ring product is also known as multiplication. However, on it is preferred that multiplication is kept to the conventional meaning as applied to multiplication of numbers. Hence, in the context of the general ring, the word product is mandatory, except in specific cases (for example, the case of matrix multiplication) where the term multiplication is established.

label: Definition:Ring Representation
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an abelian group. A ring representation of $R$ on $M$ is a ring homomorphism from $R$ to the endomorphism ring $\map {\operatorname {End} } M$.

label: Definition:Ring Representation/Unital
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $M$ be an abelian group. A unital ring representation of $R$ on $M$ is a ring representation $R \to \map \End M$ which is unital. That is, it is a unital ring homomorphism from $R$ to the endomorphism ring $\map \End M$.

label: Definition:Ring Representation Defined by Ring Action
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an abelian group. Let $\phi : R \times M \to M$ be a left linear ring action. The associated ring representation is the ring representation $\rho: R \to \map {\operatorname {End} } M$ with: $\map {\map \rho r} m = \map \phi {r, m}$

label: Definition:Ring Theory
snippet: Ring Theory is a branch of abstract algebra which studies rings and other related algebraic structures.

label: Definition:Ring of Arithmetic Functions
snippet: Let $\AA$ be the set of all arithmetic functions. Let $*$ denote Dirichlet convolution, and $+$ the pointwise sum of functions. The ring of arithmetic functions is the ring $\struct {\AA, +, *}$.

label: Definition:Ring of Bounded Continuous Real-Valued Functions
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\R$ denote the real number line. Let $\struct {\map C {S, \R}, +, *}$ be the ring of continuous real-valued functions from $S$. The ring of bounded continuous real-valued functions from $S$, denoted $\map {C^*} {S, \R}$, is the set of all bounded continuous mappings in $\map C {S, \R}$ with (pointwise) ring operations $+$ and $*$ restricted to $\map {C^*} {S, R}$.

label: Definition:Ring of Cauchy Sequences
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a normed division ring. Let $\struct {R^\N, +', \circ'}$ be the ring of sequences over $R$. Let $\CC$ be the set of Cauchy sequences on $R$. The ring of Cauchy sequences over $R$ is the subring $\struct {\CC, +', \circ'}$ of $R^\N$ with unity. The (pointwise) ring operations on the ring of Cauchy sequences over $R$ are defined as: $\forall \sequence {x_n}, \sequence {y_n} \in R^\N: \sequence {x_n} +' \sequence {y_n} = \sequence {x_n + y_n}$ $\forall \sequence {x_n}, \sequence {y_n} \in R^\N: \sequence {x_n} \circ' \sequence {y_n} =…

label: Definition:Ring of Continuous Mappings
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau_{_S} }$ be a topological space. Let $\struct {R, +, *, \tau_{_R} }$ be a topological ring. Let $\struct {R^S, +, *}$ be the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$. The ring of continuous mappings from $S$ to $R$, denoted $\map C {S, R}$, is the set of all continuous mappings in $R^S$ with (pointwise) ring operations $+$ and $*$ restricted to $\map C {S, R}$.

label: Definition:Ring of Continuous Real-Valued Functions
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau }$ be a topological space. Let $\R$ denote the real number line. The ring of continuous mappings from $S$ to $\R$, denoted $\map C {S, \R}$, is called the ring of continuous real-valued functions from $S$. The (pointwise) ring operations on the ring of continuous real-valued functions from $S$ are defined as: $\forall f, g \in \map C {S, \R} : f + g : S \to \R$ is defined by: $\forall s \in S : \map {\paren{f + g}} s = \map f x + \map g s$ $\forall f, g \in \map C {S, \R} : f g : S \to \R$ is defined by: $\forall s \in S : \map {\paren{f g}} s = \map f x \map g s$

label: Definition:Ring of Eisenstein Integers
snippet: The ring of Eisenstein integers $\struct {\Z \sqbrk \omega, +, \times}$ is the algebraic structure formed from: the set of Eisenstein integers $\Z \sqbrk \omega$, where $\omega = e^{2 \pi i / 3}$ the operation of complex addition the operation of complex multiplication.

label: Definition:Ring of Endomorphisms
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \oplus}$ be an abelian group. Let $\mathbb G$ be the set of all group endomorphisms of $\struct {G, \oplus}$. Let $*: \mathbb G \times \mathbb G \to \mathbb G$ be the operation defined as: $\forall u, v \in \mathbb G: u * v = u \circ v$ where $u \circ v$ is defined as composition of mappings. Then $\struct {\mathbb G, \oplus, *}$ is called the ring of endomorphisms of the abelian group $\struct {G, \oplus}$.

label: Definition:Ring of Gaussian Integers
snippet: The ring of Gaussian integers $\struct {\Z \sqbrk i, +, \times}$ is the algebraic structure formed from: the set of Gaussian integers $\Z \sqbrk i$ the operation of complex addition the operation of complex multiplication.

label: Definition:Ring of Idempotents
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring. Let $A$ be the set of all idempotent elements of $R$ under $\circ$: $A = \set {x \in R: x \circ x = x}$ Define a binary operation $\circ$ on $A$ by: $\forall x, y \in A: x \oplus y := x + y - 2 x \circ y$ Denote also with $\circ$ the restriction of $\circ$ to $A$. The algebraic structure $\struct {A, \oplus, \circ}$ is called the ring of idempotents of $R$. It is an idempotent ring, as shown on Ring of Idempotents is Idempotent Ring.

label: Definition:Ring of Integers
snippet: The ring of integers $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ is the set of integers under the two operations of integer addition and integer multiplication.

label: Definition:Ring of Integers Modulo m
snippet: Let $m \in \Z: m \ge 2$. Let $\Z_m$ be the set of integers modulo $m$. Let $+_m$ and $\times_m$ denote addition modulo $m$ and multiplication modulo $m$ respectively. The algebraic structure $\struct {\Z_m, +_m, \times_m}$ is the ring of integers modulo $m$.

label: Definition:Ring of Integers of Number Field
snippet: Let $K$ be a number field. The ring of integers of $K$, usually denoted $\OO_K$ or $\mathfrak o_K$, is the integral closure of $\Z$ in $K$.

label: Definition:Ring of Integers of Number Field/Also defined as
snippet: Some sources define a ring of integers specifically on an algebraic number field. The motivation behind this decision is that some mathematicians are not very interested in the general case. However, this point of view goes against the inclusivist philosophical position endorsed by .

label: Definition:Ring of Mappings
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S$ be a set. Let $R^S$ be the set of all mappings from $S$ to $R$. The ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$ is the algebraic structure $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ where $+'$ and $\circ'$ are the (pointwise) operations induced on $R^S$ by $+$ and $\circ$. From Structure Induced by Ring Operations is Ring, $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ is a ring.

label: Definition:Ring of Mappings/Additive Inverse
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ be the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$. From Structure Induced by Ring Operations is Ring, $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ is a ring. The additive inverse in the ring of mappings is defined by: $\forall f \in R^S : -f \in R^S : \forall s \in S : \map {\paren {-f} } x = -\map f x$

label: Definition:Ring of Mappings/Commutativity
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring. Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ be the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$. From Structure Induced by Commutative Ring Operations is Commutative Ring, the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$ is a commutative ring.

label: Definition:Ring of Mappings/Pointwise Addition
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ be the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$. The pointwise operation $+'$ induced by $+$ on the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$ is called pointwise addition and is defined as: $\forall f, g \in R^S: f +’ g \in R^S$ $\forall s \in S: \map {\paren {f +’ g} } x = \map f x + \map g x$

label: Definition:Ring of Mappings/Pointwise Multiplication
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ be the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$. The pointwise operation $\circ'$ induced by $\circ$ on the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$ is called pointwise multiplication and is defined as: $\forall f, g \in R^S: f \circ’ g \in R^S$ $\forall s \in S: \map {\paren {f \circ’ g} } x = \map f x \circ \map g x$

label: Definition:Ring of Mappings/Units
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity $1$. Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ be the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$. Let $f : S \to U_R$ is a mapping into the set of units $U_R$ of $R$. From Unit of Ring of Mappings iff Image is Subset of Ring Units: $f$ is a unit in the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$ and: the inverse of $f$ is the mapping defined by: $f^{-1} \in R^S : \forall x \in S: \map {\paren {f^{-1} } } x = \map f x^{-1}$

label: Definition:Ring of Mappings/Unity
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose unity is $1$. Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ be the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$. From Structure Induced by Ring with Unity Operations is Ring with Unity, the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$ is a ring with unity whose unity is the constant mapping $f_1: S \to R$ defined as: $\quad \forall s \in S : \map {f_1} x = 1$

label: Definition:Ring of Mappings/Zero
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ be the ring of mappings from $S$ to $R$. From Structure Induced by Ring Operations is Ring, $\struct {R^S, +', \circ'}$ is a ring. The zero of the ring of mappings is the constant mapping $f_0 : S \to R$ defined by: $\quad \forall s \in S : \map {f_0} x = 0$ where $0$ is the zero in $R$

label: Definition:Ring of Polynomial Forms
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $I$ be a set Let $\family {X_i: i \in I}$ be an indexed set. Let $A = R \sqbrk {\family {X_i: i \in I} }$ be the set of all polynomial forms over $R$ in $\family {X_i: i \in I}$. Let $+$ and $\circ$ denote the standard addition and multiplication of polynomial forms. The ring of polynomial forms is the ordered triple $\struct {A, +, \circ}$.

label: Definition:Ring of Quaternions
snippet: The ring of quaternions $\struct {\H, +, \times}$ is the set of quaternions under the two operations of quaternion addition and quaternion multiplication.

label: Definition:Ring of Sequences
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Given the natural numbers $\N$, the ring of sequences over $R$ is the ring of mappings $\struct {R^\N, +', \circ'}$ where: $(1): \quad R^\N$ is the set of sequences in $R$ $(2): \quad +'$ and $\circ'$ are the (pointwise) operations induced by $+$ and $\circ$. From Structure Induced by Ring Operations is Ring, $\struct {R^\N, +', \circ'}$ is a ring.

label: Definition:Ring of Sequences/Units
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity $1$. Let $\struct {R^\N, +', \circ'}$ be the ring of sequences over $R$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence over the set of units $U_R$ of $R$. From Unit of Ring of Mappings iff Image is Subset of Ring Units: $\sequence {x_n}$ is a unit in the ring of sequences over $R$ and: the inverse of $\sequence {x_n}$ is the sequence defined by: $\sequence {x_n}^{-1} \in R^\N : \sequence {x_n}^{-1} = \sequence {x_n^{-1}}$

label: Definition:Ring of Sequences/Unity
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity $1$. Let $\struct {R^\N, +', \circ'}$ be the ring of sequences over $R$. From Structure Induced by Ring with Unity Operations is Ring with Unity, the ring of sequences is a ring with unity; namely the constant sequence $\tuple {1, 1, 1, \dots}$, where $1$ is the unity in $R$.

label: Definition:Ring of Sequences/Zero
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {R^\N, +', \circ'}$ be the ring of sequences over $R$. The zero of the ring of sequences is the constant sequence $\tuple {0, 0, 0, \dots}$, where $0$ is the zero of $R$.

label: Definition:Ring of Sequences of Finite Support
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $P \sqbrk R$ be the set of all sequences in $R$ whose domain is $\N$: $P \sqbrk R = \set {\sequence {r_0, r_1, r_2, \ldots} }$ and whose support is finite. Let the operations $\oplus$ and $\odot$ on $P \sqbrk R$ be defined as follows: The ring of sequences of finite support over $R$ is the ring $\struct {P \sqbrk R, \oplus, \odot}$.

label: Definition:Ring of Square Matrices
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\map {\MM_R} n$ denote the $n \times n$ matrix space over $R$. Let $+$ denote the operation of matrix entrywise addition. Let $\times$ be (temporarily) used to denote the operation of conventional matrix multiplication. The algebraic structure: $\struct {\map {\MM_R} n, +, \times}$ is known as the ring of square matrices of order $n$ over $R$

label: Definition:Ring with Unity
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a non-null ring. Then $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ is a ring with unity the multiplicative semigroup $\struct {R, \circ}$ has an identity element. Such an identity element is known as a unity. It follows that such a $\struct {R, \circ}$ is a monoid.

label: Definition:Ring with Unity/Also known as
snippet: == Ring with Unity: Also known as == Other names for ring with unity include: ring with a one, or ring with $1$ ring with a multiplicative identity or just ring with identity unitary ring unital ring unit ring Some sources simply refer to a ring, taking the presence of the unity for granted. On , the term ring does not presuppose said presence.

label: Definition:Ringed Space
snippet: A ringed space is a pair $\struct {X, \OO_X}$ where: $X$ is a topological space $\OO_X$ is a sheaf of commutative rings with unity on $X$.

label: Definition:Ringoid (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: A ringoid is a triple $\struct {S, *, \circ}$ where: That is: {{eqn | q = \forall a, b, c \in S | l = a \circ \paren {b * c} | r = \paren {a \circ b} * \paren {a \circ c} }} {{eqn | q = \forall a, b, c \in S | l = \paren {a * b} \circ c | r = \paren {a \circ c} * \paren {b \circ c} }}

label: Definition:Rise
snippet: Let $P_1 = \tuple {x_1, y_1}$ and $P_2 = \tuple {x_2, y_2}$ be points in the Cartesian plane. The rise from $P_1$ to $P_2$ is the difference between their ordinates: $y_2 - y_1$

label: Definition:Rise/Also known as
snippet: == Rise: Also known as == The rise between two points is also known as their $y$-step.

label: Definition:Rising Factorial
snippet: Let $x$ be a real number (but usually an integer). Let $n$ be a positive integer. Then the rising factorial with $n$ terms of $x$ is defined as: $\ds x^{\overline n} := \prod_{j \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} \paren {x + j} = x \paren {x + 1} \cdots \paren {x + n - 1}$

label: Definition:Rising Factorial/Notation
snippet: == Notation for Rising Factorial == The notation $x^{\overline n}$ for $x$ to the $n$ rising is due to , who used it in $1893$. This is the notation of choice on . A more commonly seen notation (though arguably not as good) is $x^{\paren n}$. This is known as the Pochhammer function or (together with $\paren x_n$ for its falling counterpart) the Pochhammer symbol (after ). However, depending on the context, either $\paren x_n$ or $x^{\paren n}$ can be used to indicate the rising factorial.

label: Definition:Ritz Sequence
snippet: Let $\sequence {\phi_n}$ be an infinite sequence of mappings in a normed linear space, where: $\phi_n: \R \to \R$ Let this sequence be constrained by the requirements defined in the definition of the Ritz method. Then the sequence $\set {\phi_n}$ can be called a Ritz Sequence.

label: Definition:Rng
snippet: In the context of abstract algebra, a rng is a ring $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ which specifically does not have a unity. That is, such that the semigroup $\struct {R, \circ}$ does not have an identity element.

label: Definition:Robbins Constant
snippet: The Robbins constant $R$ is defined as the mean distance $D$ between $2$ points chosen at random from the interior of a unit cube: {{eqn | l = R | r = \frac {4 + 17 \sqrt 2 - 6 \sqrt3 - 7 \pi} {105} + \frac {\map \ln {1 + \sqrt 2 } } 5 + \frac {2 \, \map \ln {2 + \sqrt 3} } 5 }}

label: Definition:Rocket Science
snippet: Rocket science is the branch of physics concerned with the propulsion of rockets.

label: Definition:Rod
snippet: A rod is an idealized straight body which has: length linear mass density but whose width is approximated to zero. A rod can be defined as rigid or flexible, according to the needs of the model to which it may contribute.

label: Definition:Roman Numerals
snippet: The Roman numerals are: To express other numbers than these, symbols are placed next to each other so as to cumulate: for example: $\text {II}$ means $2$ $\text {CCXVI}$ means $216$. For brevity in presentation, the technique is used of placing a smaller denomination in front of a larger one so as to subtract the former from the latter For example: $\text {IV}$ means $4$ $\text {XCIX}$ means $99$ (although $\text {IC}$ could be used, it is not).

label: Definition:Roman Numerals/Also presented as
snippet: == Roman Numerals: Also presented as == It is commonplace to present Roman numerals in lowercase: $\text {i, v, x, l, c, d, m}$ Category:Definitions/Roman Numerals

label: Definition:Roman Numerals/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Roman Numerals == Before the adoption of the Arabic numerals, abacism was the usual technique for doing arithmetic, originating in ancient times. It is still used in rural areas of, for example, the Asian steppes, where writing materials are not to be wasted and electronic aids are un-needed. With the invention of the techniques offered by the so-called Arabic numerals in mediaeval times, an alternative method of doing arithmetic developed, called algorism. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Roman Numerals/Uses
snippet: == Uses of Roman Numerals == The Roman numerals are used today almost solely for enumeration in certain traditional contexts: $(1): \quad$ The presentation of years in dates, especially embedded in the masonry of buildings to indicate its year of construction $(2): \quad$ In the context of the cartesian plane, Roman numerals are traditionally used to enumerate the quadrants $(3): \quad$ Enumerations of lists, particularly when sublists are required which (because of the presentational style selected by the author) need different styles of presentation, for example: "See section $1 \…

label: Definition:Roman Numerals/Warning
snippet: == Roman Numerals: Warning == Because of the similarity in shape between the letter $\text I$ and the number $1$, it is a common mistake to confuse them and use $1$ where $\text I$ should be used. Consequently, hilariously clumsy-looking constructions can be found in published works (usually in [http://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/pretentious pretentious] artwork such as can often be found on the covers of contemporary musical product) such as $\text V 1 1 1$ for $\text {VIII}$. Even more hilarous is hearing muggles vocalise the above as vee wun wun wun. Category:Definitions/Roman Numerals

label: Definition:Root
snippet: Inverse ← Division/Biaction Super root/Tetraction → Analysis: Root of a number: If $y^m = x$ then $x = \sqrt [m] y$, and $x$ is the $m$th root of $y$. Root of an equation: The roots of an equation $E$ are the values of the variables for which $E$ is true. Root of a mapping (or function): The roots of a mapping $f$ are the values of $x$ for which $\map f x = 0$. Root of a polynomial: the roots of a polynomial $f$ are the values of $x$ for which $\map f x = 0$.

label: Definition:Root System
snippet: Let $E$ be a real vector space with inner product $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$. A root system $\Phi \subset E$ is a finite set of nonzero vectors in $E$ (called roots) such that: By Reflection Formula (Geometry), axiom $(3)$ may be rewritten {{axiom | n = 3 | t = $\forall \alpha, \beta \in \Phi: \beta - 2 \dfrac {\innerprod \alpha \beta} {\innerprod \alpha \alpha} \alpha \in \Phi$}} By the vector projection formula, axiom $(4)$ may be written {{axiom | n=4 | t=$\forall \alpha, \beta \in \Phi: 2 \dfrac {\innerprod \alpha \beta} {\innerprod \alpha \alpha} \in \Z$}} The notation $\innerprod \alpha…

label: Definition:Root of Congruence
snippet: Let $f$ be the congruence defined as: $\map f x \equiv 0 \pmod n$ A root of $f$ is an integer $a$ such that: $\map f a \equiv 0 \pmod n$

label: Definition:Root of Mapping
snippet: Let $f: R \to R$ be a mapping on a ring $R$. Let $x \in R$. Then the values of $x$ for which $\map f x = 0_R$ are known as the roots of the mapping $f$.

label: Definition:Root of Number
snippet: Let $x, y \in \R_{\ge 0}$ be positive real numbers. Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer such that $n \ne 0$. Then $y$ is the positive $n$th root of $x$ : $y^n = x$ and we write: $y = \sqrt[n] x$ Using the power notation, this can also be written: $y = x^{1/n}$ When $n = 2$, we write $y = \sqrt x$ and call $y$ the positive square root of $x$. When $n = 3$, we write $y = \sqrt [3] x$ and call $y$ the cube root of $x$. Note the special case where $x = 0 = y$: $0 = \sqrt [n] 0$

label: Definition:Root of Number/Also known as
snippet: == Root of Number: Also known as == A root of a number is also known as: a radical a radix.

label: Definition:Root of Number/Extraction
snippet: The process of evaluating roots of a given real number is referred to as extraction.

label: Definition:Root of Polynomial
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $f \in R \sqbrk x$ be a polynomial over $R$. A root in $R$ of $f$ is an element $x \in R$ for which $\map f x = 0$, where $\map f x$ denotes the image of $f$ under the evaluation homomorphism at $x$.

label: Definition:Root of Unity/Complex
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. The complex $n$th roots of unity are the elements of the set: $U_n = \set {z \in \C: z^n = 1}$

label: Definition:Root of Unity/Complex/First
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. In Complex Roots of Unity in Exponential Form it is shown that the complex $n$th roots of unity are the elements of the set: $U_n = \set {e^{2 i k \pi / n}: k \in \N_n}$ The root $e^{2 i \pi / n}$ is known as the first (complex) $n$th root of unity.

label: Definition:Root of Unity/Primitive
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{> 0}$ be a strictly positive integer. Let $F$ be a field. Let $U_n$ denote the set of all $n$th roots of unity.

label: Definition:Root of Unity Modulo m
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer. Let $m \in \Z_{>1}$ be a positive integer greater than one. Then $a$ is an $n^{th}$ root of unity modulo $m$ : $a^n \equiv 1 \pmod m$ Solving the following equation over the smallest integers modulo $m$: $\ds \paren {a^n - 1} = \paren {a - 1} \paren {\sum_{k \mathop = 0}^{n - 1} a^k} \equiv 0 \pmod m$ will produce the roots.
