snippet: Let $T$ be a time series whose observations are $\map z {\tau_1}, \map z {\tau_2}, \dotsb, \map z {\tau_t}, \dotsb$ at an unbroken sequence of timestamps $\tau_1, \tau_2, \dotsb, \tau_t, \dotsb$. When we have $N$ such successive observations, without a missing value, we write: $z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_t, \dotsb, z_N$ and it is understood that the subscripts correspond directly to the timestamps.

label: Definition:Successive Values of Time Series/Equispaced
snippet: Let $T$ be a time series whose observations are $\map z {\tau_1}, \map z {\tau_2}, \dotsb, \map z {\tau_t}, \dotsb$ at an unbroken sequence of timestamps $\tau_1, \tau_2, \dotsb, \tau_t, \dotsb$. Let $T$ be equispaced with time interval $h$ between adjacent observations. Then $N$ successive observations, written as: $z_1, z_2, \dotsb, z_t, \dotsb, z_N$ occur at timestamps: $\tau_0 + h, \tau_0 + 2 h, \dotsb, \tau_0 + t h, \dotsb, \tau_0 + N h$ Hence we can refer to the observations at timestamp $\tau_0 + t h$ as $z_t$.

label: Definition:Successor
snippet: Successor element: In an ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$, $a$ is a successor element to $b$ $b \prec a$. Immediate successor element: In an ordered set $\struct {S, \preceq}$, $a$ is the immediate successor element to $b$ $b \prec a$ and $\nexists c \in S: b \prec c \prec a$. Successor set: If $S$ is a set, then its successor set $S^+$ is defined as $S^+ := S \cup \set S$. Successor mapping: The mapping at the heart of a Peano structure which encapsulates its ability to sustain the Principle of Mathematical Induction.

label: Definition:Successor Mapping
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. The successor mapping $s$ is the mapping on $V$ defined and denoted: $\forall x \in V: \map s x := x \cup \set x$ where $x$ is a set in $V$.

label: Definition:Successor Ordinal
snippet: A successor ordinal is the successor set of an ordinal: $\alpha^+ := \map s \alpha = \alpha \cup \set \alpha$

label: Definition:Sufficiently Large
snippet: Let $P$ be a property of real numbers. Then: $\map P x$ holds for all sufficiently large $x$ $\exists a \in \R: \forall x \in \R: x \ge a: \map P x$ That is: There exists a real number $a$ such that for every (real) number not less than $a$, the property $P$ holds. It is not necessarily the case, for a given property $P$ about which such a statement is made, that the value of $a$ actually needs to be known, merely that such a value can be demonstrated to exist.

label: Definition:Sufficiently Small
snippet: Let $P$ be a property of real numbers. Then: $\map P x$ holds for all sufficiently small $x$ $\exists \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \forall x \in \R: \size x \le \epsilon: \map P x$ That is, : There exists a real number $\epsilon$ such that for every (real) number not more than $\epsilon$ in absolute value, the property $P$ holds. It is not necessarily the case, for a given property $P$ about which such a statement is made, that the value of $\epsilon$ actually needs to be known, merely that such a value can be demonstrated to exist.

label: Definition:Sum
snippet: Arithmetic: Under the operation of addition of two numbers $a$ and $b$, the sum is the result of the operation $a + b$. Algebra: A summation is a repeated addition on a sequence (either finite or infinite) of numbers, usually signalled by the summation sign: $\ds \sum$ Abstract Algebra, Group Theory: Definition:Direct Sum

label: Definition:Sum of Cardinals
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be the cardinals associated with $A$ and $B$ respectively. Then the sum of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is defined as: $\mathbf a + \mathbf b = \map \Card {A \sqcup B}$ where: $A \sqcup B$ denotes the disjoint union of $A$ and $B$ $\map \Card {A \sqcup B}$ denotes the cardinal associated with $A \sqcup B$.

label: Definition:Sum of Densely-Defined Linear Operators
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\struct {\map D S, S}$ and $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be densely-defined linear operators. Let: $\map D {S + T} = \map D S \cap \map D T$ Define $S + T : \map D {S + T} \to \HH$ by: $\map {\paren {S + T} } x = S x + T x$ for each $x \in \map D {S + T}$. We say that $\struct {\map D {S + T}, S + T}$ is the sum of $\struct {\map D S, S}$ and $\struct {\map D T, T}$.

label: Definition:Sum of Finite Set
snippet: Let $\mathbb A$ be one of the standard number systems $\N, \Z, \Q, \R, \C$. Let $S \subset \mathbb A$ be a finite subset. The sum of $S$ is the summation of the identity mapping on $S$ over $S$: $\ds \sum S = \sum_{s \mathop \in S} s$ Category:Definitions/Summations

label: Definition:Summation
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let $\tuple {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \in S^n$ be an ordered $n$-tuple in $S$.

label: Definition:Summation/Finite
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let the set of values of $j$ which satisfy the propositional function $\map R j$ be finite. Then the summation $\ds \sum_{\map R j} a_j$ is described as being a finite summation.

label: Definition:Summation/Finite Support
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group. Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to G$ be a mapping. Let the support $\map \supp f$ be finite. Let $g$ be the restriction of $f$ to $\map \supp f$. The summation of $f$ over $S$, denoted $\ds \sum_{s \mathop \in S} \map f s$, is the summation over the finite set $\map \supp f$ of $g$: $\ds \sum_{s \mathop \in S} \map f s = \sum_{s \mathop \in \map \supp f} \map g s$ Category:Definitions/Summations

label: Definition:Summation/Index Variable
snippet: Consider the summation, in either of the three forms: $\ds \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n a_j \qquad \sum_{1 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} a_j \qquad \sum_{\map R j} a_j$ The variable $j$, an example of a bound variable, is known as the index variable of the summation.

label: Definition:Summation/Infinite
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let an infinite number of values of $j$ satisfy the propositional function $\map R j$. Then the precise meaning of $\ds \sum_{\map R j} a_j$ is: $\ds \sum_{\map R j} a_j = \paren {\lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \sum_{\substack {\map R j \\ -n \mathop \le j \mathop < 0}} a_j} + \paren {\lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \sum_{\substack {\map R j \\ 0 \mathop \le j \mathop \le n} } a_j}$ provided that both limits exist.

label: Definition:Summation/Summand
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} \subseteq S$ be a set of elements of $S$. Let $\map R j$ be a propositional function of $j$. Let: $\ds \sum_{\map R j} a_j$ be an instance of a summation on $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$. The set of elements $\set {a_j \in S: 1 \le j \le n, \map R j}$ is called the summand.

label: Definition:Summation/Summand/Infinite
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +}$ be an algebraic structure where the operation $+$ is an operation derived from, or arising from, the addition operation on the natural numbers. Let $A = \set {a_j: j \in \Z} \subseteq S$ be a set of elements of $S$. Let $\map R j$ be a propositional function of $j$. Let: $\ds \sum_{\map R j} a_j$ be an instance of a summation on $A$. Let an infinite number of values of $j$ satisfy $\map R j = \T$. The set of elements $\set {a_j \in A: \map R j}$ is called an infinite summand.

label: Definition:Summation/Vacuous Summation
snippet: Take the summation: $\ds \sum_{\map \Phi j} a_j$ where $\map \Phi j$ is a propositional function of $j$. Suppose that there are no values of $j$ for which $\map \Phi j$ is true. Then $\ds \sum_{\map \Phi j} a_j$ is defined as being $0$. This summation is called a vacuous summation. This is because: $\forall a: a + 0 = a$ where $a$ is a number. Hence for all $j$ for which $\map \Phi j$ is false, the sum is unaffected. This is most frequently seen in the form: $\ds \sum_{j \mathop = m}^n a_j = 0$ where $m > n$.

label: Definition:Summation over Finite Index
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +}$ be a commutative monoid. Let $\family {g_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed subset of $G$ where the indexing set $I$ is finite. Let $\set {e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_n}$ be a finite enumeration of $I$. Let $\tuple {g_{e_1}, g_{e_2}, \ldots, g_{e_n} }$ be the ordered tuple formed from the composite mapping $g \circ e: \closedint 1 n \to G$. The summation over $I$, denoted $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \in I} g_i$, is defined as the summation over $\tuple {g_{e_1}, g_{e_2}, \ldots, g_{e_n} }$: $\ds \sum_{i \mathop \in I} g_i = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n g_{e_k}$

label: Definition:Sun
snippet: The Sun is the star around which Earth (and the other planets of the solar system) is in orbit.

label: Definition:Superabundant Number
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a positive integer. Then $n$ is superabundant : $\forall m \in \Z_{>0}, m < n: \dfrac {\map {\sigma_1} m} m < \dfrac {\map {\sigma_1} n} n$ where $\sigma_1$ denotes the divisor sum function. That is, $n$ has a higher abundancy index than any smaller positive integer.

label: Definition:Superabundant Number/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Superabundant Numbers == The sequence of superabundant numbers begins: $1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 120, 180, 240, 360, 720, 840, 1260, \ldots$ Category:Definitions/Abundant Numbers

label: Definition:Superadditive Function (Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, +_S}$ and $\struct {T, +_T, \preccurlyeq}$ be semigroups such that $\struct {T, +_T, \preccurlyeq}$ is ordered. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping from $S$ to $T$ which satisfies the relation: $\forall a, b \in S: \map f a +_T \map f b \preccurlyeq \map f {a +_S b}$ Then $f$ is defined as being superadditive. The usual context in which this is encountered is where $S$ and $T$ are both the set of real numbers $\R$ (or a subset of them).

label: Definition:Superdifferential
snippet: Let $\innerprod X {X'}$ be a dual system over $\R$. Let $C \subseteq X$ be a convex set. Let $f : C \to \R$ be a convex function. Let $x \in C$. We define the superdifferential of $f$ at $x$ as the (possibly empty) set of supergradients of $f$ at $x$. We denote this by $\partial \map f x$. This notation clashes with that of the subdifferential, care will be taken to distinguish the two when they simultaneously appear.

label: Definition:Superfactorial
snippet: Let $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ be a positive integer. The superfactorial of $n$ is defined as: $n\$ = \ds \prod_{k \mathop = 1}^n k! = 1! \times 2! \times \cdots \times \left({n - 1}\right)! \times n!$ where $k!$ denotes the factorial of $n$.

label: Definition:Superinductive Class
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $g: A \to A$ be a mapping on $A$. Then $A$ is superinductive under $g$ : $A$ is inductive under $g$ $A$ is closed under chain unions. That is: {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= $A$ is closed under $g$: | q = \forall x | m = \paren {x \in A \implies \map g x \in A} }}

label: Definition:Superscript
snippet: A superscript is a symbol (often a number) written above and to the right of a given symbol to identify a specific instance of the object that symbol denotes. This is often to reference an specific exponent. When placed in round brackets, it also indicates the order of a derivative.

label: Definition:Supertransitive Class
snippet: Let $A$ be a transitive class. Then $A$ is said to be a supertransitive class : $\forall x \in A: \powerset x \subseteq A$ That is, if $A$ contains the power set of all of its elements.

label: Definition:Supplemental Chords
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle. Supplemental chords are a pair of chords of $\CC$ joining a point on the circumference of $\CC$ to the two endpoints of a diameter of $\CC$.

label: Definition:Supplementary Angles
snippet: 500px Let $\angle ACB$ be a straight angle. Let $\angle BCD + \angle DCA = \angle ACB$. That is, $\angle DCA = \angle ACB - \angle BCD$. Then $\angle DCA$ is the supplement of $\angle BCD$. Hence, for any angle $\alpha$ (whether less than a straight angle or not), the supplement of $\alpha$ is $\pi - \alpha$. Measured in degrees, the supplement of $\alpha$ is $180 \degrees - \alpha$. If $\alpha$ is the supplement of $\beta$, then it follows that $\beta$ is the supplement of $\alpha$. Hence we can say that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are supplementary.

label: Definition:Support
snippet: In abstract algebra: Support of Mapping to Algebraic Structure Support of Real-Valued Function Support of Module Support of Element of Direct Product In analysis and topology: Support of Continuous Mapping Support of Continuous Real-Valued Function In functional analysis: Support of Schwartz Distribution In mapping theory: Support of Permutation Support of Characteristic Function In probability theory Support of Random Variable

label: Definition:Support of Continuous Mapping/Real-Valued
snippet: Let $f: \R^n \to \R$ be a continuous real-valued function. The support of $f$ is the closure of the set of elements $x$ of $\R^n$ whose values under $f$ are non-zero. That is: $\map \supp f = \cl \set {x \in \R^n: \map f x \ne 0}$ Category:Definitions/Real Analysis

label: Definition:Support of Mapping to Algebraic Structure
Definition:Support of Mapping to Algebraic Structure/Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. The support of $f$ is the set of elements $x$ of $S$ whose values under $f$ are non-zero: $\map \supp f := \set {x \in S: \map f x \ne 0}$

label: Definition:Support of Module
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $M$ be a unitary $A$-module. The support $\map \supp M$ of $M$ is the set of prime ideals $P$ of $A$ such that the localization of $M$ at $P$ is nonzero: $\map \supp M = \set {P \in \Spec A : M_P \ne 0}$ where $\Spec A$ is the spectrum of $A$. Category:Definitions/Module Theory

label: Definition:Support of Permutation
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $f$ be a permutation on $S$. The support of $f$ is the subset of moved elements: $\map \supp f = \set {x \in S: \map f x \ne x}$

label: Definition:Support of Vector with respect to Schauder Basis
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\GF$. Let $x \in X$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a Schauder basis for $X$. Let $\sequence {x_n^\ast}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be the coordinate functionals associated with $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We define the support of the vector $x$ $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ as the set of $n \in \N$ such that $\map {x_n^\ast} x \ne 0$, and denote it $\map \supp x$.

label: Definition:Supremum/Also known as
snippet: Particularly in the field of analysis, the supremum of a set $T$ is often referred to as the least upper bound of $T$ and denoted $\map {\mathrm {lub} } T$ or $\map {\mathrm {l.u.b.} } T$. Some sources refer to the supremum of a set as the supremum on a set. Some sources refer to the supremum of a set as the join of the set and use the notation $\bigvee T$ or $\ds \bigvee_{y \mathop \in T} y$. Some sources introduce the notation $\ds \sup_{y \mathop \in T} y$, which may improve clarity in some circumstances.

label: Definition:Supremum Metric
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $M = \struct {A', d'}$ be a metric space. Let $A$ be the set of all bounded mappings $f: S \to M$. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in A: \map d {f, g} := \sup_{x \mathop \in S} \map {d'} {\map f x, \map g x}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum. $d$ is known as the supremum metric on $A$.

label: Definition:Supremum Metric/Bounded Continuous Mappings
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $A$ be the set of all continuous mappings $f: M_1 \to M_2$ which are also bounded. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in A: \map d {f, g} := \sup_{x \mathop \in A_1} \map {d_2} {\map f x, \map g x}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum. $d$ is known as the supremum metric on $A$.

label: Definition:Supremum Metric/Bounded Real-Valued Functions
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $A$ be the set of all bounded real-valued functions $f: S \to \R$. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in A: \map d {f, g} := \sup_{x \mathop \in S} \size {\map f x - \map g x}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum. $d$ is known as the supremum metric on $A$.

label: Definition:Supremum Metric/Bounded Real Functions on Interval
snippet: Let $\closedint a b \subseteq \R$ be a closed real interval. Let $A$ be the set of all bounded real functions $f: \closedint a b \to \R$. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in A: \map d {f, g} := \sup_{x \mathop \in \closedint a b} \size {\map f x - \map g x}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum. $d$ is known as the supremum metric on $A$.

label: Definition:Supremum Metric/Bounded Real Sequences
snippet: Let $A$ be the set of all bounded real sequences. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall \sequence {x_i}, \sequence {y_i} \in A: \map d {\sequence {x_i}, \sequence {y_i} } := \sup_{n \mathop \in \N} \size {x_n - y_n}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum. $d$ is known as the supremum metric on $A$.

label: Definition:Supremum Metric/Continuous Real Functions
snippet: Let $\closedint a b \subseteq \R$ be a closed real interval. Let $A$ be the set of all continuous functions $f: \closedint a b \to \R$. Let $d: A \times A \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in A: \map d {f, g} := \sup_{x \mathop \in \closedint a b} \size {\map f x - \map g x}$ where $\sup$ denotes the supremum. $d$ is known as the supremum metric on $A$.

label: Definition:Supremum Metric/Differentiability Class
snippet: Let $\closedint a b \subseteq \R$ be a closed real interval. Let $r \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $\mathscr D^r \closedint a b$ be the set of all continuous functions $f: \closedint a b \to \R$ which are of differentiability class $r$. Let $d: \mathscr D^r \closedint a b \times \mathscr D^r \closedint a b \to \R$ be the function defined as: $\ds \forall f, g \in \mathscr D^r \closedint a b: \map d {f, g} := \sup_{\substack {x \mathop \in \closedint a b \\ i \in \set {0, 1, 2, \ldots, r} } } \size {\map {f^{\paren i} } x - \map {g^{\paren i} } x}$ where: $f^{\paren i}$ denotes the $i$th…

label: Definition:Supremum Norm/Continuous on Closed Interval Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $I = \closedint a b$ be a closed real interval. Let $\map C I$ be the space of real-valued functions continuous on $I$. Let $f \in \map C I$. Let $\size {\, \cdot \,}$ denote the absolute value. Suppose $\sup$ denotes the supremum of real-valued functions. Then the supremum norm over $\map C I$ is defined as $\ds \norm {f}_\infty := \sup_{x \mathop \in I} \size {\map f x}$

label: Definition:Supremum of Mapping
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping from $S$ to $T$. Let $f \sqbrk S$, the image of $f$, admit a supremum. Then the supremum of $f$ (on $S$) is defined by: $\ds \sup_{x \mathop \in S} \map f x = \sup f \sqbrk S$

label: Definition:Supremum of Mapping/Real-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f: S \to \R$ be a real-valued function. Let $f$ be bounded above on $S$.

label: Definition:Supremum of Sequence
snippet: A special case of a supremum of a mapping is a supremum of a sequence, where the domain of the mapping is $\N$. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Let $\set {x_n: n \in \N}$ admit a supremum. Then the supremum of $\sequence {x_n}$) is defined as: $\ds \map \sup {\sequence {x_n} } = \map \sup {\set {x_n: n \in \N} }$

label: Definition:Supremum of Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T \subseteq S$. An element $c \in S$ is the supremum of $T$ in $S$ : $(1): \quad c$ is an upper bound of $T$ in $S$ $(2): \quad c \preccurlyeq d$ for all upper bounds $d$ of $T$ in $S$. If there exists a supremum of $T$ (in $S$), we say that: $T$ admits a supremum (in $S$) or $T$ has a supremum (in $S$).

label: Definition:Supremum of Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $T \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. A real number $c \in \R$ is the supremum of $T$ in $\R$ : $(1): \quad c$ is an upper bound of $T$ in $\R$ $(2): \quad c \le d$ for all upper bounds $d$ of $T$ in $\R$. If there exists a supremum of $T$ (in $\R$), we say that: $T$ admits a supremum (in $\R$) or $T$ has a supremum (in $\R$). The supremum of $T$ is denoted $\sup T$ or $\map \sup T$.

label: Definition:Supremum of Set/Real Numbers/Propositional Function
snippet: Let $\family {a_j}_{j \mathop \in I}$ be a family of elements of the real numbers $\R$ indexed by $I$. Let $\map R j$ be a propositional function of $j \in I$. Then we can define the supremum of $\family {a_j}_{j \mathop \in I}$ as: $\ds \sup_{\map R j} a_j := \text { the supremum of all $a_j$ such that $\map R j$ holds}$ If more than one propositional function is written under the supremum sign, they must all hold.

label: Definition:Supremum of Set/Real Numbers/Propositional Function/Finite Range
snippet: Let $\family {a_j}_{j \mathop \in I}$ be a family of elements of the real numbers $\R$ indexed by $I$. Let $\map R j$ be a propositional function of $j \in I$. Let the fiber of truth of $\map R j$ be finite. Then the supremum of $\family {a_j}_{j \mathop \in I}$ can be expressed as: $\ds \max_{\map R j} a_j = \text { the maxmum of all $a_j$ such that $\map R j$ holds}$ and can be referred to as the maximum of $\family {a_j}_{j \mathop \in I}$. If more than one propositional function is written under the supremum sign, they must all hold.

label: Definition:Surd/Mixed
snippet: A mixed surd is a surd containing both irrational and rational terms.

label: Definition:Surface Charge Density
snippet: Let $B$ be a body made out of an electrically conducting substance. Let $B$ be under the influence of an electric field $\mathbf E$ under which a surface charge is induced on $B$. Let $\delta S$ be an area element which is smaller than the scale used for a macroscopic electric field, but still large enough to contain many atoms on the surface of $B$. Let $P$ be a point in the vicinity of $\delta S$ whose position vector is $\mathbf r$. Let $\delta V$ be a volume element just thick enough to enclose the whole of the surface charge $\map \sigma {\mathbf r} \delta S$ associated with $\delta S$.

label: Definition:Surface Integral
snippet: Let $S$ be a surface in a vector field $\mathbf F$. Let $\d S$ be a small element of $S$. Let $\mathbf v$ be the vector induced by $\mathbf F$ at the middle of $\d S$. Let $\mathbf {\hat n}$ denote the positive unit normal to $S$ at $\d S$. Let $\mathbf v$ make an angle $\theta$ with $\mathbf {\hat n}$. 380px Hence: $\mathbf v \cdot \mathbf {\hat n} = v \cos \theta \rd S$ where: $\cdot$ denotes dot product $v$ denotes the magnitude of $\mathbf v$.

label: Definition:Surface Integral/Physical Interpretation
snippet: == Physical Interpretation of Surface Integral == Suppose $\mathbf v$ is interpreted as the velocity of some fluid in motion through a surface $S$. Let $P$ be a point $P$ on $S$ at which a positive unit normal $\mathbf {\hat n}$ is constructed. The expression $\mathbf v \cdot \mathbf {\hat n} \rd S$ denotes the amount of fluid passing through $\d S$ perpendicular to $S$ in unit time. It is sufficient to consider this normal component, as the tangential component contributes nothing to the flow through $\d S$.

label: Definition:Surface of Revolution/Definition 1
snippet: Let $F$ be a plane figure. Let $L$ be a straight line in the same plane as $F$. Let $F$ be rotated one full turn about $L$ in $3$-dimensional space. The surface of revolution generated by $F$ around $L$ is the surface of the solid of revolution generated by $F$ around $L$. The usual scenario is that: $(1): \quad$ one of the sides of $F$ is a straight line coincident with $L$ $(2): \quad$ $L$ itself is aligned with one of the coordinate axes, usually the $x$-axis in a cartesian plane $(3): \quad$ Two other sides of $F$ are also straight lines, perpendicular to $L$ $(4): \quad$ The remaining…

label: Definition:Surface of Revolution/Definition 2
snippet: Let $H = \set {\tuple {x, y} : y \in \R_{> 0}} \subset \R^2$ be the open upper half-plane. Let $F \subset H$ be a $1$-dimensional embedded submanifold. The surface of revolution is the subset $S_F \subseteq \R^3$ such that: $S_F = \set {\tuple {x, y, z} : \tuple {\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}, z} \in F}$ where $F$ is the generating curve of the surface of revolution.

label: Definition:Surgery
snippet: Surgery is a technique for making geometric modifications to a topological manifold in order to produce a cobordant manifold with simpler homotopy groups.

label: Definition:Surgery/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Surgery == The concept of surgery was pioneered by in $1961$. It has since been shown to be a powerful tool in the study of the topology of topological manifolds.

label: Definition:Surjection

label: Definition:Surjective on Morphisms
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to be surjective on morphisms : For every morphism $g$ of $\mathbf D$, there is a morphism $f$ of $\mathbf C$ such that $F f = g$

label: Definition:Surjective on Objects
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $F: \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be a functor. Then $F$ is said to be surjective on objects : For every object $D$ of $\mathbf D$, there is an object $C$ of $\mathbf C$ such that $F C = D$.

label: Definition:Survival Function
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma, \mu}$ be a measure space. Let $f: X \to \overline \R$ be a $\Sigma$-measurable function. The survival function of $f$ is the mapping $F_f: \R \to \overline \R$ defined by: $\forall t \in \R: \map {F_f} t := \map \mu {\set {\size f \ge t} }$ where $\set {\size f \ge t}$ denotes the set $\set {x \in X: \size {\map f x} \ge t}$.

label: Definition:Switching Circuit
snippet: A switching circuit is a mechanical, electronic or electromechanical system for controlling the route of information or resources. The study of switching circuits can be considered a field of applied logic.

label: Definition:Sylow p-Subgroup
snippet: Let $p$ be prime. Let $G$ be a finite group whose order is denoted by $\left\vert{G}\right\vert$.

label: Definition:Sylow p-Subgroup/Definition 1
snippet: Let $p$ be prime. Let $G$ be a finite group whose order is denoted by $\order G$. Let $\order G = k p^n$ where $p \nmid k$. A Sylow $p$-subgroup is a $p$-subgroup of $G$ which has $p^n$ elements.

label: Definition:Sylow p-Subgroup/Definition 2
snippet: Let $p$ be prime. Let $G$ be a finite group. A Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ is a maximal $p$-subgroup $P$ of $G$. In this context, maximality means that if $Q$ is a $p$-subgroup of $G$ and $P \le Q$, then $P = Q$.

label: Definition:Sylow p-Subgroup/Definition 3
snippet: Let $p$ be prime. Let $G$ be a finite group whose order is denoted by $\order G$. Let $n$ be the largest integer such that: $p^n \divides \order G$ where $\divides$ denotes divisibility. A Sylow $p$-subgroup is a $p$-subgroup of $G$ which has $p^n$ elements.

label: Definition:Symbol
snippet: In its broadest possible sense: A symbol is an object used to represent another object. In a narrower and more "mathematical" sense, a symbol is a sign of a particular shape to which is assigned a meaning, and is used to represent a concept or identify a particular object. It is generally much more convenient to use a symbol than the plain speaking that it replaces, because it is invariably more compact. One character can replace a large number of words.

label: Definition:Symbolic Logic
snippet: Symbolic logic is the study of logic in which the logical form of statements is analyzed by using symbols as tools. Instead of explicit statements, logical formulas are investigated, which are symbolic representations of statements, and compound statements in particular. In Symbolic logic, the rules of reasoning and logic are investigated by means of formal systems, which form a good foundation for the symbolic manipulations performed in this field.

label: Definition:Symbolic Logic/Also known as
snippet: == Symbolic Logic: Also known as == Some sources refer to symbolic logic as mathematical logic, but it is generally preferred to reserve that term for its more specialised branch. The term logistic can be seen for this branch of logic, but this can be confused with the (mathematical) science of logistics. Some sources do not consider it necessary to separate the various approaches, and refer to logic, symbolic logic and mathematical logic synonymous.

label: Definition:Symbolization
snippet: Symbolization is the process whereby a statement, or set of statements, written in natural language, is converted into a symbolic sentence in the form of a well-formed formula (WFF) of symbolic logic. label: Definition:Symmetric Bilinear Form
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Let $b: M \times M \to R$ be a bilinear form. Then $b$ is symmetric : $\forall v, w, \in M: \map b {v, w} = \map b {w, v}$

label: Definition:Symmetric Bilinear Form/Nondegenerate
snippet: Let $\Bbb K$ be a field. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\Bbb K$. Let $b: V \times V \to \Bbb K$ be a symmetric bilinear form. Let $b$ be a nondegenerate bilinear form. Then $b$ is a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form.

label: Definition:Symmetric Closure
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$.

label: Definition:Symmetric Closure/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The symmetric closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^\leftrightarrow$, and is defined as the union of $\RR$ with its inverse: $\RR^\leftrightarrow = \RR \cup \RR^{-1}$

label: Definition:Symmetric Closure/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. The symmetric closure of $\RR$ is denoted $\RR^\leftrightarrow$, and is defined as the smallest symmetric relation on $S$ which contains $\RR$.

label: Definition:Symmetric Densely-Defined Linear Operator
snippet: Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a densely-defined linear operator. We say that $\struct {\map D T, T}$ is symmetric : $\innerprod {T x} y = \innerprod x {T y}$ for all $x, y \in \map D T$.

snippet: The symmetric difference between two sets $S$ and $T$ is written $S \symdif T$ and is defined as:

label: Definition:Symmetric Difference/Also known as
snippet: == Symmetric Difference: Also known as == The symmetric difference between two sets is also known as their: disjoint union Boolean sum. However, both terms have different or more specialized meanings on , so will not be used here. Another term seen occasionally is symmetric sum. Some sources are pedantically explicit and use the term symmetric difference set.

label: Definition:Symmetric Difference/Definition 2
snippet: The symmetric difference between two sets $S$ and $T$ is written $S \symdif T$ and is defined as: $S \symdif T = \paren {S \cup T} \setminus \paren {S \cap T}$ where: $\setminus$ denotes set difference $\cup$ denotes set union $\cap$ denotes set intersection. That is, $S \symdif T$ is the set of elements that are in either $S$ or $T$, but not both.

label: Definition:Symmetric Difference/Definition 3
snippet: The symmetric difference between two sets $S$ and $T$ is written $S \symdif T$ and is defined as: $S \symdif T = \paren {S \cap \overline T} \cup \paren {\overline S \cap T}$ where: $\cap$ denotes set intersection $\cup$ denotes set union $\overline S$ denotes the complement of $S$.

label: Definition:Symmetric Difference/Definition 4
snippet: The symmetric difference between two sets $S$ and $T$ is written $S \symdif T$ and is defined as: $S \symdif T = \paren {S \cup T}\cap \paren {\overline S \cup \overline T}$ where: $\cap$ denotes set intersection $\cup$ denotes set union $\overline S$ denotes the complement of $S$.

label: Definition:Symmetric Difference/Definition 5
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be any two sets. The symmetric difference of $S$ and $T$ is the set which consists of all the elements of either $S$ or $T$ but not both: $S \symdif T := \set {x: x \in S \oplus x \in T}$ where $\oplus$ denotes the exclusive or connective.

label: Definition:Symmetric Entourage
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\UU$ be a quasiuniformity on $S$. Let $u \in \UU$ be an entourage of $\UU$ such that: $u = u^{-1}$ where $u^{-1}$ is the inverse of $u$. Then $u$ is symmetric.

label: Definition:Symmetric Filter Basis
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\UU$ be a quasiuniformity on $S$. From the definition, a quasiuniformity on $S$ is also a filter on the cartesian product $S \times S$. Let $\BB \subset \powerset {S \times S}$ be a filter basis of $\UU$. Then $\BB$ is a symmetric filter basis of $\UU$ every element of $\BB$ is symmetric.

An elementary symmetric function of degree $m$ is a polynomial which can be defined by the formula: {{eqn | l = \map {e_m} U | r = \sum_{a \mathop \le j_1 \mathop < j_2 \mathop < \mathop \cdots \mathop < j_m \mathop \le b} \paren {\prod_{i \mathop = 1}^m x_{j_i} } | c = }} {{eqn | r = \sum_{a \mathop \le j_1 \mathop < j_2 \mathop < \mathop \cdots \mathop < j_m \mathop \le b} x_{j_1} x_{j_2} \cdots x_{j_m} | c…

label: Definition:Symmetric Group
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\map \Gamma S$ denote the set of permutations on $S$. Let $\struct {\map \Gamma S, \circ}$ be the algebraic structure such that $\circ$ denotes the composition of mappings. Then $\struct {\map \Gamma S, \circ}$ is called the symmetric group on $S$. If $S$ has $n$ elements, then $\struct {\map \Gamma S, \circ}$ is often denoted $S_n$.

label: Definition:Symmetric Group/Also known as
snippet: In view of the isomorphism between symmetric groups on sets of the same cardinality, the terminology symmetric group of degree $n$ is often used when the nature of the underlying set is immaterial. Some sources use the term $n$th symmetric group. These terms will sometimes be used on . Some sources refer to the symmetric group on a set as the full symmetric group (on $S$). Others use the term complete symmetric group. Similarly, the symmetric group on $n$ letters can be found referred to as the full symmetric group on $n$ letters.

label: Definition:Symmetric Group/Isomorphism
snippet: In recognition that Symmetric Groups of Same Order are Isomorphic, it is unimportant to distinguish rigorously between symmetric groups on different sets. Hence a representative set of cardinality $n$ is selected, usually (as defined here) $\N^*_{\le n} = \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$. The symmetric group $S_n$ is then defined on $\N^*_{\le n}$, and identified as the $n$th symmetric group. As a consequence, results can be proved about the symmetric group on $n$ letters which then apply to all symmetric groups on sets with $n$ elements.

label: Definition:Symmetric Group/Notation
snippet: In order not to make notation for operations on a symmetric group overly cumbersome, product notation is usually used for mapping composition. Thus $\pi \circ \rho$ is written $\pi \rho$. Also, for the same reason, rather than using $I_{S_n}$ for the identity mapping, the symbol $e$ is usually used.

label: Definition:Symmetric Group/n Letters
snippet: Let $S_n$ denote the set of permutations on $n$ letters. Let $\struct {S_n, \circ}$ denote the symmetric group on $S_n$. Then $\struct {S_n, \circ}$ is referred to as the symmetric group on $n$ letters. It is often denoted, when the context is clear, without the operator: $S_n$.

label: Definition:Symmetric Mapping (Linear Algebra)
snippet: Let $\R$ be the field of real numbers. Let $\F$ be a subfield of $\R$. Let $V$ be a vector space over $\F$ Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \mathbb F$ be a mapping. Then $\innerprod \cdot \cdot: V \times V \to \mathbb F$ is symmetric : $\forall x, y \in V: \innerprod x y = \innerprod y x$

label: Definition:Symmetric Mapping (Mapping Theory)
snippet: Let $n \in \N$ be a natural number. Let $S^n$ be an $n$-dimensional cartesian space on a set $S$. Let $f: S^n \to T$ be a mapping from $S^n$ to a set $T$. Then $f$ is a symmetric mapping : $\map f {x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n} = \map f {x_{\map \pi 1}, x_{\map \pi 2}, \dotsc x_{\map \pi n} }$ for all permutations $\pi$ on $\set {1, 2, \dotsc n}$. That is, a symmetric mapping is a mapping defined on a cartesian space whose values are preserved under permutation of its arguments.

label: Definition:Symmetric Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over a set $S$.

label: Definition:Symmetric Matrix/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over a set $S$. $\mathbf A$ is a symmetric matrix : $\mathbf A = \mathbf A^\intercal$ where $\mathbf A^\intercal$ is the transpose of $\mathbf A$. That is, : $a_{i j} = a_{j i}$ for all $i$ and $j$ for which $a_{i j}$ is defined.

label: Definition:Symmetric Matrix/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over a set $S$. $\mathbf A$ is a symmetric matrix it is symmetrical about its main diagonal.

label: Definition:Symmetric Polynomial
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $K \sqbrk {X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ be the ring of polynomial forms over $K$. A polynomial $f \in K \sqbrk {X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ is symmetric for every permutation $\pi$ of $\set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$: $\map f {X_1, \dotsc, X_n} = \map f {X_{\map \pi 1}, \dotsc, X_{\map \pi n} }$

label: Definition:Symmetric Relation/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation in $S$. $\RR$ is symmetric it is a subset of its inverse: $\RR \subseteq \RR^{-1}$

label: Definition:Symmetric Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $S \subseteq \R$ such that: $\forall x \in S: -x \in S$ That is, for every element in $S$, its negative is also in $S$. Then $S$ is a symmetric subset of $\R$, or (if $\R$ is implicit) $S$ is a symmetric set.

label: Definition:Symmetric Set/Topological Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ be a topological group. Let $A \subseteq G$. We say that $A$ is symmetric : $A = A^{-1}$ where $A^{-1}$ is the inverse of $A$.

label: Definition:Symmetric Set/Vector Space
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space over a subfield of $\C$. Let $C \subseteq V$. We say that $C$ is symmetric if whenever $x \in C$, we have $-x \in C$.

label: Definition:Symmetry
snippet: An object or an expression has (or exhibits) symmetry parts of it may be interchanged without changing the object as a whole. Algebra: Symmetric Expression Relation Theory: Symmetry (of a relation): whether a relation is symmetric, antisymmetric, asymmetric or non-symmetric. Mapping Theory: Symmetric Mapping: a mapping defined on a cartesian space whose values are preserved under permutation of its arguments: $\map f {x_1, x_2, \dotsc, x_n} = \map f {x_{\map \pi 1}, x_{\map \pi 2}, \dotsc x_{\map \pi n} }$ for all permuations $\pi$ on $\set {1, 2, \dotsc n}$ Geometry: Symmetry: A movement of…

label: Definition:Symmetry (Geometry)
snippet: A symmetry of a geometric figure $P$ is a bijection from $P$ to itself which preserves the distance between points. In other words, it is a self-congruence. Intuitively and informally, a symmetry is a movement of the figure so that it looks exactly the same after it has been moved.

label: Definition:Symmetry Group
snippet: Let $P$ be a geometric figure. Let $S_P$ be the set of all symmetries of $P$. Let $\struct {S_P, \circ}$ be the algebraic structure such that $\circ$ denotes the composition of mappings. Then $\struct {S_P, \circ}$ is called the symmetry group of $P$.

label: Definition:Symmetry Group of Rectangle
snippet: == Group Example == Let $\RR = ABCD$ be a (non-square) rectangle. 400px The various symmetries of $\RR$ are: The identity mapping $e$ The rotation $r$ (in either direction) of $180^\circ$ The reflections $h$ and $v$ in the indicated axes. The symmetries of $\RR$ form the dihedral group $D_2$.

label: Definition:Symmetry Group of Rhombus
snippet: == Group Example == Let $\RR = ABCD$ be a (non-square) rhombus. 600px The various symmetries of $\RR$ are: The identity mapping $e$ The rotation $r$ (in either direction) of $180^\circ$ The reflections $h$ and $v$ in the indicated axes. The symmetries of $\RR$ form the dihedral group $D_2$.

label: Definition:Symmetry Group of Square
snippet: == Group Example == Let $\SS = ABCD$ be a square. 600px The various symmetries of $\SS$ are: the identity mapping $e$ the rotations $r, r^2, r^3$ of $90^\circ, 180^\circ, 270^\circ$ around the center of $\SS$ anticlockwise respectively the reflections $t_x$ and $t_y$ are reflections in the $x$ and $y$ axis respectively the reflection $t_{AC}$ in the diagonal through vertices $A$ and $C$ the reflection $t_{BD}$ in the diagonal through vertices $B$ and $D$. This group is known as the symmetry group of the square, and can be denoted $D_4$.

label: Definition:Symplectic Basis
snippet: Let $\mathbb K$ be a field. Let $\struct {V, f}$ be a bilinear space over $\mathbb K$ of finite dimension $2 n > 0$. Let $\BB = \tuple {b_1, c_1, \ldots, b_n, c_n}$ be an ordered basis of $V$. Then $\BB$ is symplectic : $\map f {b_i, b_j} = \map f {c_i, c_j} = 0$ for all $i, j$ $\map f {b_i, c_j} = \delta_{i j}$ for all $i, j$ where $\delta$ denotes Kronecker delta. That is, the matrix of $f$ relative to $\BB$ has the form: $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \\ & & 0 & 1 \\ & & -1 & 0 \\ & & & & \ddots \\ & & & & & 0 & 1 \\ & & & & & -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$

label: Definition:Symplectic Geometry
snippet: Symplectic geometry is the study of the geometry of manifolds based on the structure of Hamiltonian mechanics.

label: Definition:Syndetic Subset of Natural Numbers
snippet: Let $E \subseteq \N_{>0}$ be a subset of the non-zero natural numbers. $E$ is called syndetic there exists a finite subset $F \subseteq \N_{>0}$ such that: $\ds \N_{>0} \subseteq \bigcup_{k \mathop \in F} \paren {E - k}$

label: Definition:Syndrome
snippet: Let $C$ be a linear $\tuple {n, k}$-code whose master code is $\map V {n, p}$ Let $G$ be a (standard) generator matrix for $C$. Let $P$ be a standard parity check matrix for $C$. Let $v \in \map V {n, p}$, considered as a vector in the vector space that is $\map V {n, p}$. Let $v^\intercal$ denote the transpose of $v$. The syndrome of $v$ is the element of $\map V {n - k, p}$ defined as: $\map S v := P v^\intercal$

label: Definition:Synthetic Division
snippet: Synthetic division is a technique for dividing a polynomial by a linear factor. Let $\map P x$ be a polynomial of degree $n$. Dividing $\map P x$ by $x - a$ we get: $\map P x = \paren {x - a} \map Q x + r$ where $\map Q x$ is a polynomial of degree $n - 1$ and $r$ is a constant. Applying Horner's rule to evaluate $\map P a$, the coefficient $a_n$ together with the intermediate quantities produced as each pair of brackets is removed are the coefficients of $\map q x$. Hence the final result is $r = \map P a$.

snippet: Electronics: System: a configuration of electrical devices designed for a specific utilitarian purpose. Topology: Neighborhood System: a family $\family {\NN_x}_{x \mathop \in S}$ indexed by points of $S$, such that $\NN_x$ is a local basis at $x$ for $x \in S$. label: Definition:System of Measurement
snippet: A system of measurement is a set of fundamental units of measurement with which one can measure any measurable physical property.

label: Definition:System of Neighborhoods
snippet: Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $a \in A$. Let $\NN_a$ be the set of all neighborhoods of $a$ in $M$. Then $\NN_a$ is the system of neighborhoods of the point $a$.

label: Definition:System of Open Neighborhoods
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$. Let $\map \UU x$ be the set of all open neighborhoods of $x$ in $T$. Then $\map \UU x$ is the system of open neighborhoods of the point $x$.

label: Definition:T-Score
snippet: Let $X$ be a random variable whose expectation is $\mu$ and whose standard deviation is $\sigma$. The $T$-score of $X$ is given by the transformation: $T = 50 + \dfrac {10 \paren {X - \mu} } \sigma$

label: Definition:T0 Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_0$ space : That is: $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_0$ space every two elements in $S$ are topologically distinguishable. That is: for two arbitrary distinct elements $x, y \in S$ there exists an open set of $T$ which contains one of the elements, but not the other.

label: Definition:T0 Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_0$ space no two points can be limit points of each other.

label: Definition:T1/2 Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Then $T$ is a $T_{\frac 1 2}$ space : $\forall A \subseteq S: A'$ is closed where $A'$ denotes the derivative of $A$.

label: Definition:T1 Space/Also defined as
snippet: == T1 Space: Also known as == Some sources define a $T_1$ space as follows: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_1$ space : This is trivially the same as definition $1$ but with redundancy, and so as to better match the concept of $x$ and $y$ being separated. snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_1$ space :

label: Definition:T1 Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_1$ space every pair of elements of $S$ are separated. That is:

label: Definition:T1 Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_1$ space all points of $S$ are closed in $T$.

label: Definition:T2.5 Space/Also known as
snippet: == $T_{2 \frac 1 2}$ Space: Also known as == A $T_{2 \frac 1 2}$ space is also commonly referred to as a completely Hausdorff space, for . Some sources give this as $T_{\frac 5 2}$ space, which of course evaluates to the same as a $T_{2 \frac 1 2}$ space. Some refer to it as a $T2.5$ space; on that is the style used for the page name, for pure convenience. {{SeparationAxiomNameVariants|n|Urysohn|Urysohn||$T_{2 \frac 1 2}$}}

label: Definition:T2.5 Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_{2 \frac 1 2}$ space : That is: for any two distinct elements $x, y \in S$ there exist open sets $U, V \in \tau$ containing $x$ and $y$ respectively whose closures are disjoint.

label: Definition:T2.5 Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_{2 \frac 1 2}$ space : $\forall x, y \in S, x \ne y : \exists N_x, N_y \subseteq S: \exists U, V \in \tau: x \subseteq U \subseteq N_x, y \subseteq V \subseteq N_y: N_x^- \cap N_y^- = \O$ That is: $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_{2 \frac 1 2}$ space every two points in $S$ are separated by closed neighborhoods.

label: Definition:T2 Space/Also known as
snippet: == $T_2$ Space Also known as == A $T_2$ space is also widely known as a Hausdorff space, for . These terms are used interchangeably on , depending on the context. This condition is known as the Hausdorff condition. Conveniently, a topological space is Hausdorff if any two distinct points can be housed off from one another in separate disjoint open sets. Some sources use the term separated space for $T_2$ space but this is discouraged as there already exists considerable confusion and ambiguity around the definition of the word separated in the context of topology.

label: Definition:T2 Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_2$ space : That is: $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_2$ space every two elements in $S$ are separated by open sets. That is: for two arbitrary distinct elements $x, y \in S$ there exist disjoint open sets $U, V \in \tau$ containing $x$ and $y$ respectively.

label: Definition:T2 Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_2$ space each point of $S$ is the intersection of all its closed neighborhoods.

label: Definition:T2 Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_2$ space : $\forall x, y \in S, x \ne y: \exists N_x, N_y \subseteq S: \exists U, V \in \tau: x \in U \subseteq N_x, y \in V \subseteq N_y: N_x \cap N_y = \O$ That is: $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_2$ space every two elements in $S$ are separated by neighborhoods. That is: for any two distinct elements $x, y \in S$ there exist disjoint neighborhoods $N_x, N_y \subseteq S$ containing $x$ and $y$ respectively.

label: Definition:T2 Space/Equivalence of Definitions
snippet: == Equivalence of Definitions of $T_2$ space == See Equivalence of Definitions of $T_2$ Space for a proof that these definitions of a $T_2$ space are equivalent. Note that while some sources give Definition 1 and others Definition 3, it is rarely indicated specifically that the definitions are equivalent. In particular, there may exist places on the internet where a page using Definition 3 may directly link to another page which uses Definition 1 without comment that the definitions are linguistically different. Category:Definitions/Hausdorff Spaces

label: Definition:T3.5 Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_{3 \frac 1 2}$ space : For every closed set $F \subseteq S$ and every point $y \in S$ such that $y \notin F$, there exists an Urysohn function for $F$ and $\set y$.

label: Definition:T3.5 Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_{3 \frac 1 2}$ space : there exists a uniformity $\UU$ on $S$ such that $\struct {\struct {S, \UU}, \tau}$ is a uniform space.

label: Definition:T3 Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_3$ space : That is: for an arbitrary closed set $F \subseteq S$ and an arbitrary point $y \in S$ such that $y \notin F$ there exist disjoint open sets $U, V \in \tau$ such that $F \subseteq U$, $y \in V$. That is: $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_3$ space when any closed set $F \subseteq S$ and any point not in $F$ are separated by neighborhoods.

label: Definition:T3 Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_3$ space each open set contains a closed neighborhood around each of its points: $\forall U \in \tau: \forall x \in U: \exists N_x: \relcomp S {N_x} \in \tau: \exists V \in \tau: x \in V \subseteq N_x \subseteq U$ where $N_x$ denotes a neighborhood of $x$.

label: Definition:T3 Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_3$ space each of its closed sets is the intersection of its closed neighborhoods: $\forall H \subseteq S: \relcomp S H \in \tau: H = \bigcap \set {N_H: \relcomp S {N_H} \in \tau, \exists V \in \tau: H \subseteq V \subseteq N_H}$

label: Definition:T4 Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_4$ space : That is: for two arbitrary disjoint closed sets $A, B \subseteq S$ there exist disjoint open sets $U, V \in \tau$ containing $A$ and $B$ respectively. That is: $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_4$ space when any two disjoint closed subsets of $S$ are separated by neighborhoods.

label: Definition:T4 Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_4$ space each open set $U$ contains a closed neighborhood of each closed set contained in $U$.

label: Definition:T5 Space/Definition 1
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_5$ space : That is: for two arbitrary separated sets $A, B \subseteq S$ there exist disjoint open sets $U, V \in \tau$ containing $A$ and $B$ respectively.

label: Definition:T5 Space/Definition 2
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_5$ space : $\forall Y, A \subseteq S: (A \subseteq Y^\circ \wedge A^- \subseteq Y) \implies \exists N \subseteq Y: \relcomp S N \in \tau: \exists U \in \tau: A \subseteq U \subseteq N$ That is: $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_5$ space every subset $Y \subseteq S$ contains a closed neighborhood of each $A \subseteq Y^\circ$ for which $A^- \subseteq Y$. In the above, $Y^\circ$ denotes the interior of $Y$ and $A^-$ denotes the closure of $A$.

label: Definition:T5 Space/Definition 3
snippet: A topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a $T_5$ space : every subspace of $T$ is a $T_4$ space.

label: Definition:Tableau
snippet: Linear programming: Simplex tableau: a technique for presenting information obtained by an iterative process during the course of using the simplex method. Formal systems: Tableau proof: a technique for presenting a logical argument in the form of a formal proof in a straightforward, standard form. Tableau proof: a technique for presenting a logical argument in the specific context of natural deduction. Propositional logic: Propositional tableau: an element of a specific subset of the labeled trees for propositional logic. Tableau proof: a tableau confutation of the negation of a WFF.

label: Definition:Tableau Confutation
snippet: Let $\mathbf H$ be a set of WFFs of propositional logic. A tableau confutation of $\mathbf H$ is a propositional tableau $T$ with root $\mathbf H$ such that every branch of $T$ is contradictory.

label: Definition:Tableau Proof (Propositional Tableaux)
snippet: Let $\mathbf H$ be a set of WFFs of propositional logic. Let $\mathbf A$ be a WFF. A tableau proof of $\mathbf A$ from $\mathbf H$ is a tableau confutation of $\mathbf H \cup \set {\neg \mathbf A}$. This definition also applies when $\mathbf H = \O$. Then a tableau proof of $\mathbf A$ is a tableau confutation of $\set {\neg \mathbf A}$. If there exists a tableau proof of $\mathbf A$ from $\mathbf H$, one can write: $\mathbf H \vdash_{\mathrm{PT} } \mathbf A$ Specifically, the notation: $\vdash_{\mathrm{PT} } \mathbf A$ means that there exists a tableau proof of $\mathbf A$.

label: Definition:Tail Sigma-Algebra
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of real-valued random variables on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let: $\TT_n = \map \sigma {\set {X_k: k \in \N, \, k \ge n + 1} }$ where $\map \sigma {\set {X_k: k \in \N, \, k \ge n + 1} }$ denotes the $\sigma$-algebra generated by $\set {X_k : k \in \N, \, k \ge n + 1}$. Define: $\ds \TT = \bigcap_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \TT_n$ Then we say that $\TT$ is the tail $\sigma$-algebra of $\sequence {X_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$.

label: Definition:Tally Marks
snippet: Tally marks are a system of recording (usually) small numbers. For each unit in a given natural number, a mark is made. Thus, for example, $13$ could be recorded $|||||||||||||$. It is usual for tally marks to be arranged in groups of $5$, by drawing every fifth line diagonally across the group of $4$ before it. Thus $13$ would then be recorded: File:Tally5.pngFile:Tally5.pngFile:Tally3.png It is observed that tally marks are an implementation of unary notation.

label: Definition:Tangent
snippet: Geometry and Analytic Geometry: A curve is tangent to another curve if it touches that curve but does not cross it. A straight line is tangent to a curve if it intersects that curve locally at exactly one point. Trigonometry: The tangent of an angle $\theta$ is a function defined as the opposite side divided by the adjacent. Analysis: The tangent of a real number $x$ is defined as the extension of the tangent of an angle to the real numbers.

label: Definition:Tangent Bundle
snippet: Let $M$ be a differentiable manifold. Let $p \in M$ be a point in $M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p$. The tangent bundle of $M$ is the disjoint union of all the tangent spaces of $M$: $\ds T M = \coprod_{p \mathop \in M} T_p M$

label: Definition:Tangent Circles
snippet: ' 420px In the above diagram, the two circles are tangent to each other at the point $C$. Category:Definitions/Circles Category:Definitions/Tangents

label: Definition:Tangent Curve
snippet: A set of curves is tangent to each other they have a point in common at which they have a tangent line in common.

label: Definition:Tangent Curve to Surface
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a surface in space, which may or may not be a plane. Let $P$ be a point on $\SS$. A curve $\CC$ is: tangent to $\SS$ at $P$ $\CC$ has a tangent line at $P$ which is also a tangent line to $\SS$ at $P$.

label: Definition:Tangent Function/Complex
snippet: Let $z \in \C$ be a complex number. The complex function $\tan z$ is defined as: $\tan z = \dfrac {\sin z} {\cos z}$ where: $\sin z$ is the sine of $z$ $\cos z$ is the cosine of $z$. The definition is valid for all $z \in \C$ such that $\cos z \ne 0$.

label: Definition:Tangent Function/Definition from Circle/First Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the first quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {1, 0}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the tangent of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $AB$. Hence in the first quadrant, the tangent is positive.

label: Definition:Tangent Function/Definition from Circle/Fourth Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the fourth quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {1, 0}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the tangent of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $AB$. Hence in the fourth quadrant, the tangent is negative.

label: Definition:Tangent Function/Definition from Circle/Second Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the second quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {1, 0}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the tangent of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $AB$. Hence in the second quadrant, the tangent is negative.

label: Definition:Tangent Function/Definition from Circle/Third Quadrant
snippet: Consider a unit circle $C$ whose center is at the origin of a cartesian plane. 500px Let $P$ be the point on $C$ in the third quadrant such that $\theta$ is the angle made by $OP$ with the $x$-axis. Let a tangent line be drawn to touch $C$ at $A = \tuple {1, 0}$. Let $OP$ be produced to meet this tangent line at $B$. Then the tangent of $\theta$ is defined as the length of $AB$. Hence in the second quadrant, the tangent is negative.

label: Definition:Tangent Function/Real
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The real function $\tan x$ is defined as: $\tan x = \dfrac {\sin x} {\cos x}$ where: $\sin x$ is the sine of $x$ $\cos x$ is the cosine of $x$. The definition is valid for all $x \in \R$ such that $\cos x \ne 0$.

label: Definition:Tangent Line
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Let the graph of $f$ be depicted on a Cartesian plane. 400px Let $A = \tuple {x, \map f x}$ be a point on $G$. The tangent to $f$ at $A$ is defined as: $\ds \lim_{h \mathop \to 0} \frac {\map f {x + h} - \map f x} h$ Thus the tangent to $f$ at $x$ can be considered as the secant $AB$ to $G$ where: $B = \tuple {x + h, \map f {x + h} }$ as $B$ gets closer and closer to $A$. By taking $h$ smaller and smaller, the secant approaches more and more closely the tangent to $G$ at $A$.

label: Definition:Tangent Line/Circle
snippet: ' 320px In the above diagram, the line is tangent to the circle at the point $C$.

label: Definition:Tangent Line/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note to Tangent Line == The definition of the tangent to a curve as the limit of a sequence of secants was made by . It first appeared in his , but the idea most probably dates from considerably earlier. This definition anticipates the invention of differential calculus. In fact, , in a letter that was discovered as late as $1934$, specifically states that it was the work of which inspired his own ideas about calculus.

label: Definition:Tangent Line/Limit of Secant
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a space curve. Let $\CC$ be embedded in a Cartesian plane. Let $P$ be a point on $\CC$. Let $\SS$ be a secant line to $\CC$ passing through $P$ and another point $Q$ also on $\CC$. The tangent to $\CC$ at $P$ can be considered as the limit of $\SS$ as $Q$ approaches $P$.

label: Definition:Tangent Line/Point of Contact
snippet: Let $f: \R \to \R$ be a real function. Let the graph of $f$ be depicted on a Cartesian plane. 400px Let $A = \tuple {x, \map f x}$ be a point on $G$. Let $\LL$ be tangent to $f$ at $A$. Then $A$ is known as the point of contact of $\LL$ to $f$.

label: Definition:Tangent Line to Surface
snippet: Let $\SS$ be a surface in space. Let $P$ be a point on $\SS$. A straight line $\LL$ is: tangent to $\SS$ at $P$ $\LL$ is tangent to a curve $\CC$ embedded in $\SS$ at $P$ where $P$ is also on $\CC$.

label: Definition:Tangent Plane
snippet: Let $\SS$ be the surface of a solid geometric figure. Let $Q$ be a point on $\SS$. A tangent plane to $\SS$ at $Q$ is a plane $P$ which intersects $\SS$ such that: all straight lines $\LL$ embedded in $P$ that intersect $\SS$ are tangent to $\SS$.

label: Definition:Tangent Space/Geometric Tangent Space
snippet: Let $a \in \R^n$ be an element of the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space. The geometric tangent space to $\R^n$ at $a$, denoted by $\R^n_a$, is the cartesian product of the singleton $\set a$ and $\R^n$: $\R^n_a := \set a \times \R^n = \set {\tuple {a, v} : v \in \R^n}$

label: Definition:Tangent Space (Affine Geometry)
snippet: Let $\tuple {\EE, +, -}$ be an affine space. Let $V$ be the vector space that is the codomain of $-$. Then $V$ is the tangent space of $\EE$.

label: Definition:Tangent Vector
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $m \in M$ be a point. Let $V$ be an open neighborhood of $m$. Let $\map {C^\infty} {V, \R}$ be defined as the set of all smooth mappings $f: V \to \R$.

label: Definition:Tangent Vector/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $m \in M$ be a point. Let $V$ be an open neighborhood of $m$. Let $\map {C^\infty} {V, \R}$ be defined as the set of all smooth mappings $f: V \to \R$. A tangent vector $X_m$ on $M$ at $m$ is a linear transformation: $X_m: \map {C^\infty} {V, \R} \to \R$ which satisfies the Leibniz law: $\ds \map {X_m} {f g} = \map {X_m} f \map g m + \map f m \map {X_m} g$

label: Definition:Tangent Vector/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $m \in M$ be a point. Let $V$ be an open neighborhood of $m$. Let $\map {C^\infty} {V, \R}$ be defined as the set of all smooth mappings $f: V \to \R$. Let $I$ be an open real interval with $0 \in I$. Let $\gamma: I \to M$ be a smooth curve with $\gamma \left({0}\right) = m$. Then a tangent vector $X_m$ at a point $m \in M$ is a mapping $X_m: \map {C^\infty} {V, \R} \to \R$ defined by: $\map {X_m} f := \map {\dfrac \d {\d \tau} {\restriction_0} } {\map {f \circ \gamma} \tau}$ for all $f \in \map {C^\infty} {V, \R}$.

label: Definition:Tangential Acceleration of Smooth Curve
snippet: Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a real interval. Let $M \subseteq \R^n$ be an embedded submanifold. Let $\gamma: \R \to M$ be a smooth curve. Let $\map {\gamma} t$ be the acceleration of $\gamma$ at $t \in I$. Let $T_{\map \gamma t} M$ be the tangent space at $\map \gamma t \in M$ for some $t \in I$. Let $\pi^\top : T_{\map \gamma t} \R^n \to T_{\map \gamma t} M$ be the tangential projection. The tangential acceleration of $\gamma$ at $t \in I$ is defined as: $\map {\gamma} t^\top := \map {\pi^\top} {\map {\gamma} t}$

label: Definition:Tangential Direction
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a curve in space along which a particle $P$ may be imagined to be moving The tangential direction of $P$ at a point on $\CC$ is the direction of travel of $P$ along a tangent to $\CC$ at that point.

label: Definition:Tangential Directional Derivative
snippet: Let $\R^n$ be the $n$-dimensional real vector space. Let $S \subseteq \R^n$ be an open subset of $\R^n$. Let $M \subseteq S$ be an embedded submanifold. Let $p \in S$ be a point. Let $T_p S$ be the tangent space at $p \in S$. Let $v \in T_p S$ be a vector. Let $\map {\mathfrak{X}} M$ and $\map {\mathfrak{\tilde X}} S$ be the spaces of smooth vector fields of $M$ and $S$ respectively. Let $Y \in \map {\mathfrak{X}} {M}$ and $\tilde Y \in \map {\mathfrak{X}} S$ be a vector fields. Let $\pi^\top : T_p S \to T_p M$ be the tangential projection.

label: Definition:Tangential Equation of Circle
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle embedded in the Cartesian plane of radius $r$ with its center located at the origin. Let $\LL$ be a straight line in the plane of $\CC$ whose equation is given by: $(1): \quad l x + m y + n = 0$ such that $l \ne 0$. Then the equation: $\paren {l^2 + m^2} r^2 = n^2$ is known as the tangency equation of $\CC$.

label: Definition:Tangential Projection
snippet: Let $\tilde M$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $M \subseteq \tilde M$ be an immersed or embedded Riemannian submanifold. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $\bigvalueat {T \tilde M} M$ be the tangent bundle of $\tilde M$, but restricted to $M$. Let $\pi^\top$ be a smooth bundle homomorphism such that: $\pi^\top : \bigvalueat {T \tilde M} M \to TM$ Then $\pi^\top$ is known as the tangential projection.

label: Definition:Tarski's Geometry
snippet: Tarski's geometry is an axiomatic treatment of geometry. Unless specified otherwise, will use the term Tarski's geometry to be a formal systematic treatment of geometry containing only: $(1):\quad$ The language and axioms of first-order logic, and the disciplines preceding it $(2):\quad$ The undefined terms of Tarski's Geometry $(3):\quad$ Tarski's Axioms of Geometry.

label: Definition:Tarski's Geometry/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Tarski's Geometry == Tarski's geometry was invented to treat the same subjects as Euclidean geometry, but entirely within the framework of first-order logic. Category:Historical Notes

label: Definition:Tautochrone
snippet: Let $A$ and $B$ be points in space that are neither on the same horizontal line nor on the same vertical line. A tautochrone is a curve into which a wire is to be shaped so that a bead sliding down it (without friction) takes the same time to reach the lowest point independently of where on that wire it is released from rest.

label: Definition:Tautology
snippet: A tautology is a statement which is always true, independently of any relevant circumstances that could theoretically influence its truth value. It is epitomised by the statement form: $p \implies p$ that is: if $p$ is true then $p$ is true. An example of a "relevant circumstance" here is the truth value of $p$. The archetypal tautology is symbolised by $\top$, and referred to as Top.

label: Definition:Taxicab Metric
snippet: Let $M_{1'} = \struct {A_{1'}, d_{1'} }$ and $M_{2'} = \struct {A_{2'}, d_{2'} }$ be metric spaces. Let $A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$ be the cartesian product of $A_{1'}$ and $A_{2'}$. The taxicab metric on $A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$ is defined as: $\map {d_1} {x, y} := \map {d_{1'} } {x_1, y_1} + \map {d_{2'} } {x_2, y_2}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2} \in A_{1'} \times A_{2'}$.

label: Definition:Taxicab Metric/General Definition
snippet: Let $M_{1'} = \struct {A_{1'}, d_{1'} }, M_{2'} = \struct {A_{2'}, d_{2'} }, \ldots, M_{n'} = \struct {A_{n'}, d_{n'} }$ be metric spaces. Let $\ds \AA = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_{i'}$ be the cartesian product of $A_{1'}, A_{2'}, \ldots, A_{n'}$. The taxicab metric on $\ds \AA = \prod_{i \mathop = 1}^n A_{i'}$ is defined as: $\ds \map {d_1} {x, y} := \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map {d_{i'} } {x_i, y_i}$ where $x = \tuple {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}, y = \tuple {y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n} \in \AA$.

snippet: This diagram shows the open $\epsilon$-ball $\map {B_\epsilon} {A; d_1}$ of point $A$ in the $\struct {\R^2, d_1}$ metric space where $d_1$ is the taxicab metric. 340px Note that $\epsilon = \epsilon_1 + \epsilon_2$. Neither the boundary lines nor the extreme points are actually part of the open $\epsilon$-ball.

snippet: == Historical Note on Taxicab Number == The first person to find an integer with this property was in $1657$. He discovered $5$ instances of these numbers in response to a challenge by : The name taxicab number arises from an anecdote related by about a visit to in hospital in a taxicab whose number was $1729$.

label: Definition:Taylor Polynomial
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is continuous on the closed interval $\closedint a b$ and $n$ times differentiable on the open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi \in \openint a b$. The polynomial $T_n$ defined as: $\ds \map {T_n} x = \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^n \frac {\paren {x - \xi}^i} {i!} \map {f^{\paren i} } \xi$ is known as the Taylor polynomial of degree $n$ for $f$ about $\xi$. That is, a Taylor polynomial is a Taylor series taken for $n$ initial terms.

label: Definition:Taylor Series
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is smooth on the open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi \in \openint a b$. Then the Taylor series expansion of $f$ about the point $\xi$ is: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {\paren {x - \xi}^n} {n!} \map {f^{\paren n} } \xi$ It is not necessarily the case that this power series is convergent with sum $\map f x$.

label: Definition:Taylor Series/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Taylor Series == The first proof for the convergence of a Taylor series was provided by . He used the Cauchy Form of the remainder, showing that it converges to zero.

label: Definition:Taylor Series/Remainder
snippet: Let $f$ be a real function which is smooth on the open interval $\openint a b$. Let $\xi \in \openint a b$. Consider the Taylor series expansion $\map T {\map f \xi}$ of $f$ about the point $\xi$: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^\infty \frac {\paren {x - \xi}^n} {n!} \map {f^{\paren n} } \xi$ Let $\map {T_n} {\map f \xi}$ be the Taylor polynomial: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^n \frac {\paren {x - \xi}^n} {n!} \map {f^{\paren n} } \xi$ for some $n \in \N$.

label: Definition:Telescoping Series
snippet: A telescoping series is a series whose partial sums eventually only have a fixed number of terms after cancellation through algebraic manipulation.

label: Definition:Temperature/Absolute
snippet: Absolute temperature is a measure of the amount of heat energy in a body. It is defined as: $T = \dfrac 1 k \paren {\dfrac {\partial U} {\partial \ln g} }$ where: $k$ is a constant that relates the mean kinetic energy and absolute temperature of the body $B$ $U$ is the total energy of $B$ $g$ is the number of possible states in which $B$ can be.

label: Definition:Temperature/Dimension
snippet: Temperature is frequently, at elementary levels at least, considered as one of the fundamental dimensions of physics. In dimensional analysis it is usually assigned the symbol $\Theta$. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Temperature

label: Definition:Temperature/Scales
snippet: There are several scales against which temperature is measured. Each one has two reference points. | Celsius | $\cels$ | $-273.15 \cels$ | $0 \cels$ | $99.9839 \cels$ | Fahrenheit | $\fahr$ | $-459.67 \fahr$ | $32 \fahr$ | $211.9710 \fahr$ | Kelvin | $\mathrm K$ | $0 \ \mathrm K$ | $273.15 \ \mathrm K$ | $373.1339 \ \mathrm K$ | Rankine | $\rankine$ | $0 \rankine$ | $491.67 \rankine$ | $671.641 \rankine$ There are others. snippet: Let $T: \map \SS \R \to \C$ be a tempered distribution. Then the set of all $T$ is called the tempered distribution space and is denoted by $\map {\SS'} \R$.

label: Definition:Temporal Logic
snippet: Temporal logic is a general term for systems which incorporate temporal information into a logical framework.

label: Definition:Tense Logic
snippet: Tense logic is a subcategory of modal logic designed to handle propositions whose truth values may vary with time. This can be handled by a number of approaches, but the simplest one is to add the following operators to propositional logic: {{eqn | l = \map G p | o = := | r = \text {It will always be the case that $p$} | c = General }} {{eqn | l = \map F p | o = := | r = \text {It will at some time be the case that $p$} | c = Future tense }} {{eqn | l = \map P p | o = := | r = \text {It has always been the case that $p$} | c = Past tense }} along with a number of axioms, for example: {{eqn |…

snippet: == Tense Logic: Also known as == Tense logic is also known as temporal logic, but the latter is usually reserved for the general term for systems which incorporate temporal information into a logical framework.

label: Definition:Tensor
snippet: A tensor can be informally defined as an abstract object with a set of components which are functions of position in $n$-dimensional space. Let points have $n$ coordinates in a certain Cartesian coordinate system: $x^i = \tuple {x^1, x^2, \ldots, x^n}$ Let $x^i$ have corresponding coordinates in a different Cartesian coordinate system: $\overline x^i = \tuple {\overline x^1, \overline x^2, \ldots, \overline x^n}$ A set of $n$ components, denoted $A^i$, that are functions of the $n$ coordinates $x^i$ will become a set of $n$ components, denoted $\overline A^i$, that are functions of the $n$…

label: Definition:Tensor/Notation
snippet: == Tensor: Notation == The components of a tensor are by convention identified by means of superscripts, rather than the subscripts that are general in other branches of mathematics. Thus we have such constructs as: $A^i := \set {A^1, A^2, \ldots, A^n}$ and: $x^i := \set {x^1, x^2, \ldots, x^n}$ instead of what would be more usual in the language of vector spaces: $\mathbf A := \set {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n}$ and: $\mathbf x := \set {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ Hence such suffixes are not treated as exponents in tensor notation.

label: Definition:Tensor Field
snippet: A tensor field is a set of tensors applied to a region of the Cartesian space upon which the tensor is defined.
