label: Definition:Tensor Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Tensor Theory == The field of tensor theory was initially developed by , along with as a generalization of vector analysis. It was used by in his formulation of the general theory of relativity. It is important in differential geometry and physics.

label: Definition:Term
snippet: Predicate Logic: Term Logical Term: the subject and the predicate of a simple statement in predicate logic. Algebra: Term of Expression: one of the elements of an expression: in $a \circ b$ then $a$ and $b$ are the terms. Term of Polynomial: in $x^2 + x y + y^2$, each of $x^2$, $x y$ and $y^2$ are its terms. Term of Fraction: the numerator and the denominator.

label: Definition:Term of Sequence
snippet: The elements of a sequence are known as its terms. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence. Then the $k$th term of $\sequence {x_n}$ is the ordered pair $\tuple {k, x_k}$.

label: Definition:Term of Sequence/Also defined as
snippet: == Term of Sequence: Also defined as == Some sources gloss over the fact that a sequence is a mapping and define the terms to be the elements of the range of the sequence: We call $x_n$ the $n$th term of the sequence. -- : $\S 4.2$ However, this simplistic treatment lacks the precision of the definition provided here, and does not endorse it.

label: Definition:Term of Sequence/Also known as
snippet: == Term of Sequence: Also known as == A term of a sequence is referred to by some sources as an element of the sequence. Some sources refer to the general term of a sequence when expressing it by means of a rule.

label: Definition:Term of Sequence/Index
snippet: Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence. Let $x_k$ be the $k$th term of $\sequence {x_n}$. Then the integer $k$ is known as the index of $x_k$.

label: Definition:Termial/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Termial == The termial was invented by in his . It was devised as an analogy of the factorial, so as to illustrate the extension of the latter to the real numbers.

label: Definition:Termial/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a real number. The termial of $x$ is denoted $x?$ and defined as: $x? = \dfrac {x \paren {x + 1} } 2$

label: Definition:Terminal Object
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory. A terminal object of $\mathbf C$ is an object $1 \in \mathbf C_0$ of $\mathbf C$ such that: For all $C \in \mathbf C_0$, there is a unique morphism $C \to 1$.

label: Definition:Terminal P-adic Expansion
snippet: Let $p$ be a prime number. A $p$-adic expansion $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = m}^\infty d_n p^n$ is terminal or terminates $\exists N \in \N: \forall n \ge N: d_n = 0$

label: Definition:Ternary Notation
snippet: Ternary notation is the technique of expressing numbers in base $3$. That is, every number $x \in \R$ is expressed in the form: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z} r_j 3^j$ where: $\forall j \in \Z: r_j \in \set {0, 1, 2}$

label: Definition:Ternary Relation
snippet: A ternary relation is a relation which involves $3$ operands, as follows: Let $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ be sets. A ternary relation $\RR$ on $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$ is defined as: $\RR := \struct {S_1, S_2, S_3, R}$ where $R$ is an arbitrary subset $R \subseteq S_1 \times S_2 \times S_3$.

label: Definition:Terrestrial Latitude/Also known as
snippet: == Terrestrial Latitude: Also known as == Terrestrial latitude is usually known in common parlance as just latitude. However, this term also encompasses other measurements of latitude, for example celestial latitude and galactic latitude. Hence on the full term terrestrial latitude is preferred, so as to forestall ambiguity, unless the context is clear.

label: Definition:Tessellation/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Tessellation == The word tessellation derives from the Latin tessella, meaning small square. A tessella was a small cubic piece of material used to make mosaics. The word tessella itself derives from tessera, the Latin word for square. This in turn derives from the Greek word τέσσερα (tessera), one of their words for four. The verb form of tessellation is tessellate. Hence when a tessellation can be formed from congruent copies of a polygon or a set of polygons, the polygon or set of polygons is said to tessellate the plane.

label: Definition:Tesseract
snippet: A tesseract is the $4$-dimensional regular polytope corresponding to the cube: 500px

label: Definition:Test Function Space
snippet: Denote with $\map \DD {\R^d}$ the set: $\set { \phi: \R^d \to \C, \text{$\phi$ is a test function} }$ of all test functions $\phi: \R^d \to \C$. Then $\map \DD {\R^d}$ is called the test function space. $\map \DD {\R^d}$ is a vector space over $\C$, i.e.: $\forall \psi, \phi \in \map \DD {\R^d} : \phi + \psi \in \map \DD {\R^d}$ $\forall \phi \in \map \DD {\R^d} : \forall \alpha \in \C : \alpha \cdot \phi \in \map \DD {\R^d}$ $\map \DD {\R^d}$ also has a topology.

label: Definition:Test Statistic
snippet: Let $\theta$ be a population parameter of some population $P$. Let $\Omega$ be the parameter space of $\theta$. Let $\mathbf X$ be a random sample from $P$. Let $T = \map f {\mathbf X}$ be a sample statistic. Let $\delta$ be a test procedure of the form: reject $H_0$ if $T \in C$ for some null hypothesis $H_0$ and some $C \subset \Omega$. We refer to $T$ as the test statistic of $\delta$.

label: Definition:Test of Homogeneity
snippet: The tests of homogeneity are a class of statistical tests for equality of means, variances, proportions, and so on, applied to samples from different populations.

label: Definition:Tetra-/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Use of Tetra- == The prefix tetra- can be found in the following contexts: tetrad: a set or ordered tuple with $4$ elements tetragon: a less-common name than quadrilateral for a polygon with $4$ sides and hence $4$ vertices tetrahedron: a polyhedron with $4$ faces tetravalent predicate: a predicate with a valency of $4$

label: Definition:Tetractys
snippet: The tetractys is a central concept in the mystical beliefs of the Pythagoreans. It consists of $10$ points arranged in a triangle: 300px based on the notions that: $1$ represents the point $2$ represents the line $3$ represents the surface $4$ represents the solid $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$ and therefore: $10$ represents the universe.

label: Definition:Tetrad
snippet: A tetrad is a set or tuple which has exactly $4$ elements.

label: Definition:Tetrahedral Number
snippet: Tetrahedral numbers are those denumerating a collection of objects which can be arranged in the form of a regular tetrahedron. The $n$th tetrahedral number $H_n$ is defined as: $\ds H_n = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n T_k$ where $T_k$ is the $k$th triangular number.

label: Definition:Tetrahedral Number/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Tetrahedral Numbers == The sequence of tetrahedral numbers begins as follows: $0, 1, 4, 10, 20, 35, 56, 84, 120, 165, 220, 286, 364, \ldots$

label: Definition:Tetrahedron
snippet: 300px A tetrahedron is a polyhedron which has $4$ (triangular) faces. Thus a tetrahedron is a $3$-simplex.

label: Definition:Tetrahedron/Also known as
snippet: == Tetrahedron: Also known as == A tetrahedron is also known as a triangular pyramid. In , a tetrahedron is referred to as a pyramid (with / which has) a triangular base. The first reference to it is in :

label: Definition:Tetrahedron/Apex
snippet: 300px Once the base of a tetrahedron has been identified, the vertex which does not lie on the base is called the apex of the tetrahedron. In the above diagram, given that the base of the tetrahedron $ABCD$ is the triangle $ABC$, the apex is $D$. As all faces of a tetrahedron are triangular by definition, it follows that each of its vertices is the common point of three triangles. Therefore is qualitatively immaterial which vertex is determined to be the apex. This definition is compatible with the definition of the apex of a general pyramid.

label: Definition:Tetrahedron/Base
snippet: 300px One of the faces of a tetrahedron can be chosen arbitrarily, distinguished from the others and identified as the base of the tetrahedron. In the above diagram, $ABC$ is the base of the tetrahedron $ABCD$. As all faces of a tetrahedron are triangular by definition, it is qualitatively immaterial which face is thus chosen. This definition is compatible with the definition of the base of a general pyramid.

label: Definition:Tetrahedron/Regular
snippet: A regular tetrahedron is a tetrahedron whose $4$ faces are all congruent equilateral triangles. It has: $4$ vertices $6$ edges $4$ faces The regular tetrahedron is an example of a deltahedron.

label: Definition:Tetromino
snippet: A tetromino is a $4$-omino: 500px That is, it is a polyomino consisting of exactly $4$ unit squares.

label: Definition:Thabit Number
snippet: A Thabit number is an integer in the form: $3 \times 2^n - 1$ where $n \in \Z_{\ge 0}$ is a non-negative integer.

label: Definition:Thabit Pair
snippet: A Thabit pair is an amicable pair formed by an application of Thabit's Rule: $\tuple {2^n a b, 2^n c}$ where $n$ be a positive integer such that: {{eqn | l = b | r = 3 \times 2^{n - 1} - 1 | c = }} {{eqn | l = c | r = 9 \times 2^{2 n - 1} - 1 | c = }} are all prime.

label: Definition:Thabit Prime
snippet: A Thabit prime is a Thabit number which is prime.

label: Definition:That which produces Medial Whole with Medial Area
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be in the forms: $a = \dfrac {\rho \lambda^{1/4} } {\sqrt 2} \sqrt {1 + \dfrac k {\sqrt {1 + k^2} } }$ $b = \dfrac {\rho \lambda^{1/4} } {\sqrt 2} \sqrt {1 - \dfrac k {\sqrt {1 + k^2} } }$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational $\lambda$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a - b$ is that which produces a medial whole with a medial area.

label: Definition:That which produces Medial Whole with Rational Area
snippet: Let $a, b \in \R_{>0}$ be in the forms: $a = \dfrac \rho {\sqrt {2 \left({1 + k^2}\right)} } \sqrt{\sqrt {1 + k^2} + k}$ $b = \dfrac \rho {\sqrt {2 \left({1 + k^2}\right)} } \sqrt{\sqrt {1 + k^2} - k}$ where: $\rho$ is a rational number $k$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational $\lambda$ is a rational number whose square root is irrational. Then $a - b$ is that which produces a medial whole with a rational area.

label: Definition:The Algebra of Sets/Also defined as
snippet: == The Algebra of Sets: Also defined as == Note that an algebra of sets is a more specific concept that is applied to a subset of $\powerset E$ that is closed under union, intersection and complement, and also has a unit. So while the algebra of sets is an algebra of sets, the reverse is not necessarily true. Category:Definitions/The Algebra of Sets

label: Definition:Theorem
snippet: In all contexts, the definition of the term theorem is by and large the same. That is, a theorem is a statement which has been proved to be true.

label: Definition:Theorem/Also defined as
snippet: == Theorems: Also defined as == Some sources make more of the term theorem than is perhaps merited. For example, has: Theorems are true implications which are usually of special interest. No distinction is made on between theorems that are or are not of "special interest".

label: Definition:Theorem/Formal System
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a formal language. Let $\mathscr P$ be a proof system for $\LL$. A theorem of $\mathscr P$ is a well-formed formula of $\LL$ which can be deduced from the axioms and axiom schemata of $\mathscr P$ by means of its rules of inference. That a WFF $\phi$ is a theorem of $\mathscr P$ may be denoted as: $\vdash_{\mathscr P} \phi$

label: Definition:Theorem/Logic
snippet: A theorem in logic is a statement which can be shown to be the conclusion of a logical argument which depends on no premises except logical axioms. A sequent which denotes a theorem $\phi$ is written $\vdash \phi$, indicating that there are no premises. In this context, $\vdash$ is read as: It is a theorem that ...

label: Definition:Theorem/Mathematics
snippet: The term theorem is used throughout the whole of mathematics to mean a statement which has been proved to be true from whichever axioms relevant to that particular branch. Note that statements which are taken as axioms in one branch of mathematics may be theorems in others.

label: Definition:Theoretical Physics
snippet: Theoretical physics is the branch of physics concerned with aspects of the natural universe beyond our ability to test them directly.

label: Definition:Theory
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be a set of $\LL$-formulas. Then $\FF$ is an $\LL$-theory , for every $\phi \in \LL$: $\FF \models_{\mathscr M} \phi \implies \phi \in \FF$ where $\models_{\mathscr M}$ denotes $\mathscr M$-semantic consequence.

label: Definition:Theory/Set of Formulas
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a logical language. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be a set of $\LL$-formulas. Then the $\LL$-theory of $\FF$, denoted $\map T {\FF}$ is the set: $\set {\phi \in \LL: \FF \models_{\mathscr M} \phi}$ where $\models_{\mathscr M}$ denotes $\mathscr M$-semantic consequence.

label: Definition:Theory of Algorithms
snippet: The field of the theory of algorithms is a subfield of computer science which is primarily concerned with determining the existence or non-existence of effective algorithms for the solution of certain computational problems.

label: Definition:Theory of Equations
snippet: The theory of equations is the study of polynomials and their roots.

label: Definition:Theory of Types
snippet: The theory of types is a system of axiomatic set theory which is originated by appending a further axiom to the stating: A set cannot be an element of itself.

label: Definition:Thermodynamics
snippet: Thermodynamics is the branch of physics which studies the behaviour of heat.

label: Definition:Theta-Sequence
snippet: Let $\UU$ be an open cover of a topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$. A $\theta$-sequence (that is, theta-sequence) for $\UU$ is a sequence $\sequence {\VV_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ of open covers of $T$ such that:

label: Definition:Theta Notation/Also defined as
snippet: == $\Theta$ Notation: Also defined as == Sources which utilise order notation so as to explore the behaviour of algorithms are concerned only with algorithm run times, necessarily positive. Hence they may define the $\Theta$ notation on positive real sequences only, as follows: Let $g: \N \to \R$ be a real sequence, expressed here as a real-valued function on the set of natural numbers $\N$.

label: Definition:Think of a Number
snippet: A think of a number puzzle is usually in the form of a game between two players. Player A asks player B to: Think of a number perhaps with constraints. Let this number be referred to as $n$. Player A asks player B to perform certain arithmetical manipulations on $n$. As a result, player B is left with another number, which we will refer to as $m$. The game now goes one of $2$ ways: $(1): \quad$ Player A announces: The number you have been left with is $m$. $(2): \quad$ Player A asks what $m$ is, and on learning what it is, instantaneously replies: The number you first thought of was $n$.

label: Definition:Think of a Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Think of a Number == The think of a number puzzle goes way back in time. discusses it in his posthumous ($1932$) collection as follows, presented on as a historical note: He explains that: He tells you to think of any whole number between $1$ and $100$, and then divide it successively by $3$, $5$ and $7$, telling him the remainder in each case. On receiving this information he promptly discloses the number you thought of. Note, however, that since wrote the above, the from was found to contain a number of examples of this puzzle.

label: Definition:Thomae Function
snippet: Thomae Function on $\openint 0 1$ The Thomae function $D_M: \R \to \R$ is the real function defined as: $\forall x \in \R: \map {D_M} x = \begin {cases} 0 & : x = 0 \text { or } x \notin \Q \\ \dfrac 1 q & : x = \dfrac p q : p \perp q, q > 0 \end {cases}$ where: $\Q$ denotes the set of rational numbers $p \perp q$ denotes that $p$ and $q$ are coprime (that is, $x$ is a rational number expressed in canonical form)

label: Definition:Thomas's Corkscrew
snippet: Let copies of Thomas's plank be used to construct a corkscrew in the same manner as the Tychonoff plank is used to construct the Tychonoff corkscrew. Thomas's corkscrew is the topological space that results.

label: Definition:Thomas's Plank/Definition 1
snippet: Let $L_n$ be lines embedded in the Cartesian plane $\R^2$ defined as: $\forall n \in \N: L_n = \begin {cases} \set {\tuple {x, 0}: x \in \openint 0 1} & : n = 0 \\ \set {\tuple {x, \dfrac 1 n}: x \in \hointr 0 1} & : n > 0 \end {cases}$ Let $S = \ds \bigcup {n \mathop \in \N}$. Let a topology $\tau$ be applied to $S$, defined as follows: For $n \ge 1$, each point of $L_n$ except for $\tuple {0, \dfrac 1 n}$ is open. neighborhood bases of $\tuple {0, \dfrac 1 n}$ are subsets of $L_n$ with finite complements.

label: Definition:Thomas's Plank/Definition 2
snippet: Let $L := \openint 0 1$ denote the open unit interval. Let $S_1 := L \cup \set p$ denote the Alexandroff extension of $L$. Let $S_2 := \Z_{>0} \cup \set q$ denote the Alexandroff extension of the (strictly) positive integers $\Z_{>0}$. Let $\struct {S, \tau} := \paren {S_1 \times S_2} \setminus \set {\tuple {p, q} }$ be the subspace of the product space $S_1 \times S_2$ with $\set {\tuple {p, q} }$ removed. Thomas's plank is the topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$.

label: Definition:Thousand
snippet: A thousand is $1000$: $10$ to the power of $3$: $1000 = 10^3 = 10 \times 10 \times 10$

label: Definition:Thousandth
snippet: Thousandth is the English word for $\dfrac 1 {1000}$.

label: Definition:Three-Body Problem
snippet: The three-body problem arises from this question: Given Newton's Laws of Motion and Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation, is it possible accurately to calculate the future positions and velocities of $n$ bodies in space? When $n = 2$, the problem was solved by . However, when $n = 3$, as for example Sun, Moon and Earth, the problem has still not been solved.

label: Definition:Three-Valued Logic
snippet: Three-valued logic is a class of systems of logic which a proposition three possible truth values, not only the true and false of conventional $2$-valued Aristotelian logic

label: Definition:Three (Category)
snippet: The category $\mathbf 3$, three, is the category: $\begin{xy} +{\circledast} = "x", +{\star} = "y", +{\bullet} = "z", "x";"y" **@{-} ?>*@{>}, "y";"z" **@{-} ?>*@{>}, "x";"z" **@{-} ?>*@{>} \end{xy}$ with: Three objects, $\circledast$, $\star$ and $\bullet$; and Six morphisms: The three identity morphisms $\operatorname{id}_\circledast$, $\operatorname{id}_\star$, $\operatorname{id}_\bullet$; One non-identity morphism $\circledast \to \star$; One non-identity morphism $\star \to \bullet$; One non-identity morphism $\circledast \to \bullet$.

label: Definition:Tied Ranks
snippet: Let $S$ be a set on whose elements a ranking $\RR$ has been applied. Let $2$ or more elements of $S$ be assessed as having the same rank under $\RR$. Then those elements are said to have tied ranks.

label: Definition:Time
snippet: A true definition of what time actually is has baffled philosophers from the dawn of, er, time. Therefore it will be left as an exercise for the reader. It is usually treated as a scalar quantity.

label: Definition:Time-Constructible Function/Definition 1
snippet: Let $f$ be a function. Let there exist a positive integer $n_0$ and a Turing machine $M$ such that: Given a string $1^n$ consisting of $n$ instances of $1$, $M$ stops after exactly $f \left({n}\right)$ steps for all $n \ge n_0$. Then $f$ is time-constructible.

label: Definition:Time-Constructible Function/Definition 2
snippet: Let $f$ be a function. Let there exist a positive integer $n_0$ and a Turing machine $M$ such that: Given a string $1^n$ consisting of $n$ instances of $1$, $M$ outputs the binary representation of $\map f n$ in $\map \OO {\map f n}$ time. Then $f$ is time-constructible.

label: Definition:Time/Dimension
snippet: Time is one of the fundamental dimensions of physics. In dimensional analysis it is assigned the symbol $T$ or $\mathbf T$. It is a scalar quantity which can be mapped directly to the real number line. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Time

label: Definition:Time/Fourth Dimension
snippet: In the Theory of Relativity, it is convenient to consider time as another dimension in addition to, and treated similarly to, the $3$ dimensions of ordinary space.

label: Definition:Time/Fourth Dimension/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Time as $4$th Dimension == The treatment of time as the $4$th dimension originates with . While introduced as a mathematical convenience, the concept took hold in popular culture as a pseudo-scientific backing for an entire subgenre of science fiction: the time-travel story.

label: Definition:Time/Length
snippet: A quantity of time is usually referred to in natural language in the same terms as linear measure. Thus it is usual to refer to a length of time of an elapsed quantity of time.

label: Definition:Time/Unit/Day
snippet: The day is a derived unit of time, based on the period of rotation of Earth about its axis. In common parlance, this equates to the mean solar day.

label: Definition:Time/Unit/Decade
snippet: The decade is a derived unit of time. $1$ decade $=10$ years. Category:Definitions/Time

label: Definition:Time/Unit/Season
snippet: The season is a derived unit of time. The season is measured only approximately in duration, and is not used as a scientific measure. $1$ season $= 3$ months, although exactly which months fall into which season depends on the locale and the culture. Category:Definitions/Time

label: Definition:Time/Unit/Week
snippet: The week is a derived unit of time. $1$ week $=7$ days.

label: Definition:Time/Unit/Year
snippet: The year is a derived unit of time. It is based on the orbital period of Earth round the sun.

label: Definition:Time Period
snippet: The time period of a periodic process is the period of the periodic function which models that process. Category:Definitions/Physics Category:Definitions/Applied Mathematics Category:Definitions/Time

label: Definition:Time Series
snippet: A time series is a sequence of observations of a physical process taken at a sequence of instants of time.

label: Definition:Time Series/Continuous
snippet: A continuous time series is one in which the set of timestamps of the observations forms a continuous function.

label: Definition:Titanic Prime
snippet: A titanic prime is a prime number with $1000$ digits or more.

label: Definition:Tool
snippet: A tool is a physical device used as an aid to a process. Category:Definitions/Tools Category:Definitions/Proof Techniques Category:Definitions/Language Definitions

label: Definition:Top (Logic)
snippet: Top is a constant of propositional logic interpreted to mean the canonical, undoubted tautology whose truth nobody could possibly ever question. The symbol used is $\top$.

label: Definition:Top (Logic)/Truth Table
snippet: The characteristic truth table of the top constant $\top$ of propositional logic is as follows: $\begin{array}{|c|} \hline \top \\ \hline \T \\ \hline \end{array}$

label: Definition:Topological Closed Embedding
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a (topological) closed embedding : $f$ is a topological embedding its image $f(X)$ is closed in $Y$

label: Definition:Topological Compactness
snippet: The concept of (topological) compactness is a generalization of finiteness in the context of topology. Compactness limits the number of open sets in a topology by specifying conditions that need to be satisfied by its open covers.

label: Definition:Topological Complement of Closed Vector Subspace of Banach Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $Y_1$ be a closed vector subspace of $X$. We say that $Y_2$ is the topological complement of $Y_1$ there exists a closed vector subspace $Y_2 \subseteq X$ such that: $X = Y_1 \oplus Y_2$ where $\oplus$ denotes the internal direct sum.

label: Definition:Topological Connectedness
snippet: Connectedness, in the context of topology, denies the existence of certain subsets of a topological space with the property that: $U \cap V^- = \O$ and: $U^- \cap V = \O$ where $U^-$ and $V^-$ denote the closure of $U$ and $V$ respectively. This can be found in various contexts, as follows:

label: Definition:Topological Covering Mapping
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ and $C = \struct {X, \phi}$ be topological spaces. Let $\pi: C \to T$ be a continuous surjection. $\pi$ is a (topological) covering mapping for $T$ (by $C$) every $s \in S$ has an open neighborhood which is evenly covered by $\pi$.

label: Definition:Topological Covering Mapping/Covering Space
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ and $C = \struct {X, \phi}$ be topological spaces. Let $\pi: C \to T$ be a (topological) covering mapping for $T$ by $C$. Then $C$ is called a covering space for $T$.

label: Definition:Topological Dynamical System
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $f: S \to S$ be a continuous mapping. Then $\struct {S, f}$ is called a topological dynamical system.

label: Definition:Topological Field
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +, \circ}$ be a field with zero $0_F$. Let $\tau$ be a topology on $F$. Let $\struct {F, +, \circ, \tau}$ be a topological division ring. Then $\struct {F, +, \circ, \tau}$ is a topological field. That is, a topological field is a commutative topological division ring.

label: Definition:Topological Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot}$ be a group. On its underlying set $G$, let $\struct {G, \tau}$ be a topological space.

label: Definition:Topological Group/Also defined as
snippet: == Topological Group: Also defined as == Some sources insist that a topological group has to be a $T_2$ space. Category:Definitions/Topological Groups

label: Definition:Topological Group/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot}$ be a group. On its underlying set $G$, let $\struct {G, \tau}$ be a topological space. $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ is a topological group the following conditions are fulfilled: {{axiom | n = 1 | lc= Continuous Group Product | t = $\odot: \struct {G, \tau} \times \struct {G, \tau} \to \struct {G, \tau}$ is a continuous mapping }} {{axiom | n = 2 | lc= Continuous Inversion Mapping | t = $\iota: \struct {G, \tau} \to \struct {G, \tau}$ such that $\forall x \in G: \map \iota x = x^{-1}$ is also a continuous mapping }} where $\struct {G, \tau} \times \struct {G, \tau}$ is…

label: Definition:Topological Group/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \odot}$ be a group. On its underlying set $G$, let $\struct {G, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let the mapping $\psi: \struct {G, \tau} \times \struct {G, \tau} \to \struct {G, \tau}$ be defined as: $\map \psi {x, y} = x \odot y^{-1}$ $\struct {G, \odot, \tau}$ is a topological group : $\psi$ is a continuous mapping where $\struct {G, \tau} \times \struct {G, \tau}$ is considered as $G \times G$ with the product topology.

label: Definition:Topological Group Homomorphism
snippet: Let $G$ and $H$ be topological groups. A mapping $\phi:G \to H$ is a homomorphism of topological groups if it is a continuous group homomorphism. Category:Definitions/Topological Groups Category:Definitions/Group Homomorphisms

label: Definition:Topological Isomorphism
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $\struct {X, \tau_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \tau_Y}$ be topological vector spaces over $K$. Let $T : X \to Y$ be a linear transformation. We say that $T$ is a topological isomorphism $T$ is a linear isomorphism and a homeomorphism.

label: Definition:Topological Lattice
snippet: A topological lattice is a relational structure with topology $\struct {S, \preceq, \tau}$ where $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is a lattice and $\struct {S, \tau}$ is a topological space.

label: Definition:Topological Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) second-countable locally Euclidean space of dimension $d$. Then $M$ is a topological manifold of dimension $d$.

label: Definition:Topological Manifold/Complex Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a second-countable, complex locally Euclidean space of dimension $d$. Let $\mathscr F$ be a complex analytic differentiable structure on $M$. Then $\struct {M, \mathscr F}$ is called a complex manifold of dimension $d$.

label: Definition:Topological Manifold/Differentiable Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a second-countable locally Euclidean space of dimension $d$. Let $\mathscr F$ be a $d$-dimensional differentiable structure on $M$ of class $\CC^k$, where $k \ge 1$. Then $\struct {M, \mathscr F}$ is a differentiable manifold of class $\CC^k$ and dimension $d$.

label: Definition:Topological Manifold/Smooth Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a second-countable locally Euclidean space of dimension $d$. Let $\mathscr F$ be a smooth differentiable structure on $M$. Then $\struct {M, \mathscr F}$ is called a smooth manifold of dimension $d$.

label: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary
snippet: Let $\R^n$ denote the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space. Let $\H^n$ denote the $n$-dimensional closed upper half-space of $\R^n$. A $d$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary is a second-countable $T_2$ (Hausdorff) space $M$ in which every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic either to: a) an open subset of $\R^n$ or: b) an open subset of $\H^n$.

label: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Boundary
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. The boundary of $M$, denoted $\partial M$, is the set of all its boundary points.

label: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Boundary Point
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. Let $\partial \H^n$ denote the boundary of the closed upper half-space. A point $p \in M$ is a boundary point of $M$ $p$ is in the domain of some boundary chart of $M$ that send $p$ to $\partial \H^n$.

label: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Chart
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. Let $\H^n$ denote the closed upper half-space. A chart of $M$ is an ordered pair $\struct {U, \varphi}$, where: $U$ is an open subset of $M$ $\varphi: U \to D \subseteq \R^n$ is a homeomorphism of $U$ onto an open subset $D$ of $\R^n$ or $\H^n$.

label: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Coordinate Half-Ball
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. Let $\partial \H^n$ denote the boundary of the closed upper half-space. Let $\struct {U, \varphi}$ denote a a chart where: $U$ is an open subset of $M$ $\varphi: U \to D \subseteq \R^n$ is a homeomorphism of $U$ onto an open subset $D$ of $\R^n$ or $\H^n$. Let $p \in M$. Let $r \in \R_{>0}$ be a strictly positive real number. Let $\map {B_r} p$ denote an open ball of radius $r$ centered on $p$.

label: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Interior
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. The interior of $M$, denoted $\Int M$, is the set of all its interior points.

label: Definition:Topological Manifold with Boundary/Interior Point
snippet: Let $M$ be a $n$-dimensional topological manifold with boundary. A point $p \in M$ is an interior point of $M$ $p$ is in the domain of some interior chart of $M$.

label: Definition:Topological Open Embedding
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be topological spaces. Let $f : X \to Y$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a (topological) open embedding : $f$ is a topological embedding its image $f(X)$ is open in $Y$

label: Definition:Topological Order Theory
snippet: Topological order theory is the branch of relation theory and topology which studies orderings and topological spaces.

label: Definition:Topological Property
snippet: Let $P$ be a property whose domain is the set of all topological spaces. Suppose that whenever $\map P T$ holds, then so does $\map P {T'}$, where $T$ and $T'$ are topological spaces which are homeomorphic. Then $P$ is known as a topological property. Loosely, a topological property is one which is preserved under homeomorphism.

label: Definition:Topological Ring
snippet: Let $\struct{R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. Let $\tau$ be a topology over $R$. Then $\struct {R, +, \circ, \tau}$ is a topological ring : $(1): \quad \struct {R, +, \tau}$ is a topological group $(2): \quad \struct {R, \circ,\tau}$ is a topological semigroup.

label: Definition:Topological Semigroup
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a semigroup. On that same underlying set $S$, let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Then $\struct {S, \circ, \tau}$ is a topological semigroup : $\circ: \struct {S, \tau} \times \struct {S, \tau} \to \struct {S, \tau}$ is a continuous mapping where $\struct {S, \tau} \times \struct {S, \tau}$ is considered as $S \times S$ with the product topology.

label: Definition:Topological Space
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\tau$ be a topology on $S$. That is, let $\tau \subseteq \powerset S$ satisfy the open set axioms: Then the ordered pair $\struct {S, \tau}$ is called a topological space. The elements of $\tau$ are called open sets of $\struct {S, \tau}$. In a topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$, we consider $S$ to be the universal set.

label: Definition:Topological Space/Also denoted as
snippet: == Topological Space: Also denoted as == Some authors denote a topological space using the suboptimal $\set {S, \tau}$, which leaves it conceptually unclear as to which is the set and which the topology. This adds unnecessary complexity to the underlying axiomatic justification for the existence of the very object that is being defined.

label: Definition:Topological Space/Also known as
snippet: == Topological Space: Also known as == The topological space $\struct {S, \tau}$ can be referred to as just a space if the context is clear. $\struct {S, \tau}$ can be referred to as the (topological) space $S$ if it is clear what topology is actually carried on it.

label: Definition:Topological Space Induced by Neighborhood Space
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \NN}$ be a neighborhood space. Let $\tau$ be the set of open sets of $\struct {S, \NN}$. Then $\struct {S, \tau}$ is the topological space induced by $\struct {S, \NN}$.

label: Definition:Topological Space of Real-Valued Continuous Functions on Closed Unit Interval
snippet: Let $C \closedint 0 1$ denote the topological space of real-valued continuous functions on the closed unit interval. This object is referred to on as the topological space of real-valued continuous functions on the closed unit interval.

label: Definition:Topological Subspace
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$ be a subset of $S$. Define: $\tau_H := \set {U \cap H: U \in \tau} \subseteq \powerset H$ where $\powerset H$ denotes the power set of $H$. Then the topological space $T_H = \struct {H, \tau_H}$ is called a (topological) subspace of $T$. The set $\tau_H$ is referred to as the subspace topology on $H$ (induced by $\tau$).

label: Definition:Topological Subspace/Also defined as
snippet: == Topological Subspace: Also defined as == takes the philosophical position that a topological space may be allowed to be empty. Some sources do not allow this, and insist that the underlying set of a topological space must be non-empty set. Such sources impose the additional constraint that the underlying set of a topological subspace must likewise be a non-empty set. , however, does allow for a topological subspace to be empty. Category:Definitions/Topological Subspaces

label: Definition:Topological Sum
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau_1}$ and $\struct {Y, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. The topological sum $\struct {Z, \tau_3}$ of $X$ and $Y$ is defined as: $Z = X \sqcup Y$ where: $X \sqcup Y$ denotes the disjoint union of $X$ and $Y$ $\tau_3$ is the topology generated by $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$.

label: Definition:Topological Surface
snippet: A surface, in the context of topology, is a smooth topological manifold whose dimension is $2$. More briefly, a surface is a smooth $2$-manifold. Category:Definitions/Topology Category:Definitions/Algebraic Topology

label: Definition:Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +_K, \circ_K, \tau_K}$ be a topological field. Let $\struct {X, +_X, \circ_X, \tau_X}$ be a vector space over $K$. Let $\tau_X \times \tau_X$ be the product topology of $\tau_X$ and $\tau_X$. Let $\tau_K \times \tau_X$ be the product topology of $\tau_K$ and $\tau_X$. We say that $\struct {X, \tau_X}$ is called a topological vector space : {{axiom | n = 1 | t = $+_X: \struct {X \times X, \tau_X \times \tau_X} \to \struct {X, \tau_X}$ is continuous }} {{axiom | n = 2 | t = $\circ_X : \struct {K \times X, \tau_K \times \tau_X} \to \struct {X, \tau_X}$ is continuous }}

label: Definition:Topologically Complemented Subspace of Banach Space
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $Y$ be a vector subspace of $X$. We say that $Y$ is topologically complemented in $X$ there exists a bounded projection from $X$ onto $Y$.

label: Definition:Topologically Distinguishable
snippet: topologically distinguishable]] Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x, y \in S$. Then $x$ and $y$ are topologically distinguishable they do not have exactly the same neighborhoods. That is, either: $\exists U \in \tau: x \in U \subseteq N_x \subseteq S: y \notin N_x$ or: $\exists V \in \tau: y \in V \subseteq N_y \subseteq S: x \notin N_y$ or both. That is, at least one of the elements $x$ and $y$ has a neighborhood that is not a neighborhood of the other.

label: Definition:Topologically Distinguishable/Indistinguishable
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x, y \in S$. The two points $x$ and $y$ are topologically indistinguishable they are not topologically distinguishable. That is they do not exactly the same neighborhoods: $\forall U \in \tau: x \in U \iff y \in U$

label: Definition:Topologically Equivalent Metrics
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be metric spaces on the same underlying set $A$.

label: Definition:Topologically Equivalent Metrics/Definition 1
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be metric spaces on the same underlying set $A$. $d_1$ and $d_2$ are topologically equivalent : For all metric spaces $\struct {B, d}$ and $\struct {C, d'}$: For all mappings $f: B \to A$ and $g: A \to C$: $(1): \quad f$ is $\tuple {d, d_1}$-continuous $f$ is $\tuple {d, d_2}$-continuous $(2): \quad g$ is $\tuple {d_1, d'}$-continuous $g$ is $\tuple {d_2, d'}$-continuous. Such mappings $f$ and $g$ can be referred to as homeomorphisms.

label: Definition:Topologically Equivalent Metrics/Definition 2
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A, d_2}$ be metric spaces on the same underlying set $A$. $d_1$ and $d_2$ are topologically equivalent : $U \subseteq A$ is $d_1$-open $U \subseteq A$ is $d_2$-open.

label: Definition:Topologically Nilpotent Ring Element
snippet: Let $A$ be a $T_2$ (Hausdorff) topological ring. Let $a \in A$. $a$ is topologically nilpotent the sequence of powers $a^n$ converges to $0$.

label: Definition:Topologist's Sine Curve
snippet: 420px Let $G = \set {\tuple {x, \sin \dfrac 1 x} : 0 < x \le 1}$, considered as a subset of the real number plane with the usual (Euclidean) topology $\struct {\R^2, \tau_d}$. Then the set $G \cup \set {\tuple {0, 0} }$ is called the topologist's sine curve.

label: Definition:Topology/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A topology on $S$ is a subset $\tau \subseteq \powerset S$ of the power set of $S$ that satisfies the open set axioms: If $\tau$ is a topology on $S$, then $\struct {S, \tau}$ is called a topological space. The elements of $\tau$ are called the open sets of $\struct {S, \tau}$.

label: Definition:Topology/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A topology on $S$ is a subset $\tau \subseteq \powerset S$ of the power set of $S$ that satisfies the following axioms:

label: Definition:Topology/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Topology == The word topology is derived from the Greek words τόπος, meaning place, and λόγος, meaning study. This originates from its origins as the study of situation. The word topology was coined by in a letter of $1836$. The word was first published in the title of 's $1847$ book , but never caught on until the $1920$s.

label: Definition:Topology (Mathematical Branch)
snippet: Topology is a geometry of transformations in which the only invariant is continuity. Some sources suggest that it can indeed be described simply as the study of continuity. As such, it is closely interwoven with the branch of analysis.

label: Definition:Topology (Mathematical Branch)/Also defined as
snippet: == Topology: Also defined as == Some sources define topology as: the study of the properties of shapes and space. However, this is inadequate for , as that could easily be used to define geometry.

label: Definition:Topology (Mathematical Branch)/Also known as
snippet: == Topology: Also known as == The original name of the mathematical branch known as topology was geometria situs, or analysis situs (that is: geometry / analysis of position). It is often referred to as rubber-sheet geometry.

label: Definition:Topology (Mathematical Branch)/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Topology == The mathematical branch known as topology originally arose as a sub-branch of geometry. However, it has since evolved such that it contributes to many other mathematical branches.

label: Definition:Topology Defined by Closed Sets
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $F \subseteq \powerset S$ be a subset of its power set satisfying the closed set axioms: The topology defined by $F$ is the topology whose open sets are the complements of elements of $F$: $\tau = \set {U \subseteq S : S \setminus U \in F}$

label: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Basis
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\BB$ be a synthetic basis of $S$.

label: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Basis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\BB$ be a synthetic basis of $S$. The topology on $S$ generated by $\BB$ is defined as: $\tau = \set {\bigcup \AA: \AA \subseteq \BB}$ That is, the set of all unions of sets from $\BB$.

label: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Basis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\BB$ be a synthetic basis of $S$. The topology on $S$ generated by $\BB$ is defined as: $\tau = \set {U \subseteq S: U = \bigcup \set {B \in \BB: B \subseteq U} }$

label: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Basis/Definition 3
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\BB$ be a synthetic basis of $S$. The topology on $S$ generated by $\BB$ is defined as: $\tau = \set {U \subseteq S: \forall x \in U: \exists B \in \BB: x \in B \subseteq U}$

label: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Sub-Basis
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\SS \subseteq \powerset X$ be a synthetic sub-basis on $S$.

label: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Sub-Basis/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\SS \subseteq \powerset S$ be a synthetic sub-basis on $S$. Define: $\ds \BB = \set {\bigcap \FF: \FF \subseteq \SS, \FF \text{ is finite} } \cup \O \cup S$ That is, $\BB$ is the set of all finite intersections of sets in $\SS$, together with the empty set and $S$ itself. Note that $\FF$ is allowed to be empty in the above definition.

label: Definition:Topology Generated by Synthetic Sub-Basis/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\SS \subseteq \powerset X$ be a synthetic sub-basis on $S$. The topology generated by $\SS$, denoted $\map \tau \SS$, is defined as the unique topology on $S$ that satisfies the following axioms: That is, $\map \tau \SS$ is the coarsest topology on $S$ for which every element of $\SS$ is open.

label: Definition:Topology Induced by Atlas
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A$ be an atlas on $T$. The topology induced by the atlas is the topology generated by the synthetic sub-basis: $\ds \bigcup_{\tuple {U, \, \phi} \mathop \in A} \set {\map {\phi^{-1} } V : V \text { is open in } U} \subset T$

label: Definition:Topology Induced by Metric/Also known as
snippet: == Topology Induced by Metric: Also known as == The topological space which is induced by a metric is also known as the topological space associated with the (given) metric space. When the context is clear, the phrase metric topology for $d$ can be used. The metric space whose metric induces this topology can be said to give rise to the topological space.

label: Definition:Topology Induced by Metric/Definition 1
snippet: The topology on the metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ induced by (the metric) $d$ is defined as the set $\tau$ of all open sets of $M$.

label: Definition:Topology Induced by Metric/Definition 2
snippet: The topology on the metric space $M = \struct {A, d}$ induced by (the metric) $d$ is defined as the topology $\tau$ generated by the basis consisting of the set of all open $\epsilon$-balls in $M$.

label: Definition:Topology Induced by Pseudometric
snippet: Let $\struct {X, d}$ be a pseudometric space. Let $\tau_d$ be the set of all $X \subseteq S$ which are open in the sense that: $\forall y \in X: \exists \epsilon > 0: \map {B_\epsilon} y \subseteq X$ where $\map {B_\epsilon} y$ is the open $\epsilon$-ball of $y$. We call $\tau_d$ the topology on $X$ induced by $d$.

label: Definition:Topology Induced by Quasiuniformity
snippet: Let $\UU$ be a quasiuniformity on a set $S$. Let $\NN \subseteq \powerset S$ be a subset of the power set of $S$, created from $\UU$ by: $\NN := \set {\map u x: u \in \UU, x \in S}$ where: $\forall x \in S: \map u x = \set {y: \tuple {x, y} \in u}$ That is, where $\map u x$ is the image of $x$ under $u$, where $u$ is considered as a relation on $S$. Let $\NN$ be the neighborhood system for a topology $\tau$ on $S$. Then $\tau$ is the topology induced by $\UU$ on $S$.

label: Definition:Topology on Extended Complex Plane
snippet: Let $\overline \C$ denote the extended complex plane. Let the neighborhood of $\infty$ in $\overline \C$ be defined as the complement in $\overline \C$ of the closed and bounded subsets of $\C$. Then $\overline \C$ is a topological space.

label: Definition:Topology on Extended Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\overline \R$ denote the extended real numbers. The (standard) topology on $\overline \R$ is the order topology $\tau$ associated to the ordering on $\overline \R$.

label: Definition:Topology on Étalé Space of Presheaf
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\FF$ be a presheaf of sets on $T$. Let $\map {\operatorname {\acute Et} } \FF$ be its étalé space. The topology on $\map {\operatorname {\acute Et} } \FF$ is the final topology with respect to the sections associated to elements of $\map \FF U$ with $U \subseteq S$ open.

label: Definition:Toroidal Graph
snippet: A toroidal graph is a graph which can be embedded on the surface of a torus without any of the edges meeting at points other than the vertices.

label: Definition:Torque
snippet: Torque is a measure of strength of a force to effect rotation of a body. Let $\mathbf F$ be a force acting at a point on a body $B$. Let $B$ rotate around a point $O$ as a consequence of the action of $\mathbf F$. Let $\mathbf r$ be the position vector of $P$ $O$, that is: $\mathbf r = \vec {OP}$ The torque about $O$ is defined as the cross product of the vector $\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf F$: $\bstau = \mathbf r \times \mathbf F$ Torque is a vector quantity.

snippet: Differential Geometry: Torsion of Curve Abstract Algebra: Group Theory: Torsion Element of Group Torsion Subgroup Torsion Group Commutative Algebra: Definition:Torsion Element of Module Definition:Torsion Submodule Definition:Torsion Module Algebraic Geometry Torsion Point of Elliptic Curve Torsion Point of Algebraic Group

label: Definition:Torsion Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be an abelian group. Its torsion subgroup $\map T G$ is the subgroup of all torsion elements.

label: Definition:Torsion of Curve Parameterized by Arc Length/3-Dimensional Real Vector Space
snippet: Let $\alpha : I \to \R^3$ be a (smooth) curve parameterized by arc length. Let $s \in I$ be such that the curvature $\map \kappa s \ne 0$. The torsion of $\alpha$ at $s$ is the real number $\map \tau s$ defined by: $\map {b'} s = \map \tau s \map n s$ where: $\map {b'} s$ is the derivative of the binormal vector $\map n s$ is the normal vector

label: Definition:Torus (Geometry)
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a circle. Let $\LL$ be a straight line in the same plane as $\CC$ such that $\LL$ may or may not intersect $\CC$. A torus is the surface of revolution formed by rotating $\CC$ one full turn about $\LL$.

label: Definition:Torus (Geometry)/Also defined as
snippet: == Torus in the context of Geometry: Also defined as == Some sources limit the definition of the torus to restrict the straight line so that it does not intersect the circle rotating around it.

label: Definition:Torus (Geometry)/Also known as
snippet: == Torus in the context of Geometry: Also known as == A torus is also known by its informal name anchor ring.

label: Definition:Torus (Topology)
snippet: A torus is a surface obtained by identifying both pairs of opposite sides, one with the other, of a square, while retaining the orientation: 300px Thus in the above diagram, $AB$ is identified with $DC$ and $CB$ with $DA$.

label: Definition:Torus (Topology)/Formal Construction
snippet: Let $T$ be the square embedded in the Cartesian plane defined as: $T = \closedint {-1} 1 \times \closedint {-1} 1$ Let $T'$ be the quotient space formed from $T$ using the identification mapping $p: T \to T'$ as follows: $\forall \tuple {x, y} \in T: \map p {x, y} = \begin {cases} \paren {x, y} & : -1 < x, y < 1 \\ \\ \tuple {-x, y} & : x = \pm 1 \\ \\ \tuple {x, -y} & : y = \pm 1 \end {cases}$ Then $T'$ is a torus .

label: Definition:Torus (Topology)/General/Definition 2
snippet: The $n$-dimensional torus (or $n$-torus) $\Bbb T^n$ is defined as the space whose points are those of the Cartesian product of $n$ circles: $\Bbb T^n = \underbrace{\Bbb S^1 \times \Bbb S^1 \times \ldots \times \Bbb S^1}_{n \text{ times}}$ and whose topology $\tau_{\Bbb T^n}$ is generated by the basis: $\BB = \set {U_1 \times U_2 \times \cdots \times U_n : U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n \in \tau_{\Bbb S^1}}$ where $\tau_{\Bbb S^1}$ is the topology of the $1$-sphere.

label: Definition:Total Curvature
snippet: Let $C$ be a curve defined by a real function which is twice differentiable. Let $\delta \psi$ be the angle of contingence with respect to $2$ points $P$ and $Q$ on $C$. Then $\delta \psi$ is known as the total curvature of $C$ between $P$ and $Q$.

label: Definition:Total Differential/Vector Function
snippet: Let $\map {\R^3} {x, y, z}$ denote the Cartesian $3$-space. Let $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ be the standard ordered basis on $\R^3$. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field in $\R^3$. Let $\mathbf v: \R^3 \to \mathbf V$ be a vector-valued function on $\R^3$: $\forall P = \tuple {x, y, z} \in \R^3: \map {\mathbf v} P := \map {v_1} P \mathbf i + \map {v_2} P \mathbf j + \map {v_3} P \mathbf k$ Let $v_1, v_2, v_3$ be differentiable.

label: Definition:Total Energy of Particles
snippet: Let $P$ be a physical system composed of a countable number of particles. Suppose the kinetic and potential energy of $P$ is respectively $T$ and $U$. Denote: $E = T + U$ Then $E$ is known as the total energy of $P$.

label: Definition:Total Ordering
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation on a set $S$.

label: Definition:Total Ordering/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation on a set $S$. $\RR$ is a total ordering on $S$ : $(1): \quad \RR$ is an ordering on $S$ $(2): \quad \RR$ is connected That is, $\RR$ is an ordering with no non-comparable pairs: $\forall x, y \in S: x \mathop \RR y \lor y \mathop \RR x$

label: Definition:Total Ordering/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation on a set $S$. $\RR$ is a total ordering on $S$ : {{eqn | n = 2 | l = \RR \cap \RR^{-1} | o = \subseteq | r = \Delta_S }} {{eqn | n = 3 | l = \RR \cup \RR^{-1} | r = S \times S }}

label: Definition:Total Preordering
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $\precsim$ be a preordering on $S$. Then $\precsim$ is a total preordering on $S$ $\precsim$ is connected. That is, there is no pair of elements of $S$ which is non-comparable: $\forall x, y \in S: x \precsim y \lor y \precsim x$

label: Definition:Total Relation
snippet: Let $\RR \subseteq S \times S$ be a relation on a set $S$. Then $\RR$ is defined as total : $\forall a, b \in S: \tuple {a, b} \in \RR \lor \tuple {b, a} \in \RR$ That is, every pair of elements is related (either or both ways round).

label: Definition:Total Relation/Also known as
snippet: == Total Relation: Also known as == Other terms that can be found that mean the same thing as total relation are: dichotomous relation strictly connected relation complete relation. Some sources use the term dichotomy, but this word is also used for a concept in statistics, so will not be used in this context on .

label: Definition:Total Ring of Fractions
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. The total ring of fractions of $A$ is the localization of $A$ at the set of its regular elements.

label: Definition:Total Semilattice
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \odot}$ be a semilattice. Let $\struct {S, \odot}$ have the property that every subset of $\struct {S, \odot}$ is a subsemilattice. That is, such that every subset of $\struct {S, \odot}$ is closed under $\odot$. Then $\struct {S, \odot}$ is known as a total semilattice.

label: Definition:Total Variation/Real Function/Closed Bounded Interval/Definition 1
