label: Definition:Uniform Antiprism
snippet: A uniform antiprism is an antiprism: $(1): \quad$ whose bases are both congruent regular polygons $(2): \quad$ whose lateral faces are all equilateral triangles.

label: Definition:Uniform Cauchy Criterion
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \mathbb R$. Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a sequence of real functions $S \to \R$. We say that $\sequence {f_n}$ satisfies the uniform Cauchy criterion or is uniformly Cauchy on $S$ if for all $\varepsilon \in \R_{> 0}$, there exists $N \in \N$ such that: $\size {\map {f_n} x - \map {f_m} x} N$. By Sequence of Functions is Uniformly Cauchy iff Uniformly Convergent, this criterion gives a necessary and sufficient condition for a sequence of real functions to be uniformly convergent.

label: Definition:Uniform Continuity/Metric Space
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Then a mapping $f: A_1 \to A_2$ is uniformly continuous on $A_1$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \forall x, y \in A_1: \map {d_1} {x, y} 0}$ denotes the set of all strictly positive real numbers.

label: Definition:Uniform Contraction Mapping
snippet: Let $M$ and $N$ be metric spaces. Let $f : M \times N \to M$ be a mapping. Then $f$ is a uniform contraction there exists $K<1$ such that for all $x,y\in M$ and $t\in N$: $d(f(x,t), f(y,t)) \leq K\cdot d(x,y)$.

label: Definition:Uniform Convergence/Infinite Series
snippet: Let $S \subseteq \R$. Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a sequence of real functions $S \to \R$. Let $\sequence {s_n}$ be sequence of real functions $S \to \R$ with: $\ds \map {s_n} x = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \map {f_n} x$ for each $n \in \N$ and $x \in S$. We say that: $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty f_n$ converges uniformly to a real function $f: S \to \R$ on $S$ $\sequence {s_n}$ converges uniformly to $f$ on $S$.

label: Definition:Uniform Convergence/Metric Space
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $M = \struct {A, d}$ be a metric space. Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a sequence of mappings $f_n: S \to A$. Let: $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R: \forall n \ge N, \forall x \in S: \map d {\map {f_n} x, \map f x} < \epsilon$ Then $\sequence {f_n}$ converges to $f$ uniformly on $S$ as $n \to \infty$.

label: Definition:Uniform Convergence/Real Sequence
snippet: Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a sequence of real functions defined on $D \subseteq \R$. Let: $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists N \in \R: \forall n \ge N, \forall x \in D: \size {\map {f_n} x - \map f x} < \epsilon$ Then $\sequence {f_n}$ converges to $f$ uniformly on $D$ as $n \to \infty$.

label: Definition:Uniform Convergence of Product/Compact Space
snippet: Let $X$ be a compact topological space. Let $\struct {\mathbb K, \norm{\,\cdot\,}}$ be a complete valued field. Let $\sequence {f_n}$ be a sequence of continuous mappings $f_n: X \to \mathbb K$. The infinite product $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty f_n$ converges uniformly there exists $n_0 \in \N$ such that the sequence of partial products of $\ds \prod_{n \mathop = n_0}^\infty f_n$ converges uniformly and is nonzero.

label: Definition:Uniform Distribution/Continuous
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $a, b \in \R$ such that $a < b$. $X$ is said to be uniformly distributed on the closed real interval $\closedint a b$ it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} x = \begin{cases} \dfrac 1 {b - a} & a \le x \le b \\ \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$ This is written: $X \sim \ContinuousUniform a b$

label: Definition:Uniform Distribution/Discrete
snippet: Let $X$ be a discrete random variable on a probability space. Then $X$ has a discrete uniform distribution with parameter $n$ : $\Img X = \set {1, 2, \ldots, n}$ $\map \Pr {X = k} = \dfrac 1 n$ That is, there is a number of outcomes with an equal probability of occurrence. This is written: $X \sim \DiscreteUniform n$

label: Definition:Uniform Equivalence/Metric Spaces
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Then the mapping $f: A_1 \to A_2$ is a uniform equivalence of $M_1$ with $M_2$ $f$ is a bijection such that $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are both uniformly continuous.

label: Definition:Uniform Equivalence/Metrics
snippet: Let $A$ be a set on which there are two metrics imposed: $d_1$ and $d_2$. Then $d_1$ and $d_2$ are uniformly equivalent the identity mapping of $A$ is uniformly $\tuple {d_1, d_2}$-continuous and also uniformly $\tuple {d_2, d_1}$-continuous.

label: Definition:Uniform Matroid
snippet: Let $S$ be a finite set of cardinality $n$. Let $\mathscr I_{k, n}$ be the set of all subsets of $S$ of cardinality less than or equal to $k$. Then the ordered pair $\struct {S, \mathscr I_{k, n} }$ is called the uniform matroid of rank $k$ and is denoted $U_{k, n}$.

label: Definition:Uniform Motion
snippet: Uniform motion is motion with constant velocity, speed or acceleration.

label: Definition:Uniform Polyhedron
snippet: A uniform polyhedron is a polyhedron: $(1): \quad$ which is isogonal $(2): \quad$ whose faces are all regular polygons (but not necessarily all of the same type).

label: Definition:Uniform Prism
snippet: A uniform prism is a regular prism whose lateral faces are square.

label: Definition:Uniform Space
snippet: Let $\UU$ be a uniformity on a set $S$. The quasiuniform space $\struct {\struct {S, \UU}, \tau}$ induced by $\UU$ is a uniform space.

label: Definition:Uniform Tubular Neighborhood
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $P \subseteq M$ be an embedded submanifold. Let $U \subseteq M$ be the tubular neighborhood of $P$ in $M$ with $\map \delta x = \epsilon$ where $\epsilon \in \R_{> 0}$. Then $U$ is called the uniform tubular neighborhood (or $\epsilon$-tubular neighborhood) of $P$ in $M$.

label: Definition:Uniformity
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. A uniformity on $S$ is a set of subsets $\UU$ of the cartesian product $S \times S$ satisfying the quasiuniformity axioms: and also: $(\text U 5): \forall u \in \UU: u^{-1} \in \UU$ where $u^{-1}$ is defined as: $u^{-1} := \set {\tuple {y, x}: \tuple {x, y} \in u}$ That is, all elements of $\UU$ are symmetric. These five axioms are together known as the uniformity axioms.

label: Definition:Uniformly Bounded
snippet: Let $X$ be a set and let $Y = \left({A, d}\right)$ be a metric space. Let $\FF = \family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of mappings $f_i: X \to Y$. Then $\FF$ is said to be uniformly bounded every mapping $f \in \FF$ can be bounded by the same constant. That is, there exists some $M \in \R$ such that: $\forall x, y \in X, i \in I : \map d {\map {f_i} x, \map {f_i} y} \le M$ Category:Definitions/Metric Spaces Category:Definitions/Boundedness

label: Definition:Uniformly Continuous Semigroup
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $\family {\map T t}_{t \ge 0}$ be a $\hointr 0 \infty$-indexed family of bounded linear transformations $\map T t : X \to X$. Let $\struct {\map B X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_{\map B X} }$ be the space of bounded linear transformations equipped with the canonical norm. We say that $\family {\map T t}_{t \ge 0}$ is uniformly continuous : $\ds \lim_{t \mathop \to 0^+} \norm {\map T t - I}_{\map B X} = 0$

label: Definition:Uniformly Equicontinuous
snippet: Let $X = \struct {A, d}$ and $Y = \struct {B, \rho}$ be metric spaces. Let $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of mappings $f_i: X \to Y$. Then $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is said to be uniformly equicontinuous on $S \subseteq A$ : $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0} : \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \forall i \in I: \forall x, y \in S : \map d {x, y} < \delta \implies \map \rho {\map {f_i} x, \map {f_i} y} < \epsilon$

label: Definition:Uniformly Equicontinuous Mappings
snippet: Let $M_1 = \struct {A_1, d_1}$ and $M_2 = \struct {A_2, d_2}$ be metric spaces. Let $\family {f_i: M_1 \to M_2}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be an indexed family of mappings, where $I$ is an arbitrary index set. Let $\family {f_i}$ have the property that: $\forall \epsilon \in \R_{>0}: \exists \delta \in \R_{>0}: \forall x, y \in A_1: \map {d_1} {x, y} < \delta \implies \map {d_2} {\map {f_i} x, \map {f_i} y} < \epsilon$ for all $i \in I$. Then $\family {f_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ is a family of uniformly equicontinuous mappings.

label: Definition:Uniformly Normal Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $W \subseteq M$ be a subset. Let $U_p = \map {\exp_p} {\map {B_\delta^-} 0 }$ be a closed geodesic ball around $p \in M$. Suppose there exists $\delta \in \R_{> 0}$ such that: $\forall p \in W : W \subseteq U_p$ Then $W$ is called uniformly normal (or uniformly $\delta$-normal).

label: Definition:Unimodal Distribution
snippet: A unimodal distribution is a probability distribution which has only one mode. For a discrete probability distribution $X$, if two adjacent values both have the same probability or frequency, and this is the modal value, then it is usual to regard this as a unimodal distribution.

label: Definition:Union of Family/Also denoted as
snippet: == Union of Family: Also denoted as == The set $\ds \bigcup_{i \mathop \in I} S_i$ can also be seen denoted as: $\ds \bigcup_I S_i$ or, if the indexing set is clear from context: $\ds \bigcup_i S_i$ Some sources use the form: $\bigcup \set {S_i: i \in I}$

label: Definition:Union of Relations
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\RR_1$ and $\RR_2$ be relations on $S \times T$. The union of $\RR_1$ and $\RR_2$ is the relation $\QQ$ defined by: $\QQ := \RR_1 \cup \RR_2$ where $\cup$ denotes set union. Explicitly, for $s \in S$ and $t \in T$, we have: $s \mathrel \QQ t$ $s \mathrel {\RR_1} t$ or $s \mathrel {\RR_2} t$

label: Definition:Union of Relations/General Definition
snippet: Let $S$ and $T$ be sets. Let $\mathscr R$ be a collection of relations on $S \times T$. The union of $\mathscr R$ is the relation $\RR$ defined by: $\ds \RR = \bigcup \mathscr R$ where $\bigcup$ denotes set union. Explicitly, for $s \in S$ and $t \in T$: $s \mathrel \RR t$ for some $\QQ \in \mathscr R$, $s \mathrel \QQ t$

label: Definition:Unique
snippet: Suppose $A$ and $B$ are two objects whose definition is in terms of a given set of properties. If it can be demonstrated that, in order for both $A$ and $B$ to fulfil those properties, it is necessary for $A$ to be equal to $B$, then $A$ (and indeed $B$) is unique. Equivalently, there is one and only one, or exactly one, such object. Thus, intuitively, an object is unique if there is precisely one such object.

label: Definition:Unique Period Prime
snippet: Let $b \in \N_{>1}$ be a natural number. A unique period prime base $b$ is a prime number $p$ whose reciprocal expressed base $b$ has a period shared with no other prime. If $b$ is not specified, then decimal notation (that is, base $10$) is assumed.

label: Definition:Unique up to Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $S \subseteq \map {\operatorname {Ob} } {\mathbf C}$ be a subclass of its objects. The class $S$ is unique up to isomorphism for all objects $s, t \in S$ there is a isomorphism from $s$ to $t$.

label: Definition:Unique up to Unique Isomorphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $S \subseteq \map {\operatorname {Ob} } {\mathbf C}$ be a subclass of its objects. The class $S$ is unique up to unique isomorphism for all objects $s, t \in S$ there exists a unique isomorphism from $s$ to $t$.

label: Definition:Unique up to Unique Morphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. Let $S \subseteq \map {\operatorname {Ob} } {\mathbf C}$ be a subclass of its objects.

label: Definition:Uniqueness Theorem
snippet: A uniqueness theorem is a theorem which asserts that only one particular type of object exists.

label: Definition:Unit
snippet: Arithmetic and so on: Numbers: An instance of the number $1$ (one). Abstract Algebra: Unit of Ring Set Systems: Unit of System of Sets. Set Theory: Unit set: another word for singleton Algebras: Unit of a unitary algebra The concepts are related: it is apparent that the unit of an algebra of sets $\SS$ is the unity of $\SS$ considered as a ring $\struct {\SS, *, \cap}$. Unit may also refer to: Unit of Measurement: A definite magnitude of a physical quantity which is agreed by convention. Experimental Unit: A subject of an experimental design to which a treatment is to be applied.

label: Definition:Unit-Speed Curve
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I$ be a closed real interval. Let $\gamma : \R \to M$ be a smooth curve. Suppose the speed of $\gamma$ is equal to $1$: $\size {\map {\gamma'} t}_g = 1$ where $\size {\, \cdot \,}_g$ is the Riemannian inner product norm. Then $\gamma$ is a unit-speed curve.

label: Definition:Unit (One)
snippet: A numerical quantity whose cardinality corresponds to the number $1$ (one) is called a unit. '

label: Definition:Unit Arithmetic Function
snippet: The unit arithmetic function $u: S \to \Z$ is defined by $u \left({n}\right) = 1$ for all $n$: $\forall n \in S: u \left({n}\right) = 1$ where $S$ is (in theory) any set, but in this context is usually one of the standard number sets $\Z, \Q, \R, \C$.

label: Definition:Unit Ball
snippet: Let $V$ be a normed vector space with norm $\norm {\, \cdot \,}$. The closed unit ball of $V$, denoted $\operatorname {ball} V$, is the set: $\set {v \in V: \norm v_V \mathop \le 1}$

label: Definition:Unit Circle
snippet: The unit circle is a circle with radius equal to $1$. 400px

label: Definition:Unit Cube
snippet: A unit cube is a cube each of whose edges is one unit long.

label: Definition:Unit Disk
snippet: A unit disk is a disk whose radius is equal to $1$.

label: Definition:Unit Fraction
snippet: A unit fraction is a fraction whose numerator is $1$.

label: Definition:Unit Length
snippet: A unit length is a straight line segment of arbitrary length can defined as having a length of $1$ (one). During the course of the exposition arising from the definition a unit length $L$, all subsequent lengths can then be expressed as multiples of $L$. Category:Definitions/Geometry

label: Definition:Unit Matrix
snippet: Let $R$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$ and whose unity is $1_R$. Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$ be a (strictly) positive integer. Let $\struct {\map {\MM_R} n, +, \times}$ be the ring of order $n$ square matrices over $R$. Then the unit matrix (of order $n$) of $\struct {\map {\MM_R} n, +, \times}$ is defined as: $\mathbf I_n := \sqbrk a_n: a_{i j} = \delta_{i j}$ where $\delta_{i j}$ is the Kronecker delta for $\map {\MM_R} n$. That is, it is the square matrix where every element on the diagonal is equal to $1_R$, and whose other entries all are $0_R$.

label: Definition:Unit Matrix/Also known as
snippet: == Unit Matrix: Also known as == Some sources refer to the unit matrix as the identity matrix, as it is the identity element of the ring of order $n$ square matrices over $R$. There are several variants of $\mathbf I_n$ which can frequently be found, for example: $\mathbf 1$ $\mathbf 1_n$ $\mathbb I_n$ In physics and mechanics it is common to see $\mathbf I$ used specifically to denote the $3 \times 3$ unit matrix.

label: Definition:Unit Normal
snippet: Let $S$ be a surface in ordinary $3$-space. Let $P$ be a point of $S$. Let $\mathbf n$ be a normal to $S$ at $P$ such that $\mathbf n$ is a unit vector. Then $\mathbf n$ is known as a unit normal.

label: Definition:Unit Square
snippet: A unit square is a square of side of unit length.

label: Definition:Unit Square under Lexicographic Ordering
snippet: Let $S$ be the unit square in the (real) Cartesian plane: {{eqn | l = S | r = \set {\tuple {x, y}: x, y \in \R, 0 \le x \le 1, 0 \le y \le 1} | c = }} Let $\preccurlyeq_l$ denote the lexicographic ordering applied to $S$: $\forall \tuple {x_1, y_1}, \tuple {x_2, y_2} \in S: \tuple {x_1, y_1} \preccurlyeq_l \tuple {x_2, y_2} \iff \begin {cases} x_1 < x_2 \\ x_1 = x_2 \land y_1 \le y_2 \end {cases}$ Let $\tau$ be the order topology be applied to the ordered structure $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq_l}$.

label: Definition:Unit Tangent Bundle
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $T M$ be the tangent bundle of $\struct {M, g}$. Let $p \in M$ be a point in $M$. Let $\tuple {p, v}$ be a geometric tangent vector. The unit tangent bundle $UTM \subseteq TM$ is the subset of unit vectors: $UTM = \set {\tuple {p, v} \in TM : \norm v_g = 1}$

label: Definition:Unit Vector
snippet: A unit vector is a vector quantity which has a magnitude of $1$.

label: Definition:Unit of Adjunction
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ be locally small categories. Let $\tuple {F, G, \alpha}$ be an adjunction between $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$. The unit of adjunction $\tuple {F, G, \alpha}$ is the natural transformation $\eta: \operatorname {id}_{\mathbf D} \to GF$ where: for each $D$ of $\mathbf D: \eta_{_D} = \map {\alpha_{\tuple{D, F D}}} {\operatorname {id}_{FD}}$ where $\alpha_{\tuple{D, F D}} : \map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C} } {F D, F D} \to \map {\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf D} } {D, GF D}$ is the bijection from the adjunction $\tuple {F, G, \alpha}$ $\operatorname {id}_{F D}$ is the…

label: Definition:Unit of Measurement
snippet: A unit of measurement is a specified magnitude of a given physical quantity, defined by convention. It is used as a standard for measurement of that physical quantity. Any other value of the physical quantity can be expressed as a multiple of that unit of measurement.

label: Definition:Unit of Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$.

label: Definition:Unit of Ring/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$. An element $x \in R$ is a unit of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ $x$ is invertible under $\circ$. That is, a unit of $R$ is an element of $R$ which has an inverse. $\exists y \in R: x \circ y = 1_R = y \circ x$

label: Definition:Unit of Ring/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$. An element $x \in R$ is a unit of $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ $x$ is divisor of $1_R$.

label: Definition:Unital Algebra
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Let $\struct {A, *}$ be an algebra over $R$. Then $\struct {A, *}$ is a unital algebra the algebraic structure $\struct {A, \oplus}$ has an identity element. That is: $\exists 1_A \in A: \forall a \in A: a * 1_A = 1_A * a = a$

label: Definition:Unital Associative Commutative Algebra/Definition 2
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. A unital associative commutative algebra over $R$ is a ring under $A$, that is, an ordered pair $\struct {A, f}$ where: $A$ is a commutative ring with unity $f : R \to A$ is a unital ring homomorphism.

orm {\mathbf 1_A} = 1$

label: Definition:Unital Ring Homomorphism
snippet: Let $R$ and $S$ be rings with unities $1_R$ and $1_S$ respectively. A unital ring homomorphism is a ring homomorphism $f: R \to S$ such that $\map f {1_R} = 1_S$.

label: Definition:Unitary Divisor
snippet: Let $n \in \Z$ be an integer. Let $d \in \Z$ be such that: $d$ is a divisor of $n$ $d$ and $\dfrac n d$ are coprime. Then $d$ is a unitary divisor of $n$.

label: Definition:Unitary Group
snippet: Let $n$ be a positive integer. The unitary group $\operatorname U_n$ is the group of all $n \times n$ unitary matrices under (conventional) matrix multiplication.

label: Definition:Unitary Group/Hilbert Space
snippet: Let $\HH$ be a Hilbert space. The unitary group of $\HH$ is the group consisting of the unitary operators of $\HH$.

label: Definition:Unitary Left Module
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a unitary ring whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. A unitary left module over $R$ is an $R$-algebraic structure $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ with one operation $\ast: R \times G \to G$, which satisfies the unitary left module axioms:

label: Definition:Unitary Matrix
snippet: Let $\mathbf U$ be a nonsingular square matrix over the complex numbers $\C$. Then $\mathbf U$ is a unitary matrix : $\mathbf U^{-1} = \mathbf U^\dagger$ where: $\mathbf U^{-1}$ is the inverse of $\mathbf U$ $\mathbf U^\dagger$ is the Hermitian conjugate of $\mathbf U$.

label: Definition:Unitary Module over Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. A unitary module over $R$ is an $R$-algebraic structure with one operation $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ which is either a unitary left module or a unitary right module, depending upon whether $\ast$ is defined as: $\ast: R \times G \to G$ or: $\ast: G \times R \to G$ respectively. As follows:

label: Definition:Unitary Operator
snippet: A unitary operator is an isomorphism from a Hilbert space $\HH$ to itself.

label: Definition:Unitary Perfect Number
snippet: A unitary perfect number is a positive integer which equals the sum of its positive unitary divisors apart from itself.

label: Definition:Unitary Right Module
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a unitary ring whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. A unitary right module over $R$ is an $R$-algebraic structure $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ with one operation $\ast: G \times R \to G$ which satisfies the unitary right module axioms:

label: Definition:Unitary Transformation
snippet: Let $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ be square matrices over the complex numbers $\C$. An unitary transformation is an operation of changing $\mathbf B$ to $\mathbf A$ by multiplying $\mathbf B$ by an unitary matrix $\mathbf Y$ and its inverse $\mathbf Y^{-1}$ such that: $\mathbf A = \mathbf Y^{-1} \mathbf B \mathbf Y$

label: Definition:Unitization of Algebra over Field
snippet: Let $K$ be a field. Let $A$ be an algebra over $K$. Let $A_+ = A \times K$ be the direct product of $A$ and $K$ as vector spaces over $K$ with vector addition $+_{A \times K}$ and scalar multiplication $\cdot_{A \times K}$. Define multiplication $\circ_{A \times K}$ on $A \times K$ by: $\tuple {a, \lambda} \circ_{A \times K} \tuple {b, \mu} = \tuple {a b + \lambda b + \mu a, \lambda \mu}$ for each $\tuple {a, \lambda}, \tuple {b, \mu} \in A \times K$.

label: Definition:Unity
snippet: Abstract Algebra: The concept of a unity, which is the abstraction of the concept of the number $1$ (one) The unity of a ring The unity of a field Another name (not recommended) for the identity element of a group Arithmetic, Number Theory, and so on: Another word for the number $1$ (one), when it is important to call attention to its numeric properties.

label: Definition:Unity (Abstract Algebra)/Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring. If the semigroup $\struct {R, \circ}$ has an identity, this identity is referred to as the unity of the ring $\struct {R, +, \circ}$. It is (usually) denoted $1_R$, where the subscript denotes the particular ring to which $1_R$ belongs (or often $1$ if there is no danger of ambiguity). The ring $R$ itself is then referred to as a ring with unity.

label: Definition:Univalent Relation
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a relation on a set $S$. Then $\RR$ is univalent : $\RR \circ \RR^{-1} \subseteq \Delta_S$ That is, $\RR$ composed with its inverse $\RR^{-1}$ is a subset of the diagonal relation on $S$.

label: Definition:Universal
snippet: Set Theory and Class Theory: Universal Set Universal Class Category Theory: Universal Object Universal Property Universal Morphism Universal Enveloping Algebra Topology: Universal Cover

label: Definition:Universal Affirmative
snippet: A universal affirmative is a categorical statement of the form: Every $S$ is $P$ where $S$ and $P$ are predicates. In the language of predicate logic, this can be expressed as: $\forall x: \map S x \implies \map P x$ Its meaning can be amplified in natural language as: Every object which has the property of being $S$ also has the property of being $P$.

label: Definition:Universal Affirmative/Set Theory
snippet: The universal affirmative $\forall x: \map S x \implies \map P x$ can be expressed in set language as: $\set {x: \map S x} \subseteq \set {x: \map P x}$ or, more compactly: $S \subseteq P$

label: Definition:Universal Class
snippet: The universal class is the class of which all sets are elements. The universal class is defined most commonly in literature as: $V = \set {x: x = x}$ where $x$ ranges over all sets. It can be briefly defined as the class of all sets.

label: Definition:Universal Class/Zermelo-Fraenkel Theory
snippet: == Universal Class in Zermelo-Fraenkel Set Theory == If the universal class is allowed to be a set in ZFC, then a contradiction can be derived. One equivalent of the states that: $\forall z: \forall A: \paren {A \subseteq z \implies A \in V}$ Since the universal class contains all classes, then if we assume that it is the value of some variable $z$, then all classes become elements of the universe. However, due to Russell's Paradox, this cannot be the case. Therefore, comprehension of the universal set leads to a contradiction and cannot be a value of a variable in ZF set theory.

label: Definition:Universal Cover
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $C = \struct {X, \phi}$ be a covering space for $T$. Then $C$ is a universal cover for $T$ $C$ is simply connected.

label: Definition:Universal Gas Constant
snippet: The universal gas constant is a constant of proportion that relates the average relative thermal energy of a mole of gas with the thermodynamic temperature of the gas. It is defined as Avogadro's number multiplied by Boltzmann's constant: $R = N_{\mathrm A} k$

label: Definition:Universal Graph
snippet: Let $\Bbb G$ be a set of graphs. A universal graph in $\Bbb G$ is a graph $K$ in which every element of $\Bbb G$ can be embedded in $K$. Note that $K$ need not itself be an element of $\Bbb G$.

label: Definition:Universal Gravitational Constant
snippet: == Physical Constant == The universal gravitational constant is the physical constant which is the constant of proportion in Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation. Its value in SI units is referred to as $G$ and is approximately equal to $6.674 \times 10^{-11} \, \mathrm N \, \mathrm m^2 \, \mathrm{kg}^{-2}$.

label: Definition:Universal Mapping Property (Category Theory)
snippet: A universal mapping property (or UMP) in category theory is a property that defines how morphisms from or to objects factor uniquely through a unique morphism and object.

label: Definition:Universal Model
snippet: Let $T$ be an $\LL$-theory. Let $\kappa$ be an infinite cardinal. A model $\MM$ of $T$ is $\kappa$-universal : for every model $\NN$ of $T$ whose universe has cardinality strictly less than $\kappa$, there is an elementary embedding of $\NN$ into $\MM$. That is, $\MM$ is $\kappa$-universal : for all models $\NN \models T$ with cardinality $\card \NN < \kappa$, there is an elementary embedding $j: \NN \to \MM$. We say $\MM$ is universal it is $\kappa^+$-universal where $\kappa$ is the cardinality of the universe of $\MM$ and $\kappa^+$ is the successor cardinal of $\kappa$.

label: Definition:Universal Morphism
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Let $F: \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ be a covariant functor.

label: Definition:Universal Morphism from Functor to Object
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Let $F: \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ be a covariant functor. Let the pair $\tuple{R, v}$ consist of an object $R$ of $\mathbf D$ and a morphism $v: FR \to C$ in $\mathbf C$.

label: Definition:Universal Morphism from Functor to Object/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Let $F: \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ be a covariant functor. Let the pair $\tuple{R, v}$ consist of an object $R$ of $\mathbf D$ and a morphism $v: FR \to C$ in $\mathbf C$. The pair $\tuple{R, v}$ is called a universal morphism from $F$ to $C$ : for every pair $\tuple{D, f}$ consisting of an object $D$ of $\mathbf D$ and a morphism $f: FD \to C$ in $\mathbf C$: there exists a unique morphism $f': D \to R$ with $v \circ Ff' = f$ as in the commutative diagram: $\begin{xy} +{C} = "C", +{F D} = "FD", +{F R} =…

label: Definition:Universal Morphism from Functor to Object/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Let $F: \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ be a covariant functor. Let the pair $\tuple{R, v}$ consist of an object $R$ of $\mathbf D$ and a morphism $v: FR \to C$ in $\mathbf C$. The pair $\tuple{R, v}$ is called a universal morphism from $F$ to $C$ : $\tuple{R, v}$ is a terminal object of the comma category $\paren{F \downarrow C}$ of $F$ over $C$

label: Definition:Universal Morphism from Object to Functor
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Let $F: \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ be a covariant functor. Let the pair $\tuple{R, u}$ consist of an object $R$ of $\mathbf D$ and a morphism $u: C \to FR$ in $\mathbf C$.

label: Definition:Universal Morphism from Object to Functor/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Let $F: \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ be a covariant functor. Let the pair $\tuple{R, u}$ consist of an object $R$ of $\mathbf D$ and a morphism $u: C \to FR$ in $\mathbf C$. The pair $\tuple{R, u}$ is called a universal morphism from $C$ to $F$ : for every pair $\tuple{D, f}$ consisting of an object $D$ of $\mathbf D$ and a morphism $f: C \to FD$ in $\mathbf C$: there exists a unique morphism $f': R \to D$ with $Ff' \circ u = f$ as in the commutative diagram: $\begin{xy} +{C} = "C", +{F R} = "FR", +{F D} =…

label: Definition:Universal Morphism from Object to Functor/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ and $\mathbf D$ be metacategories. Let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. Let $F: \mathbf D \to \mathbf C$ be a covariant functor. Let the pair $\tuple{R, u}$ consist of an object $R$ of $\mathbf D$ and a morphism $u: C \to FR$ in $C$. The pair $\tuple{R, u}$ is called a universal morphism from $C$ to $F$ : $\tuple{R, u}$ is an initial object of the comma category $\paren{C \downarrow F}$ of $F$ under $C$

label: Definition:Universal Negative
snippet: A universal negative is a categorical statement of the form: No $S$ is $P$ where $S$ and $P$ are predicates. In the language of predicate logic, this can be expressed as: $\forall x: \map S x \implies \neg \map P x$ Its meaning can be amplified in natural language as: Every object which has the property of being $S$ does not have the property of being $P$.

label: Definition:Universal Negative/Set Theory
snippet: The universal negative $\forall x: \map S x \implies \neg \map P x$ can be expressed in set language as: $\set {x: \map S x} \implies \set {x: \map P x} = \O$ or, more compactly: $S \subseteq \map \complement P$

label: Definition:Universal Net
snippet: Let $S$ be a non-empty set. Let $H$ be a set directed by $\preceq$. Let $f: H \to S$ be a net in $S$. Then $f$ is a universal net for each subset $A \subseteq S$, $f$ is eventually in $A$ or $f$ is eventually in $S \setminus A$. Category:Definitions/Set Theory Category:Definitions/Topology

label: Definition:Universal Object
snippet: Let $C$ be a category. A universal object of $C$ is an object that is initial or terminal.

label: Definition:Universal Quantifier
snippet: The symbol $\forall$ is called the universal quantifier. It expresses the fact that, in a particular universe of discourse, all objects have a particular property. That is: $\forall x:$ means: For all objects $x$, it is true that ... In the language of set theory, this can be formally defined: $\forall x \in S: \map P x := \set {x \in S: \map P x} = S$ where $S$ is some set and $\map P x$ is a propositional function on $S$.

label: Definition:Universal Set
snippet: Sets are considered to be subsets of some large universal set. Exactly what this universal set is will vary depending on the subject and context. When discussing particular sets, it should be made clear just what that universal set is. However, note that from There Exists No Universal Set, this universal set cannot be everything that there is.

label: Definition:Universal Set/Also known as
snippet: == Universal Set: Also known as == Some sources refer to the universal set as the universe of discourse, which name is also used for a similar concept in the field of logic. Some sources just use universe, but this has several meanings, depending on the contaxt. Some sources (particularly in the context of probability theory) refer to it as the space.

label: Definition:Universally Compatible Relation
snippet: A relation $\RR$ is universally compatible on a set $S$ it is compatible with every closed operation that can be defined on $S$. Category:Definitions/Abstract Algebra

label: Definition:Universally Congruent
snippet: A equivalence $\RR$ is universally congruent on a set $S$ it is a congruence for every closed operation that can be defined on $S$. Category:Definitions/Congruence Relations

label: Definition:Universe
snippet: Predicate Logic: Universe of Discourse Set Theory: Universal Set Grothendieck Universe Class Theory: Universal Class Statistics: Universe: another word for population. Physics, etc.: Physical Universe: the actual place where we live.

label: Definition:Unknown
snippet: An unknown is an indeterminate variable in a system of equations or inequalities whose value the solver is invited to determine.

label: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine
snippet: An unlimited register machine, abbreviated URM, is an abstract machine with the following characteristics:

label: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Unlimited Register Machine == The unlimited register machine is a more versatile and easy to understand alternative to the Turing machine, which has the same capabilities and (to a certain extent) to which it is logically equivalent. It was introduced in a paper by and published in $1963$.

label: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Program/Set
snippet: It is convenient to use $\Bbb U$ to stand for the set of all URM programs.

label: Definition:Unlimited Register Machine/Register
snippet: A URM has a sequence of registers which can store natural numbers: $\set {0, 1, 2, \ldots}$. Any given URM program may make use of only a finite number of these registers. Registers are usually referred to by the subscripted uppercase letters $R_1, R_2, R_3, \ldots$. The number held at any one time by a register is usually referred to by the corresponding lowercase letter $r_1, r_2, r_3, \ldots$.

label: Definition:Unordered Tuple
snippet: An unordered tuple is a small class in Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory that contains a finite number of elements. It is written using roster notation and is denoted: $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n}$ that is: $\set {a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n} = \set {x: x = a_1 \lor x = a_2 \lor \dots \lor x = a_n}$

label: Definition:Untouchable Number
snippet: An untouchable number is a (strictly) positive integer that is not the aliquot sum of any integer.

label: Definition:Untouchable Number/Sequence
snippet: == Sequence of Untouchable Numbers == The sequence of untouchable numbers begins: $2, 5, 52, 88, 96, 120, 124, 146, 162, 188, 206, 210, 216, 238, 246, 248, 262, \ldots$

label: Definition:Up-Complete
snippet: Let $\left({S, \precsim}\right)$ be a preordered set. Then $\left({S, \precsim}\right)$ is up-complete : every directed subset of $S$ admits a supremum in $\left({S, \precsim}\right)$.

label: Definition:Up Run
snippet: An up run is a run such that the sequence is increasing.

label: Definition:Upper Bound of Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping whose codomain is an ordered set $\struct {T, \preceq}$. Let $f$ be bounded above in $T$ by $H \in T$. Then $H$ is an upper bound of $f$.

label: Definition:Upper Bound of Number
snippet: When considering the upper bound of a set of numbers, it is commonplace to ignore the set and instead refer just to the number itself. Thus the construction: The set of numbers which fulfil the propositional function $\map P n$ is bounded above with the upper bound $N$ would be reported as: The number $n$ such that $\map P n$ has the upper bound $N$. This construct obscures the details of what is actually being stated. Its use on is considered an abuse of notation and so discouraged. This also applies in the case where it is the upper bound of a mapping which is under discussion.

label: Definition:Upper Bound of Sequence
snippet: A special case of an upper bound of a mapping is an upper bound of a sequence, where the domain of the mapping is $\N$. Let $\struct {T, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a sequence in $T$. Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be bounded above in $T$ by $H \in T$. Then $H$ is an upper bound of $\sequence {x_n}$.

label: Definition:Upper Bound of Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Let $T$ be a subset of $S$. An upper bound for $T$ (in $S$) is an element $M \in S$ such that: $\forall t \in T: t \preceq M$ That is, $M$ succeeds every element of $T$.

label: Definition:Upper Bound of Set/Real Numbers
snippet: Let $\R$ be the set of real numbers. Let $T$ be a subset of $\R$. An upper bound for $T$ (in $\R$) is an element $M \in \R$ such that: $\forall t \in T: t \le M$ That is, $M$ is greater than or equal to every element of $T$.

label: Definition:Upper Closure/Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preccurlyeq}$ be an ordered set. Let $a \in S$. The upper closure of $a$ (in $S$) is defined as: $a^\succcurlyeq := \set {b \in S: a \preccurlyeq b}$ That is, $a^\succcurlyeq$ is the set of all elements of $S$ that succeed $a$.

label: Definition:Upper Darboux Sum
Definition:Upper Darboux Sum/Rectangle
snippet: Let $R$ be a closed rectangle in $\R^n$. Let $f : R \to \R$ be a bounded real-valued function. Let $P$ be a finite subdivision of $R$. Let $S$ be the set of subrectangles of $P$. For every: $r = \closedint {a_1} {b_1} \times \dotso \times \closedint {a_n} {b_n} \in S$ define: $\ds M_r^{\paren f} = \sup_{x \mathop \in r} \map f x$ $\ds \map v r = \prod_{1 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} \paren {b_i - a_i}$ Then: $\ds \map {U^{\paren f}} P = \sum_{r \mathop \in S} M_r^{\paren f} \map v r$ is called the upper Darboux sum of $f$ on $R$ with respect to $P$.

label: Definition:Upper Limit (Topological Space)
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $f : S \to \overline \R$ be an extended real valued function. Let $x_0 \in X$. Let $\map \mho {x_0}$ be the set of open neighborhoods of $x_0$ in $\struct {S, \tau}$. We define the upper limit of $f$ at $x_0$ by: $\ds \limsup_{x \mathop \to x_0} \map f x = \inf_{V \in \map \mho {x_0} } \paren {\sup_{x \mathop \in V} \map f x}$

label: Definition:Upper Semicontinuous
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $f : S \to \overline \R$ be an extended real valued function. Let $x_0 \in S$. We say that $f$ is upper semicontinuous at $x_0$ : $\ds \limsup_{x \mathop \to x_0} \map f x = \map f {x_0}$ where $\limsup$ denotes the upper limit.

label: Definition:Upper Semicontinuous/Subset
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $f : S \to \overline \R$ be an extended real valued function. Let $A \subseteq S$. We say that $f$ is upper semicontinuous on $A$ it is upper semicontinuous at each $x_0 \in S$.

label: Definition:Upper Wythoff Sequence/Definition 1
snippet: The upper Wythoff sequence is the complementary Beatty sequence on the golden section $\phi$. It starts: $0, 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23, 26, 28, 31, 34, \ldots$

label: Definition:Upper Wythoff Sequence/Definition 2
snippet: The upper Wythoff sequence is the Beatty sequence on the square $\phi^2$ of the golden section $\phi$. It starts: $0, 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 15, 18, 20, 23, 26, 28, 31, 34, \ldots$

label: Definition:Urn
snippet: An urn is a hypothetical container from which one may draw one of a number of objects (usually defined to be balls) of assorted colours. The idea is that one cannot see the ball one is withdrawing until it is out of the urn. Therefore it is not possible to know in advance what colour ball one is taking. The probability that a particular ball being withdrawn has a particular colour depends entirely on the distribution within the urn of the various colours of the balls within. This is used as an abstraction of a randomizing device in probability theory.

label: Definition:Urysohn Function
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $A, B \subseteq S$ such that $A \cap B = \O$. Let $f: S \to \closedint 0 1$ be a continuous mapping where $\closedint 0 1$ is the closed unit interval. Then $f$ is an Urysohn function for $A$ and $B$ : $f {\restriction_A} = 0, f {\restriction_B} = 1$ That is:

label: Definition:Urysohn Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is an Urysohn space : For two arbitrary distinct elements $x, y \in S$ (that is, $x \ne y$), there exists an Urysohn function for $\set x$ and $\set y$.

label: Definition:Usual Ordering
snippet: Let $X$ be one of the sets of numbers: $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$. The usual ordering on $X$ is the conventional counting and measuring order on $X$ that is learned when one is initially introduced to numbers.

label: Definition:Usual Ordering of Ordinals
snippet: Let $\On$ denote the class of all ordinals. The usual ordering $\le$ on $\On$ is the subset relation: $a \le b \iff a \subseteq b$ and its corresponding strict version: $a < b \iff a \subsetneqq b$

label: Definition:Utilities Problem
snippet: The utilities problem is a problem in graph theory as follows: $3$ households are each to be connected to $3$ civic utilities (the archetypes being water, gas and electricity) in such a way that the conduits do not cross. This is equivalent to investigating whether the Thomsen graph (that is, the complete bipartite graph $K_{3, 3}$) is planar.

label: Definition:Utility Function
snippet: Let $G$ be a game. Let $P$ be a player of $G$. Let $C$ be the set $C$ of consequences of the moves available to $P$. A utility function on $C$ is a mapping from $C$ to the real numbers $\R$ so as to define a preference relation on $C$: $U: C \to \R$ by the condition: $\forall x, y \in C: x \succsim y \iff \map U x \ge \map U y$

label: Definition:Utility Theory
snippet: Utility theory is a branch of decision theory in which decisions are based on the concept of utility or benefit.

label: Definition:V Operator on Hilbert Space
snippet: Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\HH \times \HH$ be the Hilbert space direct sum of $\HH$ with itself. Define $V : \HH \times \HH \to \HH \times \HH$ by: $\map V {x, y} = \tuple {-y, x}$ for each $\tuple {x, y} \in \HH \times \HH$. We call $V$ the $V$ operator for $\HH$.

label: Definition:Vacuous
snippet: Logic: A vacuous truth is a statement about a collection of objects none of which exist. By definition, such a statement is understood to be true. A vacuous term is a term of a categorical syllogism $\map F x$ such that nothing in the universe of discourse has the property of the predicate $F$. Set Theory: The vacuous set is the same thing as the empty set, that is, the set with no elements. This Empty Set is Unique. Algebra: A vacuous summation is a summation over an empty set of summands. Such a sum has a value of zero.

label: Definition:Vacuous/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Vacuous == The word vacuous literally means empty. It derives from the Latin word vacuum, meaning empty space. Category:Linguistic Notes

label: Definition:Vacuous Truth
snippet: Let $P \implies Q$ be a conditional statement. Suppose that $P$ is false. Then the statement $P \implies Q$ is a vacuous truth, or is vacuously true. It is frequently encountered in the form: $\forall x: \map P x \implies \map Q x$ when the propositional function $\map P x$ is false for all $x$. Such a statement is also a vacuous truth. For example, the statement: All cats who are expert chess-players are also fluent in ancient Sanskrit is (vacuously) true, because (as far as the author knows) there are no cats who are expert chess-players.

label: Definition:Vacuum/Also known as
snippet: == Vacuum: Also known as == In certain contexts in physics, the term free space is used for a volume of space in which there is a vacuum. Category:Definitions/Vacuum

label: Definition:Vacuum Permeability
snippet: == Physical Constant == The vacuum permeability is the physical constant denoted $\mu_0$ defined as: $\mu_0:= \dfrac {2 \alpha h} {e^2 c}$ where: $e$ is the elementary charge $\alpha$ is the fine-structure constant $h$ is Planck's constant $c$ is the speed of light defined in $\mathrm m \, \mathrm s^{-1}$ Of the above, only the fine-structure constant $\alpha$ is a measured value; the others are defined. It can be defined as the capability of a magnetic field to permeate a vacuum.

label: Definition:Vacuum Permittivity
snippet: == Physical Constant == The vacuum permittivity is the physical constant denoted $\varepsilon_0$ defined as: $\varepsilon_0 := \dfrac {e^2} {2 \alpha h c}$ where: $e$ is the elementary charge $\alpha$ is the fine-structure constant $h$ is Planck's constant $c$ is the speed of light defined in $\mathrm m \, \mathrm s^{-1}$ Of the above, only the fine-structure constant $\alpha$ is a measured value; the others are defined. It can be defined as the capability of an electric field to permeate a vacuum.

label: Definition:Vague Convergence of Borel Measures
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $\sequence {\mu_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of Borel measures on $\struct {X, \tau}$. Let $\mu$ be a Borel measure on $\struct {X, \tau}$. Let $\map {C_c} X$ be the set of continuous functions $f : X \to \C$ such that: the support $\map \supp f$ is compact. We say that $\sequence {\mu_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges vaguely to $\mu$ : $\ds \int f \rd \mu_n \to \int f \rd \mu$ for all $f \in \map {C_c} X$.

label: Definition:Valid
snippet: Logic: Valid Argument Formal Systems: Valid (Formal Systems)

label: Definition:Valid Argument
snippet: A valid argument is a logical argument in which the premises provide conclusive reasons for the conclusion. When an argument is valid, we may say one of the following:

label: Definition:Valuation Ideal Induced by Non-Archimedean Norm
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm{\,\cdot\,} }$ be a non-Archimedean normed division ring with zero $0_R$. The valuation ideal induced by the non-Archimedean norm $
orm{\,\cdot\,}$ is the set: $\PP = \set{x \in R: 
orm x \lt 1}$ That is, the valuation ideal induced by the non-Archimedean norm $
orm{\,\cdot\,}$ is the open ball $B_1 \paren {0_R}$.

label: Definition:Valuation Ring Induced by Non-Archimedean Norm
snippet:
Let $\struct {R, 
orm {\,\cdot\,} }$ be a non-Archimedean normed division ring with zero $0_R$. The valuation ring induced by the non-Archimedean norm $
orm{\,\cdot\,}$ is the set: $\OO = \set {x \in R: 
orm x \le 1}$ That is, the valuation ring induced by the non-Archimedean norm $
orm{\,\cdot\,}$ is the closed ball $\map {B_1^-} {0_R}$.

label: Definition:Value
snippet: Analysis and Number Theory: Value of Variable Absolute Value Value of Continued Fraction Mapping Theory: Value: a synonym for the image of an element in the domain of a mapping Game Theory: Value of Game Value of Matrix Game Physics: Value: the number of units of a particular physical quantity that go to make up a particular physical constant.

label: Definition:Valued Field of P-adic Numbers
snippet: Let $p$ be any prime number. Let $\Q_p$ be the field of $p$-adic numbers. Let $\norm {\,\cdot\,}_p$ be the $p$-adic norm on $\Q_p$. The valued field of p-adic numbers is the valued field $\struct {\Q_p, \norm {\,\cdot\,}_p}$.

label: Definition:Van der Pol's Equation/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on van der Pol's Equation == Van der Pol's equation was introduced and investigated by from $1927$ in his investigations into the behavior of electronic circuits in early radios. However, its scope has shown itself to extend to model a number of other phenomena in physics and biology.

label: Definition:Vanish
snippet: A variable in an equation is said to vanish when (under appropriate conditions) its value becomes zero.

label: Definition:Vanishing Ideal of Set of Prime Ideals
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $V \subseteq \Spec A$ be a set of prime ideals of $A$. Its vanishing ideal is its intersection, the set of elements of $A$ that are in each $\mathfrak p \in V$: $\map I V = \bigcap V$

label: Definition:Vanishing Ideal of Subset of Affine Space
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Let $n \ge 0$ be a natural number. Let $k \sqbrk {X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ be the polynomial ring in $n$ variables over $k$. Let $S \subseteq \mathbb A^n_k$ be a subset of the standard affine space over $k$. Its vanishing ideal is the ideal: $\map I S = \set {f \in k \sqbrk {X_1, \ldots, X_n} : \forall x \in S : \map f x = 0}$

label: Definition:Vanishing Set of Subset of Ring
snippet: Let $A$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $S \subseteq A$ be a subset. The vanishing set of $S$ is the set of prime ideals of $A$ containing $S$: $\map V S = \set {\mathfrak p \in \Spec A: \mathfrak p \supseteq S}$

label: Definition:Variable
snippet: A variable is a label which is used to refer to an unspecified object. A variable can be identified by means of a symbol, for example: $x, y, z, A, B, C, \phi, \psi, \aleph$ It is often convenient to append a subscript letter or number to distinguish between different objects of a similar type: $a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n; S_\phi, S_{\phi_x}, \ldots$ The type of symbol used to define a variable is purely conventional. Particular types of object, as they are introduced, frequently have a particular range of symbols specified to define them, but there are no strict rules on the subject.

label: Definition:Variable/Also known as
snippet: When it occurs in a mathematical equation, a variable is often referred to as an unknown. In the specific context of elementary algebra, the ugly misnomer pronumeral is frequently found in Australia. This was introduced by extension of the concept of a : a symbol that stands in for a numeral, by which the term number is actually meant. Thankfully the term appears not to have caught on in general. Category:Definitions/Variables

label: Definition:Variable/Complex
snippet: A complex variable is a symbol which can stand for any one of a set of complex numbers. The symbols most often used to denote a complex variable are $w$ and $z$.

label: Definition:Variable/Descriptive Statistics/Quantitative Variable
snippet: A quantitative variable is a variable such that: The variable can be described by numbers The performing of arithmetical operations on the data is meaningful.

label: Definition:Variable/Domain
snippet: The collection of all possible objects that a variable may refer to has to be specified. This collection is the domain of the variable.

label: Definition:Variable/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Variable == The term variable, as opposed to a constant, was introduced by . However, the concept had already been established by in his work on logic.

label: Definition:Variable/Predicate Logic
snippet: In the context of predicate logic, a variable is often called an object variable or arbitrary name. As such, it is a symbol which is assigned to an arbitrarily selected object from a given universe of discourse. The understanding is that (during the scope of the argument to which it is relevant) the arbitrary name could apply equally well to any of the objects in that universe.

label: Definition:Variable/Propositional Logic
snippet: A statement variable is a variable which is used to stand for an arbitrary and unspecified statement. For a statement variable, a lowercase letter is usually used, for example: $p, q, r, \ldots{}$, and so on or lowercase Greek letters, for example: $\phi, \psi, \chi$ and so on. The citing of a statement variable can be interpreted as an assertion that the statement represented by that symbol is true. That is: $p$ means $p \text { is true}$

label: Definition:Variable/Real
snippet: A real variable is a symbol which can stand for any one of a set of real numbers. The symbols most often used to denote a real variable are $x$ and $y$.

label: Definition:Variable/Value
snippet: A variable $x$ may be (temporarily, conceptually) identified with a particular object. If so, then that object is called the value of $x$.

label: Definition:Variable Element
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a metacategory, and let $C$ be an object of $\mathbf C$. A variable element of $C$ is a morphism $f: B \to C$ with codomain $C$.

label: Definition:Variance
snippet: Variance is a measure of dispersion of a set of observations. Let $X$ be a random variable. The variance of $X$ is defined as the second central moment of $X$.

label: Definition:Variation/Complex Measure
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a complex measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $\map P A$ be the set of finite partitions of $A$ into $\Sigma$-measurable sets. We define the variation $\cmod \mu : \Sigma \to \R$ of $\mu$ by: $\ds \map {\cmod \mu} A = \sup \set {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \cmod {\map \mu {A_j} } : \set {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n} \in \map P A}$ for each $A \in \Sigma$, where the supremum is taken in the set of extended real numbers $\overline \R$.

label: Definition:Variation/Signed Measure/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \Sigma}$ be a measurable space. Let $\mu$ be a signed measure on $\struct {X, \Sigma}$. Let $\map P A$ be the set of finite partitions of $A$ into $\Sigma$-measurable sets. We define the variation $\cmod \mu : \Sigma \to \overline \R$ of $\mu$ by: $\ds \map {\cmod \mu} A = \sup \set {\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \cmod {\map \mu {A_j} } : \set {A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n} \in \map P A}$ for each $A \in \Sigma$, where the supremum is taken in the set of extended real numbers $\overline \R$. Category:Definitions/Variation of Signed Measure

label: Definition:Variation Field of Family of Curves
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $\gamma$ be an admissible curve on $M$. Let $I = \closedint a b$ is a closed real interval. Let $J$ is an open real interval. Let $\Gamma : J \times I \to M$ be the variation of $\gamma$, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product and: $\ds \forall s \in J : \forall t \in I : \tuple {s, t} \stackrel \Gamma \mapsto \map \Gamma {s, t}$ Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p \in M$.

label: Definition:Variation in Sign of Polynomial
snippet: Let $\map P x$ be a polynomial equation over the real numbers: $\pm a_n x^n \mathop \pm a_{n - 1} x^{n - 1} \mathop \pm \cdots \mathop \pm a_1 x \mathop \pm a_0 = 0$ where: the independent variable $x \in \R$ is real the coefficients $a_j \in \R_{\ge 0}$ are all non-negative constants each of the $\pm$ signs can be either positive or negative. A variation in sign of the coefficients of $\map P x$ is an instance of $j \in \set {0, 1, \ldots, n}$ in which a $\pm$ sign changes from positive to negative, or , as $j$ goes from $n$ to $0$, ignoring zero coefficients.

label: Definition:Variational Equation of Differential Equation
snippet: For $n, i \in \N$, let: $\map F {x, \sequence {\map {y^{\paren i} } x}_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n} } = 0$ where $\sequence {\map {y^{\paren i} } x}_{0 \mathop \le i \mathop \le n}$ is a sequence of derivatives of a function $y$, be a differential equation. Let $\map y x, \map g x$ be real functions which solve the given differential equation, such that $\map g x = \map y x + \map h x$ Then, neglecting $\map \OO {h^2}$, the differential equation satisfied by $h$ is called the variational equation of the differential equation $F = 0$.

label: Definition:Vector-Valued Function
snippet: Let $f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_n$ be real functions of $t$. Let $\mathbb T \subseteq \R, \mathbb Y \subseteq \R^n$ (where usually $n \ge 2$). Let $\mathbf r$ be a mapping from $\mathbb T \to \mathbb Y$ that maps each $t \in \mathbb T$ to a vector $\tuple {\map {f_1} t, \map {f_2} t, \ldots, \map {f_n} t} \in \mathbb Y$. Then $\mathbf r$ is said to be a vector-valued function (of the parameter $t$). If $\mathbb T$ is not explicitly defined, it is taken to be the intersection of all the domains of $f_1 ,f_2, \cdots, f_n$.

label: Definition:Vector/Linear Algebra
snippet: Let $V = \struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a vector space over $K$, where: $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ is the scalar ring of $V$. The elements of the abelian group $\struct {G, +_G}$ are called vectors.

label: Definition:Vector/Module
snippet: Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ be a module, where: $\struct {G, +_G}$ is an abelian group $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ is the scalar ring of $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$. The elements of the abelian group $\struct {G, +_G}$ are called vectors.

label: Definition:Vector/Real Euclidean Space
snippet: A vector is defined as an element of a vector space. We have that $\R^n$, with the operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication, forms a real Euclidean space. Hence a vector in $\R^n$ is defined as an element of the real Euclidean space $\R^n$.

label: Definition:Vector/Real Euclidean Space/Plane Vector
snippet: Consider the real Euclidean space $\R^2$. A vector in $\R^2$ can be referred to as a plane vector.

label: Definition:Vector (Vector Space)/Also defined as
snippet: == Vector: Also defined as == Some sources, in their definition of a vector space, restrict the scalar division ring to a field. That is, they insist that the scalar division ring is a commutative. This may need to be borne in mind.

label: Definition:Vector Addition/Module
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $M := \struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be the corresponding module over $R$ (either a left module or a right module). The group operation $+_G$ on $M$ is known as vector addition on $M$. Category:Definitions/Module Theory Category:Definitions/Vector Addition

label: Definition:Vector Addition/Vector Space
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$ be a field. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $V := \struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be the corresponding vector space over $F$. The group operation $+_G$ on $V$ is known as vector addition on $V$.

label: Definition:Vector Algebra
snippet: Vector Algebra is the branch of mathematics which studies the algebra of vector spaces.

label: Definition:Vector Analysis
snippet: Vector analysis is the branch of linear algebra concerned with differentiation and integration of vector spaces, primarily in Euclidean space of $3$-dimensional space.

label: Definition:Vector Analysis/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Vector Analysis == One of the earliest attempts to develop a calculus for working directly on vectors was made by in $1679$, but this was unsuccessful. 's demonstration in $1806$ of a geometrical representation of the complex plane gave the misleading impression that vectors in the Cartesian plane required them to be represented as complex numbers, which held development back for some time. published his in $1827$, which was the forerunner of the more general analysis of geometric forms developed by .

label: Definition:Vector Area
snippet: Let $S$ be a plane surface embedded in Cartesian $3$-space. The vector area of $S$ is a technique of representing $S$ using a vector quantity $\mathbf S$. 380px The magnitude of the vector is determined by the area of $S$, while its direction is defined as the unit normal $\mathbf {\hat n}$ to the plane of $S$. The sign of $\mathbf S = S \, \mathbf {\hat n}$ is determined by the right-hand rule according to the direction of rotation around $S$ when describing it. The shape of $S$ is arbitrary.

label: Definition:Vector Bundle
snippet: Let $B = \struct {E, M, \pi, F}$ be a fiber bundle. Then $B$ is a vector bundle over $M$ the model fiber $F$ is a topological vector space.

label: Definition:Vector Calculus
snippet: Vector calculus is the branch of linear algebra concerned with the application of the techniques of calculus to vector spaces.

label: Definition:Vector Cross Product
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $3$ dimensions: where $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$.

label: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Complex
snippet: Let $z_1 := x_1 + i y_1$ and $z_2 := x_2 + i y_2$ be complex numbers.

label: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Complex/Definition 1
snippet: Let $z_1 := x_1 + i y_1$ and $z_2 := x_2 + i y_2$ be complex numbers. The cross product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \times z_2 = x_1 y_2 - y_1 x_2$

label: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Complex/Definition 3
snippet: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be complex numbers. The cross product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \times z_2 := \map \Im {\overline {z_1} z_2}$ where: $\map \Im z$ denotes the imaginary part of a complex number $z$ $\overline {z_1}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z_1$ $\overline {z_1} z_2$ denotes complex multiplication.

label: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Complex/Definition 4
snippet: Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be complex numbers. The cross product of $z_1$ and $z_2$ is defined as: $z_1 \times z_2 := \dfrac {\overline {z_1} z_2 - z_1 \overline {z_2}} {2 i}$ where: $\overline {z_1}$ denotes the complex conjugate of $z_1$ $\overline {z_1} z_2$ denotes complex multiplication.

label: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $3$ dimensions: where $\tuple {\mathbf i, \mathbf j, \mathbf k}$ is the standard ordered basis of $\mathbf V$. The vector cross product, denoted $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b$, is defined as: $\mathbf a \times \mathbf b = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf i & \mathbf j & \mathbf k \\ a_i & a_j & a_k \\ b_i & b_j & b_k \\ \end{vmatrix}$ where $\begin {vmatrix} \ldots \end {vmatrix}$ is interpreted as a determinant.

label: Definition:Vector Cross Product/Definition 2
snippet:
Let $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ be vectors in a vector space $\mathbf V$ of $3$ dimensions. The vector cross product, denoted $\mathbf a 	imes \mathbf b$, is defined as: $\mathbf a 	imes \mathbf b = 
orm {\mathbf a} 
orm {\mathbf b} \sin 	heta \, \mathbf {\hat n}$ where: $
orm {\mathbf a}$ denotes the length of $\mathbf a$ $	heta$ denotes the angle from $\mathbf a$ to $\mathbf b$, measured in the positive direction $\hat {\mathbf n}$ is the unit vector perpendicular to both $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ in the direction according to the right-hand rule.

label: Definition:Vector Field
snippet: Let $F$ be a field which acts on a region of space $S$. Let the point-function giving rise to $F$ be a vector quantity. Then $F$ is a vector field.

label: Definition:Vector Field/Classification
snippet: == Classification of Vector Fields == Let $R$ be a region of space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field acting over $R$.

label: Definition:Vector Field/Classification/Illustration
snippet: == Illustration of Classification of Vector Fields == Let $R$ be a region of space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field acting over $R$. The following diagram gives a visual impression of the properties of vector fields with various combinations of properties relating to divergence and curl: 800px

label: Definition:Vector Field/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Vector Fields ==

label: Definition:Vector Field/Examples/Electric Field Strength
snippet: == Example of Vector Field == Let $R$ be a region of space in which there exists an electric field. The electric field strength in $R$ gives rise to a vector field over $R$.

label: Definition:Vector Field/Examples/Magnetic Field Strength
snippet: == Example of Vector Field == Let $R$ be a region of space in which there exists an magnetic field. The magnetic field strength in $R$ gives rise to a vector field over $R$.

label: Definition:Vector Field/Examples/Velocity of Fluid
snippet: == Example of Vector Field == In a moving fluid, the velocity $\mathbf v$ of the fluid is an example of a vector field. That is, the velocity $\mathbf v$ at a point $P$ in the fluid is the velocity of the particle which is situated at $P$ at a given instant.

label: Definition:Vector Field along Smooth Curve
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with or without boundary. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $I \subseteq \R$ be a real inverval. Let $\gamma : I \to M$ be a smooth curve. Let $V : I \to TM$ be a continuous map such that: $\forall t \in I : \map V t \in T_{\map \gamma t} M$ Then $V$ is called the vector field along (smooth) curve $\gamma$.

label: Definition:Vector Field on Smooth Manifold
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $TM$ be the tangent bundle of $M$. Let $T_p M$ be the tangent space at $p \in M$. Then by a vector field on $M$ we mean a continuous mapping $X : M \to TM$ such that: $\forall p \in M : X_p \in T_p M$ where $X_p$ denotes the value of $X$ at $p$.

label: Definition:Vector Length
snippet: The length of a vector $\mathbf v$ in a normed vector space $\struct {V, \norm {\, \cdot \,} }$ is defined as $\norm {\mathbf v}$, the norm of $\mathbf v$.

label: Definition:Vector Length/Complex Plane
snippet: == Example of Vector Length == Let $\mathbf v$ be a vector represented in the complex plane $\C$ by the complex number $z = a + b i$. The length of $\mathbf v$ is defined as: $\norm {\mathbf v} = \cmod z$ where $\cmod z = \sqrt {a^2 + b^2}$ is the modulus of $z$. Category:Definitions/Vector Length Category:Definitions/Complex Analysis

label: Definition:Vector Length/Real Number Line
snippet: == Example of Vector Length == Let $\mathbf v$ be a vector represented by an arrow on the real number line. Let: the initial point of $\mathbf v$ be $a \in \R$ the terminal point of $\mathbf v$ be $b \in \R$ The length of $\mathbf v$ is defined as: $\norm {\mathbf v} = \size {b - a}$ the absolute value of $b - a$. Category:Definitions/Vector Length

label: Definition:Vector Line
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of space in which there exists a vector field $V$ given rise to by a vector quantity $F$. Let $P$ be an arbitrary point in $V$. Let the following procedure be established: Proceed an infinitesimal distance from $P_0$ to $P_1$ in the direction of $\map F {P_0}$. Proceed an infinitesimal distance from $P_1$ to $P_2$ in the direction of $\map F {P_1}$. Continue in this manner to trace out a curve in space whose tangent at any point $Q$ gives the direction of the vector quantity $\map F Q$ at $Q$. This curve is referred to as a vector line.

label: Definition:Vector Line/Also known as
snippet: == Vector Line: Also known as == A vector line is also known as: a line of flow a flux line a field line. In contexts where the vector field in question is (or gives rise to) a force, then the term line of force can be seen.

label: Definition:Vector Normal to Pseudo-Riemannian Submanifold
snippet: Let $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be a pseudo-Riemannian manifold. Let $M \subseteq \tilde M$ be a smooth submanifold with or without boundary in $M$. Let $p \in M$ be a point. Let $T_p \tilde M$ and $T_p M$ be the tangent spaces of $\tilde M$ and $M$ at $p$ respectively. Let $v \in T_p \tilde M$ and $w \in T_p M$ be vectors. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$ be the scalar product induced by the pseudo-Riemannian metric $\tilde g$. Suppose: $\forall w \in T_p M : \innerprod v w = 0$ Then $v$ is said to be normal to $M$ (at $p$).

label: Definition:Vector Normal to Smooth Submanifold
snippet: Let $\struct {\tilde M, \tilde g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $M \subseteq \tilde M$ be a smooth submanifold with or without boundary in $M$. Let $p \in M$ be a point. Let $T_p \tilde M$ and $T_p M$ be the tangent spaces of $\tilde M$ and $M$ at $p$ respectively. Let $v \in T_p \tilde M$ and $w \in T_p M$ be vectors. Let $\innerprod \cdot \cdot$ be the inner product induced by the Riemannian metric $\tilde g$. Suppose: $\forall w \in T_p M : \innerprod v w = 0$ Then $v$ is said to be normal to $M$ (at $p$).

label: Definition:Vector Potential
snippet: Let $R$ be a region of ordinary space. Let $\mathbf V$ be a vector field over $R$. Let $\mathbf V$ be both rotational and solenoidal. Let $\mathbf A$ be a vector field such that $\mathbf V = \curl \mathbf A$. Then $\mathbf A$ is known as the vector potential of $\mathbf V$.

label: Definition:Vector Quantity
snippet: A vector quantity is a real-world concept that needs for its model a mathematical object with more than one component to specify it. Formally, a vector quantity is an element of a normed vector space, often the real vector space $\R^3$. The usual intellectual frame of reference is to interpret a vector quantity as having: A magnitude A direction.

label: Definition:Vector Quantity/Arrow Representation
snippet: A vector quantity $\mathbf v$ is often represented diagramatically in the form of an arrow such that: its length is proportional to the magnitude of $\mathbf v$ its direction corresponds to the direction of $\mathbf v$. The head of the arrow then indicates the positive sense of the direction of $\mathbf v$. It can be rendered on the page like so: 300px It is important to note that a vector quantity, when represented in this form, is not in general fixed in space. All that is being indicated using such a notation is its magnitude and direction, and not, in general, a point at which it acts.

label: Definition:Vector Space/Also known as
snippet: == Vector Space: Also known as == A vector space is also sometimes called a linear space, especially when discussing the real vector space $\R^n$. Some go further and refer to a linear vector space The notation $\struct {G, +_G, \circ, K}$ can also be seen for this concept.

label: Definition:Vector Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ be a field. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a unitary $K$-module. Then $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ is a vector space over $K$ or a $K$-vector space. That is, a vector space is a unitary module whose scalar ring is a field.

label: Definition:Vector Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ be a field whose unity is $1_K$. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct {\map {\mathrm {End} } G, +, \circ}$ be the endomorphism ring of $\struct {G, +_G}$ such that $I_G$ is the identity mapping. Let $\ast: \struct {K, +_K, \times_K} \to \struct {\map {\mathrm {End} } G, +, \circ}$ be a ring homomorphism from $K$ to $\map {\mathrm {End} } G$ which maps $1_K$ to $I_G$. Then $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ is a vector space over $K$ or a $K$-vector space.

label: Definition:Vector Space/Division Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +_K, \times_K}$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ be a unitary $K$-module. Then $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_K$ is a vector space over $K$ or a $K$-vector space. That is, a vector space is a unitary module whose scalar ring is a division ring.

label: Definition:Vector Space/Left and Right Vector Space
snippet: == Left Vector Spaces and Right Vector Spaces == In the case where the scalar division ring is a field, the difference between a left vector space and a right vector space is little more than a notational difference. This is demonstrated in: Left Module over Commutative Ring induces Right Module Right Module over Commutative Ring induces Left Module where the commutative ring in question is the scalar field of the vector space, which is of course a type of module, under discussion. But this is not the case for a scalar division ring that is not commutative.

label: Definition:Vector Space Automorphism
snippet: Let $V$ be a $K$-vector space. Let $\phi: V \to V$ be a vector space isomorphism to itself. Then $\phi$ is a vector space automorphism.

label: Definition:Vector Space Decomposition
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. A (vector space) decomposition of $V$ is a direct sum of eigenspaces that forms $V$.

label: Definition:Vector Space Monomorphism
snippet: Let $V$ and $W$ be $K$-vector spaces. Then $\phi: V \to W$ is a vector space monomorphism : $(1): \quad \phi$ is an injection $(2): \quad \forall \mathbf x, \mathbf y \in V: \map \phi {\mathbf x + \mathbf y} = \map \phi {\mathbf x} + \map \phi {\mathbf y}$ $(3): \quad \forall \mathbf x \in V: \forall \lambda \in K: \map \phi {\lambda \mathbf x} = \lambda \map \phi {\mathbf x}$

label: Definition:Vector Space of All Mappings
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +, \circ}$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_K$ be a $K$-vector space. Let $S$ be a set. Let $G^S$ be the set of all mappings from $S$ to $G$. Then $\struct {G^S, +_G', \circ}_K$ is a $K$-vector space, where: $+_G'$ is the (pointwise) addition induced on $G^S$ by $+_G$ $\forall \lambda \in K: \forall f \in G^S: \forall x \in S: \map {\paren {\lambda \circ f} } x = \lambda \circ \paren {\map f x}$ This is the $K$-vector space $G^S$ of all mappings from $S$ to $G$.

label: Definition:Vector Space of Germs of Smooth Functions
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold with or without boundary. Let $p \in M$. Let $\GG_p$ denote the set $\map {C_p^\infty} M$ of all germs of smooth functions at $p$. Let $\sqbrk f_p \in \GG_p$ denote the germ of $f$ at $p$ where $f$ is a smooth function. Then $\struct {\GG_p, +_p, \cdot_p}_\R$ is a vector space over $\R$, in which the operations: $+_p: \GG_p \times \GG_p \to \GG_p$ $\cdot_p: \R \times \GG_p \to \GG_p$ are defined as: {{axiom | lc = vector addition: | q = \forall \sqbrk f_p, \forall \sqbrk g_p \in \GG_p | ml = \sqbrk f_p +_p \sqbrk g_p | mo = := | mr = \sqbrk {f + g}_p }} {{axiom |…

label: Definition:Vector Space of Matrices
snippet: Let $m, n \in \Z_{>0}$ be (strictly) positive integers. Let $\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}$ be the $m \times n$ matrix space over a field $\GF$. Let $\struct {\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}, +}$ denote the abelian group formed from $\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}$ under matrix entrywise addition. Let $\struct {\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}, +, \times}_\GF$ denote the vector space over $\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}$ where $\times$ denotes the matrix scalar product. Then $\struct {\map {\MM_\GF} {m, n}, +, \times}_\GF$ can be referred to as the vector space of $m \times n$ matrices.

label: Definition:Vector Space of Sequences with Finite Support
snippet: Let $\struct {K, +, \circ}$ be a division ring. Let $K^\N$ be the set of sequences $\sequence{ a_n }_{n \in \N}$ in $K$. Regard $K^\N$ as a vector space of all mappings from $\N$ to $K$. The vector space of sequences with finite support is the vector subspace of $K^\N$ of sequences with finite support: $\ds \set{ f \in K^\N: \text{$f$ has finite support} }$ There is no standard symbol for the vector space of sequences with finite support.

label: Definition:Vector Space over Division Ring/Left Vector Space
Definition:Vector Space over Division Ring/Right Vector Space
Definition:Vector Space over Division Subring/Special Case
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose unity is $1_R$. Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}_R$ be the $R$-vector space. Let $S$ be a division subring of $R$, such that $1_R \in S$. Let $\circ_S$ denote the restriction of $\circ$ to $S \times R$. Then $\struct {R, +, \circ_S}_S$ is the vector space on $R$ over the division subring $S$.

label: Definition:Vector Space over Subring
snippet: Let $K$ be a division subring of the division ring $\struct {L, +_L, \times_L}$. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \circ}_L$ be a $L$-vector space. Then $\struct {G, +_G, \circ_K}_K$ is a $K$-vector space, where $\circ_K$ is the restriction of $\circ$ to $K \times G$. The $K$-vector space $\struct {G, +_G, \circ_K}_K$ is called the $K$-vector space obtained from $\struct {L, +_L, \times_L}$ by restricting scalar multiplication.

label: Definition:Vector Subspace
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $\struct {S, +, \circ}_K$ be a $K$-algebraic structure with one operation. Let $T$ be a closed subset of $S$. Let $\struct {T, +_T, \circ_T}_K$ be a $K$-vector space where: $+_T$ is the restriction of $+$ to $T \times T$ and $\circ_T$ is the restriction of $\circ$ to $K \times T$. Then $\struct {T, +_T, \circ_T}_K$ is a (vector) subspace of $\struct {S, +, \circ}_K$.

label: Definition:Vector Subspace/Hilbert Spaces
snippet: Let $K$ be a division ring. Let $\left({S, +, \circ}\right)_K$ be a $K$-algebraic structure with one operation. Let $T$ be a closed subset of $S$. Let $\left({T, +_T, \circ_T}\right)_K$ be a $K$-vector space where: $+_T$ is the restriction of $+$ to $T \times T$ and $\circ_T$ is the restriction of $\circ$ to $K \times T$. Then $\left({T, +_T, \circ_T}\right)_K$ is a (vector) subspace of $\left({S, +, \circ}\right)_K$. When considering Hilbert spaces, one wants to deal with projections onto subspaces.

label: Definition:Vector Subtraction
snippet: Let $\struct {F, +_F, \times_F}$ be a field. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $V := \struct {G, +_G, \circ}_R$ be the corresponding vector space over $F$. Let $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$ be vectors of $V$. Then the operation of (vector) subtraction on $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$ is defined as: $\mathbf x - \mathbf y := \mathbf x + \paren {-\mathbf y}$ where $-\mathbf y$ is the negative of $\mathbf y$. The $+$ on the is vector addition.

label: Definition:Vector Sum
snippet: Let $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ be vector quantities of the same physical property.

label: Definition:Vectorial Matroid
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. Let $S$ be a finite subset of $V$. Let $\struct {S, \mathscr I}$ be the matroid induced by linear independence in $V$ on $S$. Then any matroid isomorphic to $\struct {S, \mathscr I}$ is called a vectorial matroid.

label: Definition:Vectorization of Matrix
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $m, n \ge 1$ be natural numbers. Let $A = \sqbrk {a_{i j} }$ be a $m \times n$ matrix over $S$.

label: Definition:Vectorization of Matrix/Definition 1
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $m, n \ge 1$ be natural numbers. Let $A = \sqbrk {a_{i j} }$ be a $m \times n$ matrix over $S$. The vectorization of $A$ is the $m n \times 1$ column matrix: $\map {\operatorname {vec} } A = \sqbrk {a_{1 1}, \ldots, a_{m 1}, a_{1 2}, \ldots, a_{m 2}, \ldots, a_{1 n}, \ldots, a_{m n} }^\intercal$ informally obtained by stacking the columns of $A$. That is: $\map {\operatorname {vec} } A_k = a_{\floor {k / m}, k \bmod m}$ where: $\floor {\, \cdot \,}$ is the floor function $\bmod$ is the modulo operation.

label: Definition:Vectorization of Matrix/Definition 2
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. Let $m, n \ge 1$ be natural numbers. Let $A = \sqbrk {a_{i j} }$ be a $m \times n$ matrix over $S$. Let $R$ be a ring with unity. Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix over $R$. The vectorization of $A$ is its coordinate vector with respect to the standard matrix basis.

label: Definition:Velocity
snippet: The velocity $\mathbf v$ of a body $M$ is defined as the first derivative of the displacement $\mathbf s$ of $M$ from a given point of reference time $t$: $\mathbf v = \dfrac {\d \mathbf s} {\d t}$ Informally, it is described as the rate of change of position. It is important to note that as displacement is a vector quantity, then it follows by definition of derivative of a vector that so is velocity.

label: Definition:Velocity/Dimension
snippet: The dimension of measurement of velocity is $\mathsf {L T^{-1} }$.
