label: Definition:Velocity/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Velocity == The first person to treat the velocity as a vector was .

label: Definition:Velocity/Straight Line
snippet: Let $P$ be a particle in motion along a straight line $\LL$ with velocity $\map {\mathbf v} t$ as a function of time $t$. It is conventional to align $\LL$ along the $x$-axis of a Cartesian coordinate system such that the $\mathbf v$ can be expressed as $v \mathbf i$. Then the unit vector $\mathbf i$ of the component vector $v \mathbf i$ is suppressed, and $\map {\mathbf v} t$ is treated as a scalar quantity $\map v t$.

label: Definition:Velocity/Symbol
snippet: == Velocity: Symbol == The usual symbol used to denote the velocity of a body is $\mathbf v$.

label: Definition:Velocity/Unit
snippet: The SI unit of velocity is the the metre per second: $\mathrm {m \, s^{-1} }$. The CGS unit of velocity is the centimetre per second: $\mathrm {cm \, s^{-1} }$. The FPS unit of velocity is the foot per second $\mathrm {ft \, s^{-1} }$.

label: Definition:Velocity/Unit/Centimetre per Second
snippet: == CGS unit of Velocity == The CGS unit of velocity is the centimetre per second.

label: Definition:Velocity/Unit/Foot per Second
snippet: == FPS unit of velocity == The FPS unit of velocity is the foot per second.

label: Definition:Velocity/Unit/Metre per Second
snippet: == SI unit of Velocity == The SI unit of velocity is the metre per second.

label: Definition:Velocity of Main Curve
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I, J \subseteq \R$ be real intervals. Let $\map {\Gamma_s} t : J \times I \to M$ be the main curve, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product. Let $\map {\Gamma_s} t$ be differentiable on $I$. Then the velocity of the main curve is denoted by: $\partial_t \map {\Gamma} {s, t} = \map {\paren {\Gamma_s}'} t$ where: $\partial_t \map {\Gamma} {s, t} \in T_{\map \Gamma {s, t} } M$ $T_p M$ is the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$ $\map \Gamma {s, t}$ is the one-parameter family of curves on $M$.

label: Definition:Velocity of Transverse Curve
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $I, J \subseteq \R$ be real intervals. Let $\map {\Gamma^{\paren t} } s : J \times I \to M$ be the transverse curve, where $\times$ denotes the cartesian product. Let $\map {\Gamma^{\paren t} } s$ be differentiable on $J$. Then the velocity of the transverse curve is denoted by: $\partial_s \map {\Gamma} {s, t} = \map {\paren {\Gamma^{\paren t}}'} s$ where: $\partial_s \map {\Gamma} {s, t} \in T_{\map \Gamma {s, t} } M$ $T_p M$ is the tangent space of $M$ at $p \in M$ $\map \Gamma {s, t}$ is the one-parameter family of curves on $M$.

label: Definition:Venn Diagram
snippet: A Venn diagram is a technique for the graphic depiction of the interrelationship between a small number (usually $3$ or fewer) of sets. The following diagram illustrates the various operations between three sets. 500px The circles represent the sets $S_1$, $S_2$ and $S_3$. The white surrounding box represents the universal set $\mathbb U$. Each of the areas inside the various circle represents an intersection between the various sets and their complements, as follows: The gray area represents $S_1 \cap S_2 \cap S_3$. The purple area represents $S_1 \cap S_2 \cap \overline {S_3}$.

label: Definition:Veridical Paradox
snippet: A veridical paradox is a counter-intuitive result which can be demonstrated to be true.

label: Definition:Vertex
snippet: Graph Theory: Vertex of Graph: The vertices of a graph are the points, which may or may not be joined by edges. Geometry and Solid Geometry: Vertex: A point at which $2$ or more line segments meet on the boundary of a geometric figure: Vertex of Polygon: The corners of a polygon are known as its vertices. Vertex of Polyhedron: The corners of a polyhedron are known as its vertices. Vertex of Angle: The point at which the lines containing an angle meet is known as its vertex.

label: Definition:Vertex (Geometry)
snippet: A vertex is a point on the boundary of a geometric figure at which $2$ or more line segments meet.

label: Definition:Vertex Cut
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. A vertex cut of $G$ is a set of vertices $W \subseteq \map V G$ such that the vertex deletion $G \setminus W$ is disconnected.

label: Definition:Vertex Deletion
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be an (undirected) graph. Let $W \subseteq V$ be a set of vertices of $G$. Then the graph obtained by deleting $W$ from $G$, denoted by $G - W$, is the subgraph induced by $V \setminus W$. Alternatively: $G - W = \struct {V \setminus W, \set {e \in E : e \cap W = \O} }$ Informally, $G - W$ is the graph obtained from $G$ by removing all vertices in $W$ and all edges incident to those vertices. If $W$ is a singleton such that $W = \set v$, then $G - W$ may be expressed $G - v$.

label: Definition:Vertex Set
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. The set $V$ of vertices in $G$ is called the vertex set. It is often convenient to refer to the vertex set for a given graph $G$ as $\map V G$, especially if there is at any one time more than one graph under consideration.

label: Definition:Vertex Set/Also defined as
snippet: == Vertex Set: Also known as == Some sources further specify that the vertex set cannot be empty. That is, that a graph must have at least one vertex. Hence such sources do not raise the concept of a null graph.

label: Definition:Vertex of Graph/Also known as
snippet: == Vertex of Graph: Also known as == A vertex of a graph $G$, particularly when $G$ is a tree, is also known as a node.

label: Definition:Vertex of Polytope
snippet: Let $P$ be a polytope. A vertex of $P$ is one of the points at which two or more line segments meet on the boundary of $P$.

label: Definition:Vertex of Simplex
snippet: Let $S$ be a $k$-simplex for some $k \in \Z_{>0}$: $S = \set {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 0}^k \theta_i \alpha_i}$ A vertex of $S$ is one of the $k + 1$ points $\alpha_0, \alpha_1 \ldots, \alpha_k$.

label: Definition:Vertical Composition of Natural Transformations
snippet: Let $C$ and $D$ be categories. Let $F, G, H: C \to D$ be covariant functors. Let $\eta: F \to G$ and $\xi: G \to H$ be natural transformations. The vertical composition of $\eta$ and $\xi$ is the natural transformation $\xi \circ \eta : F \Rightarrow H$ with $\paren {\xi \circ \eta}_A = \xi_A \circ \eta_A$ for $A \in C$.

label: Definition:Vertical Group Action
snippet: Let $\tilde M$, $M$ be smooth manifolds. Let $\pi : \tilde M \to M$ be a surjective smooth submersion. Let $G$ be a group acting on $\tilde M$. Suppose each element of $G$ takes each fiber to itself: $\forall \phi \in G : \forall p \in \tilde M : \map \pi {\phi \cdot p} = \map \pi p$ Then the action is called to be vertical.

label: Definition:Vertical Line/Definition 1
snippet: A line is vertical it is aligned perpendicular to the horizon. File:Vertical.png

label: Definition:Vertical Line/Definition 2
snippet: A line is vertical it is parallel to the path taken by a body released from rest in a constant gravitational field. File:Vertical.png

label: Definition:Vertical Plane
snippet: A plane is vertical it contains a vertical line.

label: Definition:Vertical Section of Function
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets. Let $f : X \times Y \to \overline \R$ be an extended real-valued function. Let $x \in X$. We define the vertical section $f_x$ of $f$ by: $\map {f_x} y = \map f {x, y}$ for each $y \in Y$.

label: Definition:Vertical Section of Set
snippet: Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets. Let $E \subseteq X \times Y$. Let $x \in X$. We define the $x$-vertical section $E_x$ of $E$ by: $E_x = \set {y \in Y : \tuple {x, y} \in E}$

label: Definition:Vertical Tangent Space
snippet: Let $M, \tilde M$ be smooth manifolds. Let $\tilde g$ be a Riemannian metric on $\tilde M$. Let $\pi : \tilde M \to M$ be a smooth submersion. Let $x \in \tilde M$ be a point. The vertical tangent space at $x$, denoted by $V_x$, is defined as the tangent space to the fiber containing $x$: $V_x := \ker d \pi_x = \map {T_x} {\tilde M_{\map \pi x}}$

label: Definition:Vertical Vector Field
snippet: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. Let $x \in M$ be a base point. Let $V_x$ be the vertical tangent space. Let $Y$ be a vector field on $M$. Suppose for each $x \in M$ the value of $Y$ lies in the vertical space of $x$: $\forall x \in M : \valueat Y x \in V_x$ Then $X$ is called a vertical vector field.

label: Definition:Virtual Circle
snippet: A virtual circle is the locus in the Cartesian plane of an equation of the form: $(1): \quad \paren {x - a}^2 + \paren {y - b}^2 + r^2 = 0$ where $a$, $b$ and $r$ are real constants. There are no solutions to $(1)$ in real numbers, and so the locus of $(1)$ consists entirely of imaginary points.

label: Definition:Vitali Set
snippet: A Vitali set is a subset of the real numbers which has no Lebesgue measure.

label: Definition:Volt
snippet: The volt is the SI unit of electromotive force and electric potential. It is defined as being the difference in electric potential between two points of an electrical conductor: when an electric current of $1$ ampere dissipates $1$ watt of power between those points that will impart $1$ joule of energy per coulomb of electric charge that passes through it.

label: Definition:Volume
snippet: Volume is the measure of the extent of a body. It has three dimensions and is specified in units of length cubed. Hence the term cube as a general vague term for a quantity in three dimensions. It is a scalar quantity.

label: Definition:Volume/Also known as
snippet: == Volume: Also known as == The term capacity can sometimes be seen in texts whose emphasis is on physics and applied mathematics. In non-mathematical literature and popular puzzle pages, less precise terms can be seen, for example cubical contents.

label: Definition:Volume/Dimension
snippet: Volume is a dimension of measurement of physics. The dimension of measurement of volume is: $L^3$ length cubed. Category:Definitions/Dimensions of Measurement Category:Definitions/Volume

label: Definition:Volume Element
snippet: A volume element $\delta V$ is a (usually) infinitesimal volume of space (usually) containing a particular point $P$. In the cartesian $3$-space such a volume element is modelled as a cuboid whose edges are parallel to the coordinate axes and assigned lengths $\delta x$, $\delta y$ and $\delta z$ respectively: 300px

label: Definition:Volume of Compact Riemannian Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M, g}$ be a Riemannian manifold. Let $\rd V_g$ be the Riemannian volume form. Let $M$ be compact. Then the volume of the compact Riemannian manifold $M$, denoted by $\map {\text{Vol}} M$, is defined as: $\ds \map {\text{Vol}} M = \int_M \rd V_g$

label: Definition:Von Mangoldt Function
snippet: The von Mangoldt function $\Lambda: \N \to \R$ is defined as: $\map \Lambda n = \begin {cases} \map \ln p & : \exists m \in \N, p \in \mathbb P: n = p^m \\ 0 & : \text {otherwise} \end {cases}$ where $\mathbb P$ is the set of all prime numbers.

label: Definition:Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel Set Theory
snippet: Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel set theory is a system of axiomatic set theory. Its main feature is that it classifies collections of objects into: sets, whose construction is strictly controlled and: classes, which have fewer restrictions on how they may be generated. All sets are classes, but not all classes are sets.

label: Definition:Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel Set Theory/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel Set Theory == Von Neumann-Bernays-Gödel set theory was proposed by in $1925$ as an alternative to Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory. It was later revised by , and .

label: Definition:Von Neumann-Bounded Subset of Topological Vector Space
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $E \subseteq X$. We say that $E$ is von Neumann-bounded : for each open neighbourhood $V$ of ${\mathbf 0}_X$, there exists $s > 0$ such that $E \subseteq t V$ for each $t > s$ where $t V$ is the dilation of $V$ by $t$.

label: Definition:Von Neumann Hierarchy
snippet: Let $U$ denote the universal class. The von Neumann hierarchy is a mapping $V: \On \to U$ on the ordinals, defined via the Second Principle of Transfinite Recursion: $\map V x = \begin {cases} \O & : x = 0 \\ & \\ \powerset {\map V n} & : x = n^+ \\ & \\ \ds \bigcup_{y \mathop \in x} \map V y & : x \in \operatorname {Lim} \\ \end {cases}$ where: $\powerset x$ denotes the power set of $x$ $\operatorname {Lim}$ denotes the set of limit ordinals.

label: Definition:Waiting Time
snippet: Let $\sequence X$ be a sequence of events such that the intervals between occurrences obey a stochastic process. The waiting time of $\sequence X$ is defined as the interval between successive events.

label: Definition:Walk
snippet: Graph theory: Walk: an alternating series of vertices and edges beginning and ending with a vertex in which each edge is incident with the vertex immediately preceding it and the vertex immediately following it. Closed walk: a walk where the start and end vertices are the same Open walk: a walk where the start and end vertices are not the same Directed walk: a finite or infinite sequence $\sequence {x_k}$ of vertices such that $\forall k \in \N: k + 1 \in \Dom {\sequence {x_k} }: \tuple {x_k, x_{k + 1} } \in A$ Probability theory Random walk

label: Definition:Walk (Graph Theory)
snippet: Let $G = \struct {V, E}$ be a graph. A walk $W$ on $G$ is: an alternating sequence of vertices $v_1, v_2, \ldots$ and edges $e_1, e_2, \ldots$ of $G$ beginning and ending with a vertex in which edge $e_j$ of $W$ is incident with the vertex $v_j$ and the vertex $v_{j + 1}$. A walk between two vertices $u$ and $v$ is called a $u$-$v$ walk. To describe a walk on a simple graph it is sufficient to list just the vertices in order, as the edges (being unique between vertices) are unambiguous.

label: Definition:Wall-Sun-Sun Prime
snippet: A Wall-Sun-Sun prime is a prime number $p$ such that: $p^2 \divides F_{p - \paren {p \vert 5} }$ where: $\divides$ denotes divisibility $\paren {p \vert 5}$ denotes the Legendre symbol.

label: Definition:Wallace-Simson Line
snippet: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle. Let $P$ be a point on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$. Construct perpendiculars from $P$ to each of the sides of $\triangle ABC$. Let $D$, $E$ and $F$ be the feet of those perpendiculars. 300px The line $DEF$ called the Wallace-Simson line of the point $P$ $\triangle ABC$.

label: Definition:Wallis's Number
snippet: Wallis's number is the real root of the cubic: $x^3 - 2 x - 5 = 0$ Its approximate value is: $2 \cdotp 09455 \, 1 \ldots$

label: Definition:Wallis's Number/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wallis's Number == The cubic $x^3 - 2 x - 5 = 0$ was used by as a example to demonstrate how Newton's Method could be used to solve certain equations numerically. The real root of this equation has since become known as Wallis's number. It has subsequently been used as a test for a number of different methods of approximation. It is known to over $4000$ digits.

label: Definition:Warped Product Manifold
snippet: Let $\struct {M_1, g_1}$, $\struct {M_2, g_2}$ be Riemannian manifolds. Let $f : M_1 \to \R_{\mathop > 0}$ be a strictly positive smooth function. Let $p \in M$ be a point. Let $T_p M$ be a tangent space of $M$ at $p$. Let $v \in T_p M$ be a tangent vector. Let $g_p$ be a Riemannian metric of $M$ at $p$.

label: Definition:Wave
snippet: A wave is a disturbance in a medium which propagates through that medium with the following properties: $(1): \quad$ energy is propagated between two points in space through that medium $(2): \quad$ the disturbance travels through the medium without causing the medium itself to undergo any permanent displacement.

label: Definition:Wave-Particle Duality
snippet: Wave-particle duality is a phenomenon of quantum mechanics in which a particle can act as a wave, and a wave can act like a particle.

label: Definition:Wave/Disturbance
snippet: The disturbance of a wave at a given point and time is defined as the quantity that the medium is different from its equilibrium.

label: Definition:Wave Equation
snippet: == Equation == The wave equation is a second order PDE of the form: {{eqn | l = \dfrac 1 {c^2} \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial t^2} | r = \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial x^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial y^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial z^2} | c = }}

label: Definition:Wave Equation/Also known as
snippet: == Wave Equation: Also known as == The wave equation is referred to as the equation of wave motion by some authors, ostensibly so as not to confuse it with certain entities in the field of quantum physics. However, this confusion may not in fact be actual.

label: Definition:Wave Equation/Also presented as
snippet: == Wave Equation: Also presented as == The wave equation is also seen presented in the form: {{eqn | l = \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial t^2} | r = c^2 \paren {\dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial x^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial y^2} + \dfrac {\partial^2 \phi} {\partial z^2} } | c = }}

label: Definition:Wave Mechanics
snippet: Wave mechanics is the branch of physics concerned with the physical behaviour of waves. As such it provides the mathematical underpinning to the wave mechanical model of quantum mechanics.

label: Definition:Wave Mechanics/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wave Mechanics == Wave mechanics was developed as a form of quantum mechanics by , based on his solution of wave equations of systems of particles.

label: Definition:Wave Profile
snippet: Let $\phi$ be a wave which is propagated along the $x$-axis with velocity $c$. At $t = 0$, let $\phi = \map f x$. Then $\map f x$ is the wave profile of $\phi$. This can be expressed as: $\paren {\map \phi x}_{t \mathop = 0} = \map f x$

label: Definition:Wavelength
snippet: Wave Mechanics: Wavelength of Periodic Wave Physics: Wavelength

label: Definition:Wavelength (Physics)
snippet: The wavelength of a wave is the distance travelled in the direction of propagation between two points at the same phase of disturbance in consecutive cycles. That is, it is the distance over which the wave's shape repeats.

label: Definition:Wavelet
snippet: A wavelet is a special function the use of which other functions can be expressed, allowing greater flexibility than Fourier series.

label: Definition:Wavelet/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wavelet == The concept of the wavelet was introduced in the $1980$s as a concept in pure mathematics. It has since been used a great deal in many applied mathematical contexts.

label: Definition:Way Below Open
snippet: Let $\left({S, \preceq}\right)$ a preordered set. Let $X$ be a subset of $S$. Then $X$ is way below open : $\forall x \in X: \exists y \in X: y \ll x$ where $\ll$ denotes the way below relation.

label: Definition:Weak-* Convergence (Normed Vector Space)
snippet: Let $\Bbb F \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \norm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence of bounded linear functionals on $X$. Let $f : X \to \Bbb F$ be a bounded linear functional. Then we say that $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges weakly-$\ast$ (read as "weakly-star") : $\map {f_n} x \to \map f x$ for each $x \in X$. We say that $f$ is a weak-$\ast$ limit of $\sequence {f_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We denote this: $f_n \weakstarconv f$

label: Definition:Weak Cauchy Sequence
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, \tau}$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. Let $X^\ast$ be the topological dual of $\struct {X, \tau}$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is a weak Cauchy sequence : $\sequence {\map f {x_n} }_{n \mathop \in \N}$ is Cauchy in $\GF$ for each $f \in X^\ast$.

label: Definition:Weak Convergence
snippet: Functional Analysis: Weak Convergence (Normed Vector Space) Probability Theory: Weak Convergence (Random Variable) Measure Theory: Weak Convergence (Measure)

label: Definition:Weak Convergence (Normed Vector Space)
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot}$ be a normed vector space. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm \cdot_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm \cdot}$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $x \in X$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges weakly to $x$ : $\map f {x_n} 	o \map f x$ for each $f \in X^\ast$. We say that $x$ is a weak limit of $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$. We denote this: $x_n \weakconv x$

label: Definition:Weak Convergence (Topological Vector Space)
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. Let $X^\ast$ be the topological dual space of $X$. Suppose that: for each $x, y \in X$ with $x \ne y$, there exists $f \in X^\ast$ such that $\map f x \ne \map f y$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $x \in X$.

label: Definition:Weak Convergence (Topological Vector Space)/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. Let $X^\ast$ be the topological dual space of $X$. Suppose that: for each $x, y \in X$ with $x \ne y$, there exists $f \in X^\ast$ such that $\map f x \ne \map f y$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $x \in X$. Let $w$ be the weak topology on $X$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges weakly it converges in $\struct {X, w}$. We write: $x_n \weakconv x$ Category:Definitions/Weak Convergence (Topological Vector Spaces)

label: Definition:Weak Convergence (Topological Vector Space)/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $X$ be a topological vector space over $\GF$. Let $X^\ast$ be the topological dual space of $X$. Suppose that: for each $x, y \in X$ with $x \ne y$, there exists $f \in X^\ast$ such that $\map f x \ne \map f y$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Let $x \in X$. We say that $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges weakly to $x$ : for each $f \in X^\ast$ we have $\map f {x_n} \to \map f x$ in $\GF$. Category:Definitions/Weak Convergence (Topological Vector Spaces)

label: Definition:Weak Extremum
snippet: Let $S$ be a set of mappings. Let $y, \hat y \in S: \R \to \R$ be real functions. Let $J \sqbrk y: S \to \R$ be a functional. Suppose there exists $\epsilon \in \R_{> 0}$ such that for $\norm {y - \hat y}_1 < \epsilon$ the expression $J \sqbrk y - J \sqbrk {\hat y}$ has the same sign for all $y$. Here $\norm{\, \cdot \,}_1$ denotes the norm of in the space $C^1$. Then $y = \hat y$ is a weak extremum of the functional $J \sqbrk y$.

label: Definition:Weak Half-Space Generated by Linear Functional
snippet: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\R$. Let $f : X \to \R$ be a linear functional. Let $\alpha \in \R$. Define: $\sqbrk {f \ge \alpha} = \set {x \in X : \map f x \ge \alpha}$ and: $\sqbrk {f \le \alpha} = \set {X \in X : \map f x \le \alpha}$ We say that $\sqbrk {f \ge \alpha}$ and $\sqbrk {f \le \alpha}$ are the weak half-spaces generated by $f$.

label: Definition:Weak Hausdorff Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a weak Hausdorff space : the image $f \sqbrk K$ is closed in $T$.

label: Definition:Weak Operator Topology
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, \norm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be normed vector spaces. Let $\mathbb K = \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\map {CL} {X, Y}$ be a continuous linear transformation space. Let $F = \set {S \stackrel {p_{x,\phi} } \mapsto \size {\phi \paren{Sx - Tx} } : \map {CL} {X, Y} \to \R : x \in X : \phi \in \map {CL} {Y, \mathbb K} : T \in \map {CL} {X, Y}}$ be a set of maps. Let $\tau$ be the weakest topology on $\map {CL} {X, Y}$ such that every $y \in F$ is continuous. Then $\tau$ is called the weak operator topology on $\map {CL} {X, Y}$.

label: Definition:Weak Retract (Topology)
snippet: Let $T_1 = \struct {S_1, \tau_1}$ and $T_2 = \struct {S_2, \tau_2}$ be topological spaces. Then $T_1$ is a weak retract of $T_2$ there exists a continuous mapping $f: S_2 \to S_2$ such that: $f \circ f = f$ and: $\Img f$ and $T_1$ are homeomorphic.

label: Definition:Weakly Abnormal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.

label: Definition:Weakly Abnormal Subgroup/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. $H$ is weakly abnormal in $G$ : $\forall g \in G: g \in H^{\gen g}$ where $H^{\gen g}$ denotes the smallest subgroup of $G$ containing $H$, generated by the conjugacy action by the cyclic subgroup of $G$ generated by $g$.

label: Definition:Weakly Analytic Function
snippet:
Let $U$ be an open subset of $\C$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$ be a Banach space over $\C$. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,} }$. Let $f : U 	o X$ be a mapping. We say that $f$ is weakly analytic : for each $\phi \in X^\ast$, $\phi \circ f : U 	o \C$ is analytic.

label: Definition:Weakly Compact Linear Transformation/Definition 1
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be Banach spaces over $\GF$. Let $T : X 	o Y$ be bounded linear transformation. Let $\cl$ be the closure taken in $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$. Let $B_X^-$ be the closed unit ball in $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. We say that $T$ is weakly compact $\map \cl {T \sqbrk {B_X^-} }$ is weakly compact.

label: Definition:Weakly Compact Linear Transformation/Definition 2
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ and $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$ be Banach spaces over $\GF$. Let $T : X 	o Y$ be bounded linear transformation. Let $\cl$ be the closure taken in $\struct {Y, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_Y}$. Let $B_X^-$ be the closed unit ball in $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Let $w$ be the weak topology on $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Let $\cl_w$ be the closure taken in $\struct {X, w}$. We say that $T$ is weakly compact $\map {\cl_w} {T \sqbrk {B_X^-} }$ is weakly compact.

label: Definition:Weakly Compact Set
snippet: Let $K$ be a topological field. Let $X$ be a topological vector space with weak topology $w$. Let $C \subseteq X$. We say that $C$ is weakly compact (or $w$-compact) in $X$ $C$ is a compact in $\struct {X, w}$. That is, for every collection of weakly open sets $\SS$ such that: $\ds C \subseteq \bigcup_{S \in \SS} S$ there exists a finite subset $\set {S_1, \ldots, S_n} \subseteq \SS$ such that: $\ds C \subseteq \bigcup_{k \mathop = 1}^n S_k$ Category:Definitions/Weak Topologies on Topological Vector Spaces

label: Definition:Weakly Countably Compact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is weakly countably compact : every infinite subset of $S$ has a limit point in $S$.

label: Definition:Weakly Countably Compact Space/Also known as
snippet: == Weakly Countably Compact Space: Also known as == A space which is weakly countably compact can also be described as limit point compact.

label: Definition:Weakly Hereditary Property
snippet: Let $\xi$ be a property whose domain is the set of all topological spaces. Then $\xi$ is a weakly hereditary property : $\map \xi X \implies \map \xi Y$ where $Y$ is any closed set of $X$ when considered as a subspace. That is, whenever a topological space has $\xi$, then so does any closed subspace.

label: Definition:Weakly Lindelöf Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is a weakly Lindelöf space every open cover of $S$ has a countable subset whose union is dense in $T$.

label: Definition:Weakly Locally Compact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is weakly locally compact every point of $S$ has a compact neighborhood.

label: Definition:Weakly Locally Connected at Point
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$.

label: Definition:Weakly Locally Connected at Point/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$. The space $T$ is weakly locally connected at $x$ $x$ has a neighborhood basis consisting of connected sets.

label: Definition:Weakly Locally Connected at Point/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $x \in S$. The space $T$ is weakly locally connected at $x$ every open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ such that every two points of $V$ lie in some connected subset of $U$.

label: Definition:Weakly Measurable Function
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X,

label: Definition:Weakly Mixing Measure-Preserving Transformation
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation.

label: Definition:Weakly Mixing Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be weakly mixing : $\ds \forall A, B \in \BB : \lim_{N \mathop\to \infty} \frac 1 N \sum _{n \mathop = 0}^{N-1} \size {\map \mu {A \cap T^{-n} \sqbrk B} - \map \mu A \map \mu B} = 0$ where $T^{-n} \sqbrk B$ denotes the preimage of $B$ under the power $T^n$.

label: Definition:Weakly Mixing Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be weakly mixing : $T \times T$ is ergodic with respect to $\mu \times \mu$ where $\mu \times \mu$ denotes the product measure on $\struct {X \times X, \BB \otimes \BB}$.

label: Definition:Weakly Mixing Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 3
snippet: Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X \to X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be weakly mixing : $T \times T$ is weakly mixing in the sense of Definition 1 $\mu \times \mu$ where $\mu \times \mu$ denotes the product measure on $\struct {X \times X, \BB \otimes \BB}$.

label: Definition:Weakly Mixing Measure-Preserving Transformation/Definition 4
snippet:
Let $\struct {X, \BB, \mu}$ be a probability space. Let $T: X 	o X$ be a measure-preserving transformation. $T$ is said to be weakly mixing : for every ergodic measure-preserving system $\struct {Y, \BB_Y, 
u, S}$, the system: $\struct {X 	imes Y, \BB \otimes \BB_Y, \mu 	imes 
u, T 	imes S}$ is ergodic where $\mu 	imes 
u$ denotes the product measure on $\struct {X 	imes Y, \BB \otimes \BB_Y}$

label: Definition:Weakly Pronormal Subgroup
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$.

label: Definition:Weakly Pronormal Subgroup/Definition 1
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. $H$ is weakly pronormal in $G$ : $\forall g \in G: \exists x \in H^{\gen g}: H^x = H^g$ where: $H^{\gen g}$ denotes the smallest subgroup of $G$ containing $H$, generated by the conjugacy action by the cyclic subgroup of $G$ generated by $g$ $H^x$ denotes the conjugate of $H$ by $x$.

label: Definition:Weakly Pronormal Subgroup/Definition 2
snippet: Let $G$ be a group. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$. $H$ is weakly pronormal in $G$ : if $H \le K \le L \le G$ are such that $K$ is a normal subgroup of $L$, then $K N_L \left({H}\right) = L$ where: $H \le K$ denotes that $H$ is a subgroup of $K$ $N_L \left({H}\right)$ denotes the normalizer of $H$ in $L$.

label: Definition:Weakly Sigma-Locally Compact Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is weakly $\sigma$-locally compact : That is, $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is weakly $\sigma$-locally compact :

label: Definition:Weakly Unconditionally Cauchy Series
snippet:
Let $\GF \in \set {\R, \C}$. Let $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$ be a Banach space over $\GF$. Let $\struct {X^\ast, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_{X^\ast} }$ be the normed dual space of $\struct {X, 
orm {\, \cdot \,}_X}$. Let $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $X$. Then $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty x_n$ is weakly unconditionally Cauchy : $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \cmod {\map f {x_n} } < \infty$ for each $f \in X^\ast$.

label: Definition:Wedge Product
snippet: Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be two differential forms. Let $\alpha$ be an $x$-form. Let $\beta$ be a $y$-form. The wedge product $\alpha \wedge \beta$ is defined as the linear antisymmetric map from $F^x \times F^y \to F^{x + y}$, where $F^a$ is the set of $a$-forms in some manifold. Let $x_0$ be a specific point in a manifold $X$. Let $\alpha$ be an $x$-form. Let $\phi$ be a $1$-form. Let there be a set of vectors $\mathbf u_1, \mathbf u_2, \dotsc, \mathbf u_x, \mathbf v \in \map {T_{x_0} } X$.

label: Definition:Weibull Distribution
snippet: Let $X$ be a continuous random variable on a probability space $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$. Let $\Img X = \R_{\ge 0}$. $X$ is said to have a Weibull distribution it has probability density function: $\map {f_X} x = \alpha \beta^{-\alpha} x^{\alpha - 1} e^{-\paren {\frac x \beta}^\alpha}$ for $\alpha, \beta \in \R_{> 0}$.

label: Definition:Weight
snippet: Physics: The weight of a body is the force exerted on it by a gravitational field. Network theory: The weight of an edge or arc of a network is the functional value assigned to that edge or arc by the weight function of that network. Statistics, etc.: A weight function on a set $S$ is a mapping from $S$ to the (usually positive) real numbers. Information theory: The weight of a codeword is the number of its non-zero terms.

label: Definition:Weight (Network Theory)/Also known as
snippet: == Weight: Also known as == In the context of network analysis, the weight of an edge of a network is often referred to as a penalty. Some applications, in which a network is used to model transportation or flow between vertices, interpret the weight of an edge as a capacity. In applications in which a network models steps in a process, the weight of an edge is used to model the time that needs to elapse between activities that are modelled by the vertices.

label: Definition:Weight Function
snippet: A weight function on a set $S$ is a mapping from $S$ to the real numbers: $w: S \to \R$ It is common for the requirements of a specific application under discussion for the codomain of $w$ to be restricted to the positive reals: $w: S \to \R_{\ge 0}$ The thing that determines whether a given mapping is a weight function depends more on how it is used.

label: Definition:Weight of Topological Space
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbb B$ be the set of all bases of $T$.

label: Definition:Weight of Topological Space/Definition 1
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbb B$ be the set of all bases of $T$. The weight of $T$ is defined as: $\ds \map w T := \bigcap_{\BB \mathop \in \mathbb B} \card \BB$ where $\card \BB$ denotes the cardinality of $\BB$.

label: Definition:Weight of Topological Space/Definition 2
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $\mathbb B$ be the set of all bases of $T$. The weight of $T$ is the smallest cardinality of the elements of $\mathbb B$: $\map w T := \min \set {\card \BB: \BB \in \mathbb B}$

label: Definition:Weighted Mean
snippet: Let $S = \sequence {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a sequence of real numbers. Let $W$ be a weight function to be applied to the terms of $S$. The weighted mean of $S$ $W$ is defined as: $\bar x := \dfrac {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map W {x_i} x_i} {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map W {x_i} }$ This means that elements of $S$ with a larger weight contribute more to the weighted mean than those with a smaller weight.

label: Definition:Weighted Mean/Normalized
snippet: Let $S = \sequence {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a sequence of real numbers. Let $\map W x$ be a weight function to be applied to the terms of $S$. Let the weights be normalized. Then the weighted mean of $S$ $W$ can be expressed in the form: $\ds \bar x := \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map W {x_i} x_i$ as by definition of normalized weight function all the weights add up to $1$. This weighted mean is known as a normalized weighted mean.

label: Definition:Weighted Sum
snippet: Let $S = \sequence {x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n}$ be a sequence of real numbers. Let $\map W x$ be a weight function to be applied to the terms of $S$. The weighted sum of $S$ is defined as: $\bar x := \ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map W {x_i} x_i$ This means that elements of $S$ with a larger weight contribute more to the weighted sum than those with a smaller weight.

label: Definition:Well-Defined/Mapping
snippet: Let $f: S \to T$ be a mapping. Let $\RR$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. Let $S / \RR$ be the quotient set determined by $\RR$. Let $\phi: S / \RR \to T$ be a mapping such that: $\map \phi {\eqclass x \RR} = \map f x$ Then $\phi: S / \RR \to T$ is well-defined : $\forall \tuple {x, y} \in \RR: \map f x = \map f y$

label: Definition:Well-Defined/Relation
snippet: Let $\RR$ be an equivalence relation on $S$. For $x \in S$, let $\eqclass x \RR$ denote the equivalence class of $x$ under $\RR$. Let $S / \RR$ be the quotient set of $S$ determined by $\RR$. Let $\QQ$ be a relation on $S / \RR$. Then $\QQ$ is well-defined : for arbitrary $x, y, x', y' \in S$ such that: $x \mathrel \RR x'$ $y \mathrel \RR y'$ we have that: $\tuple {\eqclass x \RR, \eqclass y \RR} \in \QQ \iff \tuple {\eqclass {x'} \RR, \eqclass {y'} \RR} \in \QQ$

label: Definition:Well-Founded Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is well-founded it satisfies the minimal condition: Every non-empty subset of $S$ has a minimal element. That is, if the ordering $\preceq$ is a well-founded relation.

label: Definition:Well-Founded Relation/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a relational structure. $\RR$ is a well-founded relation on $S$ : $\forall T \subseteq S: T \ne \O: \exists z \in T: \forall y \in T \setminus \set z: \tuple {y, z} \notin \RR$ where $\O$ is the empty set. That is, $\RR$ is a strictly well-founded relation on $S$ : for every non-empty subset $T$ of $S$, there exists an element $z$ in $T$ such that for all $y \in T \setminus \set z$, it is not the case that $y \mathrel \RR z$.

label: Definition:Well-Founded Relation/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \RR}$ be a relational structure. $\RR$ is a well-founded relation on $S$ : for every non-empty subset $T$ of $S$, $T$ has a minimal element.

label: Definition:Well-Founded Relation/Warning
snippet: == Well-Founded Relation: Warning == According to Strictly Well-Founded Relation is Well-Founded, the Axiom of Foundation implies that every strictly well-founded relation is well-founded. As the definition quantifies over general subclasses, well-foundedness is not a first-order property. Thus it cannot be used in a formula of a theory, like NBG class-set theory, that only allow quantification over sets. For example it cannot be used with the axiom schema of specification in NBG set theory, and statements using it must generally be framed as schemas.

label: Definition:Well-Orderable Set
snippet: Let $S$ be a set. If it is possible to construct an ordering $\preccurlyeq$ on $S$ such that $\preccurlyeq$ is a well-ordering, then $S$ is defined as being well-orderable.

label: Definition:Well-Ordered Integral Domain/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \times \le}$ be an ordered integral domain whose zero is $0_D$. $\struct {D, +, \times \le}$ is a well-ordered integral domain the ordering $\le$ is a well-ordering on the set $P$ of (strictly) positive elements of $D$.

label: Definition:Well-Ordered Integral Domain/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {D, +, \times \le}$ be an ordered integral domain whose zero is $0_D$. $\struct {D, +, \times \le}$ is a well-ordered integral domain every subset $S$ of the set $P$ of (strictly) positive elements of $D$ has a minimal element: $\forall S \subseteq D_{\ge 0_D}: \exists x \in S: \forall a \in S: x \le a$ where $D_{\ge 0_D}$ denotes all the elements $d \in D$ such that $\map P d$.

label: Definition:Well-Ordered Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. Then $\struct {S, \preceq}$ is a well-ordered set the ordering $\preceq$ is a well-ordering. That is, every non-empty subset of $S$ has a smallest element: $\forall T \in \powerset S: \exists a \in T: \forall x \in T: a \preceq x$ where $\powerset S$ denotes the power set of $S$. That is, such that $\preceq$ is a well-founded total ordering.

label: Definition:Well-Ordering
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set.

label: Definition:Well-Ordering/Also defined as
snippet: == Well-Ordering: Also defined as == uses the term well-ordering to mean what calls a strict strong well-ordering. uses the term well-ordering to mean what calls a strict well-ordering. Category:Definitions/Well-Orderings

label: Definition:Well-Ordering/Class Theory
snippet: Let $V$ be a basic universe. Let $\RR \subseteq V \times V$ be a total ordering. Then $\RR$ is a well-ordering : every non-empty subclass of $\Field \RR$ has a smallest element under $\RR$ where $\Field \RR$ denotes the field of $\RR$.

label: Definition:Well-Ordering/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be an ordered set. The ordering $\preceq$ is a well-ordering on $S$ every non-empty subset of $S$ has a smallest element under $\preceq$: $\forall T \subseteq S, T \ne \O: \exists a \in T: \forall x \in T: a \preceq x$

label: Definition:Well-Ordering/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \preceq}$ be a ordered set. The ordering $\preceq$ is a well-ordering on $S$ $\preceq$ is a well-founded total ordering.

label: Definition:West Point of Horizon
snippet: Let an observer $O$ be facing the north point of the horizon $N$, facing directly away from the south point of the horizon $S$. Let the celestial equator meet the celestial horizon at the points $E$ and $W$. Let $W$ be the point on the left of $O$. This is called the west point of the horizon. 480px In the above diagram, the west point of the horizon is indicated by $W$.

label: Definition:Western Hemisphere
snippet: The western hemisphere of Earth is the hemisphere immediately to the west of the prime meridian. Points in the western hemisphere have longitude between $0 \degrees \, \mathrm W$ (the prime meridian itself) and $180 \degrees \, \mathrm W$.

label: Definition:Weyl Group
snippet: Let $\struct {E, \Phi}$ be a root system. The Weyl group $\mathscr W$ of $\struct {E, \Phi}$ is the subgroup of the general linear group $\map {GL} E$ generated by reflections through the hyperplanes orthogonal to each $\alpha \in \Phi$.

Let $H : \mathbf B \to \mathbf C$ and $K : \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$ be covariant functors. Then: the double-sided whiskered composite of $\eta$ by $K$ and $H$, denoted by $K \eta H: K \circ F \circ H \to K \circ G \circ H$, is the natural transformation defined by: for each object $B \in \mathbf B: \paren{K \eta H}_B = K \eta_{_{HB} }$ described diagramatically by: $\xymatrix{ \mathbf B \ar[rr]^H && \mathbf C…

label: Definition:Whiskered Composite of Natural Transformation/Left Whiskered
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf B$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors. Let $\eta: F \to G$ be a natural transformation. Let $H : \mathbf B \to \mathbf C$ be a covariant functor. Then: the left whiskered composite of $\eta$ by $H$, denoted by $\eta H: F \circ H \to G \circ H$, is the natural transformation defined by: for each object $B \in \mathbf B: \paren{\eta H}_B = \eta_{_{HB} }$ described diagrammatically by: $\xymatrix{ \mathbf B \ar[rr]^H && \mathbf C \ar@/^4ex/[rr]^F_{}="f" \ar@/_4ex/[rr]_G^{}="g" && \mathbf D \ar@2^\eta "f"; "g" }$

label: Definition:Whiskered Composite of Natural Transformation/Right Whiskered
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$, $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf E$ be categories. Let $F, G : \mathbf C \to \mathbf D$ be covariant functors. Let $\eta: F \to G$ be a natural transformation. Let $K : \mathbf D \to \mathbf E$ be a covariant functor. Then: the right whiskered composite of $\eta$ by $K$, denoted by $K \eta: K \circ F \to K \circ G$, is the natural transformation defined by: for each object $C \in \mathbf C: \paren{K \eta}_C = K \eta_{_C}$ described diagramatically by: $\xymatrix{ \mathbf C \ar@/^4ex/[rr]^F_{}="f" \ar@/_4ex/[rr]_G^{}="g" && \mathbf D \ar@2^\eta "f"; "g" \ar[rr]^K && \mathbf E }$

label: Definition:White Noise Process
snippet: Let $S$ be a stochastic process consisting of a time series $\map {z_r} t$ such that: the terms of the sequence $\sequence {z_r}$ are independent random variables the terms of $\sequence {z_r}$ are governed by a normal distribution with zero expectation and a given variance $\sigma^2$. Then $S$ is known as a white noise process.

label: Definition:Whole Number
snippet: The phrase whole number is an ambiguous term which could mean either: an integer a natural number a strictly positive integer. Hence it is recommended that a specific instance of the above is used instead.

label: Definition:Wholly Real/Abbreviated Notation
snippet: Let $z = a + i b$ be a complex number such that $b = 0$. That is, let $z$ be wholly real: $z = a + 0 i$, or $\tuple {a, 0}$ Despite the fact that $z$ is still a complex number, it is commonplace to use the same notation as if it were a real number, and hence say $z = a$. While it is in theory important to distinguish between a real number and its corresponding wholly real complex number, in practice it makes little difference.

label: Definition:Wholly Real/Also known as
snippet: == Wholly Real: Also known as == Variants on wholly real are: completely real entirely real and so on. Some sources gloss over the distinction between a real number and a wholly real complex number and merely refer to a number of the form $z = a + 0 i$ as a real number.

label: Definition:Wieferich Prime
snippet: A Wieferich prime is a prime number $p$ such that: $p^2 \divides 2^{p − 1} − 1$ where $\divides$ denotes divisibility.

label: Definition:Wiener Process
snippet: The Wiener process is a stochastic process $W_t$ for time $t \ge 0$ whose purpose is to model the movement of a particle under Brownian motion. Let $P$ be a particle located at the origin at $t = 0$. $W_t$ is characterised by: {{item|(2):|$W_{t + u} - W_t$ where $u \ge 0$ is independent of $W_s$ where $s \le t$}} {{item|(3):|$W_{t + u} - W_t \sim \Gaussian 0 u$ where $u \ge 0$ and $\Gaussian 0 u$ denotes the normal distribution}}

label: Definition:Wilbraham-Gibbs Constant
snippet: The Wilbraham-Gibbs constant is the real number defined as: {{eqn | l = G' | r = \int_0^\pi \dfrac {\sin u} u \rd u | c = }}

label: Definition:Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test
snippet: The Wilcoxon rank sum test is a distribution-free test of the hypothesis that two independent samples come from the same population. The alternative hypothesis may specify: a difference in median only one population distribution is stochastically larger than the other. The observations in the combined samples are arranged in ascending order and replaced by their ranks. Then the test statistic is calculated as the sum of the ranks of the observations in one of the samples. Then either $p$-values can be calculated, or critical values for given sample sizes looked up in published tables.

label: Definition:Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test
snippet: The Wilcoxon signed rank test is a distribution-free test for hypotheses about the mean or median of a symmetric distribution. Deviations of sample values from the hypothesized mean or median $M$ are ranked in order of magnitude. Those deviations are replaced by their rankings, together with a sign to indicate whether that deviation is positive or negative. The test statistic is usually taken to be the sum of the positive rankings. Critical values are tabulated for various sample sizes.

label: Definition:Wilson Prime
snippet: A Wilson prime is a prime number $p$ such that: $p^2 \divides \paren {p - 1}! + 1$ where: $\divides$ signifies divisibility $!$ is the factorial operator.

label: Definition:Wilson Prime/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Wilson Prime == The third Wilson prime was discovered by in $1953$, as a result of a computer search in which all numbers up to $10 \, 000$ were tested. This was one of the first examples of a problem in number theory being attacked by a computer. Subsequent searches have reached $2 \times 10^{13}$ without finding a $4$th such prime.

label: Definition:Winding Number
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a closed plane curve. Let $P$ be a point in the same plane as $\CC$. The winding number of $\CC$ $P$ is the number of times $\CC$ goes around $P$ in an anticlockwise direction.

label: Definition:Witch of Agnesi
snippet: 620px Let $OAM$ be a circle of radius $a$ whose center is at $\tuple {0, a}$. Let $M$ be the point such that $OM$ is a diameter of $OAM$. Let $OA$ be extended to cut the tangent to the circle through $M$ at $N$. Generate $NP$ perpendicular to $MN$ and $AP$ parallel to $MN$. As $A$ moves around the circle $OAM$, the point $P$ traces the curve known as the witch of Agnesi.

label: Definition:With Respect To
snippet: Real and complex analysis: Differentiation with respect to a variable Abstract algebra and group theory: Regular representation $\lambda_a$ or $\rho_a$ with respect to $a$

label: Definition:Witness Property
snippet: Let $\LL$ be a language of predicate logic. Let $\mathscr M$ be a formal semantics for $\LL$. Let $\FF$ be a set of $\LL$-WFFs. Suppose that, for every $\LL$-WFF of $1$ free variable $\map \phi x$, if: $\FF \models_{\mathscr M} \exists x : \map \phi x$ then there exists some term $t$ containing no variables such that: $\FF \models_{\mathscr M} \map \phi {x := t}$ Then, $\FF$ satisfies the witness property.

label: Definition:Wolstenholme Prime
snippet: A Wolstenholme prime is a prime number $p$ such that $p > 7$ which satisfies the congruence: $\dbinom {2 p - 1} {p - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod {p^4}$ where $\dbinom {2 p - 1} {p - 1}$ denotes a binomial coefficient.

label: Definition:Wonderful Demlo Number
snippet: The Wonderful Demlo numbers are the positive integers defined as the coefficients of the powers of $x$ in the expansion of: $\dfrac {1 + 10 x} {\left({1 - x}\right) \left({1 - 10 x}\right) \left({1 - 100 x}\right)}$

label: Definition:Woodall Number
snippet: A Woodall number is a positive integer of the form: $n \times 2^n - 1$

label: Definition:Woodall Prime
snippet: A Woodall prime is a Woodall number: $n \times 2^n - 1$ which is also prime.

label: Definition:Word
snippet: Abstract algebra: Word: the product of a finite number of elements of a given subset of an algebraic structure. Group Theory: Word: the product of a finite number of elements of a subset $S$ of a given group $G$. Set Theory: Associative Word on Set: an alternative name for an ordered tuple on a set Group Word on Set Formal Systems: Word (Formal Systems): a juxtaposition of symbols from a given alphabet. Natural Language: Word: a collation of letters

label: Definition:Word (Abstract Algebra)
snippet: Let $\struct {M, \circ}$ be a magma. Let $S \subseteq M$ be a subset. A word in $S$ is the product of a finite number of elements of $S$. The set of words in $S$ is denoted $\map W S$: $\map W S := \set {s_1 \circ s_2 \circ \cdots \circ s_n: n \in \N_{>0}: s_i \in S, 1 \le i \le n}$ Note that there is nothing in this definition preventing any of the elements of $S$ being repeated, neither is anything said about the order of these elements.

label: Definition:Word (Abstract Algebra)/Context
snippet: == Context of Word == It is usual for the algebraic structure of the concept of a word to be a group, a monoid or a semigroup. However, if the operation $\circ$ is not associative then this definition still holds. Category:Definitions/Words (Abstract Algebra)

label: Definition:Word (Abstract Algebra)/Monoid
snippet: Let $\struct {M, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity element is $e$. Let $S \subseteq M$ be a subset of $M$. The set of words in $S$ is denoted and defined: $\map W S := \set {\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^r n_i \cdot s_i : r \in \N, n_i \in \N, s_i \in S}$ where: $n_i \cdot s_i$ denotes the power of $s_i$: $n \cdot a = \begin {cases} e & : n = 0 \\ \paren {\paren {n - 1} \cdot a} \circ a & : n > 0 \end {cases}$ $\ds \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^r n_i \cdot s_i := \paren {n_1 \cdot s_1} \circ \paren {n_2 \cdot s_2} \circ \cdots \circ \paren {n_r \cdot s_r}$

label: Definition:Wrapped Cauchy Distribution
snippet: The wrapped Cauchy distribution is a probability distribution used to model directional data which may be clustered in an incomplete arc on the circle.

label: Definition:Wrench
snippet: A wrench is a force combined with a couple whose plane is perpendicular to the line of action of the force.

label: Definition:Wythoff Pair
snippet: A Wythoff pair is an ordered pair of integers of the form: $\tuple {\floor {k \phi}, \floor {k \phi^2} }$ where: $\phi$ denotes the golden section: $\phi = 1 \cdotp 618 \ldots$ $\floor x$ denotes the floor of $x$ $k$ signifies a positive integer: $k \in \Z_{\ge 0}$. Thus the coordinates of a Wythoff pair are corresponding terms of the lower and upper Wythoff sequences.

label: Definition:X-Y Plane
snippet: $x$-$y$ plane, $y$-$z$ plane and $x$-$z$ plane in Cartesian $3$-space ]] The $x$-$y$ plane is the Cartesian plane embedded in Cartesian $3$-space which contains the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis. It consists of all the points in $S$ such that $z = 0$.

label: Definition:X-Z Plane
snippet: $x$-$y$ plane, $y$-$z$ plane and $x$-$z$ plane in Cartesian $3$-space ]] The $x$-$z$ plane is the Cartesian plane embedded in Cartesian $3$-space which contains the $x$-axis and the $z$-axis. It consists of all the points in $S$ such that $x = 0$.

label: Definition:Y-Z Plane
snippet: $x$-$y$ plane, $y$-$z$ plane and $x$-$z$ plane in Cartesian $3$-space ]] The $y$-$z$ plane is the Cartesian plane embedded in Cartesian $3$-space which contains the $y$-axis and the $z$-axis. It consists of all the points in $S$ such that $x = 0$.

label: Definition:Yang-Mills Theory
snippet: Yang-Mills theory is a gauge theory based on a special unitary group $\map {SU} N$, or more generally any compact, reductive Lie algebra. Yang–Mills theory seeks to describe the behavior of elementary particles using these non-abelian Lie groups, and is at the core of the unification of the electromagnetic force and weak forces, that is $\map U 1 \times \map {SU} 2$, as well as quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force (based on $\map {SU} 3$). Thus it forms the basis of our understanding of the Standard Model of particle physics. Category:Definitions/Physics

label: Definition:Yates's Correction
snippet: Let $C$ be a contingency table with $2$ rows and $2$ columns. Let a $\chi$-squared test for lack of association be applied to $C$. Yates's correction is the operation of subtracting $0 \cdotp 5$ from the absolute value of each difference $\size {O_i - E_i}$ before squaring. Hence this $\chi$-squared test is an approximation to Fisher's exact test.

label: Definition:Year/Calendar
snippet: A calendar year is the number of days between dates with the same designation in adjacent years. As a year is not an integral number of days, it is necessarily an approximation to the actual year. {{eqn | r = 365 \text{ or } 366 | c = days, usually, but it depends on the calendar used }}

label: Definition:Z-Graded Ring
snippet: Let $\Z$ be the set of integers. A $\Z$-graded ring is a graded ring of type the additive group of integers. That is, it is a pair $\struct {R, f}$ where: $R$ is a ring $f$ is a family $\family {R_n}_{n \mathop \in \Z}$ of subgroups of the additive group of $R$, of which it is the internal direct sum, and such that: $\forall x \in R_n, y \in R_m: x y \in R_{m + n}$

label: Definition:Z-Module Associated with Abelian Group
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be an abelian group with identity $e$. Let $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ be the ring of integers.

label: Definition:Z-Module Associated with Abelian Group/Definition 1
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be an abelian group with identity $e$. Let $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ be the ring of integers. The $\Z$-module associated with $G$ is the $\Z$-module $\struct {G, \circ, \ast}$ with ring action: $\ast: \Z \times G \to G$: $\tuple {n, x} \mapsto \circ^n x$ where $\circ^n x$ is the $n$th power of $x$.

label: Definition:Z-Module Associated with Abelian Group/Definition 2
snippet: Let $\struct {G, \circ}$ be an abelian group with identity $e$. Let $\struct {\Z, +, \times}$ be the ring of integers. The $\Z$-module associated with $G$ is the $\Z$-module on $G$ with ring representation $\Z \to \map {\operatorname {End} } G$ equal to the initial homomorphism. {{explain|$\map {\operatorname {End} } G$}}

snippet: == $Z$-Score: Also known as == A $Z$-score is also defined as a value of a random variable which has been standardized using: $Z = \dfrac {X - \overline x} s$ where: $\overline x$ denotes the sample mean of $X$ $s$ denotes the sample standard deviation of $X$.

label: Definition:Z^Z Space
snippet: Let $Z = \struct {\Z_{\ge 0}, \tau_d}$ denote the positive integers with the discrete topology. Let $X = \ds \struct {\prod_{i \mathop \in \Z_{\ge 0} } Z, \tau}$ be the space formed on the countable Cartesian product of instances of $Z$ such that $\tau$ is the Tychonoff product topology. Then $X$ is known as the $Z^Z$ (topological) space. Thus $\tau$ can be referred to as the $Z^Z$ topology.

label: Definition:Zeckendorf Representation
snippet: Zeckendorf representation is a system for representing a positive integer $n$ by a sequence of digits which are the indices of a sequence of $r$ Fibonacci numbers.

label: Definition:Zeckendorf Representation/Definition 1
snippet: Zeckendorf representation is a system for representing a positive integer $n$ by a sequence of digits which are the indices of a sequence of $r$ Fibonacci numbers: $n := \sqbrk {k_1 k_2 k_3 \ldots k_r}_F$ where: $n = F_{k_1} + F_{k_2} + F_{k_3} + \cdots + F_{k_r}$ $k_1 \gg k_2 \gg k_3 \gg \cdots \gg k_r \gg 0$ where $n \gg k$ denotes that $n \ge k + 2$.

label: Definition:Zeckendorf Representation/Definition 2
snippet: Zeckendorf representation is a system for representing a positive integer $n$ by a sequence of digits which are the indices of a sequence of $r$ Fibonacci numbers: $n := \sqbrk {k_1 k_2 k_3 \ldots k_r}_F = \ds \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^r k_i F_i$ where: each $k_i$ equals $0$ or $1$ each pair of adjacent $\tuple {k_i, k_{i + 1} }$ satisfies $k_i k_{i + 1} = 0$ $k_1 = k+0 = 0$

snippet: Set Theory and Order Theory: The zero ordinal. The zero cardinal. Algebra: The zero of the numbers: The zero of the natural numbers, a concept which follows from, and can be defined from, the definition of the natural numbers as the isomorphism class of a naturally ordered semigroup. From this definition follow: The zero of the integers. The zero of the rational numbers. The zero of the real numbers. The zero of the complex numbers. label: Definition:Zero-Limit Sequence in Schwartz Space
snippet: Let $\map \SS \R$ be the Schwartz space. Let $\sequence {\phi_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a sequence in $\map \SS \R$. Let $\phi \in \map \SS \R$ be a Schwartz test function. Suppose: $\ds \forall l, m \in \N : \lim_{n \mathop \to \infty} \sup_{x \mathop \in \R} \size {x^l \map {\phi_n^{\paren m} } x} = 0$ where: $\phi^{\paren m}$ denotes the $m$th derivative of $\phi$ $\sup$ denotes the supremum. Then the sequence $\sequence {\phi_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ converges to $\mathbf 0$ in $\map \SS \R$. This can be denoted: $\phi_n \stackrel \SS {\longrightarrow} \mathbf 0$

label: Definition:Zero/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Zero == The Babylonians from the $2$nd century BCE used a number base system of arithmetic, with a placeholder to indicate that a particular place within a number was empty, but its use was inconsistent. However, they had no actual recognition of zero as a mathematical concept in its own right. The Ancient Greeks had no conception of zero as a number. The concept of zero was invented by the mathematicians of India. The from the $3$rd century CE contains the first reference to it.

label: Definition:Zero/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Zero == The Sanskrit word used by the early Indian mathematicians for zero was sunya, which means empty, or blank. In Arabic this was translated as sifr. This was translated via the Latin zephirum into various European languages as zero, cifre, cifra, and into English as zero and cipher. Note that the plural of zero is either zeros or zeroes. On , zeroes is preferred. The word zero can also be used as a , meaning to set (a value) to zero in the context of algorithms and computer science The word zeroize can also be seen in this context.

label: Definition:Zero (Cardinal)
snippet: The cardinal associated with the empty set $\O$ is called zero, and is denoted $0$. More informally, this means that zero is defined as being the number of elements in the empty set.

label: Definition:Zero (Category)
snippet: The category $\mathbf 0$, zero, is the empty category: $\qquad$ with: no objects and consequently: no morphisms.

label: Definition:Zero (Number)
snippet: The number zero is defined as being the cardinal of the empty set.

label: Definition:Zero (Number)/Complex
snippet: Let $\C$ denote the set of complex numbers. The zero of $\C$ is the complex number: $0 + 0 i$

label: Definition:Zero (Ordinal)
snippet: The zero ordinal, denoted $0$, is the empty set $\O$.

label: Definition:Zero Digit
snippet: Let $x \in \R$ be a number. Let $b \in \Z$ such that $b > 1$ be a number base in which $x$ is represented. By the Basis Representation Theorem, $x$ can be expressed uniquely in the form: $\ds x = \sum_{j \mathop \in \Z}^m r_j b^j$ Any instance of $r_j$ being equal to $0$ is known as a zero (digit) of $n$.

label: Definition:Zero Digit/Historical Note
snippet: == Historical Note on Zero Digit == The earliest use of a special symbol to be used as a placeholder for a missing denomination in a number expressed in a positional number system was in the Babylonian number system, at around . However, the technique was not transmitted to other cultures. The concept was reinvented by the mathematicians of the Hindu culture in the first few centuries CE. The (dated from between and ) uses it, as a heavy dot. It is also used in the of $458$, but not as a symbol as such. used a positional number system around $500$, but it did not have a zero digit.

label: Definition:Zero Dimensional Space
snippet: A topological space $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ is zero dimensional $T$ has a basis whose sets are all both closed and open.

label: Definition:Zero Dimensional Space/Linguistic Note
snippet: == Linguistic Note on Zero Dimensional Space == The thinking behind applying the term zero dimensional to the concept of a zero dimensional space arises from the idea of the small inductive dimension in the context of the topological space. The small inductive dimension of a topological space is defined to be $1$ greater than the small inductive dimension of its boundary. By Set is Clopen iff Boundary is Empty, a topological space with a basis whose sets are all clopen has no boundary. Thus it follows that such a topological space is considered to be zero dimensional.

label: Definition:Zero Element
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be an algebraic structure.

label: Definition:Zero Element/Also defined as
snippet: == Zero Element: Also defined as == Beware of the usage of the term zero element to mean the identity element under the operation of addition: $a + 0 = a = 0 + a$ While zero is indeed a zero element under the operation of multiplication: $a \times 0 = 0 = 0 \times a$ it is not, strictly speaking, a zero element of addition.

label: Definition:Zero Homomorphism
snippet: Let $\struct {R_1, +_1, \circ_1}$ and $\struct {R_2, +_2, \circ_2}$ be rings with zeroes $0_1$ and $0_2$ respectively. Consider the mapping $\zeta: R_1 \to R_2$ defined as: $\forall r \in R_1: \map \zeta r = 0_2$ Then $\zeta$ is the zero homomorphism from $R_1$ to $R_2$.

label: Definition:Zero Locus of Set of Polynomials
snippet: Let $k$ be a field. Let $n \ge 1$ be a natural number. Let $A = k \sqbrk {X_1, \ldots, X_n}$ be the polynomial ring in $n$ variables over $k$. Let $I \subseteq A$ be a set. Then the zero locus of $I$ is the set: $\map V I = \set {x \in k^n : \forall f \in I: \map f x = 0}$

label: Definition:Zero Mapping
snippet: Let $\mathbb A$ be one of the standard number systems $\N,\Z,\Q,\R,\C$. Let $S$ be a set. Let $f_0: S \to \mathbb A$ denote the constant mapping: $\forall x \in S: \map {f_0} x = 0$ Then $f_0$ is referred to as the zero mapping.

label: Definition:Zero Mapping/Vector Space
snippet: Let $Y$ be a vector space. Let $S$ be a set. Let $\mathbf 0_Y$ be the identity element of $Y$. Suppose $\mathbf 0 : S \to Y$ is a mapping such that: $\forall x \in S: \map {\mathbf 0} x = \mathbf 0_Y$ Then $\mathbf 0$ is referred to as the zero mapping.

label: Definition:Zero Matrix
snippet: Let $\Bbb F$ be one of the standard number system $\N$, $\Z$, $\Q$, $\R$ and $\C$. Let $\map \MM {m, n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix space over $\Bbb F$. The zero matrix of $\map \MM {m, n}$, denoted $\mathbf 0$, is the $m \times n$ matrix whose elements are all zero, and can be written $\sqbrk 0_{m n}$.

label: Definition:Zero Matrix/General Monoid
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \circ}$ be a monoid whose identity is $e$. Let $\map {\MM_S} {m, n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix space over $S$. The zero matrix of $\map {\MM_S} {m, n}$, denoted $\mathbf e$, is the $m \times n$ matrix whose elements are all $e$, and can be written $\sqbrk e_{m n}$.

label: Definition:Zero Matrix/Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring whose zero is $0_R$. Let $\map {\MM_R} {m, n}$ be an $m \times n$ matrix space over $R$. The zero matrix of $\map {\MM_R} {m, n}$, denoted $\mathbf 0_R$, is the $m \times n$ matrix whose elements are all $0_R$, and can be written $\sqbrk {0_R}_{m n}$.

label: Definition:Zero Morphism via Zero Object
snippet: Let $C$ be a category which has a zero object $0$. Let $a, b \in C$ be objects. The zero morphism $0$ from $a$ to $b$ is the composition of the unique morphism $a \to 0$ and the unique morphism $0 \to b$: $0: a \to 0 \to b$

label: Definition:Zero Object
snippet: Let $\mathbf C$ be a category. A zero object of $\mathbf C$ is an object which is initial and terminal.

label: Definition:Zero Operator
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space. Let $A : V \to V$ be a linear operator such that: $\forall v \in H: A v = 0_V$ where $0_V$ is the zero vector of $V$. Then $A$ is called the zero operator, and is denoted as $\mathbf 0$. Category:Definitions/Vector Spaces

label: Definition:Zero Residue Class
snippet: Let $m \in \Z$. Let $\RR_m$ be the congruence relation modulo $m$ on the set of all $a, b \in \Z$: $\RR_m = \set {\tuple {a, b} \in \Z \times \Z: \exists k \in \Z: a = b + k m}$ Let $\eqclass 0 m$ be the residue class of $0$ (modulo $m$): $\eqclass 0 m = \set {x \in \Z: \exists k \in \Z: x = k m}$ Then $\eqclass 0 m$ is known as the zero residue class (modulo $m$).

label: Definition:Zero Set
snippet: Let $\struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $H \subseteq S$. We say that $H$ is a zero set if there exists a continuous mapping $f: S \to \closedint 0 1$ such that: $H = f^{-1} \sqbrk {\set 0}$

label: Definition:Zero Subspace
snippet: Let $V$ be a vector space with zero vector $\mathbf 0$. Then the set $\paren {\mathbf 0} := \set {\mathbf 0}$ is called the zero subspace of $V$. This name is appropriate as $\paren {\mathbf 0}$ is in fact a subspace of $V$, as proved in Zero Subspace is Subspace.

label: Definition:Zero Vector
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +_R, \times_R}$ be a ring. Let $\struct {G, +_G}$ be an abelian group. Let $\struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R$ be an $R$-module. The identity of $\struct {G, +_G}$ is usually denoted $\bszero$, or some variant of this, and called the zero vector: $\forall \mathbf a \in \struct {G, +_G, \ast}_R: \bszero +_G \mathbf a = \mathbf a = \mathbf a +_G \bszero$ Note that on occasion it is advantageous to denote the zero vector differently, for example by $e$, or $\bszero_V$ or $\bszero_G$, in order to highlight the fact that the zero vector is not the same object as the zero scalar.

label: Definition:Zeroth
snippet: Zeroth is the adjectival form of the ordinal number zero.

snippet: == Historical Note on Zu Chongzhi Fraction == The Zu Chongzhi fraction $\dfrac {355} {113}$ as an approximation for $\pi$ (pi) was derived by and his son . fortuitously rediscovered it independently around the $16$th century. He did this by taking the mediant of two limits $\dfrac {377} {120}$ and $\dfrac {333} {106}$ calculated by his father. label: Definition:Zuckerman Number

label: Definition:Łukasiewicz's Polish Notation
snippet: Łukasiewicz's Polish notation is a system of prefix notation for propositional logic. Statements are represented by lowercase letters, as the conventional notation. Logical connectives are represented by uppercase letters as follows: | Negation | $\lnot p$ | $\operatorname N p$ | Conjunction | $p \land q$ | $\operatorname K p q$ | Implication | $p \implies q$ | $\operatorname C p q$ | Disjunction | $p \lor q$ | $\operatorname A p q$ | Biconditional | $p \iff q$ | $\operatorname E p q$

Let $\struct {P \sqbrk R, \oplus, \odot}$ be the polynomial ring over the set of all sequences in $R$: $P \sqbrk R = \set {\sequence {r_0, r_1, r_2, \ldots} }$ where the operations $\oplus$ and $\odot$ on $P \sqbrk R$ be defined as: Let $\struct {R \sqbrk X, +, \circ}$ be the ring of polynomials over $R$ in $X$. Then $\struct {R \sqbrk X, +, \circ}$ and $\struct {P \sqbrk R, \oplus, \odot}$ are isomorphic.

label: Definitional Abbreviation/Examples
snippet: == Examples of Definitional Abbreviations == An example of a definitional abbreviation in predicate logic is to write: $\exists! x: \map \phi x$ in place of the formally correct alternatives: $\exists x: \paren {\map \phi x \land \forall y: \paren {\map \phi y \implies x = y} }$ $\exists x: \forall y: \paren {\map \phi y \iff x = y}$ to express: there exists a unique $x$ such that $\map \phi x$ holds where $\phi$ is some unary predicate symbol. The benefit of this uniqueness quantifier readily becomes apparent when $\phi$ is already a very long formula in itself.

label: Degree-Genus Formula
snippet: Let $\CC$ be a non-singular curve in the complex projective plane. Let $\CC$ be defined by an equation of degree $d$. Then $\CC$ is a Riemann surface of genus $g$, where: $g = \dfrac {\paren {d - 1} \paren {d - 2} } 2$

label: Degree Equation
snippet: Let $E$, $K$ and $F$ be fields. Let $E / K$ and $K / F$ be finite field extensions. Then: $E / F$ is a finite field extension $\index E F = \index E K \index K F$ where $\index E F$ denotes the degree of $E / F$

label: Degree of Character equals Character of Identity Element
snippet: Let $G$ be a finite group whose identity is $e$. Let $\rho$ be a linear representation of $G$. Let $\chi_\rho$ be the character associated with $\rho$. Then $\map {\chi_\rho} e$ equals the degree of $\chi_\rho$.

label: Degree of Characteristic Polynomial of Matrix equals Order of Matrix
snippet: Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. Let $\mathbf A$ be a square matrix over $R$ of order $n > 0$. Let $\mathbf I_n$ be the $n \times n$ identity matrix. Let $R \sqbrk x$ be the polynomial ring in one variable over $R$. Let $\map {p_{\mathbf A} } x$ be the characteristic polynomial of $\mathbf A$. Then the degree of $\map {p_{\mathbf A} } x$ is equal to the order of $\mathbf A$.

label: Degree of Element of Finite Field Extension divides Degree of Extension
snippet: Let $F$ be a field whose zero is $0$ and whose unity is $1$. Let $K / F$ be a finite field extension of degree $n$. Let $\alpha \in K$ be algebraic over $F$. Then the degree of $\alpha$ is a divisor of $n$.

label: Degree of Product of Polynomials over Ring
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a commutative ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$. Let $R \sqbrk X$ be the polynomial ring over $R$ in the indeterminate $X$. Let $f, g \in R \sqbrk X$. Then: $\forall f, g \in R \sqbrk X: \map \deg {f g} \le \map \deg f + \map \deg g$ where: $\map \deg f$ denotes the degree of $f$.

label: Degree of Simple Algebraic Field Extension equals Degree of Algebraic Number
snippet: Let $F$ be a field. Let $\theta \in \C$ be algebraic over $F$ of degree $n$. Let $\map F \theta$ be the simple field extension of $F$ by $\theta$. Then $\map F \theta$ is a finite extension of $F$ whose degree is: $\index {\map F \theta} F = n$

label: Degree of Sum of Polynomials
snippet: Let $\struct {R, +, \circ}$ be a ring with unity whose zero is $0_R$. Let $R \sqbrk X$ be the ring of polynomials over $R$ in the indeterminate $X$. For $f \in R \sqbrk X$ let $\map \deg f$ be the degree of $f$. Then: $\forall f, g \in R \sqbrk X: \map \deg {f + g} \le \max \set {\map \deg f, \map \deg g}$

label: Denial of Existence/Examples/x less than or equal to 3
snippet: == Examples of Denial of Existence == Let $S \subseteq \R$ be a subset of the real numbers. Let $P$ be the statement: $\exists x \in S: x \le 3$ The negation of $P$ is the statement written in its simplest form as: $\forall x \in S: x > 3$

label: Denominators of Simple Continued Fraction are Strictly Increasing
snippet: Let $N \in \N \cup \set \infty$ be an extended natural number. Let $\sqbrk {a_0, a_1, a_2, \ldots}$ be a simple continued fraction in $\R$ of length $N$. Let $q_0, q_1, q_2, \ldots$ be its denominators. Then with the possible exception of $q_0 = q_1$, the sequence $\sequence {q_n}$ is strictly increasing.

label: Dense-in-itself iff Subset of Derivative
snippet: Let $T$ be a topological space. Let $A \subseteq T$. Then: $A$ is dense-in-itself $A \subseteq A'$ where $A'$ denotes the derivative of $A$.

label: Densely-Defined Linear Operator is Closable iff Adjoint is Densely-Defined
snippet: Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space over $\C$. Let $\tuple {\map D T, T}$ be a densely-defined linear operator. Let $\tuple {\map D {T^\ast}, T^\ast}$ be the adjoint of $\tuple {\map D T, T}$. Then $\tuple {\map D T, T}$ is closable $\tuple {\map D {T^\ast}, T^\ast}$ is densely-defined. If $T$ is closable then the closure $\overline T$ satisfies $\overline T = T^{\ast \ast} = \paren {T^\ast}^\ast$.

label: Densely-Defined Linear Operator with Real-Valued Quadratic Form is Symmetric
snippet: Let $\struct {\HH, \innerprod \cdot \cdot}$ be a Hilbert space. Let $\struct {\map D T, T}$ be a densely-defined linear operator such that: $\innerprod {T x} x \in \R$ for each $x \in \map D T$. Then $T$ is symmetric.

label: Denseness Preserved in Coarser Topology
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Let $T' = \struct {S, \tau'}$ be another topological space on $S$ such that $\tau'$ is coarser than $\tau$. Let $H \subseteq S$ be everywhere dense in $T$. Then $H$ is also everywhere dense in $T'$.

label: Density not greater than Weight
snippet: Let $T = \struct {S, \tau}$ be a topological space. Then $\map d T \le \map w T$ where $\map d T$ denotes the density of $T$, $\map w T$ denotes the weight of $T$.

label: Denumerable Class is Set
snippet: Let $A$ be a class. Let $\N$ be the natural numbers. Suppose that $F: \N \to A$ is a bijection. Then $A$ is a set.

label: Dependent Choice (Fixed First Element)
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a binary relation on a non-empty set $S$. Suppose: $\forall a \in S: \exists b \in S: a \mathrel \RR b$ that is, that $\RR$ is a left-total relation (that is, a serial relation). Let $s \in S$. Then there exists a sequence $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $S$ such that: $x_0 = s$ $\forall n \in \N: x_n \mathrel \RR x_{n + 1}$

label: Dependent Choice for Finite Sets
snippet: Let $\RR$ be a binary relation on a non-empty set $S$. For each $a \in S$, let $C_a = \set {b \in S: a \mathrel \RR b }$ Suppose that: For all $a \in S$, $C_a$ is a non-empty finite set. Let $s \in S$. Then there exists a sequence $\sequence {x_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ in $S$ such that: $x_0 = s$ $\forall n \in \N: x_n \mathrel \RR x_{n+1}$
